q: A school computer stores the marks of every student in every subject. The printed report card that shows a student's total, percentage and rank is best described as
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The report card is produced by processing (adding, comparing, ranking) the raw marks, so it is information. The raw marks themselves are data.
concept: Data means raw facts, such as individual marks, names or numbers, which have little meaning on their own. Information is data that has been processed (organised, calculated, summarised) so that it is meaningful and useful, for example for a decision. A report card that shows totals, percentages and ranks is a classic example of information. Metadata is 'data about data', such as the fact that the Marks column holds whole numbers.
why: A — Wrong. Data means raw, unprocessed facts, like the individual marks typed into the computer. The report card is the RESULT of processing those marks (totals, percentage, rank), so it is more than raw data.
B — Correct. Information is processed data that is meaningful and useful. The totals, percentage and rank on the report card were calculated from the raw marks, so the report card is information.

C — Wrong. Metadata is 'data about data', for example 'the Marks column stores whole numbers from 0 to 100'. A report card describes a student, not the structure of the stored data, so it is not metadata.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Think of data as raw ingredients and information as the cooked dish.

q: The data dictionary (also called the system catalog) of a DBMS mainly stores
opts: The actual rows of the users' tables
Backup copies of the whole database
Metadata such as table names, column data types and constraints
More than one of the above
exp: The data dictionary holds metadata — data about the data — such as names of tables and columns, their data types, constraints, views and user permissions.
concept: Metadata means 'data about data'. A DBMS keeps all metadata in a special store called the data dictionary or system catalog: names of tables and columns, data types and sizes, keys and other constraints, views, indexes and users' privileges. The DBMS reads the dictionary before it runs a statement, for example to check that a column really exists. In a relational DBMS the catalog is itself stored as tables.
why: A — Wrong. The actual rows (for example, each student's record) are the data itself and are kept in the data files. The dictionary stores only the description of those rows.
B — Wrong. Backup copies are made by the backup utility and kept on separate storage (tape, another disk, the cloud). They are not what the data dictionary holds.
C — Correct. The data dictionary is the store of metadata: table names, column names, data types, constraints, views, indexes and user permissions.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Data dictionary = system catalog = store of metadata ('data about data').

q: Which of the following are examples of METADATA for a STUDENT table?
opts: The column RollNo has the data type INTEGER
The column Name can hold at most 30 characters
More than one of the above
exp: A and C describe the structure of the table (a data type and a maximum length), so they are metadata. B is an actual stored value, i.e. data.
concept: Metadata is data that describes other data: names of tables and columns, data types, sizes, keys and constraints. Data is the actual values stored in the rows. A simple test: if the statement would still be true when the table is empty, it is metadata; if it talks about a particular student's value, it is data.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The data type of a column is part of the table's definition (its schema), so it is metadata kept in the data dictionary.
B — Wrong. 87 is an actual value stored in one row of the table. That is data, not data about data.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The maximum length of a column, as in VARCHAR(30), is part of the column's definition, so it is metadata.
D — Correct. A and C are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Empty-table test: anything that is still true for an empty table is metadata.

q: In a file-processing system, a customer's address is changed in the savings-account file but not in the loan file. Now the two files show different addresses for the same customer. This problem is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When two copies of the same data disagree, the data is inconsistent. Here the inconsistency comes from redundancy (the address is stored twice).
concept: In a file-processing system each department keeps its own files, so the same fact (like an address) is often stored in several files. This repetition is called data redundancy. If one copy is updated and another is not, the copies disagree; this is called data inconsistency. A DBMS reduces redundancy and so reduces the chance of inconsistency.
why: A — Correct. Two copies of the same fact now hold different values, which is exactly data inconsistency. It happened because the address was stored redundantly in two files.

B — Wrong. Data isolation means data is scattered in many files with different formats, so it is hard to write new programs that pull it together. The problem here is two copies that disagree, not scattered formats.
C — Wrong. A security problem means people can see or change data they are not allowed to. Nobody unauthorised acted here; one copy simply was not updated.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Redundancy (storing twice) is the cause; inconsistency (copies disagree) is the effect.

q: A bank's rule says 'the balance of an account must never fall below Rs 1000'. In its file-processing system this rule is written as code inside many separate application programs. When the bank changes the limit to Rs 2000, every program must be found and changed. Which drawback of file-processing systems does this show?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Consistency rules (integrity constraints) buried inside application code are hard to add or change; Korth calls this the integrity problem.
concept: Integrity constraints are rules that the stored data must always obey, such as 'balance must be at least 1000' or 'age must be positive'. In a file system these rules live inside program code, so adding or changing a rule means editing many programs. A DBMS lets you declare such a rule once (for example with a CHECK constraint) and enforces it for every program.
why: A — Wrong. An atomicity problem happens when a failure leaves an operation half done, for example money debited from one account but not credited to the other. No failure is described here.

B — Correct. 'Balance must not fall below Rs 1000' is an integrity (consistency) constraint. Because it is hidden inside many programs, changing it is difficult — this is the integrity problem of file systems.
C — Wrong. Data isolation means data is scattered across files in different formats, which makes new programs hard to write. Here the difficulty is changing a rule, not combining scattered data.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: In a DBMS the rule is declared once, e.g. CHECK (balance >= 1000), and checked for every program.

q: A college keeps student details in several files created by different programs at different times: one file is in CSV format and another in a fixed-width text format. Writing a new program that combines data from both files is difficult. Korth calls this problem
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Data scattered in several files with different formats is called data isolation; it makes new application programs hard to write.
concept: Korth lists the main drawbacks of file-processing systems: data redundancy and inconsistency, difficulty in accessing data, data isolation, integrity problems, atomicity problems, concurrent-access anomalies and security problems. Data isolation means the data is scattered in various files, and the files may be in different formats. A DBMS keeps all data under one common structure, so a single query can combine it.
why: A — Wrong. An integrity problem is about consistency rules (like 'marks must be between 0 and 100') being hard to enforce or change. The trouble here is different file formats, not rules.
B — Wrong. An atomicity problem is a half-finished operation after a failure (for example, a crash in the middle of a fund transfer). Nothing fails here.
C — Correct. The data is isolated in separate files with different formats, so combining it needs extra, difficult programming. That is data isolation.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following situations are matched with the correct drawback of a file-processing system?
opts: Two clerks read a balance of Rs 5000 at the same moment and each withdraws Rs 1000; the final balance is saved as Rs 4000 instead of Rs 3000 — concurrent-access anomaly
The system crashes after Rs 500 is debited from account A but before it is credited to account B — atomicity problem
A customer's address is stored in both the savings file and the loan file — data isolation
More than one of the above
exp: A is a concurrent-access anomaly (a lost update) and B is an atomicity problem, so both are matched correctly. Storing the same address in two files is data redundancy, not data isolation.
concept: A concurrent-access anomaly happens when several users change the same data at the same time without control, so one change can overwrite another. An atomicity problem happens when a failure leaves a task half done; a transfer must happen completely or not at all. Data redundancy means the same data is stored in more than one place, while data isolation means data is scattered in files of different formats.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Both clerks started from Rs 5000, so the second write overwrote the first. Uncontrolled simultaneous access gave a wrong result, which is a concurrent-access anomaly (a lost update).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A transfer must be all-or-nothing (atomic). Debit done but credit not done is exactly the atomicity problem.

C — Wrong. Keeping the same address in two files is data redundancy (which can lead to inconsistency). Data isolation means data scattered in files with different formats, which makes new programs hard to write.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Concurrency = many users at once; atomicity = all-or-nothing; redundancy = same data stored twice; isolation = scattered formats.

q: Which of the following is NOT a drawback of traditional file-processing systems?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are drawbacks of file-processing systems listed by Korth, so none of them answers the NOT question.
concept: Korth lists seven drawbacks of file-processing systems: (1) data redundancy and inconsistency, (2) difficulty in accessing data, (3) data isolation, (4) integrity problems, (5) atomicity problems, (6) concurrent-access anomalies and (7) security problems. Solving these problems is the main reason DBMSs were developed.
why: A — Wrong. Data redundancy (the same data stored in many files) and the inconsistency it causes are real drawbacks of file systems, so this option is not 'NOT a drawback'.
B — Wrong. Difficulty in accessing data is a real drawback: for each new kind of request (for example 'list all customers living in Patna') a new program has to be written.
C — Wrong. Concurrent-access anomalies are a real drawback: when many users update the same file at once without control, updates can be lost.
D — Wrong. None of A–C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three options are genuine drawbacks of file-processing systems, so none of them is 'NOT a drawback'.
tip: Korth's 7 file-system problems: redundancy/inconsistency, access difficulty, isolation, integrity, atomicity, concurrency, security.

q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of using a DBMS instead of a file-processing system?
opts: Lower initial cost of hardware, software and training
Support for many users accessing the data at the same time
More than one of the above
exp: A DBMS usually needs a high initial investment in hardware, software and training, so 'lower initial cost' is not an advantage; high cost is in fact a disadvantage.
concept: Main advantages of a DBMS: controlled redundancy, data consistency, sharing of data by many users at the same time, security (access control), integrity constraints, backup and recovery, and data independence. Main disadvantages: high cost (hardware, software licences, training), complexity, and overhead for features such as security, concurrency control and recovery that a small application may not need.
why: A — Wrong. Controlled redundancy is a key advantage of a DBMS: data is stored once (or duplicated only on purpose), which saves space and avoids inconsistency. So it does not fit the NOT question.
B — Correct. A DBMS is costly to set up: powerful hardware, software licences and trained staff such as a DBA. High initial cost is a disadvantage, so 'lower initial cost' is NOT an advantage.
C — Wrong. A DBMS lets many users read and update data at the same time safely, using concurrency control. This is a real advantage.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. B satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements about redundancy in a DBMS:
I. A DBMS removes every kind of duplicate data completely.
II. A DBMS allows controlled redundancy: some data may be stored twice on purpose, for example to make queries faster, while the copies are kept consistent.
III. Reducing redundancy saves storage space and lowers the chance of inconsistent data.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: II and III are correct. A DBMS controls redundancy rather than removing it completely, so statement I is false.
concept: Redundancy means storing the same data more than once. Uncontrolled redundancy wastes space and causes inconsistency when one copy is updated and another is not. A DBMS aims at controlled redundancy: data is normally stored once, but a designer may keep a deliberate copy (for example a precomputed total or a denormalised table) to speed up queries, and the DBMS helps keep such copies consistent (Elmasri–Navathe).
why: A — Wrong. It includes statement I, which is false: a DBMS does not remove all duplication. Foreign keys repeat key values, and designers sometimes duplicate data on purpose for speed.
B — Correct. Statement II (controlled redundancy) and statement III (less redundancy means less storage and fewer inconsistencies) are both correct, and statement I is false.
C — Wrong. It includes the false statement I and leaves out the true statement II.
D — Wrong. Exactly one combination of statements is correct (option B); the other options include a false statement or leave out a true one.
E — Wrong. Option B lists exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Remember the phrase 'controlled redundancy', not 'zero redundancy'.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of a DBMS?
opts: Compiling a C program into machine code
More than one of the above
exp: Turning C source code into machine code is the job of a compiler, not a DBMS. Concurrency control and backup/recovery are standard DBMS functions.
concept: Typical DBMS functions are: storing, retrieving and updating data; keeping a catalog of metadata; transaction support; concurrency control (many users at once); recovery after failures; authorisation (security); enforcing integrity constraints; supporting data independence; and utilities such as loading and backup.
why: A — Wrong. Concurrency control is a core DBMS function: it lets many users work on the same data at the same time without spoiling it. So it does not answer the NOT question.
B — Wrong. Backup and recovery are DBMS functions: the DBMS keeps logs and backups and can bring the database back to a correct state after a crash.
C — Correct. Compiling C code is done by a compiler such as gcc. It is not a database task, so it is NOT a DBMS function.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: According to Elmasri–Navathe, in which situation may ordinary files be preferred over a DBMS?
opts: The application is small, simple, well defined and not expected to change, and only one user needs the data
Many users must update the same data at the same time
The data must be protected by access control and restored after crashes
More than one of the above
exp: A DBMS has overhead (cost, plus security, concurrency and recovery features). For a small, simple, unchanging, single-user application that overhead may not be worth it.
concept: A DBMS is not always the best choice. Elmasri–Navathe say regular files may be better when the application is simple, well defined and not expected to change; when strict real-time needs cannot tolerate DBMS overhead; for embedded systems with little storage; or when there is no multi-user access. Whenever many users share data, or security and recovery matter, a DBMS is the right tool.
why: A — Correct. A small, fixed, single-user application does not need concurrency control, recovery or access control, so the cost and overhead of a DBMS may not be justified.
B — Wrong. Many users updating the same data at the same time need concurrency control, which is a main reason to USE a DBMS.
C — Wrong. Access control (security) and recovery after crashes are DBMS strengths; these needs point towards a DBMS, not towards plain files.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Korth's description of DBMS structure, which component translates DML statements of a query language into an evaluation plan made of low-level instructions?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This is the job of the DML compiler (which also performs query optimisation). None of the three listed components does it.
concept: Korth divides a DBMS into the query processor and the storage manager. The query processor has the DDL interpreter (reads DDL and records definitions in the data dictionary), the DML compiler (translates DML into an evaluation plan and chooses the cheapest plan, i.e. query optimisation) and the query evaluation engine (runs the plan). The storage manager has the authorization and integrity manager, transaction manager, file manager and buffer manager.
why: A — Wrong. The DDL interpreter reads DDL statements (like CREATE TABLE) and records the definitions in the data dictionary. It does not handle DML queries.
B — Wrong. The buffer manager, part of the storage manager, brings disk blocks into main memory and decides what to keep cached. It does not translate queries.
C — Wrong. The file manager, part of the storage manager, manages the space on disk and the data structures used to store information. It does not translate queries.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The component is the DML compiler. It turns a DML statement into an evaluation plan of low-level instructions and also picks the lowest-cost plan (query optimisation).
tip: Query processor = DDL interpreter + DML compiler + query evaluation engine.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the storage manager in Korth's DBMS structure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The DDL interpreter belongs to the query processor. The buffer manager and the authorization and integrity manager are parts of the storage manager.
concept: The storage manager is the part of the DBMS that connects the low-level stored data with the queries. Korth lists its components as: authorization and integrity manager (checks permissions and integrity constraints), transaction manager (keeps the database consistent despite failures and concurrent use), file manager (manages disk space and file structures) and buffer manager (moves data between disk and main memory).
why: A — Wrong. The buffer manager is a storage-manager component: it fetches data from disk into main memory and decides what to cache.
B — Wrong. The authorization and integrity manager is a storage-manager component: it checks that users have permission and that integrity constraints are satisfied.
C — Correct. The DDL interpreter is part of the query processor, not the storage manager. It interprets DDL statements and records definitions in the data dictionary.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Storage manager has four 'managers': authorization & integrity, transaction, file, buffer.

q:
Match each DBMS component with its job (Korth):
P. DDL interpreter
Q. Query evaluation engine
R. Buffer manager
1. Executes the low-level instructions generated by the DML compiler
2. Records the definitions given in DDL statements in the data dictionary
3. Fetches data from disk into main memory and decides what to keep cached
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DDL interpreter → records DDL definitions in the data dictionary (2); query evaluation engine → executes the low-level instructions (1); buffer manager → moves data between disk and memory (3).
concept: In Korth's structure the query processor contains the DDL interpreter, the DML compiler and the query evaluation engine; the storage manager contains the authorization and integrity manager, transaction manager, file manager and buffer manager. A query is compiled into a plan by the DML compiler, and the query evaluation engine runs that plan, asking the buffer manager for the disk blocks it needs.
why: A — Correct. P-2: the DDL interpreter reads DDL and stores the definitions in the data dictionary. Q-1: the query evaluation engine executes the plan of low-level instructions made by the DML compiler. R-3: the buffer manager brings disk blocks into main memory and decides what to cache.
B — Wrong. It swaps P and Q. The DDL interpreter does not execute query plans, and the query evaluation engine does not record DDL definitions.
C — Wrong. It swaps Q and R. The query evaluation engine does not manage the memory buffer, and the buffer manager does not execute query plans; it only supplies the needed disk blocks.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: According to Korth, the storage manager keeps several data structures on disk as part of the physical system implementation. Which of the following are such disk data structures?
opts: Data dictionary, which stores metadata about the structure of the database
Indices, which give fast access to data items
Buffer manager, which decides which disk blocks to keep in main memory
More than one of the above
exp: Korth lists data files, the data dictionary and indices as the data structures kept on disk. The buffer manager is a program module of the storage manager, not a data structure stored on disk.
concept: Korth separates the software modules of a DBMS from the data structures it keeps on disk. On disk the storage manager keeps: data files (the database itself), the data dictionary (metadata, such as the schema) and indices (structures for fast lookup, like the index at the back of a book). Some books also list statistical data used by the query optimiser. The buffer manager, file manager and transaction manager are programs that work on these structures.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The data dictionary is stored on disk and holds metadata, such as table definitions, constraints and user permissions.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Indices are stored on disk and let the DBMS find rows with a given value quickly, without scanning the whole file.
C — Wrong. The buffer manager is a software module of the storage manager. It moves blocks between disk and main memory; it is not a data structure stored on disk.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Modules are programs (buffer, file, transaction manager); structures are stored data (data files, data dictionary, indices).

q: A database system environment is commonly described as having five components: hardware, software, data, people (users) and
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The fifth component is procedures: the written instructions and rules for designing and using the database, for example how to log in, take backups or recover after a failure.
concept: A database system is more than the DBMS software. A common five-part description (Rob and Coronel) is: hardware (computers, disks), software (operating system, DBMS, application programs), data (the stored facts and the metadata), people (DBA, designers, programmers, end users) and procedures (the instructions and rules that govern how the system is designed and used, such as backup schedules and login steps).
why: A — Wrong. Network cables are just a part of the hardware component. They are not counted as a separate component of the database environment.
B — Correct. Procedures are the instructions and rules for using and running the database system, such as how to start the DBMS, log in, take backups and recover after a failure.
C — Wrong. A compiler is a programming tool; any software the system needs is already counted under the software component. 'Compilers' is not one of the five components.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Remember HSDPP: Hardware, Software, Data, People, Procedures.

q: A railway passenger books a ticket on a mobile app by filling in simple forms and pressing buttons. He never writes a query or a program. In Korth's classification of database users, he is a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Naive users work with the database only through application programs written by others, using forms, menus and buttons. The passenger is such a user.
concept: Korth groups database users by how they work with the system. Naive users use ready-made application programs through forms, menus or buttons (for example a bank customer at an ATM or a passenger booking a ticket). Application programmers write those programs. Sophisticated users write their requests directly in a query language or use data-analysis tools. Specialized users write special-purpose database applications, such as computer-aided design or expert systems.
why: A — Wrong. A sophisticated user does not write programs but forms requests directly in a query language such as SQL, or uses analysis tools. The passenger writes no queries.
B — Wrong. An application programmer is a computer professional who writes application programs, such as the ticket-booking app itself. The passenger only uses the app.
C — Correct. A naive user works only through an application interface such as forms and buttons, without knowing anything about queries or tables. This is exactly the passenger.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Naive = uses forms/menus; sophisticated = writes queries; application programmer = writes programs.

q:
Match each person with the type of database user (Korth):
P. A bank customer withdrawing cash at an ATM
Q. A developer writing a Java program with embedded SQL for the bank's loan section
R. A data analyst who writes SQL queries directly in a query tool to study customer trends
1. Naive user
2. Application programmer
3. Sophisticated user
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The ATM customer uses a ready-made interface (naive user), the developer writes application programs (application programmer), and the analyst writes queries directly (sophisticated user).
concept: Users differ in how they reach the data. Naive users use programs written by others. Application programmers build those programs, usually in a host language such as Java or C, with SQL embedded in the program or sent through JDBC/ODBC. Sophisticated users do not write programs; they write their own queries in SQL or use analysis tools such as OLAP or data-mining software.
why: A — Correct. P-1: the ATM customer only presses buttons on a ready-made interface (naive user). Q-2: the developer writes an application program (application programmer). R-3: the analyst writes queries directly without writing a program (sophisticated user).
B — Wrong. It swaps Q and R. The developer who writes a Java program is an application programmer, and the analyst who writes queries directly is a sophisticated user.
C — Wrong. It swaps P and R. The ATM customer does not write any queries, so he is a naive user, not a sophisticated one; the analyst is the sophisticated user.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are duties of a database administrator (DBA)?
opts: Defining the schema and deciding the storage structures and access methods
Granting and revoking users' authorization to access data
Typing in the day's sales bills through a data-entry form
More than one of the above
exp: Schema definition, storage-structure decisions and granting authorization are DBA duties (Korth). Routine data entry through forms is done by end users such as clerks.
concept: The DBA is the person who has central control over the data and over the programs that access it. Korth lists the DBA's functions: schema definition; storage structure and access-method definition; schema and physical-organization modification; granting of authorization for data access; and routine maintenance, such as periodic backups, making sure there is enough free disk space and monitoring running jobs for performance.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The DBA creates the original schema with DDL statements and decides how data is stored and which access methods (such as indices) are used.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The DBA controls security: he decides which user may read or change which data, and these permissions are recorded so that the DBMS can check them.
C — Wrong. Entering daily bills through a form is the job of an end user such as a billing clerk (a naive user). The DBA manages the database itself, not the daily data entry.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. The data administrator (DA) takes policy decisions about which data the organisation keeps and how it may be used, while the DBA provides the technical support to carry out those decisions.
II. Taking periodic backups of the database is part of the DBA's routine maintenance.
III. Naive users usually work with the database by writing SQL queries themselves.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III is false: naive users use forms and menus of application programs; it is sophisticated users who write queries.
concept: C. J. Date separates two roles. The data administrator (DA) is a manager who decides, at the policy level, what data the enterprise should store and the rules for its use. The database administrator (DBA) is the technical person who carries out those decisions: creating the database, tuning performance, controlling security and doing routine maintenance such as backups. In a small organisation one person may do both jobs.
why: A — Correct. Statement I gives the standard DA vs DBA difference (policy vs technical), and statement II is a routine DBA duty listed by Korth. Statement III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes statement III, which is false: naive users do not write SQL; they use ready-made forms and menus. It also leaves out the true statement I.
C — Wrong. It includes the false statement III and leaves out the true statement II.
D — Wrong. Exactly one combination of statements is correct (option A); the other options include a false statement or leave out a true one.
E — Wrong. Option A lists exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: DA = 'what and why' (policy); DBA = 'how' (technical).

q: In the ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture, which level describes how the data is actually stored, such as record formats, file organisation and indexes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The internal (physical) level describes the physical storage structures: how records are stored, the file organisation, indexes and access paths.
concept: The ANSI/SPARC architecture has three levels. The internal level (physical level) describes HOW data is stored on disk. The conceptual level (logical level) describes WHAT data is stored for the whole database and the relationships and constraints among the data, hiding storage details. The external level (view level) describes only the part of the database that a particular user group sees.
why: A — Correct. The internal level is the lowest level. It describes the physical storage: record formats, file organisation, indexes and access paths.
B — Wrong. The conceptual level describes the logical structure of the whole database (entities, data types, relationships, constraints) and hides physical details such as files and indexes.
C — Wrong. The external level describes the views of individual users or user groups, i.e. only the part of the database they need. It says nothing about files or indexes.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Korth's description of the levels of data abstraction, the external level of the ANSI/SPARC architecture corresponds to the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Korth names the three levels physical, logical and view. The view level is the highest level and matches the external level of ANSI/SPARC.
concept: Different books use different names for the same three levels. Internal level = physical level (how data is stored). Conceptual level = logical level (what data is stored and how it is related). External level = view level (the part of the database a user sees). The view level is the highest level of abstraction, closest to the users, and it can hide some data from users for security.
why: A — Wrong. The physical level is the lowest level, describing how data is actually stored. It matches the internal level, not the external level.
B — Wrong. The logical level describes the structure of the whole database (tables, relationships, constraints). It matches the conceptual level.
C — Correct. The view level shows each user only the part of the database he needs. This is the external level of ANSI/SPARC.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Some notes call the conceptual level the 'application level' and the internal level the 'database level'; these are not textbook names. Use External = view, Conceptual = logical, Internal = physical.

q: A database designed with the ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture supports 5 different user views. How many schemas does this database have in total, counting all three levels?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each user view has its own external schema (5), and there is exactly one conceptual schema and one internal schema: 5 + 1 + 1 = 7. Since 7 is not listed, the answer is E.
concept: In the three-schema architecture there can be many external schemas (one for each user view, also called subschemas), but only one conceptual schema and only one internal schema for the whole database. So the total number of schemas = number of external views + 2.
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the number of LEVELS, not the number of schemas. The external level alone has 5 schemas here.
B — Wrong. 6 counts the 5 external schemas and the conceptual schema but forgets the internal schema.
C — Wrong. 10 comes from wrongly giving each view its own conceptual schema (5 × 2). There is only one conceptual schema for the whole database.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The total is 5 external + 1 conceptual + 1 internal = 7 schemas, which is not among A–C.
work:
External schemas = number of user views = 5
Conceptual schema = 1 (one for the whole database)
Internal schema = 1 (one for the whole database)
Total = 5 + 1 + 1 = 7 (verify/w1_counts.py)
tip: Total schemas = number of views + 2.

q: The DBA changes the file organisation of the EMPLOYEE data from a heap file to a hashed file. To keep the conceptual schema unchanged, which mapping must be updated?
opts: The external schemas of all user groups
More than one of the above
exp: A change in physical storage is absorbed by changing the conceptual/internal mapping; the conceptual schema, and so every external schema, stays the same. This is physical data independence.
concept: A mapping is the rule that translates requests and results between two levels. The external/conceptual mapping relates each user view to the conceptual schema; the conceptual/internal mapping relates the conceptual schema to the stored files. When one level changes, only the mapping that connects it to the level above is changed, so the higher levels are not disturbed. Changes in storage (file organisation, indexes, devices) need only a change in the conceptual/internal mapping.
why: A — Wrong. The external/conceptual mapping is changed when the conceptual schema changes (this gives logical data independence). Here the conceptual schema is untouched, so this mapping need not change.
B — Correct. File organisation is part of the internal schema. Updating the conceptual/internal mapping hides this change from the conceptual level, which is physical data independence.
C — Wrong. The whole point of data independence is that user views (external schemas) do NOT have to be rewritten when the storage changes.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: A change at one level is absorbed by the mapping that links it to the level just above.

q: Which of the following statements about data independence is correct?
opts: Logical data independence is harder to achieve than physical data independence
Physical data independence is the ability to change the conceptual schema without changing the external schemas
Logical data independence is the ability to change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema
More than one of the above
exp: Logical data independence is harder because application programs and views depend heavily on the logical structure of the data. B and C swap the definitions of the two kinds of independence.
concept: Data independence is the ability to change the schema at one level without having to change the schema at the next higher level. Physical data independence: change the internal schema (for example add an index or change the file organisation) without changing the conceptual schema. Logical data independence: change the conceptual schema (for example add or remove a column, or split a table) without changing the external schemas or application programs. Logical data independence is harder to achieve, because programs and views are closely tied to the logical structure.
why: A — Correct. Programs and views refer directly to the tables and columns of the conceptual schema, so changes there are harder to hide. Physical changes are easier to hide, because programs normally do not refer to files or indexes.
B — Wrong. This is the definition of LOGICAL data independence (conceptual changes hidden from external schemas), not physical data independence.
C — Wrong. This is the definition of PHYSICAL data independence (internal changes hidden from the conceptual schema), not logical data independence.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Physical = hide storage changes (easier). Logical = hide table-structure changes (harder).

q:
How many of the following changes can be hidden from the conceptual schema by physical data independence alone (that is, they are changes at the internal, or physical, level only)?
1. Creating an index on EMP(Salary)
2. Changing the file organisation of EMP from heap to hashed
3. Adding a new column Email to EMP
4. Moving the database files from a hard disk to an SSD
5. Splitting EMP into two tables and giving old users a view that joins them
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Changes 1, 2 and 4 affect only physical storage, so they are internal-level changes. Changes 3 and 5 change the tables themselves (the conceptual schema) and need logical data independence. Count = 3.
concept: To classify a change, ask: does it change WHAT data the database holds or how the tables look (conceptual level), or only HOW and WHERE the data is stored (internal level)? Indexes, file organisation, block sizes and storage devices are internal details. Adding, removing or splitting tables or columns are conceptual changes; hiding them from users is logical data independence, often done with views.
why: A — Wrong. 2 misses one of the physical changes. A common slip is to forget that creating an index is also an internal-level change: it adds an access path, not new data.
B — Correct. Change 1 (index), change 2 (file organisation) and change 4 (storage device) are internal-level changes, so 3 changes are covered by physical data independence.
C — Wrong. 4 wrongly counts one of the conceptual changes. Adding a column (3) or splitting a table (5) changes the conceptual schema; hiding such changes from users needs logical data independence.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
1. Index on Salary -> new access path -> internal level (physical DI)
2. Heap -> hashed file -> file organisation -> internal level (physical DI)
3. Add column Email -> table structure changes -> conceptual level (logical DI)
4. HDD -> SSD -> storage device -> internal level (physical DI)
5. Split EMP + view -> table structure changes -> conceptual level (logical DI)
Physical-DI changes = 1, 2, 4 -> count = 3 (verify/w1_counts.py)
tip: Index, file organisation, block size, storage device = physical. Adding, dropping or splitting columns or tables = logical.

q: Which of the following statements about schema and instance is NOT correct?
opts: The database schema changes every time a new row is inserted
The data stored in the database at a particular moment is called an instance or database state
The schema is also called the intension, and the database state is called the extension
More than one of the above
exp: Inserting a row changes the instance (state), not the schema. The schema changes rarely, only when the structure itself is altered (for example with ALTER TABLE). B and C are correct statements.
concept: The schema is the description of the database — table names, columns, data types and constraints — fixed at design time and changed rarely. The instance (database state or snapshot) is the actual data at one moment; it changes with every insert, update or delete. Elmasri–Navathe call the schema the intension and the state the extension. Analogy: the schema is like the printed column headings of an attendance register; the instance is the entries written on a particular day.
why: A — Correct. This statement is false, so it satisfies the NOT stem. Inserting a row changes only the instance (the current data). The schema changes only when the structure itself is changed, for example by ALTER TABLE.
B — Wrong. This statement is correct: the collection of data in the database at a particular moment is the database instance, also called its state or snapshot. So it is not the NOT-item.
C — Wrong. This statement is correct: Elmasri–Navathe call the schema the intension and the database state the extension of the schema.
D — Wrong. Only A satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. A satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Schema = intension (structure, rarely changes); instance = extension (data, changes all the time).

q:
Consider the following statements about the ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture:
I. The actual data is stored only at the internal (physical) level; the conceptual and external schemas are only descriptions of data.
II. Each user group can have its own external schema, but the database has only one conceptual schema and one internal schema.
III. Logical data independence is the ability to change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III describes physical data independence, not logical data independence.
concept: In the three-schema architecture only the internal level corresponds to stored data; the other two schemas are descriptions that the DBMS uses to translate (map) requests and results between levels. There may be many external schemas but only one conceptual and one internal schema. Changing the internal schema without disturbing the conceptual schema is physical data independence; changing the conceptual schema without disturbing the external schemas is logical data independence.
why: A — Wrong. It includes statement III, which is false (it is the definition of physical data independence), and leaves out the true statement II.
B — Wrong. It includes the false statement III and leaves out the true statement I.

C — Correct. Statement I is from Elmasri–Navathe: the three schemas are only descriptions of data, and the data that actually exists is at the physical level only. Statement II is also true. Statement III is false.
D — Wrong. Exactly one combination of statements is correct (option C); the other options include a false statement or leave out a true one.
E — Wrong. Option C lists exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: The relational data model was proposed in 1970 by
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The relational model was proposed by E. F. Codd of IBM in his 1970 paper 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'. None of the three names listed is correct.
concept: Some names linked with database history: Charles Bachman designed the Integrated Data Store (IDS), the basis of the network (CODASYL) model. E. F. (Ted) Codd proposed the relational model in 1970. Peter Chen proposed the Entity–Relationship (ER) model in 1976. Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce designed SEQUEL, which later became SQL, at IBM.
why: A — Wrong. Charles Bachman developed IDS (Integrated Data Store), an early network-model DBMS that led to the CODASYL standard. He did not propose the relational model.
B — Wrong. Peter Chen proposed the Entity–Relationship (ER) model in 1976. It is used for conceptual design; it is not the relational model.
C — Wrong. Donald Chamberlin, with Raymond Boyce, designed SEQUEL (later SQL) at IBM, a language for relational databases. The relational model itself came from Codd.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The relational model was proposed by E. F. Codd in 1970, and he is not among the options.
tip: Codd 1970 = relational model; Chen 1976 = ER model; Bachman = network model (IDS).

q: IBM's IMS (Information Management System) is the best-known DBMS based on which data model?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: IMS, developed by IBM in the 1960s, organises records as trees of parent and child segments, so it follows the hierarchical model.
concept: In the hierarchical model, data is arranged like an upside-down tree: each record (except the root) has exactly one parent, and a parent can have many children (one-to-many). It works like folders inside folders in a filing cabinet. IBM's IMS is the classic example. Its weakness is many-to-many relationships, which need duplicated or virtual (pointer) records.
why: A — Correct. IMS stores data as hierarchies (trees) of parent and child records, which is the hierarchical model.
B — Wrong. The network model arranges records as a graph in which a record can have several owners. Its classic examples are IDS and CODASYL systems such as IDMS, not IMS.
C — Wrong. The relational model stores data in tables. IBM's relational work was the System R research prototype and the product DB2, not IMS.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: IMS = hierarchical; IDS/IDMS (CODASYL) = network; System R/DB2 = relational.

q: In a certain data model, records are linked through named 'set types'. Each set type links one owner record type to a member record type (a one-to-many link), and a record type can be a member in several different sets, so the data forms a graph. This model, standardised by the CODASYL DBTG, is the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Owner–member set types and the CODASYL DBTG standard belong to the network model. Because a record type can be a member in several sets, the structure is a graph, not a tree.
concept: The network model, standardised by the CODASYL Database Task Group (DBTG) in 1971, represents data as record types connected by set types. Each set type is a 1:N link from an owner record type to a member record type. Since a record type may be a member in several set types (several 'parents'), the structure is a general graph, and many-to-many relationships can be modelled through link records. Data is reached by following pointers from record to record (navigational access).
why: A — Wrong. In the hierarchical model every child record has only ONE parent, so the structure is a tree. Here a record type can be a member in several sets, which a tree does not allow.
B — Wrong. The relational model has no owner–member sets or pointers; it links tables through matching key values (foreign keys).
C — Correct. Owner and member record types joined by set types, standardised by the CODASYL DBTG, are the defining features of the network model.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a data store, each record carries its own tags or keys describing its fields, and two records of the same kind may have different fields, as in XML and JSON documents. Such data is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Self-describing data with tags or keys, where items of the same type may have different sets of attributes, is semi-structured data. XML and JSON are its standard formats.
concept: Structured data follows a fixed schema decided in advance, like the rows of a relational table where every row has the same columns. Semi-structured data is self-describing: the field names (tags or keys) are stored along with the values, and different records may have different fields; XML and JSON are typical formats. Unstructured data has no internal structure that a DBMS can use, such as free text, images or audio.
why: A — Wrong. Structured data fits a fixed schema decided in advance, as in a relational table where every row has exactly the same columns. Here the records can differ, so the data is not fully structured.
B — Correct. Data that carries its own tags/keys and allows records of the same kind to have different fields is semi-structured data, such as XML and JSON documents.
C — Wrong. Unstructured data, such as plain text, images or videos, has no tags or fields at all. XML and JSON have tags/keys that describe the data, so they are not unstructured.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Semi-structured = self-describing (tags/keys are stored with the data).

q: Which of the following are features of the object-relational data model?
opts: It extends the relational model with richer types, such as user-defined structured types and collection types
It supports inheritance between types and between tables
It stores data only as a tree of parent and child records, without tables
More than one of the above
exp: The object-relational model keeps tables but adds object-oriented features: user-defined and structured types, collections and inheritance (SQL:1999 onwards). A tree of parent and child records is the hierarchical model.
concept: The object-relational data model combines the relational model with features of the object-oriented model. Data is still stored in tables and queried with SQL, but columns can have complex types (structured types, arrays, multisets), types and tables can inherit from other types and tables, and methods can be attached to types. PostgreSQL and Oracle are examples of object-relational DBMSs. A pure object-oriented DBMS (such as ObjectDB or db4o) instead stores objects directly, with their attributes and methods, using encapsulation and inheritance, and has no tables.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Object-relational systems allow user-defined structured types (for example an Address type with street, city and PIN) and collection types such as arrays, which the plain relational model does not have.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. SQL:1999 added type inheritance (for example a Student type under a Person type) and table inheritance, borrowed from object-oriented ideas.
C — Wrong. A tree of parent and child records is the hierarchical model (like IBM's IMS). The object-relational model still stores data in tables.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. In the hierarchical model, records form a graph in which each child record can have several parent records.
II. The ER model is a high-level (conceptual) data model used mainly for database design.
III. In the network model, a record type can take part in several owner–member sets, so the structure is a graph rather than a tree.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Statements II and III are correct. Statement I is false: in the hierarchical model each child record has exactly one parent, which is why the structure is a tree.
concept: Data models can be compared by their structure. Hierarchical: a tree; each child has exactly one parent (one-to-many only). Network: a graph; a record can be a member of several sets, so it can have several owners. Relational: tables linked by key values. ER: a conceptual (high-level) model, drawn as diagrams during design and later mapped to a logical model such as the relational model.
why: A — Wrong. It includes statement I, which is false: in the hierarchical model a child record has only ONE parent, so the data forms a tree, not a graph. It also leaves out the true statement III.

B — Correct. Statement II is true: Elmasri–Navathe call the ER model a conceptual (high-level) data model, used to design the database before it is mapped to tables. Statement III is true: several owner–member sets make the network structure a graph. Statement I is false.
C — Wrong. It includes the false statement I and leaves out the true statement II.
D — Wrong. Exactly one combination of statements is correct (option B); the other options include a false statement or leave out a true one.
E — Wrong. Option B lists exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Hierarchical = tree (one parent); network = graph (many owners).

q: In a college office, a desktop program installed on each clerk's PC sends SQL queries over the network directly to a central database server; the server runs the queries and sends back the results. This is an example of
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The application runs on the client and talks directly to the database server using SQL (often through ODBC or JDBC). Client + database server = two tiers.
concept: In a one-tier architecture the user interface, the application and the DBMS are all on the same machine. In a two-tier (client–server) architecture the application runs on the client machine and sends queries directly to the DBMS on the server, often through ODBC or JDBC. In a three-tier architecture the client is only a front end (often a web browser); it talks to an application server that holds the business logic, and only the application server talks to the database server.
why: A — Wrong. In a one-tier setup the application and the DBMS run on the same computer, used directly by the user. Here the database is on a separate server.
B — Wrong. A three-tier setup needs a separate application server (middle tier) between the client and the database. Here the client program talks to the database server directly.
C — Correct. Two machines play two roles: the client runs the application and sends SQL; the server runs the DBMS. This is the classic two-tier client–server architecture.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are true about a three-tier database application architecture?
opts: The client machine acts only as a front end and does not contain direct database calls
The business logic runs on an application server, which communicates with the database server
It is meant mainly for small, single-user desktop applications
More than one of the above
exp: In a three-tier architecture the client is only a front end (A), and the application server in the middle holds the business rules and talks to the database (B). It suits large and web applications, not small single-user ones.
concept: Korth explains that in a three-tier architecture the client (often a web browser) is just a front end. It talks to an application server, which contains the business logic (rules such as 'a student can register for at most 6 courses'). The application server in turn accesses the database server. Three-tier designs suit large applications and applications on the World Wide Web, because they give better security and scale better than two-tier designs.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In Korth's words, the client machine acts merely as a front end; it sends requests to the application server, not SQL to the database.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The middle tier (application server) holds the business logic and is the tier that talks to the database server.
C — Wrong. Three-tier architecture is used for large applications and web applications with many users. A small single-user desktop program does not need a separate application server.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A database whose data is stored at several sites connected by a computer network, but which appears to its users as a single database, is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Data stored at several networked sites but presented to users as one logical database is a distributed database.
concept: A centralized database keeps all its data at one site (one computer system), even if users connect to it from many places. A distributed database spreads its data over several sites connected by a network; the distributed DBMS hides this, so users see one logical database (distribution transparency). A personal database is a small database used by one person on one computer.
why: A — Wrong. A centralized database keeps all its data at ONE site. Users may connect from far away, but the data itself is not spread across sites.
B — Correct. A distributed database stores its data at several sites linked by a network, while users see it as one database.
C — Wrong. A personal database is a small database used by a single person on a single computer, such as a contact list kept in MS Access.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Match each setup with its architecture:
P. A shopkeeper uses an MS Access database and its forms on one PC; nothing is shared over a network.
Q. A billing program on each counter PC sends SQL directly to a central MySQL server.
R. Customers use a web browser; a web/application server runs the program logic and is the only part that talks to the database server.
Each option gives the architecture of P, Q and R in that order.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: P has everything on one machine (1-tier). Q has a client program talking directly to the database server (2-tier). R has browser → application server → database server (3-tier).
concept: Count the separate layers that do different jobs. 1-tier: user interface, application and database on one machine. 2-tier: client (interface plus application logic) and database server. 3-tier: client (interface only), application server (business logic) and database server. Most web applications are three-tier.
why: A — Correct. P is 1-tier (everything on one PC), Q is 2-tier (client program + database server) and R is 3-tier (browser + application server + database server).
B — Wrong. It swaps P and Q. A single PC running MS Access has no separate server, so it is 1-tier; the counter PCs talking to a MySQL server form a 2-tier client–server system.
C — Wrong. It swaps Q and R. The billing program talks to the database directly (no middle tier), so it is 2-tier; the web setup has a middle application server, so it is 3-tier.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Ask: is there a separate middle server holding the business logic? Yes → 3-tier.

q: Which of the following is NOT a database management system?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are DBMSs: IBM Db2 and SQLite are relational DBMSs, and MongoDB is a NoSQL (document-oriented) DBMS. So none of them answers the NOT question.
concept: A DBMS is software that stores, retrieves and manages data in a database. Relational DBMSs include Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, IBM Db2, SQLite and MS Access. NoSQL DBMSs include MongoDB (document), Cassandra (column-family), Redis (key-value) and Neo4j (graph). Software such as MS Word (a word processor), a web search engine or an operating system such as Windows is not a DBMS.
why: A — Wrong. IBM Db2 is a relational DBMS from IBM, widely used in banks and large companies. So it IS a DBMS.
B — Wrong. SQLite is a small, serverless (embedded) relational DBMS that keeps a whole database in a single file; it is used inside Android apps and web browsers. It IS a DBMS.
C — Wrong. MongoDB is a NoSQL DBMS that stores JSON-like documents. It is not relational, but it is still a DBMS.
D — Wrong. None of A–C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three options are DBMSs, so none of them is 'NOT a DBMS'.
tip: Not relational does not mean not a DBMS: MongoDB, Redis and Neo4j are NoSQL DBMSs.

q: A data manipulation language in which the user states WHAT data is needed, without saying HOW to find it, is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A declarative or non-procedural DML, such as the query part of SQL, needs only a description of the wanted data; the DBMS works out how to get it.
concept: Korth divides DMLs into two kinds. A procedural DML requires the user to say what data is needed AND how to get it, step by step. A declarative (non-procedural) DML requires only what data is needed; the DBMS (its query optimiser) decides how. The query part of SQL is non-procedural. A DDL, in contrast, defines the database structure; DCL (GRANT, REVOKE) controls access and TCL (COMMIT, ROLLBACK) controls transactions.
why: A — Wrong. A procedural DML requires the user to specify both what data is needed and HOW to get it, step by step.
B — Wrong. A data definition language (DDL) defines the database structure, for example with CREATE TABLE. It is not used to state which data to retrieve.
C — Correct. A declarative (non-procedural) DML, like SQL's SELECT, describes only the required result; the DBMS decides the steps.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Declarative = WHAT only; procedural = WHAT + HOW.

q: In Elmasri–Navathe's classification of DBMS languages, the language used to specify the internal schema (storage structures and access paths) is the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Elmasri–Navathe say the storage definition language (SDL) specifies the internal schema, while the view definition language (VDL) specifies user views (external schemas).
concept: When the levels of the three-schema architecture are kept strictly apart, Elmasri–Navathe describe one language per level: DDL for the conceptual schema, SDL (storage definition language) for the internal schema and VDL (view definition language) for the external schemas (user views). In today's relational DBMSs there is no separate SDL or VDL: SQL does these jobs, and physical storage is set through parameters and commands such as CREATE INDEX.
why: A — Correct. The storage definition language specifies the internal schema: how files are stored and which access paths (such as indexes) exist.
B — Wrong. The view definition language specifies user views and their mapping to the conceptual schema, i.e. the external level, not the internal level.
C — Wrong. A DML is used to retrieve, insert, delete and modify data. It does not define any schema.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: SDL → internal schema, DDL → conceptual schema, VDL → external schemas.

q: A bank moves from an old system to a new DBMS. The DBMS utility that reads the old data files (for example text or CSV files) and inserts their contents into the new database tables is the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Elmasri–Navathe: a loading utility loads existing data files, such as text or sequential files, into the database, converting them to the required format.
concept: DBMSs come with utilities (helper programs) for the DBA. Loading utility: loads existing data files into the database, converting formats. Backup utility: makes a copy of the database (often on tape or another disk) so it can be restored after a failure. Storage reorganization utility: reorganises files and creates new access paths to improve performance. Performance-monitoring utility: watches how the database is used and gives statistics to the DBA. Other utilities sort files, compress data and monitor access by users.
why: A — Wrong. A backup utility copies the database to separate storage so that it can be restored after a crash. It does not bring in data from old files.
B — Correct. The loading utility reads existing data files and loads their contents into the database in the required format.
C — Wrong. A performance-monitoring utility collects statistics about how the database is used, to help the DBA tune it. It does not load data.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of Codd's rules states that every single data value in a relational database must be logically reachable by giving the table name, the primary-key value and the column name?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This is Codd's Rule 2, the guaranteed access rule. None of the three listed rules says this, so the answer is E.
concept: Codd published 12 rules (numbered 1 to 12, plus a foundation Rule 0) that a DBMS must follow to be called fully relational. Important ones: Rule 1 Information rule — all information is represented as values in tables. Rule 2 Guaranteed access — every value is reachable by table name + primary-key value + column name. Rule 3 Systematic treatment of NULLs. Rule 4 Active online catalog. Rule 5 Comprehensive data sublanguage. Rule 6 View updating. Rules 8 and 9 Physical and logical data independence. Rule 12 Non-subversion.
why: A — Wrong. The information rule (Rule 1) says that ALL information, including metadata, is stored as values in tables. It does not describe how to reach one particular value.
B — Wrong. Rule 3 says the DBMS must support NULL to represent missing or inapplicable information, in a uniform way that is different from zero or a blank. It is not about reaching a value.
C — Wrong. The non-subversion rule (Rule 12) says a low-level, record-at-a-time interface must not be able to bypass the integrity rules of the relational language.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The rule is the guaranteed access rule (Rule 2): table name + primary-key value + column name locate exactly one value.
tip: Guaranteed access = table + primary key + column, like a row-and-column address in a spreadsheet.

q: A relational DBMS enforces all integrity constraints when data is changed through SQL. It also offers a low-level, record-at-a-time interface through which a program can insert rows that break those constraints. Which of Codd's rules does this DBMS violate?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Codd's Rule 12 (non-subversion) says that if a low-level interface exists, it must not be usable to bypass the integrity rules expressed in the relational language. Here it can be, so Rule 12 is violated.
concept: Codd's rules aim to ensure that a DBMS is truly relational. Rule 12, the non-subversion rule, says: if a relational system offers a low-level (single-record-at-a-time) language, that language cannot be used to subvert or bypass the integrity rules and constraints expressed in the higher-level relational language. Otherwise the constraints could be quietly broken. Rule 5 needs at least one language that supports data definition, view definition, data manipulation, integrity, authorization and transactions; Rule 6 says all theoretically updatable views must be updatable by the system.
why: A — Wrong. The comprehensive data sublanguage rule (Rule 5) needs at least one language (like SQL) that supports data definition, view definition, data manipulation, integrity constraints, authorization and transactions. This DBMS has SQL with constraints, so Rule 5 is not the problem.
B — Wrong. The view updating rule (Rule 6) says all views that are theoretically updatable must be updatable by the system. The problem here is bypassing constraints, not views.
C — Correct. A low-level interface that can insert rows breaking the integrity constraints 'subverts' the relational rules. That is exactly what the non-subversion rule (Rule 12) forbids.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Non-subversion: no back door around the constraints.

q: In the ER model, the collection of all entities of the same type that share the same attributes, such as all the students of a college, is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A set of entities of the same type that share the same properties (attributes) is an entity set (Korth).
concept: An entity is a 'thing' or object in the real world that can be told apart from other objects, such as one particular student. An entity type describes the attributes shared by such things (STUDENT with RollNo, Name). An entity set is the collection of all entities of that type at a given time, for example all students of the college. In Chen notation an entity set is drawn as a rectangle.
why: A — Wrong. An attribute is a property of an entity, such as Name or RollNo. It describes entities; it is not a collection of them.
B — Wrong. A relationship set is a set of relationships of the same type among entities, for example all 'student enrols in course' pairs. It is not a set of entities.
C — Correct. All the students of the college form the entity set STUDENT: a collection of entities of the same type with the same attributes.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Chen's ER notation, a weak entity set is drawn as a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A weak entity set is shown by a double rectangle, and its identifying relationship by a double diamond.
concept: A weak entity set is one that cannot be identified by its own attributes alone and depends on an owner entity set. Chen notation: rectangle = entity set; double rectangle = weak entity set; diamond = relationship set; double diamond = identifying relationship; ellipse = attribute; underlined name = key attribute; dashed underline = partial key; double ellipse = multivalued attribute; dashed ellipse = derived attribute; single line = partial participation; double line = total participation.
why: A — Correct. A double rectangle marks a weak entity set, such as DEPENDENT owned by EMPLOYEE.
B — Wrong. A double ellipse represents a multivalued attribute, such as PhoneNumbers. It is not used for entity sets.
C — Wrong. A dashed ellipse represents a derived attribute, such as Age computed from DateOfBirth.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 'Double' for weak things: double rectangle (weak entity set), double diamond (identifying relationship).

q: DEPENDENT is a weak entity set whose owner is EMPLOYEE (primary key EmpID). The partial key (discriminator) of DEPENDENT is DepName. What is the primary key of the table created for DEPENDENT?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The primary key of a weak entity set = primary key of its owner (EmpID) + its own partial key (DepName).
concept: A weak entity set cannot be identified by its own attributes alone: two employees may each have a dependent named 'Riya'. So its key is formed from the owner's primary key plus the partial key (discriminator), which tells apart the weak entities that belong to the SAME owner. When the weak entity set is mapped to a table, EmpID also becomes a foreign key referencing EMPLOYEE.
why: A — Wrong. DepName is only a partial key: it is unique among the dependents of ONE employee, but two employees may both have a dependent called 'Riya'. So DepName alone cannot be the primary key.
B — Correct. The owner's key EmpID plus the discriminator DepName together identify each dependent uniquely, so {EmpID, DepName} is the primary key (and EmpID is also a foreign key to EMPLOYEE).
C — Wrong. One employee can have several dependents, so EmpID repeats in the DEPENDENT table and cannot be the primary key by itself.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Primary key of a weak entity set = owner's primary key + partial key.

q: Which of the following statements about a weak entity set are correct?
opts: It does not have enough attributes of its own to form a primary key
Its participation in the identifying relationship is total
Its identifying relationship with the owner must be many-to-many
More than one of the above
exp: A weak entity set lacks a primary key of its own (A), and every weak entity must be linked to an owner, so its participation is total (B). The identifying relationship is many-to-one from the weak entity set to the owner, never many-to-many.
concept: Korth: an entity set that does not have sufficient attributes to form a primary key is a weak entity set. It must be associated with an identifying (owner) entity set through an identifying relationship. The identifying relationship is many-to-one from the weak entity set to the owner (one owner, many weak entities), and the weak entity set's participation in it is total, because a weak entity cannot exist without its owner.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is the definition of a weak entity set: its own attributes cannot uniquely identify its entities.
