B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every weak entity must be related to an owner entity, so its participation in the identifying relationship is total (drawn with a double line).
C — Wrong. Each weak entity has exactly ONE owner, so the identifying relationship is many-to-one from the weak entity set to the owner (one-to-many from owner to weak entities), not many-to-many.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Every weak entity is existence-dependent on its owner entity.
II. Every entity that is existence-dependent on another entity must be a weak entity.
III. If a LOAN entity is deleted, the PAYMENT entities that are existence-dependent on it must also be deleted.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is false: an entity can be existence-dependent and still have its own key, e.g. DRIVING_LICENCE depends on PERSON but has its own LicenceNo, so it is not weak.
concept: Entity x is existence-dependent on entity y if x cannot exist without y; y is called the dominant entity and x the subordinate entity. If y is deleted, x must be deleted too. A weak entity is always existence-dependent on its owner. The reverse is not true: Elmasri–Navathe point out that a DRIVER_LICENSE cannot exist without a PERSON, yet it has its own key (the licence number), so it is a strong entity with total participation, not a weak entity.
why: A — Wrong. It includes statement II, which is false (existence dependency does not force an entity to be weak), and leaves out the true statement III.

B — Correct. Statement I is true: a weak entity cannot exist without its owner. Statement III is Korth's example: payments are existence-dependent on their loan, so deleting the loan deletes its payments. Statement II is false.
C — Wrong. It includes the false statement II and leaves out the true statement I.
D — Wrong. Exactly one combination of statements is correct (option B); the other options include a false statement or leave out a true one.
E — Wrong. Option B lists exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Weak ⇒ existence-dependent, but existence-dependent does NOT imply weak.

q: The attribute (or set of attributes) of a weak entity set that distinguishes among the weak entities belonging to the same owner entity is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This attribute is the partial key, also called the discriminator. None of the options names it, so the answer is E.
concept: A weak entity set has no key of its own, but it usually has a partial key (Elmasri–Navathe) or discriminator (Korth): an attribute that is unique among the weak entities of ONE owner. For example, for PAYMENT owned by LOAN, PaymentNo 1, 2, 3 … restarts for each loan. In Chen notation the partial key is underlined with a dashed line. Full key of the weak entity set = owner's primary key + partial key.
why: A — Wrong. A foreign key is a column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. In the mapped table the owner's key does become a foreign key, but the distinguishing attribute of the weak entity is not called a foreign key.
B — Wrong. A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies every entity in the WHOLE set. The discriminator is unique only within one owner, so it is not a candidate key.

C — Wrong. A super key is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies every entity in the set. The discriminator alone cannot do that, because different owners can have weak entities with the same discriminator value.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. It is called the partial key (Elmasri–Navathe) or discriminator (Korth), and it is shown with a dashed underline.
tip: Partial key = discriminator = dashed underline.

q: In the ER model, a simple (atomic) attribute is one that
opts: Uniquely identifies each entity in an entity set
Cannot be divided into smaller meaningful parts
Can hold several values for the same entity
More than one of the above
exp: A simple attribute is indivisible, for example Gender or RollNo. Identifying an entity is the job of a key attribute, and holding several values is a multivalued attribute — these are different ideas.
concept: Attributes are classified in several independent ways. Simple vs composite: a simple (atomic) attribute cannot be divided (Age), while a composite attribute has parts (Name = FirstName + LastName). Single-valued vs multivalued: one value per entity (DateOfBirth) or several (PhoneNumbers). Stored vs derived. A key attribute has a unique value for each entity. A key may be simple (RollNo) or composite, and a simple attribute need not be a key (Gender).
why: A — Wrong. This describes a KEY attribute, such as RollNo. Being a key is a different property: Gender is simple but not a key, and a key can even be composite.
B — Correct. A simple (atomic) attribute is indivisible — it has no meaningful sub-parts, like Age or Gender.
C — Wrong. This describes a MULTIVALUED attribute, such as PhoneNumbers, drawn as a double ellipse.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake: some notes say a simple attribute is 'also called a key attribute'. That is wrong — simple means indivisible, key means it identifies the entity. Gender is simple but not a key.

q: A PERSON entity has the attributes DateOfBirth and Age. Age can always be calculated from DateOfBirth and today's date. In the ER model, Age is a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Age is computed from DateOfBirth, so it is a derived attribute (drawn as a dashed ellipse). DateOfBirth is the stored (base) attribute.
concept: A stored (base) attribute is actually kept in the database, like DateOfBirth. A derived attribute's value can be calculated from other attributes or entities, like Age from DateOfBirth, or the number of employees of a department counted from the employee entities. Derived attributes are drawn as dashed ellipses and are usually not stored, so they never go out of date.
why: A — Correct. Age is derived: its value is calculated from the stored attribute DateOfBirth whenever it is needed.
B — Wrong. The stored (base) attribute here is DateOfBirth; Age is calculated from it, so Age is not the stored one.
C — Wrong. A composite attribute is made of smaller parts, like Address = (Street, City, PIN). Age is a single number with no sub-parts.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Match each Chen-notation symbol with what it represents:
P. Double ellipse
Q. Dashed ellipse
R. Double diamond
1. Derived attribute
2. Identifying relationship of a weak entity set
3. Multivalued attribute
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Double ellipse = multivalued attribute (3); dashed ellipse = derived attribute (1); double diamond = identifying relationship (2).
concept: Remember the symbols by meaning. 'Double' marks something special about number or dependence: double ellipse (many values), double rectangle (weak entity set), double diamond (identifying relationship), double line (total participation). 'Dashed' marks something not fully stored or not a full key: dashed ellipse (derived attribute, computed rather than stored) and dashed underline (partial key).
why: A — Wrong. It swaps P and Q: a double ellipse is a multivalued attribute, and a dashed ellipse is a derived attribute.
B — Wrong. It gets Q and R wrong: a dashed ellipse is a derived attribute (not an identifying relationship), and a double diamond is an identifying relationship (not a derived attribute).
C — Correct. P-3: double ellipse = multivalued attribute. Q-1: dashed ellipse = derived attribute. R-2: double diamond = identifying relationship that connects a weak entity set to its owner.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Double = many/dependent; dashed = derived/partial.

q: In Elmasri–Navathe notation, a PERSON entity has the attribute {CollegeDegrees(College, Year, Degree, Field)}. This attribute is
opts: A complex attribute: multivalued, where each value is a composite of College, Year, Degree and Field
A composite attribute whose parts College, Year, Degree and Field are each multivalued
A derived attribute calculated from College and Year
More than one of the above
exp: Braces { } mark a multivalued attribute and parentheses ( ) mark a composite one. So a person can have several degrees, and each degree has four parts. Such nesting of composite and multivalued attributes is called a complex attribute.
concept: Elmasri–Navathe write multivalued attributes inside braces { } and the components of a composite attribute inside parentheses ( ). When these are nested, the attribute is called a complex attribute. {CollegeDegrees(College, Year, Degree, Field)} means: a person may have many college degrees, and each degree is described by one college, one year, one degree name and one field.
why: A — Correct. The outer braces make CollegeDegrees multivalued (a person can have many degrees), and the parentheses make each value composite with four components. This nesting is a complex attribute.

B — Wrong. This reads the notation the wrong way round. The braces are around the whole CollegeDegrees, not around each part; each single degree has exactly one College, one Year, one Degree and one Field.
C — Wrong. Nothing here is calculated from other values. Degrees are stored facts, so this is not a derived attribute.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: { } = multivalued, ( ) = composite; nested together = complex attribute.

q: In the ER model, a NULL value of an attribute for a particular entity may mean
opts: The attribute does not apply to this entity (not applicable), e.g. a person who has no middle name
The value exists but is not known or not recorded (missing)
More than one of the above
exp: NULL can mean 'not applicable' or 'unknown' (missing, or not known whether it exists). NULL is not the same as zero or a blank.
concept: An entity takes a NULL for an attribute when it has no value for it. Korth and Elmasri–Navathe give the meanings: (1) not applicable — the value does not exist for this entity, e.g. no middle name or no flat number; (2) unknown — either the value exists but is missing (every person has a height, but we do not know it), or we do not know whether a value exists at all (does this person have a landline phone?). NULL is different from zero, which is a real, known number.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 'Not applicable' is one standard meaning of NULL: the attribute has no value for this entity, like a person without a middle name.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 'Unknown/missing' is the other standard meaning: the value exists in reality but has not been recorded, such as a person's height that was never measured or recorded.
C — Wrong. Zero is a definite, known value (for example 0 marks). NULL means that no value is present, so NULL is never the same as 0.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: NULL is not 0 and not a blank space; it means 'no value'.

q: Which of the following would normally be modelled as multivalued attributes of a STUDENT entity?
opts: PhoneNumbers, since a student may have several phone numbers
LanguagesKnown, since a student may know several languages
More than one of the above
exp: A student can have many phone numbers and know many languages, so both are multivalued (double ellipse). A student has only one date of birth, so it is single-valued.
concept: A single-valued attribute holds exactly one value for each entity, such as DateOfBirth or Aadhaar number. A multivalued attribute can hold a set of values for one entity, such as phone numbers, e-mail addresses, degrees or languages known. Multivalued attributes are drawn as double ellipses and, when mapped to tables, are placed in a separate table.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. One student may have a personal mobile number and a home number, so PhoneNumbers holds a set of values — a multivalued attribute.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A student may know Hindi, English and Maithili, so LanguagesKnown holds several values — a multivalued attribute.
C — Wrong. Every student has exactly one date of birth, so DateOfBirth is single-valued (and it is the stored attribute from which Age is derived).
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Chen's ER notation, which of the following symbol–meaning pairs is NOT correct?
opts: Double line between an entity set and a relationship set — total participation
More than one of the above
exp: A dashed ellipse means a derived attribute; a multivalued attribute is drawn as a double ellipse. The other two pairs are correct.
concept: The ER diagram uses a small set of shapes, and exams often test them by swapping two meanings. Chen notation: rectangle = entity set; double rectangle = weak entity set; diamond = relationship set; double diamond = identifying relationship; ellipse = attribute; underlined name = key attribute; dashed underline = partial key; double ellipse = multivalued attribute; dashed ellipse = derived attribute; single line = partial participation; double line = total participation.
why: A — Wrong. This pair is correct: a diamond represents a relationship set, such as ENROLLS. So it is not the NOT-item.
B — Correct. This pair is wrong, so it answers the NOT question. A dashed ellipse shows a DERIVED attribute (like Age); a multivalued attribute is drawn as a DOUBLE ellipse.
C — Wrong. This pair is correct: a double line means total participation (every entity takes part), and a single line means partial participation.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. B satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A relationship SUPPLY records which SUPPLIER supplies which PART to which PROJECT. The degree of SUPPLY is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Three entity sets (SUPPLIER, PART and PROJECT) take part in SUPPLY, so it is a ternary relationship of degree 3.
concept: The degree of a relationship type is the number of entity sets that take part in it. Degree 1: unary (recursive), e.g. EMPLOYEE supervises EMPLOYEE. Degree 2: binary, e.g. STUDENT enrols in COURSE (the most common kind). Degree 3: ternary, e.g. SUPPLIER supplies PART to PROJECT. In general, degree n gives an n-ary relationship.
why: A — Wrong. Degree 1 (unary or recursive) means only one entity set takes part, like EMPLOYEE supervises EMPLOYEE. SUPPLY involves three different entity sets.
B — Wrong. Degree 2 (binary) means two entity sets, like STUDENT enrols in COURSE. SUPPLY needs three entity sets to record one fact.
C — Correct. SUPPLIER, PART and PROJECT all take part in each SUPPLY instance, so the degree is 3 (ternary).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Degree = number of participating entity sets; cardinality ratio = 1:1, 1:N or M:N.

q: The relationship SUPERVISES links an employee who is a supervisor with the employees he supervises, and all of them come from the same EMPLOYEE entity set. Such a relationship is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When the same entity set takes part more than once in a relationship, in different roles, the relationship is recursive (unary, degree 1).
concept: In a recursive relationship (also called unary or self-referencing relationship), the same entity set takes part more than once, each time in a different role. Examples: EMPLOYEE supervises EMPLOYEE, COURSE is a prerequisite of COURSE, PERSON is married to PERSON. When mapped to tables, a 1:N recursive relationship usually becomes a foreign key in the same table, such as SupervisorID in EMPLOYEE referring to EmpID.
why: A — Wrong. A ternary relationship involves three entity sets, such as SUPPLIER–PART–PROJECT. SUPERVISES involves only one entity set, EMPLOYEE.
B — Correct. SUPERVISES relates EMPLOYEE entities to other EMPLOYEE entities, so it is a recursive (unary) relationship.
C — Wrong. An identifying relationship connects a weak entity set to its owner entity set (drawn as a double diamond). SUPERVISES connects strong EMPLOYEE entities with each other.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the recursive relationship PREREQUISITE on the COURSE entity set, one course takes part as 'course' and the other as 'prerequisite'. The labels 'course' and 'prerequisite' are called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Labels that show the part an entity plays in a relationship are role names (role indicators). None of the options names them, so the answer is E.
concept: Each entity set that takes part in a relationship plays a role in it. Role names are usually not needed when the entity sets are different, because the entity set's name already tells the role. In a recursive relationship the same entity set appears twice, so role names are needed to tell the two participations apart, e.g. 'supervisor' and 'supervisee' in SUPERVISES, or 'course' and 'prerequisite' in PREREQUISITE.
why: A — Wrong. A discriminator (partial key) is an attribute of a weak entity set that tells apart weak entities of the same owner. It has nothing to do with the part an entity plays in a relationship.
B — Wrong. A descriptive attribute is an attribute of a relationship, such as Grade in ENROLLS. 'course' and 'prerequisite' are not values stored for the relationship.
C — Wrong. A cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N) states how many entities can be associated with how many others. It does not name the part each entity plays.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. These labels are role names (role indicators). They are essential in recursive relationships, where the same entity set appears in two roles.
tip: Recursive relationship ⇒ role names are needed.

q: In the relationship ENROLLS between STUDENT and COURSE, the attribute Grade describes a particular student's result in a particular course. Such an attribute of a relationship set is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An attribute that belongs to a relationship rather than to any one entity is a descriptive attribute (Korth). Grade depends on both the student and the course.
concept: Relationship sets can have their own attributes, called descriptive attributes. Such an attribute describes the association, not either entity alone. Grade depends on which student AND which course, so it belongs to ENROLLS. Other examples: DepositDate in DEPOSITS, Hours in WORKS_ON. In a diagram the attribute's ellipse is attached to the diamond.
why: A — Correct. Grade describes the student–course association, so it is a descriptive attribute of the relationship ENROLLS.
B — Wrong. A derived attribute is computed from other values, like Age from DateOfBirth. Grade is an actual recorded fact, not a calculated one.
C — Wrong. A key attribute uniquely identifies the entities of an entity set, like RollNo. Many students can get the same grade, so Grade is not a key.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: If an attribute needs BOTH entities to make sense, it belongs to the relationship.

q:
Consider the following statements about attributes of relationship types:
I. An attribute of a 1:N relationship type can be moved to the entity type on the N-side.
II. An attribute of a 1:1 relationship type can be moved to either of the participating entity types.
III. An attribute of an M:N relationship type can be moved to either participating entity type without any loss of meaning.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Elmasri–Navathe: attributes of a 1:1 relationship can migrate to either side, and attributes of a 1:N relationship only to the N-side. An attribute of an M:N relationship depends on the combination of both entities, so it must stay with the relationship.
concept: Take WORKS_IN (1:N, one DEPARTMENT to many EMPLOYEEs) with attribute StartDate. Each employee has exactly one WORKS_IN instance, so StartDate can be stored with EMPLOYEE (the N-side). Storing it with DEPARTMENT would not work: one department has many employees with different start dates. In a 1:1 relationship each entity has at most one partner, so the attribute fits on either side. In an M:N relationship like ENROLLS(Grade), a student has many grades and a course has many grades, so Grade must stay with the relationship.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II follow Elmasri–Navathe's rules for moving relationship attributes; statement III is false.

B — Wrong. It includes statement III, which is false: an M:N attribute like Grade depends on the student–course pair and cannot be stored with either entity alone. It also leaves out the true statement II.
C — Wrong. It includes the false statement III and leaves out the true statement I.
D — Wrong. Exactly one combination of statements is correct (option A); the other options include a false statement or leave out a true one.
E — Wrong. Option A lists exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: 1:1 → either side; 1:N → N-side only; M:N → stays with the relationship.

q: In a bank, every loan must be taken by at least one customer, but a customer need not have any loan. In the ER diagram, the participation of LOAN in the relationship BORROWER is
opts: Partial participation, shown by a single line
Total participation, shown by a double line
Total participation, shown by a dashed line
More than one of the above
exp: Every LOAN entity must take part in BORROWER, so LOAN's participation is total, drawn with a double line. CUSTOMER's participation is partial (single line).
concept: Participation constraints say whether every entity must take part in a relationship. Total (mandatory) participation: every entity of the set takes part in at least one relationship instance; Chen notation draws it with a double line. Partial (optional) participation: some entities may not take part; drawn with a single line. Elmasri–Navathe also call total participation existence dependency.
why: A — Wrong. Partial participation would mean some loans have no borrower, but the rule says EVERY loan must have at least one customer. Partial participation belongs to CUSTOMER, not LOAN.
B — Correct. Every loan takes part in at least one BORROWER relationship, so LOAN's participation is total, shown by a double line.
C — Wrong. Total participation is right, but it is drawn with a double line, not a dashed line. Dashed shapes are used for derived attributes and partial keys.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Elmasri–Navathe's (min, max) notation, the line joining EMPLOYEE to the relationship WORKS_FOR is labelled (1,1), and the line joining DEPARTMENT to WORKS_FOR is labelled (4,N). Which statement is correct?
opts: Every employee works for exactly one department, and every department has at least 4 employees
Every department has exactly one employee, and every employee works for at least 4 departments
The participation of EMPLOYEE is partial and that of DEPARTMENT is total
More than one of the above
exp: A (min, max) pair next to an entity type tells how many relationship instances EACH entity of that type takes part in. EMPLOYEE (1,1): each employee is in exactly one WORKS_FOR instance. DEPARTMENT (4,N): each department is in at least 4 instances, i.e. has at least 4 employees.
concept: In (min, max) notation, the pair written on the line between entity type E and relationship R means: each entity of E takes part in at least min and at most max instances of R. min = 0 means partial participation; min ≥ 1 means total participation. This is read the OPPOSITE way to the 1 and N labels of the cardinality-ratio notation, which are written next to the other side. Korth's l..h notation is read the same way as (min, max).
why: A — Correct. (1,1) next to EMPLOYEE: each employee is in exactly one WORKS_FOR instance, i.e. one department. (4,N) next to DEPARTMENT: each department is in at least 4 instances, i.e. has at least 4 employees.

B — Wrong. This reads the labels from the wrong side, as one would in the 1:N notation. In (min, max) notation the label (1,1) next to EMPLOYEE limits each EMPLOYEE, and (4,N) next to DEPARTMENT limits each DEPARTMENT.
C — Wrong. Both minimums are at least 1 (EMPLOYEE 1, DEPARTMENT 4), so BOTH participations are total. Partial participation would need min = 0.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: (min, max) sits next to the entity it describes: 'each one of ME takes part min to max times'.

q: In crow's-foot notation, which of the following symbol–meaning pairs is NOT correct?
opts: Two short bars ( || ) — zero or many
More than one of the above
exp: Two bars mean 'one and only one' (mandatory one). 'Zero or many' is shown by a circle together with a crow's foot.
concept: Crow's-foot notation shows cardinality at the ends of the relationship line. A crow's foot means many, a bar ( | ) means one and a circle (O) means zero. Each end usually carries two marks: the mark next to the entity shows the maximum and the other one shows the minimum. So || = exactly one, O| = zero or one, |< (bar + crow's foot) = one or many, O< (circle + crow's foot) = zero or many.
why: A — Wrong. This pair is correct: the three-pronged crow's foot means 'many'. So it is not the NOT-item.
B — Wrong. This pair is correct: a circle means zero, i.e. taking part is optional.
C — Correct. This pair is wrong, so it answers the NOT question. Two bars mean 'one and only one' (minimum one, maximum one). 'Zero or many' is drawn as a circle with a crow's foot.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Entity set STUDENT has 5 entities and entity set COURSE has 3 entities. What is the maximum number of relationship instances in a binary relationship set between STUDENT and COURSE if the relationship is (i) many-to-many, (ii) many-to-one from STUDENT to COURSE, (iii) one-to-one?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: (i) Every student–course pair can appear once: 5 × 3 = 15. (ii) Each student can be linked to at most one course: 5. (iii) Each entity on both sides can appear at most once: min(5, 3) = 3.
concept: A relationship set is a set of pairs (student, course), so the same pair cannot appear twice. With no limit (M:N), every possible pair can be present: |S| × |C|. Many-to-one from STUDENT to COURSE means each student appears in at most one pair, so there are at most |S| pairs. One-to-one means each student and each course appears at most once, so there are at most min(|S|, |C|) pairs.
why: A — Wrong. For many-to-one from STUDENT to COURSE the limit is on students (each student at most one course), while a course may have many students. So the maximum is 5, not 3.
B — Correct. The maximums are 5 × 3 = 15 for M:N, 5 for many-to-one (one pair per student) and min(5, 3) = 3 for one-to-one.
C — Wrong. 8 = 5 + 3 is a common mistake for M:N. In M:N every student can be paired with every course, so the maximum is 5 × 3 = 15.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
(i) M:N: all pairs allowed -> 5 x 3 = 15
(ii) many-to-one STUDENT -> COURSE: each student in at most 1 pair -> 5 (a course may repeat)
(iii) 1:1: each student and each course in at most 1 pair -> min(5, 3) = 3
Brute force over all 2^15 subsets of pairs (verify/w1_counts.py): 15, 5, 3
tip: M:N → m × n; many-to-one → size of the 'many' side; 1:1 → the smaller of the two.

q: Which of the following business rules is NOT matched with the correct cardinality ratio?
opts: Each customer can place many orders; each order is placed by exactly one customer — one-to-many from CUSTOMER to ORDER
A student can enrol in many courses; a course can have many students — many-to-many
Each employee works in exactly one department; a department has many employees — one-to-one
More than one of the above
exp: In C one department is related to many employees while each employee is related to one department, so the ratio is one-to-many from DEPARTMENT to EMPLOYEE (many-to-one from EMPLOYEE), not one-to-one.
concept: To find a cardinality ratio, ask two questions: how many B's can one A be linked to, and how many A's can one B be linked to? If both answers are 'one' → 1:1; 'many' in one direction and 'one' in the other → 1:N (or N:1); 'many' in both directions → M:N. The ratio is about the maximum number of links, not about whether linking is compulsory (that is participation).
why: A — Wrong. This match is correct: one customer → many orders, one order → one customer, so 1:N from CUSTOMER to ORDER. So it is not the NOT-item.
B — Wrong. This match is correct: 'many' in both directions gives many-to-many.
C — Correct. This match is wrong, so it answers the NOT question. One department has MANY employees, so the ratio is 1:N from DEPARTMENT to EMPLOYEE (N:1 from EMPLOYEE to DEPARTMENT), not 1:1.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about participation constraints are correct?
opts: Total participation means every entity in the entity set must take part in at least one relationship instance
In (min, max) notation, min = 0 indicates partial participation and min ≥ 1 indicates total participation
In Chen notation, partial participation is drawn with a double line
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are correct. In Chen notation partial participation uses a single line; the double line is for total participation.
concept: Participation is about the MINIMUM: must every entity take part (total, mandatory) or may some stay out (partial, optional)? In Chen notation total participation is a double line and partial participation a single line. In (min, max) notation the min value shows it directly: min 0 = partial, min ≥ 1 = total. The cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N) is about the MAXIMUM.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is the definition of total (mandatory) participation, e.g. every loan must have a borrower.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. min = 0 allows an entity to take part in no instance (partial); min ≥ 1 forces every entity to take part (total).
C — Wrong. A double line marks TOTAL participation. Partial participation is drawn with an ordinary single line.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Participation = minimum (0 or at least 1); cardinality ratio = maximum (1 or N).

q: When an ER diagram is mapped to relational tables, a binary many-to-many relationship set is represented by
opts: Adding a foreign key to the table of either entity set
A separate table that contains the primary keys of both entity sets (as foreign keys) plus any attributes of the relationship
Merging the two entity tables into one table
More than one of the above
exp: An M:N relationship always needs its own table. Its primary key is the combination of the primary keys of the two entity sets, and its descriptive attributes (like Grade) go into the same table.
concept: Mapping rule for a binary M:N relationship R between E1 and E2: create a new table for R containing the primary key of E1 and the primary key of E2 as foreign keys, plus R's own attributes. The two foreign keys together form the primary key. A foreign key in one entity table cannot work, because one entity is related to many entities on the other side and a column can hold only one value in each row.
why: A — Wrong. A foreign key column holds only one value per row. In an M:N relationship a student has many courses AND a course has many students, so a foreign key on either side cannot hold all the links. That approach works only for 1:1 and 1:N.
B — Correct. The M:N relationship becomes its own table, e.g. ENROLLS(RollNo, CID, Grade), with (RollNo, CID) as the primary key.
C — Wrong. Merging two entity tables into one is the standard choice only for a 1:1 relationship with total participation on both sides. For M:N, merging would repeat data massively.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: M:N always gets its own table.

q: DEPARTMENT (key DeptNo) and EMPLOYEE (key EmpID) are linked by WORKS_IN: one department has many employees, and each employee works in one department. Without creating a separate table for WORKS_IN, where does the foreign key go?
opts: DeptNo is added as a foreign key in the EMPLOYEE table
EmpID is added as a foreign key in the DEPARTMENT table
DeptNo and EmpID must each be added as foreign keys to both tables
More than one of the above
exp: For a 1:N relationship, the primary key of the '1' side (DeptNo) is added as a foreign key to the table of the 'N' side (EMPLOYEE). Each employee row then holds exactly one DeptNo.
concept: Mapping rule for a binary 1:N relationship: put the primary key of the entity on the 1-side into the table of the entity on the N-side as a foreign key, together with any attributes of the relationship. Each N-side entity has at most one partner, so one column is enough. Putting the key the other way round would need many values in one cell, which the relational model does not allow.
why: A — Correct. EMPLOYEE is on the N-side, so it gets the column DeptNo as a foreign key referencing DEPARTMENT.
B — Wrong. A department has MANY employees, so a DEPARTMENT row would need many EmpID values in one column, which is not allowed (it breaks 1NF).
C — Wrong. Adding keys in both directions is unnecessary, and the DEPARTMENT side would still need many values per row. One foreign key on the N-side is enough.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 1:N → the foreign key goes to the N (many) side.

q: Entity sets E1 (key A1, attribute A2) and E2 (key B1, attribute B2) are linked by a one-to-many relationship R from E1 to E2. R has no attributes, and both participations are partial. What is the minimum number of relational tables needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: R needs no table: A1 is added to E2's table as a foreign key (it may be NULL for E2 rows that are not linked to any E1). Tables: E1(A1, A2) and E2(B1, B2, A1), i.e. 2 tables, which is not listed.
concept: For a 1:N relationship, the relationship does not need a separate table; the key of the 1-side goes into the N-side table as a foreign key. Partial participation of the N-side only means that this foreign key may be NULL. The two entity tables cannot be merged into one, because one E1 entity is linked to many E2 entities and merging would repeat E1's data.
why: A — Wrong. One table would mean merging E1 and E2. With 1:N, one E1 entity is linked to many E2 entities, so merging would repeat E1's data. Merging is used only for 1:1 with total participation on both sides.
B — Wrong. 3 = one table per entity set plus one for R. That design is allowed but it is not the MINIMUM: a 1:N relationship can be absorbed as a foreign key in the N-side table.
C — Wrong. 4 has no basis here: there are only two entity sets and one relationship, and nothing (such as a multivalued attribute) needs extra tables.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The minimum is 2 tables: E1(A1, A2) and E2(B1, B2, A1), where A1 is a foreign key that may be NULL.
work:
E1 -> table E1(A1, A2)
E2 -> table E2(B1, B2)
R is 1:N from E1 to E2 -> no table; add A1 as FK into E2 -> E2(B1, B2, A1)
FK A1 may be NULL (E2's participation is partial)
Total = 2 tables (verify/w1_er_mapping.py)
tip: Two entity sets + one relationship: 1:N or 1:1 (not both sides total) → 2 tables; 1:1 with both sides total → 1 table; M:N → 3 tables.

q:
An ER diagram has:
• STUDENT (RollNo, Name, multivalued {Phone})
• COURSE (CID, Title)
• DEPARTMENT (DeptNo, DName)
• ENROLLS: M:N between STUDENT and COURSE, with attribute Grade
• OFFERS: 1:N from DEPARTMENT to COURSE (each course is offered by exactly one department)
• SECTION: weak entity set (partial key SecNo, attribute Room) owned by COURSE through the identifying relationship HAS_SECTION
What is the minimum number of relational tables needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Tables: STUDENT, STUDENT_PHONE, COURSE (with DeptNo), DEPARTMENT, ENROLLS and SECTION = 6. OFFERS (1:N) and HAS_SECTION (identifying) need no tables of their own.
concept: Minimum-table rules: one table for each strong or weak entity set; one table for each M:N relationship; one table for each multivalued attribute; no separate table for a 1:N relationship (foreign key on the N-side), for a 1:1 relationship (foreign key on one side, or one merged table if both sides are total) or for an identifying relationship (the owner's key is already part of the weak entity's table).
why: A — Wrong. 5 forgets the separate table needed for the multivalued attribute Phone. A column can hold only one value, so phone numbers need their own table STUDENT_PHONE(RollNo, Phone).
B — Wrong. 8 gives a table to every entity set, every relationship and the multivalued attribute. That is not the minimum: OFFERS (1:N) and HAS_SECTION (identifying) need no tables.
C — Correct. STUDENT, STUDENT_PHONE, COURSE (+DeptNo), DEPARTMENT, ENROLLS and SECTION make 6 tables.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
STUDENT(RollNo, Name) -> 1
STUDENT_PHONE(RollNo, Phone) for multivalued Phone -> 2
COURSE(CID, Title, DeptNo) - OFFERS absorbed as FK DeptNo -> 3
DEPARTMENT(DeptNo, DName) -> 4
ENROLLS(RollNo, CID, Grade) for M:N -> 5
SECTION(CID, SecNo, Room) - HAS_SECTION absorbed (CID is part of the key and a FK) -> 6
Total = 6 (verify/w1_er_mapping.py; a naive one-per-item count gives 8)

q: Entity sets E1 (key A1, attribute A2) and E2 (key B1, attribute B2) are linked by a one-to-one relationship R with no attributes. The participation of both E1 and E2 in R is total. What is the minimum number of relational tables needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With 1:1 and total participation on both sides, every E1 entity is paired with exactly one E2 entity and vice versa, so E1, E2 and R can be merged into one table (A1, A2, B1, B2). The minimum is 1, which is not listed.
concept: Elmasri–Navathe give three ways to map a 1:1 relationship: (a) foreign-key approach — the key of one side becomes a foreign key in the other (2 tables); (b) merged-relation approach — merge both entity types and the relationship into ONE table, which is possible when both participations are total, because the two sets then always have the same number of entities, paired one-to-one; (c) cross-reference approach — a third table for R (3 tables). So the minimum is 1 when both sides are total, and 2 otherwise.
why: A — Wrong. 2 is the answer when at least one side is partial (foreign-key approach). With total participation on BOTH sides the tables can be merged into one, so 2 is not the minimum.
B — Wrong. 3 tables (E1, E2 and a separate table for R) is the cross-reference approach. It works but it is not the minimum.
C — Wrong. Nothing in this diagram needs 4 tables; there are only two entity sets and one relationship.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The minimum is 1 table: E1, E2 and R merge into a single table (A1, A2, B1, B2), because every E1 entity has exactly one E2 partner and vice versa.
work:
R is 1:1 and both sides are total -> each E1 entity is paired with exactly one E2 entity and vice versa
Merged-relation approach -> E1E2(A1, A2, B1, B2), primary key A1 (B1 is also a candidate key)
No NULLs needed and no data repeated
Minimum = 1 table (verify/w1_er_mapping.py)
tip: 1:1 with double lines on both sides → 1 table.

q: EMPLOYEE (key EmpID) and DEPARTMENT (key DeptNo) are linked by the 1:1 relationship MANAGES. Every department must have a manager (total participation), but most employees manage no department (partial participation). Using the foreign-key approach and avoiding NULL values in the foreign key, where should the foreign key go?
opts: DeptNo as a foreign key in the EMPLOYEE table
A separate MANAGES table is compulsory, because a foreign key cannot represent a 1:1 relationship
The manager's EmpID as a foreign key in the DEPARTMENT table
More than one of the above
exp: Put the foreign key in the table of the side with total participation: DEPARTMENT gets a column MgrEmpID. Every department has a manager, so this column is never NULL.
concept: For a 1:1 relationship, Elmasri–Navathe advise choosing the entity type with total participation to hold the foreign key. If the foreign key is placed on the partial side, most of its values would be NULL. In the MANAGES example, DEPARTMENT(DeptNo, DName, MgrEmpID) is better than adding a ManagesDeptNo column to EMPLOYEE, which would be NULL for most employees.
why: A — Wrong. Most employees manage no department, so a DeptNo column for MANAGES in EMPLOYEE would be NULL in most rows. This is allowed, but it is the poorer choice and does not avoid NULLs.
B — Wrong. A 1:1 relationship can be represented by a foreign key (the usual approach). A separate table (the cross-reference approach) is optional, not compulsory.
C — Correct. DEPARTMENT is the total side, so the column MgrEmpID in DEPARTMENT always has a value — no NULLs.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 1:1 → put the foreign key on the total-participation side.

q: When an ER diagram is mapped to relational tables using the minimum number of tables, which of the following does NOT need a separate table of its own?
opts: The identifying relationship between a weak entity set and its owner
More than one of the above
exp: The identifying relationship is already represented in the weak entity's table, whose key includes the owner's primary key. A multivalued attribute and an M:N relationship both need their own tables.
concept: Things that always get their own table: strong entity sets, weak entity sets, M:N relationships, multivalued attributes and relationships of degree more than two. Things absorbed into other tables: 1:1 and 1:N relationships (as foreign keys), identifying relationships (through the weak entity's key), composite attributes (as separate columns) and derived attributes (usually not stored at all).
why: A — Wrong. A multivalued attribute (like Phone) needs its own table, because one cell cannot hold many values. So it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. A many-to-many relationship needs its own table holding the keys of both sides; a single foreign key cannot represent it.

C — Correct. The weak entity's table already contains the owner's primary key as part of its own key (and as a foreign key), which fully represents the identifying relationship. No extra table is needed.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Entity set STUDENT has the attributes RollNo (key), Name as a composite attribute (FirstName, LastName), DateOfBirth, Age (derived from DateOfBirth, not stored) and a multivalued attribute {Phone}. After mapping to relations with the standard rules, how many columns does the STUDENT table have, and how many tables are there in total?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: STUDENT(RollNo, FirstName, LastName, DateOfBirth) has 4 columns. Phone goes into STUDENT_PHONE(RollNo, Phone). So 4 columns and 2 tables.
concept: Standard mapping of attribute types: a simple attribute becomes one column; a composite attribute is replaced by its simple components (Name → FirstName, LastName); a derived attribute is normally not stored; a multivalued attribute goes into a new table holding the entity's key and the value, and the two together form that table's primary key.
why: A — Wrong. 6 columns in 1 table stores Age and puts Phone inside the STUDENT table. A multivalued attribute cannot be a single column (one cell holds one value), and Age is not stored here.
B — Correct. STUDENT has RollNo, FirstName, LastName and DateOfBirth (4 columns), and Phone needs a second table STUDENT_PHONE(RollNo, Phone).
C — Wrong. 5 columns comes from also storing the derived attribute Age. The stem says Age is derived and not stored, so only 4 columns remain.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
RollNo -> 1 column
Name (composite) -> FirstName, LastName -> 2 columns
DateOfBirth -> 1 column
Age (derived, not stored) -> 0 columns
{Phone} (multivalued) -> separate table STUDENT_PHONE(RollNo, Phone)
STUDENT(RollNo, FirstName, LastName, DateOfBirth) = 4 columns; total tables = 2 (verify/w1_er_mapping.py)
tip: Composite → its parts as columns; multivalued → new table; derived → usually not stored.

q: Which of the following statements about the EER model is NOT correct?
opts: Specialization is a top-down process, while generalization is a bottom-up process
A subclass does not inherit the attributes of its superclass
In specialization, each subclass can have its own specific attributes and relationships
More than one of the above
exp: A subclass DOES inherit all attributes and relationships of its superclass (attribute inheritance). So B is false, which answers the NOT question.
concept: Specialization starts from one entity type and defines subclasses (top-down), e.g. EMPLOYEE → SECRETARY, ENGINEER, TECHNICIAN. Generalization starts from several entity types and finds a common superclass (bottom-up), e.g. CAR and TRUCK → VEHICLE. In both, the subclass–superclass link is an IS-A relationship (drawn in older Korth editions as a triangle labelled ISA), and each subclass inherits all attributes and relationships of its superclass while adding its own.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is correct: specialization goes from the general to the specific (top-down), and generalization from specific types to a common general type (bottom-up). So it is not the NOT-item.

B — Correct. This statement is false: a subclass inherits all the attributes and relationships of its superclass. For example, ENGINEER inherits EmpID and Name from EMPLOYEE. So it answers the NOT question.
C — Wrong. This statement is correct: a subclass may have specific attributes (e.g. TypingSpeed for SECRETARY) and specific relationships (e.g. ENGINEER belongs to a PROJECT).
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the NOT condition of the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two such options.
E — Wrong. B satisfies the NOT condition of the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Specialization = top-down (divide); generalization = bottom-up (combine).

q: In a university, the ternary relationship PROJ_GUIDE links INSTRUCTOR, STUDENT and PROJECT. Now each (instructor, student, project) combination must be linked to an EVALUATION entity. A basic ER relationship cannot connect to another relationship. Which modelling solution is the standard one?
opts: Aggregation: treat PROJ_GUIDE as a higher-level entity and relate it to EVALUATION through a new relationship
Generalization: merge INSTRUCTOR, STUDENT and PROJECT into one superclass
Specialization: split PROJ_GUIDE into subclasses, one for each evaluation
More than one of the above
exp: Aggregation treats a relationship set, together with its entity sets, as an abstract entity, so it can take part in another relationship, e.g. EVAL_FOR between PROJ_GUIDE and EVALUATION.
concept: One limitation of the basic ER model is that a relationship cannot take part in another relationship. Korth's example: PROJ_GUIDE (instructor, student, project) needs an EVALUATION. A quaternary relationship would repeat information, and a separate ternary relationship would not tie the evaluation to an actual PROJ_GUIDE combination. Aggregation solves this: draw a box around PROJ_GUIDE and its entity sets, treat the box as an entity, and connect it to EVALUATION through a new relationship EVAL_FOR.
why: A — Correct. Aggregation abstracts the relationship PROJ_GUIDE into a higher-level entity, which can then take part in the new relationship EVAL_FOR with EVALUATION.

B — Wrong. Generalization combines entity types that share features into a common superclass (for example STUDENT and INSTRUCTOR into PERSON). It does not let a relationship take part in another relationship.
C — Wrong. Specialization divides an entity type into subclasses. It applies to entity types, not to relationships, and it does not connect PROJ_GUIDE to EVALUATION.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Aggregation = a relationship treated as an entity (a box drawn around the diamond and its entity sets).

q: PERSON is specialized into EMPLOYEE and STUDENT. A teaching assistant can be an employee and a student at the same time. The constraint that allows one PERSON entity to belong to both subclasses is the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When an entity may belong to more than one subclass of a specialization, the specialization is overlapping (shown by 'o' in Elmasri–Navathe's circle).
concept: Two independent constraints apply to a specialization. Disjointness: disjoint (d) — an entity can be in at most one subclass; overlapping (o) — an entity can be in more than one subclass. Completeness: total — every superclass entity must be in at least one subclass; partial — some superclass entities may be in none.
why: A — Wrong. A disjoint constraint (shown by 'd' in the circle) says an entity can belong to at most ONE subclass, which would forbid a person from being both an employee and a student.
B — Wrong. Total completeness says every PERSON must belong to at least one subclass. It says nothing about belonging to two subclasses at once.
C — Correct. An overlapping specialization allows the same entity to be a member of several subclasses, like a teaching assistant who is both an EMPLOYEE and a STUDENT.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Disjoint/overlapping answers 'in how many subclasses at most?'; total/partial answers 'must it be in some subclass?'.

q: In a bank's EER model, ACCOUNT is specialized into SAVINGS_ACCOUNT and CURRENT_ACCOUNT. The rule is that every ACCOUNT entity must belong to at least one of these subclasses; no account may be left outside them. This constraint is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When every superclass entity must belong to at least one subclass, the specialization is total (the total completeness constraint). None of the options names it, so the answer is E.
concept: The completeness constraint of a specialization is either total or partial. Total: every entity of the superclass must be a member of at least one subclass (drawn with a double line from the superclass in Elmasri–Navathe's notation). Partial: an entity may belong to no subclass. Disjoint/overlapping is a separate constraint about how many subclasses an entity may belong to.
why: A — Wrong. Partial specialization would allow an account that is neither savings nor current. The rule forbids that, so it is the opposite of partial.

B — Wrong. Overlapping is about whether an entity may belong to MORE than one subclass. The rule here only says each account must be in AT LEAST one, which is a completeness rule, not a disjointness rule.
C — Wrong. Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity so that it can take part in another relationship. It is not a constraint on specialization.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The constraint is total specialization (the total completeness constraint): every ACCOUNT must belong to at least one subclass.
tip: Total specialization is drawn with a double line, just like total participation.

q: PERSON (attributes PID, Name, Address) is specialized into STUDENT (attribute CGPA) and FACULTY (attribute Salary). PERSON takes part in the relationship LIVES_IN with CITY. Which of the following are correct?
opts: A STUDENT entity has the attributes PID, Name, Address and CGPA
FACULTY entities can also take part in LIVES_IN, because a subclass inherits the relationships of its superclass
A FACULTY entity has the attribute CGPA
More than one of the above
exp: Subclasses inherit all attributes (A) and relationships (B) of their superclass. CGPA is specific to STUDENT, so FACULTY does not have it.
concept: Inheritance in the EER model: an entity of a subclass is the same real-world entity as in the superclass, so it has all the superclass's attributes and takes part in all its relationships, plus its own specific ones. Inheritance goes only DOWN, from a superclass to its subclasses; sibling subclasses do not share each other's specific attributes.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. STUDENT inherits PID, Name and Address from PERSON and adds its own attribute CGPA.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Relationships are inherited just like attributes: every FACULTY member is a PERSON, so a faculty member can be related to a CITY through LIVES_IN.
C — Wrong. CGPA is a specific attribute of STUDENT. FACULTY is a sibling subclass, not a subclass of STUDENT, so it does not inherit CGPA.
D — Correct. A and B are true, so more than one of A–C is correct.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Elmasri–Navathe's EER model, OWNER is a subclass of the union of PERSON, BANK and COMPANY: every owner is exactly one of a person, a bank or a company. Such a subclass, whose superclasses are different entity types, is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A subclass whose entities come from the UNION of several distinct entity types is a category (union type), drawn with a circle containing the ∪ symbol.
concept: A category (union type) is a subclass with two or more superclasses that are different entity types, and each of its entities belongs to only one of them. Example: a vehicle's OWNER can be a PERSON, a BANK or a COMPANY. An owner entity inherits only the attributes of the superclass it belongs to (selective inheritance). In contrast, a shared subclass (like ENGINEERING_MANAGER under ENGINEER and MANAGER) has entities that belong to ALL of its superclasses.
why: A — Correct. OWNER takes its members from the union of PERSON, BANK and COMPANY, with each owner belonging to just one of them. This is a category (union type).

B — Wrong. A shared subclass has several superclasses and each of its entities belongs to ALL of them (an intersection), like an engineering manager who is both an engineer and a manager. An owner belongs to only ONE of PERSON, BANK or COMPANY.
C — Wrong. Aggregation treats a relationship set as an entity so it can take part in another relationship. It has nothing to do with a subclass of several entity types.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Category = union (one of them); shared subclass = intersection (all of them).

q:
Consider the following statements about the EER model (Elmasri–Navathe):
I. A shared subclass, such as ENGINEERING_MANAGER under ENGINEER and MANAGER, inherits attributes from all its superclasses (multiple inheritance), and each of its entities belongs to all of those superclasses.
II. In a category (union type), each entity belongs to only one of the superclasses and inherits the attributes of that superclass only (selective inheritance).
III. A category always has exactly one superclass.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Statements I and II are correct. Statement III is false: a category has two or more superclasses, which are usually different entity types.
concept: Elmasri–Navathe contrast two kinds of subclass with more than one superclass. A shared subclass is an intersection: its entities belong to every superclass, and it inherits from all of them (multiple inheritance). A category (union type) is a union: each entity belongs to exactly one of the superclasses and inherits only that superclass's attributes (selective inheritance). Both need at least two superclasses; an ordinary specialization subclass has a single superclass.
why: A — Correct. Statement I describes a shared subclass correctly and statement II describes a category correctly. Statement III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes statement III, which is false: a category has two or more superclasses (e.g. PERSON, BANK and COMPANY for OWNER). It also leaves out the true statement I.
C — Wrong. It includes the false statement III and leaves out the true statement II.
D — Wrong. Exactly one combination of statements is correct (option A); the other options include a false statement or leave out a true one.
E — Wrong. Option A lists exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' is wrong.

q: A specialization can be disjoint or overlapping, and it can be total or partial. How many different combinations of these two constraints are possible?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The two constraints are independent, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 combinations: disjoint–total, disjoint–partial, overlapping–total and overlapping–partial.
concept: The disjointness constraint (disjoint or overlapping) and the completeness constraint (total or partial) are independent of each other, so Elmasri–Navathe list four possible kinds of specialization. Example: EMPLOYEE → SECRETARY, ENGINEER is disjoint–partial if an employee can hold at most one of these jobs and some employees hold neither; PERSON → EMPLOYEE, STUDENT would be overlapping–total if a person could be both and every person had to be at least one of them.
why: A — Wrong. 2 counts only one of the constraints (for example disjoint or overlapping). The completeness constraint (total or partial) is independent and doubles the count.
B — Wrong. 3 comes from wrongly thinking that one pair, such as overlapping with total, cannot occur together. All four combinations are allowed.
C — Correct. 2 disjointness options × 2 completeness options = 4 combinations, and all of them are valid.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Disjointness choices = 2 (disjoint, overlapping)
Completeness choices = 2 (total, partial)
Combinations = 2 x 2 = 4: disjoint-total, disjoint-partial, overlapping-total, overlapping-partial (verify/w1_counts.py)

q: In the relational model, the number of tuples (rows) in a relation is called its
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The number of tuples in a relation is its cardinality. The number of attributes (columns) is its degree, also called arity.
concept: A relation (table) has two sizes. Degree, also called arity, is the number of attributes (columns); it is fixed by the schema. Cardinality is the number of tuples (rows); it changes whenever rows are inserted or deleted. Example: a STUDENT table with 4 columns and 30 rows has degree 4 and cardinality 30.
why: A — Wrong. Degree is the number of attributes (columns) of a relation. It does not count rows.
B — Wrong. Arity is just another name for degree, i.e. the number of attributes. It does not count rows either.
C — Correct. Cardinality is the count of tuples (rows) in the relation.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Cardinality and Count both start with C: cardinality = count of rows. Degree = number of columns.

q: What are the degree and the cardinality of the relation STUDENT shown below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: STUDENT has 5 attributes (Roll, Name, Branch, Year, City), so its degree is 5, and 4 tuples, so its cardinality is 4.
concept: Degree counts the attributes (columns) in the heading of the relation. Cardinality counts the tuples (rows) in the body. The header row of a table is not a tuple; it only names the attributes.
why: A — Correct. 5 columns give degree 5 and 4 rows give cardinality 4.
B — Wrong. This swaps the two terms: 4 is the number of rows (cardinality) and 5 is the number of columns (degree).
C — Wrong. 20 = 5 × 4 is the number of cells (values) in the table. Cardinality counts only the rows.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT
Roll | Name | Branch | Year | City
101  | Asha | CSE    | 2    | Patna
102  | Ravi | IT     | 3    | Gaya
103  | Neha | CSE    | 2    | Patna
104  | Amit | ECE    | 1    | Ara
work:
Count the attributes (columns): Roll, Name, Branch, Year, City = 5, so degree = 5.
Count the tuples (rows): 101, 102, 103, 104 = 4, so cardinality = 4.
(The heading line is not a tuple.)

q: The set of tuples present in a relation at a particular moment of time is called the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A relation instance, also called a relation state, is the actual set of tuples stored at a given moment. It changes whenever data is inserted, deleted or updated.
concept: A relation schema such as STUDENT(Roll, Name, Branch) is the design: the relation name and its attributes. It rarely changes. A relation instance (state) is the data: the set of tuples present right now. Every INSERT, DELETE or UPDATE produces a new instance of the same schema. Think of a printed form layout (schema) and the pile of filled-in forms on a given day (instance).
why: A — Wrong. The relation schema is the structure: the relation name with its list of attributes, e.g. STUDENT(Roll, Name, Branch). It describes the table; it is not the data present at a moment.
B — Wrong. A domain is the set of allowed values for ONE attribute, for example all valid ages from 0 to 150. It is not the set of tuples stored in the relation.
C — Correct. The instance (state) is the current set of tuples; it changes as the data changes.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a property of a relation in the relational model?
opts: Every value in a cell is atomic (single and indivisible)
Two tuples of the relation may be exactly identical
The order of tuples in the relation has no significance
More than one of the above
exp: A relation is a SET of tuples, and a set cannot contain the same element twice, so identical tuples are not allowed. Options A and C are genuine properties of a relation.
concept: Because a relation is defined as a set of tuples, it has these properties: (1) no two tuples are identical; (2) the order of tuples does not matter; (3) the order of attributes does not matter when attributes are referred to by name; (4) each cell holds one atomic value; (5) attribute names within a relation are distinct. SQL tables relax property (1): they are multisets (bags), so a table without a primary key or UNIQUE constraint can hold duplicate rows.
why: A — Wrong. This IS a property of a relation: each cell holds one atomic value from the attribute's domain (this is also what first normal form demands). Since the question asks for what is NOT a property, A does not fit.
B — Correct. A relation is a set of tuples, so duplicate tuples are not allowed. This statement is false for relations, so it is NOT a property.
C — Wrong. This IS a property: a set has no order, so rows can be stored or shown in any order and it is still the same relation.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Careful: an SQL table CAN hold duplicate rows if it has no primary key or UNIQUE constraint; a relation in the formal model cannot.

q:
Consider the following statements about a relation R:
I. Successfully inserting a new tuple into R increases its cardinality by 1.
II. Adding a new attribute (column) to R increases its degree by 1.
III. Deleting a tuple from R decreases its degree by 1.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Cardinality counts tuples, so inserting a tuple raises it by 1. Degree counts attributes, so adding a column raises it by 1. Deleting a tuple changes the cardinality, not the degree, so III is false.
concept: Degree depends only on the schema (the number of attributes), so only schema changes such as ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN or DROP COLUMN change it. Cardinality depends on the instance (the number of tuples), so INSERT and DELETE change it. UPDATE changes values but neither the number of rows nor the number of columns.
why: A — Correct. I and II are true; III is false because deleting a row changes the cardinality, not the degree.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: deleting a tuple lowers the cardinality (row count), not the degree. It also leaves out I, which is true.
C — Wrong. It includes III (false) and leaves out II, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: According to the relational model, the domain of an attribute is a set of ______ values.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Elmasri–Navathe define a domain D as a set of atomic values: each value is indivisible as far as the relational model is concerned.
concept: A domain is the pool of values an attribute may take, for example 'all 10-digit mobile numbers' or 'integers from 0 to 150'. In the relational model each value of a domain is atomic: the DBMS treats it as one indivisible unit. Composite values (an address with parts) or multivalued values (a list of phone numbers) are not stored in one cell; they are split into separate attributes or separate relations. This rule is the basis of first normal form (1NF).
why: A — Correct. Domain values are atomic (indivisible).
B — Wrong. A composite value has parts, e.g. Address = Street + City + PIN. The relational model does not keep such a value in one cell; it splits it into simple attributes like Street, City and PIN.
C — Wrong. A multivalued value is a set of values, e.g. several phone numbers. The relational model stores these as separate tuples (usually in a separate relation), not in one cell.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following formal relational-model terms is correctly matched with its common table term?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three pairs are correct: a relation is shown as a table, a tuple is a row of that table, and an attribute is a column.
concept: The relational model uses formal mathematical words, while SQL and everyday speech use table words. Relation = table, tuple = row (record), attribute = column (field), domain = set of allowed values of a column, degree = number of columns, cardinality = number of rows. In practice they mean the same thing; the main difference is that a formal relation cannot contain duplicate rows, while an SQL table can.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A relation is represented as a two-dimensional table.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A tuple is one row (record) of the table.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. An attribute is one named column (field) of the table.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is TRUE for a relation in the (formal) relational model?
opts: Two attributes of the same relation may have the same name
The tuples must be kept sorted on the primary key
One cell may store a list of values, such as two phone numbers
More than one of the above
exp: All three are false: attribute names in a relation are distinct, tuples have no required order, and each cell holds a single atomic value.
concept: A relation has distinct attribute names, so each column can be referred to by name without confusion. Tuples form a set, so they have no fixed order; any sorting is only for display (ORDER BY in SQL) or storage. Each cell holds one atomic value; a list of phone numbers breaks this rule (and 1NF) and must be stored as separate tuples, usually in another relation such as PHONE(Roll, PhoneNo).
why: A — Wrong. Within one relation every attribute name must be unique, otherwise a reference like 'Name' would be ambiguous. (Two DIFFERENT relations may both have an attribute called Name.)

B — Wrong. A relation is a set of tuples, so it has no order at all. Keeping rows sorted is a storage or display choice (for example a clustered index or ORDER BY), not a rule of the relational model.
C — Wrong. Each cell must hold one atomic value. A list of phone numbers in one cell is a multivalued attribute, which the relational model (and 1NF) does not allow.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true. In a relation, attribute names are distinct, tuple order does not matter, and every cell holds exactly one atomic value.

q: A super key from which no attribute can be removed without losing the ability to identify tuples uniquely is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A candidate key is a minimal super key: it identifies every tuple uniquely, and no proper subset of it does.
concept: A super key is any set of attributes whose values differ for every tuple, e.g. {Roll} or {Roll, Name}. A super key may contain extra, unnecessary attributes. A candidate key is a super key with no extra attribute: if you remove any attribute, it is no longer unique. A relation can have several candidate keys; one of them is chosen as the primary key and the others are alternate keys.
why: A — Wrong. A foreign key is an attribute (set) in one relation that refers to a key of another (or the same) relation. Its values may repeat, so it need not identify tuples at all.
B — Correct. Candidate key = minimal super key.
C — Wrong. A surrogate key is an artificial, system-generated key (like an auto-increment number) with no business meaning. Being artificial has nothing to do with being a minimal super key.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a relation that has several candidate keys, a candidate key that is not chosen as the primary key is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Candidate keys that are not selected as the primary key are called alternate keys.
concept: All candidate keys can identify tuples uniquely. The designer picks ONE of them as the primary key (often the shortest or most stable one). The remaining candidate keys are called alternate keys. In SQL, alternate keys are usually declared UNIQUE (and NOT NULL) so that the DBMS still enforces their uniqueness. Example: in STUDENT(Roll, AadharNo, Email, Name), if Roll is the primary key, then AadharNo and Email are alternate keys.
why: A — Correct. Alternate keys = candidate keys − the primary key.
B — Wrong. A foreign key refers to a key of another (or the same) relation in order to link tables. It is not a leftover candidate key of the same relation.
C — Wrong. A surrogate key is an artificial key created by the system (e.g. an auto-number). An alternate key is a real candidate key that simply was not picked as the primary key.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about a primary key is correct?
opts: A table can have at most one primary key
No attribute that is part of the primary key may be NULL
A primary key may consist of more than one attribute
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true: a table has at most one primary key, primary-key attributes cannot be NULL (entity integrity), and a primary key can be composite.
concept: The primary key is the candidate key chosen to identify tuples. A table has at most one PRIMARY KEY constraint (declaring two gives an error in SQL). Its values must be unique, and none of its attributes may be NULL; this second rule is called entity integrity. A primary key made of two or more attributes, such as (RollNo, CourseID) in an ENROLL table, is called a composite (or concatenated) key.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A table has only one primary key, although that key may have several attributes and the table may have other candidate (alternate) keys declared UNIQUE.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is the entity integrity rule; in a composite key, every part must be non-NULL.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Such a key is called a composite key, for example (RollNo, CourseID).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 'One primary key' does not mean 'one column'. A single primary key can span several columns.

q: An artificial key, such as an auto-generated serial number with no business meaning, used to identify rows is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A surrogate key is a system-generated value (for example an AUTO_INCREMENT or IDENTITY number) used only to identify rows.
concept: A natural key comes from real-world data, such as an Aadhaar number, an email address or a vehicle number. A surrogate key is created by the DBMS, usually as a running number, and has no meaning outside the database. Surrogate keys are used when no good natural key exists, or when the natural key is long, composite or likely to change. In SQL they are made with AUTO_INCREMENT (MySQL), IDENTITY (SQL Server), SERIAL or IDENTITY (PostgreSQL), or a SEQUENCE (Oracle).
why: A — Wrong. A natural key is taken from real business data (Aadhaar number, PAN, email). It has meaning outside the database, which is the opposite of an artificial key.
B — Wrong. A foreign key links one table to a key of another table. It is not defined by being system-generated.
C — Correct. A surrogate key is an artificial, meaningless identifier generated by the system.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Natural = from real life (Aadhaar, PAN). Surrogate = made up by the system (1, 2, 3, …).

q: EMP.DeptNo is a foreign key that references DEPT.DeptNo. Which of the following statements about EMP.DeptNo is NOT true?
opts: It may contain NULL, unless it is declared NOT NULL
The same DeptNo value may appear in many EMP rows
Its values must all be different within EMP
More than one of the above
exp: A foreign key need not be unique: many employees can work in the same department, so the same DeptNo repeats. Statement C is false, so it is the NOT-true one.
concept: A foreign key only promises that each non-NULL value exists as a key value in the referenced table. It says nothing about uniqueness in the referencing table: in a one-to-many relationship (one department, many employees) the foreign key on the 'many' side repeats. A foreign key may be NULL (for example, an employee not yet assigned to any department) unless NOT NULL is also declared. Its name may also differ from the referenced column's name.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, so it does not answer a NOT question. A foreign key value may be NULL (meaning 'no department yet'); referential integrity checks only non-NULL values.
