B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: on the 'many' side of a one-to-many relationship the foreign key repeats, e.g. many EMP rows can have DeptNo = 10.
C — Correct. This statement is false. A foreign key does not have to be unique; only keys (primary key or UNIQUE) have to be unique.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In PostgreSQL, the table below is created and the four INSERT statements are run one by one. What happens?
opts: Only rows 1 and 2 are stored; the third and fourth INSERTs fail because UNIQUE allows only one NULL
Only row 1 is stored; the other INSERTs fail because a UNIQUE column cannot hold NULL
More than one of the above
exp: In PostgreSQL (and also in Oracle and MySQL) a UNIQUE column may hold any number of NULLs, because one NULL is never treated as equal to another NULL. So all four rows are inserted.
concept: A UNIQUE constraint forbids two rows with the same non-NULL value. In standard SQL, NULL means 'unknown', and two unknown values are not considered equal, so several NULLs do not violate UNIQUE. PostgreSQL, Oracle (for a single-column UNIQUE) and MySQL follow this rule. Microsoft SQL Server is the main exception: there a UNIQUE constraint allows only one NULL. (PostgreSQL 15 and later can be told to treat NULLs as equal with UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT, but that is not the default.)
why: A — Wrong. 'Only one NULL' is the rule of Microsoft SQL Server, not of PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL allow any number of NULLs in a UNIQUE column.
B — Correct. The non-NULL value 'a@x.in' appears once, and NULLs never clash with each other, so every row is accepted.
C — Wrong. UNIQUE does not imply NOT NULL. Only a PRIMARY KEY (or an explicit NOT NULL) forbids NULL.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Row 1: Email 'a@x.in' is new, accepted.
Row 2: Email NULL; NULLs are not compared as equal, accepted.
Row 3: Email NULL, still no clash, accepted.
Row 4: Email NULL, accepted.
Checked on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(Email) FROM CUST gives (4, 1).
tip: Common mistake (also in the notes): 'a unique key allows only one NULL'. That is true only in SQL Server; PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL allow many NULLs.

q:
Consider the following statements about the UNIQUE (unique key) constraint in standard SQL:
I. A table may have several UNIQUE constraints.
II. Once a value is stored in a UNIQUE column, it can never be updated.
III. A foreign key may reference a column that has a UNIQUE constraint.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and III are true. II is false: a UNIQUE value can be updated, as long as the new value does not clash with another row.
concept: UNIQUE says that no two rows may have the same non-NULL value in the column (or group of columns). A table has at most one primary key but may have many UNIQUE constraints, e.g. Email UNIQUE and Phone UNIQUE. UNIQUE values can be changed with UPDATE; the DBMS only checks that the new value is not already used. In standard SQL, REFERENCES may point to a primary key or to a UNIQUE column, because both guarantee that the referenced row is identified uniquely.
why: A — Wrong. It includes II, which is false: an UPDATE may change a UNIQUE value (a customer may change their email), as long as the new value is not a duplicate.
B — Wrong. It includes II (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
C — Correct. I and III are true and II is false.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB: a table with two UNIQUE columns is accepted; UPDATE of a UNIQUE value to a new value succeeds; FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCES p(code) works when code is UNIQUE.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'a unique key is non-updatable'. It is updatable; only duplicates are blocked.

q: A relation R(P, Q, S, T, U) has exactly two candidate keys: {P, Q} and {Q, S}. Which attributes of R are non-prime?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Prime attributes are those that belong to at least one candidate key: P, Q and S. The remaining attributes, T and U, are non-prime.
concept: An attribute is prime if it is part of ANY candidate key, and non-prime if it belongs to no candidate key. To find them, take the union of all candidate keys (these attributes are prime); every other attribute is non-prime. These terms matter in normalization, because the 2NF and 3NF rules talk about non-prime attributes.
why: A — Correct. T and U belong to no candidate key, so they are non-prime.
B — Wrong. P and S are prime: P is in the key {P, Q} and S is in the key {Q, S}. Being in just one candidate key is enough to be prime.
C — Wrong. P, Q and S are exactly the PRIME attributes (the union of the candidate keys), the opposite of what is asked.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Candidate keys: {P, Q} and {Q, S}.
Prime attributes = {P, Q} ∪ {Q, S} = {P, Q, S}.
Non-prime attributes = {P, Q, S, T, U} − {P, Q, S} = {T, U}.

q: In ENROLL below, a student can take many courses and a course has many students, but a student enrols in a given course only once. Which is the most suitable primary key of ENROLL?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: RollNo repeats (101 takes two courses) and CourseID repeats (CS01 has two students), but each (RollNo, CourseID) pair occurs only once. So the composite key (RollNo, CourseID) is the primary key.
concept: A table that records a many-to-many relationship (students and courses) cannot use either side's key alone, because each student and each course appears many times. The combination of both is unique, so it becomes a composite primary key. Each part is also a foreign key: RollNo references STUDENT and CourseID references COURSE.
why: A — Wrong. RollNo repeats: student 101 has taken CS01 and CS02. A primary key cannot have duplicate values.
B — Wrong. CourseID repeats: CS01 has students 101 and 102, so it cannot be the primary key on its own.
C — Correct. The pair is unique, and the business rule 'a student enrols in a course only once' guarantees this for all future data too.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
ENROLL
RollNo | CourseID | Grade
101    | CS01     | A
101    | CS02     | B
102    | CS01     | B
103    | CS02     | A
work:
RollNo values: 101, 101, 102, 103 → 101 repeats, so RollNo alone is not unique.
CourseID values: CS01, CS02, CS01, CS02 → repeats, not unique.
Pairs: (101, CS01), (101, CS02), (102, CS01), (103, CS02) → all different.

q:
Consider the following statements about the keys of a relation R:
I. Every candidate key of R is also a super key of R.
II. Every super key of R is also a candidate key of R.
III. The set of all attributes of R is always a super key of R.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I is true because a candidate key is a minimal super key. III is true because a relation has no duplicate tuples, so all attributes together always identify a tuple. II is false, because a super key may contain extra attributes.
concept: Super keys form a big family: every set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples. Candidate keys are the minimal members of this family. So 'candidate ⇒ super' always holds, but 'super ⇒ candidate' does not; for example {Roll, Name} is a super key but not a candidate key when {Roll} alone is a key. Since a relation is a set with no duplicate tuples, the set of all its attributes is the largest super key, and therefore every relation has at least one candidate key.
why: A — Correct. I and III are true; II is false.
B — Wrong. It includes II, which is false: {Roll, Name} is a super key but not minimal when {Roll} alone is a key, so it is not a candidate key. It also leaves out III, which is true.
C — Wrong. It includes II (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Looking only at the instance of EMP shown below, which of the following attribute sets can definitely NOT be a candidate key of EMP?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: {Dept, City} repeats (IT, Patna) in rows 1 and 4, and {Name, City} repeats (Ravi, Patna) in rows 1 and 3, so neither can be a key. {Name, Dept} has no repeat here, so this instance does not rule it out.
concept: A key must be unique in EVERY legal instance. So if even one instance shows two tuples with the same values for a set of attributes, that set is certainly not a key (not even a super key). The reverse is not true: a set that happens to be unique in one sample is not proved to be a key, because keys come from the meaning of the data (business rules), not from one sample. An instance can only rule keys out; it can never prove them.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Rows 1 and 4 both have (IT, Patna), so {Dept, City} does not identify tuples uniquely and cannot be a key.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Rows 1 and 3 both have (Ravi, Patna), so {Name, City} cannot be a key.

C — Wrong. {Name, Dept} has no duplicate in this instance, so the data does not rule it out. Whether it really is a key depends on the business rules, which a sample cannot prove; but the question asks which sets can definitely NOT be keys, and this is not one of them.
D — Correct. A and B are both correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
ID | Name  | Dept | City
1  | Ravi  | IT   | Patna
2  | Meena | HR   | Gaya
3  | Ravi  | HR   | Patna
4  | Amit  | IT   | Patna
5  | Neha  | HR   | Gaya
work:
{Dept, City}: row 1 = (IT, Patna), row 4 = (IT, Patna) → duplicate → cannot be a key.
{Name, City}: row 1 = (Ravi, Patna), row 3 = (Ravi, Patna) → duplicate → cannot be a key.
{Name, Dept}: (Ravi, IT), (Meena, HR), (Ravi, HR), (Amit, IT), (Neha, HR) → all different → not ruled out.
(Name alone and Dept alone both repeat, so {Name, Dept} is not obviously non-minimal either.)
tip: Sample data can prove that something is NOT a key, but it can never prove that something IS a key.

q: A relation has 4 candidate keys, and one of them is chosen as the primary key. How many alternate keys does the relation have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Alternate keys are the candidate keys that were not chosen as the primary key: 4 − 1 = 3.
concept: Candidate keys = primary key + alternate keys. A relation has exactly one primary key, so with k candidate keys there are k − 1 alternate keys. All of them are still unique identifiers; the primary key is simply the one chosen for referencing and indexing.
why: A — Wrong. 4 is the number of candidate keys. One of them became the primary key, so it is no longer an alternate key.
B — Correct. 4 candidate keys − 1 primary key = 3 alternate keys.
C — Wrong. 1 is the number of primary keys. The question asks for the remaining candidate keys.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Candidate keys = 4.
Primary key = 1 of them.
Alternate keys = 4 − 1 = 3.

q: In EMP below, MgrID holds the EmpID of the employee's manager. MgrID is best described as
opts: a foreign key that references the primary key of the same table
More than one of the above
exp: MgrID refers to EmpID of the same table, so it is a self-referencing (recursive) foreign key. It repeats (1 appears twice) and is NULL for the top manager, so it cannot be any kind of key.
concept: A foreign key may reference the primary key of its own table. This models a recursive (unary) relationship, such as 'employee is managed by employee' or 'course has prerequisite course'. In SQL: MgrID INT REFERENCES EMP(EmpID). The top-level employee has no manager, so his MgrID is NULL. Queries that pair employees with their managers use a self join.
why: A — Correct. MgrID is a self-referencing foreign key: its values must be EmpID values of the same table (or NULL).
B — Wrong. A candidate key must be unique, but MgrID = 1 appears twice (Meena and Amit share a manager).
C — Wrong. An alternate key is a candidate key that was not chosen as primary key, so it too must be unique. MgrID repeats and contains NULL, so it is not a key at all.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | MgrID
1     | Ravi  | NULL
2     | Meena | 1
3     | Amit  | 1
4     | Neha  | 2

q: In standard SQL, the columns named in  FOREIGN KEY (…) REFERENCES P(…)  may be which of the following in the parent table P?
opts: A column (or column set) of P declared UNIQUE
Any column of P, even one that has no PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint and contains duplicate values
More than one of the above
exp: Standard SQL lets a foreign key reference a primary key or a UNIQUE column, because both identify exactly one parent row. Referencing a column that may contain duplicates is rejected.
concept: Referential integrity means that each foreign-key value must match exactly one parent row. So the referenced columns must be guaranteed unique: a PRIMARY KEY or a UNIQUE constraint. If you try to reference an ordinary column, PostgreSQL reports 'there is no unique constraint matching given keys', and Oracle and SQL Server also refuse. (MySQL's InnoDB engine has a non-standard exception here; ignore it for exams.)
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is the usual case, e.g. EMP.DeptNo REFERENCES DEPT(DeptNo), where DeptNo is the primary key of DEPT.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A UNIQUE column (a candidate/alternate key) also identifies one parent row, so it may be referenced, e.g. REFERENCES DEPT(DeptCode) where DeptCode is UNIQUE.
C — Wrong. If the referenced column could hold duplicates, one child value could match two parent rows. Standard SQL (PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) rejects such a FOREIGN KEY.
D — Correct. A and B are both correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite: REFERENCES p(id) (primary key) and REFERENCES p(code) (UNIQUE) both work; REFERENCES p(plain) (no key constraint) is rejected with an error.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'a foreign key refers to the primary key'. It may also refer to any UNIQUE (alternate) key.

q: A relation R(A, B, C, D) has only one candidate key, {A}. How many super keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A super key must contain A; each of the other 3 attributes may be in or out, giving 2³ = 8 super keys.
concept: Every super key is a candidate key plus any extra attributes. If the only candidate key is a single attribute A in a relation of n attributes, then a super key = {A} + any subset of the other n − 1 attributes. There are 2^(n−1) such subsets, so there are 2^(n−1) super keys.
why: A — Wrong. 7 = 2³ − 1 forgets the super key {A} itself (choosing no extra attribute). A candidate key is also a super key.
B — Wrong. 16 = 2⁴ counts ALL subsets of {A, B, C, D}, including sets without A (like {B, C}) and the empty set, which are not super keys.
C — Correct. Each super key is {A} plus any subset of {B, C, D}: 2^(4−1) = 8.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
n = 4, only candidate key {A}.
Other attributes: B, C, D (3 of them); each may be included or not → 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8.
List: A, AB, AC, AD, ABC, ABD, ACD, ABCD → 8 (brute-force count in verify/w2_keys.py).

q: A relation R(A, B, C, D) has exactly three candidate keys: {A}, {B} and {C}. How many super keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: By inclusion–exclusion: 8 + 8 + 8 − 4 − 4 − 4 + 2 = 14. Quicker: of the 16 subsets, only {} and {D} contain no candidate key, so 16 − 2 = 14.
concept: A set of attributes is a super key exactly when it contains at least one candidate key. When there are several candidate keys, add the number of sets containing each key and subtract the overlaps (inclusion–exclusion). The overlap of 'contains K1' and 'contains K2' is 'contains K1 ∪ K2'. If a key K has k attributes in a relation of n attributes, exactly 2^(n−k) sets contain it. A shortcut that often works faster: count all subsets and remove those that contain no candidate key.
why: A — Correct. 14 subsets contain at least one of A, B, C, so R has 14 super keys.
B — Wrong. 24 = 8 + 8 + 8 adds the three groups but does not subtract the sets counted more than once (for example {A, B} contains both A and B and was counted twice).
C — Wrong. 15 = 2⁴ − 1 counts every non-empty subset, but {D} is not a super key because D alone is not a key.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Total subsets of {A, B, C, D} = 2⁴ = 16.
Contain A: 2³ = 8; contain B: 8; contain C: 8.
Contain A and B: 2² = 4; A and C: 4; B and C: 4.
Contain A, B and C: 2¹ = 2.
Super keys = 8 + 8 + 8 − 4 − 4 − 4 + 2 = 14.
Check: subsets with none of A, B, C are {} and {D} → 16 − 2 = 14.
tip: Shortcut: super keys = (all subsets) − (subsets that contain no candidate key).

q: A relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has exactly two candidate keys, {A} and {B}. How many super keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Sets containing A: 2⁴ = 16; containing B: 16; containing both: 2³ = 8. Super keys = 16 + 16 − 8 = 24.
concept: A set of attributes is a super key exactly when it contains at least one candidate key. When there are several candidate keys, add the number of sets containing each key and subtract the overlaps (inclusion–exclusion). The overlap of 'contains K1' and 'contains K2' is 'contains K1 ∪ K2'. If a key K has k attributes in a relation of n attributes, exactly 2^(n−k) sets contain it. For two single-attribute keys in n attributes this gives 2^(n−1) + 2^(n−1) − 2^(n−2).
why: A — Wrong. 32 = 16 + 16 forgets to subtract the 8 sets that contain both A and B, which were counted twice. (32 is also the number of all subsets of 5 attributes.)
B — Correct. 16 (with A) + 16 (with B) − 8 (with both) = 24 super keys.
C — Wrong. 16 counts only the super keys that contain A. Sets such as {B, C} contain the key {B} and are super keys too.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
n = 5.
Contain A: the other 4 attributes are free → 2⁴ = 16.
Contain B: 2⁴ = 16.
Contain both A and B (counted twice): the other 3 are free → 2³ = 8.
Total = 16 + 16 − 8 = 24.
Check: all subsets 32; subsets with neither A nor B = 2³ = 8; 32 − 8 = 24.

q: A relation R(A, B, C, D) has exactly two candidate keys, {A, B} and {B, C}. How many super keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Sets containing {A, B}: 2² = 4; containing {B, C}: 4; containing both, i.e. {A, B, C}: 2. Super keys = 4 + 4 − 2 = 6, which is not listed.
concept: A set of attributes is a super key exactly when it contains at least one candidate key. When there are several candidate keys, add the number of sets containing each key and subtract the overlaps (inclusion–exclusion). The overlap of 'contains K1' and 'contains K2' is 'contains K1 ∪ K2'. If a key K has k attributes in a relation of n attributes, exactly 2^(n−k) sets contain it. Here the two keys share B, so the overlap is the sets that contain A, B and C together.
why: A — Wrong. 8 = 4 + 4 adds the two groups without removing the 2 sets (ABC and ABCD) that contain both keys.
B — Wrong. 4 counts only the super keys containing {A, B}; it misses BC and BCD.
C — Wrong. 7 comes from subtracting only 1 for the overlap. The sets containing both keys are ABC and ABCD, so 2 must be subtracted.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. R has 6 super keys: AB, ABC, ABD, ABCD, BC, BCD (4 + 4 − 2).
work:
Contain {A, B}: C, D free → 2² = 4 (AB, ABC, ABD, ABCD).
Contain {B, C}: A, D free → 4 (BC, ABC, BCD, ABCD).
Contain both = contain {A, B, C}: D free → 2 (ABC, ABCD).
Total = 4 + 4 − 2 = 6: AB, ABC, ABD, ABCD, BC, BCD (brute force in verify/w2_keys.py).
tip: The overlap of 'contains AB' and 'contains BC' is 'contains ABC', not 'contains B'.

q: A relation R(A, B, C, D, E, F) has exactly two candidate keys, {A} and {B, C}. How many super keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Sets containing A: 2⁵ = 32; containing B and C: 2⁴ = 16; containing A, B and C: 2³ = 8. Total = 32 + 16 − 8 = 40.
concept: A set of attributes is a super key exactly when it contains at least one candidate key. When there are several candidate keys, add the number of sets containing each key and subtract the overlaps (inclusion–exclusion). The overlap of 'contains K1' and 'contains K2' is 'contains K1 ∪ K2'. If a key K has k attributes in a relation of n attributes, exactly 2^(n−k) sets contain it.
why: A — Wrong. 48 = 32 + 16 counts the 8 sets that contain both A and {B, C} twice.
B — Wrong. 32 counts only the super keys that contain A; sets like {B, C} or {B, C, D} are super keys too.
C — Correct. 32 (with A) + 16 (with B, C) − 8 (with A, B, C) = 40 super keys.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
n = 6.
Contain {A}: 5 other attributes free → 2⁵ = 32.
Contain {B, C}: 4 others free → 2⁴ = 16.
Contain {A, B, C}: 3 others free → 2³ = 8.
Super keys = 32 + 16 − 8 = 40 (brute-force count in verify/w2_keys.py also gives 40).

q: What is the maximum number of candidate keys that a relation with 5 attributes can have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: No candidate key can contain another, so the largest possible number is C(5, 2) = 10, reached when every pair of attributes is a candidate key.
concept: Candidate keys are minimal, so one candidate key can never be a subset of another. The largest family of subsets of n items in which no set contains another has C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) members (Sperner's theorem). So a relation with n attributes has at most C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) candidate keys: n = 4 gives C(4, 2) = 6, and n = 5 gives C(5, 2) = 10.
why: A — Correct. C(5, 2) = 10, achieved when every pair of attributes is a candidate key.
B — Wrong. 5 is what you get if each single attribute is a candidate key, but pairs allow more: with all 10 pairs as keys, no key contains another.
C — Wrong. 31 = 2⁵ − 1 is the number of non-empty subsets. They cannot all be candidate keys, because a candidate key must not contain a smaller key ({A} and {A, B} cannot both be candidate keys).
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
n = 5, ⌊5/2⌋ = 2.
C(5, 2) = 5! / (2! · 3!) = 10.
Example reaching 10: every pair AB, AC, AD, AE, BC, BD, BE, CD, CE, DE is a candidate key (each pair determines all attributes, no single attribute does).
A brute-force search over subset families of a 5-set confirms 10 is the maximum (verify/w2_keys.py).
tip: Max candidate keys with n attributes = C(n, ⌊n/2⌋): n = 3 → 3, n = 4 → 6, n = 5 → 10, n = 6 → 20.

q: In a relation R(A, B, C, D), every single attribute is a candidate key. How many super keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Every non-empty subset contains at least one candidate key, so the super keys are all non-empty subsets: 2⁴ − 1 = 15, which is not listed.
concept: If every attribute is itself a candidate key, then any non-empty set of attributes contains a key and is therefore a super key. Only the empty set fails. So the number of super keys is 2^n − 1.
why: A — Wrong. 16 = 2⁴ includes the empty set, which identifies nothing and is not a super key.
B — Wrong. 4 is the number of CANDIDATE keys ({A}, {B}, {C}, {D}). Their supersets such as {A, B} are super keys too.
C — Wrong. 11 = 16 − 1 − 4 counts only the subsets with two or more attributes; it leaves out the four single-attribute super keys.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. R has 15 super keys: all 2⁴ − 1 non-empty subsets of {A, B, C, D}.
work:
Every attribute alone is a key, so any set with at least one attribute is a super key.
All subsets = 2⁴ = 16; remove the empty set → 15.

q: The rule that no attribute of a primary key may hold a NULL value is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Entity integrity says that primary-key values cannot be NULL, because the primary key is what identifies each tuple (entity).
concept: Codd's two main integrity rules are: (1) Entity integrity: no primary-key attribute may be NULL, otherwise we could not tell some tuples apart or refer to them. (2) Referential integrity: a foreign-key value must either match an existing key value in the referenced relation or be NULL. Uniqueness of key values is called the key constraint, and the rule that every value must come from the attribute's domain is the domain constraint.
why: A — Wrong. Referential integrity is about foreign keys: each non-NULL foreign-key value must exist in the referenced table.
B — Correct. Entity integrity = primary key never NULL.
C — Wrong. Domain integrity (the domain constraint) says each value must belong to the attribute's domain: right data type, range and format. It does not single out primary keys.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A rule that the Age column of STUDENT may contain only whole numbers from 15 to 30 is an example of a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Restricting the type and range of values allowed in a column is a domain constraint.
concept: Domain constraints are the most basic integrity constraints: every value of an attribute must come from that attribute's domain, i.e. the correct data type, range, length or format. In SQL they are enforced with the column's data type, NOT NULL, CHECK (Age BETWEEN 15 AND 30), or CREATE DOMAIN. Entity integrity and referential integrity are about keys, not about the range of ordinary values.
why: A — Wrong. Entity integrity is only about the primary key: no part of it may be NULL. It says nothing about the allowed range of Age.
B — Wrong. Referential integrity is about foreign keys matching keys of another table. Age does not refer to any other table.
C — Correct. The rule limits the set of allowed values (the domain) of Age.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Roll is the primary key of STUDENT, and STUDENT.DeptID is a foreign key referencing DEPT. Which constraints does the INSERT below violate?
opts: Key constraint (uniqueness of the primary key)
More than one of the above
exp: Roll 2 already exists, so the key constraint is violated; DeptID 'D9' does not exist in DEPT, so referential integrity is violated. Roll is not NULL, so entity integrity is not violated.
concept: One INSERT can break several constraints at once. The key constraint needs the new primary-key value to differ from all existing ones. Entity integrity needs the primary-key value to be non-NULL. Referential integrity needs each non-NULL foreign-key value to exist in the referenced table. The DBMS rejects the row if any constraint fails (its error message reports the first failure it finds).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. STUDENT already has Roll = 2 (Ravi), so a second Roll 2 breaks the uniqueness of the primary key.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. DeptID 'D9' is not present in DEPT, so the foreign-key value has no matching parent row.
C — Wrong. Entity integrity is violated only when a primary-key value is NULL. Here Roll = 2 is not NULL.
D — Correct. A and B are both correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
DEPT
DeptID
D1
D2

STUDENT
Roll | Name | DeptID
1    | Asha | D1
2    | Ravi | D2

INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (2, 'Neha', 'D9');
work:
Key constraint: existing Roll values {1, 2}; new Roll = 2 → duplicate → violated.
Entity integrity: new Roll = 2 is not NULL → satisfied.
Referential integrity: DEPT.DeptID = {D1, D2}; new DeptID = D9 → not found → violated.
Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite: (2, 'Neha', 'D1') fails on the primary key alone; (3, 'Neha', 'D9') fails on the foreign key alone.

q: EMP.DNo is a foreign key referencing DEPT.DNo. What does referential integrity require?
opts: Every non-NULL DNo value in EMP must exist as a DNo value in DEPT
Every DNo value in DEPT must appear in at least one EMP row
All DNo values in EMP must be different from each other
More than one of the above
exp: Referential integrity requires every foreign-key value in the referencing table (EMP) to be either NULL or equal to some key value in the referenced table (DEPT).
concept: The referencing (child) table holds the foreign key; the referenced (parent) table holds the key it points to. Referential integrity means there are no 'dangling' references: a child row cannot point to a parent that does not exist. A NULL foreign key is allowed (it means 'no parent yet'). A parent row is not required to have any children; a department with no employees is fine.
why: A — Correct. Each non-NULL EMP.DNo must match an existing DEPT.DNo.
B — Wrong. This reverses the direction. A parent row need not be referenced at all: a new department with no employees breaks no rule.
C — Wrong. Foreign-key values may repeat; many employees can belong to the same department. Uniqueness is a property of keys, not of foreign keys.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'a foreign key must always refer to an existing primary key'. It may also be NULL, and it may refer to a UNIQUE key.

q: Which of the following is NOT an integrity constraint of the relational model?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Normalization is a design process (splitting tables to remove redundancy), not an integrity constraint. Entity integrity and referential integrity are constraints.
concept: Integrity constraints are rules that every valid database state must satisfy, and the DBMS checks them on INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. The main ones are domain constraints, key constraints, entity integrity (primary key never NULL), referential integrity (foreign key matches a key or is NULL), and general semantic constraints written with CHECK or assertions. Normalization is different: it is a schema-design technique (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) carried out by the designer to reduce redundancy and anomalies.
why: A — Wrong. Entity integrity IS a constraint (primary key never NULL), so it does not answer a NOT question.
B — Wrong. Referential integrity IS a constraint (foreign key matches a key or is NULL), so it does not answer a NOT question.
C — Correct. Normalization is a design process, not a rule checked on each data change.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Entity integrity means that no primary-key value may be NULL.
II. A foreign key may refer to the primary key of its own table.
III. A foreign-key column can never contain NULL.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true. III is false: a foreign key may be NULL unless it is also declared NOT NULL (or is part of a primary key).
concept: Entity integrity protects the identity of tuples (primary key not NULL). Referential integrity protects the links between tuples, and the link can even stay inside one table (e.g. EMP.MgrID → EMP.EmpID). A foreign key is allowed to be NULL to show 'no related row', e.g. the top manager has no manager. If the business rule demands a link (total participation), the designer adds NOT NULL.
why: A — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: a foreign key may be NULL. It also leaves out II, which is true.
B — Correct. I and II are true and III is false.
C — Wrong. It includes III (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The three tables below are linked by foreign keys declared ON DELETE CASCADE. How many rows in total (in all three tables together) are deleted by the DELETE statement?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Deleting DEPT 10 (1 row) cascades to EMP 1 and 2 (2 rows), which cascades to DEPENDENT 101, 102 and 103 (3 rows): 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 rows.
concept: ON DELETE CASCADE means: when a parent row is deleted, also delete the child rows that refer to it. Cascades chain: if those child rows are themselves parents of other rows with CASCADE, those rows are deleted too. So one DELETE can remove rows from many tables. Rows linked to other parents (like department 20) are not touched.
why: A — Wrong. 3 counts only DEPT 10 and the two EMP rows; it forgets that deleting those employees cascades again to DEPENDENT.
B — Wrong. 4 is the number of rows in DEPENDENT before the delete. Dependent 104 belongs to employee 3 of department 20, so it is not deleted.
C — Correct. 1 (DEPT) + 2 (EMP) + 3 (DEPENDENT) = 6 rows.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
DEPT(DNo PK)
DNo
10
20

EMP(EID PK, DNo REFERENCES DEPT(DNo) ON DELETE CASCADE)
EID | DNo
1   | 10
2   | 10
3   | 20

DEPENDENT(DID PK, EID REFERENCES EMP(EID) ON DELETE CASCADE)
DID | EID
101 | 1
102 | 1
103 | 2
104 | 3

DELETE FROM DEPT WHERE DNo = 10;
work:
Step 1: DEPT row 10 deleted → 1 row.
Step 2: ON DELETE CASCADE on EMP.DNo → EMP rows with DNo 10 (EID 1, 2) deleted → 2 rows.
Step 3: ON DELETE CASCADE on DEPENDENT.EID → rows with EID 1 or 2 (DID 101, 102, 103) deleted → 3 rows.
Total = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Left: DEPT {20}, EMP {3}, DEPENDENT {104}.
Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite (foreign keys ON).

q: EMP.DNo references DEPT with ON DELETE SET NULL. After the DELETE statement below, how many rows of EMP have NULL in DNo?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Employees 1 and 3 were in D1, so their DNo becomes NULL; employee 4 already had NULL. That makes 3 rows with NULL, and EMP still has all 4 rows.
concept: ON DELETE SET NULL: when a parent row is deleted, the child rows stay, but their foreign key is set to NULL (so the column must allow NULL). The referential actions are CASCADE (delete or update the child rows too), SET NULL (keep the child rows, set their foreign key to NULL), SET DEFAULT (set the foreign key to the column's default value), and RESTRICT / NO ACTION (reject the change). Only CASCADE removes child rows.
why: A — Correct. Rows 1 and 3 become NULL and row 4 was already NULL: 3 rows.
B — Wrong. 2 counts only the rows changed by the delete (EID 1 and 3) and forgets EID 4, which was NULL already.
C — Wrong. 0 would be true only if the child rows were deleted (CASCADE) or the delete were rejected (NO ACTION). SET NULL keeps the rows and blanks out the foreign key.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
DEPT
DNo
D1
D2
D3

EMP  (DNo REFERENCES DEPT(DNo) ON DELETE SET NULL)
EID | DNo
1   | D1
2   | D2
3   | D1
4   | NULL

DELETE FROM DEPT WHERE DNo = 'D1';
work:
Rows referencing D1: EID 1 and EID 3 → DNo set to NULL (rows kept).
EID 2 (D2) unchanged; EID 4 was already NULL.
Rows with NULL DNo: 1, 3, 4 → 3.
Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite: COUNT(*) = 4, rows with NULL DNo = 3.

q: EMP.DNo is a foreign key referencing DEPT.DNo, with no ON DELETE or ON UPDATE action specified. Which of the following operations can violate this referential integrity constraint?
opts: Inserting an EMP row whose DNo does not exist in DEPT
Deleting a DEPT row whose DNo is used by some EMP rows
Updating an EMP row's DNo to a value that does not exist in DEPT
More than one of the above
exp: All three can create a dangling reference: inserting or updating a child row with a missing parent value, or deleting a parent row that still has children.
concept: Referential integrity can be broken from both sides. On the child (referencing) side: an INSERT of a row with an unknown foreign-key value, or an UPDATE of the foreign key to an unknown value. On the parent (referenced) side: a DELETE of a referenced row, or an UPDATE of a referenced key value. With no ON DELETE / ON UPDATE action, the DBMS simply rejects such operations (NO ACTION). Deleting a child row or inserting a parent row can never break it.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The new child row would point to a department that does not exist.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The EMP rows using this DNo would be left pointing to nothing; with no action specified, the DBMS rejects the delete.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Changing the foreign key to a missing value creates a dangling reference, just like a bad insert.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite (foreign keys ON): each of the three operations is rejected with a foreign-key error.

q: Consider only the foreign key EMP.DNo → DEPT.DNo. Which operation can NEVER violate this referential integrity constraint?
opts: Updating the DNo of a DEPT row
More than one of the above
exp: Deleting a child (EMP) row only removes a reference; it cannot leave any foreign key pointing to a missing row. The other two operations can create dangling references.
concept: For one foreign key, operations that remove references or add parents are always safe: deleting a child row and inserting a parent row. Operations that add references or remove parents may break it: inserting a child row, updating a child's foreign key, deleting a parent row, or updating a parent's key value.
why: A — Wrong. If some EMP rows use that DNo, changing it in DEPT leaves them pointing to an old value that no longer exists (unless ON UPDATE CASCADE is declared).
B — Correct. Removing a child row cannot create a dangling reference.
C — Wrong. A new EMP row whose DNo is not in DEPT breaks referential integrity, so such an insert is rejected.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite: DELETE FROM EMP succeeds; UPDATE of a referenced DEPT key and INSERT of an EMP row with a missing DNo both raise foreign-key errors.

q: In standard SQL (for example PostgreSQL), the foreign key below is declared without any ON DELETE clause. What happens when the DELETE statement is run?
opts: DEPT row 10 is deleted, and EMP row 1 is deleted with it
The DELETE is rejected with an error, and both tables stay unchanged
DEPT row 10 is deleted, and EMP row 1 gets NULL in DNo
More than one of the above
exp: Without an ON DELETE clause the default action is NO ACTION, so deleting a parent row that is still referenced is rejected.
concept: The referential actions are CASCADE (delete or update the child rows too), SET NULL (keep the child rows, set their foreign key to NULL), SET DEFAULT (set the foreign key to the column's default value), and RESTRICT / NO ACTION (reject the change). If no action is written, the SQL-standard default is NO ACTION: the statement fails if it would leave a child row without a parent. RESTRICT behaves almost the same (it checks at once instead of at the end of the statement).
why: A — Wrong. Deleting the child rows automatically happens only with ON DELETE CASCADE, which must be written explicitly.
B — Correct. The default NO ACTION rejects the delete because EMP row 1 still refers to DEPT 10.
C — Wrong. Setting the foreign key to NULL happens only with ON DELETE SET NULL, which must be written explicitly.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
DEPT row 10 is referenced by EMP row 1.
No ON DELETE clause → default NO ACTION → the delete would leave a dangling reference → error.
PostgreSQL 16: 'update or delete on table "dept" violates foreign key constraint'. SQLite (foreign keys ON) also raises an error.
(Deleting DNo = 20, which nobody references, succeeds.)
tip: No ON DELETE clause = NO ACTION = you cannot delete a parent that still has children.

q: In PostgreSQL, the two statements below are run in order. What are the DNo values of EMP rows 1, 2, 3 and 4 afterwards?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The UPDATE cascades 20 → 40 to EMP rows 2 and 3 (ON UPDATE CASCADE), and the DELETE sets row 1's DNo to NULL (ON DELETE SET NULL). The result NULL, 40, 40, 30 is not listed.
concept: ON DELETE and ON UPDATE are separate choices for the same foreign key. ON UPDATE CASCADE copies a changed parent key value into all child rows that used the old value. ON DELETE SET NULL keeps the child rows but sets their foreign key to NULL. (Oracle supports ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL but has no ON UPDATE clause at all, which is why this question names PostgreSQL.)
why: A — Wrong. This ignores ON UPDATE CASCADE: when DEPT 20 became 40, the matching EMP rows 2 and 3 were changed to 40 as well.
B — Wrong. This ignores ON DELETE SET NULL: after DEPT 10 is deleted, EMP row 1 cannot keep 10; its DNo becomes NULL.
C — Wrong. Deleting the child row would happen with ON DELETE CASCADE, but here the delete action is SET NULL, so row 1 stays with DNo NULL.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. The values are NULL, 40, 40, 30: the update cascades 20 → 40 to rows 2 and 3, and the delete sets row 1's DNo to NULL.
code:
DEPT
DNo
10
20
30

EMP  (DNo REFERENCES DEPT(DNo)
        ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE)
EID | DNo
1   | 10
2   | 20
3   | 20
4   | 30

UPDATE DEPT SET DNo = 40 WHERE DNo = 20;
DELETE FROM DEPT WHERE DNo = 10;
work:
UPDATE DEPT 20 → 40: ON UPDATE CASCADE changes EMP rows 2 and 3 from 20 to 40.
DELETE DEPT 10: ON DELETE SET NULL sets EMP row 1's DNo to NULL (the row is kept).
Row 4 (30) is untouched.
Result: 1 → NULL, 2 → 40, 3 → 40, 4 → 30; DEPT = {30, 40}.
Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and SQLite.

q: In SQL's three-valued logic, what is the value of  FALSE AND UNKNOWN ?
opts: An error, because AND cannot take UNKNOWN
More than one of the above
exp: AND is true only if both sides are true. Since one side is already FALSE, the result is FALSE whatever the unknown value is. FALSE is not among A–C.
concept: SQL uses three truth values: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL (=, <>, <, >, even x = x) gives UNKNOWN. Think of UNKNOWN as 'could be true or could be false'. AND: FALSE wins (FALSE AND anything = FALSE; TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN). OR: TRUE wins (TRUE OR anything = TRUE; FALSE OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN). NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause keeps a row only when its condition is TRUE.
why: A — Wrong. AND can be TRUE only when both sides are TRUE, and one side here is FALSE.

B — Wrong. If the unknown side were TRUE, FALSE AND TRUE = FALSE; if it were FALSE, FALSE AND FALSE = FALSE. Both cases give FALSE, so the result is FALSE, not UNKNOWN. (It is TRUE AND UNKNOWN that gives UNKNOWN.)
C — Wrong. UNKNOWN is a normal truth value in SQL's three-valued logic; AND, OR and NOT are all defined for it.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE, because AND with a FALSE side is always FALSE.
work:
Try both possibilities for UNKNOWN: FALSE AND TRUE = FALSE; FALSE AND FALSE = FALSE.
Both give FALSE, so FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE.
Checked on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB with x NULL: (1 = 0) AND (x > 5) is FALSE.
tip: Trick: replace UNKNOWN by TRUE and then by FALSE. If both give the same answer, that is the result; if not, the result is UNKNOWN.

q:
Column x of a row is NULL. What is the value of the following SQL condition for that row?
(x > 5) OR (1 = 1 AND NOT (x = x))
opts: More than one of the above
exp: x > 5 is UNKNOWN; x = x is also UNKNOWN (NULL is not equal even to itself), so NOT (x = x) is UNKNOWN; TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN; UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN.
concept: SQL uses three truth values: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL (=, <>, <, >, even x = x) gives UNKNOWN. Think of UNKNOWN as 'could be true or could be false'. AND: FALSE wins (FALSE AND anything = FALSE; TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN). OR: TRUE wins (TRUE OR anything = TRUE; FALSE OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN). NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause keeps a row only when its condition is TRUE. So in a WHERE clause, a row for which this condition is UNKNOWN is not returned.
why: A — Wrong. OR gives TRUE only if one side is TRUE, but both sides here are UNKNOWN. (Many students think x = x must be TRUE, but with NULL it is UNKNOWN.)
B — Correct. Every part that touches x is UNKNOWN, and no FALSE in an AND or TRUE in an OR settles the answer.
C — Wrong. OR gives FALSE only when both sides are FALSE. Neither side is FALSE here.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
x > 5 → NULL > 5 → UNKNOWN.
x = x → NULL = NULL → UNKNOWN; NOT UNKNOWN → UNKNOWN.
1 = 1 → TRUE; TRUE AND UNKNOWN → UNKNOWN.
UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN → UNKNOWN.
Checked on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB: the expression returns NULL (unknown).

q:
Consider the following statements about NULL in SQL:
I. The expression 5 + NULL evaluates to NULL.
II. The condition Sal IS NULL is true for a row whose Sal value is NULL, even if the other columns of that row have values.
III. The comparison NULL = NULL evaluates to TRUE.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, so I is true. IS NULL tests one column's value, not the whole row, so II is true. NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so III is false.
concept: NULL means 'value missing or unknown'. Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 5 + NULL, or Sal * 1.1 when Sal is NULL. Any comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN, including NULL = NULL. To test for NULL you must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; these look at the value of the given column (or expression) in that row. A row as a whole is never 'NULL'.
why: A — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN. It also leaves out II, which is true.
B — Correct. I and II are true and III is false.
C — Wrong. It includes III (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB: SELECT 5 + NULL gives NULL; SELECT NULL = NULL gives NULL (unknown), not TRUE.
For rows (a, b) = (1, NULL) and (NULL, NULL), WHERE b IS NULL returns both rows.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'IS NULL is true if the row is NULL'. IS NULL checks a column's value in that row.

q: What does the query below return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Rows with NULL Sal make both comparisons UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. So only P, R and T are counted: the answer 3 is not listed.
concept: In two-valued logic, 'Sal > 4000 OR Sal <= 4000' would be always true (a tautology). In SQL's three-valued logic it is UNKNOWN when Sal is NULL, because UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only rows whose condition is TRUE, so rows with NULL Sal are silently filtered out. To include them you must add OR Sal IS NULL.
why: A — Wrong. 5 assumes the condition is always true, as in two-valued logic. For the two NULL salaries both comparisons are UNKNOWN, so those rows are dropped.
B — Wrong. 2 counts only the rows with Sal > 4000 (R and T); P also satisfies Sal <= 4000.
C — Wrong. 0 would need every row to fail, but P, R and T have real salaries and each satisfies one side of the OR.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. The query returns 3 (rows P, R and T); the two rows with NULL Sal give UNKNOWN and are not counted.
code:
EMP
Name | Sal
P    | 3000
Q    | NULL
R    | 7000
S    | NULL
T    | 5000

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMP
WHERE Sal > 4000 OR Sal <= 4000;
work:
P: 3000 > 4000 is FALSE, 3000 <= 4000 is TRUE → TRUE, counted.
Q: NULL → UNKNOWN OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN → not counted.
R: 7000 > 4000 is TRUE → counted.
S: NULL → UNKNOWN → not counted.
T: 5000 > 4000 is TRUE → counted.
COUNT(*) = 3 (PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB all return 3).
tip: A condition that seems to 'cover all values' still misses NULLs. Add OR col IS NULL if you want them.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the fundamental (basic) operations of relational algebra?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The six fundamental operations are σ, π, ρ, ∪, − and ×. Natural join is a derived operation, built from ×, σ and π.
concept: Relational algebra has six fundamental (basic) operations: selection σ (pick rows), projection π (pick columns), rename ρ, union ∪, set difference − and Cartesian product × (a few books list only five and treat rename separately). Every other operation (intersection ∩, the joins, division ÷, assignment ←) can be written using these six, so they are called derived (additional) operations; they make queries shorter but add no new power.
why: A — Wrong. Set difference IS fundamental; it cannot be built from the other basic operations. So it does not answer a NOT question.
B — Correct. Natural join = π(σ(R × S)), so it is a derived operation, not a fundamental one.
C — Wrong. Cartesian product IS fundamental: it is the only basic operation that pairs the tuples of two relations side by side, and every join is built from it. So it does not answer a NOT question.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Basic six: σ, π, ρ, ∪, −, ×. Everything else is derived.

q: Which of the following relational algebra operations is unary, i.e. works on a single relation?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Selection, projection and rename each take one relation as input, so all three are unary operations.
concept: A unary operation takes one relation: σ_condition(R), π_attribute-list(R), ρ_newname(R). A binary operation takes two relations: R ∪ S, R − S, R × S, R ∩ S, R ⋈ S, R ÷ S. The result of every operation is again a relation, so operations can be nested inside each other.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. σ_c(R) picks rows from one relation R.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. π_list(R) picks columns from one relation R.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. ρ_x(R) gives a new name to one relation (or to its attributes).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which expression is always equal to R ∩ S (R and S union-compatible)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: R − S is the part of R that is not in S; removing that part from R leaves exactly the tuples of R that are also in S, i.e. R ∩ S.
concept: Intersection is a derived operation because it can be written with set difference: R ∩ S = R − (R − S) = S − (S − R). Example: R = {1, 2, 3} and S = {2, 3, 4}. Then R − S = {1}, and R − {1} = {2, 3}, which is R ∩ S.
why: A — Correct. Taking away 'what is only in R' from R leaves 'what is in both'.
B — Wrong. R − S is already part of R, so R ∪ (R − S) is just R. With R = {1, 2, 3}, S = {2, 3, 4} it gives {1, 2, 3}, not {2, 3}.
C — Wrong. (R − S) ∪ (S − R) is the symmetric difference: tuples that are in exactly one of the two relations. In the example it is {1, 4}, the opposite of the intersection.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Example R = {1, 2, 3}, S = {2, 3, 4}:
R − (R − S) = {1, 2, 3} − {1} = {2, 3} = R ∩ S.
R ∪ (R − S) = {1, 2, 3}.
(R − S) ∪ (S − R) = {1, 4}.
Option A also equals R ∩ S on 500 random pairs (verify/w2_ra.py).

q:
Consider the following statements about joins in relational algebra:
I. The theta join R ⋈θ S is equal to σθ(R × S).
II. Adding join operations to relational algebra lets it express queries that could not be expressed before.
III. A natural join can be written using Cartesian product, selection and projection (with renaming).
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and III are true: joins are defined from ×, σ and π. Because of this, joins are only shorthand and add no new expressive power, so II is false.
concept: A theta join is a Cartesian product followed by a selection: R ⋈θ S = σθ(R × S). A natural join also equates all common attributes and keeps one copy of each: R ⋈ S = π_list(σ_R.B=S.B(R × S)). Since joins can be rewritten with the six basic operations, they are derived operations. They make queries shorter and let the DBMS evaluate them faster, but they do not let you ask any new question.
why: A — Wrong. It includes II, which is false (joins are only shorthand), and it leaves out III, which is true.
B — Wrong. It includes II (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
C — Correct. I and III are true; II is false.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In relational algebra, which operation is written with the symbol ← , as in  Temp ← π_DNo(EMP) ?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The ← operator is assignment: it stores the result of the expression on the right in a temporary relation variable named on the left.
concept: Assignment (←) lets a long query be written in steps, like variables in a program: Temp1 ← σ_Sal>5000(EMP); Result ← π_Name(Temp1). It does not change the stored database and adds no new power; it only makes queries easier to read. Rename (ρ) is a different operator: it gives a new name to a relation or to its attributes inside an expression, written ρ_x(E) or ρ_x(A1, …, An)(E).
why: A — Wrong. Rename uses the Greek letter ρ (rho), e.g. ρ_Temp(π_DNo(EMP)). It is written differently, even though both give a name to a result.
B — Correct. ← is the assignment operation.
C — Wrong. Division uses the symbol ÷ and answers 'for all' queries, such as students who took every required course.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is always true for a relation R, an attribute A of R, and selection conditions c1 and c2 on R?
opts: π_A(R) always has the same number of tuples as R
More than one of the above
exp: Selection is commutative (A), and a selection with AND can be split into a cascade of two selections (B). C is false, because projection removes duplicate tuples and can return fewer tuples than R.
concept: Selection only filters rows, so the order of two filters does not matter (commutativity), and one filter with AND equals two filters one after the other (cascade). Query optimizers use these rules to apply cheap or very selective conditions first. Projection is different: it keeps only some columns and then removes duplicate tuples, so |π_A(R)| ≤ |R|. It equals |R| only when the projected values happen to be all distinct, e.g. when A is a key.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Applying two filters in either order keeps exactly the rows that satisfy both; selection is commutative.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is the cascade (splitting) rule: a selection with AND equals one selection applied after the other.
C — Wrong. Projection removes duplicate tuples. If R has 6 employees in 3 departments, π_Dept(R) has only 3 tuples.
D — Correct. A and B are both correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked on 300 random relations (verify/w2_ra.py): A and B always hold.
Counter-example for C: EMP with 6 tuples and Dept values IT, HR, IT, Sales, HR, IT → π_Dept(EMP) has 3 tuples.

q: R and S are union-compatible relations with attributes (A, B, C), and c is a condition on A. Which of the following is NOT a valid relational algebra equivalence?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: π_A(R) has only the attribute A, so a later projection on A and B is impossible: B no longer exists. The other two are standard valid rules.
concept: Cascade of projections: π_L1(π_L2(R)) = π_L1(R) is valid only when L1 ⊆ L2, i.e. the outer list is contained in the inner list. Selection distributes over union (and also over intersection and difference): σ_c(R ∪ S) = σ_c(R) ∪ σ_c(S). Query optimizers use such rules to push selections down and to drop unneeded columns early.
why: A — Wrong. This IS valid: {A} ⊆ {A, B}, so projecting on A, B and then on A is the same as projecting on A directly.
B — Wrong. This IS valid: a tuple of R ∪ S satisfies c exactly when it is a tuple of R or of S that satisfies c.
C — Correct. This is invalid: after π_A only attribute A remains, so π_A,B cannot be applied.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked on 300 random relations (verify/w2_ra.py): A and B always hold; evaluating π_A,B on the result of π_A fails because B is missing.

q: How many tuples (rows) are produced by (i) the relational algebra expression and (ii) the SQL query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Relational algebra works on sets, so π_Dept removes duplicates and gives IT, HR, Sales = 3 tuples. SQL keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is written, so SELECT Dept returns all 6 rows.
concept: Relational algebra uses set semantics: a relation never contains duplicate tuples, so π removes them automatically. SQL uses bag (multiset) semantics for speed: removing duplicates needs sorting or hashing, so SQL does it only when asked with DISTINCT. Therefore π_list(R) corresponds to SELECT DISTINCT list FROM R.
why: A — Correct. π gives 3 distinct departments; plain SQL SELECT gives all 6 rows.
B — Wrong. 6 is right for SQL, but relational algebra projection removes duplicate tuples, so (i) gives only 3.
C — Wrong. 3 is right for π, but SQL's SELECT without DISTINCT keeps duplicate rows, so (ii) gives 6.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EID | Name  | Dept
1   | Ravi  | IT
2   | Meena | HR
3   | Amit  | IT
4   | Neha  | Sales
5   | Raj   | HR
6   | Asha  | IT

(i)  π_Dept(EMP)              -- relational algebra
(ii) SELECT Dept FROM EMP;    -- SQL
work:
Dept column: IT, HR, IT, Sales, HR, IT.
(i) π removes duplicates → {IT, HR, Sales} → 3 tuples.
(ii) SQL SELECT keeps duplicates → 6 rows.
SELECT DISTINCT Dept would give 3 (checked on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB).
tip: π = SELECT DISTINCT. Plain SELECT keeps duplicates.

q:
Which relational algebra expression is equivalent to the SQL query
SELECT DISTINCT Name FROM EMP WHERE Sal > 5000; ?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The WHERE clause filters rows, which is selection σ_Sal>5000; the SELECT list chooses columns, which is projection π_Name. So the query is π_Name(σ_Sal>5000(EMP)).
concept: A basic SQL query SELECT A1, …, An FROM R1, …, Rm WHERE P corresponds to π_A1,…,An(σ_P(R1 × … × Rm)). The FROM clause gives a Cartesian product, WHERE is selection σ, and the SELECT list is projection π (exactly π when DISTINCT is used). Note the naming trap: relational algebra's 'select' operation σ corresponds to SQL's WHERE clause, not to SQL's SELECT keyword.
why: A — Wrong. The operators are swapped: σ needs a condition and π needs a list of attributes. 'σ_Name' has no condition and 'π_Sal>5000' is not an attribute list.
B — Correct. First select the rows (σ), then project the column (π).
C — Wrong. The Cartesian product pairs every high-salary employee tuple with every name, producing extra attributes and wrong tuples. The query needs only a filter followed by a projection.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'SELECT is the same as projection'. Only the SELECT list does projection π (and keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is used); the WHERE clause does selection σ, which relational algebra confusingly calls 'select'.

q: For the union R ∪ S to be a valid relational algebra operation, which of the following conditions must hold?
opts: R and S must have the same number of attributes
For every i, the i-th attribute of R and the i-th attribute of S must have the same (compatible) domain
R and S must have the same number of tuples
More than one of the above
exp: Union compatibility needs the same degree and compatible domains for corresponding attributes. The number of tuples does not matter.
concept: Union (∪), intersection (∩) and set difference (−) work only on union-compatible (type-compatible) relations: both must have the same degree (number of attributes), and the i-th attributes of both must have the same domain. The result takes the attribute names of the first relation. The number of tuples can be anything, even zero. Cartesian product and joins do not need union compatibility.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Both relations must have the same degree; otherwise their tuples cannot be compared or merged.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Corresponding attributes must come from the same domain; you cannot unite a column of names with a column of salaries.
C — Wrong. The number of tuples may differ; a 5-tuple relation can be united with a 2-tuple relation.
D — Correct. A and B are both correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: R and S are union-compatible relations with 8 and 5 tuples respectively. What are the minimum and maximum possible numbers of tuples in R ∪ S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: R ∪ S contains all of R, so it has at least 8 tuples (when every tuple of S is already in R) and at most 8 + 5 = 13 tuples (when R and S share nothing).
concept: Union removes duplicates (set semantics), so the shared tuples are counted once. For union-compatible R and S with m and n tuples (set semantics): |R ∪ S| = m + n − |R ∩ S|, so it lies between max(m, n) and m + n; |R ∩ S| lies between 0 and min(m, n); |R − S| lies between max(0, m − n) and m.
why: A — Wrong. The union can never be smaller than the bigger relation; all 8 tuples of R are always in R ∪ S, so the minimum is 8, not 5.
B — Correct. Minimum max(8, 5) = 8 and maximum 8 + 5 = 13.
C — Wrong. The union of two non-empty relations is never empty; at least the 8 tuples of R are in it.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Maximum: no common tuples → 8 + 5 = 13.
Minimum: S ⊆ R → |R ∪ S| = |R| = 8.
Brute force over every 5-tuple S with a fixed 8-tuple R confirms the range 8 to 13 (verify/w2_ra.py).
tip: ∪: max(m, n) to m + n. ∩: 0 to min(m, n). R − S: max(0, m − n) to m.

q: R and S are union-compatible relations with 8 and 5 tuples respectively. What is the possible range of the number of tuples in R − S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: At most all 5 tuples of S can be removed from R, so R − S has at least 8 − 5 = 3 tuples; if nothing is shared it keeps all 8. The range 3 to 8 is not listed.
concept: R − S removes from R the tuples that also appear in S. At most |S| tuples can be removed, so |R − S| ≥ |R| − |S| (and never below 0); at best nothing is removed, so |R − S| ≤ |R|. For union-compatible R and S with m and n tuples (set semantics): |R ∪ S| = m + n − |R ∩ S|, so it lies between max(m, n) and m + n; |R ∩ S| lies between 0 and min(m, n); |R − S| lies between max(0, m − n) and m.
why: A — Wrong. The maximum 8 is right, but the result can never be 0: S has only 5 tuples, so at most 5 of R's 8 tuples can be removed.
B — Wrong. The maximum is 8, not 5: if R and S have nothing in common, R − S is all of R.
C — Wrong. Both ends are wrong. The result can never be 0, because at most 5 of R's 8 tuples can be removed. And 3 is the SMALLEST possible size (when S ⊆ R), not the largest; the largest is 8.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. |R − S| can be anything from 3 (all of S inside R) to 8 (no common tuples).
work:
R − S keeps the tuples of R that are not in S.
Maximum: no tuple of S is in R → nothing removed → 8.
Minimum: all 5 tuples of S are in R → 5 removed → 8 − 5 = 3.
Range 3 to 8 (brute force in verify/w2_ra.py).

q: Which of the following binary relational algebra operations is NOT commutative?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: R − S (tuples of R not in S) is in general different from S − R (tuples of S not in R), so set difference is not commutative. Union and intersection are commutative.
concept: An operation is commutative if swapping the operands does not change the result. R ∪ S = S ∪ R and R ∩ S = S ∩ R. But with R = {1, 2, 3} and S = {2, 3, 4}: R − S = {1}, while S − R = {4}. (Natural join is also commutative, apart from the order of columns.)
why: A — Wrong. Union IS commutative: R ∪ S and S ∪ R contain the same tuples.
B — Wrong. Intersection IS commutative: the common tuples are the same whichever relation is written first.
C — Correct. R − S ≠ S − R in general, e.g. {1} versus {4} in the example.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many tuples are in the result of the expression below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: π_L_Name(STUDENT) = {Clay, Shay, Stark, Noah, Singh}; π_L_Name(EMPLOYEE) = {Singh, Sinha, Stark, Gupta}. Their union, without duplicates, is {Clay, Shay, Stark, Noah, Singh, Sinha, Gupta}: 7 tuples.
concept: Union keeps every tuple that is in either relation, but each distinct tuple only once. Since π also removes duplicates, first find each projection as a set, then combine them and drop repeats: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.
why: A — Wrong. 10 = 5 + 5 is what SQL's UNION ALL would return (keeping duplicates). Relational algebra union removes duplicates.
B — Wrong. 5 counts only the student last names; the union must also include the employee-only names Sinha and Gupta.
C — Correct. 5 + 4 − 2 = 7 distinct last names.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT
Enrol | F_Name | L_Name
101   | John   | Clay
102   | Minty  | Shay
103   | Clark  | Stark
104   | Shon   | Noah
105   | Vicky  | Singh

EMPLOYEE
Emp_id | F_Name | L_Name
E001   | Ravi   | Singh
E002   | Manoj  | Sinha
E003   | Bella  | Stark
E004   | Sunny  | Gupta
E005   | Sarry  | Singh

π_L_Name(STUDENT) ∪ π_L_Name(EMPLOYEE)
work:
π_L_Name(STUDENT) = {Clay, Shay, Stark, Noah, Singh} → 5.
π_L_Name(EMPLOYEE) = {Singh, Sinha, Stark, Gupta} → 4 (Singh appears twice but is kept once).
Common names: Stark, Singh.
Union = 5 + 4 − 2 = 7: Clay, Shay, Stark, Noah, Singh, Sinha, Gupta.
SQL check: UNION gives 7 rows, UNION ALL gives 10 (PostgreSQL 16, SQLite, DuckDB).
tip: Common mistake: the union example in the notes lists only the student surnames. A union must include the names from BOTH relations.

q: Relation R has 3 attributes and 4 tuples; relation S has 2 attributes and 5 tuples. What are the degree and the cardinality of R × S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: R × S places the attributes side by side (3 + 2 = 5) and pairs every R tuple with every S tuple (4 × 5 = 20).
concept: The Cartesian product R × S pairs each tuple of R with each tuple of S. Suppose R has m attributes and p tuples, and S has n attributes and q tuples. Each result tuple has all attributes of R followed by all attributes of S, so the degree is m + n. The number of result tuples (the cardinality) is p × q. The example in the notes, a 3-tuple R times a 2-tuple S, gives 6 tuples.
why: A — Correct. Degree 3 + 2 = 5 and cardinality 4 × 5 = 20.
B — Wrong. Both numbers mix up the rules: degrees are ADDED (3 + 2 = 5, not 3 × 2 = 6) and cardinalities are MULTIPLIED (4 × 5 = 20, not 4 + 5 = 9).
C — Wrong. The degree 5 is right, but the cardinality is 4 × 5 = 20, not 4 + 5 = 9.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Degree of R × S = 3 + 2 = 5.
Cardinality of R × S = 4 × 5 = 20.

q: If relations R and S have no attribute in common, then the natural join R ⋈ S is the same as
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A natural join equates the common attributes. With no common attribute there is nothing to compare, so every R tuple pairs with every S tuple: the Cartesian product.
concept: R ⋈ S = π(σ_common attributes equal(R × S)). When there are no common attributes, the selection condition is empty (always true) and the projection removes nothing, so R ⋈ S = R × S. At the other extreme, when R and S have exactly the same attributes, R ⋈ S = R ∩ S.
why: A — Wrong. R ⋈ S equals R ∩ S in the opposite case, when R and S have ALL their attributes in common. With no common attribute there is nothing to compare, so every tuple of R is combined with every tuple of S; that is not an intersection.
B — Correct. With no common attribute, the natural join becomes the Cartesian product.
C — Wrong. The result is empty only if R or S is empty. Having no common attribute means there is no condition, so every pair is kept.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked with the small RA engine (verify/w2_ra.py): R(A, B) with 2 tuples ⋈ S(C, D) with 3 tuples equals R × S (6 tuples).
tip: No common attribute → ⋈ becomes ×. All attributes common → ⋈ becomes ∩.

q: R(A, B) has 10 tuples and S(B, C) has 6 tuples. B is not a key of either relation. What are the minimum and maximum possible numbers of tuples in R ⋈ S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: If no B value of R appears in S, the join is empty (0). If all tuples of both relations have the same B value, every pair matches and the join is as large as R × S: 10 × 6 = 60.
concept: A natural join keeps only the pairs that agree on the common attributes. In the worst case nothing agrees (0 tuples); in the extreme case everything agrees and the join is as big as the Cartesian product, |R| × |S|. Keys narrow the range: if B were a key of S, each R tuple could match at most one S tuple, so the result would have at most |R| tuples.
why: A — Correct. The join can be anything from 0 to 10 × 6 = 60 tuples.
B — Wrong. The minimum is 0, not 6: if no B value matches, the join is empty.
C — Wrong. A maximum of 10 holds only when B is a key of S (each R tuple matches at most one S tuple). Here B is not a key, so one R tuple can match all 6 S tuples, giving up to 60.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Minimum: no B value of R appears in S → 0 tuples.
Maximum: every tuple of R and of S has the same B value → all 10 × 6 = 60 pairs match.
Brute force on small sizes (|R| = 3, |S| = 3 → 0 to 9, etc.) confirms the pattern 0 to |R| × |S| (verify/w2_ra.py).

q: R(A, B) has 10 tuples and S(B, C) has 6 tuples. B is the primary key of S, and R.B is a foreign key referencing S.B that is declared NOT NULL. How many tuples are in R ⋈ S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Because R.B is a NOT NULL foreign key, each R tuple matches at least one S tuple; because B is the key of S, it matches at most one. So every R tuple produces exactly one result tuple: 10.
concept: Joining the 'many' side with the 'one' side along a foreign key gives exactly one result tuple per child tuple, as long as the foreign key is NOT NULL and referential integrity holds. If the foreign key could be NULL, those tuples would find no partner and the result could be smaller than |R|.
why: A — Wrong. 6 is the size of S. Several R tuples may refer to the same S tuple, and every R tuple appears in the result, so the size follows R, not S.
B — Correct. Exactly one match for each of the 10 R tuples.
C — Wrong. 60 = 10 × 6 is the size of the Cartesian product. The join keeps only matching pairs, and each R tuple matches only one S tuple.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Each R tuple: B is not NULL and exists in S (referential integrity) → at least 1 match.
B is the key of S → at most 1 match.
So each of the 10 R tuples gives exactly 1 joined tuple → 10 (distinct R tuples give distinct result tuples).
300 random instances in verify/w2_ra.py: always 10.
tip: Join along a NOT NULL foreign key → result size = size of the referencing (child) relation.

q: R has attributes (A, B, C) and S has attributes (B, C, D). What is the degree of the natural join R ⋈ S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The common attributes B and C appear only once in a natural join, so the result has A, B, C, D: degree 4.
concept: Degree of a natural join = deg(R) + deg(S) − (number of common attributes). Here 3 + 3 − 2 = 4. A Cartesian product or an equi join keeps both copies of the join columns, so it would have degree 6. The cardinality is a separate question and depends on the data.
why: A — Wrong. 6 = 3 + 3 is the degree of R × S or of an equi join, which keep both copies of B and C. A natural join keeps one copy of each common attribute.
B — Wrong. 3 is the degree of each input relation; the join adds S's extra attribute D to R's attributes.
C — Correct. 3 + 3 − 2 = 4 attributes: A, B, C, D.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Attributes of R: A, B, C. Attributes of S: B, C, D.
Common: B, C (kept once).
Result attributes: A, B, C, D → degree 4 = 3 + 3 − 2.

q: R(A, B) has 5 tuples and S(A, B) is empty (0 tuples). What are |R × S| and |R ∪ S|?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A product with an empty relation is empty (5 × 0 = 0), while a union with an empty relation is just R (5 tuples).
concept: The empty relation behaves like zero for × (anything × empty = empty) and like 'nothing to add' for ∪ and − (R ∪ ∅ = R, R − ∅ = R). Also R ∩ ∅ = ∅ and R ⋈ ∅ = ∅. These edge cases are popular in exams.
why: A — Correct. 5 × 0 = 0 tuples for the product; the union keeps R's 5 tuples.
B — Wrong. The union is right, but a product with an empty relation is empty: 5 × 0 = 0, not 5.
C — Wrong. The two values are swapped: the product is empty (0) and the union keeps R's 5 tuples.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
R × S: 5 × 0 = 0 tuples (there is no S tuple to pair with).
R ∪ S: all 5 tuples of R plus nothing from S → 5 tuples.

q: Which of the following statements about the equi join  R ⋈_{R.B = S.B} S  is correct?
opts: It is a theta join whose condition uses only the equality (=) operator
Its result keeps both join columns, R.B and S.B
It removes one of the two join columns, just like a natural join
More than one of the above
exp: An equi join is a theta join that uses only '=' comparisons, and it keeps all attributes of both relations, so R.B and S.B both appear (with equal values). Dropping the duplicate column is what a natural join does.
concept: Theta join: σ_θ(R × S) with any comparison (<, ≤, =, ≠, ≥, >). Equi join: a theta join whose condition uses only =. Its result has every attribute of R and every attribute of S, so the join columns appear twice with the same values. Natural join: an equi join on all common attribute names followed by a projection that keeps only one copy of each common column. So natural join = π(equi join).
