why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is the definition of an equi join: a special theta join that uses only =.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Being σ(R × S), it keeps every column of both relations, so both R.B and S.B appear, with equal values in every result tuple.
C — Wrong. Removing the duplicate join column is the job of the natural join (a projection applied after the equi join). An equi join keeps both columns.
D — Correct. A and B are both correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Example: R(A, B) = {(1, x), (2, y)}, S(B, C) = {(x, 10), (z, 20)}.
Equi join R.B = S.B → one tuple (1, x, x, 10) with 4 attributes A, R.B, S.B, C.
Natural join → (1, x, 10) with 3 attributes (verify/w2_ra.py).
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'in an equi join the common column appears only once'. That describes the natural join; an equi join keeps both columns.

q: What does the semi-join R ⋉ S return?
opts: The tuples of R that match at least one tuple of S, with only R's attributes
The matching tuples of R and S combined, with the attributes of both
The tuples of R that match no tuple of S
More than one of the above
exp: A semi-join keeps the tuples of R that have a partner in S and outputs only R's attributes: R ⋉ S = π_R(R ⋈ S).
concept: The semi-join R ⋉ S answers 'which rows of R have a match in S?'. It never adds S's columns and never repeats an R tuple. In SQL it is written with EXISTS or IN: SELECT * FROM R WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM S WHERE S.B = R.B). The opposite, the anti-join R ▷ S, keeps the R tuples with NO match (NOT EXISTS). Semi-joins are also used in distributed databases to reduce the data sent between sites.
why: A — Correct. Matched tuples of R, with R's attributes only.
B — Wrong. Combining matching tuples with the attributes of both relations is the natural (inner) join R ⋈ S.
C — Wrong. The tuples of R with no match in S are given by the anti-join R ▷ S = R − (R ⋉ S).
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Semi-join = EXISTS; anti-join = NOT EXISTS.

q: How many tuples are in EMP ⟕ DEPT, and in how many of them is DName NULL?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Every EMP tuple appears once (5 tuples). Amit (DNo NULL) and Neha (DNo 40, not in DEPT) have no matching department, so 2 tuples get NULL DName. '5 tuples, 2 with NULL' is not listed.
concept: A left outer join R ⟕ S = (R ⋈ S) plus every R tuple that has no match, padded with NULLs for S's attributes. So every R tuple appears at least once. A NULL join value never matches anything, because NULL = 10 is UNKNOWN. A right outer join keeps the unmatched S tuples instead, and a full outer join keeps the unmatched tuples of both sides.
why: A — Wrong. 5 tuples is right, but two employees have no matching department: Amit (DNo NULL; NULL never matches) and Neha (DNo 40, not in DEPT). One of them is easy to miss.

B — Wrong. 6 tuples with 2 NULL DNames is the FULL outer join, which also adds the unmatched DEPT tuple (30, Sales) with NULL EID and Name. A left outer join keeps unmatched tuples of the left relation only.
C — Wrong. 3 tuples is the inner (natural) join: Ravi, Meena and Raj. The left outer join also keeps the 2 unmatched EMP tuples.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. EMP ⟕ DEPT has 5 tuples, and 2 of them (Amit and Neha) have NULL DName.
code:
EMP
EID | Name  | DNo
1   | Ravi  | 10
2   | Meena | 20
3   | Amit  | NULL
4   | Neha  | 40
5   | Raj   | 10

DEPT
DNo | DName
10  | IT
20  | HR
30  | Sales

EMP ⟕ DEPT   (left outer natural join on DNo)
work:
Ravi (10) → IT. Meena (20) → HR. Raj (10) → IT.
Amit (NULL) → NULL matches nothing → kept with DName NULL.
Neha (40) → no DEPT 40 → kept with DName NULL.
Result: 5 tuples (every EMP tuple once), 2 of them with NULL DName.
DEPT 30 (Sales) is not in the result: a left outer join keeps unmatched tuples of the LEFT relation only.
SQL check (LEFT JOIN … ON e.DNo = d.DNo): 5 rows, 2 with NULL DName; FULL OUTER JOIN: 6 rows, 2 with NULL DName.

q: How many tuples are in R ⟗ S (full outer natural join on B)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The inner join gives 5 tuples (x matches once, each of the two y's in R matches both y's in S). Then the unmatched (4, z) from R and (w, 30) from S are added with NULLs: 5 + 1 + 1 = 7.
concept: Full outer join = inner join + unmatched tuples of R (NULL-padded) + unmatched tuples of S (NULL-padded). When a join value repeats on both sides (y twice in R and twice in S), every pair matches: 2 × 2 = 4 tuples for y. So an inner join can be larger than either input relation.
why: A — Wrong. 5 is only the inner join. A full outer join also keeps the unmatched tuples of both sides: (4, z) from R and (w, 30) from S.
B — Wrong. 6 is the size of the left outer join (or of the right outer join): it adds only one of the two unmatched tuples.
C — Correct. 5 matched + 1 unmatched from R + 1 unmatched from S = 7.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
R
A | B
1 | x
2 | y
3 | y
4 | z

S
B | C
y | 10
y | 20
w | 30
x | 40

R ⟗ S
work:
Matches on B:
(1, x) with (x, 40) → 1 tuple.
(2, y) with (y, 10), (y, 20) → 2 tuples.
(3, y) with (y, 10), (y, 20) → 2 tuples.
Inner join = 5 tuples.
Unmatched R: (4, z) → (4, z, NULL).
Unmatched S: (w, 30) → (NULL, w, 30).
Full outer join = 5 + 1 + 1 = 7.
SQL check: FULL OUTER JOIN 7 rows, INNER JOIN 5, LEFT JOIN 6 (PostgreSQL 16, SQLite, DuckDB).

q: What is the result of the anti-join R ▷ S (on DNo)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The anti-join keeps the tuples of R that have no matching DNo in S. Only (3, 40) has no partner, because S has no DNo 40.
concept: The anti-join R ▷ S returns the tuples of R that have no matching tuple in S, keeping only R's attributes. It equals R − (R ⋉ S). In SQL it is written with NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN … WHERE S.key IS NULL). Typical queries: 'employees whose department does not exist', 'customers who placed no order'.
why: A — Wrong. {(1, 10), (2, 20)} is the semi-join R ⋉ S: the R tuples that DO have a match.
B — Correct. (3, 40) is the only R tuple without a partner in S.
C — Wrong. (30, Sales) is the S tuple with no match in R, i.e. the result of S ▷ R. The anti-join R ▷ S returns tuples of R, not of S.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
R
EID | DNo
1   | 10
2   | 20
3   | 40

S
DNo | DName
10  | IT
20  | HR
30  | Sales

R ▷ S
work:
(1, 10): S has DNo 10 → matched → dropped.
(2, 20): S has DNo 20 → dropped.
(3, 40): no DNo 40 in S → kept.
R ▷ S = {(3, 40)} = R − (R ⋉ S).
SQL: SELECT * FROM R WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM S WHERE S.DNo = R.DNo) → (3, 40) on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB.

q: How many tuples are in the result of the self join below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Counting, for each employee, the employees with a strictly smaller salary gives 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 0 = 9 tuples, which is not listed.
concept: A self join joins a relation with a renamed copy of itself (ρ is needed to tell the copies apart). With a strict '>' condition, each pair of employees with different salaries gives exactly one tuple (higher, lower), a pair with equal salaries gives none, and an employee is never paired with himself.
why: A — Wrong. 10 = C(5, 2) assumes every pair of employees has one higher earner. But Q and R both earn 5000, so that pair gives no tuple.
B — Wrong. 20 = 5 × 4 is the number of ordered pairs of different employees (E1.Name ≠ E2.Name). The '>' condition keeps at most one order of each pair, and none for the equal pair.
C — Wrong. 25 = 5 × 5 is the size of the Cartesian product ρ_E1(EMP) × ρ_E2(EMP) before the condition is applied.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. The result has 9 tuples: the 10 pairs of different employees minus the one tied pair (Q, R), each counted once from higher to lower.
code:
EMP
Name | Sal
P    | 3000
Q    | 5000
R    | 5000
S    | 7000
T    | 2000

ρ_E1(EMP) ⋈_{E1.Sal > E2.Sal} ρ_E2(EMP)
work:
For each E1 tuple, count the E2 tuples with a smaller salary:
P 3000 > T 2000 → 1.
Q 5000 > P, T → 2.
R 5000 > P, T → 2 (Q and R are equal, so neither is greater than the other).
S 7000 > P, Q, R, T → 4.
T 2000 → 0.
Total = 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 0 = 9.
SQL check: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp e1, emp e2 WHERE e1.sal > e2.sal → 9.

q: In relational algebra, which operator is needed to join a relation with itself (for example, to pair each employee with his manager from the same EMP relation), so that the two copies can be told apart?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A self join needs two copies of the same relation with different names, such as ρ_E(EMP) and ρ_M(EMP); the rename operator ρ provides them.
concept: In a self join both operands come from the same relation, so a name like EMP.EID would be ambiguous. Rename (ρ) gives each copy its own name: ρ_E(EMP) ⋈_{E.MgrID = M.EID} ρ_M(EMP). The join itself still has two operands; they just happen to be copies of one relation. In SQL the same thing is done with table aliases: FROM EMP E JOIN EMP M ON E.MgrID = M.EID.
why: A — Wrong. Division answers 'for all' queries (e.g. students who took every course). It does not make a second copy of a relation.
B — Correct. ρ renames the copies so that their attributes can be told apart.
C — Wrong. Union merges the tuples of two union-compatible relations into one; it does not pair tuples and does not rename anything.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements about the division R ÷ S, where R has attributes (A, B) and S has attribute (B):
I. It is used for queries containing 'for all' or 'every', such as 'students who took every required course'.
II. Its result has the attribute A only.
III. It is a fundamental operation that cannot be expressed using other relational algebra operations.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true. III is false: division is a derived operation, R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A((π_A(R) × S) − R).
concept: R(A, B) ÷ S(B) returns those A values that are paired in R with EVERY B value in S. The result schema is R's attributes minus S's attributes. Division is derived: it can be written with projection, Cartesian product and set difference. SQL has no DIVIDE keyword; division is written with a double NOT EXISTS or with GROUP BY … HAVING COUNT(*) = (number of required values).
why: A — Wrong. It includes III, which is false (division is derived), and it leaves out II, which is true.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
C — Wrong. It includes III (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 'every' / 'all' in a query → think division.

q: What is the result of TAKES ÷ REQ?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A student is in TAKES ÷ REQ if he took every course in REQ (DBMS and OS). Asha, Ravi and Neha took both; Amit took neither.
concept: TAKES(Student, Course) ÷ REQ(Course) gives the students who are paired with EVERY course in REQ. Extra courses (like CN) neither help nor hurt. Check each student: is REQ a subset of the courses he took?
why: A — Wrong. {Asha, Neha} are the students who took DBMS, OS AND CN, i.e. every course that appears in TAKES. Division by REQ needs only DBMS and OS, so Ravi qualifies too.
B — Wrong. Amit took only CN, not DBMS or OS, so he did not take every required course. Including him would mean 'took any course at all'.
C — Correct. Asha, Ravi and Neha each took both DBMS and OS.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

TAKES
Student | Course
Asha    | DBMS
Asha    | OS
Asha    | CN
Ravi    | DBMS
Ravi    | OS
Neha    | DBMS
Neha    | CN
Neha    | OS
Amit    | CN

REQ
Course
DBMS
OS

TAKES ÷ REQ
work:
Required set = {DBMS, OS}.
Asha took {DBMS, OS, CN} ⊇ {DBMS, OS} → yes.
Ravi took {DBMS, OS} → yes.
Neha took {DBMS, CN, OS} → yes.
Amit took {CN} → no.
Result = {Asha, Ravi, Neha}. (The double NOT EXISTS SQL query gives the same on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB.)

q: R(A, B) and S(B) are relations. Which expression, using only basic operations, is equal to R ÷ S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: π_A(R) × S lists every pair (candidate, required value). Subtracting R leaves the pairs that are missing; their A values are the candidates that fail. Removing those from π_A(R) leaves R ÷ S.
concept: Division can be built in three steps: (1) T1 ← π_A(R) × S, every candidate paired with every required value; (2) T2 ← π_A(T1 − R), the candidates missing at least one required value; (3) Result ← π_A(R) − T2. This is why ÷ is called a derived operation.
why: A — Wrong. When S is not empty, π_A(π_A(R) × S) is just π_A(R) again, so this expression gives the empty relation even when some A values qualify (for TAKES ÷ REQ it gives ∅ instead of {Asha, Ravi, Neha}).
B — Wrong. This gives the A values that are MISSING at least one required B value, i.e. the candidates who fail: the complement of the answer. One more subtraction from π_A(R) is needed.
C — Correct. All candidates minus the candidates that miss something.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Test on TAKES ÷ REQ (from the division example: students Asha, Ravi, Neha, Amit; REQ = {DBMS, OS}):
π_A(R) × S = 4 students × 2 courses = 8 pairs.
(π_A(R) × S) − R = {(Amit, DBMS), (Amit, OS)} → missing pairs.
π_A of that = {Amit} (option B's result).
π_A(R) − {Amit} = {Asha, Ravi, Neha} = R ÷ S (option C).
Option A: π_A(π_A(R) × S) = all 4 students, so A gives the empty set.
Option C also equals direct division on 300 random instances (verify/w2_ra.py).

q: If R has attributes (W, X, Y, Z) and S has attributes (Y, Z), what are the attributes of R ÷ S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The result of R ÷ S has the attributes of R that are not in S: {W, X, Y, Z} − {Y, Z} = {W, X}.
concept: For R ÷ S to be defined, the attributes of S must be a subset of the attributes of R. The result schema is (attributes of R) − (attributes of S). A tuple t over (W, X) is in the result if, for every tuple s of S, the combined tuple (t, s) is in R.
why: A — Correct. R's attributes minus S's attributes: (W, X).
B — Wrong. (Y, Z) are the attributes of the divisor S; they are 'divided out' and do not appear in the result.
C — Wrong. (W, X, Y, Z) is the schema of R itself. Division always produces fewer attributes than R.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following names appear in the result of the expression below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The OR condition picks Ravi, Meena (HR but salary 52000), Amit (IT) and Neha. Meena and Amit both appear; Raj (Sales, 47000) does not.
concept: σ with ∨ (OR) keeps a tuple if at least one part of the condition is true; with ∧ (AND) both parts must be true. Then π keeps only the Name column (removing duplicates, if any). Check every tuple against each part of the condition.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Meena is not in IT, but her salary 52000 > 50000 satisfies the OR condition.
B — Wrong. Raj is in Sales and earns 47000, which is not above 50000; neither part of the OR is true, so he is not selected.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Amit is in IT; with OR, one true part is enough, even though his salary of 38000 is low.
D — Correct. A and C are both correct, so more than one of the above is true.
E — Wrong. A and C are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

1   | Ravi  | IT    | 45000
2   | Meena | HR    | 52000
3   | Amit  | IT    | 38000
4   | Neha  | IT    | 61000
5   | Raj   | Sales | 47000

π_Name(σ_{Dept = 'IT' ∨ Sal > 50000}(EMP))
work:
Condition: Dept = 'IT' OR Sal > 50000.
Ravi: IT → yes.
Meena: HR, 52000 > 50000 → yes.
Amit: IT (38000) → yes.
Neha: IT → yes.
Raj: Sales, 47000 → no.
Result = {Ravi, Meena, Amit, Neha} (SQL check on PostgreSQL 16, SQLite, DuckDB).

q: How many tuples are in the result of the expression below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The join gives 3 tuples (Ravi in 10, Ravi in 30, Amit in 10), and π_Name removes the repeated name Ravi, leaving {Ravi, Amit}: 2 tuples, which is not listed.
concept: Evaluate from the inside out: first σ on DEPT, then the join, then π. Remember that π in relational algebra removes duplicates: two different employees named Ravi become a single tuple 'Ravi' when only Name is kept. In SQL the same result needs SELECT DISTINCT.
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the number of tuples after the join. Projection on Name then removes the duplicate 'Ravi' (two different employees with the same name), leaving 2.
B — Wrong. 4 is the number of distinct names in all of EMP (Ravi, Meena, Amit, Neha); the selection keeps only the Patna departments.
C — Wrong. 5 is the number of EMP tuples; the join with Patna departments removes Meena (Gaya) and Neha (Delhi).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. The result has 2 tuples, {Ravi, Amit}: the join gives 3 tuples and π removes the repeated name Ravi.

5   | Neha  | 40

10  | IT    | Patna

30  | Sales | Patna

π_Name(EMP ⋈ σ_{Loc = 'Patna'}(DEPT))

σ_Loc='Patna'(DEPT) = {(10, IT, Patna), (30, Sales, Patna)}.
EMP ⋈ that (on DNo): (1, Ravi, 10), (3, Ravi, 30), (4, Amit, 10) → 3 tuples.
π_Name: Ravi, Ravi, Amit → duplicates removed → {Ravi, Amit} → 2 tuples.
SQL check: SELECT DISTINCT name … → Amit, Ravi; without DISTINCT → 3 rows.

q: What is the result of the expression below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The subtracted part is the set of departments that have at least one employee earning more than 40000: {10, 20, 30}. All departments {10, 20, 30, 40} minus these leaves {40}.
concept: R − S means 'in R but not in S'. Here S is 'departments with at least one employee earning more than 40000', so the result is 'departments in which NO employee earns more than 40000'. Department 40 has no employees at all, so it qualifies: an empty group satisfies a 'no one' condition.
why: A — Wrong. {10, 30} are the departments that have someone earning 40000 or less (employees 1 and 5). That answers a different question; the subtraction does not pick these.

B — Wrong. {20, 40} are the departments where nobody earns 40000 or less. The expression instead removes every department that has at least one employee earning more than 40000, and department 20 has one (45000).
C — Correct. Only department 40 has no employee with salary above 40000.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
σ_Sal>40000(EMP) = employees 2 (DNo 10), 3 (DNo 20), 4 (DNo 30).
π_DNo of that = {10, 20, 30}.
π_DNo(DEPT) = {10, 20, 30, 40}.
{10, 20, 30, 40} − {10, 20, 30} = {40}.
SQL check: SELECT dno FROM dept EXCEPT SELECT dno FROM emp WHERE sal > 40000 → 40.
tip: 'Departments with no X' → all departments − departments with some X.

q: What is the result of the expression below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The subtracted part is the set of salaries that are smaller than some other salary: {30000, 45000}. Removing these from all salaries {30000, 45000, 52000} leaves {52000}, the maximum salary.
concept: Basic relational algebra has no MAX function, but the maximum can be found by elimination: find every value that is smaller than some other value (using a product of the relation with a renamed copy of itself), then subtract those from all values. What remains has nothing bigger than it: the maximum. Two employees with 52000 give one tuple, because relations are sets.
why: A — Correct. Only 52000 is not smaller than any other salary.
B — Wrong. {30000, 45000} is only the subtracted part: the salaries that are less than some other salary.
C — Wrong. {30000} would be the MINIMUM salary, obtained with the condition EMP.Sal > D.Sal (salaries greater than some other salary) instead of <.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
Name | Sal
P    | 30000
Q    | 52000
R    | 45000
S    | 52000

π_Sal(EMP) − π_EMP.Sal(σ_{EMP.Sal < D.Sal}(EMP × ρ_D(EMP)))
tip: Max = all values − values smaller than some value. For the minimum, use > instead of <.

q: Which statement correctly compares relational algebra and relational calculus?
opts: Relational algebra is procedural; relational calculus is non-procedural (declarative)
Both relational algebra and relational calculus are procedural
Relational algebra is non-procedural; relational calculus is procedural
More than one of the above
exp: Relational algebra gives a sequence of operations (how to compute the result), so it is procedural. Relational calculus only describes the properties of the wanted tuples (what to get), so it is non-procedural.
concept: In relational algebra a query is an expression of operators applied in an order, e.g. π_Name(σ_Sal>5000(EMP)): first select, then project. In relational calculus a query is a logical formula, e.g. {t.Name | t ∈ EMP ∧ t.Sal > 5000}: it says which tuples qualify, not how to find them. Despite this difference, safe relational calculus and relational algebra can express exactly the same queries.
why: A — Correct. Algebra = how (procedural); calculus = what (declarative).
B — Wrong. Only relational algebra is procedural. Relational calculus is based on predicate logic and is declarative.
C — Wrong. This reverses the two: algebra is the procedural one.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The visual query language QBE (Query-By-Example) is based on
opts: More than one of the above
exp: QBE, developed by Moshé Zloof at IBM, is based on domain relational calculus: the user types example values (domain variables) into table skeletons. Domain relational calculus is not among A–C.
concept: Relational query languages and their bases: SQL draws on relational algebra and tuple relational calculus; QUEL (of the INGRES system) is based on tuple relational calculus; QBE is based on domain relational calculus. In QBE the user sees empty table skeletons and fills in example elements (variables such as _x) and conditions in the columns; these variables range over attribute values (domains).
why: A — Wrong. Tuple relational calculus uses variables that stand for whole tuples; it underlies QUEL and (partly) SQL. QBE's example elements stand for single attribute values, which is domain calculus.
B — Wrong. QBE is a relational query language that works on tables; it has nothing to do with the network (CODASYL) model of records and owner–member sets.
C — Wrong. QBE works on relational tables, not on the parent–child trees of the hierarchical model (such as IBM's IMS).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. QBE is based on domain relational calculus (DRC).
tip: QBE ↔ domain calculus (example values in columns). QUEL ↔ tuple calculus.

q: Which of the following tuple relational calculus expressions is unsafe (its result may be infinite)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: {t | ¬(t ∈ EMP)} asks for every possible tuple that is not in EMP. Such tuples can be built from values that appear nowhere in the database, so the answer is infinite: the expression is unsafe.
concept: A relational calculus expression is safe if its result can contain only values from the domain of the expression, i.e. values that appear in the relations or constants it mentions. Expressions that tie t to a relation (t ∈ EMP ∧ …) are safe, even with ¬ inside the condition. A bare negation such as ¬(t ∈ EMP) has no such restriction, so it is unsafe. Only safe expressions are allowed, and safe calculus has exactly the power of relational algebra.
why: A — Wrong. t is restricted to tuples of EMP, so the result is a subset of EMP: finite and safe.
B — Correct. Nothing restricts t, so infinitely many tuples satisfy 'not in EMP'.
C — Wrong. The negation applies only to a condition on t, while t is still restricted to EMP (t ∈ EMP). The result is a subset of EMP, so it is safe.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Basic relational algebra, safe tuple relational calculus and safe domain relational calculus have the same expressive power.
II. In tuple relational calculus, variables range over tuples; in domain relational calculus, variables range over attribute (domain) values.
III. Relational calculus tells the DBMS, step by step, how to compute the answer.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true. III is false: relational calculus is non-procedural; it describes what to retrieve, not how.
concept: Codd showed that relational algebra and safe relational calculus are equivalent in power. A language that can express every query of basic relational algebra is called relationally complete; SQL is relationally complete (and goes beyond it with aggregates and sorting). TRC uses tuple variables, e.g. {t | t ∈ EMP ∧ t.Sal > 5000}. DRC uses one domain variable per attribute, e.g. for EMP(Name, Sal): {<n> | ∃s (<n, s> ∈ EMP ∧ s > 5000)}.
why: A — Wrong. It includes III, which is false (calculus is declarative), and it leaves out II, which is true.
B — Wrong. It includes III (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
C — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which relational algebra expression is equivalent to the tuple relational calculus query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The query returns the students who, for EVERY course u in REQ, have a TAKES tuple with that course. 'For every' (∀) corresponds to division: TAKES ÷ REQ.
concept: In relational calculus, ∃ (there exists) corresponds to selection and join ('at least one'), and ∀ (for all) corresponds to division ('every'). In SQL, ∀ is usually written as NOT EXISTS ( … NOT EXISTS …), because ∀u P(u) is the same as ¬∃u ¬P(u).
why: A — Correct. ∀u ∈ REQ (the student took u) is exactly the division TAKES ÷ REQ.
B — Wrong. The join keeps a student who took AT LEAST ONE required course; that matches ∃ (there exists), not ∀ (for all). A student with only DBMS would wrongly be included.
C — Wrong. This gives the students who took NO required course at all, which is the opposite of the query.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Read the formula: t is a student who appears in TAKES (∃s), and for all u in REQ (∀u) there is a TAKES tuple v of that student with course u.
That means 'students who took every required course' = TAKES ÷ REQ.
Test data where the options differ: TAKES = {(Asha, DBMS), (Asha, OS), (Ravi, DBMS), (Amit, CN)}, REQ = {DBMS, OS}.
Formula and TAKES ÷ REQ → {Asha}.
Option B (join) → {Asha, Ravi}: 'took at least one required course'.
Option C → {Amit}: 'took no required course'.
The formula also equals division on 300 random instances (verify/w2_extra.py).
tip: ∃ → join; ∀ → division (or double NOT EXISTS in SQL).

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: SQL was first developed at IBM, in the System R research project, under which name?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SQL started at IBM in the early 1970s as SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language); the name was later shortened to SQL.
concept: SQL (Structured Query Language) was designed by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce at IBM for System R, one of the first relational DBMSs. Its first name was SEQUEL, Structured English QUEry Language. The name was later shortened to SQL because 'SEQUEL' was already a trademark of another company. SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987.
why: A — Wrong. QUEL was the query language of INGRES, a different relational system built at the University of California, Berkeley. It was a rival of SQL, not its old name.
B — Wrong. Datalog is a rule-based (logic) query language, similar in style to Prolog, used mainly in research. It is not an early name of SQL.
C — Correct. SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) was IBM's original name; it was later shortened to SQL.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: SEQUEL → SQL, born at IBM System R. This is why many people still pronounce SQL as 'sequel'.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which of the following command–category pairs is correctly matched?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MERGE inserts or updates rows of a table, so it is a DML command. GRANT belongs to DCL and SAVEPOINT belongs to TCL.
concept: SQL commands are grouped by what they work on. DDL (Data Definition Language) defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME, COMMENT. DML (Data Manipulation Language) changes data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE. DCL (Data Control Language) controls permissions: GRANT, REVOKE. TCL (Transaction Control Language) controls transactions: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT. SELECT is called DQL (Data Query Language) in some books and is counted under DML in others.
why: A — Correct. MERGE adds new rows and updates (or deletes) existing rows of a target table. It works on data, so it is DML.
B — Wrong. GRANT gives privileges (permissions) to users or roles. It is a DCL command, not TCL.
C — Wrong. SAVEPOINT marks a point inside a transaction so that you can roll back to it later. It is a TCL command, not DDL.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Quick rule: structure → DDL, data → DML, permission → DCL, transaction → TCL.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: SQL is called a declarative (non-procedural) language because:
opts: the programmer must write loops to read a table row by row
the user states WHAT data is wanted and the DBMS decides HOW to get it
every SQL statement must be declared before it can be used
More than one of the above
exp: In SQL you only describe the result you want; the DBMS's query optimizer chooses the steps (which index, which join order) to produce it.
concept: A procedural language, like C, tells the computer step by step HOW to do a job. A declarative language tells only WHAT result is needed. In SQL you write, for example, SELECT name FROM emp WHERE sal > 20000, and the query optimizer (the DBMS part that plans the work) decides whether to read the whole table or use an index. This is why the same SQL query can run fast or slow depending on indexes, without any change in the query text.
why: A — Wrong. Writing loops to read one row at a time is procedural, record-at-a-time programming (as in file processing or cursor code). A plain SQL statement works on a whole set of rows without loops.
B — Correct. The user describes the required result; the DBMS works out the method.
C — Wrong. There is no rule that statements must be 'declared' before use. The word 'declarative' means 'describing the result', not 'declaring statements'.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Declarative = 'what'; procedural = 'how'. SQL is 'what'.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q:
Consider the following statements about SQL:
I. SQL keywords are not case-sensitive, so SELECT and select mean the same.
II. SQL has been standardised by both ANSI and ISO.
III. SQL is a fully procedural language like C, in which every step must be coded.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Statements I and II are true. Statement III is false because SQL is a declarative language.
concept: SQL keywords are case-insensitive: SELECT, Select and select all work. (A value inside quotes, such as 'Patna', is data, and comparisons of data may be case-sensitive.) SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987; later versions include SQL-92, SQL:1999, SQL:2003 and SQL:2016. Plain SQL is declarative; procedural extensions such as Oracle PL/SQL and SQL Server T-SQL add variables, loops and IF statements on top of it.
why: A — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: plain SQL is declarative, not fully procedural.
B — Wrong. It includes III (false) and leaves out I, which is true.
C — Correct. I and II are both true and III is false.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Keywords are case-insensitive, but string values may not be: in PostgreSQL 'patna' = 'Patna' is false.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In the query  SELECT name FROM emp WHERE sal > 20000;  which relational algebra operation is performed by the WHERE clause?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: WHERE keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition, which is the job of selection σ. The SELECT list (choosing columns) does the job of projection π.
concept: Relational algebra has selection (σ), which picks ROWS that satisfy a condition, and projection (π), which picks COLUMNS. In SQL, the WHERE clause does the row-filtering job of σ, and the SELECT list does the column-choosing job of π. So this query means π name (σ sal>20000 (emp)). One small difference: π removes duplicate rows, but SQL's SELECT keeps duplicates unless you write DISTINCT.
why: A — Wrong. Projection (π) chooses columns. In this query that job is done by the SELECT list 'name', not by WHERE.
B — Correct. WHERE sal > 20000 filters rows, which is selection σ.
C — Wrong. A Cartesian product pairs every row of one table with every row of another. It comes from listing two tables in FROM, not from a WHERE condition.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (found in many notes): 'SELECT is the same as projection'. Only the SELECT list is like π; the WHERE clause is σ, which relational algebra confusingly calls 'select'.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which statement correctly adds a new column phone to an existing table STUDENT?
opts: ALTER TABLE student ADD phone VARCHAR(10);
UPDATE student ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(10);
INSERT INTO student COLUMN phone VARCHAR(10);
More than one of the above
exp: Adding a column changes the structure of the table, so it is done with the DDL command ALTER TABLE … ADD.
concept: ALTER TABLE changes the definition of an existing table. Common forms are: ALTER TABLE t ADD col type (add a column), ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN col (remove a column), ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN a TO b (rename a column), and a clause to change a column's type (MODIFY in Oracle/MySQL, ALTER COLUMN in SQL Server/PostgreSQL). Rows that already exist get NULL, or the DEFAULT value, in the new column.
why: A — Correct. ALTER TABLE … ADD is the DDL way to add a column. (PostgreSQL and MySQL also accept the optional word COLUMN: ADD COLUMN phone ….)
B — Wrong. UPDATE is a DML command that changes values in existing rows (UPDATE … SET …). It cannot change the structure of a table, so 'UPDATE … ADD COLUMN' is a syntax error.
C — Wrong. INSERT adds new rows of data, not new columns. 'INSERT INTO … COLUMN' is a syntax error.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Structure change → ALTER (DDL). Data change → UPDATE (DML). Do not mix them up.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, the statement  COMMENT ON COLUMN emp.sal IS 'Monthly salary in rupees';  stores the comment:
opts: inside every row of the EMP table
in the redo log file only
More than one of the above
exp: COMMENT is a DDL command. It saves descriptive text about a table or column as metadata in the data dictionary.
concept: The data dictionary (also called the system catalog) is a set of system tables that store metadata, that is, data about data: table names, column types, constraints, users, privileges and comments. COMMENT ON TABLE t IS '…' and COMMENT ON COLUMN t.c IS '…' add notes that help developers understand the design. In Oracle these notes can be read from views such as USER_TAB_COMMENTS and USER_COL_COMMENTS. No data row is changed.
why: A — Wrong. Rows hold the actual data values (such as 25000). A comment describes the column once; it is not copied into each row.
B — Wrong. The redo log records changes so that the database can be recovered after a crash. It is not the place where comments are kept for reading.
C — Correct. The comment is stored as metadata in the data dictionary.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: PostgreSQL also has COMMENT ON. MySQL instead uses a COMMENT 'text' clause inside CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, which of the following statements renames the table EMP to EMPLOYEE?
opts: ALTER TABLE emp RENAME TO employee;
More than one of the above
exp: Oracle accepts both RENAME old TO new and ALTER TABLE old RENAME TO new. UPDATE cannot rename a table.
concept: Renaming a table is a DDL operation. Oracle gives two forms: RENAME old_name TO new_name; and ALTER TABLE old_name RENAME TO new_name;. Other products differ: MySQL uses RENAME TABLE old TO new (or ALTER TABLE … RENAME TO …), PostgreSQL uses ALTER TABLE … RENAME TO …, and SQL Server uses the system procedure sp_rename. A column is renamed with ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN a TO b.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. RENAME old TO new is Oracle's short DDL statement for renaming a table, view, sequence or private synonym.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. ALTER TABLE … RENAME TO … is Oracle's other valid form (it also works in PostgreSQL and MySQL).
C — Wrong. UPDATE changes data values in rows. A table cannot be renamed by updating a value; the table EMP has no column table_name, so this statement fails.
D — Correct. Both A and B are valid Oracle statements for renaming a table.
E — Wrong. A and B are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Do not mix up the forms: MySQL writes RENAME TABLE emp TO employee; but Oracle's short form has no word TABLE: RENAME emp TO employee;

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In SQL Server, which statement changes the data type of the existing column sal of table EMP to DECIMAL(10,2)?
opts: ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY sal DECIMAL(10,2);
ALTER TABLE emp ALTER COLUMN sal DECIMAL(10,2);
ALTER TABLE emp CHANGE TYPE sal DECIMAL(10,2);
More than one of the above
exp: SQL Server (T-SQL) changes a column's type with ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN column new_type. MODIFY is the Oracle/MySQL keyword.
concept: Changing a column's data type is done with ALTER TABLE, but the keyword depends on the product. Oracle: ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY sal NUMBER(10,2). MySQL: ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY sal DECIMAL(10,2). SQL Server: ALTER TABLE emp ALTER COLUMN sal DECIMAL(10,2). PostgreSQL: ALTER TABLE emp ALTER COLUMN sal TYPE NUMERIC(10,2). The change fails if the existing values cannot be converted to the new type.
why: A — Wrong. MODIFY is the keyword used by Oracle and MySQL. SQL Server does not support ALTER TABLE … MODIFY.
B — Correct. ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN … new_type is the SQL Server form.
C — Wrong. There is no 'CHANGE TYPE' clause in SQL Server. (MySQL has a CHANGE clause, but its form is CHANGE old_name new_name type.)
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Oracle/MySQL → MODIFY;  SQL Server → ALTER COLUMN;  PostgreSQL → ALTER COLUMN … TYPE.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, the statements below are run one after another in the same session. What is in table T after the last statement?
opts: T is empty, because ROLLBACK undoes the INSERT
An error occurs, because ROLLBACK is not allowed after a DDL statement
T contains the row 101, because the CREATE TABLE committed the INSERT
More than one of the above
exp: Oracle performs an implicit COMMIT before (and after) every DDL statement, so the INSERT became permanent when CREATE TABLE ran; the ROLLBACK then has nothing to undo.
concept: In Oracle (and also in MySQL), DDL statements such as CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE and RENAME cause an implicit COMMIT. The open transaction is committed just before the DDL runs, and the DDL itself is committed when it finishes. So any DML done earlier becomes permanent and cannot be rolled back. PostgreSQL is different: there DDL is transactional, and BEGIN; CREATE TABLE …; ROLLBACK; really removes the new table.
why: A — Wrong. This would happen if no DDL had run in between, or in a system with transactional DDL such as PostgreSQL inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK. In Oracle the CREATE TABLE committed the INSERT first, so ROLLBACK cannot undo it.
B — Wrong. ROLLBACK is always allowed. Here it simply finds no uncommitted change to undo; no error is raised.
C — Correct. The implicit commit made row 101 permanent, so it stays after ROLLBACK.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
1. INSERT INTO t VALUES (101); → row 101 added; transaction is open and not yet committed.
2. CREATE TABLE audit_log … → Oracle first issues an implicit COMMIT (row 101 becomes permanent), then creates the table and commits again.
3. ROLLBACK; → there is no uncommitted change left, so nothing is undone (no error).
Result: T contains 101, and table AUDIT_LOG exists.
tip: Exam line: 'DDL is auto-committed in Oracle' — and it also commits any pending DML before it.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, which of the following is NOT a DDL statement?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MERGE changes the rows of a table, so it is DML. In Oracle, TRUNCATE and COMMENT are DDL statements.
concept: Oracle groups its statements into DDL (for example CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME, COMMENT) and DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE). DDL statements change structure or metadata and commit automatically in Oracle; DML statements change data and can be rolled back. Because some books classify TRUNCATE differently, the question names Oracle, whose documentation (like MySQL's) treats TRUNCATE as DDL.
why: A — Wrong. In Oracle, TRUNCATE TABLE is a DDL statement: it empties the table by releasing its storage, commits implicitly and cannot be rolled back. So it IS DDL and does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Correct. MERGE is DML: it inserts new rows and updates (or deletes) existing rows of a target table using a source table.
C — Wrong. COMMENT stores a note about a table or column in the data dictionary; Oracle lists it as a DDL statement.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: MERGE is often called an 'upsert' (UPDATE + INSERT). It touches data, so it is DML.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Table EMP has the 3 rows shown. What does the CREATE TABLE statement produce?
opts: A table EMP_COPY with the same columns as EMP and all 3 rows
A table EMP_COPY with the same columns as EMP but no rows
Nothing; an error occurs because the condition 1 = 2 is always false
More than one of the above
exp: CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT takes its columns from the query. WHERE 1 = 2 is never true, so the new table gets the columns but no rows.
concept: CREATE TABLE new_table AS SELECT … (often called CTAS) creates a new table whose columns and data types come from the SELECT, and fills it with whatever rows the SELECT returns. Adding a condition that is always false, such as WHERE 1 = 2, is a well-known trick to copy only the structure. Keys and most other constraints are not copied, so they must be added again with ALTER TABLE if needed.
why: A — Wrong. All 3 rows would be copied only without the WHERE clause, or with an always-true condition such as WHERE 1 = 1.
B — Correct. The structure (eid, name, sal) is copied, but the always-false condition returns 0 rows.
C — Wrong. An always-false condition is perfectly legal; it simply returns no rows. The table is still created.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | sal
1   | Asha  | 20000
2   | Ravi  | 15000
3   | Meena | 30000

CREATE TABLE emp_copy AS
SELECT * FROM emp WHERE 1 = 2;
work:
1. SELECT * FROM emp gives the column list and types: eid, name, sal.
2. WHERE 1 = 2 is false for every row, so the SELECT returns 0 rows.
3. EMP_COPY is created with columns eid, name, sal and 0 rows.
Verified: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp_copy → 0 in PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB (and a row can then be inserted into its 3 columns).
tip: WHERE 1 = 2 → copy structure only;  WHERE 1 = 1 (or no WHERE) → copy structure and data.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Table MARKS has 4 rows. What is the effect of the statement  DELETE FROM marks;  ?
opts: The table MARKS and its structure are removed from the database
An error occurs, because DELETE must have a WHERE clause
All 4 rows are removed, and the empty table MARKS remains
More than one of the above
exp: DELETE without WHERE removes every row but keeps the table definition, so SELECT COUNT(*) FROM marks afterwards gives 0.
concept: DELETE is a DML command that removes rows. The WHERE clause is optional: with WHERE, only the matching rows are deleted; without WHERE, all rows are deleted. The structure of the table (columns, constraints, indexes) stays, so new rows can be inserted later. To remove the table itself you need DROP TABLE.
why: A — Wrong. Removing the table together with its structure is what DROP TABLE would do. DELETE never removes the table definition.
B — Wrong. WHERE is optional in DELETE (and in UPDATE). Without it, the statement applies to every row.
C — Correct. All rows are removed and the empty table stays (checked: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM marks returns 0 in PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB).
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: In real work, a DELETE or UPDATE without WHERE changes EVERY row — always check the WHERE clause before running it.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which of the following commands can use a WHERE clause to remove only some of the rows of a table?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only DELETE accepts a WHERE clause. TRUNCATE always removes all rows, and DROP removes the whole table.
concept: DELETE FROM t WHERE condition removes only the rows that satisfy the condition. TRUNCATE TABLE t has no WHERE clause; it empties the whole table in one quick step. DROP TABLE t removes the table itself — rows, structure, indexes, triggers and constraints. So, when some rows must be kept, DELETE is the only choice of the three.
why: A — Correct. DELETE FROM t WHERE … removes only the matching rows.
B — Wrong. TRUNCATE has no WHERE clause; it always removes all rows (keeping the table structure).
C — Wrong. DROP TABLE removes the entire table including its structure; it cannot choose individual rows.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Some rows → DELETE … WHERE.  All rows, fast → TRUNCATE.  Whole table gone → DROP.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which of the following is NOT true about TRUNCATE TABLE in Oracle?
opts: It removes all rows from the table
It keeps the table's structure (columns and constraints)
It fires the DELETE triggers defined on the table for every removed row
More than one of the above
exp: TRUNCATE does not delete rows one by one, so DELETE triggers do not fire. Options A and B are true facts about TRUNCATE.
concept: TRUNCATE TABLE empties a table by deallocating (releasing) its data storage instead of deleting rows one at a time. Because of this it is fast, produces very little undo information, does not fire DELETE triggers, and in Oracle cannot be rolled back (it is DDL and commits implicitly). The table, its columns, constraints and indexes remain, so the table can be used again at once.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: TRUNCATE removes every row. The stem asks for the statement that is NOT true, so A does not fit.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: the table definition stays and only the data goes. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Correct. This statement is false: TRUNCATE does not run DELETE triggers, because it does not delete rows individually. (DELETE FROM t does fire DELETE triggers.)
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: If a DELETE trigger must run (for example to write an audit log), use DELETE, not TRUNCATE.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q:
Consider these statements comparing  DELETE FROM t;  (no WHERE clause) and  TRUNCATE TABLE t;  in Oracle:
I. Both leave table T existing but empty.
II. The DELETE can be undone with ROLLBACK before COMMIT, but the TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back.
III. For a large table, TRUNCATE is usually much faster, because it does not delete and log the rows one by one.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true, so 'I, II and III' is correct; each 'only' option leaves out a true statement.
concept: DELETE is DML: it removes rows one at a time, writes undo information for each row, fires DELETE triggers, can have a WHERE clause, and can be rolled back until COMMIT. TRUNCATE is DDL in Oracle: it releases the table's data blocks in one step, writes very little undo, does not fire DELETE triggers, has no WHERE clause, and is committed automatically, so it cannot be rolled back. Both keep the table's structure; DROP removes the structure too.
why: A — Correct. Statements I, II and III are all true.
B — Wrong. 'I and II only' says III is false, but III is true: TRUNCATE is usually much faster on a big table.
C — Wrong. 'II and III only' leaves out I, which is true: after either command the (empty) table still exists.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 'TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back' is true in Oracle and MySQL. In PostgreSQL, TRUNCATE inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK can be undone — that is why such questions should name the product.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: After the statement  DROP TABLE emp;  succeeds, what happens when  SELECT * FROM emp;  is run?
opts: It returns zero rows, because only the data was removed
It gives an error, because table EMP no longer exists
It returns the old rows, because DROP removes only the indexes
More than one of the above
exp: DROP TABLE removes the table definition together with its data, indexes, constraints and triggers, so any later use of the name EMP fails with a 'table does not exist' error.
concept: DROP TABLE is a DDL command that deletes the whole table object: its rows, its definition in the data dictionary, and objects that belong to it such as its indexes, constraints and triggers. After that the name EMP is unknown to the DBMS. To get the table back you need a backup (or, in Oracle 10g and later, FLASHBACK TABLE emp TO BEFORE DROP if the recycle bin is enabled).
why: A — Wrong. Zero rows with the table still present is what happens after DELETE FROM emp; or TRUNCATE TABLE emp; — not after DROP.
B — Correct. For example PostgreSQL says 'relation "emp" does not exist', SQLite says 'no such table: emp' and Oracle says 'ORA-00942: table or view does not exist'.
C — Wrong. DROP TABLE removes the table itself, not just its indexes. A single index is removed with DROP INDEX.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: DELETE → chosen rows go, table stays.  TRUNCATE → all rows go, table stays.  DROP → the table itself goes.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: What does the final SELECT return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Columns left out of the INSERT column list get their DEFAULT value. city has DEFAULT 'Patna'; marks has no DEFAULT, so it gets NULL.
concept: When an INSERT names only some columns, every column that is not named receives its DEFAULT value. If a column has no DEFAULT clause, its default is NULL. (If such a column is declared NOT NULL and has no default, the INSERT fails.) A numeric column does not automatically get 0, and a text column does not get an empty string.
why: A — Wrong. city is right, but marks does not become 0. A column without a DEFAULT gets NULL, which means 'unknown', not zero.
B — Wrong. marks is NULL, but city is not: its DEFAULT 'Patna' is used when the column is left out of the INSERT.
C — Correct. city takes the default 'Patna' and marks takes NULL.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
1. Columns given in the INSERT: roll = 1, name = 'Asha'.
2. city is not given → its DEFAULT 'Patna' is used.
3. marks is not given and has no DEFAULT → NULL.
4. Output: Patna | NULL.
Verified: row (1, 'Asha', 'Patna', NULL) in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB.
tip: Column missing from INSERT → its DEFAULT if defined, otherwise NULL (and an error if the column is NOT NULL).

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: What does the SELECT return after the UPDATE?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The UPDATE has no WHERE, so it adds 1000 to every row, but NULL + 1000 stays NULL. SUM skips NULL: 21000 + 16000 + 11000 = 48000, which is not listed.
concept: An UPDATE without WHERE changes every row of the table. Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, because NULL means 'unknown', and unknown + 1000 is still unknown. Aggregate functions such as SUM and AVG skip NULL values. So the NULL salary stays NULL after the raise and is not counted in SUM.
why: A — Wrong. 49000 comes from treating NULL as 0, so that Meena would get 0 + 1000 = 1000. In SQL, NULL + 1000 is NULL, not 1000.
B — Wrong. 45000 is the total before the UPDATE. An UPDATE without WHERE does change rows — all of them.
C — Wrong. 46000 would mean only one row was increased. Without WHERE, all three non-NULL salaries increase by 1000.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The true result is 48000, which is not among A–C.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | sal
1   | Asha  | 20000
2   | Ravi  | 15000
3   | Meena | NULL
4   | Kunal | 10000

UPDATE emp SET sal = sal + 1000;
SELECT SUM(sal) FROM emp;
work:
1. Salaries before: 20000, 15000, NULL, 10000 (sum 45000).
2. UPDATE without WHERE changes all 4 rows: 21000, 16000, NULL + 1000 = NULL, 11000.
3. SUM skips NULL: 21000 + 16000 + 11000 = 48000.
4. 48000 is not among A–C → answer E.
Verified: SUM(sal) = 48000 in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB.
tip: NULL in arithmetic gives NULL. To treat NULL as 0, write COALESCE(sal, 0) + 1000 (NVL(sal, 0) in Oracle).

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: The statements below are run in order. What does the final SELECT return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After the UPDATE the rows are (1,20), (2,20), (3,60); the DELETE removes (3,60); INSERT … SELECT copies the 2 remaining rows as (11,20) and (12,20). So there are 4 rows with total 80, which is not listed.
concept: Each DML statement works on the table as the previous statement left it. INSERT … SELECT inserts all the rows returned by a query — here a copy of the table's own rows with new ids. The SELECT part is evaluated completely before the new rows are added, so the copying does not go on forever.
why: A — Wrong. 2 | 40 is the state after the DELETE; it forgets that INSERT … SELECT then adds a copy of the 2 remaining rows.
B — Wrong. 4 | 120 comes from doubling id 2 as well (qty 40). The condition id <> 2 skips that row, so its qty stays 20.
C — Wrong. 6 | 200 comes from skipping the DELETE. Row 3 has qty 60, which is greater than 40, so it is removed before the copy is made.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The true result is COUNT = 4 and SUM = 80, which is not among A–C.
work:
1. After the INSERT: (1,10), (2,20), (3,30).
2. UPDATE qty = qty*2 WHERE id <> 2 → ids 1 and 3 change: (1,20), (2,20), (3,60).
3. DELETE WHERE qty > 40 → removes (3,60): (1,20), (2,20).
4. INSERT … SELECT id+10, qty → adds (11,20), (12,20).
5. COUNT(*) = 4; SUM(qty) = 20 + 20 + 20 + 20 = 80.
6. '4 | 80' is not listed → answer E.
Verified: (4, 80) in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB.
tip: In a DML trace, write the full table after every statement — most mistakes come from skipping one step.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: What does table STOCK contain after the MERGE statement?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: P2 is in both tables, so it is updated to 5 + 7 = 12; P3 is only in the source, so it is inserted; P1 has no source row and stays as it is.
concept: MERGE (standard SQL; also Oracle, SQL Server and PostgreSQL 15+) compares each source row with the target using the ON condition. For a match, the WHEN MATCHED action runs (usually UPDATE, sometimes DELETE). For a source row with no match, the WHEN NOT MATCHED action runs (INSERT). Target rows that have no matching source row are not touched. MERGE is handy for loading the day's changes into a master table in one statement.
why: A — Correct. P1 unchanged (10), P2 updated to 12, P3 inserted with 4.
B — Wrong. This replaces P2's quantity by 7. The UPDATE here adds the two quantities (s.qty + n.qty = 5 + 7 = 12); it does not just copy the new value.
C — Wrong. P1 is not removed. A target row with no matching source row is simply left alone.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STOCK (target)
item | qty
P1   | 10
P2   | 5

NEWSTOCK (source)
item | qty
P2   | 7
P3   | 4

MERGE INTO stock s
USING newstock n
ON (s.item = n.item)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET qty = s.qty + n.qty
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT VALUES (n.item, n.qty);
work:
1. Source P2 matches target P2 → UPDATE qty = 5 + 7 = 12.
2. Source P3 has no match → INSERT ('P3', 4).
3. Target P1 has no source row → unchanged (10).
4. Final STOCK: P1 10, P2 12, P3 4.
Verified in PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB (SQLite has no MERGE).
tip: MERGE = 'if the row exists, UPDATE it; otherwise INSERT it' — one statement instead of two.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Table STU is created with  CREATE TABLE stu (roll INT, name VARCHAR(10));  In PostgreSQL, which of the following statements insert a row into STU without error?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are valid: values in the table's column order, values matched to an explicit column list in any order, and INSERT … SELECT.
concept: INSERT has three common forms. (1) INSERT INTO t VALUES (…) — a value for every column, in the order the columns were created. (2) INSERT INTO t (c2, c1) VALUES (…) — the column list decides the order, and columns not listed get their DEFAULT or NULL. (3) INSERT INTO t SELECT … — the rows come from a query. Most products also allow several rows at once: VALUES (…), (…), (…).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Without a column list, the values go to roll and name in table order.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. With a column list, the values may be given in any order — here name first, then roll.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. INSERT … SELECT inserts the rows returned by a query; PostgreSQL allows a SELECT without FROM. (In Oracle you would write SELECT 7, 'Sita' FROM dual.)
D — Correct. All three statements ran without error in PostgreSQL (and in SQLite and DuckDB), so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. All of A–C are valid, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Prefer the form with a column list: it keeps working even if a column is added to the table later.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, the value 'RAM' is stored in a column declared CHAR(10). How many characters does the stored value occupy (single-byte character set)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CHAR(n) is fixed-length: Oracle pads the value with blanks up to n characters, so 'RAM' is stored as 'RAM' followed by 7 spaces — 10 characters.
concept: CHAR(n) is a fixed-length character type: every value takes exactly n characters, and shorter values are padded with blanks (spaces) on the right. VARCHAR2(n) in Oracle, or VARCHAR(n) in standard SQL, is variable-length: it stores only the characters given (up to n) plus a small length marker. CHAR suits values that always have the same length, such as a 2-letter state code 'BR'; VARCHAR2 suits names and addresses, whose length varies.
why: A — Wrong. 3 characters is what a VARCHAR2(10) column would keep, because it stores only the actual characters. CHAR(10) pads to the full length.
B — Wrong. 4 does not match CHAR(10). It looks like '3 characters + 1 length byte', which is closer to how a short VARCHAR2 value is stored.
C — Correct. 'RAM' + 7 blanks = 10 characters.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: CHAR = fixed length, padded with spaces. VARCHAR2 = variable length, no padding.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which of the following is NOT true about the Oracle data types CHAR and VARCHAR2?
opts: Inserting a 12-character string into a VARCHAR2(10) column silently stores only its first 10 characters
CHAR(n) is fixed-length and pads shorter values with blanks
VARCHAR2(n) stores only the characters actually given, up to n
More than one of the above
exp: Oracle does not cut the string silently: a value longer than the column size raises error ORA-12899 (value too large for column). B and C are true.
concept: The size n in CHAR(n) or VARCHAR2(n) is a maximum that Oracle checks; it is not used to cut values. If a value is too long, the INSERT or UPDATE fails with ORA-12899 'value too large for column'. Some products behave differently in special settings — for example MySQL in non-strict mode truncates the value with only a warning — which is why the question names Oracle.
why: A — Correct. This statement is false: Oracle raises ORA-12899 instead of cutting the string, so A satisfies the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: CHAR(n) always uses n characters, padding with blanks. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: VARCHAR2 is variable-length and keeps only the given characters. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Too-long value in Oracle → error ORA-12899, never silent truncation.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, what is the largest value that can be stored in a column declared NUMBER(5,2)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: NUMBER(5,2) allows 5 digits in total, 2 of them after the decimal point, so only 3 digits remain before the point. The largest value is 999.99, which is not listed.
concept: In NUMBER(p, s) — and in standard DECIMAL(p, s) / NUMERIC(p, s) — p is the precision, the total number of significant digits, and s is the scale, the number of digits after the decimal point. The digits allowed before the point are p − s. So NUMBER(5,2) holds values from −999.99 to 999.99, while NUMBER(7,2) holds values up to 99999.99.
why: A — Wrong. 99999.99 needs 7 digits (5 before the point + 2 after); it fits NUMBER(7,2). This mistake reads 5 as 'digits before the point'.
B — Wrong. 9999.99 needs 6 digits in total; it fits NUMBER(6,2). NUMBER(5,2) allows only 3 digits before the point.
C — Wrong. 99999 has 5 digits before the point. With scale 2, only 5 − 2 = 3 digits are allowed there.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The largest value is 999.99, which is not among A–C.
work:
1. Precision p = 5 (total digits); scale s = 2 (digits after the point).
2. Digits before the point = p − s = 5 − 2 = 3.
3. Largest value = 999.99.
4. 999.99 is not among A–C → answer E.
Checked with the equivalent PostgreSQL type NUMERIC(5,2): 999.99 is accepted; 1000 gives 'numeric field overflow'.
tip: Digits before the point = p − s. NUMBER(5,2) → 3 + 2 → 999.99.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which SQL data type can store a date together with a time of day including fractional seconds, such as 2026-10-21 14:35:07.250?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: TIMESTAMP stores year, month, day, hour, minute and seconds with a fractional part. DATE cannot keep fractions of a second, and INTERVAL stores a length of time.
concept: SQL has several date-time types. DATE stores a calendar date (in standard SQL and PostgreSQL only the date; in Oracle, DATE also keeps hours, minutes and whole seconds). TIMESTAMP stores date and time with fractional seconds (Oracle keeps 6 fractional digits by default). TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE also stores the time-zone offset. INTERVAL stores a duration, such as 3 days or 2 hours 30 minutes.
why: A — Wrong. DATE cannot keep fractions of a second. In standard SQL and PostgreSQL it holds only the date; in Oracle it holds the date and time to whole seconds only.
B — Wrong. INTERVAL stores a span of time (for example INTERVAL '2' DAY), not a particular moment.
C — Correct. TIMESTAMP keeps the date, the time and fractional seconds.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Oracle trap: Oracle DATE does contain a time part (to the second); TIMESTAMP adds fractions of a second.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, which of the following data types is NOT meant for binary (raw byte) data such as images or audio?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CLOB (Character Large OBject) stores large text. RAW and BLOB store binary data that Oracle keeps as it is, without interpreting it.
concept: Oracle has separate types for text and for binary data. Text types: CHAR, VARCHAR2, CLOB (very large text, such as a whole book) and the old LONG. Binary types store unstructured bytes that Oracle does not interpret or convert between character sets: RAW(n) for small binary values (up to 2000 bytes by default), LONG RAW (an old type kept for backward compatibility) and BLOB (Binary Large OBject) for photos, audio, video and PDF files.
why: A — Wrong. RAW does hold binary data — bytes stored exactly as given, with no character-set conversion (for example a small image or an encryption key). So it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Correct. CLOB is for large character (text) data, not binary data, so it satisfies the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. BLOB is Oracle's main type for large binary objects such as photos and videos, so it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: B-LOB = Binary; C-LOB = Character. RAW and LONG RAW are binary too.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: A bank wants to store account balances such as 1520.75 exactly, without any binary rounding error. Which data type should the balance column use?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: NUMERIC/DECIMAL is an exact numeric type that stores decimal digits exactly; FLOAT and REAL are approximate binary floating-point types.
concept: SQL numeric types are of two kinds. Exact numeric types — INTEGER, SMALLINT, BIGINT, NUMERIC(p,s), DECIMAL(p,s) and Oracle's NUMBER(p,s) — store values exactly. Approximate numeric types — FLOAT, REAL, DOUBLE PRECISION — store values in binary floating-point form, so many decimal fractions (like 0.1) cannot be stored exactly and tiny errors appear. Money should always use an exact type.
why: A — Correct. NUMERIC(12,2) keeps exactly 2 decimal places (and up to 10 digits before the point), so 1520.75 is stored exactly. In PostgreSQL, 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 is true for NUMERIC values.
B — Wrong. FLOAT is approximate: values are kept in binary floating-point. In PostgreSQL, 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 is false for DOUBLE PRECISION values because of tiny rounding errors.
C — Wrong. REAL is single-precision floating point — even less precise than DOUBLE PRECISION, and not exact.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Money → DECIMAL/NUMERIC (Oracle NUMBER). Scientific measurements → FLOAT/DOUBLE.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: A column price is declared NUMBER(5,2) in Oracle. Which of the following values can be inserted into it WITHOUT an error?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 999.99 fits exactly, and 123.456 is accepted after rounding to 2 decimal places (123.46). 1000 needs 4 digits before the point, but only 3 are allowed, so it is rejected.
concept: For NUMBER(p,s), Oracle first rounds the value to s digits after the decimal point and then checks that at most p − s digits remain before the point. Extra decimal places therefore never cause an error — they are rounded — but too many digits before the point cause error ORA-01438 (value larger than specified precision allowed for this column).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 999.99 is exactly the largest value NUMBER(5,2) can hold.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 123.456 is rounded to scale 2 and stored as 123.46; rounding extra decimals does not raise an error.
C — Wrong. 1000 has 4 digits before the decimal point, but NUMBER(5,2) allows only 3, so Oracle raises ORA-01438.
D — Correct. Both A and B can be inserted.
E — Wrong. A and B are accepted, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Column NUMBER(5,2): at most 5 − 2 = 3 digits before the point and 2 after.
A. 999.99 → 3 digits before, 2 after → fits.
B. 123.456 → rounded to 123.46 → 3 digits before → fits (stored as 123.46).
C. 1000 → 1000.00 needs 4 digits before the point → error.
Checked with PostgreSQL NUMERIC(5,2) and DuckDB DECIMAL(5,2): 999.99 and 123.456 (stored 123.46) accepted; 1000 rejected.
tip: Too many decimals → rounded quietly. Too many digits before the point → error.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which of the following is NOT a constraint that can be declared in a CREATE TABLE statement?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CHECK, UNIQUE and NOT NULL are all standard SQL constraints, so none of A–C is a 'non-constraint'.
concept: Integrity constraints are rules that the DBMS checks on every INSERT and UPDATE. The standard SQL constraints are NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY (REFERENCES) and CHECK. Clauses such as ORDER BY, GROUP BY, UNION or DISTINCT are parts of queries, not constraints. (DEFAULT supplies a value when none is given; some products, such as SQL Server, call it a 'default constraint'.)
why: A — Wrong. CHECK is a constraint: it rejects rows for which a condition such as CHECK (age >= 18) is false. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. UNIQUE is a constraint: no two rows may have the same non-NULL value in the column(s). So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. NOT NULL is a constraint: the column must always have a value. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is a non-constraint, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three options are genuine SQL constraints; none of them satisfies the NOT stem.
tip: The five classic constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK. UNION, ORDER BY and GROUP BY are NOT constraints.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Each INSERT below is run separately (a failed INSERT does not stop the others). What does the final SELECT return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Row 2 is rejected because 15 >= 18 is FALSE. Row 3 is accepted because NULL >= 18 is UNKNOWN, and a CHECK constraint rejects a row only when its condition is FALSE. So 2 rows are stored.
concept: A CHECK constraint states a condition that every row must satisfy. SQL uses three-valued logic: a comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE. A CHECK constraint rejects a row only when the condition is FALSE; TRUE and UNKNOWN are both accepted. This is the opposite of WHERE, which keeps a row only when the condition is TRUE. To forbid NULL as well, add NOT NULL to the column.
why: A — Wrong. 1 comes from thinking that the NULL age also breaks the CHECK. NULL >= 18 is UNKNOWN, and a CHECK rejects a row only when the condition is FALSE, so row 3 is accepted.
B — Correct. Rows 1 (age 20) and 3 (age NULL) are stored; row 2 (age 15) is rejected.
C — Wrong. 3 would mean the CHECK was not enforced. The INSERT with age 15 fails with a check-constraint error, so that row is never stored.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
1. (1, 20): 20 >= 18 is TRUE → accepted.
2. (2, 15): 15 >= 18 is FALSE → rejected with a CHECK constraint error.
3. (3, NULL): NULL >= 18 is UNKNOWN → accepted (CHECK rejects only FALSE).
4. Rows stored: ids 1 and 3 → COUNT(*) = 2.
Verified: PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB all store ids 1 and 3 and reject id 2.
tip: WHERE keeps only TRUE rows; CHECK rejects only FALSE rows. So a NULL passes a CHECK but fails a WHERE.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q:
In PostgreSQL, table CUST has the primary key id, and its column email is declared UNIQUE (default settings). Consider the statements:
I. Two different rows can both have NULL in email.
II. The email of an existing row can be changed with UPDATE, provided the new value is not already used by another row.
III. A table can have only one UNIQUE constraint.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true: UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct, so many NULLs are allowed, and a unique value can be updated. III is false: a table may have many UNIQUE constraints (but only one PRIMARY KEY).
concept: A UNIQUE constraint says that no two rows may have the same non-NULL value in the column (or column group). Because NULL means 'unknown', two NULLs are not treated as equal, so PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL accept many NULLs in a UNIQUE column. SQL Server is the exception: its UNIQUE constraint allows only one NULL. A UNIQUE value can be updated like any other value. A table can have only one PRIMARY KEY but any number of UNIQUE constraints (one for each alternate key).
why: A — Wrong. 'I only' says II is false, but II is true: a UNIQUE column is not frozen; its value can be updated to any value that no other row uses.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
C — Wrong. It includes III, which is false — a table can have several UNIQUE constraints, for example on email and on phone — and it leaves out I, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked in PostgreSQL 16 (also SQLite and DuckDB) on CUST(id PRIMARY KEY, email UNIQUE, phone UNIQUE):
1. INSERT (2, NULL, '222') and (3, NULL, NULL) both succeed → two NULL emails allowed → I true.
2. UPDATE cust SET email = 'b@x.in' WHERE id = 1 succeeds → II true.
3. The same table already has two UNIQUE constraints (email and phone) → III false.
Correct set: I and II only → B.
tip: Common mistake (found in many notes): a unique key is NOT 'non-updatable', and 'only one NULL allowed' is true only in SQL Server. Oracle, MySQL and PostgreSQL allow many NULLs.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Table RESULT(roll, subject, marks) needs the composite primary key (roll, subject). Which of the following can define this key? (Assume no existing data breaks the key.)
opts: A table-level clause in CREATE TABLE:  PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject)
