ALTER TABLE result ADD CONSTRAINT pk_result PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject);
Writing PRIMARY KEY after both column definitions:  roll INT PRIMARY KEY, subject VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY
More than one of the above
exp: A composite key must be declared once over both columns: as a table-level constraint in CREATE TABLE, or later with ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT. Writing PRIMARY KEY on two separate columns means two primary keys, which is an error.
concept: A composite (compound) primary key is made of two or more columns taken together. A column-level (inline) constraint is written next to one column and can refer only to that column, so a multi-column key must be written as a table-level (out-of-line) constraint: PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject). It can also be added to an existing table with ALTER TABLE … ADD [CONSTRAINT name] PRIMARY KEY (…). Naming the constraint, for example pk_result, makes it easy to identify in error messages and to drop later.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A table-level PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject) clause is the usual way to declare a composite key in CREATE TABLE.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. ALTER TABLE … ADD CONSTRAINT … PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject) adds the same key to an existing table.

C — Wrong. Writing PRIMARY KEY after each of the two columns declares two primary keys, which is not allowed (PostgreSQL: 'multiple primary keys for table "result" are not allowed'). It does not create one composite key.
D — Correct. Both A and B define the composite key correctly.
E — Wrong. A and B are both correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked in PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB:
A. CREATE TABLE … PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject) → created; inserting (1, 'Maths') twice is rejected, (1, 'Physics') is accepted.
B. ALTER TABLE result ADD CONSTRAINT pk_result PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject) → succeeds in PostgreSQL and DuckDB (SQLite cannot add constraints with ALTER TABLE); a duplicate (1, 'Maths') is then rejected.
C. roll INT PRIMARY KEY, subject VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY → error in all three engines (more than one primary key).
True options: A and B → D.
tip: One table → one PRIMARY KEY. A key over several columns is written once, at table level: PRIMARY KEY (col1, col2).

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Table EMP has a CHECK constraint named chk_sal. Which statement removes this constraint?
opts: ALTER TABLE emp DROP CONSTRAINT chk_sal;
More than one of the above
exp: A constraint is part of the table's definition, so it is removed by altering the table: ALTER TABLE … DROP CONSTRAINT name.
concept: Constraints can be added to or removed from an existing table with ALTER TABLE: ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT name … and ALTER TABLE t DROP CONSTRAINT name. This is one reason to give constraints your own names (CONSTRAINT chk_sal CHECK (sal > 0)); otherwise the DBMS makes up a name, such as SYS_C007123 in Oracle or emp_sal_check in PostgreSQL, which you must look up before dropping it. Once the constraint is dropped, its rule is no longer checked.
why: A — Correct. ALTER TABLE … DROP CONSTRAINT name is the standard form (Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server). Checked in PostgreSQL: after it, a negative salary is accepted.
B — Wrong. There is no stand-alone DROP CONSTRAINT statement; DROP must be followed by an object type such as TABLE, VIEW or INDEX. PostgreSQL reports a syntax error.
C — Wrong. DELETE is a DML command that removes rows of data. It cannot remove part of a table's definition, so this is a syntax error.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Name your constraints (CONSTRAINT chk_sal …) so that dropping them later is easy.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Table DEPT is created as shown. A FOREIGN KEY in another table may reference which of the following DEPT columns?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A foreign key must reference a column (or column set) that is guaranteed unique: a PRIMARY KEY or a UNIQUE column. dno and dcode qualify; dname has no such constraint.
concept: A foreign key (FK) is a column whose values must match a value in a key column of another (or the same) table, or be NULL. The referenced column must be declared PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE, so that each FK value points to exactly one parent row. If REFERENCES names a column without such a constraint, the DBMS refuses to create the FK (PostgreSQL: 'there is no unique constraint matching given keys'; Oracle: ORA-02270). When REFERENCES dept is written without a column name, the primary key of DEPT is used.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. dno is the PRIMARY KEY of DEPT, the most common target of a foreign key.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. dcode is declared UNIQUE (an alternate key), so a foreign key can reference it too.
C — Wrong. dname has no PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint, so two departments could share a name and an FK value could point to several rows; the DBMS rejects REFERENCES dept(dname).
D — Correct. Both dno and dcode can be referenced.
E — Wrong. A and B are both valid targets, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked in PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB:
1. e1(dno INT REFERENCES dept(dno)) → created.
2. e2(dcode VARCHAR(5) REFERENCES dept(dcode)) → created.
3. e3(dname VARCHAR(10) REFERENCES dept(dname)) → error: no unique constraint matching the referenced column.
Valid targets: dno and dcode → D.
tip: A foreign key must point to a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE column. The FK column itself may be NULL and may repeat.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In Oracle, which constraint can be declared ONLY at the column level (inline, as part of the column definition) and not as a separate table-level (out-of-line) clause?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Oracle requires NOT NULL to be written inline with its column. UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK can be written either inline or as table-level constraints.
concept: A column-level (inline) constraint is written as part of one column's definition, for example sal NUMBER NOT NULL. A table-level (out-of-line) constraint is written after the column list, for example CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE (email), and is the only way to cover several columns. Oracle's rule is: NOT NULL must be declared inline; all other constraints can be declared either way. To add NOT NULL to an existing Oracle column, you modify the column: ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY sal NOT NULL.
why: A — Correct. In Oracle, a NOT NULL constraint can only be declared inline, as part of the column definition.
B — Wrong. UNIQUE can be inline (email VARCHAR2(30) UNIQUE) or table-level (UNIQUE (email), or a multi-column UNIQUE (first_name, last_name)).
C — Wrong. A FOREIGN KEY can be inline (dno NUMBER REFERENCES dept(dno)) or table-level (FOREIGN KEY (dno) REFERENCES dept(dno)); a multi-column foreign key must be table-level.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Only NOT NULL cannot go at table level (in Oracle); keys over several columns MUST go at table level.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which statement gives user ravi permission to read (SELECT) and add (INSERT) rows in table EMP?
opts: GRANT ravi SELECT, INSERT ON emp;
ALLOW SELECT, INSERT ON emp TO ravi;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON emp TO ravi;
More than one of the above
exp: The DCL syntax is GRANT privilege_list ON object TO user.
concept: GRANT and REVOKE are the DCL (Data Control Language) commands. GRANT gives privileges: GRANT privilege_list ON object TO user_or_role [WITH GRANT OPTION]. REVOKE takes them back: REVOKE privilege_list ON object FROM user_or_role. Object privileges include SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and REFERENCES; GRANT ALL gives every privilege on the object. Normally only the owner of the object, an administrator, or a user who holds the privilege WITH GRANT OPTION can grant it.
why: A — Wrong. The order is wrong: the privileges come right after GRANT, and the user comes last, after TO. PostgreSQL reports a syntax error.
B — Wrong. ALLOW is not an SQL command. Permissions are given only with GRANT.
C — Correct. GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON emp TO ravi; is the standard form (checked in PostgreSQL).
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: GRANT … TO …;  REVOKE … FROM …  — 'give TO, take FROM'.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q:
Consider the following statements about DCL:
I. A user who receives a privilege WITH GRANT OPTION can pass that privilege on to other users.
II. Privileges are taken back with REVOKE, for example  REVOKE INSERT ON emp FROM ravi;
III. GRANT and REVOKE are TCL (Transaction Control Language) commands.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true. III is false: GRANT and REVOKE are DCL commands; the TCL commands are COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT.
concept: WITH GRANT OPTION lets the receiver of a privilege grant it again to others. REVOKE removes a privilege; note the keyword FROM, not TO. A role is a named collection of privileges; granting one role to many users makes administration easier. GRANT and REVOKE form DCL, the Data Control Language, while COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT form TCL, the Transaction Control Language.
why: A — Wrong. 'I only' leaves out II, which is true: REVOKE … ON … FROM … is the correct way to take a privilege back.
B — Correct. I and II are true and III is false.
C — Wrong. It includes III, which is false (GRANT and REVOKE are DCL, not TCL), and it leaves out I, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked in PostgreSQL 16 with a test role: GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON emp TO r; REVOKE INSERT ON emp FROM r; GRANT SELECT ON emp TO r WITH GRANT OPTION; all succeed, and the catalog then shows SELECT with is_grantable = YES.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In SQL Server, members of which fixed database role can read (SELECT) all data from all user tables of the database?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: db_datareader gives read access to all user tables and views. db_datawriter can add, change and delete data, and db_ddladmin can run DDL commands.
concept: SQL Server gives every database a set of fixed database roles, each a ready-made bundle of permissions. db_owner: all activities in the database. db_securityadmin: manage role membership and permissions. db_accessadmin: add or remove database access for logins. db_backupoperator: back up the database. db_ddladmin: run any DDL command. db_datawriter: add, delete or change data in all user tables. db_datareader: read all data from all user tables and views. db_denydatareader / db_denydatawriter: cannot read / cannot change any data.
why: A — Correct. db_datareader members can run SELECT on all user tables and views.
B — Wrong. db_datawriter members can INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE data in all user tables, but this role by itself does not give permission to read; it is usually combined with db_datareader.
C — Wrong. db_ddladmin members can run DDL commands such as CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE; this role is about structure, not about reading data.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: datareader = read; datawriter = write; ddladmin = DDL; accessadmin = who can get into the database; securityadmin = permissions and roles.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In SQL Server, which of the following is NOT a fixed database-level role?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: sysadmin is a fixed SERVER role (it works on the whole SQL Server instance), not a database role. db_owner and db_securityadmin are fixed database roles.
concept: SQL Server has two levels of fixed roles. Fixed server roles apply to the whole server instance: sysadmin (can do anything on the server), serveradmin, securityadmin, processadmin, setupadmin, bulkadmin, diskadmin and dbcreator. Fixed database roles apply inside one database and start with db_: db_owner, db_securityadmin, db_accessadmin, db_backupoperator, db_ddladmin, db_datawriter, db_datareader, db_denydatawriter and db_denydatareader. A role named db_sysadmin does not exist.
why: A — Wrong. db_owner IS a fixed database role (its members can do all configuration and maintenance work in the database), so it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. db_securityadmin IS a fixed database role (its members manage role membership and permissions), so it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Correct. sysadmin is a fixed server role, not a database-level role.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Fixed database roles start with db_. sysadmin has no db_ prefix because it works at server level; 'db_sysadmin' is a made-up option.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In standard SQL, database objects are organised in a hierarchy. Which is the correct form of a fully qualified table name?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A catalog contains schemas, and a schema contains tables, views and other objects, so the full name goes from the biggest container to the smallest: catalog.schema.table.
concept: The SQL standard arranges names in levels: catalogs contain schemas, and each schema contains objects such as tables, views and domains. A name like college.academics.student means table STUDENT in schema ACADEMICS of catalog COLLEGE. Products map this differently: in PostgreSQL and SQL Server the catalog is the database (database.schema.table); in Oracle a schema is the set of objects owned by one user (user.table).
why: A — Wrong. The top two levels are swapped: a schema lives inside a catalog, so the catalog must come first.
B — Correct. Catalog → schema → table, from the largest container to the object.
C — Wrong. This writes the levels from smallest to largest. SQL qualified names start with the outermost container.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Like a folder path, the largest container comes first: catalog.schema.table.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Table T(id) already contains the committed rows 1 and 2. The statements below are then run as one transaction. Which rows does T contain at the end?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: ROLLBACK TO s1 undoes only the work done after s1 (the INSERT of 4 and the DELETE of 1). The INSERT of 3, made before s1, stays; then 5 is inserted and everything is committed: 1, 2, 3, 5.
concept: A savepoint is a named marker inside a transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes every change made after that marker but keeps the changes made before it, and the transaction stays open. Savepoints set after the marker (here s2) are removed too. COMMIT then makes all remaining changes of the transaction permanent. Rows committed before the transaction began are not affected by any rollback.
why: A — Wrong. This keeps the DELETE of row 1. But the DELETE ran after s1, so ROLLBACK TO s1 undoes it and row 1 comes back.
B — Wrong. This ignores the ROLLBACK TO s1. Row 4 was inserted after s1, so it is undone and is not in the final table.
C — Wrong. This treats ROLLBACK TO s1 like a full ROLLBACK. Only the work after s1 is undone; the INSERT of 3, made before s1, is kept.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The final rows are 1, 2, 3 and 5, which is not among A–C.
work:
Start (committed): 1, 2.
1. INSERT 3 → 1, 2, 3.
2. SAVEPOINT s1.
3. INSERT 4 → 1, 2, 3, 4.
4. SAVEPOINT s2.
5. DELETE id = 1 → 2, 3, 4.
6. ROLLBACK TO s1 → steps 3–5 undone → 1, 2, 3 (s2 is discarded; the transaction is still open).
7. INSERT 5 → 1, 2, 3, 5.
8. COMMIT → 1, 2, 3, 5 made permanent.
9. '1, 2, 3, 5' is not among A–C → E.
Verified in PostgreSQL (inside BEGIN … COMMIT) and SQLite: rows 1, 2, 3, 5.
tip: In a savepoint trace, cross out only the statements between the savepoint and the ROLLBACK TO — nothing else.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Inside a transaction, the statement  ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;  is executed. Which of the following is true just after it?
opts: Changes made after sp1 are undone, and the transaction is still active
All changes of the transaction are undone, and the transaction ends
Changes made before sp1 are committed (made permanent)
More than one of the above
exp: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work done after the savepoint; it neither ends the transaction nor commits anything.
concept: TCL has three main commands. COMMIT ends the transaction and makes all its changes permanent. ROLLBACK (without TO) ends the transaction and undoes all its changes. SAVEPOINT name marks a point inside the transaction, and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes only the changes made after that point. After ROLLBACK TO, the transaction continues: you can do more work and then COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The earlier changes are still uncommitted, so a later plain ROLLBACK would remove them as well.
why: A — Correct. Work after sp1 is undone; the transaction stays open, and sp1 itself still exists (you could roll back to it again).
B — Wrong. That describes a plain ROLLBACK (without TO). ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT is only a partial rollback.
C — Wrong. Nothing is committed by ROLLBACK TO. The changes made before sp1 remain uncommitted, and a later ROLLBACK would still undo them.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Verified in PostgreSQL and SQLite: BEGIN; INSERT 1; SAVEPOINT a; INSERT 2; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT a; INSERT 3; ROLLBACK; → the table ends up empty.
1. INSERT 3 after ROLLBACK TO worked → the transaction was still open.
2. The final ROLLBACK also removed row 1 → row 1 had not been committed by ROLLBACK TO.
tip: ROLLBACK TO = partial undo, the transaction continues. ROLLBACK = full undo, the transaction ends.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: In PostgreSQL, table T(id) already contains the committed rows 1 and 2. Then the statements below are run. Which rows does T contain at the end?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: RELEASE SAVEPOINT only removes the marker p; it does not commit anything. The final ROLLBACK undoes the whole transaction (rows 3 and 4), leaving the earlier committed rows 1 and 2.
concept: RELEASE SAVEPOINT name (standard SQL; supported by PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite, but not by Oracle) destroys a savepoint, so you can no longer roll back to it. The changes made after the savepoint stay part of the transaction and are still uncommitted. Only COMMIT makes changes permanent, and a plain ROLLBACK undoes everything since the transaction began. Rows committed by earlier transactions are never touched by a later ROLLBACK.
why: A — Wrong. This treats RELEASE SAVEPOINT as a COMMIT. Releasing a savepoint only removes the marker; rows 3 and 4 were still uncommitted, so ROLLBACK undoes them.
B — Wrong. This assumes that the work done before the savepoint (row 3) became permanent. Nothing in this transaction was committed, so ROLLBACK removes row 3 as well.
C — Wrong. ROLLBACK undoes only the current transaction. Rows 1 and 2 were committed earlier, so they stay.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. T contains only rows 1 and 2, which is not among A–C.
work:
Start (committed): 1, 2.
1. BEGIN → a new transaction starts.
2. INSERT 3 → 1, 2, 3 (3 is uncommitted).
3. SAVEPOINT p.
4. INSERT 4 → 1, 2, 3, 4.
5. RELEASE SAVEPOINT p → marker p removed; rows 3 and 4 are still uncommitted.
6. ROLLBACK → the whole transaction is undone → 1, 2.
7. '1, 2' is not among A–C → E.
Verified in PostgreSQL and SQLite: rows 1, 2.
tip: RELEASE SAVEPOINT is not COMMIT. Only COMMIT makes changes permanent.

topic: SQL: DDL, DML, DCL, TCL & Data Types
q: Which of the following statements ends the current transaction?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: COMMIT ends the transaction by saving its changes; ROLLBACK ends it by undoing them. SAVEPOINT only marks a point inside the transaction, which continues.
concept: A transaction is a group of operations treated as one unit. It ends in one of two ways: COMMIT, which makes all its changes permanent and visible to other users, or ROLLBACK, which undoes all its changes. After either one, the next SQL statement starts a new transaction. SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT work inside a transaction and do not end it. (In Oracle and MySQL, a DDL statement also ends the transaction, because it causes an implicit COMMIT.)
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. COMMIT makes all changes of the transaction permanent and ends it.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. ROLLBACK (without TO) undoes all changes of the transaction and ends it.
C — Wrong. SAVEPOINT sp1 only places a named marker inside the running transaction; the transaction continues and still needs COMMIT or ROLLBACK to end.
D — Correct. Both COMMIT and ROLLBACK end the transaction.
E — Wrong. A and B are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: A transaction ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK (and, in Oracle/MySQL, with the implicit commit of a DDL statement). SAVEPOINT never ends it.

q: In the logical processing order of a SELECT query, in which order are the clauses applied?
opts: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
FROM → GROUP BY → WHERE → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
More than one of the above
exp: The DBMS first takes the rows FROM the tables, filters them with WHERE, makes groups with GROUP BY, filters the groups with HAVING, then computes the SELECT list, and finally sorts with ORDER BY.
concept: We WRITE a query starting with SELECT, but the DBMS logically EVALUATES it in a different order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT (then DISTINCT) → ORDER BY. Each step works on the output of the step before it. This order explains many rules: a column alias made in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE (WHERE runs earlier), but it can be used in ORDER BY (ORDER BY runs later).
why: A — Wrong. This is the order in which we WRITE the clauses, not the order in which the DBMS evaluates them. SELECT cannot be evaluated first, because the rows it needs come from FROM.
B — Correct. Rows come from FROM, are filtered by WHERE, grouped by GROUP BY, the groups are filtered by HAVING, the SELECT list is computed, and ORDER BY sorts the final rows.
C — Wrong. WHERE always works on single rows BEFORE groups are formed. Filtering after grouping is the job of HAVING, so GROUP BY cannot come before WHERE.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Memory line: 'Fruits Will Grow Healthy, Students Order' = FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.

q: In Oracle, MySQL and PostgreSQL, the query below stops with an error such as "column Annual does not exist". What is the reason?
opts: A column alias cannot be given to an arithmetic expression such as Salary * 12.
The WHERE clause cannot compare a calculated value with a number.
WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list, so the alias Annual does not exist yet.
More than one of the above
exp: An alias is created when the SELECT list is evaluated, and that happens after WHERE. So WHERE cannot see Annual; write WHERE Salary * 12 > 500000 instead.
concept: A column alias (AS name) is a temporary heading created in the SELECT step. Because the logical order is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY, the clauses WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING run before the alias exists. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so ORDER BY Annual is allowed. To filter on a calculated value, repeat the expression in WHERE or use a subquery in FROM.
why: A — Wrong. Giving an alias to an expression is perfectly legal: SELECT Name, Salary * 12 AS Annual FROM EMP; runs without any problem. The error comes only from using Annual inside WHERE.
B — Wrong. WHERE can compare any expression with a value; WHERE Salary * 12 > 500000 is valid. The trouble is the alias name, not the calculation.
C — Correct. The SELECT list (where Annual is defined) is evaluated after WHERE, so when WHERE is checked the name Annual is still unknown.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP(EmpID, Name, Salary)

SELECT Name, Salary * 12 AS Annual
FROM EMP
WHERE Annual > 500000;
work:
PostgreSQL 16: ERROR: column "annual" does not exist (pointing at WHERE Annual).
Fix 1: WHERE Salary * 12 > 500000 → runs.
Fix 2: ORDER BY Annual DESC → runs, because ORDER BY comes after SELECT.
(SQLite and DuckDB accept the alias in WHERE as their own extension; standard SQL, Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL do not.)
tip: Standard SQL: a column alias is NOT allowed in WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING, but it is allowed in ORDER BY. (MySQL also accepts it in GROUP BY and HAVING, and PostgreSQL in GROUP BY, but Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL all reject it in WHERE.)

q: How many rows does the query below return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DISTINCT removes rows whose whole (Dept, City) pair is repeated. The distinct pairs are (IT, Patna), (HR, Gaya), (HR, NULL) and (IT, Gaya), so 4 rows are returned.
concept: DISTINCT works on the complete row of the SELECT list, not on the first column only: two rows are duplicates only when every listed column matches. For DISTINCT (and also for GROUP BY), two NULLs are treated as 'not distinct', so they collapse into one row — even though NULL = NULL is not TRUE inside a WHERE condition.
why: A — Correct. The four different (Dept, City) pairs are (IT, Patna), (HR, Gaya), (HR, NULL) and (IT, Gaya).
B — Wrong. 5 comes from treating the two (HR, NULL) rows as different. For DISTINCT, NULLs count as duplicates of each other, so only one (HR, NULL) row is kept.
C — Wrong. 2 is the number of different Dept values (IT and HR). DISTINCT applies to the combination of all selected columns, not to the first column alone.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STAFF
Name  | Dept | City
Ravi  | IT   | Patna
Meena | HR   | Gaya
Amit  | IT   | Patna
Sita  | HR   | NULL
Kiran | HR   | NULL
Arjun | IT   | Gaya

SELECT DISTINCT Dept, City FROM STAFF;
work:
FROM: 6 rows.
SELECT Dept, City: (IT, Patna), (HR, Gaya), (IT, Patna), (HR, NULL), (HR, NULL), (IT, Gaya)
DISTINCT: (IT, Patna) twice → keep one; (HR, NULL) twice → keep one
Result: (IT, Patna), (HR, Gaya), (HR, NULL), (IT, Gaya) → 4 rows
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: 4 rows in all three.
tip: DISTINCT and GROUP BY treat NULLs as equal (one NULL row survives); the = operator never does.

q: Which of the following queries display the Name column under the heading EmpName?
opts: SELECT Name AS EmpName FROM EMP;
SELECT Name FROM EMP AS EmpName;
More than one of the above
exp: A column alias can be written with or without the keyword AS, so A and B both show the heading EmpName. In C, EmpName is an alias of the table, so the column heading stays Name.
concept: An alias is a temporary name that lives only for one query. A column alias changes the heading in the output: SELECT Name AS EmpName (AS is optional, so SELECT Name EmpName also works). A table alias gives the table a short name to use inside the query, for example FROM EMP E ... E.Name; it does not change any heading. Note: Oracle does not allow the word AS before a table alias (write FROM EMP E).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. AS EmpName is the standard way to give a column a new heading.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The keyword AS is optional for a column alias, so Name EmpName also renames the heading.
C — Wrong. Here EmpName is an alias for the TABLE EMP, not for the column, so the heading remains Name. (Oracle would even reject AS before a table alias.)
D — Correct. A and B both give the column the heading EmpName; C only renames the table.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
code: EMP(EmpID, Name, Dept, Salary)
work:
Column headings read from the result (cursor description) in SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB:
A → EmpName
B → EmpName
C → Name (EmpName is only the table alias)
(PostgreSQL prints empname in small letters and Oracle prints EMPNAME in capitals, because unquoted names are not case-sensitive and each product folds them to one case; the heading is still the alias.)
tip: An alias with a space needs double quotes: SELECT Name AS "Emp Name" FROM EMP;

q: What does the keyword ALL do in the query SELECT ALL Dept FROM EMP; ?
opts: It removes duplicate Dept values from the result.
It displays every column of the table, just like *.
It causes an error, because ALL can be used only with a subquery, as in > ALL (…).
More than one of the above
exp: ALL is the default 'set quantifier' of SELECT: it keeps every row, duplicates included. SELECT ALL Dept gives IT, HR, IT, HR — exactly the same as SELECT Dept.
concept: Right after the word SELECT you may write DISTINCT or ALL. DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result; ALL keeps all rows, duplicates included. ALL is the default, so people rarely write it. The same word ALL is also a separate comparison operator used with subqueries (Salary > ALL (subquery)) — that is a different use.
why: A — Wrong. Removing duplicates is the job of DISTINCT, which is the opposite of ALL.
B — Wrong. * means 'all columns'. ALL here means 'all rows'; the query still shows only the Dept column.
C — Wrong. SELECT ALL is valid syntax in standard SQL and in Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL. The comparison > ALL (subquery) is a different use of the same word.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. ALL keeps every row, including duplicates. It is the default, so SELECT ALL Dept is the same as SELECT Dept (result: IT, HR, IT, HR).
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept
1     | Ravi  | IT
2     | Meena | HR
3     | Amit  | IT
4     | Sita  | HR

SELECT ALL Dept FROM EMP;
work:
FROM EMP: 4 rows.
SELECT ALL Dept: IT, HR, IT, HR (duplicates kept).
SELECT DISTINCT Dept would give only IT, HR.
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: SELECT ALL Dept and SELECT Dept return identical rows.
tip: SELECT ALL = plain SELECT (the default). SELECT DISTINCT = remove duplicate rows.

q:
Consider the query SELECT Name FROM EMP WHERE Salary > 40000; and the statements:
I. The WHERE clause does the job of the selection (σ) operation of relational algebra.
II. The column list after SELECT does the job of the projection (π) operation.
III. Like π, the SELECT clause removes duplicate rows automatically.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: WHERE picks rows (like σ) and the SELECT list picks columns (like π). But SQL keeps duplicate rows unless DISTINCT is written, while π in relational algebra always removes them, so III is false.
concept: Relational algebra has σ (selection: choose the ROWS that satisfy a condition) and π (projection: choose COLUMNS). In SQL, the WHERE clause plays the role of σ and the column list after SELECT plays the role of π — so the SQL keyword SELECT is closer to projection, not to relational 'selection'. Another difference: relational algebra works on sets, so π removes duplicates, but SQL works on multisets (bags) and keeps duplicates unless you write DISTINCT.
why: A — Correct. Statement I (WHERE ≈ σ) and statement II (SELECT list ≈ π) are true and statement III is false, so 'I and II only' is the right combination.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: SQL's SELECT keeps duplicates (SELECT Dept FROM EMP shows IT many times) unless DISTINCT is used. It also leaves out I, which is true.
C — Wrong. Statement III is false, so 'all three' cannot be right.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Relational algebra form of the query: π Name (σ Salary > 40000 (EMP))
WHERE Salary > 40000 → σ (choose rows)
SELECT Name → π (choose columns)
Duplicate test on the 7-row EMP table: SELECT Dept FROM EMP WHERE Salary > 40000 returned HR, IT, IT on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB → duplicates kept, so III is false.
tip: Common mistake (also in the notes): 'SELECT is the same as projection'. Only the SELECT column list ≈ π, the WHERE clause ≈ σ, and SQL keeps duplicates while π removes them.

q: How many rows does the query below return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: AND is evaluated before OR, so the condition means Dept = 'HR' OR (Dept = 'IT' AND Salary > 45000). That gives Meena and Sita (HR) plus Ravi and Arjun (IT, above 45000) = 4 rows.
concept: When a condition mixes AND and OR without brackets, SQL applies NOT first, then AND, then OR — just as × is done before + in arithmetic. So P OR Q AND R means P OR (Q AND R). If you want (P OR Q) AND R, you must write the brackets yourself.
why: A — Wrong. 2 is the answer to (Dept = 'HR' OR Dept = 'IT') AND Salary > 45000, i.e. if OR were done first (only Ravi and Arjun). Without brackets, AND is done first.
B — Wrong. 3 would come from (Dept = 'HR' OR Dept = 'IT') AND Salary >= 45000 (Ravi, Sita, Arjun) — wrong grouping and also the wrong operator.
C — Correct. Dept = 'HR' OR (Dept = 'IT' AND Salary > 45000) is TRUE for Ravi, Meena, Sita and Arjun.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Name FROM EMP
WHERE Dept = 'HR' OR Dept = 'IT' AND Salary > 45000;
work:
SQL reads the condition as: Dept = 'HR' OR (Dept = 'IT' AND Salary > 45000)
Dept = 'IT' AND Salary > 45000 → Ravi (50000), Arjun (60000)
Dept = 'HR' → Meena, Sita
WHERE keeps: Ravi, Meena, Sita, Arjun → 4 rows
(Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.)
tip: Precedence: NOT > AND > OR. When in doubt, add brackets.

q: When a WHERE condition uses NOT, AND and OR without brackets, which operator is applied first?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The precedence of the logical operators in SQL is NOT first, then AND, then OR.
concept: SQL logical operators have a fixed priority (precedence): NOT is applied first, then AND, then OR. Comparison operators such as =, < and > are evaluated even before NOT. So NOT a = 1 AND b = 2 OR c = 3 is read as ((NOT (a = 1)) AND (b = 2)) OR (c = 3).
why: A — Correct. NOT has the highest precedence of the three; it applies to the condition written just after it.
B — Wrong. AND comes second: it is applied after NOT but before OR.
C — Wrong. OR has the lowest precedence, so it is applied last.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: NOT > AND > OR, just like unary minus > × > + in arithmetic.

q: Which employees does the query below return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: NOT applies only to Dept = 'IT', so the condition is (Dept <> 'IT') AND (Age < 25). Only Kiran (SALES, 24) satisfies both, and 'Kiran only' is not given in A–C.
concept: NOT has higher precedence than AND and OR, so without brackets it negates only the single condition written right after it. NOT Dept = 'IT' AND Age < 25 means (NOT Dept = 'IT') AND (Age < 25). To negate the whole condition you must write NOT (Dept = 'IT' AND Age < 25).
why: A — Wrong. Amit is the result of Dept = 'IT' AND Age < 25, i.e. if NOT were ignored. Amit works in IT, so NOT Dept = 'IT' is FALSE for him.
B — Wrong. 'Everyone except Amit' is the result of NOT (Dept = 'IT' AND Age < 25), i.e. if NOT covered the whole condition. Without brackets NOT covers only Dept = 'IT'.
C — Wrong. Meena's age is exactly 25, and 25 < 25 is FALSE. Meena would appear only with Age <= 25.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. Only Kiran (SALES, age 24) satisfies (Dept <> 'IT') AND (Age < 25), and that result is not among A–C.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Name FROM EMP
WHERE NOT Dept = 'IT' AND Age < 25;
work:
SQL reads: (NOT Dept = 'IT') AND (Age < 25)
NOT Dept = 'IT' → Meena, Sita, Kiran, Pooja
of these, Age < 25 → Kiran (24); Meena (25), Sita (28), Pooja (27) fail
Result: Kiran only (checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB)

q: Which employees does the query below return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: By De Morgan's law, NOT (Dept = 'HR' OR Salary < 40000) = (Dept <> 'HR' AND Salary >= 40000), which gives Ravi, Amit and Arjun. Then Age < 30 removes Ravi (32), leaving Amit and Arjun.
concept: De Morgan's laws: NOT (P OR Q) = (NOT P) AND (NOT Q), and NOT (P AND Q) = (NOT P) OR (NOT Q). The opposite of < is >=, so NOT (Salary < 40000) means Salary >= 40000 (40000 itself is included). Brackets are evaluated first, then NOT, then AND, then OR.
why: A — Correct. Only Amit (IT, 40000, 23) and Arjun (IT, 60000, 29) are outside HR, earn at least 40000 and are younger than 30.
B — Wrong. Ravi, Amit and Arjun is the result before the last condition. Ravi is 32, so Age < 30 removes him.
C — Wrong. This comes from reading NOT (Salary < 40000) as Salary > 40000, which drops Amit. The opposite of < 40000 is >= 40000, so Amit's 40000 qualifies.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Name FROM EMP
WHERE NOT (Dept = 'HR' OR Salary < 40000) AND Age < 30;
work:
Step 1 (brackets): Dept = 'HR' OR Salary < 40000 is TRUE for Meena, Sita, Kiran, Pooja
Step 2 (NOT): rows left → Ravi (IT, 50000, 32), Amit (IT, 40000, 23), Arjun (IT, 60000, 29)
Step 3 (AND Age < 30): Ravi (32) removed
Result: Amit, Arjun (checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB)

q: In Oracle, which of the following can be used as the 'not equal to' comparison operator in a WHERE clause?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: <> is the ISO standard 'not equal to' operator, and Oracle also accepts != (and ^=). There is no >< operator.
concept: The standard SQL 'not equal to' operator is <>. Oracle also accepts != and ^= with the same meaning, and MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL accept != too. There is no >< operator in SQL. Remember that every comparison with NULL, including <>, gives UNKNOWN, so Dept <> 'IT' does not return rows whose Dept is NULL.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. <> is the ISO standard not-equal operator and Oracle supports it.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Oracle (like MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL) accepts != as another way of writing <>.
C — Wrong. >< is not an operator in Oracle or in any major SQL product; writing it gives a syntax error.
D — Correct. Both <> and != mean 'not equal to' in Oracle; >< does not exist.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work:
Oracle documentation lists !=, ^= and <> as the inequality operators.
Check on the 7-row EMP table in PostgreSQL 16, SQLite and DuckDB:
WHERE Dept <> 'IT' → 4 rows
WHERE Dept != 'IT' → 4 rows
WHERE Dept >< 'IT' → error in all three
tip: Oracle has three spellings of not-equal: <>, != and ^=. Only <> is the ISO standard one.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: Which condition is NOT equivalent to Salary BETWEEN 30000 AND 50000?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: BETWEEN includes both end values, so it equals >= 30000 AND <= 50000. Option B uses strict > and <, so it leaves out salaries of exactly 30000 and 50000.
concept: x BETWEEN low AND high is a short form of x >= low AND x <= high — both end values are included (inclusive). NOT BETWEEN means x < low OR x > high. BETWEEN works on numbers, dates and text, and the smaller value must be written first.
why: A — Wrong. This is exactly the definition of BETWEEN (both ends included), so it IS equivalent and does not satisfy the stem.
B — Correct. Strict > and < exclude the end values: a salary of exactly 30000 or 50000 satisfies BETWEEN but not this condition, so B is NOT equivalent.
C — Wrong. By De Morgan's law, NOT (Salary < 30000 OR Salary > 50000) = Salary >= 30000 AND Salary <= 50000, which is the same as BETWEEN (and for a NULL salary both give UNKNOWN).
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is not equivalent, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Test on the 7-row EMP table (salaries 50000, 30000, 40000, 45000, 30000, 60000, 35000):
BETWEEN 30000 AND 50000 → 6 rows (all except 60000)
A → the same 6 rows
B → only 40000, 45000, 35000 (3 rows; both 30000s and the 50000 are lost)
C → the same 6 rows
(Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.)
tip: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends: think '>= and <='.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: What value does the query below print? (Look carefully at the order of the two limits.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 30000 means Salary >= 50000 AND Salary <= 30000, which is FALSE for every salary. NOT makes it TRUE for the 5 non-NULL salaries; for Sita's NULL salary it stays UNKNOWN, so the count is 5.
concept: BETWEEN never swaps its limits: x BETWEEN a AND b always means x >= a AND x <= b. If a is larger than b, no value can satisfy it, so BETWEEN returns no rows and NOT BETWEEN returns every row with a non-NULL value. A NULL value makes both BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN UNKNOWN, so such a row never qualifies. (PostgreSQL has a special BETWEEN SYMMETRIC that does swap the limits.)
why: A — Wrong. 1 (only Arjun's 60000) is what you get if the limits were swapped automatically, i.e. NOT BETWEEN 30000 AND 50000. Standard BETWEEN does not swap them.
B — Wrong. 6 also counts Sita, but her Salary is NULL: NULL NOT BETWEEN … is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE.
C — Correct. BETWEEN 50000 AND 30000 is FALSE for every real salary, so NOT BETWEEN is TRUE for the 5 rows that have a non-NULL salary.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Salary
1     | Ravi  | 50000
2     | Meena | 30000
3     | Amit  | 40000
4     | Sita  | NULL
5     | Kiran | 30000
6     | Arjun | 60000

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMP
WHERE Salary NOT BETWEEN 50000 AND 30000;
work:
BETWEEN 50000 AND 30000 ≡ Salary >= 50000 AND Salary <= 30000 → FALSE for every number
NOT BETWEEN → TRUE for Ravi, Meena, Amit, Kiran, Arjun (5 rows)
Sita: NULL >= 50000 is UNKNOWN → NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN → row rejected
COUNT(*) = 5 (SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB all print 5)
Compare: NOT BETWEEN 30000 AND 50000 → 1 (Arjun); PostgreSQL NOT BETWEEN SYMMETRIC 50000 AND 30000 → 1
tip: Always write the smaller value first in BETWEEN. Reversed limits → BETWEEN finds nothing.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: The condition Dept IN ('HR', 'SALES') is equivalent to which of the following?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: IN is a short form of several = comparisons joined by OR: the row qualifies if Dept equals any one value in the list.
concept: x IN (v1, v2, …) is TRUE when x equals at least one of the listed values, so it is the same as x = v1 OR x = v2 OR …. NOT IN means x <> v1 AND x <> v2 AND …. The list can also come from a subquery, for example Dept IN (SELECT DeptName FROM DEPT).
why: A — Correct. IN ('HR', 'SALES') is TRUE exactly when Dept = 'HR' or Dept = 'SALES'.
B — Wrong. With AND, one Dept value would have to equal 'HR' and 'SALES' at the same time, which is impossible, so this condition returns no rows.
C — Wrong. BETWEEN 'HR' AND 'SALES' is an alphabetical range; it also accepts every value in between, such as 'IT' or 'MARKETING', so it is not the same as a list of two values.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: IN = many ORs of =; NOT IN = many ANDs of <>.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: Which name is NOT returned by the query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: '_a%' means exactly one character, then the letter a, then anything — so the SECOND letter must be 'a'. Asha's second letter is 's', so Asha is not returned; Rahul, Kavya and Sagar are.
concept: In LIKE patterns, _ (underscore) matches exactly one character and % matches any number of characters (zero, one or many). So '_a%' = second character is a; 'a%' = starts with a; '%a' = ends with a; '%a_' = second-last character is a; '___' = exactly three characters.
why: A — Wrong. Rahul = R + a + hul: one character, then 'a', then the rest. It matches, so it IS returned.
B — Wrong. Sagar = S + a + gar: the second letter is 'a', so it IS returned.
C — Correct. Asha = A + s + ha: the second letter is 's', not 'a', so Asha is NOT returned. (Its first letter is A, but '_a%' checks the second position.)
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. Asha is not returned, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT
Roll | Name
1    | Asha
2    | Rahul
3    | Kavya
4    | Aman
5    | Neha
6    | Sagar

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE Name LIKE '_a%';
work:
Pattern '_a%': position 1 = any one character, position 2 = 'a', then anything
Asha → 2nd letter s ✗
Rahul → a ✓
Kavya → a ✓
Aman → m ✗
Neha → e ✗
Sagar → a ✓
Result: Rahul, Kavya, Sagar (same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB)
tip: _ = exactly one character; % = zero or more characters.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: Which of the following names are returned by the query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: '%a_' means anything, then 'a', then exactly one more character — so the second-last letter must be 'a'. Aman (a-n) and Sagar (a-r) match; Kavya ends in y-a, so its second-last letter is 'y'.
concept: Read a LIKE pattern position by position. % stands for any number of characters, _ for exactly one. In '%a_' the _ is at the end, so the 'a' must be the second-last character. Compare: '%a' (last letter a) and '_a%' (second letter a).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Aman ends in 'a' followed by one character 'n', so it matches '%a_'.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Sagar ends in 'a' followed by one character 'r', so it matches.
C — Wrong. Kavya's last two letters are 'y' and 'a', so its second-last letter is 'y'. Kavya would match '%a' (ends with a), not '%a_'.
D — Correct. Both Aman and Sagar are returned; Kavya is not.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
code:
STUDENT
Roll | Name
1    | Asha
2    | Rahul
3    | Kavya
4    | Aman
5    | Neha
6    | Sagar

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT
WHERE Name LIKE '%a_';
work:
Pattern '%a_': any characters, then 'a', then exactly one character (second-last letter = a)
Asha → second-last h ✗
Rahul → u ✗
Kavya → y ✗
Aman → a ✓
Neha → h ✗
Sagar → a ✓
Result: Aman, Sagar (same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB)
tip: '%a_' = second-last letter a; '_a%' = second letter a. Look at which side the _ is on.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: A STUDENT table has two names, 'Asha' and 'arun'. Which statements about SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE 'a%'; are correct?
opts: In PostgreSQL it returns only 'arun', because LIKE is case-sensitive there.
In MySQL, with its default case-insensitive collation, it returns both 'Asha' and 'arun'.
In Oracle it returns both names, because LIKE ignores letter case by default.
More than one of the above
exp: Whether LIKE cares about capital letters depends on the product: PostgreSQL and Oracle compare case-sensitively by default (only 'arun'), while MySQL's default collation is case-insensitive (both names).
concept: LIKE compares characters using the column's collation (the rules for comparing text). In PostgreSQL and Oracle the default comparison is case-sensitive, so 'a%' does not match 'Asha'; PostgreSQL offers ILIKE for case-insensitive matching, and in Oracle you can write UPPER(Name) LIKE 'A%'. MySQL's default collations (names ending in _ci = case-insensitive) and SQL Server's usual default collation ignore case, so there 'a%' matches 'Asha' too.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. PostgreSQL's LIKE is case-sensitive, and 'Asha' starts with a capital A, so only 'arun' matches (ILIKE would match both).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. MySQL's default collation (for example utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci, where ci = case-insensitive) treats 'A' and 'a' as equal, so both names match.
C — Wrong. Oracle's LIKE is case-sensitive by default (binary comparison), so it returns only 'arun'. To ignore case in Oracle you write UPPER(Name) LIKE 'A%'.
D — Correct. A and B are true; C is false.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work:
Two-row table ('Asha', 'arun'):
PostgreSQL 16: LIKE 'a%' → arun; ILIKE 'a%' → Asha, arun
DuckDB: LIKE 'a%' → arun (case-sensitive)
SQLite: LIKE 'a%' → Asha, arun (case-insensitive for English letters, like MySQL's default)
Oracle: case-sensitive by default (NLS_COMP = BINARY) → arun only
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): "LIKE 'john' also returns JOHN". That is true only in case-insensitive setups such as MySQL or SQL Server defaults, not in Oracle or PostgreSQL. Also, the [abc] and [^abc] wildcards shown in the notes work only in SQL Server and MS Access.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: Which WHERE condition returns only the offers whose Discount contains a real % sign (D1 and D3)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: ESCAPE '!' tells LIKE that the character just after ! must be taken literally. So '%!%%' means: anything, a real % sign, anything — which matches '50%' and '25% off' only.
concept: In LIKE, % and _ are wildcards. To search for these characters themselves, choose an escape character with the ESCAPE clause and write it just before the wildcard: LIKE '%!%%' ESCAPE '!' finds a literal %, and LIKE '%!_%' ESCAPE '!' finds a literal underscore. Any character that does not occur in the data can be the escape character (! and # are common choices).
why: A — Wrong. Without ESCAPE every % is a wildcard, so '%%%' just means 'any string' and returns all four rows (D1, D2, D3, D4).
B — Correct. The % after ! is a literal percent sign, and the outer % signs allow any text before and after it, so only '50%' (D1) and '25% off' (D3) match.
C — Wrong. = does not use wildcards at all; it looks for a Discount that is exactly the one-character string '%', so no row is returned.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
OFFER
Code | Discount
D1   | 50%
D2   | 50
D3   | 25% off
D4   | half
work:
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB:
A: LIKE '%%%' → D1, D2, D3, D4 (all rows)
B: LIKE '%!%%' ESCAPE '!' → D1, D3
C: = '%' → no rows

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: What exactly does the condition Phone IS NULL test?
opts: Whether the whole row is empty, i.e. every column of the row is NULL
Whether the Phone value is the number 0
Whether the value of the Phone column in that row is NULL (missing or unknown)
More than one of the above
exp: IS NULL is a test on one value: it is TRUE when the Phone value of the row being checked is NULL, whatever the other columns contain.
concept: NULL means 'value missing or unknown'; it is not zero and not a space. Because any comparison with NULL (=, <>, < …) gives UNKNOWN, SQL provides special tests: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. Phone IS NULL looks only at the Phone value of each row; the other columns of that row do not matter.
why: A — Wrong. IS NULL checks one column's value, not the whole row. A row with Name 'Ravi' and a missing Phone still satisfies Phone IS NULL.
B — Wrong. 0 is a real, known number. Phone = 0 is an ordinary comparison, and a Phone of 0 is NOT NULL.
C — Correct. Phone IS NULL is TRUE exactly for the rows whose Phone value is NULL.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'IS NULL is TRUE if the row is NULL'. It tests whether a column VALUE is NULL.

subtopic: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and NULL tests
q: What value does the query below print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: City = NULL is never TRUE — any comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN — so WHERE keeps no rows and COUNT(*) prints 0. To find the two missing cities you must write City IS NULL.
concept: SQL uses three-valued logic: a condition can be TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL using =, <>, <, > … is UNKNOWN, even NULL = NULL. WHERE keeps only the rows where the condition is TRUE, so WHERE City = NULL returns nothing. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL to test for NULL.
why: A — Wrong. 2 is the result of WHERE City IS NULL (Meena and Sita). With = the comparison is UNKNOWN, not TRUE, for those rows.
B — Wrong. 3 is the number of rows whose City is NOT NULL (Ravi, Amit, Kiran); = NULL does not select them either.
C — Wrong. 5 is the total number of rows; WHERE removes all of them because no comparison with NULL is TRUE.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. No row satisfies City = NULL, so COUNT(*) counts zero rows and prints 0.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | City
1     | Ravi  | Patna
2     | Meena | NULL
3     | Amit  | Gaya
4     | Sita  | NULL
5     | Kiran | Patna

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMP
WHERE City = NULL;
work:
Ravi: 'Patna' = NULL → UNKNOWN ✗
Meena: NULL = NULL → UNKNOWN ✗
Amit, Sita, Kiran: UNKNOWN ✗
Rows left after WHERE: 0 → COUNT(*) = 0
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: City = NULL → 0; City IS NULL → 2; City IS NOT NULL → 3
tip: '= NULL' is always a trap: it selects 0 rows. (Only old SQL Server code with SET ANSI_NULLS OFF behaved differently.)

q: In the query SELECT Name, Salary FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary; neither ASC nor DESC is written. In what order are the rows shown?
opts: In the order in which the rows were inserted
More than one of the above
exp: ASC (ascending) is the default sort direction of ORDER BY, so the smallest salary comes first and the largest comes last.
concept: ORDER BY sorts the final result. Each sort column can be followed by ASC (ascending: small to large, A to Z, old date to new date) or DESC (descending: large to small). If nothing is written, ASC is used. Without any ORDER BY clause, SQL does not promise any particular order of rows at all.
why: A — Correct. When the direction is left out, ORDER BY sorts in ascending order, so the lowest salary appears first.
B — Wrong. Largest-first order needs the keyword DESC written after the column: ORDER BY Salary DESC.
C — Wrong. The query has an ORDER BY clause, so the rows are sorted by Salary. Insertion order is never guaranteed in SQL, even when there is no ORDER BY.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: No direction written = ASC. Write DESC only when you want large-to-small.

q: What is the SECOND row of the output of the query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DESC applies only to Dept, so departments come as SALES, IT, HR. Salary has no direction, so inside each department it is ascending: Kiran (30000) first, then Pooja (35000).
concept: With several sort columns, the first column decides the main order and the next column only breaks ties between rows that have the same value in the first column. ASC or DESC applies only to the one column it is written after; every column without a keyword is sorted ascending.
why: A — Wrong. Kiran is the FIRST row (SALES, smallest salary). It would be the second row only if DESC also applied to Salary, but DESC covers only Dept.
B — Correct. The SALES rows come first (Dept DESC), sorted by Salary ascending: Kiran 30000, then Pooja 35000.
C — Wrong. Sita would be second if Dept were sorted ascending (HR first: Meena, Sita). Here Dept is DESC, so HR comes last.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Name, Dept, Salary
FROM EMP
ORDER BY Dept DESC, Salary;
work:
FROM: 7 rows; no WHERE, no GROUP BY.
SELECT: Name, Dept, Salary of all 7 rows.
ORDER BY Dept DESC → SALES, then IT, then HR.
Ties broken by Salary ASC:
1. Kiran | SALES | 30000
2. Pooja | SALES | 35000
3. Amit | IT | 40000
4. Ravi | IT | 50000
5. Arjun | IT | 60000
6. Meena | HR | 30000
7. Sita | HR | 45000
Same order on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.
(ORDER BY Dept DESC, Salary DESC would start Pooja, Kiran.)
tip: ORDER BY a DESC, b means a descending, b ASCENDING. DESC does not carry over to the next column.

q: Which name appears in the FIRST row of the output?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: ORDER BY 2 means 'sort by the 2nd column of the SELECT list', which is Salary. With DESC, the highest salary comes first: Arjun (60000).
concept: In ORDER BY you may write a number instead of a column name. The number is the position of a column in the SELECT list (1 = first column listed after SELECT), not its position in the table and not a row number. This positional form works in Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server, PostgreSQL and SQLite, but writing the column name is clearer.
why: A — Wrong. Sita comes first when the sort is on Name DESC. Name is the 2nd column of the TABLE (after EmpID), but ORDER BY 2 counts columns of the SELECT list, where column 2 is Salary.
B — Correct. Column 2 of SELECT Name, Salary is Salary; sorted in descending order, Arjun's 60000 is the highest.
C — Wrong. Meena is the employee with EmpID 2. The number in ORDER BY is a column position, not a key value or a row number.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Column Bonus contains some NULL values. Consider these statements about ORDER BY Bonus (ascending):
I. In Oracle and PostgreSQL, the NULL rows appear at the END.
II. In MySQL and SQL Server, the NULL rows appear at the BEGINNING.
III. Oracle and PostgreSQL let you choose the position yourself with NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Oracle and PostgreSQL treat NULL as larger than every value (last in ASC); MySQL and SQL Server treat NULL as smaller than every value (first in ASC); and Oracle and PostgreSQL support NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST. All three statements are true.
concept: Where NULLs go in a sort is decided by each product. Oracle and PostgreSQL sort NULL as if it were the largest value: last in ASC, first in DESC. MySQL, SQL Server and SQLite sort NULL as the smallest value: first in ASC, last in DESC. The standard clause NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST (supported by Oracle and PostgreSQL) fixes the position explicitly.
why: A — Wrong. It leaves out statement III, which is true: Oracle and PostgreSQL both accept ORDER BY Bonus NULLS FIRST (or NULLS LAST).
B — Wrong. It leaves out statement I, which is true: in Oracle and PostgreSQL the default for ascending order is NULLS LAST.
C — Correct. Statement I (Oracle/PostgreSQL: NULLs last in ASC), statement II (MySQL/SQL Server: NULLs first in ASC) and statement III (NULLS FIRST/LAST syntax) are all true.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Test table: Ravi 500, Meena NULL, Amit 200.
PostgreSQL 16, ORDER BY Bonus → Amit 200, Ravi 500, Meena NULL (NULL last, as in Oracle)
PostgreSQL 16, ORDER BY Bonus DESC → Meena NULL first
SQLite, ORDER BY Bonus → Meena NULL, Amit 200, Ravi 500 (NULL first, as in MySQL and SQL Server)
ORDER BY Bonus NULLS FIRST → NULL first in PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB.
Oracle documentation: NULLS LAST is the default for ascending order. MySQL and SQL Server documentation: NULL values come first in ascending order.
tip: Oracle/PostgreSQL: NULL behaves like the BIGGEST value. MySQL/SQL Server: NULL behaves like the SMALLEST value.

q: Which of the following is NOT an aggregate (group) function?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: UPPER is a scalar (single-row) string function: it changes the letters of one value to capitals and gives one result per row. AVG and MIN are aggregate functions.
concept: An aggregate (group) function takes MANY rows and returns ONE value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN. A scalar (single-row) function works on one value of one row at a time and returns one result for every row: UPPER, LOWER, ROUND, SUBSTR, LENGTH and so on.
why: A — Wrong. AVG returns the average of a whole set of values, so it IS an aggregate function.
B — Wrong. MIN returns the smallest value of a whole set of values, so it IS an aggregate function.
C — Correct. UPPER('ravi') = 'RAVI' works on one value per row, so it is a scalar function, NOT an aggregate.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. UPPER is not an aggregate, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Aggregate = many rows in, one value out (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN).

q: What does the query below print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: COUNT(*) counts all 5 rows; COUNT(City) skips Sita's NULL, giving 4; COUNT(DISTINCT City) counts the different non-NULL cities Patna, Gaya and Ranchi, giving 3.
concept: COUNT(*) counts rows, whatever they contain. COUNT(column) counts only the rows where that column is NOT NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts the different non-NULL values. All other aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN) also ignore NULLs.
why: A — Wrong. This treats the NULL city as a counted value. COUNT(City) and COUNT(DISTINCT City) both skip NULLs, so they give 4 and 3, not 5 and 4.
B — Correct. 5 rows in total, 4 non-NULL cities, and 3 different cities (Patna, Gaya, Ranchi).
C — Wrong. COUNT(*) does not skip rows that contain a NULL; it counts every row, so it is 5, not 4.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | City
1     | Ravi  | Patna
2     | Meena | Gaya
3     | Amit  | Patna
4     | Sita  | NULL
5     | Kiran | Ranchi

SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(City), COUNT(DISTINCT City)
FROM EMP;
work:
FROM: 5 rows; no WHERE; the whole table is one group.
COUNT(*) → 5 rows
COUNT(City) → Patna, Gaya, Patna, Ranchi (Sita's NULL skipped) → 4
COUNT(DISTINCT City) → {Patna, Gaya, Ranchi} → 3
Result: 5, 4, 3 (same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB)
tip: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values.

q: What value does the query below print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: AVG ignores the NULL bonus: it adds the 3 known values (10 + 20 + 30 = 60) and divides by 3, giving 20.
concept: AVG(column) = SUM(column) / COUNT(column): both the sum and the count use only the non-NULL values. A NULL is NOT treated as 0. If you want NULL counted as 0, write AVG(COALESCE(Bonus, 0)), which here would give 60 / 4 = 15.
why: A — Correct. 60 / 3 = 20, because Amit's NULL bonus is left out of both the sum and the count.
B — Wrong. 15 = 60 / 4 treats the NULL as 0 and divides by all 4 rows. AVG does not do that; it divides by COUNT(Bonus) = 3.
C — Wrong. A NULL makes ordinary arithmetic such as 10 + NULL give NULL, but aggregate functions simply skip NULLs. AVG returns NULL only when there is no non-NULL value at all.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Bonus
1     | Ravi  | 10
2     | Meena | 20
3     | Amit  | NULL
4     | Sita  | 30

SELECT AVG(Bonus) FROM EMP;
work:
FROM: 4 rows; no WHERE; one group.
Non-NULL bonuses: 10, 20, 30 → SUM = 60, COUNT(Bonus) = 3 (COUNT(*) = 4)
AVG = 60 / 3 = 20
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: 20.
tip: AVG(col) = SUM(col) / COUNT(col), not SUM(col) / COUNT(*).

q: No employee works in the ADMIN department. What does the query below return?
opts: No row at all (an empty result)
More than one of the above
exp: With no GROUP BY, an aggregate query always returns exactly one row, even when WHERE keeps no rows. COUNT(*) of zero rows is 0, but SUM of zero values is NULL, so the row is 0 and NULL — not listed in A–C.
concept: When an aggregate is computed over an empty set of rows: COUNT(*) and COUNT(col) give 0, while SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN give NULL (there is no value to add, average or compare). A query that has aggregates but no GROUP BY treats all the remaining rows as one group, so it still returns one row.
why: A — Wrong. COUNT(*) is 0, but SUM of no values is NULL, not 0. (You get 0 only if you write COALESCE(SUM(Salary), 0).)
B — Wrong. SUM is NULL, but COUNT never returns NULL; counting zero rows gives 0.
C — Wrong. Without GROUP BY, the whole (empty) set of rows is one group, so one result row is still returned. (With GROUP BY Dept, there would be no groups and no rows.)
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The query returns one row: COUNT(*) = 0 and SUM(Salary) = NULL.

4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(Salary)
FROM EMP
WHERE Dept = 'ADMIN';

FROM: 7 rows.
WHERE Dept = 'ADMIN': 0 rows survive.
No GROUP BY → the empty set is one group.
COUNT(*) over 0 rows = 0; SUM over 0 values = NULL
Result: one row (0, NULL) on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB. AVG and MAX would also be NULL.

q: The query SELECT Dept FROM EMP WHERE AVG(Salary) > 40000 GROUP BY Dept; gives an error. Where should the condition AVG(Salary) > 40000 be written?
opts: In a HAVING clause, after GROUP BY Dept
More than one of the above
exp: WHERE checks one row at a time before groups exist, so it cannot use an aggregate. A condition on a group value such as AVG(Salary) belongs in HAVING: SELECT Dept FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept HAVING AVG(Salary) > 40000;
concept: Aggregate functions need a group of rows. WHERE runs before GROUP BY and looks at single rows, so aggregates are not allowed in WHERE. HAVING runs after GROUP BY and filters whole groups, so it is the place for conditions such as COUNT(*) > 2 or AVG(Salary) > 40000.
why: A — Wrong. The SELECT list chooses what to display; a condition written there (for example as a column) does not remove any row or group.
B — Wrong. ORDER BY only sorts the result; it never filters rows or groups.
C — Correct. HAVING AVG(Salary) > 40000 is checked for each department group after GROUP BY, which is exactly what is needed.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
On the 7-row EMP table:
WHERE AVG(Salary) > 40000 → error in all three engines (PostgreSQL: 'aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE').
GROUP BY Dept HAVING AVG(Salary) > 40000 → IT (average 50000) on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.
tip: Aggregate condition → HAVING. Row condition → WHERE.

q: What does the query below print?
opts: An error, because MAX and MIN work only on numbers
More than one of the above
exp: MAX and MIN also work on text, using alphabetical (dictionary) order. The last name alphabetically is Sita and the first is Amit.
concept: MAX and MIN work on any data type that can be ordered: numbers, text (alphabetical order according to the collation) and dates (latest / earliest). SUM and AVG, on the other hand, need numbers.
why: A — Wrong. MAX and MIN accept text and dates as well as numbers; only SUM and AVG need numeric values.
B — Correct. In alphabetical order the names run Amit, Arjun, Kiran, Meena, Pooja, Ravi, Sita, so MAX = Sita and MIN = Amit.
C — Wrong. Ravi and Pooja are the first and last rows of the table. MAX and MIN compare the values; they do not look at the position of the rows.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
