(Amit before Arjun because the 2nd letters are m < r)
MAX(Name) = Sita, MIN(Name) = Amit — same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.
tip: MAX/MIN: numbers, text and dates. SUM/AVG: numbers only.

q:
Consider the statements:
I. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN are aggregate functions of standard SQL.
II. COMPUTE is an aggregate function.
III. FIRST(column) and LAST(column) are aggregate functions of ISO standard SQL.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The five standard aggregate functions are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN. COMPUTE was a clause of old SQL Server, not a function, and FIRST()/LAST() come from MS Access, not from the SQL standard.
concept: Standard SQL's basic aggregate functions are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN; each turns many rows into one value. COMPUTE was a Transact-SQL (SQL Server) clause that printed extra summary rows; it was removed in SQL Server 2012 and was never an aggregate function. FIRST(column) and LAST(column) are MS Access functions, not standard SQL; standard SQL instead has the window functions FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE.
why: A — Correct. Only statement I is true. Statements II and III are false, as explained in B and C.
B — Wrong. Statement II is false: COMPUTE (as in COMPUTE SUM(Salary)) was a separate clause of old SQL Server for printing summary rows, not an aggregate function.

C — Wrong. Statement III is false: FIRST(column) and LAST(column) are MS Access functions. The ISO standard does not define them, and Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server have no FIRST(column) or LAST(column) aggregate. (Oracle uses the words FIRST and LAST only inside a special KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST ORDER BY …) clause, which is a different thing.)
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): FIRST() and LAST() listed as SQL aggregate functions. They are MS Access only. The five to remember: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN.

q: How many rows does Query 1 return, and what value does Query 2 print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DISTINCT keeps one NULL as a separate value, so Query 1 returns Patna, Gaya and NULL (3 rows). COUNT(DISTINCT City) ignores NULLs, so Query 2 prints 2. '3 rows; 2' is not in A–C.
concept: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows, and for this purpose all NULLs count as duplicates of each other, so exactly one NULL row survives. Aggregate functions, including COUNT(DISTINCT column), skip NULLs completely. So the number of rows from SELECT DISTINCT col can be one more than COUNT(DISTINCT col).
why: A — Wrong. Query 2 is 2, but Query 1 does not drop NULLs: DISTINCT keeps one NULL row, so it returns 3 rows, not 2.
B — Wrong. Query 1 is 3 rows, but COUNT(DISTINCT City) does not count NULL as a value, so Query 2 is 2, not 3.
C — Wrong. 4 rows would mean the two NULLs are treated as different values. For DISTINCT, NULLs are treated as the same, so only one NULL row is kept.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. Query 1 returns 3 rows (Patna, Gaya, NULL) and Query 2 prints 2.
code:
CUST
ID | City
1  | Patna
2  | NULL
3  | Gaya
4  | Patna
5  | NULL

Query 1: SELECT DISTINCT City FROM CUST;
Query 2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT City) FROM CUST;
work:
Query 1: FROM → 5 rows; SELECT City → Patna, NULL, Gaya, Patna, NULL
DISTINCT → Patna (once), Gaya, NULL (once) → 3 rows
Query 2: non-NULL cities → Patna, Gaya, Patna → distinct {Patna, Gaya} → 2
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: 3 rows and 2.
tip: SELECT DISTINCT keeps one NULL; COUNT(DISTINCT) throws NULL away.

q: Name is a VARCHAR (text) column of EMP containing names such as 'Ravi' and 'Meena'. Which statement about SELECT SUM(Name) FROM EMP; is correct?
opts: Every SQL product returns 0, because SUM treats text as 0.
Every SQL product returns all the names joined into one string.
PostgreSQL rejects it with an error, because SUM has no version that accepts a text (VARCHAR) argument.
More than one of the above
exp: SUM and AVG need numbers. PostgreSQL (and also SQL Server and Oracle) give an error for text such as 'Ravi'. Only MySQL-style loose conversion turns such text into 0 and returns 0.
concept: SUM and AVG are numeric aggregate functions. Strict products refuse a text argument: PostgreSQL says 'function sum(character varying) does not exist', SQL Server says the varchar data type is invalid for the sum operator, and Oracle tries to convert the text to a number and fails with 'invalid number'. MySQL and SQLite instead convert non-numeric text to 0 and return 0 (MySQL only adds a warning). MAX and MIN, by contrast, work on text.
why: A — Wrong. Returning 0 is MySQL's (and SQLite's) loose behaviour, not a rule of SQL. PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle raise an error instead.
B — Wrong. SUM never joins strings. Joining text values is done by other functions, for example STRING_AGG in PostgreSQL or LISTAGG in Oracle.
C — Correct. PostgreSQL defines SUM for number types (and a few others such as interval), but not for VARCHAR, so it reports 'function sum(character varying) does not exist'.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
SELECT SUM(Name) FROM EMP on the 7-row EMP table:
PostgreSQL 16 → ERROR: function sum(character varying) does not exist
DuckDB → Binder Error: no function matches sum(VARCHAR)
SQLite → 0 (loose conversion, like MySQL)
SQL Server → error (varchar invalid for sum operator); Oracle → ORA-01722 invalid number.
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'SUM/AVG of a text column returns 0'. That is MySQL behaviour only; strict products give an error.

q: Which statement about GROUP BY is NOT correct?
opts: Rows that have the same value in the GROUP BY column are put into one group.
The groups are always returned sorted by the GROUP BY column, even when no ORDER BY is written.
A plain GROUP BY query without HAVING returns one output row for each group.
More than one of the above
exp: GROUP BY only forms groups; it does not promise any order. Only ORDER BY guarantees sorted output.
concept: GROUP BY collects rows with equal values in the grouping column(s) into groups, and the query then produces one summary row per group (HAVING may remove some groups). The order of those rows is not defined unless ORDER BY is written; different products, or even the same product with a different plan, may return the groups in different orders.
why: A — Wrong. This is the definition of GROUP BY, so it IS correct and does not satisfy the stem.
B — Correct. This statement is NOT correct: without ORDER BY the order of groups is not guaranteed. (Old MySQL 5.x sorted GROUP BY output as a side effect; MySQL 8.0 no longer does.)
C — Wrong. This is correct: each group gives one summary row, for example one row per department.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is not correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept (7-row EMP, no ORDER BY):
SQLite → HR, IT, SALES
PostgreSQL 16 → SALES, IT, HR
DuckDB → IT, HR, SALES
Three engines, three different orders → GROUP BY does not sort. Each engine returned 3 rows (one per group).
tip: Want sorted groups? Add ORDER BY. GROUP BY alone gives no order.

q: Which departments appear in the output of the query below?
opts: No department, because no single salary is above 70000
More than one of the above
exp: The department totals are IT 150000, HR 75000 and SALES 65000. HAVING keeps the groups whose total is above 70000: IT and HR.
concept: HAVING tests a condition on each GROUP after GROUP BY has formed the groups, so HAVING SUM(Salary) > 70000 compares the department TOTAL with 70000, not each employee's salary. To test single rows, use WHERE.
why: A — Wrong. HR's total 30000 + 45000 = 75000 is also above 70000, so HR is kept as well.
B — Wrong. That would be the result of WHERE Salary > 70000, which tests single rows. HAVING tests the group total, and two totals exceed 70000.
C — Correct. IT (150000) and HR (75000) pass the HAVING condition; SALES (65000) does not.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Dept, SUM(Salary)
FROM EMP
GROUP BY Dept
HAVING SUM(Salary) > 70000;
work:
FROM: 7 rows; no WHERE.
GROUP BY Dept:
IT → 50000 + 40000 + 60000 = 150000
HR → 30000 + 45000 = 75000
SALES → 30000 + 35000 = 65000
HAVING SUM > 70000 → IT ✓, HR ✓, SALES ✗
SELECT → (IT, 150000), (HR, 75000) — same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.

q: What is the output of the query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: WHERE first keeps the 4 rows with Salary >= 40000 (Ravi, Amit, Sita, Arjun). Grouping gives IT 3 and HR 1, and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps only IT 3.
concept: The clauses work in the order FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT. WHERE removes rows BEFORE the groups are formed, so the counts are made only from the surviving rows. HAVING then removes whole groups.
why: A — Correct. After WHERE, IT has 3 rows (50000, 40000, 60000) and HR has 1 row (45000); only IT has more than 1.
B — Wrong. This is the result if WHERE is ignored (all 7 rows grouped). WHERE runs first and removes Meena, Kiran and Pooja.
C — Wrong. This comes from reading >= as >, which drops Amit (40000). Salary >= 40000 includes 40000, so IT has 3 rows.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) AS N
FROM EMP
WHERE Salary >= 40000
GROUP BY Dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
work:
FROM: 7 rows.
WHERE Salary >= 40000 → Ravi (IT 50000), Amit (IT 40000), Sita (HR 45000), Arjun (IT 60000)
GROUP BY Dept → IT: 3 rows; HR: 1 row
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 → IT ✓, HR ✗
SELECT → IT | 3
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB. (Without WHERE: HR 2, IT 3, SALES 2. With Salary > 40000: IT 2.)
tip: WHERE filters rows before counting; HAVING filters groups after counting.

q: In standard SQL (for example in Oracle or PostgreSQL), which query is NOT valid?
opts: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;
SELECT Dept, Name, MAX(Salary) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept;
More than one of the above
exp: In a grouped query every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function. Name is neither, and a department has many names, so query B is rejected.
concept: After GROUP BY Dept, each output row stands for a whole department. A column like Dept has one value per group, and an aggregate like MAX(Salary) gives one value per group, but Name has several values in a group, so SQL cannot choose one. Rule: every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY. The reverse is not required: a GROUP BY column need not be shown in SELECT.
why: A — Wrong. Dept is in GROUP BY and COUNT(*) is an aggregate, so this query is valid (it shows the number of employees per department).

B — Correct. This query is NOT valid: Name is neither grouped nor aggregated. Oracle gives ORA-00979 'not a GROUP BY expression' and PostgreSQL says Name 'must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function'.
C — Wrong. This query is valid: the grouping column does not have to appear in the SELECT list. It returns one count per department (3, 2 and 2 for the 7-row EMP table).
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is not valid, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: EMP(EmpID, Name, Dept, Salary)
work:
On the 7-row EMP table:
A → (HR, 2), (IT, 3), (SALES, 2) on all three engines
B → PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: error 'column Name must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function'
   (SQLite accepts it as a non-standard extension, as does MySQL when ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is switched off)
C → 2, 2, 3 (one count per group) on all three engines
tip: SELECT columns ⊆ GROUP BY columns + aggregates. Not the other way round.

q: Which departments appear in the output of the query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The average salaries are IT 50000, HR 37500 and SALES 32500. HAVING AVG(Salary) < 40000 keeps HR and SALES.
concept: HAVING with AVG compares the average of each group with the given value. AVG of a group = sum of its non-NULL values ÷ number of non-NULL values in that group.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. HR's average is (30000 + 45000) / 2 = 37500, which is below 40000.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. SALES's average is (30000 + 35000) / 2 = 32500, which is below 40000.
C — Wrong. IT's average is (50000 + 40000 + 60000) / 3 = 50000, which is not below 40000. (IT does contain one salary of 40000, but HAVING tests the average, not single rows.)
D — Correct. Both HR and SALES appear; IT does not.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Dept, AVG(Salary)
FROM EMP
GROUP BY Dept
HAVING AVG(Salary) < 40000;
work:
FROM: 7 rows; no WHERE.
GROUP BY Dept:
IT → 150000 / 3 = 50000
HR → 75000 / 2 = 37500
SALES → 65000 / 2 = 32500
HAVING AVG < 40000 → HR ✓, SALES ✓, IT ✗
Result: (HR, 37500), (SALES, 32500) on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.

q: What is the output of the query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: WHERE removes Ravi (50000) and Arjun (60000). The remaining groups are HR (2 rows, max 45000), IT (1 row, max 40000) and SALES (2 rows, max 35000). Only HR has MAX > 40000, so the output is HR | 2, which is not listed.
concept: Work clause by clause: WHERE removes rows first, GROUP BY groups the survivors, HAVING keeps the groups whose aggregate passes, and SELECT shows the aggregates of the surviving groups. The COUNT(*) in SELECT counts every row of the group that passed WHERE; the HAVING condition does not change it.
why: A — Wrong. IT | 3 appears only if WHERE is ignored (IT's maximum would then be 60000). WHERE runs before grouping and removes Ravi and Arjun, leaving IT with just Amit.
B — Wrong. IT's maximum after WHERE is exactly 40000, and 40000 > 40000 is FALSE. IT would appear only with >= 40000.
C — Wrong. COUNT(*) counts all HR rows that passed WHERE (Meena and Sita = 2). HAVING MAX(Salary) > 40000 decides only whether the group is kept; it does not filter the rows being counted.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The only output row is HR | 2.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Dept, COUNT(*)
FROM EMP
WHERE Salary < 50000
GROUP BY Dept
HAVING MAX(Salary) > 40000;
work:
FROM: 7 rows.
WHERE Salary < 50000 → Meena (HR 30000), Amit (IT 40000), Sita (HR 45000), Kiran (SALES 30000), Pooja (SALES 35000); Ravi and Arjun removed
GROUP BY Dept → HR: 2 rows, MAX 45000; IT: 1 row, MAX 40000; SALES: 2 rows, MAX 35000
HAVING MAX > 40000 → HR ✓, IT ✗ (40000 is not > 40000), SALES ✗
SELECT → HR | 2
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB. (Without WHERE: HR 2, IT 3. With >= 40000: HR 2, IT 1.)

q: In the output of the query below, what is shown for the staff members who have no department?
opts: No row; GROUP BY leaves out the rows whose Dept is NULL
More than one of the above
exp: GROUP BY puts all NULL Dept values into ONE group, so Meena and Kiran form a single group. COUNT(*) counts its 2 rows, but COUNT(Dept) counts non-NULL Dept values, of which there are 0.
concept: For grouping, NULLs are treated as equal, so all rows with NULL in the grouping column form one group (the same idea as DISTINCT). Inside that group, COUNT(*) counts the rows, while COUNT(Dept) counts only non-NULL Dept values, so it is 0.
why: A — Wrong. GROUP BY does not drop NULLs; rows with a NULL Dept form their own group and appear in the output.
B — Correct. The NULL group has 2 rows (Meena, Kiran), so COUNT(*) = 2, and none of them has a non-NULL Dept, so COUNT(Dept) = 0.
C — Wrong. Two separate rows would mean each NULL is a different group. For GROUP BY, NULLs count as the same value, so they form one group.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STAFF
Name  | Dept
Ravi  | IT
Meena | NULL
Amit  | IT
Sita  | HR
Kiran | NULL

SELECT Dept, COUNT(*), COUNT(Dept)
FROM STAFF
GROUP BY Dept;
work:
FROM: 5 rows; no WHERE.
GROUP BY Dept → IT {Ravi, Amit}; HR {Sita}; NULL {Meena, Kiran}
SELECT:
IT | 2 | 2
HR | 1 | 1
NULL | 2 | 0
3 output rows — same values on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB (only the position of the NULL row differs, because no ORDER BY is given).
tip: GROUP BY and DISTINCT: all NULLs together in one bucket.

q: Which departments does the query below return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: COUNT(*) counts all rows of a group, COUNT(Bonus) only the non-NULL bonuses. They are equal only when nobody in the group has a NULL bonus: IT (3 and 3). HR has 2 and 1, SALES has 2 and 0.
concept: Comparing COUNT(col) with COUNT(*) is a neat trick: COUNT(*) − COUNT(col) is the number of NULLs in that column for the group. HAVING COUNT(Bonus) = COUNT(*) therefore means 'every row in this group has a bonus'.
why: A — Wrong. HR and SALES are the departments where some bonus is missing; they would be returned by the opposite condition HAVING COUNT(Bonus) < COUNT(*).
B — Wrong. This assumes COUNT(Bonus) also counts NULLs, so it would always equal COUNT(*). In fact COUNT(column) skips NULLs.
C — Correct. Only IT has COUNT(Bonus) = COUNT(*) = 3; every IT employee has a bonus.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
Name  | Dept  | Bonus
Ravi  | IT    | 5000
Meena | HR    | NULL
Amit  | IT    | 2000
Sita  | HR    | 3000
Kiran | SALES | NULL
Arjun | IT    | 4000
Pooja | SALES | NULL

SELECT Dept
FROM EMP
GROUP BY Dept
HAVING COUNT(Bonus) = COUNT(*);
work:
FROM: 7 rows; no WHERE.
GROUP BY Dept:
IT → rows 3, non-NULL bonuses 3
HR → rows 2, non-NULL bonuses 1 (Meena NULL)
SALES → rows 2, non-NULL bonuses 0
HAVING COUNT(Bonus) = COUNT(*) → IT ✓, HR ✗, SALES ✗
SELECT → IT (same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB)
tip: COUNT(*) − COUNT(col) = number of NULLs in col.

q: What is the LAST row of the output of the query below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The counts are IT 3, HR 2, SALES 2. Sorting by N descending puts IT first; HR and SALES tie on 2, and the second sort key Dept (ascending) puts HR before SALES. So SALES | 2 is last.
concept: ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it may use a column alias such as N (in standard SQL an alias cannot be used in WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING). When rows tie on the first sort key, the next key in ORDER BY decides their order.
why: A — Wrong. HR ties with SALES on N = 2, but the tie is broken by Dept ascending, and 'HR' comes before 'SALES' alphabetically, so HR is second, not last.
B — Correct. Order: IT 3, HR 2, SALES 2 — SALES is last.
C — Wrong. IT has the largest count, and N DESC puts the largest first, so IT is the FIRST row.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) AS N
FROM EMP
GROUP BY Dept
ORDER BY N DESC, Dept;
work:
FROM: 7 rows; no WHERE.
GROUP BY Dept → IT 3, HR 2, SALES 2
SELECT → Dept, N
ORDER BY N DESC → IT 3 first; HR 2 and SALES 2 tie
Tie broken by Dept ASC → HR, then SALES
Output: IT 3, HR 2, SALES 2 (same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB). Last row: SALES 2.
tip: Aliases work in ORDER BY because ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT.

q: What does the query below return on the 7-row EMP table?
opts: An error, because HAVING cannot be used without GROUP BY
More than one of the above
exp: Without GROUP BY, HAVING treats the whole table as ONE group. That group has COUNT(*) = 7, and 7 > 10 is FALSE, so the only group is removed and the query returns no rows at all.
concept: HAVING is allowed without GROUP BY (standard SQL, Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server, PostgreSQL). Then all rows that passed WHERE form a single group. If the HAVING condition is TRUE, one row comes out; if it is FALSE, the result is empty (zero rows). This differs from a plain aggregate query, which always returns one row.
why: A — Wrong. 7 would be printed only if the HAVING condition were TRUE (for example HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). Since 7 > 10 is FALSE, the group is filtered out.
B — Wrong. HAVING does not change the value of COUNT(*) to 0; it either keeps the group's row (showing 7) or removes it completely.
C — Wrong. HAVING without GROUP BY is legal; the whole result is treated as one group.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. The result is empty: no row is returned.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM EMP
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
work:
FROM: 7 rows; no WHERE.
No GROUP BY → all 7 rows form one group.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10 → 7 > 10 is FALSE → the group is removed.
SELECT: nothing left → 0 rows.
SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: empty result. (With HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 they return one row: 7.)
tip: Aggregate without GROUP BY → always 1 row. Add a false HAVING → 0 rows.

q:
Consider these statements about the order in which the clauses of a SELECT statement are WRITTEN in standard SQL:
I. WHERE is written before GROUP BY.
II. HAVING must be written before GROUP BY.
III. ORDER BY is written after HAVING.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The written order is SELECT … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY. So I and III are true, and II is false because HAVING comes after GROUP BY.
concept: Written order of a SELECT statement: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY (row-limiting clauses such as LIMIT or FETCH FIRST, where used, come at the very end). This is different from the logical processing order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY), in which only SELECT changes place.
why: A — Wrong. It leaves out statement III, which is true: ORDER BY is the last of these clauses, so it comes after HAVING.
B — Correct. Statements I and III are true and statement II is false.

C — Wrong. Statement II is false: standard SQL writes GROUP BY first and HAVING after it. (Oracle happens to accept both orders, but no product requires HAVING first.) C also leaves out the true statement I.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY Dept → syntax error near GROUP in SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.
SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM EMP WHERE … GROUP BY Dept HAVING … ORDER BY … → valid in all three.
tip: Written order: 'Some Funny Woman Gave Her Orange' = SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.

q: In Oracle, what does SELECT ROUND(1234.567, -2) FROM DUAL; print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A negative second argument rounds to the LEFT of the decimal point: −2 means 'to the nearest hundred'. 1234.567 lies between 1200 and 1300, and its last part 34.567 is less than 50, so it rounds down to 1200.
concept: ROUND(n, d) rounds n to d decimal places. Positive d counts places to the right of the decimal point; d = 0 (or left out) gives a whole number; negative d rounds to the left: −1 = nearest ten, −2 = nearest hundred, −3 = nearest thousand. Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL all support negative d (SQLite does not).
why: A — Correct. To the nearest hundred, 1234.567 becomes 1200 because the remainder 34.567 is below 50.
B — Wrong. 1234.57 is ROUND(1234.567, 2) — two places to the RIGHT of the decimal point. A minus sign moves the rounding to the left.
C — Wrong. 1300 would need the part after the hundreds (34.567) to be 50 or more; it is not, so the value rounds down.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT ROUND(1234.567, -2) FROM DUAL;
work:
−2 → round to the nearest 100.
1234.567 lies between 1200 and 1300; remainder 34.567 < 50 → round down → 1200.
Checked without DUAL: PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB print 1200. (SQLite ignores negative digits and prints 1235 — one reason why such questions name Oracle.)
Compare: ROUND(1234.567, 2) = 1234.57; ROUND(1250, -2) = 1300.
tip: ROUND(x, -1) → tens, ROUND(x, -2) → hundreds, ROUND(x, -3) → thousands.

q: In Oracle, what does SELECT ROUND(2.5), ROUND(-2.5) FROM DUAL; print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: For exact numbers (Oracle NUMBER, DECIMAL), ROUND rounds a half AWAY from zero: 2.5 → 3 and −2.5 → −3.
concept: ROUND on exact numeric values (Oracle NUMBER, DECIMAL/NUMERIC in MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL) rounds a value that is exactly halfway away from zero: 2.5 → 3, −2.5 → −3, 0.5 → 1. 'Banker's rounding' (round half to even, the IEEE 754 default) is used only for binary floating-point types such as Oracle BINARY_DOUBLE or PostgreSQL double precision, where ROUND(2.5) gives 2.
why: A — Wrong. 2 and −2 is banker's rounding (round half to the even number). It applies to binary floating-point values, not to the exact NUMBER literals 2.5 and −2.5 used here.
B — Wrong. −2 would come from always rounding a half UP towards +∞ (like FLOOR(x + 0.5)). SQL ROUND treats the sign symmetrically: −2.5 goes away from zero to −3.
C — Correct. Half away from zero: 2.5 → 3 and −2.5 → −3.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT ROUND(2.5), ROUND(-2.5) FROM DUAL;
work:
2.5 is exactly halfway between 2 and 3 → away from zero → 3
−2.5 is exactly halfway between −2 and −3 → away from zero → −3
Checked without DUAL on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: 3, −3.
For contrast, PostgreSQL ROUND(2.5::float8), ROUND(-2.5::float8) → 2, −2 (half to even on a binary float).
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): 'ROUND uses IEEE banker's rounding, so 5.5 → 6 because 6 is even'. For SQL exact numbers the rule is half away from zero: ROUND(2.5) = 3, ROUND(-2.5) = -3.

q: In Oracle, what does SELECT TRUNC(65.76, 1), ROUND(65.76, 1) FROM DUAL; print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: TRUNC simply cuts off the digits after 1 decimal place (65.76 → 65.7), while ROUND looks at the next digit 6 and rounds up (65.76 → 65.8).
concept: TRUNC(n, d) (Oracle; TRUNCATE(n, d) in MySQL, TRUNC in PostgreSQL) chops a number to d decimal places WITHOUT rounding. ROUND(n, d) rounds to d decimal places, going up when the next digit is 5 or more. With no second argument both work to 0 decimal places: TRUNC(65.76) = 65, ROUND(65.76) = 66.
why: A — Wrong. TRUNC never rounds up; it only drops the extra digits, so TRUNC(65.76, 1) is 65.7, not 65.8.
B — Correct. TRUNC(65.76, 1) = 65.7 (the 6 is dropped) and ROUND(65.76, 1) = 65.8 (the 6 makes it round up).
C — Wrong. 65 and 66 are TRUNC(65.76) and ROUND(65.76) with no second argument (0 decimal places). Here the second argument 1 keeps one decimal place.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT TRUNC(65.76, 1), ROUND(65.76, 1) FROM DUAL;
work:
Keep 1 decimal place: 65.7|6
TRUNC → drop the 6 → 65.7
ROUND → next digit 6 ≥ 5 → round up → 65.8
Checked without DUAL: PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB print 65.7, 65.8; SQLite (no TRUNC) CAST(65.76*10 AS INTEGER)/10.0 = 65.7 and ROUND(65.76, 1) = 65.8.
tip: TRUNC cuts, ROUND rounds.

q: In Oracle, what does SELECT CEIL(-4.3), FLOOR(-4.3) FROM DUAL; print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CEIL gives the smallest integer that is >= the number, and FLOOR the largest integer that is <= it. On the number line −4.3 lies between −5 and −4, so CEIL(−4.3) = −4 and FLOOR(−4.3) = −5 — the pair '−4 and −5' is not listed.
concept: CEIL (CEILING in SQL Server) always moves UP the number line to the next integer; FLOOR always moves DOWN. For positive numbers that feels like 'round up / cut off' (CEIL(4.3) = 5, FLOOR(4.3) = 4), but for negative numbers 'up' means towards zero: CEIL(−4.3) = −4 and FLOOR(−4.3) = −5.
why: A — Wrong. This swaps the two answers. CEIL moves up to −4 (−4 is greater than −4.3) and FLOOR moves down to −5.
B — Wrong. −4 for both is just dropping the decimal part (truncation). FLOOR must go DOWN to −5, because −4 is greater than −4.3.
C — Wrong. −5 for both treats the minus sign as if it made the number 'bigger'. CEIL(−4.3) must be ≥ −4.3, and −5 is smaller.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.
E — Correct. CEIL(−4.3) = −4 and FLOOR(−4.3) = −5.
code: SELECT CEIL(-4.3), FLOOR(-4.3) FROM DUAL;
work:
Number line: −5 … −4.3 … −4
CEIL → smallest integer ≥ −4.3 → −4
FLOOR → largest integer ≤ −4.3 → −5
Checked without DUAL on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: −4, −5. (For +4.3: CEIL 5, FLOOR 4.)
tip: CEIL = go up (to the right), FLOOR = go down (to the left), even for negative numbers.

q: Which of the following expressions does NOT return the value 2?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: POWER(2, 3) = 2³ = 8. MOD(17, 5) is the remainder of 17 ÷ 5 = 2, and SQRT(4) = 2.
concept: Common numeric functions: MOD(m, n) = remainder of m divided by n (also written m % n in MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL); POWER(m, n) = m raised to the power n; SQRT(n) = square root; ABS(n) = value without its sign.
why: A — Wrong. 17 = 3 × 5 + 2, so the remainder MOD(17, 5) is 2. It DOES return 2.
B — Correct. POWER(2, 3) = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, not 2, so this is the expression that does NOT return 2.
C — Wrong. The square root of 4 is 2, so SQRT(4) DOES return 2.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. POWER(2, 3) does not return 2, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
MOD(17, 5)
POWER(2, 3)
SQRT(4)
work:
MOD(17, 5): 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2 → 2
POWER(2, 3): 2 × 2 × 2 → 8
SQRT(4) → 2
Checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: SELECT MOD(17,5), POWER(2,3), SQRT(4), ABS(-2) → 2, 8, 2, 2.

q: In Oracle, what does SELECT SUBSTR('DATABASE', 3, 4) FROM DUAL; print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SUBSTR(string, start, length) starts at position 3 (positions are counted from 1) and takes 4 characters: D-A-[T-A-B-A]-S-E → TABA.
concept: SUBSTR(s, start, length) returns part of a string. Positions start at 1 (not 0), and the third argument is the NUMBER of characters to take, not an end position. If the length is left out, it takes everything up to the end: SUBSTR('DATABASE', 5) = 'BASE'. Standard SQL writes SUBSTRING(s FROM 3 FOR 4); SQL Server uses SUBSTRING(s, 3, 4); MS Access uses MID.
why: A — Correct. Positions: D1 A2 T3 A4 B5 A6 S7 E8. Starting at 3 and taking 4 characters gives T, A, B, A.
B — Wrong. ABAS comes from counting positions from 0 (D = 0, A = 1, T = 2, A = 3), so 'position 3' would be the second A and the 4 characters would be A, B, A, S. SQL string positions start at 1.
C — Wrong. TA comes from treating 4 as an END position (characters 3 to 4). The third argument is the number of characters to take.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT SUBSTR('DATABASE', 3, 4) FROM DUAL;
work:
D(1) A(2) T(3) A(4) B(5) A(6) S(7) E(8)
Start at 3, take 4 characters → positions 3, 4, 5, 6 → T A B A
Checked without DUAL on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: TABA (also SUBSTRING('DATABASE' FROM 3 FOR 4) = TABA).
tip: SUBSTR(s, start, HOW MANY) — positions start at 1.

q: In Oracle, what does the query below print? (Each quoted string has TWO spaces before SQL and TWO spaces after it.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: TRIM removes spaces from both ends, leaving 'SQL' (length 3). RTRIM removes spaces only from the right end, leaving '  SQL' (length 5).
concept: TRIM(s) removes leading and trailing spaces (both ends). LTRIM(s) removes only the LEFT (leading) spaces and RTRIM(s) only the RIGHT (trailing) spaces. Spaces inside the string are never removed. LENGTH(s) counts every character, spaces included (SQL Server's LEN is different: it ignores trailing spaces).
why: A — Correct. LENGTH('SQL') = 3 and LENGTH('  SQL') = 5 (the two leading spaces remain after RTRIM).
B — Wrong. 3 for RTRIM would mean it also removed the leading spaces. RTRIM ('right trim') removes only trailing spaces, so the two spaces on the left stay.
C — Wrong. 7 is the length of the original string. TRIM removes the spaces at both ends, so its result has length 3.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
SELECT LENGTH(TRIM('  SQL  ')), LENGTH(RTRIM('  SQL  '))
FROM DUAL;
work:
Original: '␣␣SQL␣␣' → 7 characters
TRIM → 'SQL' → LENGTH 3
RTRIM → '␣␣SQL' → LENGTH 5
(LTRIM would give 'SQL␣␣' → 5)
Checked without DUAL on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: 3, 5 (and LTRIM 5, original 7).
tip: L = left, R = right, TRIM = both sides.

q: Some notes list the following as SQL functions. Which of them is NOT a function of ISO standard SQL?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: UCASE() and MID() are MS Access (and MySQL) names. Standard SQL uses UPPER() to convert to capitals and SUBSTRING() to take part of a string.
concept: Some function names in popular notes come from MS Access or MySQL rather than from standard SQL: UCASE/LCASE (standard: UPPER/LOWER), MID (standard: SUBSTRING; Oracle SUBSTR), LEN (SQL Server/Access; standard CHAR_LENGTH, Oracle/MySQL/PostgreSQL LENGTH), FORMAT, FIRST and LAST. UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTRING, TRIM and CHAR_LENGTH are defined by the ISO standard. UPPER and LOWER work in Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL and PostgreSQL; for the others some products use their own names (Oracle: SUBSTR and LENGTH; SQL Server: LEN).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. UCASE() is the MS Access/MySQL name; the standard function is UPPER(), and Oracle and PostgreSQL have no UCASE.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. MID() is the MS Access/MySQL name; the standard function is SUBSTRING() (SUBSTR in Oracle).
C — Wrong. UPPER() IS a standard SQL function (it converts text to capital letters) and works in Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL and PostgreSQL.
D — Correct. Both UCASE() and MID() are not part of standard SQL; UPPER() is.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work:
PostgreSQL 16: UPPER('sql') → SQL; UCASE('sql') → error 'function ucase does not exist'; MID('DATABASE',1,4) → error 'function mid does not exist'; SUBSTRING('DATABASE' FROM 1 FOR 4) → DATA.
SQLite: UPPER works; UCASE and MID → 'no such function'.
(DuckDB happens to accept UCASE as an alias, like MySQL, but rejects MID.)
tip: Common mistake (in the notes): UCASE, LCASE, MID, LEN, FORMAT, FIRST, LAST as 'SQL functions'. Standard names: UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTRING, CHAR_LENGTH.

q: In Oracle, which of the following expressions give the string '00042'?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: LPAD fills '0's on the LEFT until the length is 5 → '00042', and || joins '000' and '42' → '00042'. RPAD fills on the RIGHT → '42000'.
concept: LPAD(s, n, c) pads string s on the LEFT with character c until it is n characters long; RPAD pads on the RIGHT. The operator || joins (concatenates) two strings in Oracle, PostgreSQL and standard SQL; Oracle's CONCAT(a, b) does the same but takes exactly two arguments. SQL Server joins strings with + and MySQL normally with CONCAT().
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. '42' has 2 characters, so LPAD adds three '0's on the left: '00042'.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. || is Oracle's concatenation operator, so '000' || '42' = '00042'.
C — Wrong. RPAD pads on the RIGHT, giving '42000', not '00042'.
D — Correct. A and B both give '00042'; C gives '42000'.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
work:
LPAD: '42' (2 chars) → need 3 more → '000' + '42' = '00042'
||: '000' joined to '42' = '00042'
RPAD: '42' + '000' = '42000'
Checked on PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB (same Oracle-style LPAD/RPAD/||): '00042', '00042', '42000'. SQLite: '000' || '42' = '00042'. CONCAT('000', '42') = '00042' on all three.
tip: LPAD = pad on the Left, RPAD = pad on the Right.

q: In Oracle, what does SELECT INSTR('BANANA', 'AN'), REPLACE('BANANA', 'AN', 'X') FROM DUAL; print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: INSTR returns the position (counted from 1) of the FIRST occurrence of 'AN', which starts at position 2. REPLACE replaces EVERY occurrence of 'AN': B-AN-AN-A → B-X-X-A = BXXA.
concept: INSTR(s, sub) (Oracle, MySQL, SQLite) returns the position where sub first appears in s, counting from 1, or 0 if it does not appear; the standard form is POSITION(sub IN s) and SQL Server uses CHARINDEX. REPLACE(s, old, new) replaces ALL occurrences of old with new, not just the first one.
why: A — Wrong. The position 2 is right, but REPLACE changes every 'AN', not only the first, so the result is BXXA, not BXANA.
B — Wrong. BXXA is right, but 1 comes from counting positions from 0. SQL counts from 1: B is 1 and the first 'AN' starts at 2.
C — Correct. 'AN' first appears at position 2, and replacing both 'AN's with 'X' gives BXXA.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
SELECT INSTR('BANANA', 'AN'), REPLACE('BANANA', 'AN', 'X')
FROM DUAL;
work:
B(1) A(2) N(3) A(4) N(5) A(6)
'AN' occurs at positions 2–3 and 4–5 → INSTR = 2 (first occurrence)
REPLACE: B | AN | AN | A → B | X | X | A → BXXA
Checked without DUAL: SQLite and DuckDB INSTR → 2, REPLACE → BXXA; PostgreSQL 16 STRPOS / POSITION('AN' IN 'BANANA') → 2, REPLACE → BXXA.
tip: INSTR finds the FIRST match; REPLACE changes ALL matches.

q: In Oracle, what does the query below print for Ravi?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, so 50000 + NULL = NULL. NVL(Comm, 0) replaces the NULL with 0, so the second column is 50000 + 0 = 50000.
concept: NULL means 'unknown', so an expression such as Salary + Comm becomes NULL when Comm is NULL. NVL(expr, value) (Oracle) returns value when expr is NULL, otherwise expr itself. The standard function COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first non-NULL argument; MySQL also has IFNULL and SQL Server has ISNULL for the same job.
why: A — Wrong. The first column does not treat NULL as 0; plain arithmetic with NULL always gives NULL. Only the NVL column converts NULL to 0.
B — Correct. Salary + Comm = 50000 + NULL = NULL, and Salary + NVL(Comm, 0) = 50000 + 0 = 50000.
C — Wrong. NULL arithmetic gives NULL, not 0. (Amit's Comm is a real 0, which is different from NULL.)
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Salary | Comm
1     | Ravi  | 50000  | NULL
2     | Meena | 30000  | 2000
3     | Amit  | 40000  | 0

SELECT Salary + Comm AS Total1,
       Salary + NVL(Comm, 0) AS Total2
FROM EMP
WHERE Name = 'Ravi';
work:
FROM: 3 rows.
WHERE Name = 'Ravi' → 1 row (50000, NULL)
SELECT: Total1 = 50000 + NULL = NULL; Total2 = 50000 + NVL(NULL, 0) = 50000 + 0 = 50000
Checked with NVL translated to COALESCE on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB: (NULL, 50000). For Meena both are 32000; for Amit both are 40000.
tip: NULL + anything = NULL. Use NVL (Oracle) or COALESCE (standard) to replace NULL first.

q: In Oracle, which statement is correct?
opts: DUAL is a dummy table with exactly one row and one column, used for queries such as SELECT SYSDATE FROM DUAL;
More than one of the above
exp: DUAL is Oracle's one-row, one-column table used to evaluate an expression once. NULLIF(5, 5) returns NULL (the two values are equal), and COALESCE(NULL, 0, 7) returns 0 (the first non-NULL value).
concept: In Oracle (before version 23ai) every SELECT needs a FROM clause, so Oracle provides DUAL (one column DUMMY, one row 'X') for computing values: SELECT SYSDATE FROM DUAL; shows the current date and time. Other products use CURRENT_DATE (standard), NOW() (MySQL, PostgreSQL) or GETDATE() (SQL Server). NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a = b, otherwise a. COALESCE(x1, x2, …) returns the first argument that is not NULL.
why: A — Correct. DUAL has one column (DUMMY) and one row, so an expression selected from it is shown exactly once.
B — Wrong. NULLIF returns NULL when its two arguments are equal; 5 = 5, so NULLIF(5, 5) is NULL. (NULLIF(5, 3) would return 5.)
C — Wrong. COALESCE stops at the FIRST non-NULL argument, which is 0. The value 0 is a real value, not NULL, so 7 is never reached.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
SELECT NULLIF(5,5), NULLIF(5,3), COALESCE(NULL,0,7), COALESCE(NULL,NULL,7) on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB → NULL, 5, 0, 7.
Oracle documentation: DUAL has one column DUMMY VARCHAR2(1) containing one row with the value 'X'.
tip: NULLIF(a, b): equal → NULL. COALESCE: first non-NULL wins (0 is not NULL).

q: In how many rows of the output is Grade equal to 'Low'?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Roll 4 (39) and Roll 6 (25) fail both WHEN tests, and Roll 3's NULL makes both tests UNKNOWN (not TRUE), so it also falls to ELSE. That gives 3 'Low' rows.
concept: A searched CASE checks its WHEN conditions from top to bottom and returns the THEN value of the FIRST condition that is TRUE; later WHENs are not looked at. A condition that is UNKNOWN (for example NULL >= 60) counts as not TRUE. If no condition is TRUE, the ELSE value is returned; if there is no ELSE, the result is NULL.
why: A — Correct. Rolls 3, 4 and 6 get 'Low'.
B — Wrong. 2 forgets the NULL row. NULL >= 60 and NULL >= 40 are UNKNOWN, neither WHEN is TRUE, so CASE returns the ELSE value 'Low' for Roll 3.
C — Wrong. 4 also counts Roll 2, but 40 >= 40 is TRUE, so Roll 2 gets 'Mid'.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
RESULT
Roll | Marks
1    | 75
2    | 40
3    | NULL
4    | 39
5    | 60
6    | 25

SELECT Roll,
       CASE WHEN Marks >= 60 THEN 'High'
            WHEN Marks >= 40 THEN 'Mid'
            ELSE 'Low'
       END AS Grade
FROM RESULT;
work:
FROM: 6 rows; no WHERE. CASE is evaluated in SELECT for each row:
Roll 1: 75 >= 60 TRUE → High (second WHEN not checked)
Roll 2: 40 >= 60 FALSE; 40 >= 40 TRUE → Mid
Roll 3: NULL >= 60 UNKNOWN; NULL >= 40 UNKNOWN → ELSE → Low
Roll 4: 39 → both FALSE → Low
Roll 5: 60 >= 60 TRUE → High
Roll 6: 25 → both FALSE → Low
'Low' rows: 3, 4, 6 → 3 (same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB)
tip: In CASE, a NULL fails every WHEN test and lands in ELSE (or gives NULL if there is no ELSE).

q: In SQL Server (version 2012 or later), which query is NOT a valid way to list the 3 highest-paid employees?
opts: SELECT TOP 3 Name FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary DESC;
SELECT Name FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY;
SELECT Name FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary DESC LIMIT 3;
More than one of the above
exp: SQL Server limits rows with TOP or with OFFSET … FETCH (SQL Server 2012 and later). LIMIT belongs to MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite; SQL Server reports a syntax error for it.
concept: Each product limits the number of rows differently: SQL Server and MS Access use SELECT TOP n; MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite use LIMIT n at the end; Oracle uses ROWNUM (old way) or FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY (12c and later). The standard form is OFFSET … ROWS FETCH FIRST/NEXT n ROWS ONLY, which SQL Server (2012+), Oracle (12c+) and PostgreSQL support. Always combine row limiting with ORDER BY, otherwise 'the first n rows' is not well defined.
why: A — Wrong. TOP is SQL Server's own row-limiting keyword, so this query IS valid there.
B — Wrong. OFFSET … FETCH NEXT … ROWS ONLY (with ORDER BY) has been valid in SQL Server since version 2012, so this query IS valid.
C — Correct. SQL Server has no LIMIT clause, so this query is NOT valid there (it is the MySQL/PostgreSQL form).
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is not valid in SQL Server, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Logic checked on the 7-row EMP table: PostgreSQL 16 ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY → Arjun, Ravi, Sita; LIMIT 3 → Arjun, Ravi, Sita on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB.
SQL Server documentation: row limiting with TOP or with ORDER BY … OFFSET … FETCH; LIMIT is not part of T-SQL.
tip: TOP → SQL Server/Access; LIMIT → MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQLite; ROWNUM / FETCH FIRST → Oracle.

q: In MySQL or PostgreSQL, what does the query below return?
opts: An error, because LIMIT must be written before ORDER BY
More than one of the above
exp: ORDER BY Salary DESC sorts the rows from the highest salary down, and LIMIT 2 then keeps the first two: Arjun (60000) and Ravi (50000).
concept: In MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite, LIMIT n is written at the very end of the query, after ORDER BY, and it is applied after sorting. ORDER BY … DESC LIMIT n is the usual way to get the 'top n' rows.
why: A — Correct. After sorting by Salary descending, the first two rows are Arjun (60000) and Ravi (50000).
B — Wrong. Ravi and Meena are simply the first two rows stored in the table. LIMIT is applied after ORDER BY, so it takes the first two rows of the SORTED result.
C — Wrong. The opposite is true: LIMIT is written after ORDER BY. Writing LIMIT 2 before ORDER BY is the version that gives a syntax error.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27

SELECT Name
FROM EMP
ORDER BY Salary DESC
LIMIT 2;
work:
FROM: 7 rows; no WHERE.
ORDER BY Salary DESC → Arjun 60000, Ravi 50000, Sita 45000, Amit 40000, Pooja 35000, Meena/Kiran 30000
LIMIT 2 → Arjun, Ravi
Same on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB. 'LIMIT 2 ORDER BY …' → syntax error in all three.

q: In Oracle 12c or later, which queries are guaranteed to return the names of the 2 highest-paid employees of EMP?
opts: SELECT Name FROM (SELECT Name FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary DESC) WHERE ROWNUM <= 2;
SELECT Name FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary DESC FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY;
SELECT Name FROM EMP WHERE ROWNUM <= 2 ORDER BY Salary DESC;
More than one of the above
exp: ROWNUM is numbered while rows are fetched, BEFORE ORDER BY. So the sorting must happen first, in a subquery (A), or you use the 12c clause FETCH FIRST (B). Query C picks any 2 rows first and only then sorts those two.
concept: Oracle's ROWNUM is a pseudocolumn that numbers rows 1, 2, 3 … as they are fetched, before ORDER BY of the same query is applied. To get a 'top n', first sort in an inline view (subquery in FROM) and then apply ROWNUM <= n in the outer query. Since Oracle 12c, the standard row-limiting clause ORDER BY … FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY does the same job more simply.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The inner query sorts first, so ROWNUM <= 2 in the outer query keeps the two highest salaries (Arjun, Ravi).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY (Oracle 12c and later) is applied after ORDER BY, so it returns Arjun and Ravi.
C — Wrong. WHERE ROWNUM <= 2 is applied before ORDER BY, so it keeps whichever two rows are fetched first (for example Ravi and Meena) and then merely sorts those two. That is not the top 2.
D — Correct. A and B are correct top-2 queries; C is not.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is wrong.
code:
EMP
EmpID | Name  | Dept  | Salary | Age
1     | Ravi  | IT    | 50000  | 32
2     | Meena | HR    | 30000  | 25
3     | Amit  | IT    | 40000  | 23
4     | Sita  | HR    | 45000  | 28
5     | Kiran | SALES | 30000  | 24
6     | Arjun | IT    | 60000  | 29
7     | Pooja | SALES | 35000  | 27
work:
Translated to engines that have no ROWNUM:
A ≈ SELECT Name FROM (SELECT Name FROM EMP ORDER BY Salary DESC) t LIMIT 2 → Arjun, Ravi (SQLite, PostgreSQL 16, DuckDB)
B: ORDER BY Salary DESC FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY → Arjun, Ravi (PostgreSQL 16, DuckDB)
C ≈ take the first 2 rows fetched (storage order: Ravi, Meena), then ORDER BY Salary DESC → Ravi, Meena ✗
Oracle documentation: if ORDER BY follows ROWNUM in the same query, the rows are reordered after ROWNUM is assigned; put ORDER BY in a subquery to apply ROWNUM after sorting.
tip: Oracle top-n: sort INSIDE, ROWNUM OUTSIDE — or use FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY (12c+).

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the tables EMP and DEPT shown, how many rows does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An inner join returns only matching pairs. Asha and Meena match dno 10 (Sales) and Ravi matches 20 (HR). Kunal (NULL) and Sohan (40) have no match, and IT has no employee, so there are 3 rows.
concept: INNER JOIN … ON condition pairs each row of the first table with each row of the second table for which the condition is TRUE. Rows with no partner are dropped from both sides. A NULL in the join column never matches anything, because NULL = 10 is UNKNOWN, not TRUE. INNER JOIN is the default join type: writing just JOIN means INNER JOIN.
why: A — Correct. Asha–Sales, Ravi–HR and Meena–Sales: 3 rows.
B — Wrong. 5 is the row count of a LEFT OUTER JOIN, which keeps every employee, including Kunal and Sohan with a NULL dname. An inner join drops them.
C — Wrong. 2 counts the departments that have employees (Sales and HR). But Sales matches two employees, so it appears twice: there is one output row per matching pair.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

DEPT
dno | dname | loc
10  | Sales | Patna
20  | HR    | Gaya
30  | IT    | Patna

SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM emp e INNER JOIN dept d
ON e.dno = d.dno;
work:
Match each EMP row on dno:
1. Asha (10) → Sales: match.
2. Ravi (20) → HR: match.
3. Meena (10) → Sales: match.
4. Kunal (NULL) → no match (NULL = anything is UNKNOWN).
5. Sohan (40) → no DEPT row 40.
DEPT 30 (IT) has no employee → not shown.
Rows = 3. Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB.
tip: Inner join: one output row for every matching PAIR, and nothing for unmatched rows.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the tables EMP and DEPT shown, how many rows does this query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every row of the left table (EMP). The 3 matching rows appear with their dname, and Kunal and Sohan appear with dname NULL: 5 rows.
concept: LEFT [OUTER] JOIN returns all the rows of the inner join, plus every row of the LEFT table that found no match, with NULL in the columns of the right table. Unmatched rows of the RIGHT table are not shown. So the result has at least as many rows as the left table (more if some left row matches several right rows).
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the inner-join count. A LEFT JOIN also keeps the unmatched employees Kunal and Sohan.
B — Wrong. 6 is the FULL OUTER JOIN count, which also adds the unmatched department IT. A LEFT JOIN does not keep unmatched rows of the right table.
C — Correct. 3 matched rows + 2 unmatched employees (Kunal and Sohan, with dname NULL) = 5.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

DEPT
dno | dname | loc
10  | Sales | Patna
20  | HR    | Gaya
30  | IT    | Patna

SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM emp e LEFT OUTER JOIN dept d
ON e.dno = d.dno;
work:
1. Matched rows: Asha–Sales, Ravi–HR, Meena–Sales (3).
2. Unmatched EMP rows kept with NULL dname: Kunal–NULL, Sohan–NULL (2).
3. The unmatched DEPT row (IT) is NOT kept in a LEFT join.
Total = 5. Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the tables EMP and DEPT shown, how many rows does this query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: FULL OUTER JOIN = 3 matched rows + 2 unmatched EMP rows (Kunal, Sohan) + 1 unmatched DEPT row (IT) = 6 rows, which is not listed.
concept: FULL [OUTER] JOIN keeps everything: the matching pairs, the unmatched rows of the left table (right-side columns NULL) and the unmatched rows of the right table (left-side columns NULL). A quick formula: rows = matched pairs + unmatched left rows + unmatched right rows. MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN; there it is written as a LEFT JOIN combined by UNION with a RIGHT JOIN.
why: A — Wrong. 5 is the LEFT OUTER JOIN count (3 matched + Kunal + Sohan). It forgets the unmatched department IT.
B — Wrong. 4 is the RIGHT OUTER JOIN count (3 matched + IT). It forgets the unmatched employees Kunal and Sohan.
C — Wrong. 15 = 5 × 3 is the CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product) count. An outer join pairs rows only when the ON condition is true.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The result has 6 rows (3 + 2 + 1), which is not among A–C.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

DEPT
dno | dname | loc
10  | Sales | Patna
20  | HR    | Gaya
30  | IT    | Patna

SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM emp e FULL OUTER JOIN dept d
ON e.dno = d.dno;
work:
1. Matched pairs: Asha–Sales, Ravi–HR, Meena–Sales → 3.
2. Unmatched EMP rows: Kunal (dno NULL), Sohan (dno 40) → 2, with dname NULL.
3. Unmatched DEPT rows: IT (dno 30) → 1, with name NULL.
4. Total = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 → not listed → E.
Verified: COUNT(*) = 6 in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB (LEFT = 5, RIGHT = 4, INNER = 3).
tip: Outer-join counting: matched pairs + unmatched left (LEFT) + unmatched right (RIGHT); FULL adds both.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Table EMP has 5 rows and table DEPT has 3 rows. How many rows does  SELECT * FROM emp CROSS JOIN dept;  return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product: every EMP row is paired with every DEPT row, so 5 × 3 = 15 rows.
concept: CROSS JOIN (Cartesian product) pairs each row of the first table with each row of the second, with no condition. If the tables have m and n rows, the result has m × n rows, and its number of columns is the sum of the two tables' column counts. Writing FROM emp, dept with no join condition in WHERE gives the same result.
why: A — Wrong. 8 = 5 + 3 adds the row counts. A Cartesian product multiplies them. (Adding is right for the number of COLUMNS, not rows.)
B — Correct. Each of the 5 EMP rows is paired with each of the 3 DEPT rows: 5 × 3 = 15 rows.
C — Wrong. 5 is just the number of EMP rows. A CROSS JOIN repeats every EMP row once for each DEPT row.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Rows = rows(EMP) × rows(DEPT) = 5 × 3 = 15.
Verified with a 5-row EMP and a 3-row DEPT: COUNT(*) = 15 in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB.
tip: CROSS JOIN: rows multiply, columns add.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: EMP and DEPT have exactly one common column, dno. With SELECT *, which of the following joins shows the dno column only ONCE in the result?
opts: FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dno = d.dno
More than one of the above
exp: NATURAL JOIN and JOIN … USING merge the common column into a single column. An equi join written with ON keeps both e.dno and d.dno.
concept: An equi join is a join whose condition uses only equality, such as ON e.dno = d.dno; with SELECT * it shows the dno column of both tables. A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins on all columns with the same name and shows each such column only once. JOIN … USING (col) joins on the named common column(s) and also shows them once. So: natural join = equi join on all common columns + removal of the duplicate columns.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. NATURAL JOIN joins on all same-named columns (here only dno) and keeps a single dno column.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. USING (dno) names the join column, and the result has a single dno column.
C — Wrong. With ON e.dno = d.dno, SELECT * returns both dno columns (eid, name, dno, sal, dno, dname, loc). This is a plain equi join.
D — Correct. Both A and B show dno only once.
E — Wrong. A and B are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Column lists from SELECT * (checked in PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB):
A. NATURAL JOIN → eid, name, dno, sal, dname, loc (6 columns, one dno; PostgreSQL lists dno first).
B. JOIN … USING (dno) → the same 6 columns, one dno.
C. JOIN … ON e.dno = d.dno → eid, name, dno, sal, dno, dname, loc (7 columns, dno twice).
True options: A and B → D.
tip: Common mistake (found in many notes): 'equi join shows the common column only once'. That is the natural join; an equi join keeps both columns.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Table STAFF stores each employee's manager id in mgr. Which (employee, manager) rows does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This is a self join: STAFF is used twice, as s (employee) and m (manager). Each employee is paired with the row whose sid equals his mgr. Anil has mgr NULL, so the inner join drops him.
concept: A self join joins a table with itself. Two different aliases (here s and m) make the two copies separate, as if they were two tables. Self joins are used for hierarchies stored in one table, such as employee–manager, or for comparing rows of the same table. Because this is an inner join, an employee without a manager (mgr NULL) does not appear; a LEFT JOIN would keep him with a NULL manager.
why: A — Wrong. The row Anil–NULL would appear only with a LEFT JOIN. In an inner join, NULL = m.sid is never true, so Anil is dropped.
B — Correct. Bina (mgr 1) → Anil, Charu (mgr 1) → Anil, Dev (mgr 2) → Bina.
C — Wrong. This swaps the roles. s.name is the employee and m.name is the manager, so the first name of each pair is the employee: Bina–Anil, not Anil–Bina.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

sid | name  | mgr
1   | Anil  | NULL
2   | Bina  | 1
3   | Charu | 1
4   | Dev   | 2

SELECT s.name, m.name
FROM staff s JOIN staff m
ON s.mgr = m.sid;

s = employee copy, m = manager copy; match s.mgr = m.sid:
1. Anil: mgr NULL → no match → dropped.
2. Bina: mgr 1 → sid 1 is Anil → (Bina, Anil).
3. Charu: mgr 1 → Anil → (Charu, Anil).
4. Dev: mgr 2 → Bina → (Dev, Bina).
Result: 3 rows. Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB (with LEFT JOIN, (Anil, NULL) is added).

To keep them, put the condition in the ON clause, or add OR d.dname IS NULL.

C — Correct. Only Asha–Sales and Meena–Sales make dname <> 'HR' TRUE.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Which join returns the matching rows and ALSO the unmatched rows of BOTH tables, filling the missing side with NULLs?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps the unmatched rows of the left table and of the right table, padding the other side with NULLs.
concept: Join types differ in which unmatched rows they keep. INNER JOIN keeps only matching pairs. LEFT OUTER JOIN also keeps unmatched rows of the left table; RIGHT OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows of the right table. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows of both tables. In every outer join, the columns of the missing side are filled with NULL.
why: A — Wrong. LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows of the LEFT table only; unmatched rows of the right table are lost.
B — Correct. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.
C — Wrong. INNER JOIN keeps no unmatched rows at all — only the matching pairs.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN; it is written as (LEFT JOIN) UNION (RIGHT JOIN).

q: Using the tables EMP and DEPT shown, which of the following queries correctly lists the departments that have no employees (the expected answer is IT)?

SELECT dname FROM dept d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM emp e WHERE e.dno = d.dno);

concept: To find rows with no match, three patterns are common: NOT IN (subquery), NOT EXISTS (correlated subquery) and LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.key IS NULL. NOT EXISTS is TRUE when the subquery returns no row, and NULLs in the other table do not disturb it. The LEFT JOIN pattern keeps unmatched departments with NULL employee columns and then picks them out. NOT IN gives the same answer only when the subquery cannot return NULL.
why: A — Wrong. NOT IN fails here: the subquery returns 10, 20, 10, NULL, 40, and the NULL makes '30 NOT IN (…)' UNKNOWN, so even IT is not returned. The query returns no rows.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The LEFT JOIN gives IT with all EMP columns NULL; e.eid (the primary key) is NULL only for such unmatched rows, so the result is IT.

If the subquery returns no rows, there is nothing that x fails to beat, so the condition is TRUE (it is 'vacuously true'). In contrast, x > ANY (empty set) is FALSE, because there is no value that x beats. An empty subquery used with ALL, ANY, IN or EXISTS is not an error.

B — Wrong. 0 would be the result of > ANY (empty set), which is FALSE. With ALL, an empty set makes the condition TRUE.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Which of the following WHERE clauses gives the same result as  WHERE dno IN (SELECT dno FROM dept WHERE loc = 'Patna')?
opts: WHERE dno = ANY (SELECT dno FROM dept WHERE loc = 'Patna')
WHERE dno = SOME (SELECT dno FROM dept WHERE loc = 'Patna')
WHERE dno = ALL (SELECT dno FROM dept WHERE loc = 'Patna')
More than one of the above
exp: = ANY and = SOME both mean 'equal to at least one returned value', which is exactly what IN means. = ALL means 'equal to every returned value', which is different.
concept: In SQL, SOME is just another word for ANY. x = ANY (subquery) is TRUE when x equals at least one returned value, so it is equivalent to x IN (subquery). x = ALL (subquery) is TRUE only when x equals every returned value, which can happen only if all the returned values are the same. Note also that NOT IN is equivalent to <> ALL (not to <> ANY).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. = ANY is TRUE when dno equals at least one Patna department number — exactly the meaning of IN.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. SOME is a synonym of ANY, so = SOME is also equivalent to IN.

C — Wrong. = ALL requires dno to equal every Patna department number (10 and 30) at the same time, which is impossible here; on the sample EMP/DEPT data it returns no rows, while IN returns Asha and Meena.
D — Correct. Both = ANY and = SOME are equivalent to IN.
E — Wrong. A and B are both equivalent to IN, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked on the usual EMP/DEPT data (Patna departments: 10 and 30) in PostgreSQL and DuckDB:
IN → Asha, Meena; = ANY → Asha, Meena; = SOME → Asha, Meena; = ALL → no rows.
True options: A and B → D.
tip: IN ≡ = ANY ≡ = SOME;  NOT IN ≡ <> ALL.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q:
Consider the following statements about subqueries:
I. A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer query.
II. A correlated subquery is, in principle, evaluated again for each row of the outer query.
III. A non-correlated subquery must be evaluated again for each row of the outer query.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II describe a correlated subquery correctly. III is false: a non-correlated subquery does not depend on the outer row, so it needs to be evaluated only once.
concept: A non-correlated (simple) subquery is independent of the outer query: it can run once, and its result is then used by the outer query, e.g. WHERE sal > (SELECT AVG(sal) FROM emp). A correlated subquery uses a value from the current outer row, e.g. WHERE sal > (SELECT AVG(sal) FROM emp WHERE dno = e.dno); logically it is re-evaluated for every outer row, because e.dno changes from row to row. EXISTS and NOT EXISTS are usually used with correlated subqueries. (The optimizer may internally rewrite either kind, but the meaning stays the same.)
why: A — Wrong. 'I only' leaves out II, which is true: because a correlated subquery uses the outer row's values, it is (conceptually) run once per outer row.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false, and it leaves out I, which is true.
C — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Correlated = the inner query 'looks outside' at the current outer row, so it is repeated for each row.

Kunal's dno is NULL, so his subquery average is NULL and the comparison is UNKNOWN. Only Meena is returned.
concept: In a correlated subquery the inner query uses a value from the current outer row (here e.dno). For each employee, the DBMS computes the average salary of that employee's department and then compares. Two traps: an employee who is alone in his department equals his department's average, so '>' fails; and when e.dno is NULL, the condition dno = NULL matches no row, AVG over no rows is NULL, and sal > NULL is UNKNOWN.
why: A — Wrong. Asha, Meena is the result of comparing with the overall average (26000). The subquery is correlated (dno = e.dno), so each employee is compared with his own department's average; Asha's 30000 is below department 10's average of 35000.
B — Wrong. This uses >= instead of >. Ravi and Sohan are alone in their departments, so each salary equals the department average and is not greater than it.
C — Wrong. Kunal's dno is NULL, so the subquery finds no rows (dno = NULL is never TRUE), AVG returns NULL, and 20000 > NULL is UNKNOWN. Kunal is not returned.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Only Meena is returned, which is not among A–C.

4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000

WHERE sal > (SELECT AVG(sal) FROM emp
             WHERE dno = e.dno);

Department averages: 10 → (30000 + 40000) / 2 = 35000; 20 → 25000; 40 → 15000; NULL → subquery finds no rows → AVG = NULL.

More than one of the above
exp: With the single-row operator =, the subquery must return at most one row. Department 10 has two salaries (30000 and 40000), so Oracle raises ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row.
concept: A single-row subquery returns at most one row and is used with single-row operators (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=). A multi-row subquery can return many rows and must be used with IN, ANY/SOME, ALL or EXISTS. If a subquery used with = returns two or more rows, Oracle stops with ORA-01427; PostgreSQL similarly reports 'more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression'. The fix is to use IN (or = ANY) instead of =.
why: A — Wrong. Asha and Meena would be returned by WHERE sal IN (SELECT sal FROM emp WHERE dno = 10). With = the query is invalid when the subquery returns two rows.
B — Wrong. Oracle does not quietly pick the first row of the subquery. (SQLite does behave like this, which is why the question names Oracle.)
C — Correct. Oracle raises ORA-01427: single-row subquery returns more than one row.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE sal = (SELECT sal FROM emp
             WHERE dno = 10);
work:
1. Subquery: sal of dno 10 → 30000, 40000 (2 rows).
2. '=' needs a single value → error ORA-01427 in Oracle.
Checked: PostgreSQL and DuckDB also raise an error ('more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression'); SQLite silently uses the first row and returns Asha, which is why the product must be named.
tip: If a subquery may return many rows, use IN, not =.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the table EMP shown, what does this query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The subquery in FROM (a derived table) gives each department's total: 10 → 70000, 20 → 25000, 40 → 15000, NULL → 20000. The outer MAX picks 70000.
concept: A subquery in the FROM clause is called a derived table (or inline view). It is computed first and then used like a temporary table; it is usually given an alias (here t), and MySQL and SQL Server require one. Derived tables let you apply an aggregate to the result of another aggregate, such as the largest of the department totals.
why: A — Wrong. 40000 is the highest single salary (Meena's). The query takes the maximum of the department TOTALS, not of individual salaries.
B — Correct. Department 10's total, 30000 + 40000 = 70000, is the largest.
C — Wrong. 130000 is the sum of all salaries. The outer query applies MAX to the per-department totals, not SUM.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

SELECT MAX(total)
FROM (SELECT dno, SUM(sal) AS total
      FROM emp
      GROUP BY dno) t;
work:
1. Inner query (GROUP BY dno): 10 → 30000 + 40000 = 70000; 20 → 25000; 40 → 15000; NULL → 20000 (all NULLs form one group).
2. Outer query: MAX(70000, 25000, 15000, 20000) = 70000.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB.
tip: An aggregate of an aggregate (the max of sums) needs a derived table or a CTE.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Tables R and S are shown. How many rows does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: UNION combines both results and removes duplicates: 1, 2, 3, 4 — 4 rows.
concept: UNION returns every row that appears in either query, with duplicates removed (like the set union ∪). UNION ALL keeps all rows, including duplicates, so it is faster (no duplicate check) and its row count is simply the sum of the two counts. INTERSECT returns the rows common to both, and EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle) returns the rows of the first query that are not in the second.
why: A — Correct. The distinct values from both tables are 1, 2, 3 and 4.
B — Wrong. 7 = 4 + 3 is the UNION ALL count, which keeps duplicates. UNION removes them.
C — Wrong. 2 is the INTERSECT count (only 2 and 3 are in both tables). UNION keeps values found in either table.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

S

SELECT x FROM r
UNION
SELECT x FROM s;

1. R gives 1, 2, 2, 3; S gives 2, 3, 4.
2. All together: 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4 (7 rows = UNION ALL).
3. Remove duplicates: 1, 2, 3, 4 → 4 rows.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB (UNION ALL gives 7).

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Tables R and S are shown. What does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: INTERSECT returns the distinct values present in both results: 2 and 3.
concept: INTERSECT returns the rows that appear in the results of both queries (the set intersection ∩), without duplicates. INTERSECT ALL (supported by PostgreSQL, DuckDB and newer Oracle versions) keeps duplicates, as many times as the smaller of the two counts. Older MySQL versions had no INTERSECT; there the same result is written with IN or a join.
why: A — Wrong. INTERSECT removes duplicates, so 2 appears only once. (Even INTERSECT ALL gives 2 only once here, because S contains a single 2.)
B — Wrong. 1 and 4 are the values found in only ONE table (1 only in R, 4 only in S). INTERSECT returns the values found in both.
C — Correct. 2 and 3 are in both tables.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Oracle's set operator MINUS is equivalent to which operator of standard SQL (used, for example, in PostgreSQL and SQL Server)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MINUS and EXCEPT both return the distinct rows of the first query that do not appear in the second query — the set difference.
concept: Both MINUS (Oracle) and EXCEPT (standard SQL; PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite) return the distinct rows of the first query that are not in the second — the set difference (−) of relational algebra. The order matters: A MINUS B is not the same as B MINUS A. Recent Oracle versions (21c onwards) also accept the keyword EXCEPT.
why: A — Wrong. INTERSECT returns rows that are in BOTH queries (set intersection), not rows of the first that are missing from the second.
B — Correct. EXCEPT is the standard name of the set-difference operator that Oracle calls MINUS.
C — Wrong. UNION ALL joins the two results together and keeps duplicates; it never removes rows.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: MINUS = Oracle's name for EXCEPT; both mean 'rows of the first query minus rows of the second'.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: To combine two SELECT statements with UNION, which of the following is NOT required?
opts: Both SELECTs return the same number of columns
Corresponding columns have compatible data types
Corresponding columns have the same names
More than one of the above
exp: Column names do not need to match; the result simply takes its column names from the first SELECT. The same number of columns and compatible types are required (union compatibility).
concept: Set operators (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT) need union-compatible inputs: the same number of columns, and each pair of corresponding columns (1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd, and so on) must have compatible data types. Column names may differ; the result uses the names of the first SELECT. For example, SELECT roll FROM student UNION SELECT eid FROM emp is valid, and its single column is called roll.
why: A — Wrong. This IS required: a different number of columns causes an error (PostgreSQL: 'each UNION query must have the same number of columns'). So it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. This IS required: for example, an INTEGER column cannot be matched with a DATE column (PostgreSQL: 'UNION types integer and date cannot be matched'). So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Correct. The names need not be the same; the result takes its column names from the first SELECT.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked: SELECT roll FROM s UNION SELECT eid FROM t runs in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB (result column named roll); one column UNION two columns → error in all three; INTEGER UNION DATE → error in PostgreSQL.
tip: Union compatibility = same number of columns + compatible types, position by position. Names do not matter.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
