q: In a query of the form  SELECT … UNION SELECT …  (without parentheses), where may an ORDER BY clause be written?
opts: Only once, after the last SELECT; it sorts the whole combined result
After each SELECT, before the UNION keyword
More than one of the above
exp: The combined result is one table, so ORDER BY may appear only once, at the very end, and it sorts the final combined rows.
concept: When queries are combined with UNION, INTERSECT or EXCEPT, the result is one table and ORDER BY may appear only once, at the very end; it sorts the final result. It usually refers to the column names (or positions) of the first SELECT, e.g. ORDER BY 1. Each individual SELECT may still have its own WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING clauses.
why: A — Correct. One ORDER BY, at the end, sorting the combined result.

B — Wrong. An ORDER BY placed before UNION is a syntax error (SQLite: 'ORDER BY clause should come after UNION not before'). Sorting the separate parts would be pointless anyway, because the combined result is formed afterwards.
C — Wrong. The first SELECT comes before the UNION keyword, so an ORDER BY there is the same syntax error as in B.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: One combined result → one ORDER BY, at the end.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Which of the following is NOT true about an ordinary (non-materialized) view?
opts: It is a virtual table defined by a stored query
It can be queried with SELECT just like a table
It stores its own separate copy of the rows of its base tables
More than one of the above
exp: An ordinary view stores only its defining query, not the rows. Each time it is used, the query runs on the current base tables.
concept: A view is created with CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT …. Only the query (the view's definition) is stored in the data dictionary; no rows are stored. Each time the view is used, the DBMS runs the stored query on the current base tables, so the view always shows up-to-date data. That is why views are called virtual tables. A materialized view is different: it does store the query result.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: a view is a virtual table whose definition is a stored SELECT. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: a view can be used in FROM, joined, filtered and so on, like a table. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Correct. This statement is false: an ordinary view keeps no copy of the data; storing the result is what a materialized view does.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: View = stored query, not stored data.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the table EMP shown, what does the final SELECT return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A view stores only its query. When RICH is queried, the query runs on the current EMP, which now includes Tara (35000 > 20000): Asha, Ravi, Meena and Tara → 4.
concept: A view is not a snapshot taken when it is created. It is a saved query that is executed every time the view is used. Therefore rows inserted, updated or deleted in the base table later are automatically reflected when the view is queried again.
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the count at the time the view was created (Asha, Ravi, Meena). A view is not a snapshot; Tara, inserted later, is included because the query is run again.
B — Correct. Asha, Ravi, Meena and Tara have sal > 20000.
C — Wrong. 6 is the number of rows in EMP. The view keeps only rows with sal > 20000, so Kunal (20000, not greater) and Sohan (15000) are excluded.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

CREATE VIEW rich AS
  SELECT eid, name, sal FROM emp
  WHERE sal > 20000;

INSERT INTO emp VALUES (6, 'Tara', 20, 35000);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rich;
work:
1. EMP after the INSERT: 6 rows.
2. Rows with sal > 20000: Asha 30000, Ravi 25000, Meena 40000, Tara 35000 (Kunal's 20000 is not greater; Sohan 15000).
3. COUNT = 4. Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB (count 3 before the INSERT, 4 after).
tip: Base table changes → the view shows them at once, because the view's query is run every time.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In PostgreSQL, the statements below are run on the table EMP shown. Afterwards, how many rows do EMP and the view RICH contain?
opts: An error occurs; EMP still has 5 rows and RICH has 3
EMP has 6 rows and RICH has 4
EMP has 5 rows and RICH has 4
More than one of the above
exp: RICH is a simple view on one table, so PostgreSQL inserts the row into EMP (EMP: 6 rows). Without WITH CHECK OPTION the row is accepted even though 15000 > 20000 is false — so Tara is not visible through the view (RICH: still 3 rows).
concept: A simple view (one base table, no GROUP BY, DISTINCT, aggregates or set operators) is updatable: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the view are passed on to the base table. By default the DBMS does not check that a new or changed row still satisfies the view's WHERE condition, so a row can 'disappear' from the view right after being inserted through it. Adding WITH CHECK OPTION to CREATE VIEW makes the DBMS reject such rows.
why: A — Wrong. The error happens only when the view is created WITH CHECK OPTION. This view has no check option, so the INSERT succeeds.
B — Wrong. EMP does get 6 rows, but Tara's salary of 15000 does not satisfy sal > 20000, so she does not appear in RICH; RICH still has 3 rows.
C — Wrong. A view stores no rows of its own; the inserted row goes into EMP. So EMP gets 6 rows, and RICH, which just runs its query again, still shows 3.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. EMP has 6 rows and RICH has 3, which is not among A–C.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

CREATE VIEW rich AS
  SELECT eid, name, dno, sal FROM emp
  WHERE sal > 20000;

INSERT INTO rich VALUES (6, 'Tara', 20, 15000);
work:
1. RICH is a simple single-table view → automatically updatable in PostgreSQL.
2. INSERT INTO rich … → the row (6, Tara, 20, 15000) is stored in EMP → EMP has 6 rows.
3. No WITH CHECK OPTION → the row is not checked against sal > 20000.
4. RICH runs its query: Asha, Ravi, Meena → 3 rows (Tara fails sal > 20000).
5. '6 and 3' is not among A–C → E.
Verified in PostgreSQL 16: EMP 6, RICH 3. With WITH CHECK OPTION the INSERT fails ('new row violates check option for view "rich"').
tip: WITH CHECK OPTION means: rows added or changed through the view must stay visible in the view.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In standard SQL (for example in PostgreSQL, with no INSTEAD OF triggers or rules), a view CANNOT be updated directly if its defining query contains:
opts: GROUP BY with an aggregate function such as SUM
a WHERE clause on a single base table
More than one of the above
exp: To be updatable, each view row must map to exactly one base-table row. GROUP BY with aggregates and DISTINCT merge several base rows into one view row, so such views are read-only. A WHERE clause on one table keeps the one-to-one mapping.
concept: A view is updatable when each of its rows corresponds to exactly one row of one base table, so the DBMS knows which base row to change. Features that make a view NOT updatable include GROUP BY, HAVING, aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT, …), DISTINCT and set operators such as UNION. A view with only a column list and a WHERE clause on a single table is updatable. Non-updatable views can be made writable with INSTEAD OF triggers.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A row of such a view (for example dno 10 with total 70000) is built from several base rows, so an UPDATE on it cannot be passed to one base row; PostgreSQL says 'cannot update view'.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. DISTINCT can merge several identical base rows into one view row, so the DBMS cannot tell which base row to change.
C — Wrong. A WHERE clause only filters rows; each view row still maps to one base row, so the view stays updatable (PostgreSQL ran UPDATE v3 SET sal = 99 WHERE eid = 3 successfully).
D — Correct. Both GROUP BY with aggregates and DISTINCT make a view non-updatable.
E — Wrong. A and B are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked in PostgreSQL 16 on EMP:
A. CREATE VIEW v1 AS SELECT dno, SUM(sal) AS tot FROM emp GROUP BY dno; UPDATE v1 … → 'cannot update view "v1"'.
B. CREATE VIEW v2 AS SELECT DISTINCT dno, sal FROM emp; UPDATE v2 … → 'cannot update view "v2"'.
C. CREATE VIEW v3 AS SELECT eid, name, sal FROM emp WHERE dno = 10; UPDATE v3 SET sal = 99 WHERE eid = 3 → succeeds and EMP changes.
True options: A and B → D.
tip: Updatable view = one view row ↔ one base row. GROUP BY, aggregates, DISTINCT and UNION break this.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Which of the following is NOT true about a materialized view?
opts: It re-runs its query every time it is read, so it is never out of date
It physically stores the result of its query
It can make repeated heavy queries, such as summaries, faster
More than one of the above
exp: A materialized view returns its stored result when read; it does not re-run its query, so its data can be stale until it is refreshed. B and C are true.
concept: A materialized view (Oracle, PostgreSQL; SQL Server has a similar 'indexed view') stores the result of its query on disk, like a table. Reading it is fast because the work is already done, which is useful for reports and data warehouses. The price is that the stored data can become stale (out of date) when the base tables change, so it must be refreshed — for example with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW in PostgreSQL, or with Oracle's refresh options such as ON DEMAND or ON COMMIT.
why: A — Correct. This statement is false: a materialized view does not re-run its query on every read, and its data can be stale until it is refreshed. Re-running the query on every use is what an ordinary view does.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: storing the result physically is exactly what 'materialized' means. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: because the result is computed in advance, repeated heavy queries become fast. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Ordinary view = stored query (always fresh, computed when read). Materialized view = stored result (fast, but needs refreshing).

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q:
Consider the following statements about views:
I. A view can hide some columns or rows of a table from a user, so views help in security.
II. Dropping a view with DROP VIEW also deletes the rows of its base table.
III. A view can be defined on another view.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and III are true. II is false: DROP VIEW removes only the view's definition; the base table and its rows are not touched.
concept: Views are used for security (a user is given SELECT on a view that shows only some columns or rows, instead of on the base table), for simplicity (a complex join is hidden behind a simple name), and for logical data independence (old queries keep working when tables change). A view can be built on tables or on other views. DROP VIEW name removes only the stored query from the data dictionary; base tables and their data are unaffected.
why: A — Wrong. It includes II, which is false (DROP VIEW never deletes base-table rows), and it leaves out III, which is true.
B — Correct. I and III are true; II is false.
C — Wrong. It includes II, which is false, and it leaves out I, which is true.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Checked in PostgreSQL 16: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT eid, name, sal FROM emp; CREATE VIEW vv AS SELECT name FROM v WHERE sal > 20000 → works (III true). DROP VIEW vv; DROP VIEW v; → EMP still has all 5 rows (II false).
tip: DROP VIEW removes only the 'window', never the data behind it.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the table EMP shown, what does this query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The CTE dt has one row per department, including one group for the NULL dno: totals 70000, 25000, 15000 and 20000. Their average is 130000 / 4 = 32500.
concept: The WITH clause defines a common table expression (CTE): a named, temporary result that exists only for the query that follows it. It works like a derived table, but it is written first and given a name, which makes complex queries easier to read. Remember also that GROUP BY puts all NULLs of the grouping column into ONE group, so Kunal (dno NULL) forms a group of his own.
why: A — Wrong. 26000 is the average salary per EMPLOYEE (130000 / 5). The outer AVG works on the CTE's rows, which are department totals (4 rows), not employees.
B — Wrong. 36666.67 = (70000 + 25000 + 15000) / 3 ignores the NULL group. GROUP BY does not drop NULLs; they form one group (total 20000).
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno  | sal
1   | Asha  | 10   | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20   | 25000
3   | Meena | 10   | 40000
4   | Kunal | NULL | 20000
5   | Sohan | 40   | 15000

WITH dt AS (
  SELECT dno, SUM(sal) AS tot
  FROM emp
  GROUP BY dno
)
SELECT AVG(tot) FROM dt;
work:
1. CTE dt (GROUP BY dno): 10 → 70000; 20 → 25000; 40 → 15000; NULL → 20000 (4 rows).
2. AVG(tot) = (70000 + 25000 + 15000 + 20000) / 4 = 130000 / 4 = 32500.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB: AVG = 32500 and the CTE has 4 rows.
tip: GROUP BY makes one group for all the NULLs — count that group too.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: What does this query (PostgreSQL / MySQL 8 syntax) return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The anchor gives 1; the recursive part adds x + 1 while x < 5, giving 2, 3, 4 and 5. It stops when x = 5. Sum = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
concept: A recursive CTE has two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor (non-recursive) query that gives the starting rows, and a recursive query that refers to the CTE itself and produces new rows from the previous ones. The process repeats until the recursive part returns no new rows. Recursive CTEs are used for number series and for hierarchies such as employee–manager chains. PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and SQLite write WITH RECURSIVE; SQL Server and Oracle write just WITH.
why: A — Correct. The rows are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and their sum is 15.
B — Wrong. 10 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 stops one step too early. When x = 4, the condition 4 < 5 is still true, so x + 1 = 5 is produced.
C — Wrong. 21 = 1 + … + 6 goes one step too far. From x = 5 the condition 5 < 5 is false, so 6 is never produced.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
1. Anchor: x = 1.
2. From 1: 1 < 5 → 2. From 2 → 3. From 3 → 4. From 4: 4 < 5 → 5.
3. From 5: 5 < 5 is false → no new row; the recursion stops.
4. Rows: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 → SUM = 15.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB (x < 4 would give 10; x < 6 would give 21).
tip: In a recursive CTE, the WHERE condition is tested on the OLD row; the new row x + 1 can be equal to the limit.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: A common table expression (CTE) is defined with the WITH clause. For how long does it exist?
opts: Until it is removed with a DROP statement
Until the end of the current session
Until the current transaction is committed
More than one of the above
exp: A CTE exists only for the single SQL statement in which it is defined; even the next statement of the same transaction cannot use it.
concept: The WITH clause creates a temporary, named result set — a 'temporary relation' — for the query on which it is defined. It is not stored in the data dictionary like a view, and it is not a temporary table that lasts for a session. Once that statement finishes, the CTE is gone. To reuse a query across many statements, create a view or a temporary table instead.
why: A — Wrong. DROP is used for stored objects such as tables and views. A CTE is never stored, so there is nothing to drop.
B — Wrong. Lasting until the end of the session describes a temporary table (CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE …), not a CTE.
C — Wrong. A CTE does not even last until the end of the transaction; a second statement in the same transaction cannot refer to it.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.

E — Correct. A CTE lives only for the one statement in which it is defined, which is not among A–C. (Checked in PostgreSQL: inside one transaction, WITH dt AS (…) SELECT … FROM dt works, but a following SELECT … FROM dt fails with 'relation "dt" does not exist'.)
tip: CTE = for one statement only; temporary table = for the session; view = permanent (until DROP VIEW).

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: What is the main purpose of creating an index on column name of table EMP (CREATE INDEX idx_name ON emp(name);)?
opts: To find rows with a given name quickly, without scanning the whole table
To make INSERT statements on EMP run faster
To stop NULL values from being stored in name
More than one of the above
exp: An index is an extra sorted structure on the column that lets the DBMS jump directly to the rows with a given value, like the index at the back of a book.
concept: An index is a separate data structure (usually a B+ tree) that keeps the values of one or more columns in sorted order, with pointers to the rows — like the index at the back of a book. It speeds up searches such as WHERE name = 'Ravi', and can also help joins and ORDER BY on that column. The cost is extra storage and slower INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, because the index must be updated as well. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX additionally prevents duplicate values.
why: A — Correct. Fast lookup of rows by the indexed column is the main purpose of an index.
B — Wrong. An index makes INSERT slightly slower, not faster, because every new row must also be added to the index.
C — Wrong. Preventing NULLs is the job of a NOT NULL constraint. An ordinary index allows NULLs (and in most products even a UNIQUE index allows NULLs).
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Index = faster reads, slower writes.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Which of the following can be used to generate unique numbers automatically, for example for a key column?
opts: An IDENTITY column in SQL Server
More than one of the above
exp: All three are automatic number generators: MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT, SQL Server's IDENTITY and Oracle's SEQUENCE.
concept: Products give different tools for automatic numbering. MySQL: a column declared AUTO_INCREMENT gets the next number when a row is inserted without a value for it. SQL Server: IDENTITY(1,1) on a column does the same (start 1, step 1). Oracle: CREATE SEQUENCE s START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1, and then s.NEXTVAL gives the next number (Oracle 12c and later also have identity columns). PostgreSQL has sequences, SERIAL and GENERATED … AS IDENTITY. Such generated numbers are often used as surrogate keys.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In MySQL, an AUTO_INCREMENT column automatically receives the next number for each new row.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In SQL Server, IDENTITY(seed, increment) makes a column generate numbers automatically.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In Oracle, a SEQUENCE is a separate object whose NEXTVAL returns a new unique number each time.
D — Correct. All three generate unique numbers automatically, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Same idea, different names: AUTO_INCREMENT (MySQL), IDENTITY (SQL Server), SEQUENCE (Oracle, PostgreSQL).

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In Oracle, a SYNONYM is:
opts: a copy of a table stored on another disk
a constraint that forces two columns to hold equal values
an alternative name (alias) for a database object such as a table or view
More than one of the above
exp: A synonym is just another name for an object; it stores no data of its own.
concept: A synonym is an alias: another name for a table, view, sequence, procedure or other object. It stores no data. Synonyms hide the owner or location of an object (for example, CREATE SYNONYM emp FOR hr.employees lets users write emp instead of hr.employees), and they let objects be moved without changing applications. A PUBLIC synonym is visible to all users.
why: A — Wrong. A synonym holds no data at all, only a name that points to an object. A copy of a table kept elsewhere would be a replica or a materialized view.
B — Wrong. A synonym has nothing to do with data rules. A rule that two columns must be equal would be written as a CHECK constraint, such as CHECK (a = b).
C — Correct. A synonym is an alternative name for an object.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Synonym = a nickname for a database object.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In PostgreSQL, table EMP has 5 rows. Two AFTER UPDATE triggers are defined on EMP; the function add_log() inserts one row into table LOG every time a trigger fires. LOG is empty at first. How many rows are in LOG after the UPDATE?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The row-level trigger fires once for each of the 5 updated rows (5 log rows); the statement-level trigger fires once for the whole UPDATE statement (1 log row). Total 6.
concept: A trigger is code that the DBMS runs automatically when an event (INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE) happens on a table. A row-level trigger (FOR EACH ROW) fires once for every row affected by the statement and can see the old and new values of that row. A statement-level trigger (FOR EACH STATEMENT, the default in Oracle and PostgreSQL when FOR EACH ROW is not written) fires once per statement, however many rows it changes — even none.
why: A — Wrong. 2 counts each trigger only once. The row-level trigger fires once per affected row, so it alone adds 5 rows.
B — Correct. 5 (row-level) + 1 (statement-level) = 6.
C — Wrong. 10 treats both triggers as row-level. The statement-level trigger fires only once for the whole UPDATE.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
1. The UPDATE has no WHERE, so it changes all 5 EMP rows.
2. t_row (FOR EACH ROW) fires 5 times → 5 LOG rows.
3. t_stmt (FOR EACH STATEMENT) fires once → 1 LOG row.
4. Total = 6.
Verified in PostgreSQL 16 with exactly these two triggers and one shared add_log() function: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM log → 6.
tip: Row-level: once per affected row. Statement-level: once per statement.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In an Oracle row-level UPDATE trigger, which reference gives the value of column sal as it was BEFORE the update?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: :OLD holds the column values before the change, and :NEW holds the values after the change.
concept: Inside an Oracle row-level trigger, two pseudo-records describe the row being changed: :OLD holds the values before the change and :NEW holds the values after it. For INSERT, the :OLD values are NULL (there is no old row); for DELETE, the :NEW values are NULL (there is no new row); for UPDATE both are available. A BEFORE trigger can even change :NEW values before they are saved. (In the trigger's WHEN condition, and in PostgreSQL, they are written OLD and NEW without the colon.)
why: A — Wrong. :NEW.sal is the value AFTER the update (the new salary).
B — Wrong. OLD_VALUE is not an Oracle function; old values are read through the :OLD pseudo-record.
C — Correct. :OLD.sal is the salary before the update.
D — Wrong. Only C is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. C is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Salary-raise audit: INSERT INTO sal_audit VALUES (:OLD.sal, :NEW.sal) — old first, new second.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Which of the following is NOT true about a database trigger?
opts: It must be called explicitly by name, like a procedure, before it runs
It runs automatically when a specified event, such as an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table, occurs
It can be defined to fire BEFORE or AFTER the triggering event
More than one of the above
exp: A trigger is never called by name; the DBMS fires it automatically when its event occurs. B and C are true.
concept: A trigger is a stored program attached to a table (or a view, or a database event). It is never called directly: the DBMS fires it automatically when its event happens. Triggers are used for auditing (logging changes), enforcing complex business rules and keeping derived data up to date. A trigger is defined with its timing (BEFORE, AFTER, or INSTEAD OF for views), its event (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and its level (row or statement). A stored procedure, by contrast, runs only when it is called.
why: A — Correct. This statement is false: a trigger runs automatically; being called explicitly by name is how a stored procedure runs.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: firing automatically on an event is the defining feature of a trigger. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE: triggers can be BEFORE or AFTER triggers (and INSTEAD OF on views). So it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Procedure = you call it. Trigger = the event calls it.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In Oracle PL/SQL, which of the following is true about a stored FUNCTION?
opts: It must return a value to its caller with a RETURN statement
A function that does not change data can be used inside an SQL statement, e.g. SELECT tax(sal) FROM emp;
More than one of the above
exp: A function must return a value, and (if it does no DML) it can be called inside SQL statements. Functions can take parameters, so C is false.
concept: Both procedures and functions are named PL/SQL blocks stored in the database. A function must return exactly one value — its header has RETURN datatype and its body must execute RETURN value — so it can be used inside expressions, including SQL statements such as SELECT, as long as it does not modify data. A procedure does not return a value through RETURN; it is called as a statement and can send results back through OUT parameters. Both can take IN, OUT and IN OUT parameters.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A function's header declares RETURN datatype; if the function ends without executing a RETURN with a value, Oracle raises ORA-06503 (function returned without value).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Functions can be called in SELECT lists and WHERE clauses; only a function that performs DML is not allowed inside a query (Oracle raises ORA-14551).
C — Wrong. Functions can take parameters, for example FUNCTION tax(p_sal NUMBER) RETURN NUMBER.
D — Correct. Both A and B are true facts about PL/SQL functions, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Function: returns a value, usable inside SQL. Procedure: performs an action, called as a statement.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: What is the correct order of steps for using an explicit cursor in PL/SQL?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The cursor is first declared with its query, then opened (the query runs), then rows are fetched one at a time, and finally it is closed.
concept: A cursor is a pointer to the result set of a query, used to process the rows one at a time. Oracle creates an implicit cursor automatically for every DML statement and SELECT INTO. For a multi-row query you use an explicit cursor: DECLARE it (name + query) in the declaration section; OPEN it (the query runs and the pointer is placed before the first row); FETCH rows one by one into variables, usually in a loop until %NOTFOUND; and CLOSE it to release its memory. A cursor FOR loop does OPEN, FETCH and CLOSE automatically.
why: A — Correct. Declare, open, fetch (repeatedly), close.
B — Wrong. A cursor must be declared before it can be opened; OPEN needs to know the cursor's query.
C — Wrong. FETCH before OPEN is an error (Oracle raises ORA-01001: invalid cursor), because the query has not been run yet.
D — Wrong. Only A is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. A is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Memory aid: D-O-F-C — Declare, Open, Fetch, Close.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In Oracle PL/SQL (with SERVEROUTPUT on), the query of cursor c1 below returns 5 rows. What value is printed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: For an explicit cursor, %ROWCOUNT is the number of rows fetched so far. After three successful FETCH statements it is 3, which is not listed.
concept: Explicit cursor attributes: %ISOPEN is TRUE if the cursor is open; %FOUND is TRUE if the last FETCH returned a row; %NOTFOUND is TRUE if the last FETCH returned no row (used to exit loops); %ROWCOUNT is the number of rows fetched so far. Just after OPEN, %ROWCOUNT is 0, and it goes up by one with each successful FETCH. For the implicit cursor, SQL%ROWCOUNT gives the number of rows affected by the last DML statement.
why: A — Wrong. 5 is the total number of rows in the result set. %ROWCOUNT counts only the rows fetched so far, not all the rows the query will return.
B — Wrong. 0 is the value just after OPEN, before any FETCH. Each successful FETCH adds 1.
C — Wrong. 2 is an off-by-one count. Three FETCH statements each returned a row, so the count is 3.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. c1%ROWCOUNT is 3 (three rows fetched), which is not among A–C.
work:
1. OPEN c1 → %ROWCOUNT = 0.
2. 1st FETCH (row 1) → 1.
3. 2nd FETCH (row 2) → 2.
4. 3rd FETCH (row 3) → 3.
5. PUT_LINE prints 3 → not listed → E.
(Oracle documentation: for an explicit cursor, %ROWCOUNT returns the number of rows fetched so far.)
tip: %ROWCOUNT = rows fetched so far, not the size of the result set.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: In embedded SQL (for example Oracle Pro*C), how is a host-language variable written inside an SQL statement?
opts: With a colon before it, as :sal
With an @ sign before it, as @sal
More than one of the above
exp: Host variables are prefixed with a colon, for example EXEC SQL SELECT sal INTO :sal FROM emp WHERE eid = :id;
concept: Embedded SQL means writing SQL statements inside a program in a host language such as C or COBOL. Each statement starts with EXEC SQL, and a precompiler converts it into ordinary library calls before the program is compiled. Program variables used inside SQL are called host variables and are written with a colon prefix, e.g. EXEC SQL SELECT sal INTO :sal FROM emp WHERE eid = :id; The SQLCA (SQL Communication Area) or the SQLCODE variable tells the program whether the statement succeeded.
why: A — Wrong. Double quotes in SQL mark a quoted identifier, i.e. the name of a column or table such as "sal", not a program variable.
B — Correct. The colon tells the precompiler that :sal is a host-program variable, not a column.
C — Wrong. @sal is how local variables are written in SQL Server's T-SQL; it is not the embedded-SQL host-variable notation.
D — Wrong. Only B is correct here; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be correct.
E — Wrong. B is correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: EXEC SQL starts the statement; a colon marks a host variable.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q:
Consider the following statements:
I. In dynamic SQL, the text of an SQL statement is built and prepared while the program is running.
II. In static embedded SQL, the SQL statements are fixed when the program is written and are processed by a precompiler.
III. ODBC can connect an application only to Microsoft SQL Server, not to other DBMSs.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true and III is false (ODBC works with almost every DBMS). The correct choice, 'I and II only', is not among A–C.
concept: Static SQL: the statements are written in the program and known at compile time; a precompiler checks and translates them (EXEC SQL …). Dynamic SQL: the program builds the statement as a string at run time and then prepares and executes it (PREPARE / EXECUTE, or EXECUTE IMMEDIATE in Oracle); it is needed when, for example, the table name or the condition is chosen by the user. ODBC (Open Database Connectivity, from Microsoft) and JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) are call-level APIs: the program calls library functions, and a driver for each DBMS (Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, …) translates them.
why: A — Wrong. 'I only' leaves out II, which is true: static embedded SQL is fixed in the source code and handled by a precompiler.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false, and it leaves out I, which is true.
C — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: ODBC is a general standard with drivers for Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL and many other DBMSs.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The correct set is 'I and II only', which is not among A–C.
tip: Static SQL = fixed at compile time. Dynamic SQL = built at run time. ODBC/JDBC = one API, many DBMSs (through drivers).

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the table EMP shown, the query below is meant to list the employees with the 3 highest salaries. How many rows does it actually return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A row is kept when fewer than 3 employees earn more than it. That is true for Meena and Tara (0), Asha and Sohan (2) and also Kunal, whose NULL salary makes every comparison UNKNOWN, so his count is 0. Only Ravi (4) fails: 5 rows.
concept: A correlated subquery uses a column of the outer row (here e.sal), so it is evaluated again for every outer row. The pattern 'number of rows greater than me < N' keeps the top N rows plus every row tied with them (the same rows as RANK() ≤ N), so it can return more than N rows. COUNT(*) of an empty set is 0, not NULL; so for a row whose own value is NULL, every comparison x.sal > NULL is UNKNOWN, nothing is counted, and the test 0 < 3 is TRUE.
why: A — Wrong. 3 is what the query is meant to return, but 'fewer than 3 people earn more' also keeps ties: Asha and Sohan (30000) both have exactly 2 people above them. Kunal's NULL salary adds one more row.
B — Wrong. 4 (Meena, Tara, Asha, Sohan) forgets Kunal. For his NULL salary, x.sal > NULL is UNKNOWN for every x, so COUNT(*) is 0 and 0 < 3 is TRUE.
C — Correct. Asha, Meena, Kunal, Sohan and Tara are returned; only Ravi is left out.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno | sal
1   | Asha  | 10  | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20  | 25000
3   | Meena | 10  | 40000
4   | Kunal | 20  | NULL
5   | Sohan | 40  | 30000
6   | Tara  | 30  | 40000

SELECT name FROM emp e
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp x
       WHERE x.sal > e.sal) < 3;
work:
For each row e, the subquery counts the employees who earn more than e:
Asha (30000): Meena, Tara → 2 → 2 < 3 TRUE
Ravi (25000): Asha, Meena, Sohan, Tara → 4 → FALSE
Meena (40000): nobody → 0 → TRUE
Kunal (NULL): x.sal > NULL is UNKNOWN for every x → 0 rows counted → 0 < 3 TRUE
Sohan (30000): Meena, Tara → 2 → TRUE
Tara (40000): 0 → TRUE
Result: Asha, Meena, Kunal, Sohan, Tara → 5 rows.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MariaDB: 5 rows.
tip: COUNT of an empty set is 0. A NULL in the outer row can make a correlated 'COUNT … < N' test TRUE.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the tables shown, what does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The double NOT EXISTS keeps a student when there is no CS course that the student has not taken, i.e. students who have taken ALL CS courses (C1 and C2): Amit and Bina.
concept: Relational division (R ÷ S) answers 'for all' questions, such as 'students who have taken every CS course'. SQL has no division operator, so it is written with two NOT EXISTS: 'there is no CS course that this student has not taken'. Extra courses outside the divisor (here C3) do not matter, but missing even one course of the divisor does.
why: A — Correct. Amit and Bina have both C1 and C2 (Bina's extra course C3 does not matter).

B — Wrong. Bina only would be the answer if the query divided by ALL courses (without c.dept = 'CS'), because she is the only student enrolled in C1, C2 and C3. With the CS filter, Amit also qualifies.
C — Wrong. Chetan has only one CS course (C1). The query asks for students who have taken EVERY CS course, not at least one.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT
sid | sname
1   | Amit
2   | Bina
3   | Chetan
4   | Divya

COURSE
cid | dept
C1  | CS
C2  | CS
C3  | Maths

ENROLL
sid | cid
1   | C1
1   | C2
2   | C1
2   | C2
2   | C3
3   | C1
3   | C3
4   | C3

SELECT s.sname FROM student s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT * FROM course c
  WHERE c.dept = 'CS'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT * FROM enroll e
    WHERE e.sid = s.sid
    AND e.cid = c.cid));
work:
Meaning: keep s if there is NO CS course c that s has NOT taken.
CS courses = {C1, C2}.
Amit: C1 taken, C2 taken → no missing CS course → outer NOT EXISTS is TRUE → returned.
Bina: C1, C2 taken (C3 is extra) → returned.
Chetan: C2 not taken → a missing CS course exists → not returned.
Divya: C1 and C2 not taken → not returned.
Result: Amit, Bina.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MariaDB (without the CS filter the result would be Bina only).
tip: 'For all' in SQL = NOT EXISTS ( … NOT EXISTS ( … ) ).

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the table EMP shown, what does this query return?
opts: An error, because the subquery returns a NULL
More than one of the above
exp: The subquery returns {25000, NULL}. sal > NULL is UNKNOWN, so sal > ALL (…) is never TRUE for any row, and the query returns no rows.
concept: x > ALL (subquery) is TRUE only if x > v is TRUE for every value v returned. If the subquery returns a NULL, x > NULL is UNKNOWN, so > ALL can be FALSE or UNKNOWN but never TRUE, and WHERE drops the row. NOT IN behaves the same way, because x NOT IN (…) means x <> ALL (…). Aggregates such as MAX ignore NULLs, so x > (SELECT MAX(…)) is NOT the same as x > ALL (…) when the subquery contains NULLs.
why: A — Wrong. These 4 rows are what you get with sal > (SELECT MAX(sal) …), because MAX ignores the NULL and returns 25000. > ALL does not ignore the NULL: the comparison with it is UNKNOWN.
B — Wrong. Meena and Tara have the highest salary, but even for them 40000 > NULL is UNKNOWN, so the whole > ALL condition is UNKNOWN, not TRUE.
C — Wrong. A NULL value in a subquery result is not an error; it only makes some comparisons UNKNOWN.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The query returns no rows: because the subquery contains a NULL, sal > ALL (…) is never TRUE.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno | sal
1   | Asha  | 10  | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20  | 25000
3   | Meena | 10  | 40000
4   | Kunal | 20  | NULL
5   | Sohan | 40  | 30000
6   | Tara  | 30  | 40000

SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE sal > ALL (SELECT sal FROM emp
                 WHERE dno = 20);
work:
1. Subquery: salaries in dno 20 → {25000, NULL} (Ravi and Kunal).
2. sal > ALL {25000, NULL} means (sal > 25000) AND (sal > NULL).
3. sal > NULL is UNKNOWN for every row:
   Meena, Tara (40000): TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN
   Asha, Sohan (30000): TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN
   Ravi (25000): FALSE AND UNKNOWN = FALSE
   Kunal (NULL): UNKNOWN
4. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows → no rows.
Verified in PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MariaDB (SQLite does not support ALL): empty result.
tip: One NULL in the subquery makes > ALL (and NOT IN) return nothing. Add WHERE sal IS NOT NULL inside the subquery.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the table EMP shown, which of the following queries return ALL six rows of EMP?
opts: SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT x.sal FROM emp x WHERE x.sal IS NULL);
SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT MAX(x.sal) FROM emp x WHERE x.dno = 99);
SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM emp x WHERE x.sal = NULL);
More than one of the above
exp: EXISTS is TRUE whenever the subquery returns at least one row, even a row that holds only NULL. Query A returns Kunal's NULL salary and query B returns one row (MAX of nothing = NULL), so both return all 6 rows; query C's subquery returns no rows.
concept: EXISTS (subquery) is TRUE if the subquery returns at least one row, whatever values that row holds — even if they are all NULL. EXISTS itself is never UNKNOWN. Two traps: an aggregate query without GROUP BY or HAVING (such as SELECT MAX(…) or SELECT COUNT(*)) always returns exactly one row, even when no rows match; and a test like col = NULL is never TRUE, so it matches no rows (use IS NULL instead).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The subquery returns one row (Kunal's sal, which is NULL). EXISTS only asks whether a row exists, not what is in it, so it is TRUE for every outer row and all 6 names are returned.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. No employee is in dno 99, but an aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row; here MAX over no rows gives one row containing NULL. A row exists, so EXISTS is TRUE and all 6 names are returned.
C — Wrong. x.sal = NULL is never TRUE (it is UNKNOWN even for Kunal), so the subquery returns no rows, EXISTS is FALSE and this query returns no rows at all.
D — Correct. Queries A and B both return all six rows, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno | sal
1   | Asha  | 10  | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20  | 25000
3   | Meena | 10  | 40000
4   | Kunal | 20  | NULL
5   | Sohan | 40  | 30000
6   | Tara  | 30  | 40000
work:
A: subquery → 1 row (sal = NULL for Kunal) → EXISTS TRUE for every outer row → 6 rows.
B: subquery → SELECT MAX(sal) over 0 matching rows → 1 row containing NULL → EXISTS TRUE → 6 rows.
C: x.sal = NULL is UNKNOWN for every row → subquery returns 0 rows → EXISTS FALSE → 0 rows.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MariaDB: 6, 6 and 0 rows.
tip: EXISTS checks for rows, not for values. SELECT MAX(…) without GROUP BY always returns one row.

topic: SQL Joins, Subqueries, Views & Database Objects
q: Using the tables EMP and DEPT shown, how many rows do queries Q1 and Q2 return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In Q1 the test d.loc = 'Patna' is part of the ON condition, so it only decides which DEPT rows match; all 6 EMP rows are kept. In Q2 the WHERE filter runs after the join and keeps only Asha, Meena and Tara.
concept: In an outer join, ON and WHERE do different jobs. ON is the matching rule: a left row that finds no matching right row is still kept, with NULLs in the right-table columns. WHERE is a filter applied after the join: it keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE, so a WHERE test on a right-table column removes the NULL-padded rows and the LEFT JOIN acts like an inner join. (For an INNER JOIN, putting the condition in ON or in WHERE gives the same result.)
why: A — Wrong. Q2 does return 3 rows, but Q1 returns 6. A condition in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN only decides which DEPT rows match; it never removes EMP rows. Unmatched employees are kept with NULL dname.
B — Correct. Q1 keeps all 6 employees (Ravi, Kunal and Sohan get NULL dname); Q2 keeps only the 3 employees whose department is in Patna.
C — Wrong. The numbers are swapped. It is the WHERE clause (Q2) that removes rows after the join; the ON condition (Q1) keeps every row of the left table.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
eid | name  | dno | sal
1   | Asha  | 10  | 30000
2   | Ravi  | 20  | 25000
3   | Meena | 10  | 40000
4   | Kunal | 20  | NULL
5   | Sohan | 40  | 30000
6   | Tara  | 30  | 40000

DEPT
dno | dname | loc
10  | Sales | Patna
20  | HR    | Gaya
30  | IT    | Patna

-- Q1
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM emp e LEFT JOIN dept d
ON e.dno = d.dno AND d.loc = 'Patna';

-- Q2
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM emp e LEFT JOIN dept d
ON e.dno = d.dno
WHERE d.loc = 'Patna';
work:
Q1 (filter in ON): an EMP row matches a DEPT row only if the dno is equal AND that department is in Patna.
 Asha (10) → Sales; Ravi (20) → HR is in Gaya → no match → NULL; Meena (10) → Sales; Kunal (20) → NULL; Sohan (40) → no dept 40 → NULL; Tara (30) → IT.
 LEFT JOIN keeps every EMP row → 6 rows (3 of them with dname NULL).
Q2 (filter in WHERE): first the LEFT JOIN on dno only → Asha–Sales, Ravi–HR, Meena–Sales, Kunal–HR, Sohan–NULL, Tara–IT (6 rows).
 Then WHERE d.loc = 'Patna': 'Gaya' = 'Patna' is FALSE; NULL = 'Patna' is UNKNOWN → only Asha, Meena, Tara are kept → 3 rows.
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MariaDB: Q1 = 6 rows, Q2 = 3 rows.
tip: LEFT JOIN: a filter in ON keeps all left rows; a filter in WHERE can remove them.

q: According to Korth, the basic steps in processing an SQL query, in the correct order, are
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The query is first parsed and translated into relational algebra, then the optimizer chooses the cheapest evaluation plan, and finally the evaluation engine runs that plan.
concept: Korth lists three steps of query processing. (1) Parsing and translation: the parser checks the syntax of the query, checks that the named tables and columns exist (using the catalog), and translates the query into an internal form, a relational-algebra expression. (2) Optimization: among the many equivalent ways (plans) to compute the same answer, the optimizer chooses the one with the lowest estimated cost. (3) Evaluation: the query-execution engine runs the chosen plan and returns the answer.
why: A — Wrong. The optimizer works on the relational-algebra form of the query, so the query must be parsed and translated first. Optimization cannot come before parsing.
B — Correct. Parse and translate → choose the cheapest plan → run it.
C — Wrong. A plan must be chosen (optimized) before it is run. Evaluating first and optimizing afterwards is like planning a journey after you have already reached the destination.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In query processing, a relational-algebra operation annotated with instructions on how to evaluate it (for example, 'use the index on Dept for this selection') is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Korth calls one annotated operation an evaluation primitive; a sequence of such primitives that computes a whole query is a query-evaluation (query-execution) plan.
concept: An SQL query can be computed in many ways. To say exactly how, the system annotates each relational-algebra operation with the algorithm or index to use; one such annotated operation is called an evaluation primitive. A sequence (usually drawn as a tree) of evaluation primitives that computes the whole query is called a query-evaluation plan or query-execution plan. The query-execution engine takes this plan, runs it and returns the result.
why: A — Correct. One relational-algebra operation plus the instruction on how to compute it (which algorithm, which index) is an evaluation primitive.
B — Wrong. A parse tree is produced by the parser and shows the grammatical structure of the SQL statement. It says nothing about which algorithm or index to use.
C — Wrong. A query-evaluation plan is the whole sequence (tree) of evaluation primitives for the complete query, not a single annotated operation. The stem describes one operation.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following does a cost-based query optimizer read from the system catalog (data dictionary) to estimate the cost of a plan?
opts: n_r, the number of tuples in relation r
V(A, r), the number of distinct values of attribute A in relation r
Which indices exist on each relation, and on which attributes
More than one of the above
exp: All three are kept in the catalog and used by the optimizer: tuple counts and distinct-value counts give size estimates, and index information tells it which access paths are possible.
concept: The catalog (data dictionary) stores metadata, that is, data about the data. For each relation r, Korth's optimizer uses statistics such as n_r (number of tuples), b_r (number of blocks), l_r (size of one tuple in bytes), f_r (blocking factor: tuples that fit in one block) and V(A, r) (number of distinct values of attribute A). The catalog also stores the definitions of indices (and details such as the height of a B+-tree). The optimizer combines these to estimate the sizes of intermediate results and the cost of each possible plan.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. n_r is the most basic statistic; for example, the size of σ_{A = v}(r) is estimated as n_r / V(A, r).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. V(A, r) is used to estimate the sizes of selections and joins and the number of groups produced by GROUP BY.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The optimizer can consider an index scan only if the catalog tells it that the index exists.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. All of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Korth's cost model, which of the following is NOT included in the estimated cost of an operation such as a selection or a join?
opts: The number of blocks transferred from disk
The number of disk seeks (random accesses)
The cost of writing the final result of the operation back to disk
More than one of the above
exp: Korth counts block transfers and seeks, but his cost formulas leave out writing the final result of the operation to disk; that is counted separately when needed (for example, in materialized evaluation).
concept: Disk access is far slower than work in main memory, so Korth measures cost by disk I/O: the number of block transfers (b) and the number of seeks (S). With t_T = time to transfer one block and t_S = time for one seek (head movement plus rotational delay), the time is b × t_T + S × t_S. CPU cost is ignored for simplicity, and the cost of writing an operation's final output to disk is not included in the formulas; it is added separately only when the result really has to be written.
why: A — Wrong. Block transfers ARE counted (the b × t_T part), so this does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. Seeks ARE counted too (the S × t_S part); because a seek takes much longer than a block transfer, they matter a lot. So this does not satisfy the NOT stem.
C — Correct. Korth's cost estimates leave out the cost of writing the final result of an operation back to disk; it is counted separately when required.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A query-evaluation plan needs 600 block transfers and 50 seeks. If t_T = 0.1 ms (time to transfer one block) and t_S = 4 ms (time for one seek), what is its estimated time according to Korth's cost measure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Time = b × t_T + S × t_S = 600 × 0.1 + 50 × 4 = 60 + 200 = 260 ms, which is not listed.
concept: Korth estimates the time of a plan from disk I/O only: time = (number of block transfers) × t_T + (number of seeks) × t_S. A seek (moving the disk head and waiting for the disk to rotate) is much slower than transferring one block, so a plan that reads data sequentially (few seeks) is much faster than a plan that jumps around the disk, even if both read a similar number of blocks.
why: A — Wrong. 60 ms counts only the block transfers (600 × 0.1) and forgets the 50 seeks.
B — Wrong. 2405 ms comes from swapping the two times: 600 × 4 + 50 × 0.1. Each block transfer costs t_T and each seek costs t_S, not the other way round.
C — Wrong. 200 ms counts only the seeks (50 × 4) and forgets the block transfers.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The estimated time is 60 + 200 = 260 ms, which is not listed.
code:
Plan: b = 600 block transfers, S = 50 seeks
t_T = 0.1 ms per block transfer
t_S = 4 ms per seek
work:
Formula: time = b × t_T + S × t_S
Transfers: 600 × 0.1 ms = 60 ms
Seeks: 50 × 4 ms = 200 ms
Total = 60 + 200 = 260 ms (not among A–C)

q: Relation r occupies b_r = 1000 blocks, and the file is sorted on its key attribute A. For the selection σ_{A = 25}(r), which of the following block-transfer counts are correct?
opts: Linear search, worst case: 1000 block transfers
Linear search, average case: 500 block transfers
Binary search on the sorted file: ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10 block transfers
More than one of the above
exp: Linear search reads all 1000 blocks in the worst case and, because A is a key, can stop at the match, so on average it reads b_r / 2 = 500. Binary search needs ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10 block reads. All three are correct.
concept: Linear search (a file scan) reads the blocks one after another and tests every record; it works for any file and any condition, and costs b_r block transfers. If the condition is equality on a key, the scan can stop as soon as the one matching record is found, so on average it reads b_r / 2 blocks. If the file is sorted on the attribute, binary search can be used: each read halves the remaining blocks, so about ⌈log2 b_r⌉ block reads find the right block (plus extra blocks if several records match a non-key value).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. If the record is in the last block (or does not exist at all), the scan reads all 1000 blocks.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Since A is a key, at most one record matches, so the scan stops when it finds it; on average that is half the file.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each step of binary search reads the middle block and throws away half of the remaining blocks: 1000 → 500 → 250 → … → 1 takes 10 reads.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all correct, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. All of A–C are correct, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Linear search, worst case: read every block = b_r = 1000
Linear search, average (key equality, stop at the match): b_r / 2 = 1000 / 2 = 500
Binary search: 2^9 = 512 < 1000 ≤ 1024 = 2^10, so ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10
A, B and C are all correct → D
tip: Linear search: b_r (worst), b_r / 2 (average, equality on a key). Binary search: ⌈log2 b_r⌉.

q: Relation EMP has a secondary B+-tree index of height h_i = 3 on Dept, which is not a key. 40 employees work in 'Sales', and in the worst case each of them is stored in a different block. Using Korth's formula, how many block transfers does σ_{Dept = 'Sales'}(EMP) need when it uses this index?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: For a secondary index on a non-key attribute, cost = h_i + n = 3 index blocks + 40 data blocks = 43 block transfers.
concept: A primary (clustering) index is built on the attribute the file is sorted on, so the matching records sit together in a few consecutive blocks. A secondary (non-clustering) index is on some other attribute, so the matching records can be scattered all over the file. Korth's cost with a secondary B+-tree index: equality on a key = h_i + 1 (walk down the tree, then read one record); equality on a non-key = h_i + n, because each of the n matching records may be in a different block. This is why a secondary index can be slower than a plain linear scan when very many records match.
why: A — Wrong. 4 = h_i + 1 is the cost when the indexed attribute is a key, so only ONE record is fetched. Here Dept is not a key and 40 records match.
B — Correct. 3 blocks to walk down the index plus one block for each of the 40 scattered records gives 43.
C — Wrong. 40 counts only the data blocks and forgets the 3 index blocks read while walking down the B+-tree.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP: secondary B+-tree index on Dept (not a key), height h_i = 3
σ_{Dept = 'Sales'}(EMP) matches n = 40 records, each in a different block (worst case)
work:
Walk down the B+-tree from the root to a leaf: h_i = 3 block transfers
Fetch each matching record: n = 40 records, each in its own block = 40 block transfers
Total = h_i + n = 3 + 40 = 43
tip: Secondary index + many matching records = many random block reads. When n is large, a linear scan can be cheaper.

q: Relation r has a B+-tree index on A, a B+-tree index on B and a composite index on (A, B). Which of the following is NOT a correct way to evaluate the conjunctive selection σ_{A = 5 ∧ B = 7}(r)?
opts: Use the index on A to fetch the records with A = 5, then test B = 7 on each fetched record in memory
Search the composite index on (A, B) directly for the pair (5, 7)
Get the record pointers for A = 5 and for B = 7 from the two separate indices, intersect the two pointer sets, then fetch only those records
More than one of the above
exp: All three are standard, correct methods for a conjunctive selection (Korth's A7, A8 and A9 in the 6th-edition numbering; the 5th edition calls them A8, A9 and A10), so none of them satisfies the NOT stem.
concept: A conjunctive selection has the form σ_{θ1 ∧ θ2}(r): a record must satisfy every condition. Korth (6th-edition numbering) describes three index-based methods: (A7) use one index for one condition (preferably the most selective) and test the other conditions in memory on each fetched record; (A8) use a composite index (an index on several attributes together) if one exists for those attributes; (A9) take the intersection of the record pointers obtained from several indices and fetch only the records in the intersection. A linear scan of the whole file is always possible as well.
why: A — Wrong. This method is correct (Korth's A7): every record returned by the index already has A = 5, and testing B = 7 in memory removes the rest. So it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. This method is correct (Korth's A8): a composite index on (A, B) can look up the pair (5, 7) directly. It does not satisfy the NOT stem.

C — Wrong. This method is correct (Korth's A9): a record satisfies both conditions only if its pointer is in both sets, so the intersection gives exactly the right records. It does not satisfy the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. None of A–C satisfies the NOT stem (all three are correct methods), so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three are correct ways to evaluate the conjunctive selection, so none of them is 'NOT correct'.
tip: For OR conditions (disjunctive selection), the union of pointer sets works only if EVERY condition has an index; otherwise a linear scan is needed.

q: External sort-merge is used to sort a relation of b_r = 1000 blocks with M = 11 buffer blocks in main memory. How many sorted runs are created in the first (run-creation) stage?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each run is made by reading M = 11 blocks, sorting them in memory and writing them out, so the number of runs = ⌈1000 / 11⌉ = ⌈90.9⌉ = 91.
concept: External sorting is used when a relation is too big to fit in main memory. In the first stage, external sort-merge reads M blocks at a time (as many as fit in memory), sorts them in memory and writes them back as one sorted 'run'; this gives ⌈b_r / M⌉ runs. In the second stage, the runs are merged, up to M − 1 at a time (one block is kept for the output), until a single sorted run remains.
why: A — Wrong. 100 = 1000 / 10 uses M − 1. The run-creation stage uses all M = 11 buffer blocks to hold data; M − 1 is the number of runs merged at once in the merge stage.
B — Wrong. 90 rounds down. 90 runs of 11 blocks hold only 990 blocks; the remaining 10 blocks form one more run, so take the ceiling, not the floor.
C — Correct. ⌈1000 / 11⌉ = 91 runs: 90 full runs of 11 blocks and one last run of 10 blocks.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
b_r = 1000 blocks
M = 11 buffer blocks
work:
Each run holds M = 11 blocks (the last run may be smaller)
Number of runs = ⌈b_r / M⌉ = ⌈1000 / 11⌉ = ⌈90.9…⌉ = 91
(90 full runs × 11 blocks = 990 blocks, plus 1 last run of 10 blocks)
tip: Run creation divides by M; merging uses M − 1 (one buffer block is kept for the output).

q: A relation of b_r = 8000 blocks is sorted by external sort-merge with M = 20 buffer blocks (one buffer block per run). After the run-creation stage, how many merge passes are needed? (Do not count the run-creation stage.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Runs = 8000 / 20 = 400. Each merge pass merges M − 1 = 19 runs at a time: 400 → 22 → 2 → 1, so 3 merge passes (⌈log_19 400⌉ = 3, since 19² = 361 < 400).
concept: In external sort-merge, each merge pass reduces the number of runs by a factor of M − 1, because one of the M buffer blocks is needed for the output. So the number of merge passes is ⌈log_{M−1}(b_r / M)⌉. A common mistake is to use log base M; when the number of runs is just above a power of M − 1, this gives one pass too few.
why: A — Wrong. 2 comes from log base M: 20² = 400, so ⌈log_20 400⌉ = 2. But only M − 1 = 19 runs can be merged at a time, and 19² = 361 is less than 400, so 2 passes are not enough.
B — Correct. 400 → 22 → 2 → 1 needs 3 merge passes.
C — Wrong. 4 also counts the run-creation stage (1 + 3). The question asks for merge passes only.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: b_r = 8000 blocks, M = 20 buffer blocks, one buffer block per run
work:
Initial runs = ⌈8000 / 20⌉ = 400
Runs merged at once = M − 1 = 19
Pass 1: ⌈400 / 19⌉ = 22 runs
Pass 2: ⌈22 / 19⌉ = 2 runs
Pass 3: ⌈2 / 19⌉ = 1 run (fully sorted)
Check: 19² = 361 < 400 ≤ 19³ = 6859, so ⌈log_19 400⌉ = 3 merge passes

q: A relation of b_r = 900 blocks is sorted by external sort-merge with M = 10 buffer blocks (one buffer block per run). Count the reading and the writing of every block in every stage, except the final write of the fully sorted result (as Korth does). How many block transfers does the sort need in total?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Runs = 900 / 10 = 90; merge passes = ⌈log_9 90⌉ = 3 (9² = 81 < 90). Total = b_r(2 × 3 + 1) = 900 × 7 = 6300 block transfers, which is not listed.
concept: Korth's cost of external sort-merge (one buffer block per run): the run-creation stage reads and writes every block once (2b_r), and each merge pass also reads and writes every block (2b_r per pass). The write of the final, fully sorted result is not counted, because the result may be passed straight to the next operation. So total block transfers = b_r(2⌈log_{M−1}(b_r / M)⌉ + 1). Note that the number of merge passes uses log base M − 1.
why: A — Wrong. 7200 = 900 × 8 also counts the final write of the sorted result. The question (like Korth's formula) leaves that write out, so 900 must be subtracted.
B — Wrong. 4500 = 900 × (2 × 2 + 1) uses only 2 merge passes, from log base M (10² = 100 ≥ 90). But only M − 1 = 9 runs can be merged at once, and 9² = 81 < 90, so 3 merge passes are needed.

C — Wrong. 5400 = 2 × 900 × 3 counts only the reading and writing in the three merge passes. It forgets the run-creation stage, which also reads and writes all 900 blocks, and it does not take off the final write.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The total is 900 × (2 × 3 + 1) = 6300 block transfers, which is not listed.
code:
b_r = 900 blocks, M = 10 buffer blocks, one buffer block per run
The final write of the sorted output is NOT counted
work:
Runs = ⌈900 / 10⌉ = 90
Merge passes (9 runs merged at a time): 90 → 10 → 2 → 1, so 3 passes (9² = 81 < 90 ≤ 729 = 9³)
Run creation: read 900 + write 900 = 1800
Merge passes: 3 × (read 900 + write 900) = 5400
Sum = 1800 + 5400 = 7200; minus the final write (900) = 6300
Formula check: b_r(2P + 1) = 900 × (2 × 3 + 1) = 900 × 7 = 6300 (not among A–C)
tip: Korth's sort cost (one buffer per run): b_r(2⌈log_{M−1}(b_r / M)⌉ + 1). Books that also count the final write get 2b_r × (merge passes + 1).

q:
Consider the following statements about external sort-merge with M buffer blocks (one buffer block per run):
I. Each merge step can merge at most M − 1 runs, because one buffer block is kept for the output.
II. Each merge pass reduces the number of runs by a factor of about M − 1.
III. Even when the whole relation fits in memory (b_r ≤ M), at least one merge pass is needed.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are correct. III is false: if b_r ≤ M, the whole relation is read and sorted in memory as one run, so no merge pass is needed.
concept: External sort-merge has two stages. Run creation: read M blocks, sort them in memory and write them out as a sorted run; repeat until the relation is used up, giving ⌈b_r / M⌉ runs. Merging: with M buffers, M − 1 runs are read side by side (one input block each), and the smallest remaining tuple is moved again and again to the single output block; so each pass divides the number of runs by M − 1. If there is only one run (b_r ≤ M), the relation is already sorted after the first stage.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: when b_r ≤ M there is just one run, so ⌈log_{M−1} 1⌉ = 0 merge passes are needed.
C — Wrong. It leaves out II, which is also true: merging M − 1 runs into one at every step divides the number of runs by M − 1 in each pass.

D — Wrong. Each of A–C names a different exact set of correct statements (note the word 'only'), so at most one of them can be right; here that is A. 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: STUDENT has n_r = 4000 tuples in b_r = 200 blocks, and ENROLL has n_s = 20,000 tuples in b_s = 800 blocks. They are joined by the simple (tuple-at-a-time) nested-loop join with STUDENT as the outer relation. In the worst case (memory holds only one block of each relation), how many block transfers are needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: For each of the 4000 STUDENT tuples, the whole of ENROLL (800 blocks) is read; STUDENT itself is read once: 4000 × 800 + 200 = 3,200,200.
concept: The simple nested-loop join takes each tuple of the outer relation r and scans the entire inner relation s for matching tuples. In the worst case only one block of each relation fits in memory, so s is read once for every TUPLE of r: cost = n_r × b_s + b_r block transfers (plus n_r + b_r seeks). It needs no index and works for any join condition, but it is very expensive.
why: B — Wrong. 160,200 = 200 × 800 + 200 is the worst-case cost of the BLOCK nested-loop join, which scans the inner relation once per outer BLOCK, not once per outer tuple.
C — Wrong. 4,000,800 = 20,000 × 200 + 800 is the cost with ENROLL as the outer relation. The question fixes STUDENT as the outer relation.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT (outer): n_r = 4000 tuples, b_r = 200 blocks
ENROLL (inner): n_s = 20,000 tuples, b_s = 800 blocks
Simple nested-loop join, worst case
work:
Inner relation scanned once per outer tuple: n_r × b_s = 4000 × 800 = 3,200,000
Outer relation read once: b_r = 200
Total = 3,200,000 + 200 = 3,200,200 block transfers
tip: Nested loop: n_r × b_s + b_r (one inner scan per outer TUPLE). Block nested loop: b_r × b_s + b_r (one inner scan per outer BLOCK).

q: COURSE occupies 150 blocks and STUDENT occupies 600 blocks. They are joined by block nested-loop join. In the worst case (memory holds only one block of each relation), how many block transfers are needed if the better relation is chosen as the outer relation?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Worst case = b_r × b_s + b_r. COURSE outer: 150 × 600 + 150 = 90,150; STUDENT outer: 600 × 150 + 600 = 90,600. The smaller relation (COURSE) as outer is better: 90,150.
concept: Block nested-loop join reads the outer relation block by block, and for each outer BLOCK it scans the whole inner relation, pairing every tuple of the outer block with every tuple of the inner block. Worst-case cost = b_r × b_s + b_r block transfers (and 2b_r seeks). The product b_r × b_s is the same either way, so the cost is lower when the smaller relation is the outer one (the + b_r part is smaller). In the best case, when the smaller relation fits entirely in memory, the cost falls to b_r + b_s.
why: A — Wrong. 90,600 is the cost with the larger relation (STUDENT) as the outer relation. That is the worse choice, because the + b_r part becomes 600 instead of 150.
B — Wrong. 750 = 150 + 600 is the BEST-case cost, when the smaller relation fits completely in memory and each relation is read only once. The question asks for the worst case.
C — Correct. With COURSE as the outer relation, 150 × 600 + 150 = 90,150.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
COURSE: 150 blocks
STUDENT: 600 blocks
Block nested-loop join, worst case (one block of each relation in memory)
work:
COURSE as outer: 150 × 600 + 150 = 90,000 + 150 = 90,150
STUDENT as outer: 600 × 150 + 600 = 90,000 + 600 = 90,600
Better choice: COURSE (the smaller relation) as outer → 90,150

q: STUDENT (b_r = 200 blocks) is joined with ENROLL (b_s = 800 blocks) by block nested-loop join, with STUDENT as the outer relation. Memory has M = 12 buffer blocks. Using Korth's method (M − 2 blocks hold the outer relation, one block for the inner relation and one for the output), how many block transfers are needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The outer relation is read in chunks of M − 2 = 10 blocks: ⌈200 / 10⌉ = 20 chunks. ENROLL is scanned once per chunk: 20 × 800 + 200 = 16,200.
concept: When more memory is available, block nested-loop join keeps M − 2 blocks of the outer relation in memory at once and uses the remaining two blocks for the inner relation and the output. The inner relation is then scanned once per chunk of M − 2 outer blocks instead of once per outer block: cost = ⌈b_r / (M − 2)⌉ × b_s + b_r block transfers (and 2⌈b_r / (M − 2)⌉ seeks). More memory means fewer scans of the inner relation.
why: A — Wrong. 13,800 uses chunks of M = 12 blocks: ⌈200 / 12⌉ = 17, and 17 × 800 + 200 = 13,800. But two of the 12 buffers are needed for the inner relation and the output, so only 10 can hold the outer relation.
B — Wrong. 15,400 uses chunks of M − 1 = 11 blocks: ⌈200 / 11⌉ = 19, and 19 × 800 + 200 = 15,400. It forgets that one buffer block is also needed for the output.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT (outer): b_r = 200 blocks
ENROLL (inner): b_s = 800 blocks
M = 12 buffer blocks: M − 2 for the outer relation, 1 for the inner, 1 for the output
work:
Outer chunk size = M − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10 blocks
Number of chunks = ⌈200 / 10⌉ = 20
Inner scans: 20 × 800 = 16,000
Outer relation read once: 200
Total = 16,000 + 200 = 16,200 block transfers
tip: With M buffers: ⌈b_r / (M − 2)⌉ × b_s + b_r. Sort-merge merges M − 1 runs; block nested loop holds M − 2 outer blocks.

q: Relation R has 2,000 tuples stored in 40 blocks, and relation S has 10,000 tuples stored in 1,000 blocks. R ⋈ S is computed with the simple (tuple-at-a-time) nested-loop join, worst case (only one block of each relation in memory). What is the smallest number of block transfers the optimizer can get by choosing the outer relation?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Cost = n_outer × b_inner + b_outer. R outer: 2,000 × 1,000 + 40 = 2,000,040. S outer: 10,000 × 40 + 1,000 = 401,000. So S (the larger relation, with fewer tuples per block) should be the outer one: 401,000.
concept: For the simple nested-loop join, the inner relation is scanned once for every TUPLE of the outer relation, so the cost is n_r × b_s + b_r. Comparing the two choices (n_r × b_s against n_s × b_r), the better outer relation is the one with fewer tuples per block (smaller blocking factor), which is not always the smaller relation. This differs from block nested-loop join, where the inner relation is scanned once per outer BLOCK and the smaller relation should be the outer one.
why: A — Wrong. 2,000,040 is the cost with R as the outer relation. R is smaller, but each of its 2,000 tuples causes a scan of all 1,000 blocks of S; this choice is about five times worse.
B — Correct. With S as the outer relation, the 40-block relation R is scanned 10,000 times: 10,000 × 40 + 1,000 = 401,000, the smaller of the two costs.
C — Wrong. 40,040 = 40 × 1,000 + 40 is the worst-case cost of BLOCK nested-loop join with R outer. The question uses the simple tuple-at-a-time nested-loop join.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
R: n = 2,000 tuples, b = 40 blocks (50 tuples per block)
S: n = 10,000 tuples, b = 1,000 blocks (10 tuples per block)
Simple nested-loop join, worst case
work:
R as outer: n_R × b_S + b_R = 2,000 × 1,000 + 40 = 2,000,040
S as outer: n_S × b_R + b_S = 10,000 × 40 + 1,000 = 400,000 + 1,000 = 401,000
Minimum = 401,000 (S as the outer relation)
Reason: S has fewer tuples per block (10) than R (50)
tip: Common mistake: 'always put the smaller relation outside' is the rule for BLOCK nested loop. For tuple-at-a-time nested loop, compare n_r × b_s with n_s × b_r.

q: ORDERS (the outer relation: n_r = 10,000 tuples in b_r = 500 blocks) is joined with CUSTOMER by indexed nested-loop join. CUSTOMER has a B+-tree index of height 3 on the join attribute cust_id (its key), so each lookup reads 3 index blocks and then 1 data block. How many block transfers are needed (Korth)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Cost = b_r + n_r × c, where c = 3 + 1 = 4 block transfers per lookup: 500 + 10,000 × 4 = 40,500.
concept: Indexed nested-loop join replaces the scan of the inner relation by an index lookup: for each tuple of the outer relation r, the index on the inner relation s finds the matching tuples. Korth's cost is b_r(t_T + t_S) + n_r × c, where c is the cost of one index lookup plus fetching the matching record; counted in block transfers, that is b_r + n_r × c. It is much cheaper than a plain nested-loop join when such an index exists.
why: A — Correct. Read ORDERS once (500) and do one 4-block lookup per ORDERS tuple (10,000 × 4): 500 + 40,000 = 40,500.
B — Wrong. 30,500 = 500 + 10,000 × 3 counts only the index blocks of each lookup and forgets the data block that holds the matching CUSTOMER record.
C — Wrong. 40,000 counts only the lookups and forgets that the 500 blocks of ORDERS must also be read.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
ORDERS (outer): n_r = 10,000 tuples, b_r = 500 blocks
CUSTOMER (inner): B+-tree index on cust_id (key), height 3
One lookup = 3 index blocks + 1 data block
work:
Cost of one lookup c = 3 (index) + 1 (data) = 4 block transfers
Lookups: n_r × c = 10,000 × 4 = 40,000
Read the outer relation once: b_r = 500
Total = 500 + 40,000 = 40,500 block transfers
tip: Korth: if both relations have an index on the join attribute, it is usually best to make the relation with fewer tuples the outer one.

q: STUDENT occupies 200 blocks and ENROLL occupies 800 blocks. Which of the following cost estimates (in block transfers) for the equi-join STUDENT ⋈ ENROLL are correct?
opts: Merge join, when both relations are already sorted on the join attribute: 1,000
