Hash join with STUDENT as the build input, both relations partitioned once (no recursive partitioning), partly filled blocks ignored: 3,000
Block nested-loop join, worst case, with STUDENT as the outer relation: 1,000
More than one of the above
exp: Merge join on sorted inputs reads each block once: 200 + 800 = 1,000 (A true). Hash join costs about 3(b_r + b_s) = 3 × 1,000 = 3,000 (B true). Block nested-loop join in the worst case costs 200 × 800 + 200 = 160,200, not 1,000 (C false).
concept: Typical costs in block transfers (Korth): merge join on inputs already sorted on the join attribute = b_r + b_s, because each block is read once; if the inputs are not sorted, the cost of sorting is added. Hash join partitions both relations (read + write = 2(b_r + b_s)) and then reads every partition once more to build and probe (b_r + b_s): about 3(b_r + b_s), plus a small extra for partly filled blocks. (If the whole build input fits in memory, no partitioning is needed and hash join costs only b_r + b_s.) Block nested-loop join costs b_r × b_s + b_r in the worst case and b_r + b_s only in the best case, when the smaller relation fits in memory.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Both inputs are scanned once, side by side, like merging two sorted lists, so each block is read once: 200 + 800 = 1,000.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Partitioning reads and writes both relations (2 × 1,000), and the build-and-probe phase reads every partition once more (1,000): 3,000 in total.

C — Wrong. 1,000 = b_r + b_s is the BEST case of block nested-loop join (the smaller relation fits in memory). In the worst case the inner relation is read once per outer block: 200 × 800 + 200 = 160,200.
D — Correct. A and B are true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT: b_r = 200 blocks
ENROLL: b_s = 800 blocks
Equi-join on the common attribute ID
work:
A: merge join (both sorted) = b_r + b_s = 200 + 800 = 1,000 → TRUE
B: hash join ≈ 3(b_r + b_s) = 3 × (200 + 800) = 3,000 → TRUE
C: block nested-loop worst case = b_r × b_s + b_r = 200 × 800 + 200 = 160,200 ≠ 1,000 → FALSE
Two of A–C are true → D
tip: Quick costs: merge join (sorted inputs) b_r + b_s; hash join ≈ 3(b_r + b_s); block nested loop b_r × b_s + b_r (worst case).

q: Which of the following join algorithms can NOT be used to evaluate a join whose condition is r.A < s.B (a non-equi-join)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Hash join works only for equi-joins and natural joins, because it relies on matching tuples having EQUAL join values that hash to the same partition. Nested-loop and block nested-loop joins test any condition on every pair of tuples.
concept: Nested-loop and block nested-loop joins compare every tuple of r with every tuple of s, so they work with ANY join condition (=, <, >, <> or combinations of these). Hash join places tuples into partitions by hashing the join attribute; only tuples with equal values are sure to land in partitions with the same number, so it can be used only for equi-joins and natural joins. Merge join also needs an equality condition (equi-join or natural join).
why: A — Wrong. Nested-loop join can evaluate any join condition, because it checks the condition on every pair of tuples. So it does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Correct. Hash join can be used only when the join condition is an equality; values such as 5 and 9, which satisfy 5 < 9, hash to unrelated partitions and would never be compared.
C — Wrong. Block nested-loop join also tests every pair of tuples (block by block), so it works for r.A < s.B. It does not satisfy the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the NOT stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. B satisfies the NOT stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Equi-join only: hash join and merge join. Any condition: nested-loop and block nested-loop join.

q:
Consider the following statements about the hash join of r and s on attribute A:
I. Both relations are partitioned using the same hash function on A.
II. The relation used as the build input should preferably be the smaller one.
III. Both relations must first be sorted on A.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are correct. III is false: sorting both inputs is needed for merge join, not for hash join.
concept: Hash join first partitions both r and s with the same hash function h on the join attribute, so tuples with equal join values always go to partitions with the same number. Then, for each partition number i, it loads partition i of the build input into memory, builds an in-memory hash index on it, and reads partition i of the probe input, looking up each tuple in that index. Korth recommends the smaller relation as the build input, so that each of its partitions fits in memory. No sorting is needed.
why: A — Wrong. It leaves out II, which is also true: the build partitions must fit in memory, so the smaller relation is the better build input.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.
C — Wrong. It includes III, which is false; sorting both inputs on the join attribute is the first step of merge join, not of hash join.

D — Wrong. Each of A–C names a different exact set of correct statements (note the word 'only'), so at most one of them can be right; here that is B. 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In pipelined evaluation, each operation is implemented as an iterator with open(), next() and close() functions, and the parent operation repeatedly calls next() on its child to get the next tuple. This form of pipelining is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When the top of the pipeline pulls tuples by asking its child for the next one, the pipeline is demand-driven (lazy); Korth notes that it is usually implemented with iterators having open(), next() and close().
concept: Pipelining passes the output tuples of one operation directly to the next operation, without storing them in a temporary relation on disk. In demand-driven (lazy, 'pull') pipelining, the system repeatedly requests tuples from the operation at the top of the pipeline; each operation computes its next tuple only when asked, and asks its own inputs for tuples when it needs them. In producer-driven (eager, 'push') pipelining, each operation produces tuples as fast as it can and puts them into a buffer for its parent, waiting only when the buffer is full.
why: A — Correct. The parent pulls tuples by calling next(), and each operator works only when asked: this is demand-driven (lazy) pipelining, implemented with iterators.
B — Wrong. In producer-driven (eager) pipelining, operations do not wait to be asked; they generate tuples on their own and push them into a buffer for the parent.

C — Wrong. Materialized evaluation computes each operation completely and stores its result in a temporary relation (usually on disk) before the next operation starts; there is no tuple-by-tuple pipeline.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A blocking operation is one that cannot output any result until it has examined all of its input. Which of the following is NOT a blocking operation?
opts: A selection σ_{marks > 60}(r) that tests each tuple as it arrives
A hash join that must read and partition both of its inputs completely before it outputs any tuple
More than one of the above
exp: A selection can pass each tuple on as soon as it is tested, so it is not blocking. Sorting is inherently blocking, and Korth notes that hash join (which must partition both inputs first) is blocking too.
concept: Some operations can be pipelined tuple by tuple, but blocking operations cannot output anything until all of their input has been seen. Sorting is inherently blocking: the smallest tuple may be the last one read. Korth also notes that the hash-join algorithm is blocking, since both inputs must be fully read and partitioned first, whereas indexed nested-loop join can output result tuples as soon as it gets tuples of the outer relation. Simple per-tuple operations such as selection, and projection without duplicate elimination, are not blocking.
why: A — Wrong. Sorting IS blocking: the first output tuple (the smallest) may be the last tuple of the input, so nothing can be output until all input is read. It does not satisfy the NOT stem.
B — Correct. Each tuple is tested on its own and passed on at once if marks > 60, so the selection produces output while its input is still arriving.
C — Wrong. As described, this hash join is blocking: it outputs nothing until both inputs are completely read and partitioned. It does not satisfy the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the NOT stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. B satisfies the NOT stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements about evaluating a query-evaluation plan:
I. In materialized evaluation, the result of each intermediate operation is stored in a temporary relation, usually on disk, and then read by the next operation.
II. Pipelining saves the cost of writing intermediate results to disk and reading them back.
III. Every operation, including sorting, can be fully pipelined.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are correct. III is false: sorting is a blocking operation and cannot be fully pipelined.
concept: In materialized evaluation, operations are evaluated one at a time, starting from the bottom of the plan tree; each result is materialized (stored) in a temporary relation, usually on disk, and the next operation reads it. Its cost = the cost of all the operations + the cost of writing the intermediate results. Pipelining instead passes tuples directly from one operation to the next, which saves those writes and reads and produces answers sooner. But blocking operations such as sorting need all their input before producing output, so they cannot be fully pipelined.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II are true and III is false.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false: sorting cannot output its first tuple until it has read every input tuple, so it cannot be fully pipelined.
C — Wrong. It includes III (false) and leaves out II (true): avoiding the writing and re-reading of temporary results is the main benefit of pipelining.

D — Wrong. Each of A–C names a different exact set of correct statements (note the word 'only'), so at most one of them can be right; here that is A. 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Korth: double buffering (two output buffers, one being written to disk while the other is being filled) makes materialized evaluation faster.

q: According to Korth, how many different join orders are possible for the join r1 ⋈ r2 ⋈ r3 ⋈ r4 ⋈ r5 (counting every join-tree shape and every arrangement of the relations)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Number of join orders for n relations = (2(n − 1))! / (n − 1)!. For n = 5: 8! / 4! = 40320 / 24 = 1680.
concept: Because join is commutative and associative, n relations can be joined in many orders. Korth gives the number of different join orders as (2(n − 1))! / (n − 1)!: 12 for 3 relations, 1680 for 5, 665,280 for 7 and more than 17.6 billion for 10. Since trying all of them is impossible for large n, optimizers use dynamic programming and often consider only left-deep join trees, of which there are n!.
why: A — Wrong. 120 = 5! counts only the left-deep join trees (one tree shape, all orders of the relations). Bushy and other tree shapes are also possible join orders.
C — Wrong. 14 is only the number of different binary-tree SHAPES with 5 leaves. Each shape can have the 5 relations arranged in 5! = 120 ways, giving 14 × 120 = 1680.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: r1 ⋈ r2 ⋈ r3 ⋈ r4 ⋈ r5   (n = 5 relations)
work:
Formula: (2(n − 1))! / (n − 1)!
n = 5: (2 × 4)! / 4! = 8! / 4!
8! = 40320, 4! = 24
40320 / 24 = 1680
Check: 14 tree shapes × 5! (= 120) leaf orders = 1680; left-deep trees only: 5! = 120
Brute-force enumeration of all join trees for n = 5 also gives 1680

q: STUDENT has n_r = 6000 tuples, V(dept, STUDENT) = 12 and V(year, STUDENT) = 4. Assuming values are uniformly distributed and the two conditions are independent, what is the estimated number of tuples in σ_{dept = 'CS' ∧ year = 2}(STUDENT)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: σ_{dept = 'CS'} gives 6000 / 12 = 500 tuples and σ_{year = 2} gives 6000 / 4 = 1500. For a conjunction, multiply the selectivities: 6000 × 1/12 × 1/4 = 125, which is not listed.
concept: The optimizer estimates result sizes from catalog statistics. For an equality selection, size(σ_{A = v}(r)) ≈ n_r / V(A, r), assuming each value appears equally often. The fraction s_i / n_r is called the selectivity of condition θ_i. For a conjunction θ1 ∧ θ2 (assuming independence) the selectivities are multiplied: n_r × (s1 / n_r) × (s2 / n_r). For a disjunction the formula is n_r × [1 − (1 − s1 / n_r)(1 − s2 / n_r)].
why: A — Wrong. 500 = 6000 / 12 is the estimate for dept = 'CS' alone; it ignores the second condition year = 2.
B — Wrong. 1500 = 6000 / 4 is the estimate for year = 2 alone; it ignores dept = 'CS'.

C — Wrong. 2000 = 500 + 1500 adds the two sizes. Even for OR this would count twice the tuples that satisfy both conditions; for AND a tuple must satisfy both, so the fractions are multiplied, giving a much smaller number.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The estimate is 6000 × 1/12 × 1/4 = 125 tuples, which is not listed.
code:
STUDENT: n_r = 6000
V(dept, STUDENT) = 12
V(year, STUDENT) = 4
σ_{dept = 'CS' ∧ year = 2}(STUDENT)
work:
s1 = size of σ_{dept = 'CS'} = 6000 / 12 = 500 (selectivity 1/12)
s2 = size of σ_{year = 2} = 6000 / 4 = 1500 (selectivity 1/4)
Conjunction: n_r × (s1 / n_r) × (s2 / n_r) = 6000 × 1/12 × 1/4 = 6000 / 48 = 125
125 is not among A–C

q: Relations r(A, B) and s(A, C) have n_r = 1,000 and n_s = 2,000 tuples, with V(A, r) = 50 and V(A, s) = 100. A is not a key of either relation. Using Korth's method, what is the estimated size of the natural join r ⋈ s?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Korth gives two estimates, n_r × n_s / V(A, s) = 2,000,000 / 100 = 20,000 and n_r × n_s / V(A, r) = 2,000,000 / 50 = 40,000, and takes the lower one: 20,000.
concept: Estimating join size (Korth): if r and s have no common attribute, r ⋈ s is a Cartesian product with n_r × n_s tuples. If the common attribute is a key of r, each s tuple joins with at most one r tuple, so the size is at most n_s (exactly n_s if it is also a foreign key from s to r). Otherwise, each tuple of r is assumed to match n_s / V(A, s) tuples of s, giving n_r × n_s / V(A, s); working the other way gives n_r × n_s / V(A, r). The two can differ, and the lower one is probably more accurate, i.e. n_r × n_s / max(V(A, r), V(A, s)).
why: A — Wrong. 2,000,000 = n_r × n_s is the size of the Cartesian product r × s; that is the natural-join size only when r and s have no common attribute.
B — Wrong. 40,000 divides by the smaller value V(A, r) = 50. Korth computes both estimates and keeps the lower one, because it is probably the more accurate.
C — Correct. The lower of the two estimates is 2,000,000 / 100 = 20,000.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
r(A, B): n_r = 1,000, V(A, r) = 50
s(A, C): n_s = 2,000, V(A, s) = 100
A is not a key of r or s; estimate the size of r ⋈ s
tip: Join size ≈ n_r × n_s / max(V(A, r), V(A, s)) when A is not a key. If A is a key of r and a foreign key in s, the size is exactly n_s.

q: Which of the following equivalences is NOT valid in general? (E1 and E2 have the same schema, θ, θ1 and θ2 are selection conditions and L is a list of attributes.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A (cascade of selections) and B (selection distributes over set difference) are Korth's equivalence rules. C fails: projection does not distribute over set difference.
concept: Equivalence rules say that two relational-algebra expressions always give the same result, so the optimizer may replace one with the other. Examples: a conjunctive selection can be split into a cascade of selections; selection distributes over ∪, ∩ and −, and for − it is enough to apply it to the left operand, σ_θ(E1 − E2) ≡ σ_θ(E1) − E2; projection distributes over union. But projection does NOT distribute over set difference (or intersection), because two different tuples can become the same tuple after projection.
why: A — Wrong. This is valid (cascade of σ): a tuple satisfies θ1 ∧ θ2 exactly when it passes θ2 and then also passes θ1. It does not satisfy the NOT stem.

B — Wrong. This is valid (one of Korth's rules): a tuple of E1 − E2 is in E1 and not in E2, so filtering only E1 is enough; filtering E2 as well would give the same answer. It does not satisfy the NOT stem.

C — Correct. This is not valid. Counterexample (attributes A, B; L = A): E1 = {(1, x), (1, y)} and E2 = {(1, x)}. Then π_A(E1 − E2) = {(1)} but π_A(E1) − π_A(E2) is empty, because (1, y) and (1, x) both project to (1).
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Projection distributes over ∪ but NOT over − or ∩. Selection distributes over ∪, ∩ and −.

q: The equivalence rule σ_{θ0}(E1 ⋈_θ E2) ≡ σ_{θ0}(E1) ⋈_θ E2 lets the optimizer push a selection below a join. When can it be applied?
opts: When θ0 uses only attributes of E1
When θ0 uses attributes of both E1 and E2
When θ0 uses only attributes of E2
More than one of the above
exp: A condition can be checked on E1 before the join only if every attribute it mentions belongs to E1.
concept: Pushing selections down the query tree (performing them as early as possible) is one of the most important heuristics: it makes the inputs of the join smaller, so the join is cheaper. Korth's rule: σ_{θ0}(E1 ⋈_θ E2) ≡ σ_{θ0}(E1) ⋈_θ E2 when all the attributes in θ0 belong to E1. If the condition is θ1 ∧ θ2, where θ1 uses only E1 and θ2 uses only E2, then each part is pushed to its own side: σ_{θ1}(E1) ⋈_θ σ_{θ2}(E2).
why: A — Correct. If θ0 mentions only E1's attributes, it can be tested on each E1 tuple before the join, and the join result is the same.
B — Wrong. A condition that compares attributes of E1 with attributes of E2 (for example E1.x > E2.y) cannot be tested on E1 alone; it must stay above the join or be merged into the join condition.
C — Wrong. If θ0 uses only E2's attributes, the selection can be pushed to E2 (σ_{θ0}(E2)), not to E1 as the rule in the stem does; E1 does not even have those attributes.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements about query optimization:
I. Heuristic optimization applies rules such as 'perform selections as early as possible'.
II. In a left-deep join tree, the right-hand input of every join is a stored relation, not the result of another join.
III. A cost-based optimizer always chooses the plan that is actually fastest when the query runs.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are correct. III is false: a cost-based optimizer chooses the plan with the lowest ESTIMATED cost, and estimates based on statistics can be wrong.
concept: Cost-based optimization generates many equivalent plans, estimates the cost of each from catalog statistics, and picks the cheapest. Heuristic optimization uses rules of thumb, such as performing selections and projections early and avoiding Cartesian products, to reduce the work. Many optimizers consider only left-deep join trees, where the right input of every join is a base relation; such trees suit pipelining and need far fewer choices (n! orders). Because size and cost estimates rest on assumptions such as uniform distribution of values, the chosen plan is not guaranteed to be the truly fastest.
why: A — Wrong. It leaves out II, which is also true: that is exactly the definition of a left-deep join tree.
B — Wrong. It includes III, which is false; the optimizer minimises the ESTIMATED cost, and estimates (based on assumptions such as uniform distribution of values) can be wrong.
C — Correct. I and II are true; III is false.

D — Wrong. Each of A–C names a different exact set of correct statements (note the word 'only'), so at most one of them can be right; here that is C. 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A materialized view v = r ⋈ s is kept up to date by incremental view maintenance. A set of tuples i_r is inserted into r. What is the new value of v?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only the new tuples of r can create new join results, so the system computes i_r ⋈ s and adds it to the old view: v_new = v ∪ (i_r ⋈ s).
concept: A materialized view stores the result of its query. When base tables change, recomputing the whole view is expensive, so incremental view maintenance computes only the change (the 'differential'). For v = r ⋈ s: after inserting i_r into r, v_new = v_old ∪ (i_r ⋈ s); after deleting d_r from r, v_new = v_old − (d_r ⋈ s). Similar rules exist for selection, projection (using a count of how many ways each tuple is derived) and aggregates such as COUNT and SUM. Maintenance can be immediate (inside the updating transaction) or deferred (done later).
why: A — Correct. (r ∪ i_r) ⋈ s = (r ⋈ s) ∪ (i_r ⋈ s), so only the join of the new tuples with s has to be computed and added.
B — Wrong. Subtracting a join is the rule for DELETING tuples d_r from r: v − (d_r ⋈ s). Insertions can only add join results, never remove them.
C — Wrong. i_r has the schema of r, not of the view; the new r tuples must first be joined with s before they can be added to v.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Join view: insert into r → add (i_r ⋈ s); delete from r → remove (d_r ⋈ s).

q: What values of r and d does the query show for Dev?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Scores in descending order: 90, 90, 85, 85, 80. RANK leaves gaps after ties (1, 1, 3, 3, 5) and DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2, 2, 3), so Dev (80) gets r = 5 and d = 3.
concept: RANK() and DENSE_RANK() number the rows in the order given by OVER (ORDER BY …), and tied rows get the same number. RANK() then skips numbers: after two rows tied at rank 1, the next row gets rank 3 (its rank = 1 + the number of rows ahead of it). DENSE_RANK() does not skip: the next distinct value simply gets the next number. ROW_NUMBER() gives every row a different number even when values tie.
why: A — Correct. Four students score more than Dev, so RANK = 4 + 1 = 5; 80 is the third distinct score, so DENSE_RANK = 3.
B — Wrong. 3 is right for DENSE_RANK, but RANK leaves a gap after each tie: the ranks are 1, 1, 3, 3, 5, so Dev's RANK is 5, not 3.
C — Wrong. 5 is right for RANK, but DENSE_RANK never skips numbers: 90 → 1, 85 → 2, 80 → 3, so Dev's DENSE_RANK is 3.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
MARKS
Name   | Score
Asha   | 90
Bina   | 85
Chetan | 90
Dev    | 80
Esha   | 85

SELECT Name, Score,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY Score DESC) AS r,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Score DESC) AS d
FROM MARKS;
work:
Sort by Score DESC: Asha 90, Chetan 90, Bina 85, Esha 85, Dev 80
RANK: 90 → 1, 1; 85 → 3, 3 (two rows ahead); 80 → 5 (four rows ahead)
DENSE_RANK: 90 → 1; 85 → 2; 80 → 3
Dev: r = 5, d = 3
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MySQL/MariaDB (all give 5 and 3)
tip: RANK = 1 + (number of rows strictly ahead). DENSE_RANK = position of the value among the DISTINCT values.

q: Which of the following SQL ranking functions never skip a number (they always use 1, 2, 3, … with no gaps), even when some rows have equal values?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: ROW_NUMBER() gives every row a different consecutive number, and DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same number but continues with the very next number; only RANK() leaves gaps after ties.
concept: For scores 90, 90, 85, 85, 80 sorted in descending order: ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (tied rows get different numbers, in any order unless the ORDER BY decides it); RANK gives 1, 1, 3, 3, 5 (ties share a number and then numbers are skipped); DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 (ties share a number, no gaps). All three are window functions written with OVER (ORDER BY …), optionally with PARTITION BY to restart the numbering in each group.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. ROW_NUMBER() numbers the rows 1, 2, 3, … one by one; tied rows simply get different numbers.
B — Wrong. RANK() skips numbers after ties: two rows tied at 1 are followed by rank 3, so 2 is missing.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. DENSE_RANK() gives tied rows the same number, and the next value gets the very next number: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3.
D — Correct. A and C are true (B is false), so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Scores 90, 90, 85, 85, 80 (descending):
ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 → no gaps
RANK: 1, 1, 3, 3, 5 → 2 and 4 are skipped
DENSE_RANK: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 → no gaps
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MySQL/MariaDB

q: What does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: PARTITION BY Dept restarts the numbering in each department, so rn = 1 marks the highest-paid employee of each department: Amit (IT), Deepa (HR) and Farid (Sales).
concept: PARTITION BY divides the rows into groups (here, one per department), and the window function is computed separately inside each group; ROW_NUMBER() restarts at 1 in every partition. Unlike GROUP BY, the rows are not collapsed, so other columns such as Name are still available. A window function cannot be used directly in WHERE (WHERE is evaluated before window functions), so the query computes it in a subquery and filters outside: this is the standard 'top-N per group' pattern.
why: A — Wrong. Amit alone would be the result without PARTITION BY: the whole table would be numbered once, so only the overall top earner would have rn = 1.

B — Wrong. Amit, Bela and Gita are the three highest salaries overall (they are all in IT); that would need WHERE rn <= 3 without PARTITION BY. With PARTITION BY Dept, exactly one row per department has rn = 1.
C — Correct. Each department's highest salary gets rn = 1: Amit (IT, 70000), Deepa (HR, 55000) and Farid (Sales, 45000).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
Name   | Dept  | Sal
Amit   | IT    | 70000
Bela   | IT    | 65000
Chandu | HR    | 50000
Deepa  | HR    | 55000
Esha   | Sales | 40000
Farid  | Sales | 45000
Gita   | IT    | 60000

SELECT Name
FROM (SELECT Name,
             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Dept ORDER BY Sal DESC) AS rn
      FROM EMP) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY Name;
work:
HR: Deepa 55000 → rn 1, Chandu 50000 → rn 2
IT: Amit 70000 → 1, Bela 65000 → 2, Gita 60000 → 3
Sales: Farid 45000 → 1, Esha 40000 → 2
Rows with rn = 1: Deepa, Amit, Farid → ordered by Name: Amit, Deepa, Farid
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MySQL/MariaDB
tip: Top-N per group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY value DESC) in a subquery, then WHERE rn <= N outside.

q: What value of run does the query show for the two rows with Day = 2?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With ORDER BY and no frame clause, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which includes all rows with the same Day (peers). So both Day = 2 rows show 100 + 50 + 30 = 180.
concept: SUM(…) OVER (ORDER BY col) gives a running (cumulative) total. When ORDER BY is given without a frame clause, standard SQL uses the frame RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW: the sum covers every earlier row AND all rows with the same ORDER BY value as the current row (called peers). So tied rows get the same running total. To add the rows strictly one at a time, write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (and make the ORDER BY unique).
why: A — Wrong. 130 and 180 would come from adding the tied rows one at a time (a ROWS frame, with 30 taken before 50). The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE, which treats rows with equal Day as peers and includes all of them.
B — Correct. Both Day = 2 rows are peers, so each sum includes 100, 50 and 30: 180.
C — Wrong. 80 = 50 + 30 is the total of Day 2 alone, which PARTITION BY Day would give. ORDER BY Day makes a running total that also includes the earlier Day 1 row.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
SALES
Day | Amt
1   | 100
2   | 50
2   | 30
3   | 20

SELECT Day, Amt,
       SUM(Amt) OVER (ORDER BY Day) AS run
FROM SALES
ORDER BY Day, Amt;
work:
Day 1: 100 → run = 100
Day 2 rows are peers (same Day): frame = all rows with Day ≤ 2 → 100 + 50 + 30 = 180 for BOTH rows
Day 3: 180 + 20 = 200
Output: (1, 100, 100), (2, 30, 180), (2, 50, 180), (3, 20, 200)
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MySQL/MariaDB. With ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW the two Day-2 rows would instead get different totals (130/180 or 150/180, depending on which tied row comes first).
tip: Common mistake: assuming SUM() OVER (ORDER BY …) always adds one row at a time. Rows that tie in the ORDER BY get the same running total unless you write ROWS BETWEEN … .

q: How many rows does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A window function does not collapse rows: every one of the 6 EMP rows is returned, each with the size of its department (IT 3, HR 2, Sales 1).
concept: GROUP BY Dept would return one row per department (3 rows). A window function with OVER (PARTITION BY Dept) also computes the aggregate per department, but it attaches the result to every input row instead of merging the rows. So the query returns as many rows as the table has, and each row can show both its own details (Name) and information about its group (dept_size).
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the number of departments, which is what GROUP BY Dept would return. A window function keeps every row.
B — Correct. All 6 rows are returned, each with its department's count.
C — Wrong. 1 row would come from COUNT(*) used as an ordinary aggregate with no GROUP BY. With OVER (…), COUNT(*) becomes a window function and no rows are merged.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
Name  | Dept
Ravi  | IT
Meena | HR
John  | IT
Sara  | Sales
Anil  | IT
Tina  | HR

SELECT Name, Dept,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY Dept) AS dept_size
FROM EMP;
work:
Rows in EMP: 6 → a window function keeps all 6 rows
dept_size: IT = 3 (Ravi, John, Anil), HR = 2 (Meena, Tina), Sales = 1 (Sara)
Output: 6 rows, e.g. (Ravi, IT, 3), (Meena, HR, 2), (Sara, Sales, 1), …
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MySQL/MariaDB (6 rows)

q: The query SELECT region, product, year, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY CUBE(region, product, year); computes aggregates for how many groupings (grouping sets), including the grand total?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CUBE on n columns forms every subset of the columns: 2^n = 2^3 = 8 groupings.
concept: CUBE and ROLLUP are extensions of GROUP BY used for OLAP (data analysis); they are supported by PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server, while MySQL has only GROUP BY … WITH ROLLUP. GROUP BY CUBE(a, b, c) computes the aggregate for every subset of {a, b, c}: (a,b,c), (a,b), (a,c), (b,c), (a), (b), (c) and () — 2^n groupings for n columns. GROUP BY ROLLUP(a, b, c) computes only the hierarchy (a,b,c), (a,b), (a) and () — n + 1 groupings. In the output, a rolled-up column shows NULL (the GROUPING() function tells such NULLs apart from real NULLs).
why: A — Wrong. 3 is just the number of columns. CUBE groups by every combination of them, not by each column once.
B — Wrong. 4 = n + 1 is the number of groupings for ROLLUP(region, product, year): (r,p,y), (r,p), (r), (). CUBE also includes combinations such as (product, year) and (year).
C — Correct. 2^3 = 8 groupings, including the grand total ().
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Columns: region, product, year → n = 3
CUBE: all subsets = 2^3 = 8
(region, product, year), (region, product), (region, year), (product, year), (region), (product), (year), ()
ROLLUP would give only n + 1 = 4

q: In standard SQL (for example PostgreSQL), how many rows does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: CUBE(Region, Product) produces 4 groupings: (Region, Product) gives 4 rows, (Region) 3 rows, (Product) 2 rows and () 1 row: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10.
concept: The number of output rows of CUBE or ROLLUP is the sum, over all its groupings, of the number of distinct value combinations that actually occur in the data. Combinations that do not occur (such as North–Pen here) produce no row. CUBE(a, b) = GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), (b), ()); ROLLUP(a, b) = GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ()).
why: A — Correct. 4 (Region, Product) groups + 3 Region subtotals + 2 Product subtotals + 1 grand total = 10 rows.
B — Wrong. 8 = 4 + 3 + 1 is the result of ROLLUP(Region, Product), which has no per-Product subtotals. CUBE adds the 2 Product subtotal rows (Pen 45, Ink 35).
C — Wrong. 12 assumes that all 3 × 2 = 6 Region–Product pairs exist. Only 4 pairs occur (West has no Ink and North has no Pen), and groups are formed only for combinations present in the data.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
SALES
Region | Product | Amt
East   | Pen     | 10
East   | Ink     | 20
West   | Pen     | 30
West   | Pen     | 5
North  | Ink     | 15

SELECT Region, Product, SUM(Amt)
FROM SALES
GROUP BY CUBE(Region, Product);
work:
(Region, Product): East-Pen, East-Ink, West-Pen, North-Ink → 4 rows (the two West-Pen rows, 30 and 5, form one group)
(Region): East, West, North → 3 rows
(Product): Pen, Ink → 2 rows
(): grand total → 1 row
Total = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10
Verified in PostgreSQL and DuckDB (10 rows; ROLLUP gives 8). SQLite has no CUBE; MySQL/MariaDB support only WITH ROLLUP.

q: In standard SQL (for example PostgreSQL), how many rows does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: GROUPING SETS ((Class), (Stream)) is the union of GROUP BY Class (2 rows: 11, 12) and GROUP BY Stream (3 rows: Sci, Com, Arts) = 5 rows. No grand-total row is produced because () is not listed. 5 is not among A–C.
concept: GROUP BY GROUPING SETS lists exactly the groupings wanted; the result is the union of the separate GROUP BY results, with NULL in the columns that are not part of a grouping. Only the listed groupings are produced: a grand total appears only if the empty grouping () is listed. ROLLUP and CUBE are shorthands for particular lists of grouping sets.
why: A — Wrong. 6 adds a grand-total row. A grand total is produced only when the empty grouping () is listed, as it is inside ROLLUP and CUBE; here it is not.
B — Wrong. 4 is the number of distinct (Class, Stream) pairs, i.e. the result of GROUP BY Class, Stream. That grouping is not in the list.
C — Wrong. 10 = 4 + 2 + 3 + 1 is the result of CUBE(Class, Stream), which uses all four groupings.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The query returns 2 + 3 = 5 rows, which is not listed.
code:
RESULT
Class | Stream | Marks
11    | Sci    | 80
11    | Com    | 70
12    | Sci    | 90
12    | Arts   | 60
12    | Sci    | 75

SELECT Class, Stream, COUNT(*)
FROM RESULT
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((Class), (Stream));
work:
Grouping (Class): 11 (2 rows), 12 (3 rows) → 2 output rows
Grouping (Stream): Sci (3), Com (1), Arts (1) → 3 output rows
No () in the list → no grand total
Total = 2 + 3 = 5 (not among A–C)
Verified in PostgreSQL and DuckDB: (11, NULL, 2), (12, NULL, 3), (NULL, Arts, 1), (NULL, Com, 1), (NULL, Sci, 3)

q: What does the query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: AllPre is the transitive closure of PREREQ (every direct or indirect prerequisite): C2→C1, C3→C2, C3→C1, C4→C2, C4→C1, C5→C4, C5→C2, C5→C1 — 8 pairs.
concept: A recursive query can compute the transitive closure of a relation: all pairs connected by a chain of any length. The anchor (non-recursive) part gives the direct pairs; the recursive part joins the pairs found in the previous round with the base table to extend each chain by one step. The rounds repeat until one adds no new pair — a fixed point. UNION (rather than UNION ALL) removes duplicates, which also guarantees that the query stops even if the data contains a cycle.
why: A — Wrong. 4 counts only the direct prerequisites from the anchor part; the recursive part adds the indirect ones.
B — Wrong. 7 stops after one recursive step (chains of length 2). The chain C5 → C4 → C2 → C1 has length 3, so (C5, C1) is added in the next step.
C — Correct. 4 direct pairs + 3 two-step pairs + 1 three-step pair = 8.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
PREREQ
Course | Pre
C3     | C2
C2     | C1
C4     | C2
C5     | C4

WITH RECURSIVE AllPre(Course, Pre) AS (
  SELECT Course, Pre FROM PREREQ
  UNION
  SELECT a.Course, p.Pre
  FROM AllPre a JOIN PREREQ p ON a.Pre = p.Course
)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AllPre;
work:
Round 0 (anchor): (C3,C2), (C2,C1), (C4,C2), (C5,C4) → 4 rows
Round 1: (C3,C2)+(C2,C1) → (C3,C1); (C4,C2)+(C2,C1) → (C4,C1); (C5,C4)+(C4,C2) → (C5,C2); (C2,C1) cannot be extended → 3 new, total 7
Round 2 (extend the 3 new pairs): (C5,C2)+(C2,C1) → (C5,C1); (C3,C1) and (C4,C1) cannot be extended (C1 has no prerequisite) → 1 new, total 8
Round 3: (C5,C1) cannot be extended → nothing new → fixed point
COUNT(*) = 8
Verified in SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MySQL/MariaDB

q: Which of the following statements about recursive queries (WITH RECURSIVE) in SQL are correct?
opts: The recursive part is applied again and again until no new tuples are produced, that is, until a fixed point is reached
A typical use is finding a transitive closure, such as all direct and indirect prerequisites of a course
The SQL standard puts no restriction on the recursive part; for example, it may apply COUNT or NOT EXISTS to the recursive view itself
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are true. C is false: as Korth explains, SQL requires recursive queries to be monotonic, so the recursive part may not use aggregation or NOT EXISTS on the recursive view.
concept: A recursive view is evaluated by repeating its definition until nothing new is added (a fixed point). This works correctly only if the query is monotonic: adding tuples to the recursive view can only add tuples to the result, never remove them. Aggregation, NOT EXISTS or EXCEPT applied to the recursive view are non-monotonic, so the SQL standard does not allow them in the recursive part; PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB give an error if, for example, an aggregate is used there. Recursive queries are used for transitive closure, organisation charts, bills of materials and reachability in graphs.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each round uses the rows found in the previous round to produce new ones; when a round adds nothing, the result is complete.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The anchor gives the direct prerequisites, and each recursive round extends the chains by one step.

C — Wrong. SQL requires recursive queries to be monotonic. Aggregation, NOT EXISTS or EXCEPT on the recursive view could make tuples disappear as the view grows, so they are not allowed in the recursive part; PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB reject such queries.
D — Correct. A and B are true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Test of C: WITH RECURSIVE t(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT MAX(n) + 1 FROM t HAVING MAX(n) < 3) SELECT * FROM t;
PostgreSQL: error 'aggregate functions are not allowed in a recursive query's recursive term'
SQLite: error 'recursive aggregate queries not supported'
MariaDB: error 'Restrictions imposed on recursive definitions are violated'
(DuckDB accepts it as a non-standard extension.)
tip: Korth: a recursive view must be monotonic — no aggregation, NOT EXISTS or EXCEPT on the recursive view.

q: In a functional dependency X → Y, the attribute set X (on the left side of the arrow) is called the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In X → Y, the left side X is the determinant (it decides the value of Y) and the right side Y is the dependent.
concept: A functional dependency (FD) X → Y says that the value of X decides (determines) the value of Y. The left side X is called the determinant and the right side Y is called the dependent. Example: in STUDENT, Roll_no → Name; Roll_no is the determinant and Name is the dependent. X and Y can each be a single attribute or a set of attributes.
why: A — Wrong. The dependent is the RIGHT side Y, whose value is decided by X. X is the side that does the deciding.
B — Correct. X decides (determines) the value of Y, so X is called the determinant.

C — Wrong. A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that determines ALL attributes of the relation. The left side of an FD need not be a key: in EMP(EmpID, DeptNo, DeptName), DeptNo → DeptName holds, but DeptNo is not a key of EMP.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Determinant = the side that Determines (left). Dependent = the side that Depends (right).

q: The functional dependency X → Y holds on a relation R(X, Y, Z). Which statement must be true?
opts: Any two tuples that have the same X value also have the same Y value
Any two tuples that have the same Y value also have the same X value
X must be a candidate key of R
More than one of the above
exp: X → Y means: whenever two tuples agree on X, they must also agree on Y. It promises nothing in the reverse direction, and X need not be a key.
concept: Formally, X → Y holds on R if, in every legal state of R, any two tuples t1 and t2 with t1[X] = t2[X] also have t1[Y] = t2[Y]. In simple words, one X value can never be paired with two different Y values. The reverse is not promised: many different X values may share the same Y value. X is a key only if it determines every attribute of R, which an ordinary FD does not require.
why: A — Correct. This is exactly the definition of X → Y: equal X values force equal Y values.
B — Wrong. This describes the reverse FD, Y → X. X → Y allows two different X values to have the same Y value (two students with different roll numbers can both be named 'Amit').
C — Wrong. X → Y only says X decides Y. Nothing is said about Z, so X may not determine Z and need not be a key. X would be a superkey only if it determined every attribute of R.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Look at this instance of R(A, B, C). Which functional dependency is satisfied by this instance?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only A → B is satisfied: the repeated value A = 1 always comes with B = x. A → C fails on rows 1–2 and B → A fails on rows 3–4.
concept: To test X → Y on a table instance, look for two rows with the same X value. If any such pair has different Y values, the FD is violated. If no pair breaks it (or the X values never repeat), the instance satisfies the FD. One violating pair is enough to show that the FD does not hold.
why: A — Wrong. Rows 1 and 2 have the same A value (1) but different C values (p and q). One A value is paired with two C values, so A → C is violated.
B — Wrong. Rows 3 and 4 have the same B value (y) but different A values (2 and 3). So B → A is violated.
C — Correct. The only repeated A value is 1, and both rows with A = 1 have B = x. No pair of rows breaks the rule, so the instance satisfies A → B.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
R
A | B | C
1 | x | p
1 | x | q
2 | y | p
3 | y | r
work:
A → C: rows 1 and 2 both have A = 1 but C = p and C = q, so it is violated.
B → A: rows 3 and 4 both have B = y but A = 2 and A = 3, so it is violated.
A → B: A = 1 appears twice, both times with B = x; A = 2 and A = 3 appear once each, so it is satisfied.

q: Which of the following functional dependencies is satisfied by this instance of WORKS?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each of the three FDs is broken by a pair of rows, so none of A–C is satisfied by this instance.
concept: An FD X → Y is violated by an instance as soon as two rows agree on X but differ on Y. In WORKS an employee can work on several projects, so EmpID alone cannot decide Proj; the pair (EmpID, Proj) is what identifies a row.
why: A — Wrong. E1 appears in two rows with two different projects (P1 and P2). One EmpID value has two Proj values, so EmpID → Proj is violated. (An employee can work on many projects.)
B — Wrong. Project P1 has 10 hours in both of its rows, but P2 has 20 hours in row 2 and 30 hours in row 4. So Proj → Hours is violated.
C — Wrong. Department D1 appears with employees E1 and E3. One Dept value has two EmpID values, so Dept → EmpID is violated.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three FDs are violated by this instance. FDs that ARE satisfied here include EmpID → Dept (E1 always has D1) and (EmpID, Proj) → Hours.
code:
WORKS
EmpID | Dept | Proj | Hours
E1    | D1   | P1   | 10
E1    | D1   | P2   | 20
E2    | D2   | P1   | 10
E3    | D1   | P2   | 30
work:
EmpID → Proj: E1 appears with P1 (row 1) and P2 (row 2), so it is violated.
Proj → Hours: P2 appears with 20 (row 2) and 30 (row 4), so it is violated.
Dept → EmpID: D1 appears with E1 (rows 1–2) and E3 (row 4), so it is violated.
For comparison: EmpID → Dept is satisfied (E1 always has D1; E2 and E3 appear once), and (EmpID, Proj) → Hours is satisfied (no (EmpID, Proj) pair repeats).

q:
Consider the following statements about functional dependencies (FDs):
I. One table instance can prove that an FD does NOT hold on the relation schema.
II. One table instance can prove that an FD will hold in all future states of the relation.
III. FDs are decided from the meaning (semantics) of the attributes, that is, from real-world rules.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A single instance can disprove an FD (one violating pair is enough) but cannot prove it for all future states; FDs come from the meaning of the data. So I and III are correct.
concept: An FD is a constraint on the relation schema: it must hold in every legal state (instance) of the relation, now and in the future. The designer finds FDs from real-world rules, for example 'each roll number belongs to exactly one student'. Today's rows can show that an FD is false (two rows agree on X but differ on Y), but they cannot show that the FD will always be true, because a new row may break it tomorrow.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is false. A table may satisfy an FD today by chance (for example, all current students happen to have different names), but a new row could break it tomorrow. So 'I and II only' is wrong.
B — Correct. I is true (one pair of rows with the same X and a different Y disproves X → Y). III is true (FDs come from real-world meaning). II is false. So the correct set is I and III.
C — Wrong. II is false, as explained above, so any option that contains II is wrong.
D — Wrong. Only option B names exactly the correct statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at the same time, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option B is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: An instance can only say 'NO, this FD does not hold'. It can never say 'YES, it will always hold'.

q: Which of the following are derived inference rules, that is, rules that can be proved from Armstrong's three axioms instead of being axioms themselves?
opts: Union rule: if X → Y and X → Z, then X → YZ
Pseudotransitivity rule: if X → Y and WY → Z, then WX → Z
Augmentation rule: if X → Y, then XZ → YZ
More than one of the above
exp: Union and pseudotransitivity are derived rules; augmentation is one of the three basic axioms.
concept: Armstrong's three axioms are reflexivity (if Y ⊆ X then X → Y), augmentation (if X → Y then XZ → YZ) and transitivity (if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z). Using only these three we can prove extra rules: union (X → Y and X → Z give X → YZ), decomposition (X → YZ gives X → Y), and pseudotransitivity (X → Y and WY → Z give WX → Z). These extra rules are called derived (secondary) rules.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The union rule can be proved: augment X → Y with X to get X → XY; augment X → Z with Y to get XY → YZ; then transitivity gives X → YZ.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Pseudotransitivity can be proved: augment X → Y with W to get WX → WY, then use transitivity with WY → Z to get WX → Z.
C — Wrong. Augmentation is one of Armstrong's three basic axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity). It is not derived from the others.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Axioms = RAT (Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity). Derived rules = UDP (Union, Decomposition, Pseudotransitivity).

q: The inference rule 'if Y ⊆ X, then X → Y' is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: If Y is a subset of X, then X → Y always holds; this is the reflexivity axiom, and the FDs it gives are trivial FDs.
concept: Reflexivity says that a set of attributes always determines any of its own subsets: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y. For example, {Roll_no, Name} → Name. FDs produced by reflexivity are trivial FDs, because they hold in every relation whatever data it contains.
why: A — Wrong. Augmentation says: if X → Y holds, then XZ → YZ holds (the same attributes Z may be added to both sides). It starts from an FD that already holds.
B — Wrong. Transitivity says: if X → Y and Y → Z hold, then X → Z holds. It chains two FDs together.
C — Correct. Reflexivity: any set of attributes determines its own subsets, so Y ⊆ X gives X → Y.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Armstrong's axioms are said to be complete. What does 'complete' mean here?
opts: Every FD derived using the axioms really holds in every relation that satisfies F
Every FD in F+ (every FD implied by F) can be derived by applying the axioms again and again
Applying the axioms always produces a minimal cover of F
More than one of the above
exp: Complete means the axioms can derive every FD that is logically implied by F, that is, all of F+. Option A describes soundness.
concept: Armstrong's axioms are sound and complete. Sound means they never produce a wrong FD: everything they derive is really implied by F. Complete means they miss nothing: every FD in the closure F+ can be derived from F using them. Together this means F+ is exactly the set of FDs that can be derived with the axioms.
why: A — Wrong. This is the meaning of SOUND, not complete. Soundness says the axioms never derive an FD that is false.
B — Correct. This is completeness: by using the axioms repeatedly we can reach every FD in F+.

C — Wrong. A minimal cover is found by a separate algorithm (split right sides, remove extraneous attributes, remove redundant FDs). The axioms generate FDs; they do not by themselves give a minimal cover.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Sound = no wrong answers. Complete = no missing answers.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E) has the FD set F = {A → B, B → C, CD → E}. Which of the following FDs is implied by F (that is, belongs to F+)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A+ = {A, B, C} contains C, and (AD)+ = {A, B, C, D, E} contains E, so A → C and AD → E are implied; B+ = {B, C} does not contain E.
concept: To test whether an FD X → Y is implied by F, compute the attribute closure X+ using F. If every attribute of Y is in X+, the FD is in F+; otherwise it is not. This closure test is quicker and safer than trying Armstrong's axioms by hand.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A+ = {A, B, C} contains C. (This is transitivity: A → B and B → C give A → C.)

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. (AD)+ = {A, B, C, D, E} contains E: A gives B and C, and then C together with D gives E through CD → E (this is pseudotransitivity).
C — Wrong. B+ = {B, C}. E is missing, because CD → E also needs D, and nothing gives D starting from B. So B → E is not implied.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following functional dependencies is trivial?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In all three FDs the right side has an attribute that is not on the left side (B, B and C respectively), so none of them is trivial.
concept: An FD X → Y is trivial if Y ⊆ X; it holds in every relation (for example {Roll_no, Name} → Name). It is non-trivial if Y is not a subset of X, that is, Y has at least one attribute that is not in X. It is completely non-trivial if X and Y have no attribute in common (X ∩ Y = ∅). Every completely non-trivial FD is non-trivial, but not the other way round.
why: A — Wrong. B is not part of the left side {A}, so A → B is non-trivial. In fact it is completely non-trivial, because the two sides share no attribute.

B — Wrong. The right side {A, B} contains B, which is not on the left side {A}. An FD is trivial only when the WHOLE right side lies inside the left side. A → AB is non-trivial (but not completely non-trivial, because A is on both sides).
C — Wrong. The right side contains C, which is not in {A, B}. So AB → BC is non-trivial (but not completely non-trivial, because B is on both sides).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. None of the three is trivial. A trivial FD has its whole right side inside its left side, for example AB → B or A → A; such FDs hold in every relation.
work:
Rule: X → Y is trivial only if every attribute of Y is also in X.
A → B: B is not in {A}, so non-trivial (the sides share nothing, so it is also completely non-trivial).
A → AB: B is not in {A}, so non-trivial (A is common, so not completely non-trivial).
AB → BC: C is not in {A, B}, so non-trivial (B is common, so not completely non-trivial).
Result: none of the three is trivial.

q: Which of the following inferences is NOT valid for functional dependencies?
opts: From XY → Z, infer X → Z
From X → Y and WY → Z, infer WX → Z
From X → YZ, infer X → Y
More than one of the above
exp: XY → Z does not give X → Z, because the left side of an FD cannot be shrunk; the other two are the valid pseudotransitivity and decomposition rules.
concept: Valid rules come from Armstrong's axioms. You may split the RIGHT side (decomposition: X → YZ gives X → Y), join right sides (union), add attributes to the left side (augmentation, reflexivity), and chain FDs (transitivity, pseudotransitivity). But you may NOT drop attributes from the LEFT side: XY → Z does not mean X alone decides Z. Example: (Roll_no, Subject) → Marks holds, but Roll_no → Marks does not.
why: A — Correct. This inference is NOT valid, so it fits the stem. Shrinking the left side is not allowed. Example: (Roll_no, Subject) → Marks holds, but Roll_no alone does not decide Marks, because one student has different marks in different subjects.
B — Wrong. This is a valid rule (pseudotransitivity), so it does not fit the stem. Augment X → Y with W to get WX → WY, then transitivity with WY → Z gives WX → Z.
C — Wrong. This is a valid rule (decomposition), so it does not fit the stem. Reflexivity gives YZ → Y, and transitivity with X → YZ gives X → Y.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The right side may be split; the left side may NOT. (Roll, Subject) → Marks does not give Roll → Marks.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G) has F = {A → C, BC → D, D → E, G → B}. What is the attribute closure (AB)+?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Starting from {A, B}: A → C adds C, BC → D adds D, D → E adds E. G is never added, so (AB)+ = {A, B, C, D, E}.
concept: The closure X+ of an attribute set X is the set of all attributes that X determines under F. Algorithm: start with result = X; repeatedly find an FD L → R whose whole left side L is already inside result, and add R to result; stop when nothing changes. If X+ contains every attribute of the relation, X is a superkey.
why: A — Wrong. {A, B, C} is what you have after using only A → C. The algorithm must continue: BC is now inside the set, so BC → D adds D, and then D → E adds E.
B — Wrong. G is not determined by AB. The FD G → B goes from G to B, not from B to G; it can be used only when G is already in the set. So (AB)+ does not contain G (and AB is not a superkey of R).
C — Correct. A → C adds C; BC → D adds D; D → E adds E. G → B can never be used because G is not in the set. So (AB)+ = {A, B, C, D, E}.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: An FD can be used only when its WHOLE left side is already in the set. Never use an FD backwards.

q: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → A}. Which option lists ALL the candidate keys of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: D never appears on a right side, so it is in every key. A, B and C determine one another, so AD, BD and CD each determine all four attributes, and no smaller set does.
concept: Shortcut for finding candidate keys: an attribute that appears on no right side must be in every key. Add other attributes to it until the closure covers the whole relation, and keep only minimal sets. When attributes form a cycle such as A → B → C → A, any one of them can take the place of the others, which gives several candidate keys.
why: A — Correct. (AD)+, (BD)+ and (CD)+ all equal {A, B, C, D}, while no single attribute is a key (A+ = {A, B, C}, D+ = {D}). So the candidate keys are AD, BD and CD.
B — Wrong. A+ = {A, B, C} misses D (and so do B+ and C+). D is never determined by anything, so every key must contain D. Hence A, B and C alone are not keys.
C — Wrong. AD is a candidate key, but not the only one. Because the cycle A → B → C → A lets B or C replace A, BD and CD are also minimal keys.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G) has F = {AB → C, C → A, AD → E, E → G, G → D}. How many candidate keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: B must be in every key; A or C (they replace each other once B is present) and one of D, E, G complete the key: 2 × 3 = 6 keys (ABD, ABE, ABG, BCD, BCE, BCG).
concept: To count candidate keys, first fix the attributes that appear on no right side (they are in every key). Then look for groups of attributes that can replace one another. If a key needs one attribute from a group of 2 and one from a group of 3, and the choices are independent, there are 2 × 3 keys. Always confirm each candidate with a closure and check that it is minimal.
why: A — Wrong. 4 is too few. It would come from noticing only two of the three choices D, E and G (2 × 2 = 4). But E alone also works: E → G and G → D give D and G, so ABE and BCE are keys too.
B — Correct. Keys = B + (A or C) + (D or E or G) = ABD, ABE, ABG, BCD, BCE, BCG. Each closure is the whole of R, and every 2-attribute subset fails, so there are 6 candidate keys.
C — Wrong. 8 is too many. Sets such as ABDE or BCDG are superkeys but not minimal, and a set such as ABC is not even a superkey ((ABC)+ = {A, B, C}). Only the 6 minimal superkeys are candidate keys.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Count keys as 'core × choices': core attributes are fixed, interchangeable groups multiply.

q: R(P, Q, S, T, U) has F = {PQ → S, S → T, T → Q}. Which of the following is a non-prime attribute of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The candidate keys are PQU, PSU and PTU, so Q, S and T are all prime; in fact every attribute of R is prime.
concept: A prime attribute belongs to at least one candidate key; a non-prime attribute belongs to no candidate key. To classify attributes you must first find ALL candidate keys, not just one. Here Q, S and T form a cycle (with P, Q gives S; S gives T; T gives Q), so each of them can sit in a key in place of the others.
why: A — Wrong. Q is part of the candidate key PQU, so Q is prime, not non-prime.
B — Wrong. S is part of the candidate key PSU ((PSU)+ = {P, Q, S, T, U}), so S is prime.
C — Wrong. T is part of the candidate key PTU ((PTU)+ = {P, Q, S, T, U}), so T is prime.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The candidate keys are PQU, PSU and PTU, so every attribute (P, Q, S, T, U) is prime and R has no non-prime attribute at all.
tip: Find ALL candidate keys before calling an attribute non-prime. Checking only one key is a common mistake.

q: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. Which of the following is NOT a candidate key of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: ABD is a superkey but not a candidate key, because its proper subsets AB and BD are already keys.
concept: A superkey is any set of attributes whose closure is the whole relation. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: removing any attribute from it makes it stop being a superkey. So every candidate key is a superkey, but a superkey that contains a smaller key inside it is not a candidate key.
why: A — Wrong. (BC)+ = {A, B, C, D}, while B+ = {B} and C+ = {A, C, D} are not the whole relation. So BC is a minimal superkey, i.e., a candidate key. It does not fit the stem.
B — Correct. (ABD)+ = {A, B, C, D}, so ABD is a superkey, but it is not minimal: AB alone (and BD alone) already determines everything. So ABD is NOT a candidate key, which is what the stem asks.
C — Wrong. (BD)+ = {A, B, C, D} (D → A gives A, then AB → C gives C). B+ = {B} and D+ = {A, D} are not keys, so BD is a candidate key. It does not fit the stem.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Using attribute closure, a set of attributes X is a superkey of relation R exactly when
opts: X+ contains every attribute of R
X appears on the left side of some FD in F
More than one of the above
exp: X is a superkey when its closure X+ is the whole relation schema, because then X determines every attribute.
concept: The closure X+ lists every attribute that X determines. If X+ contains all attributes of R, then X decides every attribute, so two different tuples can never agree on X: X is a superkey. If, in addition, no proper subset of X has this property, X is a candidate key.
why: A — Correct. If X+ is the full set of attributes of R, X decides every attribute and therefore identifies each tuple uniquely: X is a superkey.

B — Wrong. Being the left side (determinant) of some FD does not make X a key. In EMP(EmpID, DeptNo, DeptName), DeptNo → DeptName has DeptNo on the left, but DeptNo does not determine EmpID, so it is not a superkey.
C — Wrong. X+ = X means X determines nothing beyond itself (only trivial FDs). That is not the superkey test; in that case X would be a superkey only if X were already the whole of R.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
R(A, B, C, D, G) has F = {A → B, BC → G, DG → A}. Consider the statements:
I. Every candidate key of R contains both C and D.
II. Attribute A belongs to every candidate key of R.
III. R has exactly three candidate keys.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The candidate keys are ACD, BCD and CDG: all contain C and D (I true), there are three (III true), and two of them do not contain A (II false).
concept: A systematic way to find all keys: (1) put every attribute that appears on no right side into a 'core'; it must be in every key. (2) If the core's closure is not the whole relation, add one attribute at a time, then two, and so on. (3) Keep only the minimal sets. Attributes in some key are prime; the rest are non-prime.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is false: BCD and CDG are candidate keys that do not contain A. So 'I and II only' is wrong.
B — Wrong. Statement II is false (BCD and CDG have no A), so this option is wrong.
C — Correct. I is true: C and D appear on no right side, so every key contains them. III is true: the keys are ACD, BCD and CDG. II is false. So the correct statements are I and III.
D — Wrong. Only option C names exactly the correct statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at the same time, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option C is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a relation R with FD set F, some attribute appears on the right-hand side of no non-trivial FD in F. Which statement about this attribute is true?
opts: It must be part of every candidate key of R
It is, by itself, always a candidate key of R
It is always a non-prime attribute
More than one of the above
exp: The closure algorithm can only add attributes that appear on some right side, so no set without this attribute can determine it; every key must therefore contain it.
concept: Two useful shortcuts for finding keys: (1) an attribute that appears on no right side (only on left sides, or in no FD at all) must be in every candidate key, because nothing else can produce it in a closure; (2) an attribute that appears only on right sides and never on a left side is in no candidate key, because it never helps to determine anything else. Attributes that appear on both sides need closure checks.
why: A — Correct. When computing any closure S+, new attributes come only from right sides of FDs. Since this attribute is on no right side, it is in S+ only if it was in S from the start. So every superkey, and hence every candidate key, must contain it.
B — Wrong. Not always. In R(A, B, C) with F = {B → C}, B is on no right side, but B+ = {B, C} misses A, so B alone is not a key; the only key is AB.
C — Wrong. It is the opposite: because it belongs to every candidate key, it is a prime attribute.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Counter-example for B and C: R(A, B, C), F = {B → C}. A and B are on no right side.
B+ = {B, C} ≠ {A, B, C}, so B alone is not a key (option B fails).
(AB)+ = {A, B, C} and A+ = {A}, B+ = {B, C}, so the only key is AB; A and B are prime (option C fails).
tip: Only on the left (or in no FD) → in every key. Only on the right → in no key. On both sides → check with closures.

opts: F covers G, but G does not cover F
G covers F, but F does not cover G
F does not cover G, and G does not cover F
More than one of the above
exp: Every FD of G follows from F and every FD of F follows from G, so F and G cover each other: they are equivalent. Each of A–C denies at least one of these covers.
concept: F covers G if every FD of G can be derived from F (G ⊆ F+). To test an FD X → Y of G, compute X+ using F and check that Y ⊆ X+. Two FD sets are equivalent when F covers G AND G covers F; then F+ = G+, so they describe exactly the same constraints.
why: A — Wrong. The first half is true (F covers G), but the second half is false: G also covers F. Under G, A+ = {A, B, C} gives A → B and AB → C, and D+ = {A, B, C, D, E} gives D → AC and D → E.
B — Wrong. The first half is true (G covers F), but F also covers G. Under F, A+ = {A, B, C} gives A → BC and D+ = {A, B, C, D, E} gives D → AE. So 'F does not cover G' is false.
C — Wrong. Both covers hold, as the closures in the working show, so this statement is false.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. F covers G AND G covers F, so the two sets are equivalent (F+ = G+). That is why each of the one-sided statements A, B and C is false.
work:
Does F cover G? (closures computed with F)
  A+ = {A, B, C} ⊇ {B, C}, so A → BC follows from F.
  D+ = {A, B, C, D, E} ⊇ {A, E}, so D → AE follows from F.
  So F covers G.
Does G cover F? (closures computed with G)
  A+ = {A, B, C}, so A → B follows from G.
  (AB)+ = {A, B, C}, so AB → C follows from G.
  D+ = {A, B, C, D, E}, so D → AC and D → E follow from G.
  So G covers F.
Both directions hold, so F and G are equivalent (F+ = G+).

q: Which of the following is a minimal cover of F = {A → BC, B → C, AB → D}?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Split A → BC, reduce AB → D to A → D (B is extraneous because A → B), and drop A → C (it follows from A → B and B → C). The result is {A → B, B → C, A → D}.
concept: A minimal cover (Elmasri–Navathe) of F is an equivalent FD set in which (1) every right side has a single attribute, (2) no left side has an extraneous attribute, and (3) no FD is redundant. Steps: split the right sides; remove extraneous left-side attributes (A is extraneous in XA → Y if X+ already contains Y); then delete any FD that can be derived from the others. Korth's canonical cover is the same idea but combines FDs with the same left side (here {A → BD, B → C}).
why: A — Wrong. This set loses B → C: under {A → B, A → C, A → D}, B+ = {B}, so B → C cannot be derived. A cover must be equivalent to F, so this is wrong.
B — Wrong. This set is equivalent to F but is not minimal: in AB → D the attribute B is extraneous, because A alone gives B (A+ = {A, B, C, D}). AB → D must be reduced to A → D.

C — Correct. Split right sides, remove the extraneous B from AB → D, and drop the redundant A → C (it follows from A → B and B → C). What remains is {A → B, B → C, A → D}, which is equivalent to F and minimal.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Step 1 (single attribute on the right): A → B, A → C, B → C, AB → D.
Step 2 (extraneous left-side attributes in AB → D):
  A+ = {A, B, C, D} contains D, so B is extraneous; AB → D becomes A → D.
  B+ = {B, C} has no D, so A is not extraneous.
Step 3 (redundant FDs), set is now A → B, A → C, B → C, A → D:
  without A → C: A+ = {A, B, C, D} still has C, so A → C is redundant; remove it.
  without A → B: A+ = {A, D} has no B, so keep A → B.
  without B → C: B+ = {B} has no C, so keep B → C.
  without A → D: A+ = {A, B, C} has no D, so keep A → D.
Minimal cover = {A → B, B → C, A → D}.

q: F = {PQ → S, Q → T, T → P}. Which attribute on the left side of PQ → S is extraneous (can be removed without changing F+)?
opts: No attribute; PQ → S is already left-reduced
More than one of the above
exp: Q+ = {P, Q, S, T} already contains S, so P is extraneous and PQ → S can be replaced by Q → S. P+ = {P} does not contain S, so Q is needed.
concept: An attribute A on the left side of X → Y is extraneous if (X − A) → Y can already be derived from F. Test: compute (X − A)+ using the full F; if it contains Y, A is extraneous and can be deleted. Removing extraneous attributes is one step in finding a minimal (canonical) cover.
why: A — Correct. Q alone already reaches S: Q → T, T → P, and then PQ → S. So P adds nothing to the left side; it is extraneous, and PQ → S can be replaced by Q → S.
B — Wrong. Without Q the left side would be just P, and P+ = {P} does not contain S. So Q is needed and is not extraneous.
C — Wrong. P is extraneous, as Q+ = {P, Q, S, T} shows, so PQ → S is not left-reduced.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a property of a minimal cover G of an FD set F (as defined by Elmasri–Navathe)?
opts: Every FD in G has a single attribute on its right-hand side
No FD can be removed from G without changing G+
G is unique: every FD set F has exactly one minimal cover
More than one of the above
exp: A minimal cover need not be unique: F = {A → B, B → A, A → C, B → C} has two different minimal covers, {A → B, B → A, A → C} and {A → B, B → A, B → C}.
concept: A minimal cover of F is a set G that is equivalent to F (G+ = F+) and as small as possible: a single attribute on each right side, no extraneous attribute on any left side, and no redundant FD. Every F has at least one minimal cover, but it can have more than one, depending on the order in which the FDs are examined.
why: A — Wrong. This IS a property (Elmasri's first condition: one attribute on each right side), so it does not fit the stem.
B — Wrong. This IS a property: a minimal cover contains no redundant FD. It does not fit the stem.
C — Correct. This is NOT a property, so it fits the stem. One FD set can have several minimal covers; the working shows an example with two.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
F = {A → B, B → A, A → C, B → C}.
G1 = {A → B, B → A, A → C}: B+ = {A, B, C} gives B → C, so G1 ≡ F; removing any FD of G1 loses it.
G2 = {A → B, B → A, B → C}: A+ = {A, B, C} gives A → C, so G2 ≡ F; removing any FD of G2 loses it.
Both are minimal covers of F, so a minimal cover is not unique.

q: In the table STUDENT(Roll_no, Name, Branch, HOD) with key Roll_no, a newly started branch and its HOD cannot be recorded until at least one student joins that branch. This problem is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Being unable to add one fact (a new branch) without some other fact (a student) is an insertion anomaly.
concept: When facts about two different things (students and branches) are kept in one table, three anomalies appear. Insertion anomaly: a fact cannot be added without another fact (no student, so no row for the branch, because the key Roll_no cannot be NULL). Deletion anomaly: deleting one fact also removes another (deleting the last student of a branch loses the branch's HOD). Update anomaly: one fact is stored many times, so changing it needs many updates and a missed row causes inconsistency. Normalization removes these by splitting the table.
why: A — Correct. We cannot insert the branch fact on its own, because every row needs a Roll_no (the key cannot be NULL). This is an insertion anomaly.

B — Wrong. A deletion anomaly is when deleting a row removes some other useful fact, for example deleting the only student of a branch also deletes that branch's HOD. Here we are trying to add data, not delete it.

C — Wrong. An update anomaly is when one fact is stored in many rows, so changing it (say, a new HOD) needs many updates, and a missed row makes the data inconsistent. This question is about adding new data.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Can't ADD → insertion. Lose extra info on DELETE → deletion. Must CHANGE many rows → update.

q: STUDENT_BRANCH stores student facts and branch facts together (Branch → HOD, Office). Which of the following anomalies can occur in this table?
opts: Insertion anomaly: a new branch cannot be added until some student joins it
Deletion anomaly: deleting student 104 also loses the fact that Dr. Sinha heads ECE in Block B
Update anomaly: changing the HOD of CSE needs three rows to be changed, and missing one makes the data inconsistent
More than one of the above
exp: The table mixes two themes (students and branches), so all three anomalies occur; the cure is to split it into STUDENT(Roll_no, Name, Branch) and BRANCH(Branch, HOD, Office).
concept: Redundancy (the same fact stored many times) is the root of insertion, deletion and update anomalies. Here Branch → HOD, Office holds but Branch is not a key, so each branch's facts repeat for every student of that branch. Decomposing into STUDENT(Roll_no, Name, Branch) and BRANCH(Branch, HOD, Office) stores each branch fact once and removes all three anomalies (this is the step from 2NF to 3NF, removing the transitive dependency Roll_no → Branch → HOD).
