why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every row needs a Roll_no (the key cannot be NULL), so a branch that has no students cannot be stored.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Student 104 is the only ECE student, so deleting that row removes the only record of ECE's HOD and office.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 'Dr. Rao heads CSE' is stored three times. If only two rows are changed, the table shows two different HODs for CSE.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT_BRANCH (key: Roll_no)
Roll_no | Name  | Branch | HOD       | Office
101     | Ravi  | CSE    | Dr. Rao   | Block A
102     | Meena | CSE    | Dr. Rao   | Block A
103     | Arjun | CSE    | Dr. Rao   | Block A
104     | Priya | ECE    | Dr. Sinha | Block B

q: Which of the following is NOT a goal of normalization?
opts: Avoiding insertion, deletion and update anomalies
Making every query faster by reducing the number of joins
More than one of the above
exp: Normalization splits tables, so queries often need MORE joins; reducing joins to speed up reads is the aim of denormalization, not normalization.
concept: Normalization is the step-by-step decomposition of relations, guided by FDs and normal forms, to reduce redundancy and remove insertion, deletion and update anomalies, which improves data integrity. Its cost is that data is spread over more tables, so many queries need joins and may run slower. Denormalization makes the opposite trade-off: it adds controlled redundancy to speed up reads.
why: A — Wrong. Reducing redundancy is the main aim of normalization, so this does not fit the stem.
B — Wrong. Removing anomalies is exactly why we normalize, so this does not fit the stem.

C — Correct. This is NOT a goal of normalization, so it fits the stem. Normalized designs usually need more joins, which can make some queries slower; cutting joins for speed is what denormalization does.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In this STUDENT table, the Subjects column holds lists such as 'OS, CN'. What is the lowest normal form that this table fails to satisfy?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 1NF requires every value to be atomic (single and indivisible). A cell holding 'OS, CN' is multi-valued, so the table is not in 1NF.
concept: First normal form (1NF) says every attribute value must be atomic: one value per cell, with no lists, sets or repeating groups. A multi-valued attribute such as Subjects is fixed by giving each subject its own row or, better, by moving it to a separate table STUDENT_SUBJECT(Roll_no, Subject). Every higher normal form (2NF, 3NF, BCNF, ...) assumes 1NF, so a table that breaks 1NF fails all of them; that is why the question asks for the LOWEST form it fails.
why: A — Correct. The cell 'OS, CN' is not atomic, which breaks the basic rule of 1NF. 1NF is the lowest normal form, so it is the lowest one this table fails.
B — Wrong. 2NF is about partial dependencies on part of a composite key. The table does fail 2NF as well (every higher form needs 1NF), but 2NF is not the LOWEST form it fails.
C — Wrong. 3NF is about transitive dependencies. The table fails 3NF too, but 3NF is not the lowest normal form it fails; 1NF is.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT
Roll_no | Name  | Subjects
101     | Raj   | OS, CN
102     | Sohan | C, C++
103     | Vijay | Java

q: In normalization, a partial dependency means that
opts: a non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute
a non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset (part) of a candidate key
an attribute set determines one of its own attributes
More than one of the above
exp: A partial dependency is X → A where X is a proper part of a candidate key and A is non-prime; 2NF forbids it.
concept: Let (Roll_no, Course_id) be the key of RESULT(Roll_no, Course_id, Marks, Student_name). Marks needs the whole key, so it is fully functionally dependent on the key. Student_name needs only Roll_no, a part of the key: this is a partial dependency. A relation in 1NF with no partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on any candidate key is in 2NF. A partial dependency can exist only when some candidate key has two or more attributes.
why: A — Wrong. Non-prime → non-prime (for example Dept → DeptHead when the key is EmpID) is a transitive dependency, which 3NF removes. It is not a partial dependency.
B — Correct. This is the definition: a proper subset of a candidate key determines a non-prime attribute, for example Roll_no → Student_name when the key is (Roll_no, Course_id).
C — Wrong. A set determining one of its own attributes (for example {Roll_no, Name} → Name) is a trivial FD. It holds in every relation and causes no problem.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Partial = depends on PART of the key (2NF problem). Transitive = depends on a non-key attribute (3NF problem).

q: In the 3NF test, a non-trivial FD X → A whose left side X is NOT a superkey is still allowed when
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 3NF requires, for every non-trivial X → A, that X is a superkey or A is prime. So when X is not a superkey, the FD is allowed only if A is prime.
concept: Definition (Elmasri–Navathe, Korth): R is in 3NF if for every non-trivial FD X → A in F+, either (a) X is a superkey of R, or (b) A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key). BCNF drops condition (b), so BCNF is stricter. Hence 3NF is violated whenever a non-prime attribute is decided by something that is not a superkey: a non-prime attribute, a part of a key, or a mixture.
why: A — Wrong. Even if X has only prime attributes, X → A breaks 3NF when A is non-prime. Example: key (Roll_no, Course_id) and Roll_no → Student_name; Roll_no is prime, but this partial dependency violates 2NF and therefore 3NF.

B — Correct. This is condition (b) of 3NF: X → A may stay when A is prime, even though X is not a superkey. Example: in R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B, the keys are AB and AC, and C → B is allowed in 3NF because B is prime.
C — Wrong. This is the opposite of the rule. When X is not a superkey and A is non-prime, X → A VIOLATES 3NF.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (notes): '3NF only forbids non-prime → non-prime'. The real test is 'X is a superkey OR A is prime'. A mixed left side such as BC → D (B prime, C and D non-prime) also breaks 3NF.

q: A relation R is in Boyce–Codd normal form (BCNF) if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y that holds on R,
opts: X is a superkey of R
More than one of the above
exp: BCNF requires the left side (determinant) of every non-trivial FD to be a superkey; unlike 3NF, it gives no exception for prime attributes.
concept: BCNF (Boyce–Codd normal form, sometimes called 3.5NF) is a stricter form of 3NF. 3NF allows X → A when X is a superkey OR A is prime; BCNF keeps only the first condition: every determinant must be a superkey. So every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but a 3NF relation with an FD such as C → B (B prime, C not a superkey) is not in BCNF.
why: A — Correct. This is the BCNF condition: the determinant of every non-trivial FD is a superkey, so it decides the whole tuple.
B — Wrong. 'Y is prime' is the extra escape clause that 3NF allows. BCNF removes this escape: even if Y is prime, X must be a superkey.

C — Wrong. In BCNF it does not matter whether X has prime or non-prime attributes; only whether X is a superkey. A left side made of prime attributes only (for example, part of a key) can still violate BCNF, and even 2NF.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: BCNF in one line: 'Every determinant is a superkey.'

q: In STUDENT(Roll_no, Name, Dept, HOD), Roll_no → Dept and Dept → HOD hold, and Dept does not determine Roll_no. The dependency Roll_no → HOD, obtained through Dept, is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Roll_no → HOD holds only through the non-key attribute Dept (Roll_no → Dept → HOD), so it is a transitive dependency, which 3NF removes.
concept: X → Z is a transitive dependency when it holds through a third set Y: X → Y and Y → Z, where Y is not a key (Y does not determine X) and Z is not in Y. 3NF does not allow any non-prime attribute to be transitively dependent on a candidate key. The cure is to move Y and Z to their own table: STUDENT(Roll_no, Name, Dept) and DEPT(Dept, HOD).
why: A — Wrong. A partial dependency is a dependency on PART of a composite key. Here the key Roll_no is a single attribute, so no partial dependency is possible.
B — Correct. Roll_no → Dept and Dept → HOD give Roll_no → HOD through the non-key attribute Dept. That is exactly a transitive dependency.

C — Wrong. A multivalued dependency X →→ Y means one X value is linked to a SET of Y values, independent of the other attributes. Here each student has exactly one HOD, so this is an ordinary FD reached through transitivity.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {AB → C, C → D}. What is the highest normal form of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The only key is AB; no part of it determines a non-prime attribute, so R is in 2NF, but C → D (C not a superkey, D non-prime) breaks 3NF.
concept: Procedure for the highest normal form: (1) find ALL candidate keys and split the attributes into prime and non-prime; (2) 2NF: no proper subset of a candidate key determines a non-prime attribute; (3) 3NF: for every non-trivial FD X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime; (4) BCNF: for every non-trivial FD X → A, X is a superkey. Stop at the first test that fails; the previous level is the answer (1NF is assumed because values are atomic).
why: A — Wrong. BCNF needs every determinant to be a superkey. C+ = {C, D} is not the whole relation, so C → D breaks BCNF.
B — Wrong. 3NF fails because of C → D: C is not a superkey and D is non-prime. This is the transitive dependency AB → C → D.

C — Correct. No part of the key AB determines a non-prime attribute (A+ = {A}, B+ = {B}), so R is in 2NF. The transitive dependency C → D stops it from reaching 3NF, so the highest normal form is 2NF.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
A and B are on no right side, so every key contains AB.
(AB)+ = {A, B, C, D}, so AB is the only candidate key.
Prime: A, B. Non-prime: C, D.
2NF: A+ = {A}, B+ = {B}; no part of the key gives a non-prime attribute, so 2NF holds.
3NF: C → D with C+ = {C, D} (C is not a superkey) and D non-prime, so 3NF fails.
Highest normal form = 2NF.

q: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {AB → CD, B → C}. What is the highest normal form of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: AB is the only candidate key, and B → C makes the non-prime attribute C depend on part of that key. R is not in 2NF, so its highest normal form is 1NF, which is not listed.
concept: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of any candidate key. When the key is composite (AB) and a part of it (B) alone decides a non-prime attribute (C), 2NF is violated and the relation stays at 1NF (values are assumed atomic). Fix: decompose into R1(B, C) and R2(A, B, D).
why: A — Wrong. 2NF fails: B → C is a partial dependency (B is a part of the key AB and C is non-prime).
B — Wrong. 3NF requires 2NF first; moreover B → C has a non-superkey left side and a non-prime right side. R is not in 3NF.
C — Wrong. BCNF fails: B is a determinant but not a superkey (B+ = {B, C}).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The only candidate key is AB and B → C is a partial dependency, so R is not even in 2NF. Its highest normal form is 1NF, which is not among A–C.
work:
A and B are on no right side, so every key contains AB.
(AB)+ = {A, B, C, D}, so AB is the only candidate key.
Prime: A, B. Non-prime: C, D.
2NF: B+ = {B, C}; B is a proper part of the key and gives the non-prime C, so B → C is a partial dependency.
So R is not in 2NF. Highest normal form = 1NF.

q: R(A, B, C) has F = {AB → C, C → B}. What is the highest normal form of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The candidate keys are AB and AC, so every attribute is prime and R is in 3NF; but C → B has a non-superkey left side, so R is not in BCNF.
concept: This is the classic '3NF but not BCNF' pattern: two overlapping candidate keys (AB and AC) and an FD C → B from a non-superkey into a prime attribute. 3NF allows it because B is prime; BCNF does not, because C is not a superkey. Korth's example is dept_advisor(s_ID, i_ID, dept_name) with i_ID → dept_name and (s_ID, dept_name) → i_ID. Decomposing such a relation into BCNF loses the dependency AB → C.
why: A — Wrong. R is in 2NF (all attributes are prime, so no non-prime attribute can depend partially), but it also passes the 3NF test, so 2NF is not the HIGHEST form.
B — Correct. Every attribute is prime (keys AB and AC), so every FD passes the 3NF test. But C → B has a left side that is not a superkey, so BCNF fails. Highest normal form = 3NF.
C — Wrong. BCNF fails because of C → B: C+ = {B, C} is not the whole relation, so C is not a superkey.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
A is on no right side, so every key contains A; A+ = {A}.
(AB)+ = {A, B, C} and (AC)+ = {A, B, C}, so the candidate keys are AB and AC.
Prime: A, B, C (all). Non-prime: none, so 2NF and 3NF hold.
BCNF: C → B with C+ = {B, C} (not a superkey), so BCNF fails.
Highest normal form = 3NF.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G) has F = {AB → CD, D → A, BC → E, E → G}. What is the highest normal form of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The keys are AB and BD (prime A, B, D). No part of a key determines a non-prime attribute, so R is in 2NF, but BC → E and E → G (non-superkey to non-prime) break 3NF.
concept: When several FDs are given, check each one with closures to decide 'superkey or not'. The 2NF test looks only at proper subsets of candidate keys. A left side such as BC, which mixes part of a key (B) with a non-prime attribute (C), is not a part of any key, so BC → E is a 3NF problem (transitive-type), not a 2NF problem.
why: A — Correct. Keys AB and BD; proper parts A+ = {A}, B+ = {B}, D+ = {A, D} give no non-prime attribute, so R is in 2NF. BC → E and E → G break 3NF. Highest normal form = 2NF.
B — Wrong. 3NF fails: BC → E has (BC)+ = {B, C, E, G}, not a superkey, and E is non-prime; E → G has the same problem.
C — Wrong. BCNF fails already at D → A (D is not a superkey), besides the 3NF violations.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G) has F = {AB → C, BC → D, D → E, E → A, B → G}. What is the highest normal form of R?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The candidate keys are AB, BC, BD and BE, so G is the only non-prime attribute. B → G makes G depend on a part of a key, so R is not in 2NF: its highest normal form is 1NF.
concept: With many candidate keys, most attributes become prime, and only FDs whose right side is non-prime can break 2NF or 3NF. So after finding all keys, focus on those FDs. Here the only non-prime attribute is G, and B → G comes from a part of the keys, which is a partial dependency.
why: A — Wrong. 3NF fails: B → G has a non-superkey left side (B+ = {B, G}) and a non-prime right side.
B — Wrong. 2NF fails: B is a proper part of the candidate key AB (and of BC, BD, BE), and B alone decides the non-prime attribute G. That is a partial dependency.

C — Correct. Keys are AB, BC, BD, BE; the only non-prime attribute is G, and B → G is a partial dependency. So R is not in 2NF, and the highest normal form is 1NF. (D → E and E → A are harmless for 2NF/3NF because E and A are prime.)
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: ORDER_ITEM(OrderID, ProductID, Qty, ProductName, UnitPrice) has key (OrderID, ProductID). The only FDs are (OrderID, ProductID) → Qty and ProductID → ProductName, UnitPrice. Why is ORDER_ITEM NOT in 2NF?
opts: Qty depends on the whole key (OrderID, ProductID)
ProductName and UnitPrice depend on ProductID alone, which is only a part of the key
UnitPrice depends on ProductName, a non-key attribute
More than one of the above
exp: ProductID → ProductName, UnitPrice is a partial dependency (non-prime attributes depend on part of the composite key), and that breaks 2NF.
concept: 2NF removes partial dependencies. Here product details depend on ProductID alone, so they repeat in every order line for that product. Fix: decompose into PRODUCT(ProductID, ProductName, UnitPrice) and ORDER_ITEM(OrderID, ProductID, Qty). Now each product's name and price are stored once, and Qty stays with the full key.
why: A — Wrong. Qty depending on the WHOLE key is a full functional dependency, which is exactly what 2NF wants. It does not cause the violation.
B — Correct. ProductID is a proper part of the key, and it alone determines the non-prime attributes ProductName and UnitPrice. This partial dependency is why the table is not in 2NF.

C — Wrong. No FD ProductName → UnitPrice is given, and it does not follow from the given FDs (ProductName+ = {ProductName}). Even if it held, a non-key → non-key dependency would be a 3NF (transitive) problem, not the reason for failing 2NF.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Key: (OrderID, ProductID). Prime: OrderID, ProductID. Non-prime: Qty, ProductName, UnitPrice.
ProductID+ = {ProductID, ProductName, UnitPrice}: a proper part of the key gives non-prime attributes, so this is a partial dependency.
OrderID+ = {OrderID}.
Hence ORDER_ITEM is not in 2NF (its highest normal form is 1NF).

q:
R(A, B, C, D) has F = {AB → CD, D → A}. Consider the statements:
I. R is in 3NF.
II. R is in BCNF.
III. The FD D → A violates BCNF.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The keys are AB and BD, so A is prime. D → A is allowed in 3NF (A is prime) but breaks BCNF (D is not a superkey). So I and III are true, II is false.
concept: A relation can be in 3NF but not in BCNF when some FD goes from a non-superkey into a prime attribute (here D → A, where A is part of the key AB). 3NF tolerates this; BCNF does not. Such cases need overlapping candidate keys (AB and BD share B).
why: A — Wrong. II is false: D → A has a left side that is not a superkey (D+ = {A, D}), so R is not in BCNF.

B — Correct. I is true: the keys are AB and BD; the only non-prime attribute C is determined only through superkeys, and D → A goes into the prime attribute A, which 3NF allows. III is true: D is not a superkey, so D → A breaks BCNF. II is false.
C — Wrong. III is true, but I is also true, so 'III only' leaves out a correct statement.
D — Wrong. Only option B names exactly the correct statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at the same time, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option B is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following kinds of relation is always in BCNF?
opts: Any relation with exactly two attributes
Any relation in which every attribute is prime
Any relation that has no non-trivial functional dependency (an 'all-key' relation)
More than one of the above
exp: A two-attribute relation and a relation with no non-trivial FDs are always in BCNF; 'all attributes prime' guarantees only 3NF.
concept: Useful facts: (1) every relation with only two attributes is in BCNF; (2) a relation with no non-trivial FDs (all attributes together form the only key) is in BCNF, because BCNF only restricts non-trivial FDs; (3) if every attribute is prime, the relation is at least in 3NF, but not necessarily in BCNF; (4) if every candidate key has a single attribute, the relation is at least in 2NF.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. With attributes A and B, the only possible non-trivial FDs are A → B and B → A. If A → B holds, A determines both attributes, so A is a superkey; the same holds for B → A. So every determinant is a superkey.
B — Wrong. 'Every attribute prime' guarantees only 3NF. Example: R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B has keys AB and AC (all attributes prime), but C → B breaks BCNF because C is not a superkey.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. BCNF only restricts non-trivial FDs. If there are none, nothing can violate BCNF; the whole attribute set is the only key.
D — Correct. A and C are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Two attributes: the possible FD sets are {}, {A → B}, {B → A}, {A → B, B → A}; in each case every determinant is a superkey, so BCNF (checked by the toolkit).
All prime but not BCNF: R(A, B, C), F = {AB → C, C → B}: keys AB and AC; C+ = {B, C} is not all of R, so C → B breaks BCNF (the relation is 3NF only).
No non-trivial FD: there is nothing to test, so the relation is in BCNF.
tip: Two attributes → always BCNF. All attributes prime → at least 3NF (not necessarily BCNF).

q:
Assume every relation is in 1NF. Consider the statements:
I. If every attribute of R is prime, R is at least in 3NF.
II. If every candidate key of R has only one attribute, R is at least in 2NF.
III. If every candidate key of R has only one attribute, R is at least in 3NF.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are standard facts; III is false because single-attribute keys do not prevent transitive dependencies (R(A, B, C) with A → B, B → C is only in 2NF).
concept: Two shortcuts from the notes are correct: all attributes prime ⇒ at least 3NF (the 3NF condition 'X is a superkey or A is prime' is always met), and only single-attribute candidate keys ⇒ at least 2NF (a partial dependency needs a composite key). But single-attribute keys do not stop a non-prime attribute from depending on another non-prime attribute, so they do not guarantee 3NF.
why: A — Correct. I is true: every right-side attribute is prime, so each FD passes the 3NF test. II is true: a single-attribute key has no proper non-empty subset, so no partial dependency can exist. III is false (see the counter-example). So the correct set is I and II.
B — Wrong. III is false. Counter-example: R(A, B, C) with A → B and B → C has the single key A, but B → C is a transitive dependency, so R is only in 2NF.
C — Wrong. III is false, as the counter-example R(A, B, C) with A → B, B → C shows.
D — Wrong. Only option A names exactly the correct statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at the same time, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option A is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Check III with R(A, B, C), F = {A → B, B → C}:
A+ = {A, B, C}, B+ = {B, C}, C+ = {C}
A is the only candidate key (a single attribute).
B → C: B is not a superkey and C is non-prime, so 3NF fails; R is in 2NF only. So III is false.
I and II: also checked by brute force on 20 000 random FD sets over 4 attributes (verify/w5_checks.py), with no counter-example.

q: Which of the following statements about decomposition algorithms is correct?
opts: The 3NF synthesis algorithm always gives a lossless-join decomposition
The 3NF synthesis algorithm always gives a dependency-preserving decomposition
The BCNF decomposition algorithm always gives a dependency-preserving decomposition
More than one of the above
exp: 3NF synthesis guarantees both a lossless join and dependency preservation; BCNF decomposition guarantees a lossless join but not dependency preservation.
concept: Design trade-off: we can always reach 3NF with a decomposition that is both lossless and dependency preserving, but reaching BCNF sometimes forces us to lose a dependency (checking it would then need a join). That is why 3NF is generally considered adequate for practical RDBMS design, and BCNF is chosen when no needed FD is lost.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The synthesis algorithm makes one relation per FD of a canonical cover and adds a relation containing a candidate key if none already has one; this guarantees a lossless join.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each FD of the canonical cover lies completely inside one of the new relations, so every dependency is preserved.
C — Wrong. BCNF decomposition is always lossless but NOT always dependency preserving. Example: R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B; the BCNF split (B, C), (A, C) loses AB → C.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Example for C: R(A, B, C), F = {AB → C, C → B}. BCNF split: R1(B, C), R2(A, C).
R1 ∩ R2 = {C}, C+ = {B, C} ⊇ R1, so the split is lossless.
Projected FDs: C → B on R1; no non-trivial FD on R2. AB → C cannot be derived from them, so it is NOT preserved.
tip: 3NF: lossless + dependency preserving, always. BCNF: lossless always, dependency preserving not always.

q: A relation is in BCNF. Which kind of redundancy can it still have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: BCNF removes all redundancy that comes from FDs, but redundancy caused by independent multi-valued facts (MVDs) can remain; 4NF removes it.
concept: BCNF is free only from redundancy caused by functional dependencies. Example: TEACH(Course, Teacher, Book), where a course has several teachers and several books chosen independently. The table has no non-trivial FD, so it is in BCNF, yet every teacher is repeated with every book. This MVD-based redundancy is removed by 4NF, by splitting into (Course, Teacher) and (Course, Book).
why: A — Wrong. Partial dependencies are removed already at 2NF, so a BCNF relation cannot have them.
B — Wrong. Transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes are removed at 3NF, so a BCNF relation cannot have them.
C — Correct. BCNF says nothing about multivalued dependencies. Independent multi-valued facts stored together still repeat data; 4NF handles this.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (notes): 'BCNF is free from redundancy'. Correct: BCNF is free only from FD-based redundancy; MVD redundancy needs 4NF.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true?
opts: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
Every relation in a relational database is at least in 1NF
More than one of the above
exp: Normal forms are nested (BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF), but 3NF does not imply BCNF: R(A, B, C) with AB → C, C → B is in 3NF but not in BCNF.
concept: The normal forms form a chain: 5NF ⊂ 4NF ⊂ BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF. A relation in a higher form automatically satisfies every lower form, but not the other way round. In the relational model every relation is in 1NF by definition, because every value must be atomic.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true (BCNF is stricter than 3NF), so it does not fit the stem.

B — Correct. This statement is NOT true, so it fits the stem. A 3NF relation may have an FD from a non-superkey into a prime attribute (for example C → B in R(A, B, C) with AB → C), which BCNF forbids.
C — Wrong. This statement is true: the relational model requires atomic values, so every relation is at least in 1NF. It does not fit the stem.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {AB → C, C → D, D → E}. Which of the following decompositions of R is lossy?
opts: R1(A, B, C), R2(C, D, E)
R1(A, B, C, D), R2(D, E)
R1(A, B, D), R2(C, D, E)
More than one of the above
exp: In option C the common attribute D determines only {D, E}, which is neither R1 nor R2, so the join is lossy; in A and B the common attribute is a key of R2.
concept: Binary lossless-join test (Korth, Elmasri–Navathe): a decomposition of R into R1 and R2 (with R1 ∪ R2 = R) is lossless if and only if (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2 is in F+. In words: the common attributes must form a superkey of at least one of the two parts.
why: A — Wrong. The common attribute is C, and C+ = {C, D, E} contains all of R2, so C is a key of R2: the decomposition is lossless.
B — Wrong. The common attribute is D, and D+ = {D, E} contains all of R2, so D is a key of R2: lossless.
C — Correct. The common attribute is D, but D+ = {D, E} contains neither R1 = {A, B, D} nor R2 = {C, D, E} (C is missing). The test fails, so this decomposition is lossy.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Option A: R1 ∩ R2 = {C}; C+ = {C, D, E} ⊇ R2, so lossless.
Option B: R1 ∩ R2 = {D}; D+ = {D, E} ⊇ R2, so lossless.
Option C: R1 ∩ R2 = {D}; D+ = {D, E}, which contains neither {A, B, D} nor {C, D, E}, so lossy.
(The tableau/chase test in verify/w5_checks.py gives the same three results.)

q: R(A, B, C) is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). Which FD, if it holds on R, is enough to make this decomposition lossless?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The common attribute is B; the split is lossless when B is a key of R1 (B → A) or of R2 (B → C). A → B does not help.
concept: The notes give R(Student, Course, Instructor) → (Student, Course), (Course, Instructor) as lossless without any condition. That is incomplete. Using FDs, the split is lossless only if the common attribute Course is a key of one part, that is, Course → Instructor (each course has one instructor) or Course → Student. If a course has many students AND many instructors, the join pairs every student of that course with every instructor of that course, so it creates spurious (Student, Instructor) pairs unless every such pair really is in R (that special case is the multivalued dependency Course →→ Instructor, studied in 4NF).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The common attribute is B; B → A makes B a key of R1(A, B), so the test (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 passes.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. B → C makes B a key of R2(B, C), so the test (R1 ∩ R2) → R2 passes.

C — Wrong. A → B says nothing about what B determines, so B still need not be a key of either part. Counter-example: the rows (1, x, p) and (2, x, q) satisfy A → B, but the join of their projections has 4 rows, 2 of them spurious.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
R1 ∩ R2 = {B}.
With B → A: B+ = {A, B} ⊇ R1, so lossless.
With B → C: B+ = {B, C} ⊇ R2, so lossless.
With A → B only: B+ = {B}, so the test fails.
Instance (A, B, C) = (1, x, p), (2, x, q): π_AB = {(1, x), (2, x)}, π_BC = {(x, p), (x, q)}; the join has 4 rows (1, x, p), (1, x, q), (2, x, p), (2, x, q), so 2 rows are spurious.
tip: Common mistake (notes): a split is not lossless just because the parts share a column. With FDs, the shared column must be a key of one part (for example Course → Instructor).

q: Which statement about a lossy decomposition is NOT correct?
opts: Joining the decomposed relations gives back fewer tuples than the original relation
Joining the decomposed relations can produce extra (spurious) tuples
From the joined result we cannot tell which tuples were in the original relation
More than one of the above
exp: Projection followed by natural join never loses an original tuple; a lossy decomposition ADDS spurious tuples. So 'fewer tuples' is the incorrect statement.
concept: For any decomposition of R into R1 and R2, R ⊆ π_R1(R) ⋈ π_R2(R): the join never loses an original tuple. If the decomposition is lossy, the join contains extra, wrong tuples called spurious tuples. 'Loss' means loss of information (we can no longer tell which tuples are real), not loss of rows. A natural join of the projections does not create NULLs either.
why: A — Correct. This statement is NOT correct, so it fits the stem. Every original tuple comes back after projecting and joining (R ⊆ R1 ⋈ R2 always). A lossy join gives MORE tuples, never fewer.
B — Wrong. This statement is correct (the extra tuples are called spurious tuples), so it does not fit the stem.

C — Wrong. This statement is correct: real and spurious tuples look alike, so information is lost even though the row count grows. That is why the decomposition is called 'lossy'. It does not fit the stem.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (notes): 'a lossy join loses rows or creates duplicates/NULLs'. Correct: it creates EXTRA (spurious) rows.

q: R is decomposed into R1 = π_A,B(R) and R2 = π_B,C(R). How many tuples are there in R1 ⋈ R2 (natural join)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Grouping on B: B = x gives 2 × 2 = 4 tuples, B = y gives 2 × 1 = 2, B = z gives 1, so the join has 7 tuples (5 original + 2 spurious).
concept: To find the size of a natural join of projections, group by the common attribute: for each value b of B, the join has (number of A values with b) × (number of C values with b) tuples. Projection removes duplicate rows (set semantics), so (y, r) appears only once in R2. Tuples that are in the join but not in R are spurious; their presence proves that the decomposition is lossy.
why: A — Wrong. 5 would be right only for a lossless decomposition. Here B is not a key of either part (x goes with A = 1, 2 and with C = p, q), so the join gives extra tuples.
B — Wrong. 6 counts only one spurious tuple. For B = x, both (1, x, q) and (2, x, p) are spurious.
C — Wrong. 20 = 5 × 4 is the size of the Cartesian product R1 × R2. The natural join keeps only pairs with equal B values.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. R1 ⋈ R2 has 7 tuples: the 5 original tuples plus 2 spurious tuples, (1, x, q) and (2, x, p). 7 is not listed.
code:
R
A | B | C
1 | x | p
2 | x | q
3 | y | r
4 | y | r
5 | z | s

R1 = π_A,B(R)
R2 = π_B,C(R)
work:
R1 = π_A,B(R) = {(1, x), (2, x), (3, y), (4, y), (5, z)}: 5 tuples.
R2 = π_B,C(R) = {(x, p), (x, q), (y, r), (z, s)}: 4 tuples (the duplicate (y, r) is kept once).
Join on B:
  B = x: A ∈ {1, 2}, C ∈ {p, q}: 2 × 2 = 4 tuples
  B = y: A ∈ {3, 4}, C ∈ {r}: 2 × 1 = 2 tuples
  B = z: A ∈ {5}, C ∈ {s}: 1 × 1 = 1 tuple
Total = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 tuples = 5 original + 2 spurious ((1, x, q) and (2, x, p)).

q: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → A, A → D, D → E, E → D}. It is decomposed into R1(A, B), R2(B, C), R3(A, D) and R4(C, E). Which FDs of F are NOT preserved by this decomposition?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: D → E and E → D are lost: D and E are never together in one part, and neither can reach the other through the parts. C → A is still preserved through C → B (in R2) and B → A (in R1).
concept: A decomposition is dependency preserving if the FDs that hold inside the separate parts (the projections of F+) together imply every FD of F; then each FD can be checked inside single tables without joins. An FD whose attributes all lie in one part is clearly preserved. For the others use Korth's test: start with result = X and keep adding (result ∩ Ri)+ ∩ Ri for each part Ri; X → Y is preserved if Y ends up inside result.
why: A — Wrong. C → A IS preserved: C → B holds inside R2 and B → A holds inside R1, so C → A follows. Also D → E and E → D are lost, so 'C → A only' is wrong on both counts.

B — Correct. D appears only in R3(A, D), where D determines nothing new, and E appears only in R4(C, E), where E determines nothing new. So neither D → E nor E → D can be checked in the parts: both are lost.
C — Wrong. A → D is preserved directly, because A and D are both in R3. And D → E, E → D are lost, so this option is wrong.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
FDs inside one part: A → B (R1), B → C (R2), A → D (R3) are preserved directly.
C → A (Korth's test): result = {C}; via R2: ({C})+ ∩ {B, C} = {B, C}; via R1: ({B})+ ∩ {A, B} = {A, B}; result = {A, B, C} contains A, so preserved.
D → E: result = {D}; via R3: ({D})+ ∩ {A, D} = {D}; no other part contains D; result stays {D}, so NOT preserved (D+ = {D, E}, but E is never reached through the parts).
E → D: result = {E}; via R4: ({E})+ ∩ {C, E} = {E}; result stays {E}, so NOT preserved.
Lost FDs: D → E and E → D.

q: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. Which decomposition is BOTH lossless-join and dependency preserving?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Splitting along the chain keeps each FD inside one part, and each shared attribute is a key of the next part, so (A, B), (B, C), (C, D) is lossless and dependency preserving.
concept: A good decomposition must be lossless (no spurious tuples) and, if possible, dependency preserving (each FD checkable in one table). For a chain A → B → C → D, the split (A, B), (B, C), (C, D) keeps every FD inside one table, and every shared attribute is a key of a neighbouring part, so the joins are lossless. Splitting everything around the key A is also lossless, but it hides B → C and C → D.
why: A — Correct. Every FD lies inside one part (A → B in R1, B → C in R2, C → D in R3), so all are preserved. Lossless: C is a key of R3, so R2 ⋈ R3 = (B, C, D) is lossless; then B is a key of (B, C, D), so joining with R1 is lossless too.
B — Wrong. This decomposition is lossless (A is a key of every part), but B → C and C → D are lost: the parts give only A → B, A → C, A → D, from which B+ = {B} and C+ = {C}.
C — Wrong. R1 and R2 share no attribute, so their natural join is a Cartesian product: the decomposition is lossy. B → C is also lost.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Option A: R2 ∩ R3 = {C}, C+ = {C, D} ⊇ R3, so R2 ⋈ R3 = R23(B, C, D) is lossless;
  R1 ∩ R23 = {B}, B+ = {B, C, D} ⊇ R23, so lossless. Each FD lies in one part, so dependency preserving.
Option B: R1 ∩ R2 = {A}, A+ = {A, B, C, D} covers both parts, so lossless; but the projected FDs are only A → B, A → C, A → D, so B → C and C → D are NOT preserved.
Option C: R1 ∩ R2 = ∅, so the join is a Cartesian product: lossy. B → C (B in R1, C in R2) is NOT preserved.
(The chase test and Korth's preservation test in verify/w5_checks.py confirm all three.)

q: In STUDENT(Roll_no, Name, Marks), each roll number has exactly one name and one marks value, so Roll_no → {Name, Marks} holds, while Name and Marks do not determine each other. What kind of dependency is Roll_no → {Name, Marks}?
opts: A multivalued dependency and not a functional dependency, because Name and Marks do not determine each other
More than one of the above
exp: Each Roll_no has exactly ONE Name and ONE Marks, so this is an ordinary FD (the same as Roll_no → Name plus Roll_no → Marks). An MVD needs a SET of values for each Roll_no.
concept: An FD X → Y says each X value has exactly one Y value. A multivalued dependency (MVD) X →→ Y says each X value has a SET of Y values, and this set does not depend on the remaining attributes Z: if (x, y1, z1) and (x, y2, z2) are in the table, then (x, y1, z2) and (x, y2, z1) must also be there. By the replication rule every FD is also an MVD (each X value simply has a set of exactly one Y value); a genuine MVD that is not just an FD needs several Y values for the same X. Such MVDs are the basis of 4NF.
why: A — Wrong. This is the mistake in the notes. Roll_no → {Name, Marks} certainly IS a functional dependency (each Roll_no has one Name and one Marks), so 'not a functional dependency' is false. A genuine multivalued dependency X →→ Y needs one X value to be linked to a SET of several Y values, independent of the other attributes (for example, one course with several teachers and several books). Whether Name and Marks determine each other is irrelevant.
B — Wrong. A transitive dependency needs a middle attribute (X → Y → Z). Here Roll_no decides Name and Marks directly.

C — Correct. Roll_no → {Name, Marks} is a normal FD: the same Roll_no always has the same Name and the same Marks. By the decomposition rule it equals Roll_no → Name plus Roll_no → Marks. Whether Name and Marks depend on each other does not change its type.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake (notes): 'roll_no → {name, marks} is a multivalued dependency'. It is an ordinary FD; 'multivalued' means one X value has MANY Y values.

q: Which of the following dependencies is satisfied by this instance of TEACH?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DBMS has two teachers, so Course → Teacher fails; but for DBMS every teacher appears with every book, so Course →→ Teacher and Course →→ Book both hold.
concept: X →→ Y (X multidetermines Y) holds in R if, whenever two tuples agree on X, the tuple that takes Y from the first and the remaining attributes Z from the second is also in R. Informally: for each X value, its set of Y values and its set of Z values are independent, so every combination appears. MVDs come in pairs: X →→ Y implies X →→ Z (complementation rule). An FD X → Y is the special case where each set of Y values has only one element.
why: A — Wrong. DBMS appears with two teachers (Rao and Jha), so one Course value has two Teacher values: Course → Teacher is violated.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. For DBMS the teachers are {Rao, Jha} and the books are {Korth, Navathe}, and all 2 × 2 = 4 combinations are present; OS has only one row. So a course's set of teachers does not depend on the book: Course →→ Teacher holds.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. By the complementation rule, Course →→ Teacher gives Course →→ Book (Book is the rest of the attributes). The same four DBMS combinations show it directly.
D — Correct. B and C are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
TEACH
Course | Teacher | Book
DBMS   | Rao     | Korth
DBMS   | Rao     | Navathe
DBMS   | Jha     | Korth
DBMS   | Jha     | Navathe
OS     | Rao     | Galvin
work:
Course → Teacher: DBMS appears with Rao and with Jha, so it is violated.
Course →→ Teacher: for rows with the same Course, swapping their Book values must give rows that exist.
  DBMS: teachers {Rao, Jha} × books {Korth, Navathe} = 4 combinations; all 4 rows are present.
  OS: only one row, nothing to check.
  So Course →→ Teacher holds.
Course →→ Book: the same 4 combinations (complementation), so it holds.
For contrast, Teacher →→ Book fails: (DBMS, Rao, Korth) and (OS, Rao, Galvin) agree on Rao, but the swapped row (OS, Rao, Korth) is missing.

q:
Consider the statements:
I. Every relation in 4NF is also in BCNF.
II. An MVD X →→ Y on R is trivial if Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y = R.
III. Every functional dependency X → Y is also a multivalued dependency X →→ Y.
Which statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are standard facts: 4NF ⊂ BCNF, the definition of a trivial MVD, and the replication rule (every FD is an MVD).
concept: A relation R is in 4NF if, for every non-trivial MVD X →→ Y that holds on R, X is a superkey of R. An MVD is trivial if Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y = R (it then holds in every relation). Because every FD is also an MVD, 4NF is stricter than BCNF (4NF ⊂ BCNF). To reach 4NF, a relation with a non-trivial MVD X →→ Y (X not a superkey) is split into (X ∪ Y) and (X ∪ (R − Y)).
why: A — Wrong. Statement III is also true, so 'I and II only' leaves out a correct statement.
B — Wrong. Statement I is also true, so 'II and III only' leaves out a correct statement.

C — Correct. I is true: 4NF needs every non-trivial MVD to have a superkey on the left; since every FD is an MVD, every non-trivial FD also has a superkey on the left, which is BCNF. II is the textbook definition of a trivial MVD. III is the replication rule: if each X value has one Y value, that single value trivially combines with every value of the other attributes.
D — Wrong. Only option C names exactly the correct statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at the same time, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option C is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: TEACH(Course, Teacher, Book) has no non-trivial functional dependencies, so its only key is (Course, Teacher, Book). The teachers and the books of a course are independent of each other, so Course →→ Teacher holds. What is the highest normal form of TEACH?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: TEACH has no non-trivial FD, so it is in BCNF; but the non-trivial MVD Course →→ Teacher has a non-superkey left side, so it is not in 4NF. The highest normal form is BCNF, which is not listed.
concept: An all-key relation (no non-trivial FDs) is automatically in BCNF, but it can still contain independent multi-valued facts. Such a relation fails 4NF, and its redundancy (each teacher repeated with each book) is removed by splitting into CT(Course, Teacher) and CB(Course, Book). This is the standard example showing that BCNF does not remove all redundancy.
why: A — Wrong. TEACH is in 3NF, but 3NF is not the HIGHEST form it reaches: with no non-trivial FD it also satisfies BCNF.
B — Wrong. 4NF fails: Course →→ Teacher is a non-trivial MVD (Teacher is not inside Course, and Course ∪ Teacher is not all of TEACH), and Course is not a superkey.
C — Wrong. 5NF requires 4NF first (every 5NF relation is in 4NF), and TEACH is not in 4NF.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.

E — Correct. TEACH is in BCNF (it has no non-trivial FD) but not in 4NF, because the non-trivial MVD Course →→ Teacher has a left side (Course) that is not a superkey. Its highest normal form is BCNF, which is not among A–C.

q: Fifth normal form (5NF), also called project–join normal form (PJNF), is defined using which kind of dependency?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 5NF (PJNF) is based on join dependencies: every non-trivial join dependency must be implied by the candidate keys.
concept: A join dependency (JD) *(R1, R2, ..., Rn) on R says that R can always be rebuilt, with no spurious tuples, by joining its projections on R1, ..., Rn (a lossless n-way decomposition). An MVD is a JD with only two parts. R is in 5NF (PJNF) if every non-trivial JD on R is implied by its candidate keys. 5NF handles tables that can be split losslessly into three or more parts but not into two.
why: A — Wrong. Multivalued dependencies are the basis of 4NF. An MVD is only the two-part special case of a join dependency, so 5NF uses the more general idea.
B — Correct. 5NF requires every non-trivial join dependency to be implied by the candidate keys. A join dependency *(R1, ..., Rn) means R always equals the join of its projections on R1, ..., Rn.
C — Wrong. Transitive dependencies are the concern of 3NF.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 4NF ↔ multivalued dependency; 5NF ↔ join dependency.

q: Which of the following statements about denormalization is NOT correct?
opts: It removes all redundancy from the database
It is usually done to make frequent read queries faster by reducing joins
It can bring back update anomalies, so extra care (for example triggers) is needed to keep the copies consistent
More than one of the above
exp: Denormalization deliberately ADDS controlled redundancy to speed up reads; it does not remove redundancy.
concept: Denormalization is the deliberate step of combining tables or storing duplicate/derived data in a normalized design to improve read performance. It trades extra storage and the risk of update anomalies for fewer joins. It is common in reporting systems and data warehouses (star schemas). It is a conscious choice made after normalization, not a replacement for it.
why: A — Correct. This statement is NOT correct, so it fits the stem. Denormalization does the opposite: it deliberately ADDS controlled redundancy (for example, storing the customer name inside ORDERS).
B — Wrong. This statement is correct, so it does not fit the stem: fewer joins make frequent reads, reports and warehouse queries faster.
C — Wrong. This statement is correct, so it does not fit the stem: duplicated data must be kept in step, so update anomalies can return; designers use triggers or application code to manage this.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G) has F = {A → B, BG → D, CD → E, D → A, E → G}. How many candidate keys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: C is on no right side, so it is in every key. CD is a key. A key without D must produce D through BG → D, so it needs A or B (A → B) and E or G (E → G): ACE, ACG, BCE, BCG. Total 5 candidate keys.
concept: To find all candidate keys: (1) every attribute that appears on no right-hand side must be in every key; (2) add as few attributes as possible to this core and test each set with a closure; (3) a set is a candidate key only if its closure is all of R and no smaller part of it is a key. Once a small key such as CD is found, a bigger set that contains it (like ACD) is only a superkey, not a candidate key.
why: A — Wrong. 4 counts only the four 3-attribute keys that follow the pattern C + (A or B) + (E or G), and forgets the 2-attribute key CD.
B — Wrong. 6 is too many. Sets such as ACD or CDE are superkeys but not minimal (they contain the key CD), and a set such as ABC is not a superkey at all ((ABC)+ = {A, B, C}).
C — Correct. The candidate keys are CD, ACE, ACG, BCE and BCG.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
C is on no right-hand side → C is in every key; (C)+ = {C}.
Two-attribute sets containing C:
(CD)+: CD → E adds E; D → A adds A; E → G adds G; A → B adds B → {A, B, C, D, E, G} → key.
(AC)+ = {A, B, C}; (BC)+ = {B, C}; (CE)+ = {C, E, G}; (CG)+ = {C, G} → not keys.
Any other key must not contain D (else it would contain the key CD). The only FD that gives D is BG → D, so the key must produce B (from A or B) and G (from E or G):
(ACE)+: A → B adds B; E → G adds G; BG → D adds D → all of R.
(ACG)+: A → B adds B; BG → D adds D; CD → E adds E → all of R.
(BCE)+: E → G adds G; BG → D adds D; D → A adds A → all of R.
(BCG)+: BG → D adds D; CD → E adds E; D → A adds A → all of R.
Each is minimal, because its 2-attribute subsets containing C are not keys.
Candidate keys: CD, ACE, ACG, BCE, BCG → 5. (Brute force over all 63 subsets in Python: 5.)
tip: Fix the 'never on the right' attributes first, then search by size: 2-attribute sets, then 3-attribute sets that do not contain a smaller key.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G) has F = {AD → BC, B → C, D → E}. R is decomposed into BCNF with the usual algorithm: whenever an FD X → Y of F violates BCNF in a relation Ri (X ⊆ Ri, X is not a superkey of Ri, and Y' = the attributes of Y that lie in Ri is not empty), Ri is replaced by X ∪ Y' and Ri − Y'. The FDs may be used in any order (here every order gives the same result). How many relations does the final BCNF decomposition contain?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The only key of R is ADG. Splitting on AD → BC, B → C and D → E gives BC, ABD, DE and ADG, and each of these is in BCNF, so there are 4 relations.
concept: BCNF decomposition: take an FD X → Y that holds on a relation Ri where X is not a superkey of Ri, and split Ri into (X ∪ Y), in which X determines every attribute, and (Ri − Y), which keeps X so the two parts can be joined back without spurious tuples. Repeat until every relation is in BCNF. After every split, check BOTH new relations again, using every FD that holds on them (including FDs implied by F). The result can depend on the order of the splits, so a question must fix the order or use an F where the order does not matter.
why: A — Wrong. 3 is what you get if you stop too early: after splitting on AD → BC and D → E you have ABCD, DE and ADG, but ABCD is still not in BCNF, because B → C holds in it and B is not a key of ABCD.
B — Correct. The final relations are BC, ABD, DE and ADG.
C — Wrong. 5 would need one more split, but all four relations are already in BCNF: BC has key B, ABD has key AD (its only FD is AD → B), DE has key D, and ADG has no non-trivial FD at all.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Key of R: A, D and G are on no right side; (ADG)+ = {A, B, C, D, E, G} → the only key is ADG.
Split 1: AD → BC in ABCDEG: (AD)+ = ABCDE, not a superkey → ABCD and ADEG.
Split 2: B → C in ABCD: (B)+ = BC, not a superkey of ABCD → BC and ABD.
Split 3: D → E in ADEG: (D)+ = DE, not a superkey of ADEG → DE and ADG.
Check: BC (key B; FD B → C) ✓; ABD (key AD; FD AD → B; (AB)+ ∩ ABD = AB, so nothing else) ✓; DE (key D) ✓; ADG (no non-trivial FD) ✓.
Result: BC, ABD, DE, ADG → 4 relations.
(Python: all 6 orders of the FDs give exactly these 4 relations; every relation passes a full BCNF test on the projection of F+; the decomposition is lossless.)
tip: After each BCNF split, test both parts again — the part that keeps the old key often still violates BCNF.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G, H) has F = {A → B, AB → C, C → D, A → D, E → G, G → H}. The 3NF synthesis algorithm is applied: find a minimal (canonical) cover, make one relation for each group of FDs with the same left side, and add one relation for a candidate key if no relation contains a key. How many relations are produced?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The minimal cover is {A → B, A → C, C → D, E → G, G → H}. Grouping by left side gives ABC, CD, EG and GH; the only key AE is in none of them, so AE is added: 5 relations.
concept: The 3NF synthesis (Bernstein) algorithm: (1) find a minimal cover — one attribute on each right side, no extraneous attribute on any left side, no redundant FD; (2) for each left side X, make one relation with X and everything X determines in the cover; (3) if no relation contains a candidate key, add one relation consisting of a candidate key; (4) remove any relation contained in another. The result is always in 3NF, lossless and dependency-preserving.
why: A — Correct. ABC, CD, EG, GH and the key relation AE.
B — Wrong. 4 forgets the key relation. ABC, CD, EG and GH do not contain the candidate key AE, so the algorithm adds AE; without it the join of the parts would not be lossless.
C — Wrong. 6 comes from making separate relations AB and AC instead of putting the FDs with the same left side (A → B and A → C) into one relation ABC.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Minimal cover:
AB → C: B is extraneous, because (A)+ = {A, B, C, D} already contains C → replace by A → C.
A → D is redundant: without it, (A)+ = {A, B, C, D} (A → C, C → D) still contains D → remove it.
Minimal cover = {A → B, A → C, C → D, E → G, G → H} (Python: this is the only minimal cover).
Group by left side: A → BC, C → D, E → G, G → H → relations ABC, CD, EG, GH.
Candidate key: A and E are on no right side; (AE)+ = {A, B, C, D, E, G, H} → the only key is AE.
No relation contains AE → add relation AE.
No relation is contained in another.
Result: ABC, CD, EG, GH, AE → 5 relations.
tip: 3NF synthesis = minimal cover → one table per left side → add a key table if none holds a key.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {A → D, C → A, D → E, E → A, E → C}. It is decomposed into R1(A, B, E), R2(A, C) and R3(C, D). Which FD of F is NOT preserved by this decomposition?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A, C, D and E all determine one another, and the parts link them in a chain E–A (R1), A–C (R2), C–D (R3). So A → D, E → C and D → E can all be derived from FDs inside the parts: every FD is preserved.
concept: An FD is preserved by a decomposition if it can be derived from the FDs that hold inside the separate parts (the projections of F+ on each part). An FD whose attributes are spread over several parts may still be preserved through a chain of FDs, one link in each part. Korth's test for X → Y: start with result = X; for each part Ri, add (result ∩ Ri)+ ∩ Ri; repeat until nothing changes. X → Y is preserved if Y ends up inside result.
why: A — Wrong. A → D is preserved, even though A and D are never in the same part: A → C holds in R2 (A → D → E → C) and C → D holds in R3 (C → A → D), so A → C → D is enforced through R2 and R3.
B — Wrong. E → C is preserved: E → A holds in R1 and A → C holds in R2, so E → A → C.
C — Wrong. D → E is preserved: D → C holds in R3 (D → E → C), C → A in R2 and A → E in R1 (A → D → E), so D → C → A → E.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All five FDs of F are preserved, so none of A–C is a lost FD; the decomposition is dependency-preserving (and also lossless).
work:
FDs that hold inside each part (projection of F+):
R1(A, B, E): A → E, E → A.  R2(A, C): A → C, C → A.  R3(C, D): C → D, D → C.
E → A (inside R1) and C → A (inside R2) are preserved directly.
A → D: result = {A}; R1: (A)+ ∩ ABE = {A, E} → {A, E}; R2: (A)+ ∩ AC = {A, C} → {A, C, E}; R3: (C)+ ∩ CD = {C, D} → {A, C, D, E} contains D → preserved.
D → E: result = {D}; R3: (D)+ ∩ CD = {C, D} → {C, D}; R2: (C)+ ∩ AC = {A, C} → {A, C, D}; R1: (A)+ ∩ ABE = {A, E} → {A, C, D, E} contains E → preserved.
E → C: result = {E}; R1: (E)+ ∩ ABE = {A, E} → {A, E}; R2: (A)+ ∩ AC = {A, C} → {A, C, E} contains C → preserved.
No FD is lost. (Python: Korth's test for every FD; the chase test also shows the decomposition is lossless.)
tip: Do not mark an FD as lost just because no single table holds all its attributes — always run the closure test across the parts.

q: R(A, B, C, D, E, G) has F = {AB → C, C → A, B → D, D → E, AE → G}. How many superkeys does R have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The candidate keys are AB and BC. Supersets of AB: 2^4 = 16; of BC: 2^4 = 16; of both (ABC): 2^3 = 8. Superkeys = 16 + 16 − 8 = 24.
concept: A superkey is any set of attributes whose closure is the whole relation, so every superset of a candidate key is a superkey. In a relation with n attributes, a key of k attributes has 2^(n − k) supersets (each of the other attributes is either in or out). For two candidate keys K1 and K2 use inclusion–exclusion: superkeys = 2^(n − |K1|) + 2^(n − |K2|) − 2^(n − |K1 ∪ K2|).
why: A — Wrong. 32 = 16 + 16 adds the supersets of AB and of BC but counts twice the 8 sets that contain both keys (all sets containing A, B and C).
B — Correct. 16 + 16 − 8 = 24 superkeys.

C — Wrong. 28 subtracts only 2^2 = 4 for the overlap, as if the keys had no common attribute (that formula is for keys like AB and CD). AB and BC share B, so their union ABC has 3 attributes and the overlap is 2^(6 − 3) = 8.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
B is on no right side → B is in every key. (B)+ = {B, D, E}.
(AB)+: AB → C adds C; B → D adds D; D → E adds E; AE → G adds G → all of R → key.
(BC)+: C → A adds A; B → D adds D; D → E adds E; AE → G adds G → all of R → key.
From B, D, E, G alone we can never get A or C ((BDEG)+ = {B, D, E, G}), so every key contains A or C → the candidate keys are exactly AB and BC.
Supersets of AB: C, D, E, G are free → 2^4 = 16.
Supersets of BC: A, D, E, G are free → 2^4 = 16.
Supersets of both = supersets of ABC: D, E, G are free → 2^3 = 8 (counted twice).
Superkeys = 16 + 16 − 8 = 24. (Brute force over all 63 subsets in Python: 24.)
tip: Two keys: add the supersets of each key, then subtract the supersets of their UNION.

q: A transaction has executed its final statement, but its changes have not yet been made permanent in the database. In which state is it?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After the last statement runs, the transaction enters the partially committed state; it becomes committed only after its changes are safely recorded.
concept: A transaction moves through states. Active: it is running its reads and writes. Partially committed: its final statement has run, but its output may still be only in main memory (RAM). Committed: the changes are safely recorded and will survive a failure. Failed: normal execution cannot continue. Aborted: it has been rolled back and the database is restored to its state before the transaction began.
why: A — Wrong. Active is the starting state, while the transaction is still executing its operations. Here the final statement has already run, so it has left the active state.

B — Correct. Partially committed means 'all statements done, but the commit is not yet complete'. The changes may still sit in the main-memory buffer, so a failure at this moment could still force an abort.
C — Wrong. Committed is reached only after the changes are safely recorded (for example, the commit log record is on stable storage). The stem says the changes are not yet permanent.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Partially committed = finished working, not yet finished saving.

q: In the simple read/write model of a transaction, what does the operation read(X) do?
opts: Writes the value of X from the transaction's buffer to the database on disk
Places an exclusive lock on X so that no other transaction can use it
Copies data item X from the database into a variable X in the transaction's main-memory buffer
More than one of the above
exp: read(X) brings the value of X from the database into a local variable of the transaction; write(X) does the opposite.
concept: A transaction works with the database through two basic operations. read(X) copies data item X from the database into a variable (also called X) in the main-memory buffer of that transaction. write(X) copies the value of the variable X from the transaction's buffer back to data item X in the database (the disk block may be written to disk at once or a little later). Calculations such as X := X - 50 happen on the local copy in memory.
why: A — Wrong. This describes write(X), which works in the opposite direction: from the transaction's buffer to the database.
B — Wrong. Locking is done by the concurrency-control manager through separate lock requests (lock-S, lock-X). read(X) itself only transfers data; it is not a lock operation.
C — Correct. read(X) moves the value from the database into the transaction's own buffer so that the transaction can use it in calculations.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: read = database to memory (variable); write = memory to database.

q: Which of the following state transitions is NOT allowed in the transaction state diagram of Silberschatz–Korth?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three transitions are allowed. A transition that is not allowed is, for example, Committed → Aborted or Aborted → Committed.
concept: The allowed arrows in the state diagram are: Active → Partially committed, Active → Failed, Partially committed → Committed, Partially committed → Failed, and Failed → Aborted. Committed and Aborted are final states (a transaction in either is said to be terminated). Once a transaction is committed it can never be aborted; its effect can only be reversed by running a new 'compensating' transaction. (Elmasri–Navathe draw a similar diagram without a separate aborted state: a failed transaction goes to a single 'terminated' state. That is why this question names Silberschatz–Korth.)
why: A — Wrong. This transition IS allowed: when the last statement finishes, an active transaction becomes partially committed. So it does not fit a NOT-allowed question.

B — Wrong. This transition IS allowed: a hardware or system failure while the changes are being written out can stop a partially committed transaction from committing, so it moves to the failed state.
C — Wrong. This transition IS allowed: a failed transaction is rolled back, and after the rollback it is in the aborted state.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is a forbidden transition, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three listed transitions are allowed. Forbidden ones include Committed → Aborted, Committed → Active and Aborted → Committed.
tip: Committed is a one-way door: a committed transaction can never be rolled back.

q: A transaction has entered the aborted state. According to the standard transaction model, which actions can the system then take?
opts: Restart the transaction as a new transaction, if it was aborted because of a hardware or software error not caused by its own logic
Kill the transaction, if it was aborted because of an internal logical error such as bad input
Mark the transaction as committed so that its partial changes are kept
More than one of the above
exp: After an abort, the system can either restart the transaction (for external errors) or kill it (for internal logical errors). It can never commit it.
concept: When a transaction fails, its changes are rolled back and it enters the aborted state. The system then has two choices. Restart: used when the abort was caused by something outside the transaction's own logic, such as a hardware or software failure; the restarted run is treated as a new transaction. Kill: used when the transaction itself is faulty, for example because of bad input or because the data it needs is not in the database.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The standard model (Silberschatz–Korth) says a transaction aborted because of a hardware or software error that is not caused by its own logic can be restarted; the restarted run counts as a new transaction.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. If the problem is inside the transaction itself (bad input, missing data, a logical error), restarting would just fail again, so the system kills it.
C — Wrong. An aborted transaction has already been rolled back. Aborted → Committed is not a possible transition, and keeping partial changes would break atomicity.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a state in the standard transaction state diagram?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The standard states are active, partially committed, failed, aborted and committed (plus terminated in some books). 'Suspended' is not one of them.
concept: Silberschatz–Korth list five transaction states: active, partially committed, failed, aborted and committed. Elmasri–Navathe also show a terminated state, which a transaction reaches after it commits or aborts. A transaction that is waiting for a lock is still in the active state; there is no separate 'suspended' state in the transaction state diagram.
why: A — Correct. 'Suspended' is not in the transaction state diagram (it sounds like an operating-system process state). A transaction waiting for a lock is still counted as active. So this option correctly names a NOT-state.
B — Wrong. Partially committed IS a standard state: the final statement has run but the commit is not yet complete. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Wrong. Failed IS a standard state: normal execution can no longer continue because of an error. So it does not fit a NOT question.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Remember the five: Active, Partially committed, Committed, Failed, Aborted (+ Terminated in Elmasri–Navathe).

q: Rs 500 is debited from account A, and then the system crashes before account B is credited. Which ACID property requires the DBMS to undo the debit?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Atomicity means 'all or nothing'. Since the transfer did not finish, its partial effect (the debit) must be undone.
concept: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability. Atomicity means either all operations of a transaction are reflected in the database or none are. If a transaction stops halfway (because of a crash or an error), the DBMS uses the log to undo the part that was done. In the bank example, money must not disappear: either both the debit and the credit happen, or neither happens.
why: A — Wrong. Isolation is about transactions running at the same time: each should behave as if it were running alone. The problem here is a crash in the middle of one transaction, not interference between transactions.

B — Wrong. Durability protects the changes of a COMMITTED transaction from being lost after a failure. This transfer never committed, so durability does not apply; in fact its changes must be removed, not kept.
C — Correct. Atomicity is the 'all-or-nothing' rule. The debit without the credit is a half-done transaction, so the debit must be rolled back.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Half-done work after a crash → Atomicity. Finished (committed) work after a crash → Durability.

q: A train-booking site shows 'Ticket booked' after the booking transaction commits. One second later the server loses power. Which ACID property guarantees that the booking is still there after the restart?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Durability guarantees that the changes of a committed transaction survive later system failures.
concept: Durability means that once a transaction has committed, its changes are permanent, even if the system crashes right after. The DBMS achieves this by writing log records (or the data itself) to stable, non-volatile storage before it reports success; after a crash, the recovery system redoes committed work from the log if needed.
why: A — Correct. The transaction had committed before the power failure, so durability requires that its effect (the booking) is not lost.

B — Wrong. Consistency means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state (rules such as 'seats booked ≤ seats available' stay true). It does not by itself protect committed data from crashes.
C — Wrong. Isolation deals with concurrent transactions not seeing each other's half-done work. A power failure is not a concurrency problem.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: According to the commonly used table of ACID responsibilities, which DBMS component ensures Isolation?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Isolation is ensured by the concurrency-control manager, using locking, timestamps or similar protocols.
concept: Isolation means that concurrent transactions should not interfere with each other; the result should be as if they had run one after another. The part of the DBMS that controls the interleaving of transactions is the concurrency-control manager (concurrency-control system). Every textbook agrees on this match. The tables differ only for atomicity: many Indian notes say 'transaction manager', while Silberschatz–Korth say the recovery system ensures both atomicity and durability.
why: A — Wrong. The recovery manager uses the log to undo incomplete transactions and redo committed ones after a failure. That supports atomicity and durability, not isolation.

B — Correct. The concurrency-control manager decides which operations of concurrent transactions may run and in what order (for example by granting and refusing locks), which is exactly what isolation needs.
C — Wrong. The query optimizer chooses an efficient plan (join order, index use) for a single query. It has nothing to do with keeping transactions apart.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common table: Atomicity – transaction manager, Consistency – application programmer, Isolation – concurrency-control manager, Durability – recovery manager. Korth: the recovery system handles both A and D.

q:
Consider the following statements about ACID properties:
I. Ensuring consistency for an individual transaction is mainly the responsibility of the application programmer who writes it.
II. Isolation requires that each transaction behave as if it were running alone, unaware of other transactions running at the same time.
III. Durability means that a value written by a committed transaction can never be changed later by any other transaction.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are correct. III is wrong: durability only says committed changes survive failures; later transactions are free to update the same data.
concept: Consistency: if the database is correct before a transaction runs alone, it is correct after. The DBMS checks declared constraints, but the logic (for example, debit and credit the same amount) is written by the application programmer, so Silberschatz–Korth say consistency of a single transaction is the programmer's responsibility. Isolation: concurrent transactions must not see each other's partial work. Durability: committed changes are not lost because of crashes; it does not freeze the data.
why: A — Correct. Statement I matches Silberschatz–Korth's wording, and statement II is the definition of isolation. Statement III is false, so 'I and II only' is the right choice.

B — Wrong. This includes statement III, which is false. A committed balance of Rs 1,000 can of course be changed tomorrow by another transaction; durability only protects it from being lost in a crash.
C — Wrong. Statement II is also correct, so 'I only' leaves out a true statement.
D — Wrong. Only option A gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option A is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The log (journal) kept by a DBMS is directly used to provide which of the following ACID properties?
opts: Atomicity, by undoing the changes of transactions that did not complete
Durability, by redoing the changes of committed transactions after a crash
Isolation, by stopping two transactions from reading the same item at the same time
More than one of the above
exp: The log supports atomicity (undo using old values) and durability (redo using new values). Isolation comes from concurrency control.
concept: Each update log record looks like <T, X, old value, new value>. Old values let the recovery system UNDO changes of transactions that never committed (atomicity). New values and <T commit> records let it REDO changes of committed transactions that were lost from memory (durability). Keeping transactions from interfering with each other (isolation) is a separate job done by locking or timestamp protocols.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The log stores old values, so after a failure the changes of incomplete transactions can be undone. This is how 'all or nothing' (atomicity) is enforced.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The log stores new values and commit records on stable storage, so committed changes that had not reached the disk can be redone. This is how durability is enforced.

C — Wrong. The log does not control concurrent access. Isolation is enforced by the concurrency-control manager (locks, timestamps). Also, two transactions reading the same item at the same time is not even a conflict.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Log = old value (for UNDO → atomicity) + new value (for REDO → durability).

q: T1 updates the price of an item from Rs 100 to Rs 120 but has not committed. T2 reads the price as Rs 120. Then T1 rolls back. Which problem has T2 faced?
opts: More than one of the above
