exp: T2 read a value written by an uncommitted transaction that was later rolled back; this is a dirty read (also called the temporary-update problem, a write–read conflict).
concept: A dirty read happens when a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed. If the writer later rolls back, the reader has used a value that officially never existed. Elmasri–Navathe call this the temporary update problem. It comes from a write–read (WR) conflict. The READ COMMITTED isolation level and higher prevent it.
why: A — Wrong. A lost update happens when two transactions both read and then write the same item and one write overwrites the other. Here T2 only reads.
B — Correct. T2 read Rs 120, a value written by T1 before T1 committed. T1 then rolled back, so T2 used 'dirty' (never committed) data.

C — Wrong. A phantom read happens when a transaction runs the same query twice and new rows appear (or rows vanish) because another transaction inserted or deleted rows that match the condition. No rows were inserted here.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Dirty = uncommitted. Reading uncommitted data = dirty read.

q: Two transactions run with the interleaving shown. What is the final value of X, and which problem has occurred?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: T2 read X before T1 wrote it and then overwrote T1's result, so the final value is 1300 and T1's update is lost.
concept: The lost update problem happens when two transactions read the same item, both change it, and the later write overwrites the earlier one, so the effect of one transaction disappears. Any serial order (T1 then T2, or T2 then T1) would give 1000 - 200 + 300 = 1100. Locking (for example 2PL with an exclusive lock taken before reading an item that will be written) prevents this.
why: A — Wrong. 1100 is what a serial execution would give, but this interleaving does not produce it. Both transactions read the old value 1000, so one change is lost.

B — Wrong. 800 is the value T1 wrote at time 5, but T2 overwrites it at time 6. Also, no transaction reads uncommitted data written by another: both reads see the original 1000, so this is not a dirty read.
C — Correct. T2's write of 1300 at time 6 overwrites T1's 800. The -200 of T1 has vanished, which is the lost update problem.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Initial value: X = 1000

Time | T1              | T2
1    | read(X)         |
2    | X := X - 200    |
3    |                 | read(X)
4    |                 | X := X + 300
5    | write(X)        |
6    |                 | write(X)
work:
Time 1: T1 reads X = 1000 into its local copy.
Time 2: T1's local X = 1000 - 200 = 800.
Time 3: T2 reads X = 1000 (T1 has not written yet).
Time 4: T2's local X = 1000 + 300 = 1300.
Time 5: T1 writes 800 to the database.
Time 6: T2 writes 1300, overwriting 800.
Final X = 1300. A serial run would give 1000 - 200 + 300 = 1100.
T1's update (-200) is lost → lost update problem.
tip: Lost update pattern: R1(X) R2(X) W1(X) W2(X) — both read the old value, the last writer wins.

q: T1 adds up two balances while T2 transfers money, as shown. T1 reports a total of 850. Which concurrency problem is this?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: T1 read A before the transfer and B after it, so its sum mixes old and new values: this is the incorrect summary problem.
concept: The incorrect summary (inconsistent analysis) problem happens when one transaction computes an aggregate (a sum, a count) over several items while another transaction is updating some of those items. The aggregate sees some values before the update and some after, so the result matches no correct database state. Here the true total is always 800, but T1 reports 850.
why: A — Correct. T1's sum uses A = 500 (before the transfer) and B = 350 (after the transfer). This mix of old and new values is exactly the incorrect summary problem.
B — Wrong. A dirty read needs a read of UNCOMMITTED data. T2 committed before T1 read B, and T1 read A before T2 changed it, so T1 never read uncommitted data.
C — Wrong. A lost update needs two transactions to write the same item, with one write overwriting the other. T1 writes nothing, and all of T2's updates are kept.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Initial values: A = 500, B = 300 (true total = 800)

T1 (computes total)          | T2 (transfers 50 from A to B)
sum := 0                     |
read(A); sum := sum + A      |
                             | read(A); A := A - 50; write(A)
                             | read(B); B := B + 50; write(B)
                             | commit
read(B); sum := sum + B      |
work:
T1 reads A = 500 → sum = 500.
T2 changes A to 450 and B to 350, then commits (total still 800).
T1 reads B = 350 (already committed) → sum = 500 + 350 = 850.
T1 used the OLD A and the NEW B → total is 50 too high.

q: Under the SQL standard, which isolation level prevents dirty reads but still allows non-repeatable reads?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: READ COMMITTED allows reading only committed data (no dirty reads), but if another transaction commits a change between two reads, the second read can return a different value.
concept: The SQL standard defines four isolation levels by the anomalies they allow. READ UNCOMMITTED: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms are all possible. READ COMMITTED: no dirty reads; non-repeatable reads and phantoms possible. REPEATABLE READ: no dirty or non-repeatable reads; phantoms possible. SERIALIZABLE: none of these. A non-repeatable read means reading the same row twice and getting different values because another transaction updated it and committed in between.
why: A — Wrong. REPEATABLE READ prevents non-repeatable reads too (rows you have read cannot change under you). The stem wants a level that still ALLOWS them.
B — Correct. READ COMMITTED shows only committed values, so no dirty reads, but it does not keep rows stable across two reads, so non-repeatable reads can still happen.
C — Wrong. SERIALIZABLE is the strongest level; it prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Ladder: READ UNCOMMITTED (allows all three) → READ COMMITTED (stops dirty) → REPEATABLE READ (stops non-repeatable) → SERIALIZABLE (stops phantoms).

q: Under the SQL standard, which anomaly is NOT prevented by the REPEATABLE READ isolation level?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the SQL standard, REPEATABLE READ still allows phantom reads; only SERIALIZABLE prevents them.
concept: A phantom read: T1 runs a query with a condition (for example, WHERE dept = 'IT') twice; between the runs, T2 inserts (or deletes) a matching row and commits, so T1 sees a different set of rows. Protecting only the rows already read (as REPEATABLE READ does) cannot stop new matching rows from being inserted, so the SQL standard allows phantoms at this level. SERIALIZABLE prevents them, for example with predicate or index-range locks.
why: A — Wrong. Dirty reads are prevented already at READ COMMITTED, and therefore also at REPEATABLE READ. So it does not fit a NOT-prevented question.
B — Wrong. Preventing non-repeatable reads is exactly what REPEATABLE READ is named for: rows you have read keep the same values. So it does not fit.
C — Correct. The SQL standard allows phantoms at REPEATABLE READ, because new rows that match a search condition can still be inserted by other transactions. This is the anomaly NOT prevented.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Product note: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is stricter than the standard and also blocks phantoms; exam questions follow the SQL standard table.

q: Under the SQL standard, which isolation level permits dirty reads?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only READ UNCOMMITTED permits dirty reads, and it is not among the options.
concept: READ UNCOMMITTED is the lowest isolation level: a transaction may read values written by other transactions that have not committed yet (dirty reads). Every higher level (READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE) forbids dirty reads.
why: A — Wrong. READ COMMITTED is the first level that forbids dirty reads: it lets a transaction read only committed data.
B — Wrong. REPEATABLE READ is stronger than READ COMMITTED, so it also forbids dirty reads.
C — Wrong. SERIALIZABLE is the strongest level and forbids all three standard anomalies, including dirty reads.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The level that permits dirty reads is READ UNCOMMITTED, which is not listed.

q: A schedule in which the operations of different transactions are interleaved (mixed together) is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Interleaving makes a schedule non-serial (concurrent). Whether it is serializable is a separate question.
concept: A schedule is the order in which the operations of several transactions are executed. Serial schedule: one transaction runs completely, then the next (no interleaving). Non-serial (concurrent) schedule: operations of different transactions are interleaved. Serializable schedule: a schedule (usually non-serial) whose effect is equivalent to some serial schedule. So 'serial vs non-serial' is about the shape of the schedule; 'serializable vs non-serializable' is about whether it is correct.
why: A — Correct. Interleaving the operations of different transactions is exactly what makes a schedule non-serial (also called concurrent).
B — Wrong. In a serial schedule each transaction runs from start to finish before the next begins, so there is no interleaving.
C — Wrong. An interleaved schedule may very well be serializable (equivalent to a serial schedule). 'Non-serializable' describes an incorrect result, not the mere fact of interleaving.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake: 'Non-serializable schedule (parallel)'. Correct pairing: serial vs non-serial (parallel/concurrent); serializable vs non-serializable is a separate idea.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Every serial schedule is serializable.
II. Every non-serial (concurrent) schedule is non-serializable.
III. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial schedule of the same transactions.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and III are true. II is false: many non-serial schedules are serializable.
concept: A serial schedule is trivially serializable, because it is equivalent to itself. A serializable schedule is defined as one that is equivalent (conflict- or view-equivalent) to some serial schedule. Interleaving does not automatically make a schedule wrong. Example: R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) W2(A) R1(B) W1(B) R2(B) W2(B) is non-serial, yet all its conflicts go from T1 to T2, so it is equivalent to the serial order T1 → T2.
why: A — Wrong. This includes statement II, which is false. A non-serial schedule can be serializable, as the example in the concept shows.
B — Correct. Statement I is true (a serial schedule is equivalent to itself) and statement III is the definition of serializability. Statement II is false.
C — Wrong. Statement I is also true, so 'III only' leaves out a correct statement.
D — Wrong. Only option B gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option B is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake: thinking 'concurrent' means 'non-serializable'. Concurrency control exists precisely to allow non-serial schedules that are still serializable.

q: Ti and Tj are different transactions and X is the same data item. Which pair of operations is NOT a conflicting pair?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Two operations conflict only if at least one of them is a write. Two reads never conflict.
concept: Two operations in a schedule conflict when all three conditions hold: they belong to different transactions, they access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write. Conflicting operations cannot be swapped without possibly changing the result. Read–read pairs can be swapped freely because neither changes the data.
why: A — Wrong. Read–write on the same item by different transactions IS a conflict: the value read depends on whether the read comes before or after the write. So it does not fit a NOT question.
B — Wrong. Write–write IS a conflict: the final value of X depends on which write comes last. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Correct. Two reads of the same item do not change anything, so their order does not matter. This pair is NOT a conflict.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Consider schedule S of transactions T1, T2 and T3. Which statement about S is correct?
opts: S is conflict-serializable and equivalent to T1 → T2 → T3
S is conflict-serializable and equivalent to T3 → T1 → T2
More than one of the above
exp: The precedence graph has the cycle T1 → T2 → T3 → T1, so S is not conflict-serializable.
concept: To test conflict serializability, draw a precedence graph: one node per transaction, and an edge Ti → Tj whenever an operation of Ti conflicts with a LATER operation of Tj. If the graph has no cycle, the schedule is conflict-serializable and any topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial order. If the graph has a cycle, no serial order can respect all the conflicts, so the schedule is not conflict-serializable.
why: A — Correct. The edges are T1 → T2 (item A), T2 → T3 (item B) and T3 → T1 (item C). They form a cycle, so no serial order is possible.
B — Wrong. T1 → T2 → T3 respects the conflicts on A and B, but the conflict on C (W3(C) before R1(C)) needs T3 before T1. Looking only at the first two conflicts is a common mistake.
C — Wrong. T3 → T1 → T2 respects the conflicts on C and A, but the conflict on B (W2(B) before R3(B)) needs T2 before T3, which this order breaks.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: S: R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) R2(B) W2(B) R3(B) R3(C) W3(C) R1(C)
work:
Conflicting pairs (different transactions, same item, at least one write):
Item A: W1(A) before R2(A) → edge T1 → T2
Item B: W2(B) before R3(B) → edge T2 → T3
Item C: W3(C) before R1(C) → edge T3 → T1
Precedence graph: T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 → cycle.
A cycle means no serial order exists → not conflict-serializable.
(Each transaction reads an item before writing it, so there are no blind writes; S is not view-serializable either — checked by brute force over all 6 serial orders.)
tip: Check every pair of conflicting operations; a cycle can be hidden across three transactions even when each pair looks fine.

q: Schedule S is conflict-serializable. To which serial schedule is it conflict-equivalent?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The edges T3 → T1, T1 → T2 and T3 → T2 give the single topological order T3 → T1 → T2.
concept: When the precedence graph has no cycle, the equivalent serial orders are its topological orders: repeatedly pick, from the remaining transactions, one that has no incoming edge. If at every step exactly one transaction has no incoming edge, the serial order is unique.
why: A — Wrong. This puts T1 before T3, but W3(A) comes before R1(A), which forces T3 before T1.
B — Wrong. This puts T2 before T1, but R1(A) before W2(A) and W1(B) before R2(B) force T1 before T2.
C — Correct. The edges T3 → T1, T1 → T2 and T3 → T2 are all respected, and it is the only order that does so.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: S: R3(A) R1(B) W3(A) R1(A) W1(B) R2(B) W2(A)
work:
Conflicting pairs:
W3(A) before R1(A) → T3 → T1
R3(A) before W2(A) and W3(A) before W2(A) → T3 → T2
R1(A) before W2(A) → T1 → T2
W1(B) before R2(B) → T1 → T2
(R1(B) and R2(B) are both reads → no edge)
Edges: T3 → T1, T3 → T2, T1 → T2 → no cycle.
Topological order: T3 (no incoming edge), then T1, then T2.
Checking all 6 permutations: only T3 → T1 → T2 satisfies every edge.

q: How many serial schedules are conflict-equivalent to schedule S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The precedence graph has only the edges T1 → T2 and T3 → T4, so there are 4!/(2!·2!) = 6 topological orders.
concept: The number of conflict-equivalent serial schedules equals the number of topological orders of the precedence graph. For independent chains you can count by merging: if one chain has a transactions and another has b, the number of ways to merge them while keeping each chain's internal order is (a + b)! / (a! × b!).
why: A — Wrong. 2 counts only the two 'one whole chain first' orders (T1T2T3T4 and T3T4T1T2) and misses interleaved orders such as T1T3T2T4.
B — Wrong. 4 = 2! × 2! is a wrong formula. The merge count is 4! / (2! × 2!) = 6.
C — Wrong. 24 = 4! counts every order of the four transactions and ignores the two edges T1 → T2 and T3 → T4.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. There are 6 conflict-equivalent serial schedules: T1T2T3T4, T1T3T2T4, T1T3T4T2, T3T1T2T4, T3T1T4T2 and T3T4T1T2.
code: S: R1(A) R3(B) W2(A) R4(C) W4(B) R2(C) R1(D) R3(D)
work:
Conflicting pairs:
R1(A) before W2(A) → T1 → T2
R3(B) before W4(B) → T3 → T4
Items C and D are only read → no edges.
Graph: T1 → T2 and T3 → T4 (two separate chains), no cycle.
Orders of 4 transactions with T1 before T2 and T3 before T4:
4! / (2! × 2!) = 24 / 4 = 6
The 6 orders: T1T2T3T4, T1T3T2T4, T1T3T4T2, T3T1T2T4, T3T1T4T2, T3T4T1T2 (confirmed by brute force).
tip: Number of conflict-equivalent serial orders = number of topological sorts of the precedence graph.

q: In the precedence graph of a schedule, an edge Ti → Tj (i ≠ j) is drawn when, for some data item Q,
opts: Ti executes write(Q) before Tj executes read(Q)
Ti executes read(Q) before Tj executes write(Q)
Ti executes write(Q) before Tj executes write(Q)
More than one of the above
exp: An edge is drawn for every conflicting pair (W–R, R–W, W–W) in the order the operations occur. Only R–R gives no edge.
concept: The precedence (serialization) graph has a node for each transaction. For each pair of conflicting operations — same data item, different transactions, at least one write — draw an edge from the transaction whose operation comes first to the one whose operation comes later. Read–read pairs never create edges.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is a write–read conflict: Tj reads the value written by Ti, so Ti must come before Tj in any equivalent serial order.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is a read–write conflict: Ti read Q before Tj changed it, so Ti must come first.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is a write–write conflict: the final value of Q depends on which write is last, so Ti must come first.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which statement about conflict serializability and view serializability is correct?
opts: Testing view serializability is easy: a precedence-graph test decides it in polynomial time
More than one of the above
exp: Conflict serializability is the stricter test, so every conflict-serializable schedule is also view-serializable, but not the other way round.
concept: Conflict-serializable schedules form a subset of view-serializable schedules. A schedule can be view-serializable without being conflict-serializable when it has blind writes (a write of an item by a transaction that has not read that item). Testing conflict serializability is cheap (a cycle check in the precedence graph), but testing view serializability is NP-complete, so practical protocols aim for conflict serializability.
why: A — Wrong. This is the reverse of the truth. For example, R1(Q) W2(Q) W1(Q) W3(Q) is view-serializable (equivalent to T1, T2, T3), but its precedence graph has the cycle T1 → T2 → T1.
B — Correct. Conflict equivalence implies view equivalence, so conflict serializability is the stricter condition and every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable.
C — Wrong. Testing view serializability is NP-complete; no efficient (polynomial-time) algorithm is known. The simple precedence-graph cycle test works for conflict serializability.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Conflict-serializable ⊂ view-serializable. Schedules that are view- but not conflict-serializable always contain blind writes.

q: Schedule S is not conflict-serializable. To which serial schedule is it view-equivalent?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In S, T2 reads the initial X and T3 writes the final X. Only T2 → T1 → T3 keeps both facts.
concept: Two schedules are view-equivalent if (1) a transaction that reads the initial value of an item in one schedule also does so in the other, (2) each read reads the value written by the same transaction in both schedules, and (3) the same transaction does the final write of each item in both. W1(X) and W3(X) here are blind writes (T1 and T3 write X without reading it), which is why S can be view-serializable though not conflict-serializable.
why: A — Correct. T2 runs first, so it reads the initial X, as in S. T3 runs last, so it writes the final X, as in S. All three view conditions hold.
B — Wrong. In T1 → T2 → T3, T2 would read the value written by T1, but in S T2 reads the initial value. The initial-read condition fails.
C — Wrong. In T3 → T2 → T1, T2 would read T3's value and T1 would make the final write. Both differ from S.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: S: R2(X) W1(X) W2(X) W3(X)
work:
Conflict check: R2(X) before W1(X) → T2 → T1; W1(X) before W2(X) → T1 → T2 → cycle → not conflict-serializable.
View facts of S:
- Initial read: T2 reads the initial value of X (no write before R2(X)).
- Final write: W3(X) is the last write → T3.
Check serial orders:
T2 T1 T3: T2 reads initial X ✓, final writer T3 ✓ → view-equivalent.
T1 T2 T3: T2 reads X written by T1 ✗.
T3 T2 T1: T2 reads X written by T3 ✗; final writer T1 ✗.
Brute force over all 6 orders: only T2 → T1 → T3 matches.
tip: For view equivalence check three things: who reads the initial value, who reads from whom, and who writes last.

q: A schedule that is view-serializable but not conflict-serializable always contains
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Every view-serializable schedule that is not conflict-serializable has at least one blind write.
concept: A blind write is a write(Q) by a transaction that has not read Q before writing it. Blind writes can 'hide' a conflict cycle: the overwritten value is never read by anyone, so the order of those writes does not affect what any transaction sees, and view equivalence still holds. Silberschatz–Korth note that every view-serializable schedule that is not conflict-serializable has blind writes.
why: A — Wrong. A deadlock is a situation in locking where transactions wait for each other forever. It belongs to the execution of a locking protocol, not to the serializability class of a schedule.
B — Wrong. Cascading rollback is about recoverability (one abort forcing others to abort). It is unrelated to the gap between view and conflict serializability.
C — Correct. Blind writes are exactly what allow a schedule to be view-equivalent to a serial one while its precedence graph has a cycle.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A single transaction failure forces several other transactions to roll back, because they had read data written by the failed transaction. This is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When a rollback spreads to transactions that read uncommitted data, it is a cascading rollback (cascading abort).
concept: If T2 reads a value written by T1 before T1 commits, and T1 then fails, T2 must also be rolled back because it used a value that never officially existed. If T3 had read from T2, T3 must roll back too, and so on. This chain is a cascading rollback. Cascadeless schedules avoid it by letting transactions read only committed data; strict 2PL produces such schedules.
why: A — Wrong. A deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting for each other's locks so that none can proceed. No transaction is failing because of another's rollback.
B — Correct. One failure spreading to all transactions that read its uncommitted data is exactly a cascading rollback.
C — Wrong. Starvation means a transaction waits indefinitely (or is rolled back again and again) while others keep going. It is not a chain of rollbacks caused by one failure.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How should schedule S be classified?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: T2 reads A from uncommitted T1 and commits before T1, so S is not even recoverable; hence it is neither cascadeless nor strict.
concept: Recoverable: if Tj reads data written by Ti, then Ti must commit before Tj commits. Cascadeless: Tj may read data written by Ti only after Ti has committed. Strict: no transaction may read OR write an item written by Ti until Ti commits or aborts. Each condition is stronger than the one before: every strict schedule is cascadeless, and every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.
why: A — Wrong. T2 read from T1 but committed first. If T1 now aborts, T2 has already committed with a dirty value and cannot be rolled back, so S is not recoverable.
B — Wrong. T2 read A before T1 committed, so S is not cascadeless.
C — Wrong. Strictness forbids even reading A until T1 finishes; T2 reads it earlier, so S is not strict.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. S is non-recoverable: T2 reads from T1 and commits before T1 commits. A non-recoverable schedule cannot be cascadeless or strict.
code:
S: W1(A) R2(A) W2(B) C2 C1
(Ci = commit of Ti)
work:
R2(A) comes after W1(A) while T1 has not committed → T2 reads from T1 (a dirty read).
Recoverable needs C1 before C2. In S, C2 comes before C1 → NOT recoverable.
Cascadeless needs C1 before R2(A) → violated.
Strict needs T1 to commit/abort before any read/write of A by another transaction → violated.
Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable, so failing 'recoverable' fails all three.
tip: Check recoverability first: if it fails, the schedule is automatically neither cascadeless nor strict.

q: How should schedule S be classified?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The commits follow the reads-from order (C1, C2, C3), so S is recoverable; but T2 and T3 read uncommitted data, so S is not cascadeless or strict.
concept: A recoverable schedule can always be repaired after an abort, but it may need cascading rollbacks. In this schedule, a failure of T1 before its commit would force T2 to roll back, and that would in turn force T3 to roll back: a cascade of length two. To avoid this, a schedule must be cascadeless, i.e. transactions must read only committed data.
why: A — Correct. T2 reads from T1 and T3 reads from T2, and the commits come in the same order (C1, then C2, then C3). This satisfies the recoverability rule.
B — Wrong. T2 reads A and T3 reads B before their writers commit, so a failure could cascade. The schedule is not cascadeless.
C — Wrong. A strict schedule must first be cascadeless. Since S is not cascadeless, it cannot be strict.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
S: W1(A) R2(A) W2(B) R3(B) C1 C2 C3
(Ci = commit of Ti)
work:
Reads-from:
R2(A) reads from T1 (W1(A) earlier, T1 not yet committed).
R3(B) reads from T2 (W2(B) earlier, T2 not yet committed).
Recoverable? T2 reads from T1: C1 before C2 ✓. T3 reads from T2: C2 before C3 ✓ → recoverable.
Cascadeless? R2(A) happens before C1 ✗ → not cascadeless.
Strict? Not cascadeless → not strict.
If T1 aborted before C1, T2 and then T3 would have to roll back (a cascade).
tip: Serializability and recoverability are separate checks: this schedule is conflict-serializable (edges T1 → T2 → T3) and still has dirty reads. Common mistake: 'serializability prevents dirty reads'.

q: Which of the following describe schedule S?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: No transaction reads another's uncommitted data, so S is recoverable and cascadeless. But T2 overwrites T1's uncommitted A, so S is not strict.
concept: The difference between cascadeless and strict is writes. Cascadeless: you may not READ uncommitted data. Strict: you may neither READ nor WRITE an item until the transaction that last wrote it has committed or aborted. Strictness makes undo simple: when an aborted transaction's write is undone by restoring the item's old value (its before-image), this can never wipe out another transaction's write.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. No transaction reads a value written by another transaction, so the recoverability rule can never be broken.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Cascadeless only restricts READS of uncommitted data. T2 never reads A; it only overwrites it, so no rollback can cascade.

C — Wrong. Strict also forbids WRITING an item written by an uncommitted transaction. W2(A) comes before C1, so S is not strict. (If T1 aborted, restoring A's old value would wrongly erase T2's write.)
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
S: R1(A) W1(A) W2(A) R2(B) C1 C2
(Ci = commit of Ti)
work:
Reads in S: R1(A) (T1 reads the initial A) and R2(B) (B is never written) → no transaction reads data written by another.
Recoverable: no reads-from pairs between transactions → ✓.
Cascadeless: no read of uncommitted data written by another → ✓.
Strict: W2(A) overwrites A while T1 (which wrote A) has not committed → ✗.
Result: recoverable and cascadeless, but not strict.
tip: Cascadeless looks only at reads; strict looks at reads and writes.

q:
Consider the following statements about schedules:
I. Every strict schedule is cascadeless.
II. Every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.
III. Every recoverable schedule is cascadeless.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable, so I and II are true; III is false.
concept: The three classes are nested: strict schedules are a subset of cascadeless schedules, which are a subset of recoverable schedules. The containments are proper: W1(A) R2(A) C1 C2 is recoverable but not cascadeless, and W1(A) W2(A) C1 C2 is cascadeless but not strict.
why: A — Wrong. Statement III is false: in W1(A) R2(A) C1 C2, T2 reads uncommitted data, so the schedule is not cascadeless, yet T1 commits before T2, so it is recoverable.
B — Wrong. This includes the false statement III.

C — Correct. I: strictness forbids reading uncommitted data, so a strict schedule is cascadeless. II: if Tj reads only committed data, the writer committed before Tj's read, and hence before Tj's commit, so the schedule is recoverable.
D — Wrong. Only option C gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option C is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Transaction T1 holds a shared (S) lock on data item Q. Transaction T2 now requests a lock on Q. Which statement is correct?
opts: T2 can get an exclusive (X) lock on Q at once
T2 can get a shared (S) lock on Q at once
T2 cannot get any lock on Q until T1 commits
More than one of the above
exp: S is compatible with S, so T2's shared lock is granted at once; an exclusive lock request must wait.
concept: Lock compatibility: S with S → compatible (many readers at once). S with X, X with S, X with X → not compatible (the request must wait). A shared lock lets a transaction read an item; an exclusive lock lets it read and write. When a requested lock is incompatible with a lock already held by another transaction, the requester waits until that lock is released.
why: A — Wrong. X is not compatible with S. Granting T2 an exclusive lock would let T2 write Q while T1 is reading it, so T2 must wait.
B — Correct. Two shared locks are compatible: both transactions only read Q, so they cannot harm each other.
C — Wrong. Too strong: T2 can get a shared lock immediately. Only an exclusive lock request has to wait (until T1 releases its S lock).
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Only S–S is compatible; any pair involving X conflicts.

q: In the two-phase locking protocol, the point in a transaction's schedule at which it obtains its final lock (the end of its growing phase) is called the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The lock point is the moment a transaction acquires its last lock; transactions can be serialized in the order of their lock points.
concept: Under 2PL each transaction has a growing phase (it may acquire locks but not release any) and then a shrinking phase (it may release locks but not acquire any). The lock point is the instant the growing phase ends, i.e. when the last lock is obtained. Ordering transactions by their lock points gives an equivalent serial order, which is why 2PL ensures conflict serializability.
why: A — Wrong. The commit point is when the transaction's commit record is safely in the log and the transaction becomes committed. Under basic 2PL, locks may be released before commit, so these two points can differ.
B — Wrong. A checkpoint is a recovery technique: the DBMS writes buffered changes and a <checkpoint> log record to reduce work after a crash. It has nothing to do with one transaction's locks.
C — Correct. The lock point is defined as the point where the transaction holds all its locks, just before it may start releasing them.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Basic two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees which of the following?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability only. It can still deadlock and can still produce cascading rollbacks.
concept: Basic 2PL: a transaction must acquire all its locks before releasing any. This guarantees conflict-serializable schedules (equivalent to the order of lock points). It does NOT prevent deadlock (two transactions can each hold one lock and wait for the other's) and does NOT prevent cascading rollback or dirty reads (an exclusive lock released in the shrinking phase before commit lets another transaction read uncommitted data). Strict 2PL fixes cascading rollback; conservative 2PL fixes deadlock.
why: A — Correct. This is the main theorem of 2PL: every schedule produced by 2PL is conflict-serializable.
B — Wrong. 2PL can deadlock: T1 locks A and waits for B, while T2 locks B and waits for A. Both are still in their growing phases, so 2PL allows this.
C — Wrong. Under basic 2PL, T1 may release its exclusive lock on A in the shrinking phase before committing; T2 can then read A. If T1 later aborts, T2 must roll back too.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common mistake: '2PL prevents dirty reads'. Basic 2PL does not; strict 2PL (hold X locks until commit) does.

q: Which variant of two-phase locking requires a transaction to hold all its exclusive locks until it commits or aborts, while allowing its shared locks to be released earlier?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Strict 2PL keeps exclusive (write) locks until commit or abort; shared locks may be released earlier in the shrinking phase.
concept: Variants of 2PL: Basic 2PL – a growing phase, then a shrinking phase. Strict 2PL – in addition, all exclusive locks are held until commit or abort; other transactions can never read or write uncommitted data, so schedules are strict and cascadeless. Rigorous 2PL – ALL locks (shared and exclusive) are held until commit or abort; transactions can be serialized in the order in which they commit. Conservative (static) 2PL – all locks are acquired before the transaction starts; this prevents deadlock.
why: A — Wrong. Conservative 2PL is about acquiring locks: the transaction must lock everything it needs before it starts. It says nothing about holding X locks until commit.
B — Correct. Strict 2PL is exactly this: X locks are held until commit or abort, and S locks may be released earlier.
C — Wrong. Rigorous 2PL holds ALL locks, including shared locks, until commit or abort, so it does not allow shared locks to be released early.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following variants of two-phase locking does NOT guarantee freedom from deadlock?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Strict and rigorous 2PL can both deadlock; only conservative 2PL is deadlock-free.
concept: A deadlock needs 'hold and wait': a transaction holds some locks while waiting for more. Strict and rigorous 2PL change only the rules for RELEASING locks, so hold-and-wait still happens and deadlocks are possible. Conservative (static) 2PL removes hold-and-wait by predeclaring and acquiring all locks at the start, so it is deadlock-free (but it is rarely used, because a transaction often does not know in advance which items it will need).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Strict 2PL controls when exclusive locks are released, not how they are acquired. Two transactions can still each hold one lock and wait for the other's, so deadlock is possible.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Rigorous 2PL also only delays the release of locks; locks are still acquired one by one during execution, so a cycle of waits can form.

C — Wrong. Conservative 2PL makes a transaction obtain all its locks before it starts (if any lock is unavailable, it takes none and waits). It never holds some locks while waiting for others, so deadlock cannot occur. Therefore it does not fit the NOT question.
D — Correct. Both strict 2PL and rigorous 2PL can deadlock, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Each sequence shows only the lock actions of a single transaction (its reads and writes are omitted). Which sequence follows the two-phase locking protocol with lock conversion?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only Sequence C acquires and upgrades all its locks before its first unlock.
concept: 2PL with lock conversion: in the growing phase a transaction may acquire locks and upgrade S to X; in the shrinking phase it may release locks and downgrade X to S. Any acquisition or upgrade after the first release breaks the protocol.
why: A — Wrong. Lock-X(C) is requested after Unlock(A). Acquiring a lock in the shrinking phase violates 2PL.
B — Wrong. Upgrading S(A) to X(A) is a form of lock acquisition. It happens after Unlock(B), i.e. in the shrinking phase, so 2PL is violated.
C — Correct. All acquisitions (S on A, S on B, the upgrade of A) come first, then only releases. This is a valid two-phase pattern.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Lock-S = shared lock, Lock-X = exclusive lock, Upgrade = convert own S lock to X

Sequence A: Lock-S(A), Lock-S(B), Unlock(A), Lock-X(C), Unlock(B), Unlock(C)
Sequence B: Lock-S(A), Lock-X(B), Unlock(B), Upgrade(A), Unlock(A)
Sequence C: Lock-S(A), Lock-S(B), Upgrade(A), Unlock(B), Unlock(A)
work:
Rule: after the first Unlock, no new lock and no upgrade may occur (an upgrade counts as acquiring a lock).
A: Unlock(A) is followed by Lock-X(C) → violates 2PL.
B: Unlock(B) is followed by Upgrade(A) → upgrade in the shrinking phase → violates 2PL.
C: Lock-S(A), Lock-S(B), Upgrade(A) all happen before the first Unlock(B) → growing phase, then shrinking phase → follows 2PL.
tip: Upgrade = acquire (growing phase only); downgrade = release (shrinking phase only).

q: In two-phase locking with lock conversion, upgrading a lock (S → X) is allowed only in the ____ phase, and downgrading (X → S) only in the ____ phase.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An upgrade gains a stronger lock, so it belongs to the growing phase; a downgrade gives up lock strength, so it belongs to the shrinking phase.
concept: Lock conversion lets a transaction start with a weaker lock and change it later. Upgrade: S → X, needed when a transaction that read an item now wants to write it. Downgrade: X → S, used when a transaction no longer needs to write an item. In 2PL an upgrade acts like acquiring a lock and a downgrade acts like releasing one, so they must follow the growing/shrinking rule.
why: A — Correct. Upgrading acquires more power over the item, which is allowed only while growing. Downgrading gives up power, which is allowed only while shrinking.
B — Wrong. This is reversed: an upgrade in the shrinking phase would mean acquiring a lock after releasing one, which breaks 2PL.
C — Wrong. A downgrade releases part of a lock. Allowing it in the growing phase would let the transaction release and later acquire again, breaking the two-phase rule.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Under the basic timestamp-ordering protocol, which operation is the first to be rejected (causing its transaction to be rolled back)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: W2(A) is rejected because the younger T3 (TS 30) has already read A; T2 (TS 20) is too late to write it.
concept: Basic timestamp ordering gives each transaction a timestamp TS when it starts (older = smaller TS). Each item keeps R-TS (largest TS of any transaction that read it) and W-TS (largest TS of any transaction that wrote it). Read by Ti: rejected if TS(Ti) < W-TS(X); otherwise allowed and R-TS(X) = max(R-TS(X), TS(Ti)). Write by Ti: rejected if TS(Ti) < R-TS(X) or TS(Ti) < W-TS(X); otherwise allowed and W-TS(X) = TS(Ti). A rejected transaction is rolled back and restarted with a new timestamp.
why: A — Wrong. R3(A) is allowed: no one has written A yet (W-TS(A) = 0), so T3 may read it. R-TS(A) becomes 30.
B — Correct. When T2 wants to write A, R-TS(A) = 30 > TS(T2) = 20. A younger transaction has already read the old value of A, so T2's write arrives 'too late' and T2 is rolled back.
C — Wrong. W3(B) is allowed: TS(T3) = 30 is not smaller than R-TS(B) = 20 or W-TS(B) = 10. It also comes after W2(A), so it cannot be the first rejection.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
TS(T1) = 10, TS(T2) = 20, TS(T3) = 30
Initially R-TS and W-TS of A and B are 0.

S: R1(A) R3(A) W1(B) R2(B) W2(A) W3(B)
work:
R1(A): TS 10 ≥ W-TS(A) 0 → OK; R-TS(A) = 10
R3(A): TS 30 ≥ W-TS(A) 0 → OK; R-TS(A) = 30
W1(B): TS 10 ≥ R-TS(B) 0 and ≥ W-TS(B) 0 → OK; W-TS(B) = 10
R2(B): TS 20 ≥ W-TS(B) 10 → OK; R-TS(B) = 20
W2(A): TS 20 < R-TS(A) 30 → REJECT, roll back T2
W3(B): TS 30 ≥ R-TS(B) 20 and ≥ W-TS(B) 10 → OK; W-TS(B) = 30
tip: A write is rejected if a YOUNGER transaction has already read or written the item.

q: Under the timestamp-ordering protocol with Thomas' write rule, what happens when W1(X) is issued?
opts: W1(X) is executed and W-TS(X) becomes 5
W1(X) is rejected and T1 is rolled back
W1(X) is ignored, and T1 continues
More than one of the above
exp: W1(X) is obsolete (the younger T2 has already written X) and no younger transaction has read X, so Thomas' write rule simply ignores it.
concept: Thomas' write rule changes only the write test of timestamp ordering. If TS(Ti) < R-TS(X): reject and roll back Ti, as usual. Else if TS(Ti) < W-TS(X): the write is obsolete — in timestamp order, the younger transaction's write would overwrite it anyway — so it is simply ignored. Otherwise: execute it and set W-TS(X) = TS(Ti). This rule allows some schedules that are view-serializable but not conflict-serializable.
why: A — Wrong. W1(X) is not executed. If it were, the older T1's value would replace the value of the younger T2, which in timestamp order should be the final one.
B — Wrong. This is what basic timestamp ordering (without Thomas' rule) would do. Thomas' rule avoids the rollback for obsolete writes.
C — Correct. TS(T1) = 5 is not less than R-TS(X) = 5, but it is less than W-TS(X) = 10, so the write is obsolete and ignored; T1 goes on.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
TS(T1) = 5, TS(T2) = 10
Initially R-TS(X) = W-TS(X) = 0

S: R1(X) W2(X) W1(X)
work:
R1(X): TS 5 ≥ W-TS 0 → OK; R-TS(X) = 5
W2(X): TS 10 ≥ R-TS 5 and ≥ W-TS 0 → OK; W-TS(X) = 10
W1(X): is TS 5 < R-TS(X) 5? No → no reader-based rejection.
       TS 5 < W-TS(X) 10 → obsolete write.
Basic TO: reject and roll back T1.
Thomas' write rule: ignore the obsolete write; T1 continues.

q: Which of the following concurrency-control protocols is NOT a lock-based protocol?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Multiversion timestamp ordering and the validation (optimistic) protocol do not use locks; rigorous 2PL does.
concept: Concurrency-control protocols fall into families. Lock-based: 2PL and its variants (strict, rigorous, conservative) and graph-based protocols. Timestamp-based: basic timestamp ordering, Thomas' write rule, and multiversion timestamp ordering (an MVCC scheme). Optimistic (validation-based): read phase → validation phase → write phase; good when conflicts are rare. MVCC (multiversion concurrency control) keeps old versions of data so that a reader can read a suitable version instead of waiting.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Multiversion timestamp ordering keeps several versions of each item and uses timestamps to decide which version a read sees; it uses no locks. In this scheme a read request never fails and never waits.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The optimistic (validation-based) protocol lets a transaction run without locks: in the read phase it works on local copies, in the validation phase it is checked for conflicts, and only then does the write phase make its changes permanent.
C — Wrong. Rigorous 2PL is a lock-based protocol: it holds all shared and exclusive locks until commit or abort. So it does not fit the NOT question.
D — Correct. Both multiversion timestamp ordering and the validation-based protocol are not lock-based, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Three families: locks (2PL), timestamps (TO, Thomas, MVTO), validation (optimistic: read → validate → write).

q: In multiple-granularity locking, a transaction wants to read ALL records of file F without locking each record separately, and to update a few of those records (locking only those records in X mode). Which single lock mode should it hold on F?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The right mode is SIX (shared and intention-exclusive): S on the whole file for reading, plus the right to place X locks on individual records.
concept: Multiple-granularity locking lets a transaction lock at different levels (database → file → page → record). Intention modes are placed on ancestors to announce finer locks below. IS: S locks will be taken below. IX: X (or S) locks will be taken below. S: the whole subtree is read-locked. SIX = S + IX: the whole subtree is read-locked, and X locks will be taken on some descendants. To lock a node in S or IS, the parent must be held in IS or IX; to lock a node in X, SIX or IX, the parent must be held in IX or SIX.
why: A — Wrong. IS allows only S or IS locks below. The transaction would have to lock every record it reads, and it could not take X locks on records at all.
B — Wrong. IX allows X locks on records, but it does not cover reading the whole file: the transaction would still have to S-lock every record it reads, which the stem wants to avoid.
C — Wrong. S on F lets the transaction read every record, but S does not permit X locks on descendants, so it cannot update any record.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The required mode is SIX (shared + intention-exclusive), which is not listed: the S part covers reading the whole file, and the IX part permits X locks on the few records being updated.
tip: SIX = 'read everything, write a few'.

q: Under the wait-die deadlock-prevention scheme, what happens in cases (i) and (ii)?
opts: (i) T2 waits; (ii) T2 is rolled back
(i) T2 is rolled back; (ii) T2 waits
More than one of the above
exp: In wait-die an older requester waits and a younger requester dies. T2 is younger than T1 (so it dies) and older than T3 (so it waits).
concept: Wait-die and wound-wait use timestamps to prevent deadlock; each allows waiting in only one direction of age, so a cycle of waits cannot form. Wait-die (non-preemptive): an older requester waits; a younger requester is rolled back ('dies'). Wound-wait (preemptive): an older requester 'wounds' the younger holder (the holder is rolled back); a younger requester waits. In both, a rolled-back transaction restarts with its ORIGINAL timestamp, so it eventually becomes the oldest and cannot starve.
why: A — Wrong. This is the reverse of wait-die. In (i) the requester T2 is younger than the holder T1, so it may not wait; in (ii) T2 is older than T3, so it is allowed to wait.
B — Correct. (i) T2 (TS 10) is younger than the holder T1 (TS 5), so T2 dies. (ii) T2 (TS 10) is older than the holder T3 (TS 15), so T2 waits.
C — Wrong. In wait-die only an older requester may wait. In case (i) T2 is the younger one, so it must die rather than wait.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
TS(T1) = 5, TS(T2) = 10, TS(T3) = 15 (smaller timestamp = older)

(i)  T2 requests a lock on an item currently locked by T1.
(ii) T2 requests a lock on an item currently locked by T3.
work:
Wait-die rule: if the requester is OLDER than the holder, it waits; if it is YOUNGER, it dies (is rolled back and later restarts with its original timestamp).
(i) Requester T2 (TS 10) vs holder T1 (TS 5): T2 is younger → T2 dies (rolled back).
(ii) Requester T2 (TS 10) vs holder T3 (TS 15): T2 is older → T2 waits.
(For comparison, wound-wait: (i) T2 waits; (ii) T2 wounds T3, i.e. T3 is rolled back.)
tip: Wait-die: Old Waits, Young Dies. Wound-wait: Old Wounds, Young Waits. In both, the older transaction gets its way.

q:
Consider the following statements about deadlocks:
I. A deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph contains a cycle.
II. Hold-and-wait is one of the necessary conditions for a deadlock.
III. In the timeout scheme, a transaction that has waited longer than a fixed time for a lock is rolled back and restarted.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are standard facts: a cycle in the wait-for graph means deadlock; hold-and-wait is a necessary (Coffman) condition; timeouts roll back long waiters.
concept: A deadlock is a set of transactions each waiting for a lock held by another in the set. Four necessary conditions (Coffman): mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Handling: prevention (conservative 2PL, ordering of data items, wait-die, wound-wait); detection (wait-for graph with an edge Ti → Tj when Ti waits for a lock held by Tj; a cycle means deadlock, and a victim is rolled back); and timeouts (simple, but may roll back transactions that were not deadlocked, and a good time limit is hard to choose).
why: A — Correct. I is the standard detection rule (Silberschatz–Korth: a deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph contains a cycle). II is one of the four Coffman conditions. III correctly describes the timeout-based scheme.
B — Wrong. Statement III is also correct, so 'I and II only' leaves out a true statement.
C — Wrong. Statements II and III are also correct, so 'I only' leaves out two true statements.
D — Wrong. Only option A gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option A is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Starvation: if the same transaction is chosen as the deadlock victim again and again it may never finish; counting its past rollbacks in the victim-selection cost avoids this.

q: Which statement about the wait-die and wound-wait schemes is correct?
opts: In wait-die, an older transaction that requests a lock held by a younger transaction is rolled back
In wound-wait, a younger transaction that requests a lock held by an older transaction forces the older one to roll back
In both schemes, a rolled-back transaction is restarted with a new, larger timestamp
More than one of the above
exp: All three are false: in wait-die the older requester waits; in wound-wait the younger requester waits; and restarted transactions keep their original timestamps.
concept: Wait-die: older requester waits, younger requester dies. Wound-wait: older requester wounds (rolls back) the younger holder, younger requester waits. A transaction that is rolled back in either scheme restarts with its ORIGINAL timestamp. Over time it becomes the oldest active transaction and is then never rolled back, so starvation is avoided.
why: A — Wrong. In wait-die the older requester is allowed to WAIT. Only a younger requester dies.
B — Wrong. In wound-wait a younger requester WAITS for the older holder. Only an older requester wounds a younger holder.
C — Wrong. Restarting with a new (larger) timestamp would make the transaction look young again, so it could be rolled back again and again (starvation). Both schemes keep the original timestamp.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.

E — Correct. All three statements are false. The correct facts: wait-die – older waits, younger dies; wound-wait – older wounds, younger waits; a restarted transaction keeps its original timestamp, which prevents starvation.

q: T1 has 4 operations and T2 has 3 operations, as shown. Every schedule of T1 and T2 must keep the operations of each transaction in their own order. How many of the possible schedules are non-serial (concurrent)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: There are C(7, 3) = 7! / (4! × 3!) = 35 ways to interleave the two transactions. Exactly 2 of them are serial (T1 then T2, or T2 then T1), so 35 − 2 = 33 are non-serial.
concept: A schedule may mix (interleave) the operations of different transactions, but it must keep each transaction's own operations in their original order. For T1 with m operations and T2 with n operations, a schedule is fixed by choosing which m of the m + n time slots belong to T1, so there are C(m + n, m) = (m + n)! / (m! × n!) schedules. Exactly 2 of them are serial (all of T1 first, or all of T2 first); all the others are non-serial (concurrent).
why: A — Wrong. 35 = C(7, 3) is the TOTAL number of schedules. It still includes the 2 serial schedules (T1 → T2 and T2 → T1), which are not non-serial.
B — Correct. Total schedules = 7! / (4! × 3!) = 35; taking away the 2 serial schedules leaves 33 non-serial schedules.
C — Wrong. 5040 = 7! counts every ordering of the 7 operations, including orders that change the order inside a transaction (for example W1(A) before R1(A)). A schedule is not allowed to do that.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Total operations = 4 + 3 = 7.
A schedule = a choice of which 4 of the 7 positions hold T1's operations (the order inside each transaction is fixed).
Number of schedules = C(7, 4) = C(7, 3) = 7! / (4! × 3!) = 5040 / (24 × 6) = 35.
Serial schedules: T1 then T2, and T2 then T1 → 2.
Non-serial schedules = 35 − 2 = 33.
(Confirmed by listing all interleavings in Python: 35 in total, 2 serial, 33 non-serial.)
tip: Schedules of T1 (m operations) and T2 (n operations) = (m + n)! / (m! × n!); non-serial = that number − 2.

q: Schedule S of transactions T1, T2 and T3 is shown. To how many different serial schedules is S conflict-equivalent?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The precedence graph has only one edge, T3 → T2 (from item B and from item D); T1 conflicts with nobody. The serial orders with T3 before T2 are T1T3T2, T3T1T2 and T3T2T1, so the answer is 3, which is not listed.
concept: Two operations conflict only if they belong to different transactions, use the same data item, and at least one of them is a write. Each conflicting pair gives an edge Ti → Tj (Ti's operation comes first) in the precedence graph. If the graph has no cycle, S is conflict-serializable, and every topological order of the graph (an order in which all edges point forward) is a conflict-equivalent serial schedule. A transaction with no edges can be placed anywhere in the order.
why: A — Wrong. 1 would be right only if the edges fixed a single chain such as T3 → T2 → T1. But T1 has no conflict with anyone: R1(A) and R2(A) are both reads, and only T1 uses item C, so T1 can be placed anywhere.
B — Wrong. 2 comes from wrongly treating R1(A) and R2(A) as a conflict (adding an edge T1 → T2). Two reads of the same item never conflict, because neither changes the value.
C — Wrong. 6 = 3! counts every order of the three transactions. It ignores the real edge T3 → T2: R3(B) comes before W2(B), and R3(D) comes before W2(D), so T3 must come before T2.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. S is conflict-equivalent to 3 serial schedules: T1 → T3 → T2, T3 → T1 → T2 and T3 → T2 → T1.
code: S: R1(A) R2(A) R3(B) W1(C) W2(B) R3(D) W2(D) R1(A)
work:
Pairs on the same item from different transactions:
A: R1(A), R2(A), R1(A) → all reads → no conflict.
B: R3(B) before W2(B) → conflict → edge T3 → T2.
C: only W1(C) → no pair.
D: R3(D) before W2(D) → conflict → edge T3 → T2 (the same edge again).
Precedence graph: T3 → T2 only; T1 has no edges. No cycle → conflict-serializable.
Serial orders with T3 before T2: T1T3T2, T3T1T2, T3T2T1 → 3 of the 3! = 6 orders.
(Confirmed by checking all 6 orders in Python.)
tip: Read–read pairs never give an edge. A transaction with no edges can sit anywhere in the serial order.

q: T1 and T2 are shown. Consider every schedule (interleaving) of T1 and T2 that keeps each transaction's own order. How many of these schedules are conflict-serializable?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: There are C(6, 2) = 15 schedules. One is equivalent to T2 → T1 (T2 runs entirely first) and 6 are equivalent to T1 → T2 (both T2 operations come after W1(A)), so 7 are conflict-serializable.
concept: To count conflict-serializable schedules, count the schedules equivalent to each serial order separately and add them. A schedule is conflict-equivalent to T1 → T2 exactly when, in every conflicting pair, T1's operation comes first. Counting the allowed 'gaps' (places between T1's operations) where the other transaction's operations may go is much faster than listing every schedule.
why: A — Correct. 6 schedules are equivalent to T1 → T2 and 1 schedule is equivalent to T2 → T1, giving 6 + 1 = 7.

B — Wrong. 2 counts only the two serial schedules. Some non-serial schedules are also conflict-serializable, for example R1(A) W1(A) R2(A) W2(A) R1(B) W1(B): T2 uses only A, and only after T1 has finished with A.

C — Wrong. 15 = 6! / (4! × 2!) is the total number of schedules. Schedules that begin R1(A) R2(A) W1(A) W2(A) … contain the cycle T1 → T2 → T1 (R1(A) before W2(A), R2(A) before W1(A)) and are not conflict-serializable.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Total schedules = 6! / (4! × 2!) = 15.
Conflicts are only on A: R1(A), W1(A) against R2(A), W2(A). Item B is used by T1 alone.
Equivalent to T2 → T1: both T2 operations must come before R1(A) → 1 schedule (the serial schedule T2 T1).
Equivalent to T1 → T2: R2(A) and W2(A) must both come after W1(A). T1 = R1(A) W1(A) R1(B) W1(B) has 3 gaps after W1(A): after W1(A), after R1(B), after W1(B).
Placing 2 ordered operations into 3 gaps (two may share a gap) = C(3 + 2 − 1, 2) = C(4, 2) = 6.
Every other placement has at least one T2 operation before W1(A) and at least one after R1(A) → edges T2 → T1 and T1 → T2 → cycle.
Conflict-serializable schedules = 6 + 1 = 7.
(Brute force over all 15 schedules in Python: 7.)
tip: Count 'equivalent to T1 → T2' and 'equivalent to T2 → T1' separately, then add.

q: Under basic (non-strict) two-phase locking, a transaction takes a shared lock on an item it only reads and an exclusive lock on an item it writes. It may take a lock at any time before it first uses the item and may release a lock at any time after its last use, but it may not take any lock after it has released one. Which of the schedules shown could be produced under this protocol?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: S1 is not conflict-serializable, so 2PL can never produce it. S2 is conflict-serializable, but T1 would have to hold a lock on B while T3 writes B. S3 is possible: T1 locks A and B at the start, releases A after W1(A) and releases B after W1(B).
concept: Every schedule produced by two-phase locking (2PL) is conflict-serializable, but not every conflict-serializable schedule can be produced by 2PL. To test a schedule, look at each moment when a transaction Ti must give up a lock (because another transaction needs a conflicting lock on that item). Ti may release only if it already holds every lock it will need later, so any item Ti uses later must be locked before that release and held until Ti uses it. If another transaction needs a conflicting lock on that item in between, 2PL cannot produce the schedule.
why: A — Wrong. S1 is not even conflict-serializable: R1(A) before W2(A) gives T1 → T2, and R2(B) before W1(B) gives T2 → T1, a cycle. 2PL never produces a schedule that is not conflict-serializable.

B — Wrong. S2 is conflict-serializable (equivalent to T3 → T1 → T2), but 2PL cannot produce it. T1 must release its lock on A before W2(A). Because T1 still needs B later, it must lock B before that release and keep the lock until R1(B). W3(B) needs an exclusive lock on B in between, which conflicts with T1's lock.

C — Correct. A valid locking exists: T1 takes X(A) and X(B) at the start, reads and writes A, and releases A; T2 takes S(A), reads A, takes X(C), writes C; T1 writes B and releases B; T2 takes S(B), reads B, and then releases all its locks. Each transaction takes all its locks before its first release.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
S1: R1(A) before W2(A) → T1 → T2; R2(B) before W1(B) → T2 → T1 → cycle → not conflict-serializable → impossible under 2PL.
S2: R1(A) before W2(A) → T1 → T2; W3(B) before R1(B) → T3 → T1 → no cycle (serial order T3, T1, T2).
   2PL check: T1 must unlock A before W2(A). T1 still needs B, so it must lock B before unlocking A and hold it until R1(B).
   W3(B) comes in between and needs X(B) → conflict → impossible.
S3: edges T1 → T2 only (on A and on B) → serializable. One valid lock sequence:
   T1: X-lock(A), X-lock(B), R1(A), W1(A), unlock(A)
   T2: S-lock(A), R2(A), X-lock(C), W2(C)
   T1: W1(B), unlock(B)
   T2: S-lock(B), R2(B), unlock(A), unlock(B), unlock(C)
   Both transactions take all their locks before their first unlock → 2PL.
Checked in Python by trying every possible lock point for every transaction (with and without S → X upgrades): only S3 is possible.
tip: 2PL ⇒ conflict-serializable, but not the other way round. A transaction that releases a lock must already hold every lock it will need later.

q: Schedule S runs under the basic timestamp-ordering protocol (without Thomas' write rule). A rolled-back transaction's remaining operations in S are not executed; it is restarted only after S ends. Which of the following transactions is rolled back?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: W1(A) is rejected because the younger T2 has already written A, and W2(B) is rejected because the younger T3 has already read B. Every operation of T3 is allowed, so T1 and T2 are rolled back.
concept: In basic timestamp ordering, each transaction gets a timestamp TS when it starts (smaller = older), and each item X keeps R-TS(X) and W-TS(X), the largest timestamps of transactions that have read and written it. A read by Ti is rejected if TS(Ti) < W-TS(X). A write by Ti is rejected if TS(Ti) < R-TS(X) or TS(Ti) < W-TS(X). In short: an older transaction may not read or write an item after a younger one has used it in a conflicting way. With Thomas' write rule, a write rejected only because TS(Ti) < W-TS(X) is simply ignored instead of causing a rollback.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. T1 is rolled back at W1(A): W-TS(A) = 20 (written by the younger T2) and TS(T1) = 10 < 20, so T1's write comes too late.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. T2 is rolled back at W2(B): R-TS(B) = 30 because the younger T3 has already read B, and TS(T2) = 20 < 30.
C — Wrong. T3 is not rolled back. It is the youngest transaction: R3(B), W3(A) (30 ≥ R-TS(A) = 10 and 30 ≥ W-TS(A) = 20) and W3(C) (30 ≥ R-TS(C) = 20) are all allowed.
D — Correct. T1 and T2 are both rolled back, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
TS(T1) = 10, TS(T2) = 20, TS(T3) = 30
Initially R-TS and W-TS of every item are 0.

S: R1(A) R3(B) W2(A) R2(C) W1(A) W2(B) W3(A) W3(C)
work:
R1(A): TS 10 ≥ W-TS(A) 0 → OK; R-TS(A) = 10
R3(B): TS 30 ≥ W-TS(B) 0 → OK; R-TS(B) = 30
W2(A): TS 20 ≥ R-TS(A) 10 and ≥ W-TS(A) 0 → OK; W-TS(A) = 20
R2(C): TS 20 ≥ W-TS(C) 0 → OK; R-TS(C) = 20
W1(A): TS 10 < W-TS(A) 20 → REJECT → T1 rolled back
W2(B): TS 20 < R-TS(B) 30 → REJECT → T2 rolled back
W3(A): TS 30 ≥ R-TS(A) 10 and ≥ W-TS(A) 20 → OK; W-TS(A) = 30
W3(C): TS 30 ≥ R-TS(C) 20 and ≥ W-TS(C) 0 → OK; W-TS(C) = 30
Rolled back: T1 and T2; T3 completes.
(Python simulator; the result is the same whether or not the timestamps set by T2's earlier operations are undone, and no transaction read a value written by T1 or T2.)
tip: With Thomas' write rule, W1(A) would only be ignored (it is an obsolete write), and only T2 would be rolled back.

q: A power failure wipes out the contents of main memory, but the data on disk is not damaged. This kind of failure is classified as a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Loss of volatile storage (main memory) while non-volatile storage (disk) survives is a system crash.
concept: Failure types: (1) Transaction failure – one transaction cannot continue because of a logical error (bad input, constraint violation) or a system error (for example, it is chosen as a deadlock victim). (2) System crash – a hardware fault, power failure or software bug that loses the contents of volatile storage (RAM, buffers) while the disk survives. (3) Disk failure – a head crash or similar damage destroys data on disk; recovery then needs a backup (archival dump) on other media plus the log.
why: A — Correct. A power cut loses main memory but not the disk, which is exactly a system crash. Recovery uses the log to undo incomplete transactions and redo committed ones.
B — Wrong. A transaction failure affects one transaction (for example, division by zero or a constraint violation). The rest of the system and its memory keep running.
C — Wrong. A disk failure means the data on disk itself is lost or damaged. The stem says the disk is not damaged.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: System crash = RAM lost, disk safe. Disk failure = disk lost → restore from backup + log.

q: The rule that all log records for a change must be written to stable storage before the changed data block itself is written to the database on disk is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This is the write-ahead logging (WAL) rule: log first, data later.
concept: Write-ahead logging (WAL) says: before a block of data in main memory is written to the database on disk, all log records for the changes in that block must already be on stable storage; and a transaction counts as committed only after its <T commit> log record is on stable storage. Because the log always holds the old value before the disk changes, an incomplete change can always be undone, and committed changes can always be redone.
why: A — Wrong. Shadow paging avoids a log for undo: it keeps a shadow page table pointing to the old pages and writes changes to new pages. It is a different recovery technique, not a rule about the order of log and data writes.
B — Correct. WAL is exactly the rule 'write the log record ahead of the data'.
C — Wrong. A checkpoint periodically writes all modified buffer blocks and a <checkpoint> log record to reduce recovery work. It is not the rule about the order of log and data writes.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: WAL: Log before Data.

q: In the deferred database modification (deferred-update) technique, which operations are needed to recover from a system crash?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Deferred update never writes uncommitted changes to the database, so no undo is needed; committed changes may need redo. It is a NO-UNDO/REDO method.
concept: Deferred update: a transaction's writes are recorded only in the log (and local buffers) until it commits; the database on disk is updated only after commit. After a crash, uncommitted transactions have changed nothing on disk, so they need no undo — they are simply ignored (and restarted). Committed transactions may not have reached the disk, so they are redone from the log. Immediate update, by contrast, may write uncommitted changes to disk, so it needs both UNDO and REDO.
why: A — Wrong. Undo is needed only when uncommitted changes can reach the disk, which deferred update never allows.
B — Wrong. Undo plus redo is the immediate-update method (UNDO/REDO), where changes may reach the disk before commit.
C — Correct. Only committed transactions ever change the database, so recovery just redoes them (the log may even hold only their new values).
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Deferred = NO-UNDO/REDO. Immediate = UNDO/REDO. Shadow paging = NO-UNDO/NO-REDO.

q: The log below uses the immediate-update technique; {T2} in the checkpoint record lists the transactions active at the checkpoint. Using the classical checkpoint-based UNDO/REDO recovery algorithm, which transactions must be redone and which must be undone?
opts: Redo T1, T2, T3; undo T4
More than one of the above
exp: T1 committed before the checkpoint, so it needs nothing. T2 and T3 committed after it and are redone; T4 never committed and is undone.
concept: At a checkpoint the DBMS writes all modified buffer blocks to disk and writes <checkpoint L> to the log, where L lists the active transactions. After a crash, only the transactions in L and those that started after the checkpoint need attention: committed ones go into the redo list, those without a commit record into the undo list. Undo uses old values (scanning the log backward); redo uses new values (scanning forward).
why: A — Correct. T2 (active at the checkpoint) and T3 both have commit records, so they are redone; T4 has no commit record, so it is undone.
B — Wrong. T1 committed before the checkpoint. The checkpoint already forced its changes to disk, so it does not need to be redone.
C — Wrong. T2 has a <T2 commit> record, so it must be redone, not undone. Being active at the checkpoint does not make a transaction a loser.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Log at the time of crash (immediate update; format <T, item, old value, new value>):
<T1 start>
<T1, A, 100, 150>
<T2 start>
<T1 commit>
<T2, B, 200, 250>
<checkpoint {T2}>
<T3 start>
<T3, C, 300, 350>
<T2, D, 400, 450>
<T2 commit>
<T4 start>
<T4, A, 150, 180>
<T3 commit>
--- system crash ---
work:
Last checkpoint: <checkpoint {T2}> → T2 was active.
Transactions to consider: T2 (active at the checkpoint) + T3, T4 (started after it).
T1 committed before the checkpoint → its changes were forced to disk → ignore.
T2: <T2 commit> present → redo.
T3: <T3 commit> present → redo.
T4: no commit → undo (A goes back to 150).
Redo list = {T2, T3}; undo list = {T4}.
tip: Committed before the checkpoint → ignore; committed after → redo; never committed → undo.

q: After recovery with the immediate-update UNDO/REDO method, what are the values of X, Y and Z in the database?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: T3's write to X is undone (X back to 50), and T2's writes are redone (Y = 60, Z = 70).
concept: Undo restores the OLD value of each update made by an uncommitted transaction; redo re-applies the NEW value of each update made by a committed transaction. The result is as if committed transactions ran completely and uncommitted ones never ran. Here T1 and T2 committed and T3 did not.
why: A — Wrong. X = 90 is T3's uncommitted value. Since T3 has no commit record, its write must be undone.
B — Correct. X goes back to 50 (T1's committed value, which is the old value in T3's log record); Y = 60 and Z = 70 come from redoing the committed T2.
C — Wrong. Y = 30 would mean T2's update of Y was undone, but T2 committed, so Y must be 60.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Log at the time of crash (immediate update; format <T, item, old value, new value>):
<T1 start>
<T1, X, 20, 50>
<T2 start>
<T2, Y, 30, 60>
<T1 commit>
<checkpoint {T2}>
<T3 start>
<T3, X, 50, 90>
<T2, Z, 40, 70>
<T2 commit>
--- system crash ---
work:
Consider T2 (in the checkpoint list) and T3 (started after the checkpoint).
T1 committed before the checkpoint → X = 50 is already on disk.
T2 has <T2 commit> → redo: Y = 60, Z = 70.
T3 has no commit → undo: X = old value 50.
Final: X = 50, Y = 60, Z = 70.
(Checked by simulating every possible set of blocks flushed after the checkpoint, with both undo-first and redo-first orders: always X = 50, Y = 60, Z = 70.)

q: Which of the following are benefits of taking checkpoints in log-based recovery?
opts: After a crash, the system does not have to scan and process the entire log from its beginning
Transactions that committed before the last checkpoint do not need to be redone
Once a checkpoint is taken, undoing uncommitted transactions never needs log records written before the checkpoint
More than one of the above
exp: Checkpoints shorten the log scan and avoid redoing transactions committed before the checkpoint, but undo may still need older log records.
concept: A checkpoint: (1) writes all log records in main memory to stable storage, (2) writes all modified buffer blocks to disk, (3) writes <checkpoint L>, where L lists the active transactions. Benefits: recovery does not scan the whole log, and work committed before the checkpoint needs no redo. Transactions in L may still need undo using log records from before the checkpoint.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Without checkpoints, recovery would have to search the whole log. With checkpoints, it starts from the last checkpoint (going back only as far as needed for the transactions active at that time).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. At the checkpoint all modified blocks were forced to disk, so the changes of transactions committed before it are already safe.
