C — Wrong. False. A transaction that was active at the checkpoint may have made updates before it; undoing them needs the old values in log records written BEFORE the checkpoint.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about shadow paging is NOT correct?
opts: It keeps two page tables: a current page table and a shadow page table
A transaction commits by making the current page table the new shadow page table in one atomic step
After a crash, committed transactions must be redone using the log
More than one of the above
exp: Shadow paging needs neither undo nor redo after a crash (NO-UNDO/NO-REDO), so statement C is wrong.
concept: Shadow paging: when a transaction starts, the current page table is copied into a shadow page table, which is kept on disk and not changed during the transaction. Updated pages are written to NEW disk pages, and only the current page table points to them. Commit = atomically switch the database pointer so that the current page table becomes the shadow. Crash before commit: discard the current table; the shadow still describes the old database. Crash after commit: the new pages are already in place. Drawbacks: data gets scattered on disk, old pages need garbage collection, and copying page tables is costly.
why: A — Wrong. This IS correct: the shadow table describes the database as it was before the transaction; the current table includes its changes. So it does not fit a NOT question.
B — Wrong. This IS correct: commit is a single atomic pointer switch, after which the current table becomes the shadow table. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Correct. This is NOT correct: after a crash, the shadow page table simply describes the last committed state, so nothing needs to be redone or undone.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Shadow paging = NO-UNDO/NO-REDO; its price is scattered data and garbage collection.

q: After recovery using the deferred-update technique, what are the values of A and C?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Redo T1 and T3 and ignore the uncommitted T2: A = 50 and C = 30, which is not among A–C.
concept: With deferred update, the log keeps only new values, because an uncommitted transaction has never touched the database and so never needs undo. Recovery redoes the committed transactions in log order. Redo is idempotent (doing it twice gives the same result), so it is safe even if some of the changes had already reached the disk.
why: A — Wrong. A = 70 is T2's value, but T2 never committed, so under deferred update its write never reaches the database.
B — Wrong. C = 40 is the value before T3. T3 committed, so its new value C = 30 must be redone.
C — Wrong. A = 10 is the value before T1. T1 committed, so A = 50 must be redone.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. After redoing T1 and T3 and ignoring T2: A = 50 and C = 30 (and B = 80). This pair is not listed.
code:
Deferred-update log at the time of crash (format <T, item, new value>):
<T1 start>
<T1, A, 50>
<T1, B, 80>
<T1 commit>
<T2 start>
<T2, A, 70>
<T3 start>
<T3, C, 30>
<T3 commit>
--- system crash ---
Values on disk before T1 started: A = 10, B = 20, C = 40
work:
Committed: T1, T3 → redo them in log order.
Redo T1: A = 50, B = 80.
T2 has no commit → ignored (deferred update never wrote it to disk; no undo needed).
Redo T3: C = 30.
Final: A = 50, B = 80, C = 30.

q: A file organization stores the records of two or more relations in the same disk block — for example, each DEPARTMENT record together with its EMPLOYEE records — so that joins on department are fast. It is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Storing related records of different relations together in the same block is multitable clustering file organization.
concept: Common file organizations: Heap (pile) – a record goes anywhere there is space; no order. Sequential (ordered) – records are kept sorted by a search key. Hashing – a hash function on some attribute decides the block (bucket) of a record. Multitable clustering – related records of several relations (for example, linked by a foreign key) are stored together in the same block, which speeds up joins but slows queries that need only one of the relations.
why: A — Correct. Keeping DEPARTMENT and its EMPLOYEE records in the same block is exactly multitable clustering.
B — Wrong. A heap file puts records wherever free space exists, with no attempt to place related records together.
C — Wrong. A sequential file keeps the records of one file sorted by a search key; it does not mix records of different relations in one block.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A file has 10,000 fixed-length records of 120 bytes each. The block size is 2048 bytes and records are unspanned (a record may not cross a block boundary). How many blocks does the file need?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: bfr = ⌊2048/120⌋ = 17, so the file needs ⌈10000/17⌉ = 589 blocks, which is not listed.
concept: Blocking factor (bfr) = number of whole records that fit in one block = ⌊block size / record size⌋. With unspanned records, the leftover bytes in each block are wasted. Number of blocks = ⌈number of records / bfr⌉ (round up, because a partly filled last block is still a block).
why: A — Wrong. 586 = ⌈10000 × 120 / 2048⌉ treats the file as one long stream of bytes, which is valid only for spanned records. With unspanned records each block wastes 8 bytes, so more blocks are needed.
B — Wrong. 625 = 10000 / 16 uses a wrong blocking factor of 16; the correct value is ⌊2048 / 120⌋ = 17.
C — Wrong. 17 is the blocking factor (records per block), not the number of blocks.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The file needs ⌈10000 / 17⌉ = 589 blocks.
work:
Blocking factor bfr = ⌊B / R⌋ = ⌊2048 / 120⌋ = ⌊17.07⌋ = 17 records per block.
Unused space per block = 2048 − 17 × 120 = 8 bytes.
Number of blocks b = ⌈r / bfr⌉ = ⌈10000 / 17⌉ = ⌈588.2⌉ = 589.
tip: Unspanned: floor for records per block, ceiling for number of blocks.

q: A data file of 1000 blocks is sorted on its key field. About how many block accesses does a binary search on that key need, in the worst case, to find a record?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Binary search on b ordered blocks needs about ⌈log2 b⌉ = ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10 block accesses.
concept: If a file is ordered on a field, a binary search on that field reads about ⌈log2 b⌉ blocks for a file of b blocks. A linear search through an unordered (heap) file reads b/2 blocks on average for a key field (if the record exists), and all b blocks if it does not exist or the field is not a key.
why: A — Wrong. 500 = b/2 is the AVERAGE cost of a LINEAR search for a key value, not of binary search.
B — Correct. ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10, because 2^10 = 1024 is the first power of two that is at least 1000.
C — Wrong. 1000 = b is the cost of a full linear scan (for example, an unsuccessful search of an unordered file).
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Binary search halves the remaining blocks at each step.
Block accesses ≈ ⌈log2 b⌉ = ⌈log2 1000⌉.
2^9 = 512 < 1000 ≤ 1024 = 2^10 → ⌈log2 1000⌉ = 10.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. In a heap (unordered) file, a new record is placed wherever there is space (usually at the end), so insertion is cheap.
II. In a sequential (ordered) file, insertion is cheap because no order has to be maintained.
III. Searching a heap file for a record with a given key value needs a linear search, reading about half the blocks on average.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and III are true. II is false: an ordered file must keep its records in sorted order, so insertion is expensive.
concept: Heap file: fast insertion, slow search (linear: about b/2 blocks on average for an existing key, b blocks otherwise). Sequential (ordered) file: fast binary search and fast ordered reading on the ordering key, but insertion and deletion are expensive because records must be moved to keep the order (often an overflow area is used and the file is reorganized from time to time).
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is false: an ordered file must keep its sort order, so a new record has to go into its correct position, moving other records or using overflow blocks.
B — Wrong. This again includes the false statement II.
C — Correct. I is true (a heap file just appends) and III is true (no order, so only linear search, about b/2 blocks on average when the key exists).
D — Wrong. Only option C gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option C is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An index that has an index entry for every search-key value that occurs in the data file is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A dense index has an entry for every search-key value; a sparse index has entries for only some values (for example, one per block).
concept: Dense index: an index record for every search-key value in the file. Sparse (non-dense) index: index records for only some search-key values, typically one per data block (the first key in the block, called the block anchor); it works only when the file is sorted on the search key. Multilevel index: an index built on top of another index (an outer index on the inner index) to cut search cost when the index itself is large.
why: A — Wrong. A sparse index has entries for only SOME search-key values, for example one per block.
B — Correct. 'An entry for every search-key value' is the definition of a dense index.
C — Wrong. Multilevel describes how many levels of index there are (an index on the index), not whether every key value has an entry.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q:
Consider the following statements about indexes:
I. A sparse index can be used only if the data file is sorted on the search key of the index.
II. A primary index on the ordering key field of a sorted file can be sparse, with one entry per data block.
III. A dense index usually needs more space than a sparse index on the same file, but can locate a record faster.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are standard facts about dense and sparse indexes.
concept: A sparse index finds the block whose first key is the largest key ≤ the search value and then searches inside that block, so the file must be in search-key order. That is why the primary index of a sorted file can be sparse (one entry per block, using block anchors). A dense index has more entries (more space and more maintenance on insert and delete) but points straight at the record. Silberschatz–Korth: it is generally faster to locate a record with a dense index, while sparse indices need less space and less maintenance.
why: A — Wrong. Statement III is also correct, so this leaves out a true statement.
B — Wrong. Statement I is also correct, so this leaves out a true statement.
C — Correct. I: a sparse index depends on the file being sorted. II: one entry per block is the classic sparse primary index. III: dense = more space but faster lookup.
D — Wrong. Only option C gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option C is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A sparse primary index with one entry per data block is built on the key field. How many blocks does the index occupy?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 2500 data blocks give 2500 index entries; 256 entries fit in a block, so the index needs ⌈2500/256⌉ = 10 blocks.
concept: Steps for the size of an index: (1) data blocking factor = ⌊B/R⌋; (2) number of data blocks; (3) number of index entries (one per block for a sparse primary index, one per record for a dense index on a key); (4) index blocking factor = ⌊B / entry size⌋, also called the fan-out; (5) index blocks = ⌈entries / index blocking factor⌉.
why: A — Correct. Correct chain: 20 records per block → 2500 data blocks → 2500 index entries → 256 entries per index block → 10 index blocks.
B — Wrong. 196 = ⌈50000 / 256⌉ would be the size of a DENSE index (one entry per record). A sparse primary index needs one entry per data block only.
C — Wrong. 2500 is the number of index ENTRIES (equal to the number of data blocks), not the number of index blocks.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Data file: r = 50,000 records, record size R = 200 bytes, block size B = 4096 bytes, unspanned.
The file is sorted on its key field.
Index entry = key (10 bytes) + block pointer (6 bytes) = 16 bytes.
work:
Data bfr = ⌊4096 / 200⌋ = 20 records per block.
Data blocks b = ⌈50000 / 20⌉ = 2500.
Index entries = one per data block = 2500.
Index bfr = ⌊4096 / 16⌋ = 256 entries per block.
Index blocks = ⌈2500 / 256⌉ = ⌈9.77⌉ = 10.
(Binary search on this index: ⌈log2 10⌉ + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5 block accesses.)

q: Using binary search on this single-level secondary index, how many block accesses are needed to fetch the record with a given SSN?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The dense index has 196 blocks; binary search reads ⌈log2 196⌉ = 8 index blocks, plus 1 data block = 9 accesses.
concept: A secondary index is built on a field that is not the file's ordering field. Because the records are not in order of that field, an index on a key field must be dense (one entry per record). Even though it is larger than a primary index, searching it (log2 of its block count, plus one data block) is far cheaper than a linear search of the data file.
why: A — Wrong. 8 counts only the index blocks read by the binary search and forgets the final access to the data block that holds the record.
B — Correct. ⌈log2 196⌉ = 8 index-block reads + 1 data-block read = 9.
C — Wrong. 1250 = 2500 / 2 is the average cost of a linear search on the data file without any index — exactly what the index saves us from.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Data file: r = 50,000 records, record size R = 200 bytes, block size B = 4096 bytes, unspanned. (2500 data blocks)
The file is NOT sorted on field SSN, which is a key field.
A dense secondary index on SSN has one entry per record; entry = 10-byte key + 6-byte pointer = 16 bytes.
work:
Index entries = 50,000 (one per record).
Index bfr = ⌊4096 / 16⌋ = 256.
Index blocks = ⌈50000 / 256⌉ = ⌈195.3⌉ = 196.
Binary search on the index: ⌈log2 196⌉ = 8 (2^7 = 128 < 196 ≤ 256 = 2^8).
Plus 1 access to read the data block → 8 + 1 = 9.

q: The index is turned into a multilevel index (each higher level indexes the blocks of the level below, until a level fits in one block). How many block accesses are needed to fetch a record through this multilevel index?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: There are two index levels (196 blocks, then 1 block), so a lookup reads 2 index blocks + 1 data block = 3 blocks.
concept: A multilevel index treats the first-level index as an ordered file and builds a sparse index on it, repeating until the top level fits in one block. With fan-out fo, the number of levels is about ⌈log_fo(r1)⌉, where r1 is the number of first-level entries. A lookup reads one block per level plus the data block, which is far less than a binary search (log2) on a single-level index.
why: A — Wrong. 2 is the number of index LEVELS; the data block must also be read, giving 3.
B — Wrong. 9 is the cost of binary search on the single-level index (8 index blocks + 1 data block). The multilevel index is cheaper.
C — Correct. 2 index levels + 1 data block = 3 block accesses.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Dense secondary index on key field SSN of a 50,000-record file: 50,000 entries of 16 bytes each; block size 4096 bytes.
→ index blocking factor (fan-out) fo = 256, first-level index = 196 blocks.
work:
Level 1: 196 blocks (so level 2 needs 196 entries).
Level 2: ⌈196 / 256⌉ = 1 block → top level reached.
Number of levels t = 2 (also t = ⌈log_256 50000⌉ = 2).
Access cost = one block per level + one data block = 2 + 1 = 3.
tip: Multilevel index cost = (number of levels) + 1. Single-level index with binary search = ⌈log2(index blocks)⌉ + 1.

q: Using the definitions of Elmasri–Navathe (primary, clustering and secondary indexes), which statement is NOT correct?
opts: A file can have at most one primary index or one clustering index, but not both
A file can have several secondary indexes
A primary index is built on a non-key ordering field whose values may repeat
More than one of the above
exp: In Elmasri–Navathe, an index on a non-key ordering field is a CLUSTERING index; a primary index is on the ordering KEY field.
concept: Elmasri–Navathe: Primary index – on the ordering key field of a sorted file (unique values); sparse, one entry per block. Clustering index – on an ordering field that is NOT a key (values repeat); one entry per distinct value. Secondary index – on any non-ordering field; a file may have many. Since a file can be physically sorted on only one field, it can have at most one primary or one clustering index. (Silberschatz–Korth use 'primary index' as another name for any clustering index, key or not; this question uses Elmasri–Navathe's terms.)
why: A — Wrong. This IS correct: a file can be physically ordered on only one field, so it can have a primary index (ordering key) or a clustering index (ordering non-key), but not both. So it does not fit a NOT question.
B — Wrong. This IS correct: secondary indexes do not depend on the physical order, so any number of them can be built. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Correct. This is NOT correct in Elmasri–Navathe's terms: an index on a non-key ordering field with repeating values is a clustering index. A primary index needs the ordering field to be a key.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Ordering + key → primary; ordering + non-key → clustering; non-ordering → secondary (Elmasri–Navathe).

q: Which of the following are properties of a B+ tree index?
opts: All leaf nodes are at the same level (the tree is balanced)
Pointers to the data records are stored only in the leaf nodes
The leaf nodes are linked together so that keys can be read in sorted order
More than one of the above
exp: A B+ tree is balanced, keeps record pointers only in its leaves, and links its leaves for sequential access.
concept: B+ tree vs B-tree: both are balanced multiway search trees used for indexes. In a B-tree every key appears once, and internal nodes also carry record pointers. In a B+ tree all keys appear at the leaf level (some are repeated in internal nodes as separators), record pointers are only in the leaves, and the leaves are chained. Because internal nodes carry no record pointers, more keys fit per internal node, so the fan-out is higher and the tree is shallower.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Like a B-tree, a B+ tree is height-balanced: every path from the root to a leaf has the same length.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In a B+ tree, internal nodes hold only keys and tree pointers to guide the search; record (data) pointers appear only in the leaves. (In a B-tree, internal nodes also hold record pointers.)

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each leaf has a pointer to the next leaf, so a range query or an ordered scan can walk along the leaf level.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all properties of a B+ tree, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a B+ tree, the order p of an internal node is the maximum number of tree pointers it can hold (it then holds p − 1 keys). If the block size is 1024 bytes, a key is 10 bytes and a tree (block) pointer is 6 bytes, what is p?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: To find the order of a B+ tree internal node, add the space used by p pointers and p − 1 keys and keep it within the block size: p·P + (p − 1)·K ≤ B. Always round DOWN, because a node must fit in one block. Leaf nodes use a different formula, because they hold record pointers and one next-leaf pointer.
why: A — Wrong. 102 = ⌊1024 / 10⌋ counts only keys and forgets the pointers.
B — Correct. p = 64 is the largest value with 6p + 10(p − 1) ≤ 1024 (it uses 1014 bytes).
C — Wrong. 65 comes from rounding 64.6 up; with 65 pointers and 64 keys the node needs 1030 bytes, which is more than the block.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Order convention matters: here order = maximum number of children (pointers). Always round down.

q: A B+ tree leaf node holds p_leaf pairs of (key, record pointer) plus one pointer to the next leaf. The block size is 1024 bytes, a key is 10 bytes, a record pointer is 7 bytes and a block pointer is 6 bytes. What is the largest possible p_leaf?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 17·p_leaf + 6 ≤ 1024 gives p_leaf ≤ 59.9, so p_leaf = 59.
concept: A B+ tree leaf stores (key, record pointer) pairs and a single pointer to the next leaf, so p_leaf·(K + Pr) + P ≤ B. Internal nodes instead store p tree pointers and p − 1 keys, so the leaf capacity and the internal order are usually different numbers.
why: A — Correct. 59 pairs use 59 × 17 = 1003 bytes, plus 6 for the next-leaf pointer = 1009 bytes, which fits; 60 pairs would not.
B — Wrong. 60 comes from rounding 59.88 up; 60 × 17 + 6 = 1026 bytes, more than the block.
C — Wrong. 64 is the order of an INTERNAL node with these sizes (6p + 10(p − 1) ≤ 1024). Leaves store a 7-byte record pointer with every key, so fewer entries fit.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Leaf node: p_leaf × (key + record pointer) + one next-leaf pointer ≤ block size
p_leaf × (10 + 7) + 6 ≤ 1024
17 p_leaf ≤ 1018
p_leaf ≤ 59.88 → p_leaf = 59
Check: 59 × 17 + 6 = 1009 ≤ 1024 ✓; 60 × 17 + 6 = 1026 > 1024 ✗.

q: Consider a B-tree of order 5, where order means the maximum number of children a node can have. What are the minimum and maximum numbers of keys in a non-root node?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Maximum keys = m − 1 = 4; a non-root node has at least ⌈5/2⌉ = 3 children, so at least 2 keys.
concept: B-tree of order m (convention: m = maximum number of children): every node has at most m children and m − 1 keys; every non-root node has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children (if internal) and at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys; the root, if not a leaf, has at least 2 children (so at least 1 key); all leaves are at the same level.
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the minimum number of CHILDREN (⌈5/2⌉) and 5 is the maximum number of children. The question asks for keys, which are one less.
B — Wrong. The minimum of 2 is right, but a node with at most 5 children can hold at most 4 keys, not 5.
C — Correct. Keys range from ⌈5/2⌉ − 1 = 2 to 5 − 1 = 4.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Order m = 5 → at most 5 children → at most m − 1 = 4 keys.
Every non-root internal node has at least ⌈m/2⌉ = ⌈2.5⌉ = 3 children → at least 3 − 1 = 2 keys.
(A non-root leaf also holds at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 = 2 keys.)
Answer: minimum 2, maximum 4.
tip: Keys = children − 1. Order m (max children): a non-root node has ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 to m − 1 keys.

q: In the Cormen (CLRS) convention, a B-tree has minimum degree t: every non-root node has between t − 1 and 2t − 1 keys, and the root has at least 1 key. What is the minimum number of keys in a B-tree with t = 3 and height h = 2 (the root is at depth 0 and the leaves are at depth 2)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The sparsest tree has 1 + 2×2 + 6×2 = 17 keys, matching 2t^h − 1 = 17; 17 is not listed.
concept: In a B-tree of minimum degree t, the root has at least 1 key (2 children) and every other node at least t − 1 keys (t children if internal). Counting the sparsest tree of height h gives n ≥ 2t^h − 1, i.e. h ≤ log_t((n + 1)/2). This is why B-tree height grows only logarithmically. (The other common convention uses 'order m' = maximum number of children; minimum degree t = 3 corresponds to m = 2t = 6.)
why: A — Wrong. 26 = 3^3 − 1 treats the root like the other nodes (2 keys, 3 children). The root may have just 1 key and 2 children, so the minimum is smaller.
B — Wrong. 18 = 2t^h forgets the '− 1' in the bound n ≥ 2t^h − 1.
C — Wrong. 8 = 3^2 − 1 counts only two levels of nodes, but a tree of height 2 has three levels (depths 0, 1 and 2).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The minimum number of keys is 2t^h − 1 = 2 × 3^2 − 1 = 17, which is not listed.
work:
Sparsest tree: the root has 1 key and 2 children.
Depth 1: 2 nodes, each with t − 1 = 2 keys and t = 3 children → 4 keys, 6 children.
Depth 2 (leaves): 6 nodes × 2 keys = 12 keys.
Total = 1 + 4 + 12 = 17.
Formula (CLRS): n ≥ 2t^h − 1 = 2 × 9 − 1 = 17.
tip: CLRS: minimum degree t → each non-root node has t − 1 to 2t − 1 keys; n ≥ 2t^h − 1.

q: A B-tree has order 4, where order means the maximum number of children of a node. What is the maximum number of keys it can store if it has exactly 3 levels (the root, one middle level and the leaf level)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With every node full: 1 + 4 + 16 = 21 nodes × 3 keys = 63 keys = m^L − 1.
concept: When every node of a B-tree of order m is full, level i holds m^(i−1) nodes, each with m − 1 keys. For L levels the total is (m − 1)(1 + m + … + m^(L−1)) = m^L − 1. This upper bound, together with the lower bound from minimum fill, gives the height bounds of a B-tree.
why: B — Wrong. 64 = 4^3 forgets the '− 1' in the formula m^L − 1. A full tree has 1 + 4 + 16 = 21 nodes with 3 keys each, i.e. 63 keys.
C — Wrong. 48 counts only the keys in the leaf level. In a B-tree, internal nodes also store keys (unlike a B+ tree, where every key is repeated in the leaves).
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Each node: at most 4 children and 3 keys.
Level 1 (root): 1 node → 3 keys.
Level 2: 4 nodes → 12 keys.
Level 3 (leaves): 16 nodes → 48 keys.
Total = 3 + 12 + 48 = 63 = 4^3 − 1.

q: In static hashing, which of the following can cause bucket overflow?
opts: Too few buckets for the number of records
Skew: many records hash to the same bucket (for example, many records share one search-key value, or the hash function is not uniform)
Building a dense index on the same file
More than one of the above
exp: Bucket overflow comes from insufficient buckets or from skew; building an index is unrelated.
concept: In static hashing, a hash function h(K) maps each search-key value to one of a FIXED number of buckets (disk blocks). Overflow happens when a bucket has no room for a new record: either there are too few buckets, or the records are skewed. It is handled with overflow buckets chained to the full bucket (overflow chaining). Because the number of buckets is fixed, performance degrades as the file grows; dynamic hashing (extendible, linear) solves this.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. If the number of buckets was chosen too small for the actual number of records, buckets fill up and overflow.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Even with enough buckets in total, a skewed distribution can overload some buckets while others stay nearly empty.
C — Wrong. An index is a separate structure; it does not change how many records the hash function places in each bucket.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about extendible hashing are correct?
opts: It uses a directory (bucket address table) of 2^d entries, where d is the global depth
Several directory entries may point to the same bucket
Every split of a bucket doubles the size of the directory
More than one of the above
exp: Extendible hashing uses a 2^d-entry directory whose entries can share buckets; the directory doubles only when a full bucket's local depth equals the global depth.
concept: Extendible hashing is a dynamic hashing method. Global depth d: the number of hash bits used to index the directory. Local depth d' of a bucket: the number of bits its records have in common. On overflow: if d' < d, split the bucket into two (each with local depth d' + 1) and fix the pointers; if d' = d, first double the directory (d becomes d + 1), then split. Linear hashing is another dynamic method that grows the file one bucket at a time without a directory.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The first (or last) d bits of the hash value index a directory of 2^d bucket pointers; d is the global depth.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A bucket whose local depth d' is smaller than d is shared by 2^(d − d') directory entries.

C — Wrong. False. The directory doubles only when the overflowing bucket's local depth equals the global depth. If the local depth is smaller, the bucket is split and only some directory pointers change.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a dynamic hashing technique?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Static hashing uses a fixed number of buckets; overflow chaining only patches overflow. Extendible and linear hashing are dynamic.
concept: Dynamic hashing techniques let the number of buckets grow (and shrink) with the file. Extendible hashing uses a directory that can double. Linear hashing has no directory: it splits buckets one by one in a fixed (linear) order and uses a pair of hash functions. Static hashing fixes the number of buckets when the file is created; overflow buckets chained to full buckets keep it working, but it gets slower as the chains grow.
why: A — Wrong. Extendible hashing IS dynamic: the directory doubles and buckets split as the file grows. So it does not fit the NOT question.
B — Wrong. Linear hashing IS dynamic: it adds buckets one at a time in linear order. So it does not fit the NOT question.
C — Correct. Static hashing keeps a fixed number of buckets; chaining overflow buckets does not change that number. So it is NOT dynamic.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which RAID level keeps an identical copy of every disk on a second disk (disk mirroring)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: RAID 1 is mirroring: every write goes to two disks.
concept: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines several disks. RAID 0: block striping, no redundancy — fastest, but one disk failure loses data. RAID 1: mirroring (often combined with striping as RAID 1+0) — every block is stored on two disks; high reliability, 50% usable space; good for logs and frequently updated data. RAID 5: block-interleaved distributed parity — parity blocks are spread over all disks; survives one disk failure; usable space (n − 1)/n.
why: A — Wrong. RAID 0 only stripes data across disks for speed and keeps no copy, so it has no redundancy.
B — Correct. RAID 1 writes every block to two disks (a mirror), so either disk can serve the data if the other fails.
C — Wrong. RAID 5 protects data with parity blocks spread across all disks, not with full copies.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A RAID 5 array is built from 5 disks of 2 TB each. What is its usable storage capacity?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: RAID 5 gives up one disk's worth of space to parity: (5 − 1) × 2 = 8 TB, which is not listed.
concept: Usable capacity with n equal disks of size s: RAID 0 → n·s (no redundancy); RAID 1 (mirroring) → n·s/2; RAID 5 (single distributed parity) → (n − 1)·s, survives one disk failure; RAID 6 (double parity) → (n − 2)·s, survives two disk failures.
why: A — Wrong. 10 TB = 5 × 2 TB is the raw total, which only RAID 0 gives (no parity).
B — Wrong. 5 TB = half of the raw space, which is what mirroring (RAID 1) would give.
C — Wrong. 6 TB = (5 − 2) × 2 TB is the RAID 6 figure (two parity blocks per stripe).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. RAID 5 usable capacity = (n − 1) × disk size = 4 × 2 TB = 8 TB.
work:
RAID 5 stores one parity block per stripe, spread over all disks.
In total, parity uses the space of 1 disk.
Usable = (n − 1) × disk size = (5 − 1) × 2 TB = 8 TB.
tip: RAID 5 loses one disk to parity; RAID 6 loses two; RAID 1 loses half.

q: In a distributed database, the EMPLOYEE relation is split so that the rows of Patna employees are stored at the Patna site and the rows of Delhi employees at the Delhi site. This is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Splitting a relation into subsets of ROWS (by a selection condition) is horizontal fragmentation.
concept: Fragmentation divides a relation into pieces stored at different sites. Horizontal fragmentation: each fragment is a subset of rows chosen by a condition (σ city = 'Patna'); the relation is rebuilt by UNION. Vertical fragmentation: each fragment is a subset of columns (π), and every fragment must include the primary key (or a tuple-id) so the relation can be rebuilt by a natural JOIN. Hybrid (mixed) fragmentation applies both. Replication is different: it stores copies of the same data at several sites.
why: A — Correct. Each site gets a subset of ROWS chosen by a condition on city: that is horizontal fragmentation.
B — Wrong. Vertical fragmentation would split the COLUMNS (for example, name and address at one site, salary at another), not the rows.
C — Wrong. Replication keeps COPIES of the same data at more than one site. Here each row is stored at only one site.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Horizontal = rows (σ, rebuild by UNION); vertical = columns (π + key, rebuild by JOIN).

q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of replicating data at several sites of a distributed database?
opts: Higher availability when a site fails
Faster reads, because a query can use a nearby copy
More than one of the above
exp: Replication helps availability and read speed, but makes updates more costly, because every copy must be updated consistently.
concept: Replication means storing copies of a relation (or fragment) at more than one site. Advantages: availability (if one site fails, another copy can be used) and increased parallelism, i.e. faster reads (queries can run at a nearby site, many in parallel). Disadvantage: increased overhead on update — every replica must be changed, and keeping the copies consistent needs extra protocols (for example primary copy, two-phase commit).
why: A — Correct. This is NOT an advantage: with replication each update must be applied to every copy and coordinated across sites, so updates become MORE complex and costly.
B — Wrong. This IS an advantage: if one site fails, the data is still available from another copy. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Wrong. This IS an advantage: reads can be served locally and in parallel at several sites. So it does not fit a NOT question.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Replication: reads get better, updates get worse.

q: What are the two phases of the two-phase commit (2PC) protocol used for distributed transactions?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 2PC has a prepare (voting) phase and a commit (decision) phase. None of A–C names them.
concept: Two-phase commit makes a distributed transaction commit at all sites or at none. Phase 1 (prepare / voting): the coordinator sends <prepare T>; each participant force-writes its log and replies <ready T> (vote yes) or <abort T> (vote no). Phase 2 (commit / decision): if all voted ready, the coordinator logs and sends <commit T>; if any voted no (or did not reply in time), it sends <abort T>. Each participant then commits or aborts and acknowledges.
why: A — Wrong. Growing and shrinking are the phases of two-phase LOCKING (2PL), a concurrency-control protocol.
B — Wrong. Read, validation (and write) are the phases of the optimistic (validation-based) concurrency-control protocol.
C — Wrong. Analysis, redo (and undo) are the passes of the ARIES recovery algorithm after a crash.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The phases of 2PC are (1) the prepare (voting) phase and (2) the commit (decision) phase.
tip: Do not mix up the 'two-phase' protocols: 2PL = growing/shrinking (locks); 2PC = prepare/commit (distributed commit).

q: In a distributed database, users can write a query on a relation without knowing at which site (computer) its data is physically stored. This property is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Not needing to know WHERE the data is stored is location transparency.
concept: Distributed databases hide details from users. Fragmentation transparency: users need not know that a relation is split into fragments. Replication transparency: users need not know that copies exist at several sites. Location transparency: users need not know the site where the data is stored. Naming transparency: each data item has a unique name that does not depend on its site.
why: A — Wrong. Fragmentation transparency hides the fact that a relation is divided into pieces; the stem is about the storage site. (A system with fragmentation transparency usually hides the sites too, but the property whose name and definition is 'users need not know where the data is stored' is location transparency.)
B — Wrong. Replication transparency hides the existence of multiple copies; the stem is about where the data lives.
C — Correct. Hiding the physical site of the data is location transparency.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In two-phase commit, the coordinator of transaction T fails. Every active participant has <ready T> in its log, and none of them has <commit T> or <abort T>. What must the participants do?
opts: Commit T, since every active participant voted ready
Abort T, since the coordinator has failed
Wait until the coordinator recovers; T stays blocked
More than one of the above
exp: Since every active participant has only <ready T>, the coordinator might have decided either way; the participants must wait (the blocking problem of 2PC).
concept: Once a participant votes ready, it promises to obey the coordinator's decision and may not decide alone. If the coordinator fails and no active site knows the decision, the participants can neither safely commit (the coordinator might have decided abort, for example because a site that has since failed voted no) nor safely abort (it might have decided commit, and some failed site may already have committed). They keep their locks and wait: this is the blocking problem of 2PC. Three-phase commit (3PC) was designed to reduce blocking.
why: A — Wrong. Unsafe: the coordinator may have received a 'no' vote from a site that has since failed and decided to abort. Committing could make the sites disagree.
B — Wrong. Unsafe: the coordinator may already have decided commit, and a site that has since failed may have committed. Aborting could make the sites disagree.
C — Correct. With only <ready T> records at every active site, the decision is unknown, so the participants must block until the coordinator recovers.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Rules when the coordinator fails (Silberschatz–Korth):
1. Some active site has <commit T> → commit T.
2. Some active site has <abort T> → abort T.
3. Some active site has no <ready T> → the coordinator cannot have decided commit → abort T.
4. Otherwise (all active sites have only <ready T>) → the decision cannot be known → wait for the coordinator (blocking).
Here case 4 applies → wait.

q: According to W. H. Inmon's definition, which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a data warehouse?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Inmon defined a data warehouse as subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and NON-volatile. 'Volatile' is the opposite.
concept: Inmon: a data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile collection of data in support of management's decision-making. Subject-oriented: organized around subjects such as customer, product or sales. Integrated: data from many sources is cleaned and made consistent. Time-variant: it keeps history (data is tied to time periods). Non-volatile: data is loaded and read, not updated or deleted by day-to-day transactions.
why: A — Wrong. Subject-oriented IS a characteristic: the warehouse is organized by business subjects, not by applications. So it does not fit a NOT question.
B — Correct. A warehouse is NON-volatile: once loaded, data is normally not changed. 'Volatile' is therefore NOT a characteristic.
C — Wrong. Time-variant IS a characteristic: the warehouse stores historical data over long periods. So it does not fit a NOT question.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Inmon's four: Subject-oriented, Integrated, Time-variant, Non-volatile.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. OLTP systems handle a large number of short transactions that read and update current data.
II. OLAP queries are usually complex and work on large amounts of historical, summarized data.
III. OLAP databases are usually kept highly normalized and are updated row by row in real time by clerks.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II describe OLTP and OLAP correctly; III describes OLTP-style operation, not OLAP.
concept: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing): day-to-day operations such as bookings and payments; many short read/write transactions; current, detailed data; highly normalized schemas; fast response for many users. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing): decision support; fewer but complex queries (aggregation, roll-up, drill-down, slicing) over large historical data; mostly read-only, loaded in batches by ETL; often denormalized star or snowflake schemas.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also correct, so 'I only' leaves out a true statement.
B — Correct. I describes OLTP and II describes OLAP correctly. III is false.
C — Wrong. Statement III is false: OLAP data is loaded in batches (not updated row by row by clerks) and is often denormalized for fast analysis.
D — Wrong. Only option B gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option B is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A data warehouse schema has one central fact table (for example SALES) connected directly to denormalized dimension tables such as TIME, PRODUCT and STORE. This schema is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: One fact table with directly attached, denormalized dimension tables is a star schema.
concept: Fact table: stores measures (quantity, amount) and foreign keys to the dimensions. Dimension tables: describe the context (time, product, store). Star schema: one fact table, each dimension a single denormalized table, so the diagram looks like a star. Snowflake schema: dimension tables are normalized into several related tables (for example PRODUCT → CATEGORY), so the diagram branches like a snowflake. Fact constellation (galaxy): several fact tables share dimension tables.
why: A — Wrong. In a snowflake schema the dimensions are normalized into extra tables; the stem says the dimensions are denormalized and attached directly.
B — Correct. A single fact table at the centre with denormalized dimension tables around it is the star schema.
C — Wrong. A fact constellation has SEVERAL fact tables sharing dimensions; here there is only one fact table.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Star = denormalized dimensions; snowflake = normalized dimensions.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. ETL stands for Extract, Transform and Load, the process that brings data from source systems into a data warehouse.
II. A data mart is a smaller warehouse focused on one subject area or department.
III. Data mining means entering the day's sales transactions into the operational database.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are correct. Data mining is discovering hidden patterns in large data sets, not data entry.
concept: ETL: Extract data from sources (OLTP databases, files), Transform it (clean, convert, integrate, summarize), and Load it into the warehouse. Data mart: a subset of warehouse data for one department or subject (for example, a sales mart). Data mining (knowledge discovery): finding useful patterns such as association rules ('customers who buy bread also buy butter'), classification and clustering in large amounts of data.
why: A — Correct. I gives the correct meaning of ETL, and II the correct meaning of a data mart. III is false.
B — Wrong. This includes statement III, which is false: entering daily transactions is OLTP work, not data mining.
C — Wrong. This includes the false statement III and leaves out the true statement I.
D — Wrong. Only option A gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option A is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about NoSQL systems are correct?
opts: Apache Cassandra is a column-family (wide-column) store
By the CAP theorem, a distributed data store can always guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance at the same time
More than one of the above
exp: Neo4j is a graph database and Cassandra a column-family store; the CAP theorem says all three of C, A and P cannot be guaranteed together.
concept: NoSQL ('not only SQL') systems drop the fixed relational schema to scale out across many machines. Main types: key-value (Redis, Amazon DynamoDB), document (MongoDB, CouchDB – JSON-like documents), column-family/wide-column (Cassandra, HBase) and graph (Neo4j). CAP theorem (Brewer): of Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance, a distributed system can fully guarantee at most two; since network partitions cannot be ruled out, a system must choose between consistency and availability during a partition. Many NoSQL systems favour availability with eventual consistency (BASE).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Neo4j stores data as nodes and relationships (edges) with properties, which is the graph data model.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Cassandra groups columns into column families and stores rows that can have different sets of columns, which is the wide-column model.
C — Wrong. The CAP theorem says the opposite: when a network partition happens, a distributed system must give up either consistency or availability; it cannot guarantee all three at once.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: NoSQL types with examples: key-value – Redis; document – MongoDB; column-family – Cassandra, HBase; graph – Neo4j.

q: In an object-oriented database, every object has a unique, system-generated identifier that does not change during the object's lifetime and does not depend on its attribute values. It is called the
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Object identity in an OODBMS is provided by an immutable, system-generated object identifier (OID).
concept: Object-oriented databases (OODBMS) store objects as in object-oriented programming. Key features: object identity (OID), complex objects (attributes can be sets, lists or other objects), encapsulation (data together with methods), classes and inheritance, and the ODMG standard with its query language OQL. Unlike a primary key, an OID is not visible business data and never changes, even if all attribute values change.
why: A — Correct. The OID is generated by the system, is unique, never changes and does not depend on the object's values — exactly what the stem describes.

B — Wrong. A primary key is made of attribute values chosen by the designer (like a roll number); it is visible data and can, in principle, be changed. It is a relational concept, not object identity.
C — Wrong. A foreign key is an attribute that refers to a key of another (or the same) relation; it does not identify the object itself.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The keys shown are inserted, in that order, into an empty B+ tree of order 4 (every node holds at most 3 keys; an internal node has at most 4 children). Split rules: an overflowing leaf (4 keys) splits into two leaves of 2 keys each, and the smallest key of the new right leaf is COPIED into the parent. An overflowing internal node (4 keys) keeps its 2 smallest keys, MOVES its third key up to the parent, and puts its largest key in a new right node. After all ten insertions, how many levels does the tree have, and what does the root hold?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Inserting 50 splits the leaf [35, 40, 45, 50] and copies 45 up; the root [15, 25, 35, 45] then overflows, keeps [15, 25], gives [45] to a new right node and moves 35 up into a new root. The tree has 3 levels with root [35].
concept: In a B+ tree every key is stored in a leaf; internal nodes hold only separator keys that guide the search. When a leaf overflows, it splits and a COPY of the first key of the new right leaf goes up (the key stays in the leaf). When an internal node overflows, it also splits, but its middle key MOVES up and is not kept below. If the root splits, a new root is created and the tree becomes one level taller; this is the only way a B+ tree grows in height, so all leaves stay at the same level.
why: A — Correct. The last insertion (50) splits a leaf and then the root, so a new root [35] is created above the internal nodes [15, 25] and [45]: 3 levels.

B — Wrong. Root [25] would come from the other internal-split convention (the left node keeps only 1 key and the 2nd key moves up). The question says the left node keeps its 2 smallest keys and the THIRD key, 35, moves up.
C — Wrong. This is the tree after the first 9 insertions. Inserting 50 overflows the leaf [35, 40, 45], and the key copied up (45) overflows the root, so the tree grows to 3 levels.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Leaf split: copy up. Internal split: move up. A B+ tree grows taller only when the root splits.

q: Extendible hashing uses h(k) = k mod 32, written as a 5-bit binary number. The directory is indexed by the LOW-ORDER (rightmost) d bits of h(k), where d is the global depth. A bucket holds at most 2 keys. At the start d = 1 and there are two empty buckets, each of local depth 1. When a key must go into a full bucket: if the bucket's local depth equals d, the directory is doubled first; then the bucket is split on its next bit (and split again if it is still full). After the keys shown are inserted, what are the global depth and the number of buckets?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The directory doubles twice (at 6 and at 24), so d = 3 with 8 directory entries. Two buckets of local depth 2 are each shared by two entries, so there are only 6 buckets: {16, 24}, {4, 20}, {10}, {6, 22}, {9}, {7, 31}.
concept: Extendible hashing keeps a directory of 2^d bucket pointers (d = global depth). Each bucket has a local depth d' ≤ d, and a bucket with d' < d is shared by 2^(d − d') directory entries. When a bucket overflows: if d' < d, only that bucket is split (no doubling); if d' = d, the directory is doubled first. Because buckets can be shared, the number of buckets is usually smaller than the number of directory entries.
why: A — Wrong. 8 = 2^3 is the number of DIRECTORY ENTRIES at global depth 3, not the number of buckets. The buckets {9} and {7, 31} have local depth 2, and each is pointed to by two entries.
B — Wrong. Global depth 4 with 7 buckets is what you get if you index the directory with the high-order (leftmost) bits. The question says to use the low-order (rightmost) bits.
C — Correct. Final state: d = 3, 8 directory entries, 6 distinct buckets.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Directory entries = 2^d, but buckets ≤ 2^d. Double the directory only when the full bucket's local depth equals the global depth.

q: A file has 400,000 records. A dense secondary index is built on a non-ordering key field: one index entry per record, each entry = 12-byte key + 8-byte record pointer. The block size is 2048 bytes and entries do not span blocks. The index is made multilevel: each higher level indexes the blocks of the level below, until a level fits in one block. How many levels does the multilevel index have, and how many block accesses are needed to fetch one record through it?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Fan-out = ⌊2048 / 20⌋ = 102. The levels have 3922, 39 and 1 blocks, so there are 3 levels; a search reads one block per level plus the data block = 4 accesses.
concept: A multilevel index treats the first-level index as an ordered file and builds an index on it, then an index on that, and so on. The fan-out fo = ⌊block size / entry size⌋ is the number of entries in one index block. Each level has about 1/fo as many blocks as the level below; stop when a level fits in ONE block. The number of levels is t = ⌈log_fo(r1)⌉, where r1 is the number of first-level entries. A search reads one block at each level and then one data block.
why: A — Wrong. 3 levels is right, but reading one block per index level only gives the address of the record. One more access is needed to read the data block itself, so 4 accesses.
B — Correct. 3 index levels (3922, 39 and 1 blocks) + 1 data block = 4 block accesses.
C — Wrong. After level 2 there are still 39 blocks. A multilevel index keeps adding levels until the top level fits in ONE block, so a third level is needed (and then 4 accesses).
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Entry size = 12 + 8 = 20 bytes.
Fan-out fo = ⌊2048 / 20⌋ = ⌊102.4⌋ = 102 entries per block.
Level 1: 400,000 entries → ⌈400,000 / 102⌉ = ⌈3921.6⌉ = 3922 blocks.
Level 2: 3922 entries → ⌈3922 / 102⌉ = ⌈38.45⌉ = 39 blocks.
Level 3: 39 entries → 1 block (top level).
Levels t = 3 (check: ⌈log_102 400,000⌉ = ⌈2.79⌉ = 3).
Block accesses = 3 index blocks + 1 data block = 4.
tip: Block accesses through a multilevel index = number of levels + 1 (the data block).

q: A data file has 30,000 records of 100 bytes each and is sorted on its primary key. The block size is 1024 bytes, and neither records nor index entries span blocks. An index entry is a 9-byte key plus a 6-byte block pointer. How many blocks are needed for (i) a dense index on the primary key (one entry per record) and (ii) a sparse index on the primary key (one entry per data block)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The index holds ⌊1024 / 15⌋ = 68 entries per block. Dense: ⌈30,000 / 68⌉ = 442 blocks. The file has 30,000 / 10 = 3000 data blocks, so sparse: ⌈3000 / 68⌉ = 45 blocks.
concept: A dense index has one entry for every record; a sparse (non-dense) index has one entry for every data block, so it can be used only when the file is sorted on the search key. Index blocks needed = ⌈number of entries / index blocking factor⌉, where index blocking factor = ⌊block size / entry size⌋. Round the blocking factor DOWN (part of an entry cannot be stored) and the number of blocks UP (a partly filled block is still a block).
why: A — Correct. Dense: ⌈441.18⌉ = 442 blocks; sparse: ⌈44.12⌉ = 45 blocks.
B — Wrong. 441 and 44 round DOWN (⌊441.18⌋ and ⌊44.12⌋). The leftover entries still need one more block each time, so the counts must be rounded UP: 442 and 45.
C — Wrong. 30,000 and 3,000 are the numbers of index ENTRIES (one per record, one per data block), not blocks. Each index block holds 68 entries.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Data blocking factor = ⌊1024 / 100⌋ = 10 records per block.
Data blocks b = 30,000 / 10 = 3000.
Index entry = 9 + 6 = 15 bytes (entries do not span blocks) → index blocking factor = ⌊1024 / 15⌋ = ⌊68.27⌋ = 68 entries per block.
(i) Dense: 30,000 entries → ⌈30,000 / 68⌉ = ⌈441.18⌉ = 442 blocks.
(ii) Sparse: 3000 entries (one per data block) → ⌈3000 / 68⌉ = ⌈44.12⌉ = 45 blocks.
tip: Blocking factor: round down. Number of blocks: round up.

q: Each B-tree node is stored in one disk block of 512 bytes. A node of order p holds p tree pointers and p − 1 (key, data pointer) pairs. A key is 9 bytes, a data (record) pointer is 7 bytes and a tree pointer is 6 bytes. With the largest possible p, what is the maximum number of keys a B-tree with exactly 3 levels (root, one middle level, leaves) can hold?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 6p + 16(p − 1) ≤ 512 gives p = 24. A full 3-level tree has 1 + 24 + 576 = 601 nodes with 23 keys each = 13,823 = 24^3 − 1 keys.
concept: In a B-tree every node stores its keys together with their data pointers, so the node size condition is p × (tree pointer) + (p − 1) × (key + data pointer) ≤ block size; take the largest whole p. When every node is full, level i has p^(i−1) nodes, each with p − 1 keys, so L levels hold (p − 1)(1 + p + … + p^(L−1)) = p^L − 1 keys.
why: A — Wrong. 13824 = 24^3 forgets the '− 1'. A node with 24 children holds only 23 keys, so a full tree of 3 levels has 24^3 − 1 keys.

B — Wrong. 13248 counts only the leaf level (576 leaves × 23 keys). In a B-tree, unlike a B+ tree, the root and middle nodes also store keys with their data pointers, so their 23 + 552 = 575 keys must be added.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Node size: 6p + (9 + 7)(p − 1) ≤ 512
6p + 16p − 16 ≤ 512
22p ≤ 528 → p ≤ 24 → p = 24 (uses exactly 144 + 368 = 512 bytes; p = 25 would need 534 bytes).
Each full node: 24 children and 23 keys.
Level 1 (root): 1 node → 23 keys
Level 2: 24 nodes → 552 keys
Level 3 (leaves): 576 nodes → 13,248 keys
Total = 23 + 552 + 13,248 = 13,823 = 24^3 − 1.
tip: B-tree node: p·P_tree + (p − 1)(K + P_data) ≤ B. A full tree of L levels holds p^L − 1 keys.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following storage media is NOT volatile (that is, it keeps its data when the power is switched off)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Flash memory keeps its contents without power, so it is non-volatile. Cache and main memory lose their contents when the power goes off.
concept: Volatile storage loses its contents when the power is switched off or the system crashes. In Korth's storage hierarchy, cache and main memory are volatile. Flash memory, magnetic disk, optical disk and magnetic tape are non-volatile: their data survive a power failure. This is why a database must finally keep its data (and its log) on non-volatile storage.
why: A — Wrong. Cache is the fastest and smallest memory, close to the CPU. It is volatile: its contents are lost when the power goes off. So it does not fit a NOT question.
B — Wrong. Main memory (RAM) holds the data being processed. It is volatile: a power failure or crash wipes it out. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Correct. Flash memory (used in pen drives and SSDs) keeps its data even when the power is off, so it is NOT volatile. This is the option the question asks for.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: In Korth's (Silberschatz) storage hierarchy, magnetic tapes and optical-disk jukeboxes are referred to as
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Korth calls the lowest, slowest and cheapest level of the hierarchy — magnetic tape and optical-disk jukeboxes — tertiary or off-line storage.
concept: Korth groups storage media into three levels. Primary storage: the fastest media, cache and main memory (volatile). Secondary or on-line storage: the next level, for example magnetic disks and flash-based SSDs (non-volatile, fairly fast). Tertiary or off-line storage: the lowest level, for example magnetic tape and optical-disk jukeboxes (non-volatile, cheapest per byte, slowest; used for backups and archives).
why: A — Correct. Tape and optical-disk jukeboxes form the lowest level of the hierarchy. They are slow but very cheap per byte and are used for backup and archival copies, so Korth calls them tertiary (off-line) storage.
B — Wrong. Secondary (on-line) storage means media such as magnetic disks, which stay connected and give access in milliseconds. Tape and jukeboxes are slower and lie lower in the hierarchy.
C — Wrong. Primary storage means the fastest media that the CPU works with directly: cache and main memory. They are volatile, unlike tape.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Primary = cache + RAM; secondary = disks (and SSDs); tertiary = tape + optical jukeboxes.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following statements about magnetic tape is NOT correct?
opts: It is non-volatile and has a very low cost per byte, so it is used for backups and archives
It supports fast direct (random) access, so any block can be reached in a few milliseconds
It is a sequential-access medium: to reach a block, the tape must be wound past all the data before it
More than one of the above
exp: Tape is a sequential-access medium; reaching a far position can take seconds or even minutes, not milliseconds. So statement B is the incorrect one.
concept: Sequential access means data can be reached only in order, one after another, like a song on an old audio cassette. Direct (random) access means the device can jump to any block, like a magnetic disk whose arm moves straight to the right track. Magnetic tape is sequential-access, slow to position and very cheap per byte, so it is used for backup and archival data, not for data that queries use all the time.
why: A — Wrong. This is correct: tape keeps data without power and is the cheapest medium per byte, which makes it ideal for backups and archives. So it does not fit a NOT question.

B — Correct. This is NOT correct, so it is the answer. Tape cannot jump to a block; the drive must wind the tape to that position, which may take seconds or even minutes. Fast direct access in milliseconds is a feature of magnetic disks.
C — Wrong. This is correct: tape is the standard example of a sequential-access device. So it does not fit a NOT question.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following statements about NAND flash memory (as used in SSDs and pen drives) are correct?
opts: The data stored in it survive a power failure
A page that has already been written cannot be overwritten in place; it must first be erased, and erasing is done for a whole erase block of many pages
A random read from flash is slower than a random read from a magnetic disk, because flash must move a read–write head to the data
More than one of the above
exp: Statements A and B are true facts about flash memory. C is false, because flash has no moving head and reads much faster than a disk.
concept: Flash memory is non-volatile semiconductor storage. NAND flash, used in SSDs, reads and writes in units called pages. A written page cannot simply be overwritten: its whole erase block must be erased first, and each block can be erased only a limited number of times. So SSD controllers write new data to fresh pages and spread the writes evenly over the blocks (wear leveling). Because there is no mechanical movement, random reads are much faster than on a magnetic disk.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Flash memory is non-volatile: the data stay even when the power is switched off.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. This is the 'erase-before-write' rule of flash. Since erasing works on a big erase block, an SSD writes the new version of a page to a fresh, already-erased page and updates a mapping table instead.

C — Wrong. This statement is false. Flash has no moving parts and no read–write head. A random page read takes only tens of microseconds, far faster than a disk, which needs several milliseconds for seek and rotation.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: On a magnetic disk with several platters, the tracks that are at the same arm position on all the recording surfaces (for example, track 25 of every surface) together form a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The i-th tracks of all the surfaces together are called the i-th cylinder; all of them can be read without moving the arm.
concept: A magnetic disk has one or more platters (circular plates), and each platter has two recording surfaces. Each surface is divided into circles called tracks, and each track into sectors, the smallest unit that is read or written. There is one read–write head per surface, and all the heads move together on one arm assembly. So the tracks under the heads at one arm position — track i of every surface — form cylinder i. Data in the same cylinder can be read without a new seek.
why: A — Wrong. A sector is a small part of one track (for example 512 bytes or 4 KB). It is the smallest unit the disk reads or writes, not a group of tracks.
B — Correct. Track i of all the surfaces lie one above another in the shape of a cylinder, and all of them are under the heads at the same arm position, so no seek is needed to move among them.
C — Wrong. A platter is one physical circular plate of the disk, with two surfaces. It holds many tracks, but a platter is not the set of tracks at one arm position.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A disk pack has 4 platters, and both surfaces of every platter are used for recording. Each surface has 2048 tracks, each track has 256 sectors, and each sector holds 512 bytes. What is the total capacity of the disk pack? (Take 1 GB = 2^30 bytes.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector = 8 × 2048 × 256 × 512 = 2^31 bytes = 2 GB.
concept: Disk capacity = (number of recording surfaces) × (tracks per surface) × (sectors per track) × (bytes per sector). A platter has two surfaces, so when both are used the number of surfaces is twice the number of platters. Working in powers of two keeps the arithmetic easy: here 2^3 × 2^11 × 2^8 × 2^9 = 2^31 bytes.
why: A — Wrong. 1 GB is what you get if you count only 4 surfaces (one per platter). The stem says both surfaces of each platter are used, so there are 8 surfaces.
B — Wrong. 4 GB is double the right value; it would need 16 surfaces or 1024-byte sectors. 8 × 2048 × 256 × 512 = 2^31 bytes, which is 2 GB.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Recording surfaces = 4 platters × 2 surfaces = 8
Bytes per track = 256 sectors × 512 bytes = 131,072 bytes (128 KB)
Bytes per surface = 2048 tracks × 131,072 bytes = 268,435,456 bytes (256 MB)
Total = 8 surfaces × 268,435,456 bytes = 2,147,483,648 bytes = 2^31 bytes
2^31 / 2^30 = 2 GB
tip: Count surfaces, not platters: surfaces = 2 × platters when both sides are used.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A disk rotates at 7200 rpm (rotations per minute). What is its average rotational latency, that is, the average time for the required sector to come under the head once the head is on the right track?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: One rotation takes 60,000 / 7200 = 8.33 ms; on average the head waits half a rotation, so the average latency is about 4.17 ms.
concept: Rotational latency is the waiting time until the wanted sector rotates under the read–write head. In the worst case the disk must turn one full rotation; in the best case the wait is zero. Since the sector is equally likely to be anywhere on the track, the average is half a rotation: average latency = (1/2) × (60 / rpm) seconds.
why: A — Correct. Full rotation = 60 / 7200 s = 8.33 ms; average latency = half of that ≈ 4.17 ms.
B — Wrong. 8.33 ms is the time of one full rotation, which is the worst-case (maximum) latency, not the average.
C — Wrong. 2.08 ms is a quarter of a rotation. The average waiting time is half a rotation, not a quarter.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Rotations per second = 7200 / 60 = 120
Time for one full rotation = 1/120 s = 1000/120 ms = 8.33 ms
On average the sector is half a rotation away
Average rotational latency = 8.33 / 2 = 4.17 ms
tip: Remember: 7200 rpm → 8.33 ms per rotation → 4.17 ms average latency; 15,000 rpm → 4 ms per rotation → 2 ms average.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A disk has an average seek time of 8 ms and rotates at 6000 rpm. Its data transfer rate is 8 MB per second (take 1 MB = 1000 KB). What is the average time to read one 8 KB block from a random position on the disk (seek time + rotational latency + transfer time)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Time = average seek + average rotational latency + transfer = 8 + 5 + 1 = 14 ms, which is not among A–C.
concept: Time to read a block from a random place on a disk = seek time (move the arm to the right track) + rotational latency (wait for the sector to come under the head; on average half a rotation) + transfer time (block size ÷ transfer rate). Korth calls seek time + rotational latency the access time; adding the transfer time gives the total time for one random block read.
why: A — Wrong. 19 ms = 8 + 10 + 1 uses a FULL rotation (10 ms) as the latency. The average latency is half a rotation, 5 ms.
B — Wrong. 13 ms = 8 + 5 leaves out the transfer time of 1 ms (8 KB at 8000 KB per second).
C — Wrong. 9 ms = 8 + 1 leaves out the rotational latency of 5 ms.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The average time is 8 ms (seek) + 5 ms (half of a 10 ms rotation) + 1 ms (transfer) = 14 ms, which is not listed.
work:
Average seek time = 8 ms
One rotation = 60,000 ms / 6000 = 10 ms, so average rotational latency = 10 / 2 = 5 ms
Transfer rate = 8 MB/s = 8000 KB/s, so transfer time = 8 KB / 8000 KB per s = 0.001 s = 1 ms
Total = 8 + 5 + 1 = 14 ms
tip: Three parts, always: seek + half a rotation + transfer. Check that each one is in your sum.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: The mean time to failure (MTTF) of one disk is 200,000 hours. A disk array has 50 such disks. Assuming that the disks fail independently and using the simple rule given in Korth, what is the mean time until SOME disk in the array fails?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With 50 disks, failures happen 50 times as often, so the mean time until some disk fails = 200,000 / 50 = 4,000 hours.
concept: Mean time to failure (MTTF) is the average time a disk is expected to run before it fails. When many disks work together, the chance that at least one of them fails grows with the number of disks: MTTF of some disk in an array of N disks ≈ MTTF of one disk ÷ N. Korth's example: 100,000 hours ÷ 100 disks = 1,000 hours, about 42 days. This is why large disk arrays need redundancy (RAID).
why: A — Wrong. 200,000 hours is the MTTF of a single disk. With 50 disks running at once, some disk fails much sooner.
B — Correct. 200,000 / 50 = 4,000 hours (about 167 days).
C — Wrong. 10,000,000 hours comes from multiplying by 50. More disks make a failure MORE likely, so the time until some disk fails becomes shorter, not longer.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
With N independent disks, a failure of some disk is N times as likely in any hour
MTTF of some disk in the array = MTTF of one disk / N
= 200,000 / 50 = 4,000 hours (about 167 days)

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: While an update on a block is in progress, the buffer manager must not write that block back to disk. In Korth's terms, a block that is not allowed to be written back to disk is said to be
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Korth: a block that is not allowed to be written back to disk is said to be pinned.
concept: The buffer manager keeps copies of disk blocks in main memory (the buffer). While a block is in use, for example while a transaction is updating it, the block is pinned so that it is neither thrown out nor written back at that moment. When the work is done, the block is unpinned and may again be written back or replaced. Many systems keep a pin count: a block can be replaced only when its pin count is 0.
why: A — Correct. Pinning a block stops the buffer manager from writing it back to disk (or replacing it) until it is unpinned.

B — Wrong. A dirty block is one that has been changed in the buffer but not yet written to disk. A dirty block CAN be written back — that is how changes reach the disk — so 'dirty' does not mean 'not allowed to be written'.
C — Wrong. 'Shadow' comes from shadow paging, a recovery method that keeps an old (shadow) copy of the page table. It is not the buffer-manager term for a block that must stay in memory.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: In a nested-loop join, the blocks of the inner relation are read again, in the same order, for every tuple (or block) of the outer relation. According to Korth, which buffer-replacement strategy is best for the inner relation's blocks?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A block of the inner relation that was just used will be needed again only after all the other inner blocks, so throwing out the most recently used block (MRU) is best; LRU throws out exactly the block that is needed next.
concept: Operating systems usually replace the least recently used (LRU) block. A DBMS knows the access pattern of a query and can do better. In a nested-loop join the inner relation is scanned again and again in the same order. If the buffer cannot hold the whole inner relation, LRU (and FIFO) always throw out the block that will be needed soonest, so almost every read misses. Korth says the best choice here is MRU: once a block is unpinned, replace the most recently used block, because it will be needed again only at the end of the next scan.
