For the outer relation Korth suggests toss-immediate: free a block as soon as its last tuple has been processed.
why: A — Wrong. LRU is the usual operating-system strategy, but for a repeated scan in the same order it is the worst choice: it throws out the oldest block, which is exactly the next one the scan needs again.
B — Wrong. FIFO throws out the block that came in earliest. In a repeated scan in the same order that is again the block needed next, so it behaves as badly as LRU here.
C — Correct. After a block is used, it will be needed again only after all the other inner blocks have been read, so it is the best block to throw out.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Repeated scans of the same blocks → MRU; outer relation of a nested-loop join → toss-immediate.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Sometimes the buffer manager writes a block back to disk even though the buffer space it occupies is not needed for another block — for example, so that log records reach stable storage before a transaction commits. In Korth's terms, such a write is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A write of a block to disk that is done even though its buffer space is not needed is called forced output; none of A–C names it.
concept: Normally a changed block in the buffer is written back to disk only when its space is needed for another block. But recovery needs some blocks on disk at definite times — for example, the log records of a transaction must be on stable storage before the transaction commits, and before the data blocks they describe are written to disk (the write-ahead logging rule). Writing a block to disk even though its buffer space is not needed is called forced output of the block. Other buffer-manager terms: pinned block (may not be written back now), toss-immediate (free a block right after its last tuple is used), LRU / MRU (which block to replace when space is needed).
why: A — Wrong. Pinning means the opposite: the block may NOT be written back to disk for now (for example while an update on it is in progress).
B — Wrong. Toss-immediate frees a block's buffer space as soon as the last tuple of that block has been processed. It is about freeing space, not about writing a block whose space is not needed.
C — Wrong. MRU is a replacement policy: when space IS needed, it chooses the most recently used block to throw out. It does not describe a write done when no space is needed.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Korth calls this the forced output of a block: the block is written to disk on purpose, even though its buffer space is not needed.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: In the slotted-page structure used to store variable-length records, the records inside a block may be moved (for example, to keep all the free space together). To make this safe, pointers from outside the block (for example, from an index) point to
opts: The record's entry (slot) in the block header
The first byte of the record itself
The end of the free space in the block
More than one of the above
exp: Outside pointers point to the record's entry in the block header; that entry holds the record's current location and size, so the record can move without breaking any pointer.
concept: In Korth's slotted-page structure, each block begins with a header that holds: the number of record entries, the end of the free space, and an array with the location and size of each record. Records are packed at the end of the block, and the free space lies between the header array and the records. When a record is deleted or changes size, other records can be moved and only their header entries are updated. So pointers from outside never point directly at a record; they point at its entry in the header.
why: A — Correct. The header entry is a fixed place that always holds the record's current location, so moving the record inside the block only changes this entry, and outside pointers stay valid.
B — Wrong. If outside pointers pointed straight at the record, every move of the record inside the block would leave those pointers dangling (pointing to the wrong place).
C — Wrong. The end-of-free-space value is kept in the header for the block's own use when new records are inserted. It is not where pointers to a particular record point.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q:
Consider the following statements about storing records in disk blocks:
I. In an unspanned organization a record is never split across two blocks, so some space at the end of a block may be left unused.
II. In a spanned organization a record may be split across blocks (with a pointer to the rest), so a record larger than a block can be stored.
III. When fixed-length records are deleted, no gaps are ever left in the file, so a free list is never needed.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II correctly describe unspanned and spanned organization. III is false: deletions leave empty slots, which are either filled by moving records or kept on a free list.
concept: A block holds several records. Unspanned: each record lies wholly inside one block; if the space left at the end of a block is smaller than a record, it is wasted. Spanned: a record may continue in another block, linked by a pointer; this uses space fully and is necessary when a record is bigger than a block. With fixed-length records, deleting a record leaves an empty slot; Korth describes either moving records to close the gap or keeping a free list (a linked list of the empty slots, starting from the file header) so that later insertions reuse them.
why: A — Wrong. Statement I is true, but III is false: deleting fixed-length records does leave empty slots.
B — Correct. I (unspanned can waste space at the end of a block) and II (spanned allows splitting and very large records) are both true, and III is false.
C — Wrong. II is true, but III is false; and I, which is true, is left out.
D — Wrong. Only option B gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option B is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A relation has 80,000 records. Its attribute grade takes exactly 4 distinct values and is never NULL. A bitmap index on grade keeps one bitmap per value, with one bit per record. What is the total size of these bitmaps? (1 byte = 8 bits.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 4 bitmaps × 80,000 bits = 320,000 bits = 40,000 bytes.
concept: A bitmap index on attribute A has one bitmap (bit vector) for each value of A. Each bitmap has one bit per record: bit i is 1 if record i has that value, otherwise 0. So the size is (number of distinct values) × (number of records) bits. Bitmaps are small when there are few distinct values, and conditions on several attributes can be answered with fast bitwise AND and OR.
why: B — Wrong. 10,000 bytes is the size of only ONE bitmap (80,000 bits). The index has a bitmap for each of the 4 values.
C — Wrong. 320,000 is the number of BITS. Dividing by 8 gives the size in bytes: 40,000.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
One bitmap = one bit per record = 80,000 bits = 80,000 / 8 = 10,000 bytes
Number of bitmaps = number of distinct values = 4
Total = 4 × 10,000 = 40,000 bytes (= 320,000 bits)

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A relation has 6 records, numbered 1 to 6 from left to right in the bitmaps below. Which records satisfy city = 'Patna' AND dept = 'IT'?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The bitwise AND 101101 AND 110100 = 100100, so only records 1 and 4 satisfy both conditions.
concept: With bitmap indices, a condition joined by AND is answered by the bitwise AND (intersection) of the bitmaps; OR uses the bitwise OR (union); NOT uses the complement. Bit operations on whole machine words are very fast, so queries on several attributes become cheap. Only after the final bitmap is found are the actual records with 1-bits fetched from disk.
why: A — Wrong. Records 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 is the bitwise OR (111101): the records that satisfy city = 'Patna' OR dept = 'IT'. The question uses AND.
B — Wrong. Records 1, 3, 4 and 6 is just the bitmap for city = 'Patna'; it ignores the condition dept = 'IT'.
C — Correct. Only records 1 and 4 have a 1 in both bitmaps.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Bitmap for city = 'Patna' : 1 0 1 1 0 1
Bitmap for dept = 'IT'    : 1 1 0 1 0 0
work:
AND the two bitmaps bit by bit:
record 1: 1 AND 1 = 1
record 2: 0 AND 1 = 0
record 3: 1 AND 0 = 0
record 4: 1 AND 1 = 1
record 5: 0 AND 0 = 0
record 6: 1 AND 0 = 0
Result 100100 → records 1 and 4

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following statements about indices are correct?
opts: A bitmap index is most useful for an attribute that takes only a small number of distinct values, such as gender or grade
A covering index stores the values of some extra (non-search-key) attributes along with the record pointers, so some queries can be answered from the index alone
For a condition such as dept = 'IT' AND salary = 50000, only one index can ever be used, even if there are separate indices on dept and on salary
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are true. C is false: two indices can be used together by intersecting the sets of record pointers that they return.
concept: Multiple-key access means answering conditions on several attributes. Korth lists ways to do it: use an index on one attribute and test the other condition on each fetched record; use indices on both attributes and intersect the two sets of record pointers; use one composite index on (dept, salary); or use bitmap indices and AND the bitmaps. A covering index carries extra attribute values, so some queries never need to read the data file at all.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. With few distinct values there are only a few bitmaps, so the index is small, and AND / OR of bitmaps answers conditions on several attributes quickly.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Korth calls these covering indices: they store some attribute values besides the search key, so a query that needs only those attributes is answered without reading the actual records.

C — Wrong. This statement is false. With separate indices on dept and salary, the system can use both: take the set of record pointers from each index, intersect the two sets, and fetch only the records in the intersection.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Covering index = the index 'covers' every column the query needs.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which RAID level uses P + Q redundancy (two independent sets of check information per stripe), so that the data survive the failure of ANY two disks at the same time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: RAID 6 stores two kinds of redundant information (P + Q, for example Reed–Solomon codes), so it can rebuild the data after any two disk failures.
concept: RAID levels that use parity (3, 4 and 5) keep one parity block per stripe, so they can rebuild the data of only ONE failed disk. RAID 6, the P + Q redundancy scheme, stores extra error-correcting information (for example Reed–Solomon codes) — in total the space of two disks — and can survive any two disk failures at the same time. Usable capacity of RAID 6 with n equal disks = (n − 2) disks.
why: A — Wrong. RAID 4 keeps one parity block per stripe on one dedicated parity disk. One parity block can rebuild only one failed disk.
B — Wrong. RAID 5 spreads the parity blocks over all the disks, but it still has only ONE parity block per stripe, so it survives only one disk failure.
C — Correct. With two independent check blocks (P and Q) per stripe, any two lost blocks of a stripe can be recomputed.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A disk array has 8 disks of 4 TB each. What is its usable (data) capacity under RAID 6 and under RAID 1+0 (RAID 10: striping over mirrored pairs of disks), respectively?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: RAID 6 uses two disks' worth of space for P + Q data: 6 × 4 = 24 TB. RAID 1+0 stores every block twice: 32 / 2 = 16 TB.
concept: Usable capacity of n equal disks of size s: RAID 0 (striping only, no redundancy) = n × s; RAID 1 and RAID 1+0 (mirroring) = n × s / 2; RAID 5 (one parity block per stripe) = (n − 1) × s; RAID 6 (P + Q) = (n − 2) × s. RAID 1+0 combines mirroring (for safety) with striping (for speed).
why: A — Correct. RAID 6: (8 − 2) × 4 = 24 TB; RAID 1+0: (8 / 2) × 4 = 16 TB.
B — Wrong. 28 TB = (8 − 1) × 4 is the capacity under RAID 5 (one parity block per stripe). RAID 6 needs space for two check blocks per stripe.
C — Wrong. 32 TB is the raw capacity, as in RAID 0 (no redundancy). With mirroring (RAID 1+0) half of the space holds copies, so only 16 TB is usable.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Raw capacity = 8 × 4 TB = 32 TB
RAID 6: two disks' worth of space holds the P and Q check data → (8 − 2) × 4 = 24 TB
RAID 1+0: the disks are mirrored in pairs, so every block is stored twice → (8 / 2) × 4 = 16 TB
tip: Usable disks: RAID 0 → n; RAID 5 → n − 1; RAID 6 → n − 2; RAID 1 / 1+0 → n / 2.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following statements about RAID levels is NOT correct?
opts: RAID 3 (bit-interleaved parity) needs only one parity disk, because the disk controller can detect which sector has failed, so one parity bit is enough to rebuild it
RAID 2 (memory-style error-correcting codes) needs fewer extra (check) disks than RAID 3
In RAID 4 (block-interleaved parity) all parity blocks are on one disk, so that disk takes part in every write and can become a bottleneck
More than one of the above
exp: RAID 2 uses Hamming-type codes and needs several check disks (Korth's example: 3 for 4 data disks), while RAID 3 needs only one parity disk. So statement B is false.
concept: RAID 2 uses memory-style error-correcting codes (like Hamming codes); Korth's example needs 3 check disks for 4 data disks. RAID 3 improves on this: a disk controller already knows WHICH sector has failed, so a single parity bit per position is enough to rebuild the missing bit, and one parity disk is sufficient — that is why RAID 2 is not used in practice. RAID 4 keeps block-level parity on a single parity disk; every write must update that disk, so it becomes a bottleneck. RAID 5 removes the bottleneck by spreading the parity blocks over all the disks.
why: A — Wrong. This is correct (Korth): because the failed sector is known, one parity bit can rebuild it, so RAID 3 needs only one parity disk. So it does not fit a NOT question.

B — Correct. This is NOT correct, so it is the answer. RAID 2 needs MORE check disks than RAID 3 (for example 3 check disks for 4 data disks, against only 1 for RAID 3). That is why RAID 3 replaced RAID 2.

C — Wrong. This is correct: every write changes a parity block, and in RAID 4 all parity blocks are on the same disk, so that disk becomes the bottleneck. RAID 5 fixes this by distributing the parity. So it does not fit a NOT question.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: RAID 2 → 3 → 4 → 5: Hamming code → one parity disk (bit level) → one parity disk (block level) → parity spread over all disks.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: In a parallel database architecture, each processor has its own main memory and its own disks, and the processors communicate with each other only over an interconnection network. This architecture is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When the processors share neither memory nor disks and talk only through the network, the architecture is shared nothing.
concept: Korth lists four parallel database architectures. Shared memory: all processors share one common main memory (fast communication, but hard to grow beyond a few dozen processors). Shared disk: each processor has its own memory, but all processors can reach all the disks over a network (good fault tolerance). Shared nothing: each node has its own processor, memory and disks, and nodes communicate only by messages over the network (scales to thousands of processors). Hierarchical: a mix, for example shared-nothing nodes each of which is itself a shared-memory system.
why: A — Wrong. In shared memory, all the processors use one common main memory. Here each processor has its own memory, so it is not shared memory.
B — Wrong. In shared disk, processors have private memories but every processor can access ALL the disks directly. Here the disks are private too.
C — Correct. Neither memory nor disk is shared; the only thing shared is the interconnection network.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A query takes 120 seconds on a parallel database system. On a larger system with 4 times the resources (processors, disks and memory), the same query takes 40 seconds. Using Korth's definitions, what is the speedup, and what kind of speedup is it?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Speedup = 120 / 40 = 3. Linear speedup would be N = 4, so a speedup of 3 is sub-linear.
concept: Speedup asks: if the task stays the same and the resources grow, how much faster does it run? Speedup = TS / TL, where TS is the time on the smaller system and TL the time on a system N times larger. Linear speedup means speedup = N; if the speedup is less than N it is sub-linear. Reasons for sub-linear speedup include start-up costs, interference (processors competing for shared resources) and skew (unequal work on different processors).
why: A — Wrong. 4 would be the speedup if the time had dropped to 120 / 4 = 30 seconds. The actual time is 40 seconds.
B — Correct. 120 / 40 = 3, which is less than N = 4, so the speedup is sub-linear.
C — Wrong. 0.33 = 40 / 120 is the ratio turned upside down. Speedup is old time ÷ new time, so it is more than 1 when the larger system is faster.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Speedup = TS / TL (time on the small system ÷ time on the large system)
= 120 / 40 = 3
The large system has N = 4 times the resources
Linear speedup would be 4; since 3 < 4, the speedup is sub-linear
tip: Speedup: same task, bigger system → compare with N. Scaleup: N-times bigger task on an N-times bigger system → compare with 1.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: On a small parallel system, a task Q runs in 50 seconds. On a system 5 times larger, a task 5 times bigger (5Q) runs in 60 seconds. Using Korth's definitions (scaleup = TS / TL, and linear scaleup means TL = TS), what is the scaleup, and what kind of scaleup is it?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Scaleup = 50 / 60 ≈ 0.83, which is less than 1 (TL > TS), so it is sub-linear; no option gives 0.83 with sub-linear.
concept: Scaleup asks: if the task grows N times and the system also grows N times, does the time stay the same? Scaleup = TS / TL, where TS is the time of task Q on the small system and TL is the time of the N-times-bigger task on the N-times-bigger system. Linear scaleup: TL = TS (scaleup = 1). Sub-linear scaleup: TL > TS (scaleup < 1). Scaleup matters for systems whose data or number of users keeps growing.
why: A — Wrong. 1.2 = 60 / 50 turns the ratio upside down; scaleup is TS / TL. Also, linear scaleup would need equal times, and 60 ≠ 50.
B — Wrong. The value 0.83 is right, but the scaleup is not linear: linear scaleup needs TL = TS (scaleup exactly 1). Since 60 > 50, it is sub-linear.
C — Wrong. 'Sub-linear' is right, but 1.2 is the inverted ratio TL / TS. The scaleup is TS / TL = 0.83.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Scaleup = 50 / 60 ≈ 0.83, and since it is less than 1 (TL > TS) the scaleup is sub-linear. No option gives this pair.
work:
TS = 50 s (task Q on the small system)
TL = 60 s (task 5Q on the 5-times-larger system)
Scaleup = TS / TL = 50 / 60 = 0.83
Linear scaleup needs TL = TS, i.e. scaleup = 1
Here TL > TS (scaleup < 1), so the scaleup is sub-linear
Answer: 0.83, sub-linear — not listed
tip: Linear scaleup = the bigger job on the bigger machine takes the same time as the small job on the small machine.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q:
Consider the following statements about partitioning a relation across n disks of a parallel database:
I. Round-robin partitioning spreads the tuples evenly, but a point query such as WHERE id = 105 has to be sent to all n disks.
II. Hash partitioning on attribute A is good for point queries on A, but a range query on A usually has to be sent to all n disks.
III. Range partitioning cannot suffer from skew (very unequal amounts of data or work on different disks).
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true (Korth). III is false: range partitioning can put many more tuples in some ranges than in others, which is skew.
concept: Korth describes three ways to partition a relation over n disks. Round-robin: tuple i goes to disk i mod n — perfectly even, best for scanning the whole relation, but any point or range query must look at every disk. Hash partitioning: a hash function on attribute A chooses the disk — good for point queries on A (only one disk is searched), but hashing scatters nearby values, so range queries must look at all disks. Range partitioning: each disk gets one range of A values — good for point AND range queries on A, but it can cause skew (some partitions get many more tuples or much more work than others), which spoils the parallel speedup.
why: A — Correct. I and II are true; III is false because range partitioning is the technique most open to skew when the ranges are badly chosen.
B — Wrong. II is true, but III is false: if the data are not spread evenly over the ranges, some disks get far more tuples than others (partition skew).
C — Wrong. III is false, so 'I, II and III' cannot be right.
D — Wrong. Only option A gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option A is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Korth divides intra-query parallelism (making a single query run faster) into two forms. Which of the following is NOT a form of intra-query parallelism?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Inter-query parallelism runs DIFFERENT queries in parallel; it is not a form of intra-query parallelism.
concept: Inter-query parallelism: different queries or transactions run in parallel on different processors; it raises throughput (queries per second) but does not make any single query faster. Intra-query parallelism: one query runs on several processors to reduce its response time. It has two forms: intra-operation parallelism (one operation, such as a sort or a join, is split across processors, each working on part of the data) and inter-operation parallelism (different operations of the same query run at the same time, either pipelined or independently).
why: A — Wrong. Intra-operation parallelism IS a form of intra-query parallelism: a single operation (for example a parallel sort) is divided among processors. So it does not fit a NOT question.

B — Wrong. Inter-operation parallelism IS a form of intra-query parallelism: different operations of the same query (for example two joins in a pipeline) run at the same time. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Correct. Inter-query parallelism runs several DIFFERENT queries at once. It improves throughput but does not speed up a single query, so it is not a form of intra-query parallelism.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Inter = between, intra = within. Inter-query = between queries; intra-query = within one query.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: An analyst is viewing total sales for each city. She now wants total sales for each state, by climbing up the location hierarchy (city → state). This OLAP operation is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Going from a detailed level (city) to a more summarized level (state) of a concept hierarchy is roll-up.
concept: OLAP (online analytical processing) lets users look at a data cube at different levels of detail. Roll-up (drill-up) summarizes data by climbing up a concept hierarchy (city → state → country) or by removing a dimension. Drill-down is the reverse: from less detail to more detail (year → quarter → month), or adding a dimension. Slice selects one value on one dimension; dice selects on two or more dimensions; pivot (rotate) turns the axes to give another view of the same data.
why: A — Wrong. Drill-down goes the other way: from summary to detail (for example from state to city, or from year to month).
B — Correct. Moving from city level to state level adds up the data at a higher level of the hierarchy, which is roll-up.
C — Wrong. Slice picks a single value of one dimension (for example time = 'Q1') and gives a sub-cube. It does not change the level of detail of the location dimension.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: From a 3-D sales cube with dimensions time, location and item, an analyst selects the sub-cube in which location is 'Patna' or 'Gaya', time is 'Q1' or 'Q2', and item is 'Books' or 'Pens'. In Han–Kamber's terms, this OLAP operation is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Selecting on two or more dimensions to get a sub-cube is dice; slice selects on only one dimension.
concept: Han–Kamber: slice performs a selection on ONE dimension of the cube (for example time = 'Q1') and gives a sub-cube. Dice defines a sub-cube by performing a selection on TWO OR MORE dimensions. Pivot (rotate) only changes the orientation of the axes to show the same data in another way; it does not select anything.
why: A — Wrong. Slice selects on a single dimension only (for example time = 'Q1'). Here conditions are placed on all three dimensions.
B — Wrong. Pivot (rotate) rearranges the axes of the view (for example swapping rows and columns); it does not choose a subset of values.
C — Correct. Conditions on location, time and item together pick out a smaller cube, which is dice.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Slice = one cut along one dimension; dice = cut on several dimensions into a small cube.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A data cube has three dimensions. Time has the concept hierarchy day < month < year (3 levels), location has city < state (2 levels), and item has only item_name (1 level). Using Han–Kamber's formula, which also counts the virtual top level 'all' of each dimension, how many cuboids does the full cube have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Number of cuboids = (3 + 1) × (2 + 1) × (1 + 1) = 24, which is not among A–C.
concept: A data cube is a lattice of cuboids; each cuboid is one group-by. Without hierarchies, n dimensions give 2^n cuboids (each dimension is either grouped or not), from the base cuboid (all n dimensions) up to the apex cuboid (one grand total). With concept hierarchies, each dimension can be grouped at any one of its L_i levels or not at all ('all'), so Han–Kamber's total is the product of (L_i + 1) over all dimensions.
why: A — Wrong. 8 = 2^3 is the count for three dimensions WITHOUT hierarchies. Here time and location each have several levels.
B — Wrong. 6 = 3 × 2 × 1 multiplies the numbers of levels but forgets the extra choice 'all' (dimension not grouped) for every dimension.
C — Wrong. 12 = 4 × 3 × 1 adds 'all' for time and location but forgets it for item, which also has two choices: item_name or all.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The cube has (3 + 1) × (2 + 1) × (1 + 1) = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cuboids, which is not listed.
work:
Han–Kamber: total cuboids = product of (L_i + 1), where L_i = number of levels of dimension i; the + 1 is for the virtual level 'all'
time: 3 + 1 = 4 choices (day, month, year, all)
location: 2 + 1 = 3 choices (city, state, all)
item: 1 + 1 = 2 choices (item_name, all)
Total = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 (checked by listing all combinations in Python)
tip: No hierarchies: 2^n cuboids. With hierarchies: multiply (levels + 1) over all dimensions.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following OLAP server types are correctly matched with the way they store data?
opts: ROLAP – stores data in relational tables and uses a relational or extended-relational DBMS
MOLAP – stores data in multidimensional arrays (array-based storage)
HOLAP – keeps all data only on magnetic tape for archiving
More than one of the above
exp: ROLAP (relational tables) and MOLAP (multidimensional arrays) are correctly matched; HOLAP is a hybrid of the two, not tape storage.
concept: OLAP servers come in three main kinds (Han–Kamber). ROLAP (relational OLAP) stores data in a relational DBMS and turns OLAP operations into SQL on star or snowflake tables; it scales well to large data. MOLAP (multidimensional OLAP) stores data in multidimensional arrays; it gives very fast access to precomputed summaries but can waste space on sparse data. HOLAP (hybrid OLAP) combines both, for example detailed data in relational tables and aggregates in a MOLAP store.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Relational OLAP servers sit between a relational back-end and the client tools and turn OLAP operations into SQL on relational tables.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Multidimensional OLAP servers keep the cube in multidimensional array structures, giving very fast access to precomputed summaries.

C — Wrong. This statement is false. HOLAP (hybrid OLAP) combines ROLAP and MOLAP: for example, detailed data stay in a relational database while aggregates are kept in a MOLAP store. It has nothing to do with tape.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: R = Relational tables, M = Multidimensional arrays, H = Hybrid of both.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following statements about data-warehouse schemas are correct?
opts: A fact table stores numeric measures (such as units_sold and amount) together with foreign keys that refer to the dimension tables
In a snowflake schema, some dimension tables are normalized, that is, split into additional tables
A fact constellation (galaxy) schema has exactly one fact table
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are true. C is false: a fact constellation (galaxy) schema has more than one fact table, sharing some dimension tables.
concept: A star schema has one central fact table joined directly to denormalized dimension tables. A snowflake schema normalizes some dimension tables into extra tables, so the diagram branches like a snowflake. A fact constellation (galaxy) schema has several fact tables that share some dimension tables. Measures are the numeric values being analysed (sales amount, quantity); dimensions are the perspectives used to analyse them (time, item, location).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The fact table is the central table; each row records the measures of one business event and the keys of its dimensions (time_key, item_key, …).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. For example, the location dimension may be split into a location table and a separate city table. This saves some space but needs more joins.

C — Wrong. This statement is false. A fact constellation has SEVERAL fact tables (for example SALES and SHIPPING) that share dimension tables; it looks like a group of stars, hence the name galaxy schema.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Using the 8 transactions below, what are the support and the confidence of the association rule {bread, milk} ⇒ {butter}?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 3 of the 8 transactions contain all three items (support 37.5%), and 3 of the 5 transactions that contain bread and milk also contain butter (confidence 60%).
concept: For a rule X ⇒ Y: support = the fraction of ALL transactions that contain both X and Y (that is, X ∪ Y); confidence = among the transactions that contain X, the fraction that also contain Y = support count(X ∪ Y) / support count(X). A rule is called strong if its support and confidence are at least the minimum support and minimum confidence chosen by the user.
why: A — Correct. Support = 3/8 = 37.5%; confidence = 3/5 = 60%.
B — Wrong. 62.5% = 5/8 is the support of {bread, milk} alone (the left-hand side). The support of a rule counts the transactions that contain ALL the items of X and Y.
C — Wrong. 50% = 3/6 divides by the 6 transactions that contain butter. That is the confidence of the reverse rule {butter} ⇒ {bread, milk}; the confidence of X ⇒ Y divides by the count of X.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
TID | Items
T1  | bread, milk, butter
T2  | bread, milk
T3  | bread, butter
T4  | milk, butter
T5  | bread, milk, butter
T6  | bread, milk, jam
T7  | milk, butter, jam
T8  | bread, milk, butter, jam
work:
Transactions containing {bread, milk}: T1, T2, T5, T6, T8 → 5
Transactions containing {bread, milk, butter}: T1, T5, T8 → 3
Support = 3 / 8 = 37.5%
Confidence = count(bread, milk, butter) / count(bread, milk) = 3 / 5 = 60%
tip: Support: divide by ALL transactions. Confidence: divide by the transactions that contain the LEFT side.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: In the Apriori algorithm, the frequent 2-itemsets are L2 = {AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CE} (items in alphabetical order). C3 is formed by joining two itemsets of L2 that have the same first item, and then pruning every candidate that has a 2-item subset not in L2. How many candidate 3-itemsets remain in C3?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The join gives ABC, ABD, ACD and BCD; ACD and BCD are pruned because CD is not frequent, so 2 candidates remain.
concept: Apriori finds frequent itemsets level by level. The Apriori property says that every non-empty subset of a frequent itemset must also be frequent (so if an itemset is not frequent, none of its supersets can be frequent). To build the candidates Ck, Apriori joins pairs of itemsets in L(k−1) that agree on their first k − 2 items, and then prunes every candidate that has some (k − 1)-item subset not in L(k−1). Only the surviving candidates are counted in the database.
why: A — Wrong. 4 is the number of candidates after the join step only (ABC, ABD, ACD, BCD). The prune step removes ACD and BCD.
B — Correct. After pruning, only ABC and ABD remain, because every 2-item subset of each of them is in L2.
C — Wrong. 3 would mean that only one of ACD and BCD was pruned. Both contain CD, which is not in L2, so both are pruned.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Join step (pairs with the same first item):
AB + AC → ABC; AB + AD → ABD; AC + AD → ACD
BC + BD → BCD
CE has no partner starting with C
Prune step (every 2-item subset must be in L2):
ABC: AB, AC, BC all in L2 → keep
ABD: AB, AD, BD all in L2 → keep
ACD: CD not in L2 → prune
BCD: CD not in L2 → prune
C3 = {ABC, ABD} → 2 candidates (checked by brute force in Python)
tip: A candidate survives only if ALL its (k − 1)-item subsets are frequent.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Han–Kamber describe knowledge discovery from data (KDD) as a sequence of steps. Which of the following is NOT one of these steps?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The KDD steps are data cleaning, data integration, data selection, data transformation, data mining, pattern evaluation and knowledge presentation. Data replication is a distributed-database technique, not a KDD step.
concept: Han–Kamber list the KDD process as: 1. data cleaning (remove noise and inconsistent data), 2. data integration (combine data from several sources), 3. data selection (take the data relevant to the task), 4. data transformation (convert the data into forms suitable for mining, for example by aggregation), 5. data mining (apply intelligent methods to extract patterns), 6. pattern evaluation (pick out the truly interesting patterns), 7. knowledge presentation (show the knowledge to users, for example with visualization). Data mining is only one step of KDD, though the term is often used for the whole process.
why: A — Wrong. Data integration (combining data from several sources) IS a KDD step (step 2). So it does not fit a NOT question.
B — Wrong. Pattern evaluation (picking out the truly interesting patterns) IS a KDD step; it comes right after data mining. So it does not fit a NOT question.
C — Correct. Data replication means keeping copies of data at several sites of a distributed database for availability. It is not a step of the KDD process.
D — Wrong. Only C fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. C fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: KDD order: Clean → Integrate → Select → Transform → Mine → Evaluate → Present.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A bank builds a model from past loan records that are already labelled 'safe' or 'risky', and then uses the model to put each new applicant into one of these two groups. This data-mining task is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Learning from labelled examples and assigning new items to predefined classes is classification, which is not among A–C.
concept: Classification is supervised learning: the training data already carry class labels ('safe', 'risky'), a model such as a decision tree is learned from them, and the model then predicts the class of new data. Regression is similar but predicts a numeric value. Clustering is unsupervised: it groups objects by similarity when no labels are given. Association rule mining finds items that occur together (X ⇒ Y). Outlier analysis finds objects that do not fit the general pattern, for example in fraud detection.
why: A — Wrong. Clustering groups objects by similarity WITHOUT predefined class labels (unsupervised learning). Here the labels 'safe' and 'risky' are known in advance.
B — Wrong. Association rule mining finds items that often occur together, like {bread} ⇒ {butter}. It does not put each applicant into a class.
C — Wrong. Outlier analysis looks for unusual objects that do not fit the general behaviour (for example fraud). Here every applicant is put into one of two known classes.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Learning a model from labelled examples and using it to assign new items to predefined classes is classification (supervised learning).
tip: Labels given → classification; no labels → clustering; numeric value predicted → regression.
