q: Which of the following are requirements for an XML document to be well-formed?
opts: It has exactly one root element that contains all the other elements

Every start tag has a matching end tag (or the element is written as an empty-element tag such as
), and the elements are properly nested
It conforms to a DTD or an XML Schema
More than one of the above
exp: One root element and matching, properly nested tags are well-formedness rules. Conforming to a DTD or an XML Schema is the extra condition for being valid.
concept: A well-formed XML document follows the basic syntax rules: exactly one root element, every start tag closed (or written as an empty-element tag), proper nesting, case-sensitive tag names, and quoted attribute values. A valid XML document is a well-formed document that ALSO conforms to a DTD or an XML Schema. So every valid document is well-formed, but a well-formed document need not be valid.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A document such as <a/><b/>, with two top-level elements, is not well-formed (an XML parser rejects it).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A document such as is rejected by an XML parser, because the tags overlap instead of nesting.
C — Wrong. This statement is false. Conforming to a DTD or an XML Schema makes a document VALID. A document can be well-formed without having any DTD or schema at all.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. At least two of A–C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Checked with the lxml parser: '' and '' raise a syntax error (not well-formed); '
' parses without any DTD.
tip: Well-formed = syntax rules obeyed; valid = well-formed + obeys its DTD or schema.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: What does the XPath expression /library/book[price > 400]/title return for the XML document below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The predicate [price > 400] keeps the books priced 450 and 520, so their titles DBMS and OS are returned.
concept: XPath picks out parts of an XML document with path expressions. '/' steps to child elements, '//' to descendants at any depth, '@' selects attributes, and a predicate in square brackets filters the nodes of a step, for example book[price > 400] or book[@year = '2021']. XQuery builds on XPath with FLWOR expressions — for, let, where, order by, return — which work much like SELECT … FROM … WHERE in SQL.
why: A — Correct. DBMS (price 450) and OS (price 520) are the books whose price is greater than 400, so their titles are returned.
B — Wrong. Networks (price 300) is exactly the book that FAILS the condition price > 400.
C — Wrong. This ignores the predicate [price > 400]; without it, /library/book/title would return all three titles.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
<library>
  <book year="2019"><title>DBMS</title><price>450</price></book>
  <book year="2021"><title>Networks</title><price>300</price></book>
  <book year="2021"><title>OS</title><price>520</price></book>
</library>
work:
/library → the root element library
/book → its three book children
[price > 400] → keep the books whose price child is greater than 400: DBMS (450) yes, Networks (300) no, OS (520) yes
/title → the title children of the kept books: DBMS, OS
Checked with lxml: ['DBMS', 'OS']
tip: In XPath, [ ] works like a WHERE clause on the nodes of that step.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q:
Consider the following statements:
I. A DTD can only say that an element contains text (#PCDATA); it cannot require that text to be an integer or a date.
II. An XML Schema (XSD) is itself written in XML and provides built-in data types such as xs:integer and xs:date.
III. A JSON document must be checked against a DTD before an application can use it.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true: a DTD cannot give data types to element text, while XML Schema is written in XML and has rich data types. III is false: JSON does not use DTDs.
concept: A DTD (Document Type Definition) states which elements and attributes may appear and how they nest, but element text is just #PCDATA (character data); a DTD cannot say 'this must be an integer'. XML Schema (XSD) is written in XML syntax and supports many built-in types (xs:integer, xs:decimal, xs:date, xs:string), user-defined types and limits on the number of occurrences. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lighter semi-structured format made of objects (name/value pairs inside { }) and arrays (inside [ ]); it does not use DTDs (a separate, optional JSON Schema standard exists).
why: A — Wrong. Statement I is true, but statement II is also true and is missing from this set.
B — Wrong. II is true, but III is false: JSON has nothing to do with DTDs; a JSON document only has to follow JSON syntax to be used.
C — Correct. I and II are true, and III is false.
D — Wrong. Only option C gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option C is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: Which of the following statements about object-based databases is NOT correct?
opts: An object-relational DBMS is built by adding persistence to an object-oriented programming language such as C++ or Java, and it does not use SQL
OQL, the query language of the ODMG standard, uses an SQL-like select … from … where syntax
In an object database, a subclass inherits the attributes and methods of its superclass
More than one of the above
exp: An object-relational DBMS extends a RELATIONAL DBMS and SQL with richer types; adding persistence to an object-oriented language describes an object-oriented DBMS. So statement A is incorrect.
concept: There are two routes to object-based databases. Object-relational DBMS (ORDBMS): start from the relational model and SQL and add richer types — user-defined structured types, arrays and multisets, inheritance and references (as in SQL:1999; PostgreSQL and Oracle have such features). Object-oriented DBMS (OODBMS): start from an object-oriented programming language (C++, Java) and add persistence, so program objects can be stored and shared; the ODMG standard defines an object model, ODL for schemas and OQL, a query language with SQL-like syntax. Both support object identity and inheritance.
why: A — Correct. This is NOT correct, so it is the answer. Adding persistence to an object-oriented programming language describes an OODBMS (a persistent programming language). An ORDBMS builds on the relational model and is queried with extended SQL.
B — Wrong. This is correct: an OQL query looks like select e.name from Employees e where e.salary > 50000, closely following SQL. So it does not fit a NOT question.

C — Wrong. This is correct: inheritance is a basic feature of the object model — a subclass (for example Student) gets the attributes and methods of its superclass (Person) and may add its own. So it does not fit a NOT question.
D — Wrong. Only A fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. A fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: ORDBMS = relational + objects (SQL-based). OODBMS = object-oriented language + persistence (ODMG, OQL).

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q: A login program builds its SQL query by joining strings, as shown below. A user types the user name ravi and the password  x' OR '1'='1  . The USERS table has the 4 rows shown. How many rows does the resulting query return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The input closes the quote and adds OR '1'='1'. Since AND is evaluated before OR, the WHERE condition is true for every row, so all 4 rows are returned.
concept: SQL injection happens when user input is pasted directly into an SQL string, so specially crafted input changes the meaning of the query. Here the quote in the input ends the string literal, and the rest (OR '1'='1') becomes part of the SQL. Because AND has higher precedence than OR, the condition becomes (uname = 'ravi' AND pwd = 'x') OR '1'='1', which is true for every row — the attacker gets in without knowing any password. The standard defence is a prepared (parameterized) statement, for example cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE uname = %s AND pwd = %s", (uname, pwd)), where the input is always treated as a value, never as SQL code.
why: A — Wrong. 0 rows is what a prepared (parameterized) statement would give: the whole input would be compared as one password value, and no row has that password. With string joining, however, the input changes the SQL itself.
B — Correct. The query becomes ... WHERE uname = 'ravi' AND pwd = 'x' OR '1'='1', that is (uname = 'ravi' AND pwd = 'x') OR '1'='1'. Since '1'='1' is true for every row, all 4 rows are returned.
C — Wrong. 1 row would need the OR to be evaluated first: uname = 'ravi' AND (pwd = 'x' OR '1'='1'). But in SQL, AND has higher precedence than OR, and there are no brackets around the OR.
D — Wrong. Only B fits the question; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to fit.
E — Wrong. B fits the question, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
USERS
uname | pwd
ravi  | r@123
meena | m#456
amit  | a$789
sita  | s%000

# Python code of the login program
q = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE uname = '" + uname + "' AND pwd = '" + pwd + "'"
cursor.execute(q)

# input typed by the user
uname : ravi
pwd   : x' OR '1'='1
work:
Substituting the input gives:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE uname = 'ravi' AND pwd = 'x' OR '1'='1'
AND is evaluated before OR, so the condition is (uname = 'ravi' AND pwd = 'x') OR ('1' = '1')
uname = 'ravi' AND pwd = 'x' is false for all rows, but '1' = '1' is true for every row
So every row qualifies → 4 rows
Verified on SQLite, PostgreSQL, DuckDB and MySQL (MariaDB): 4 rows. With the brackets uname = 'ravi' AND (pwd = 'x' OR '1'='1') the result would be 1 row; with a parameterized query it is 0 rows.
tip: Never build SQL by joining strings with user input; use placeholders (prepared statements).

topic: Storage, Parallel DBs, Warehousing, Mining, XML & Security
q:
In the Bell–LaPadula model of mandatory access control (as described in Elmasri–Navathe), the security classes are ordered Top Secret > Secret > Confidential > Unclassified. A subject S has clearance Secret. Consider:
I. S may read an object classified Confidential.
II. S may write (update) an object classified Confidential.
III. S may read an object classified Top Secret.
Which of the statements are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The simple security property ('no read up') allows I and forbids III; the star property ('no write down') forbids II. So only I is correct.
concept: Discretionary access control (DAC) lets the owner of data grant and revoke privileges to other users (SQL GRANT and REVOKE). Mandatory access control (MAC) gives every subject (user, program) and every object (table, row) a security class, and the system enforces two Bell–LaPadula rules: 1. Simple security property: S may read O only if class(S) ≥ class(O) — 'no read up'. 2. Star (*) property: S may write O only if class(S) ≤ class(O) — 'no write down', so secret data cannot leak into a lower-class object.
why: A — Wrong. I is true, but II is false: writing to a Confidential object would be a 'write down' from Secret, which the star property forbids, because it could leak secret data to a lower level.
B — Correct. Only I is allowed: Secret ≥ Confidential, so reading is permitted. II breaks 'no write down' and III breaks 'no read up'.
C — Wrong. I is true, but III is false: a Secret subject cannot read Top Secret data, because reading needs class(S) ≥ class(O) — 'no read up'.
D — Wrong. Only option B gives the right set of statements; 'More than one of the above' would need two of A–C to be right at once, which cannot happen here.
E — Wrong. Option B is right, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Bell–LaPadula: no read UP, no write DOWN.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, a database named school already exists. Which command makes school the current (default) database, so that the following CREATE TABLE and SELECT statements work inside it?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: USE school; selects school as the current (default) database for the session. After it, table names refer to the tables of school.
concept: One MySQL server can hold many databases. CREATE DATABASE school; makes a new, empty database, and SHOW DATABASES; lists all of them. USE school; selects one database as the current (default) database for your session. After USE, SHOW TABLES; lists the tables of that database and CREATE TABLE puts new tables into it. The function call SELECT DATABASE(); only tells you which database is current now.
why: A — Wrong. MySQL has no OPEN statement for databases, so this gives a syntax error. (OPEN is used inside stored programs to open a cursor, not a database.)
B — Correct. USE db_name; makes db_name the default database for all the following statements in the session.
C — Wrong. This is not valid syntax. The real function is SELECT DATABASE(); (with brackets and no name), and it only shows the name of the current database; it does not change it.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Tested on MariaDB (same syntax as MySQL 8): USE x2school → OK, then SELECT DATABASE() → x2school; OPEN x2school → ERROR 1064 (syntax error); SELECT DATABASE x2school → ERROR.
tip: NCERT practical order: CREATE DATABASE school; → USE school; → CREATE TABLE …; → SHOW TABLES; → DESC table;

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, which of the following statements can be used to list the names of all the databases on the server?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SHOW DATABASES; and its synonym SHOW SCHEMAS; both list all the databases. SELECT DATABASE(); only returns the name of the current database.
concept: In MySQL the words DATABASE and SCHEMA mean the same thing: CREATE SCHEMA is a synonym of CREATE DATABASE, and SHOW SCHEMAS is a synonym of SHOW DATABASES. SHOW DATABASES lists every database you are allowed to see. The function DATABASE() returns just one value: the name of the current (default) database chosen with USE, or NULL if no database has been selected yet.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. SHOW DATABASES; is the usual NCERT command to list all the databases.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In MySQL, SHOW SCHEMAS is a synonym of SHOW DATABASES, because schema and database mean the same thing in MySQL.
C — Wrong. DATABASE() is a function that returns only the name of the current database (one row, one value), or NULL if no database is selected. It does not list all the databases.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Tested on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): SHOW DATABASES and SHOW SCHEMAS gave the same list of databases; SELECT DATABASE() returned one value — the current database name, or NULL when no database was selected.
tip: In MySQL, DATABASE = SCHEMA (CREATE SCHEMA, SHOW SCHEMAS). In Oracle a schema means the set of objects owned by one user — a different idea.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: Table STUDENT has a column called name, of type VARCHAR(20). Which of the following statements is NOT valid in MySQL?
opts: ALTER TABLE student ALTER COLUMN name VARCHAR(30);
ALTER TABLE student MODIFY name VARCHAR(30);
ALTER TABLE student ADD phone CHAR(10);
More than one of the above
exp: In MySQL, the data type or size of a column is changed with MODIFY (or CHANGE). ALTER COLUMN name VARCHAR(30) is the SQL Server form and gives a syntax error in MySQL.
concept: ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table. In MySQL: ADD adds a new column (ALTER TABLE student ADD phone CHAR(10);), DROP removes a column, MODIFY changes the data type, size or constraint of a column but keeps its name, and CHANGE can rename a column and change its definition together. MySQL's ALTER [COLUMN] clause cannot change a data type; it only sets or drops a column's default value (and, from MySQL 8.0.23, makes a column visible or invisible). Products differ here: SQL Server writes ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN col type, and Oracle writes ALTER TABLE … MODIFY (col type).
why: A — Correct. This is the SQL Server way of changing a column's type. In MySQL, ALTER COLUMN cannot change a data type (it is used for things like setting a default value), so this statement gives a syntax error — it is the NOT-valid one.
B — Wrong. This statement is valid: MODIFY changes the size of name from VARCHAR(20) to VARCHAR(30) and keeps the same column name.
C — Wrong. This statement is valid: ADD puts a new column phone of type CHAR(10) at the end of the table (the word COLUMN is optional).
D — Wrong. Only A satisfies the NOT stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. A satisfies the NOT stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested on MariaDB (same syntax as MySQL 8):
ALTER TABLE student ALTER COLUMN name VARCHAR(30) → ERROR 1064 (syntax error)
ALTER TABLE student MODIFY name VARCHAR(30) → OK; DESC shows name varchar(30)
ALTER TABLE student ADD phone CHAR(10) → OK; DESC shows phone char(10)
tip: Change a column's type — MySQL: MODIFY; Oracle: MODIFY (…); SQL Server: ALTER COLUMN.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL 8, table STUDENT has a column called name, of type VARCHAR(20). Which of the following statements rename this column to sname (keeping the type VARCHAR(20))?
opts: ALTER TABLE student CHANGE name sname VARCHAR(20);
ALTER TABLE student MODIFY name sname VARCHAR(20);
ALTER TABLE student RENAME COLUMN name TO sname;
More than one of the above
exp: CHANGE old_name new_name definition renames a column (and restates its type). RENAME COLUMN old TO new (MySQL 8.0 and later) only renames it. MODIFY can never rename a column.
concept: MySQL gives three clauses for changing an existing column. CHANGE old_name new_name type renames the column and (re)defines its type, so the type must always be written, even if it does not change. MODIFY col type changes only the definition; the name stays the same. RENAME COLUMN old TO new (added in MySQL 8.0) changes only the name, and no type is written.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. CHANGE takes the old name, the new name and the full definition, so it renames name to sname and keeps VARCHAR(20).
B — Wrong. MODIFY takes only one column name followed by the definition. Here MySQL reads sname as a data type and gives an error, because MODIFY cannot rename a column.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. RENAME COLUMN old TO new, available from MySQL 8.0, renames a column without touching its type.
D — Correct. A and C both rename the column, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. A and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested on MariaDB 10.11 (same syntax as MySQL 8.0):
MODIFY name sname VARCHAR(20) → ERROR (sname is read as an unknown data type)
CHANGE name sname VARCHAR(20) → OK; DESC shows sname varchar(20)
RENAME COLUMN sname TO fullname → OK; DESC shows fullname varchar(20)
tip: CHANGE = new name + type (write both names). MODIFY = type only. RENAME COLUMN = name only (MySQL 8).

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q:
Table STUDENT(roll, name) was created in MySQL without a primary key. Consider the following statements:
I. ALTER TABLE student ADD PRIMARY KEY (roll); fails with an error if roll already contains a duplicate value.
II. ALTER TABLE student DROP PRIMARY KEY; removes the primary key without naming its column.
III. After roll has been made the primary key, ALTER TABLE student ADD PRIMARY KEY (name); adds a second primary key on name.
Which of these are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true. III is false: a table can have only one primary key, so MySQL rejects a second ADD PRIMARY KEY with the error 'Multiple primary key defined'.
concept: A primary key can be added after the table is created: ALTER TABLE student ADD PRIMARY KEY (roll); MySQL first checks the existing rows, and the statement fails if roll has duplicate values (or, in MySQL's default strict SQL mode, NULLs). Because a table has at most one primary key, it is removed simply with ALTER TABLE student DROP PRIMARY KEY; — no column name is needed. A primary key may cover several columns (a composite key, such as PRIMARY KEY (roll, subject)), but it is still only one key.
why: A — Wrong. Statement I is true, but this option leaves out statement II, which is also true.
B — Wrong. Statement III is false: a table can have only one primary key, so a second ADD PRIMARY KEY gives the error 'Multiple primary key defined'. This option also leaves out the true statement I.
C — Correct. I is true (duplicate values break the primary key rule, so the ALTER fails) and II is true (DROP PRIMARY KEY needs no column name); III is false.
D — Wrong. Only option C matches the correct set of statements; the other options list a wrong set, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. Option C gives exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested on MariaDB (same behaviour in MySQL 8):
roll values 1, 2, 2 → ADD PRIMARY KEY (roll) → ERROR 1062 Duplicate entry '2' for key 'PRIMARY' (I true)
roll values 1, 2 → ADD PRIMARY KEY (roll) → OK; DROP PRIMARY KEY → OK and DESC no longer shows PRI (II true)
After adding PRIMARY KEY (roll) again: ADD PRIMARY KEY (name) → ERROR 1068 Multiple primary key defined (III false)
tip: One table → at most ONE primary key (it may have many columns). DROP PRIMARY KEY needs no column name.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL 8 (InnoDB table), the statements below are run one after another in one session. What does the final SELECT show?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pen gets 1 and Ink gets 2 (NULL also means 'generate the next number'). Inserting 10 by hand moves the counter to 11. Deleting row 10 does not move the counter back, so Bag gets 11.
concept: An AUTO_INCREMENT column gets the next number automatically when you leave it out of the INSERT or give it NULL. If you insert a value larger than the current maximum, the counter jumps to that value + 1. Deleting rows never lowers the counter, so deleted numbers are not reused. A table can have only one AUTO_INCREMENT column, and it must be a key (usually the primary key).
why: A — Correct. The ids given are 1 (Pen), 2 (Ink), 10 (Book, later deleted) and 11 (Bag). After the DELETE, the rows left are 1, 2 and 11.
B — Wrong. 3 would be right only if the manual value 10 had never been inserted. Inserting 10 pushed the counter to 11, and deleting row 10 does not bring it back to 3.
C — Wrong. AUTO_INCREMENT does not reuse a deleted number. The counter stays at 11 after row 10 is deleted, so Bag gets 11, not 10.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
1. INSERT 'Pen' (id left out) → id 1; counter → 2
2. INSERT (NULL, 'Ink') → NULL means 'generate' → id 2; counter → 3
3. INSERT (10, 'Book') → 10 is larger than the maximum → counter → 11
4. DELETE id 10 → row removed; counter stays 11
5. INSERT 'Bag' → id 11
Rows left: 1, 2, 11
Run on MariaDB (InnoDB): SELECT * FROM item → (1,'Pen'), (2,'Ink'), (11,'Bag'); SHOW CREATE TABLE shows AUTO_INCREMENT=12.
tip: AUTO_INCREMENT only goes up: a deleted number is not reused, and a bigger manual value makes it jump. (Only TRUNCATE TABLE, unlike DELETE, resets it to the start value.)

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, which of the following statements does NOT display the structure (column names, data types, NULL and key information) of table STUDENT?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three show the table structure: DESC is the short form of DESCRIBE, EXPLAIN followed by a table name is a synonym of DESCRIBE, and SHOW COLUMNS FROM gives the same Field / Type / Null / Key / Default / Extra list. So none of them fits the NOT stem.
concept: To see the structure (schema) of a table in MySQL, NCERT uses DESCRIBE student; or its short form DESC student;. The output has one row per column, with Field, Type, Null, Key (PRI for the primary key), Default and Extra (for example auto_increment). MySQL treats DESCRIBE and EXPLAIN as synonyms: with a table name they show its columns, and with a SELECT statement they show the query's execution plan. SHOW COLUMNS FROM student; gives the same information.
why: A — Wrong. DESC student; is the short form of DESCRIBE student; and shows the structure, so it does not satisfy the NOT stem.

B — Wrong. Many students know EXPLAIN only for query plans, but in MySQL EXPLAIN followed by a table name is a synonym of DESCRIBE and shows the same list of columns. So it does display the structure.
C — Wrong. SHOW COLUMNS FROM student; returns the same Field, Type, Null, Key, Default and Extra rows as DESCRIBE, so it does display the structure.
D — Wrong. None of A–C satisfies the NOT stem, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three statements display the structure of STUDENT, so none of them is the 'does NOT' option.
work:
Run on MariaDB for CREATE TABLE student(roll INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20)):
DESC student → rows for roll (PRI) and name, with Field, Type, Null, Key, Default, Extra
DESCRIBE student → same rows
EXPLAIN student → same rows
SHOW COLUMNS FROM student → same rows
(For contrast: SHOW TABLES student → syntax error; SHOW TABLES lists tables, not columns.)
tip: In MySQL: DESC = DESCRIBE = EXPLAIN <table> = SHOW COLUMNS FROM <table>.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what is the largest length n that can be declared for a CHAR(n) column?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MySQL allows CHAR(n) with n from 0 to 255 characters. Longer text needs VARCHAR (up to 65,535 bytes in a row) or TEXT.
concept: CHAR(n) is a fixed-length string type: every value takes the full n characters, padded on the right with spaces. In MySQL, n can be 0 to 255. VARCHAR(n) is variable-length: it stores only the characters given, plus 1 or 2 bytes that record the length, and n can go up to 65,535 (shared with the other columns, because a MySQL row can have at most 65,535 bytes). Other products have other limits: in Oracle, CHAR goes up to 2000 bytes and VARCHAR2 up to 4000 bytes (standard setting).
why: A — Wrong. 65,535 is the upper limit for VARCHAR(n) in MySQL (it is really the maximum row size), not for CHAR.
B — Correct. MySQL CHAR(n) takes n from 0 to 255; CHAR(256) gives the error 'Column length too big … (max = 255)'.
C — Wrong. 2000 bytes is the maximum size of CHAR in Oracle, not in MySQL.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work: Tested on MariaDB (same limit in MySQL 8): CREATE TABLE t1(c CHAR(255)) → OK; CREATE TABLE t2(c CHAR(256)) → ERROR 1074 Column length too big for column 'c' (max = 255); use BLOB or TEXT instead. CREATE TABLE t3(v VARCHAR(300)) → OK.
tip: MySQL: CHAR up to 255, VARCHAR up to 65,535. Oracle: CHAR up to 2000, VARCHAR2 up to 4000.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q:
Consider the following statements about MySQL data types:
I. A DATE value is written and displayed in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD', for example '2024-08-15'.
II. A DATETIME value stores both the date and the time, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss'.
III. FLOAT stores numbers exactly, so it is the best type for money amounts such as 1234.50.
Which of these are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true. III is false: FLOAT is an approximate (floating-point) type; money should be stored in DECIMAL, which is exact.
concept: MySQL's date and time types: DATE holds only a date as 'YYYY-MM-DD' (year first); DATETIME holds a date and a time as 'YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss'; TIME holds only a time. For numbers: INT stores whole numbers; FLOAT and DOUBLE are approximate floating-point types, so a value such as 0.1 cannot be stored exactly; DECIMAL(p, s) is an exact fixed-point type with p digits in total and s digits after the decimal point, for example DECIMAL(8,2) for amounts like 123456.78.
why: A — Correct. Statements I and II describe DATE and DATETIME correctly, and statement III is false.
B — Wrong. Statement II is also true: DATETIME keeps both the date and the time of day, written 'YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss'.
C — Wrong. Statement III is false. FLOAT keeps only an approximation (for example, 0.1 + 0.2 stored as FLOAT is not exactly 0.3), so money should use the exact type DECIMAL.
D — Wrong. Only option A matches the correct set of statements; the other options list a wrong set, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. Option A gives exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested on MariaDB (same rules as MySQL 8):
INSERT '2024-08-15' into a DATE column and '2024-08-15 10:30:00' into a DATETIME column → shown as 2024-08-15 and 2024-08-15 10:30:00; '15-08-2024' → Incorrect date value error
FLOAT column with 0.1 and 0.2: SUM = 0.30000000447…, and SUM = 0.3 is false
DECIMAL(10,2) column with 0.1 and 0.2: SUM = 0.30, and SUM = 0.3 is true
tip: Money → DECIMAL, never FLOAT. MySQL dates are year first: 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL 8 (default settings), the statements below are run. The inserted value 'RAM  ' has TWO spaces after RAM. What does the SELECT return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MySQL pads a CHAR value with spaces when it stores it, but removes the trailing spaces when it reads it back, so LENGTH(c) = 3. VARCHAR keeps exactly what was inserted, including the two spaces, so LENGTH(v) = 5.
concept: CHAR(n) is fixed-length: on disk MySQL fills the value with spaces up to n characters (NCERT: 'city' in CHAR(10) takes space for 10 characters). But when a CHAR value is retrieved, MySQL removes all trailing spaces (unless the special SQL mode PAD_CHAR_TO_FULL_LENGTH is turned on). VARCHAR(n) is variable-length: it stores only the given characters plus a length byte, and trailing spaces are kept both when storing and when reading. Oracle behaves differently: there LENGTH of a CHAR(10) value is always 10.
why: A — Wrong. 10 is what Oracle would report for a CHAR(10) value, because Oracle returns the padded value. MySQL strips the trailing spaces of a CHAR value when it reads it, so it reports 3.
B — Wrong. 5 is right for the VARCHAR column, but MySQL does not keep the trailing spaces of a CHAR value when it reads it back, so LENGTH(c) is 3, not 5.
C — Correct. CHAR loses its trailing spaces on retrieval ('RAM' → 3), while VARCHAR keeps them ('RAM' + 2 spaces → 5).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
c CHAR(10): stored as 'RAM' + 7 spaces (10 characters); when read, MySQL removes trailing spaces → 'RAM' → LENGTH 3
v VARCHAR(10): stored as 'RAM  ' (5 characters + 1 length byte); trailing spaces kept → LENGTH 5
Run on MariaDB (same rule as MySQL 8): LENGTH(c), LENGTH(v) → 3, 5; CONCAT(c,'|') → 'RAM|'; CONCAT(v,'|') → 'RAM  |'
tip: MySQL CHAR: pads when storing, trims when reading. VARCHAR: keeps the spaces exactly as typed.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what does SELECT MOD(-17, 5), MOD(17, -5); return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MySQL's MOD gives a remainder with the same sign as the dividend (the first number): -17 = 5 × (-3) + (-2), so MOD(-17, 5) = -2; and 17 = (-5) × (-3) + 2, so MOD(17, -5) = 2. The answer '-2 and 2' is not listed.
concept: MOD(N, M) (also written N % M or N MOD M in MySQL) returns the remainder when N is divided by M. MySQL divides, cuts off the fraction (truncates toward zero), and then remainder = N − M × quotient. So the remainder always has the same sign as N, the dividend; the sign of M does not matter. This is like C and Java, but different from Python, where -17 % 5 is 3.
why: A — Wrong. 3 and -3 come from 'floor' division, where the remainder takes the sign of the divisor (as in Python: -17 % 5 = 3 and 17 % -5 = -3). MySQL truncates toward zero instead.
B — Wrong. 2 is right for MOD(17, -5), but MOD(-17, 5) is -2 in MySQL, not 3, because the remainder keeps the sign of -17.
C — Wrong. -2 is right for MOD(-17, 5), but MOD(17, -5) is +2: the dividend 17 is positive, so the remainder is positive.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. MySQL returns -2 and 2, which is not among A–C.
code: SELECT MOD(-17, 5), MOD(17, -5);
tip: MySQL MOD: the sign of the answer = the sign of the FIRST number. (Python's % follows the second number.)

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what does SELECT ROUND(1458.65, -2), TRUNCATE(1458.65, -2); return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A negative second argument works on the digits to the LEFT of the decimal point; -2 means 'to the hundreds'. ROUND rounds 1458.65 to the nearest hundred, 1500; TRUNCATE just cuts it, giving 1400.
concept: ROUND(x, d) rounds x to d decimal places, while TRUNCATE(x, d) simply cuts x after d decimal places without rounding. When d is negative, both work to the left of the decimal point: d = -1 → tens, d = -2 → hundreds, and the digits after that place become 0. In MySQL, TRUNCATE always needs two arguments (TRUNCATE(7.9) gives an error); Oracle calls the same function TRUNC. Do not confuse the function TRUNCATE(x, d) with the command TRUNCATE TABLE.
why: A — Wrong. 1500 is right for ROUND, but TRUNCATE never rounds up; it just drops everything after the hundreds place, giving 1400.
B — Correct. ROUND(1458.65, -2) = 1500 (the part 58.65 is 50 or more, so round up) and TRUNCATE(1458.65, -2) = 1400 (simply cut).
C — Wrong. 1400 is right for TRUNCATE, but ROUND goes to the nearest hundred, and 1458.65 is nearer to 1500 than to 1400.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT ROUND(1458.65, -2), TRUNCATE(1458.65, -2);
work:
Split 1458.65 at the hundreds place: 14 | 58.65
ROUND: 58.65 ≥ 50 → round up → 1500
TRUNCATE: drop the part after the hundreds → 1400
Run on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): ROUND(1458.65,-2) → 1500, TRUNCATE(1458.65,-2) → 1400 (also ROUND(1458.65,1) → 1458.7, TRUNCATE(1458.65,1) → 1458.6)
tip: TRUNCATE never rounds — it only cuts. A negative d works on the left side of the decimal point.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, which of the following expressions does NOT return the value 8?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three give 8: POW(2, 3) = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, SQRT(64) = 8, and TRUNCATE(8.99, 0) cuts off the decimals to give 8. So none of them is the NOT option.
concept: Common MySQL maths functions: POWER(x, y) or POW(x, y) gives x raised to the power y; SQRT(x) gives the square root; MOD(x, y) gives the remainder; ROUND(x, d) rounds to d decimal places; TRUNCATE(x, d) cuts after d decimal places without rounding. So TRUNCATE(8.99, 0) is 8 (no rounding up), while ROUND(8.99, 0) would be 9.
why: A — Wrong. POW is a synonym of POWER; POW(2, 3) = 2³ = 8, so it does return 8.
B — Wrong. SQRT(64) = 8, because 8 × 8 = 64, so it does return 8.
C — Wrong. TRUNCATE(8.99, 0) removes all digits after the decimal point without rounding, giving 8. (ROUND(8.99, 0) would give 9.)
D — Wrong. None of A–C satisfies the NOT stem, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Every expression returns 8, so none of them 'does NOT return 8'.
work:
POW(2, 3) = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8
SQRT(64) = 8 (8 × 8 = 64)
TRUNCATE(8.99, 0) → drop .99 → 8
Run on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): POW(2,3) → 8, SQRT(64) → 8, TRUNCATE(8.99,0) → 8; for contrast ROUND(8.99,0) → 9
tip: TRUNCATE cuts, ROUND rounds: TRUNCATE(8.99, 0) = 8 but ROUND(8.99, 0) = 9.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what does SELECT UCASE(MID('informatics', 3, 4)); return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MID('informatics', 3, 4) takes 4 characters starting at position 3: f, o, r, m → 'form'. UCASE turns it into capital letters: 'FORM'.
concept: MID(str, pos, n) is MySQL's synonym of SUBSTRING(str, pos, n) and SUBSTR(str, pos, n): it returns n characters starting at position pos, where the first character is position 1. If n is left out, it returns everything from pos to the end. UCASE(str) is a synonym of UPPER(str), and LCASE(str) of LOWER(str). UCASE, LCASE and MID are MySQL names; standard SQL uses UPPER, LOWER and SUBSTRING.
why: A — Correct. Positions 3 to 6 of 'informatics' are f, o, r, m; in capitals that is FORM.
B — Wrong. NFOR comes from counting the first character as position 0. In SQL the first character is position 1, so position 3 is 'f', not 'n'.
C — Wrong. FORMATICS is what you get when the length argument is left out (MID('informatics', 3) returns everything from position 3). Here the length is 4.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT UCASE(MID('informatics', 3, 4));
work:
i(1) n(2) f(3) o(4) r(5) m(6) a(7) t(8) i(9) c(10) s(11)
MID(…, 3, 4) → positions 3–6 → 'form'
UCASE('form') → 'FORM'
Run on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): UCASE(MID('informatics',3,4)) → FORM; MID('informatics',3) → formatics
tip: In MySQL: MID = SUBSTR = SUBSTRING; UCASE = UPPER; LCASE = LOWER. Positions start at 1.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what does SELECT SUBSTR('INFORMATICS', -5, 3); return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A negative start position is counted from the END of the string: -1 is the last letter S, so -5 is A. Taking 3 characters from there gives ATI.
concept: In MySQL, SUBSTR / SUBSTRING / MID accept a negative start position: the start is then counted from the end of the string, with -1 meaning the last character. The length still runs forward (to the right). So SUBSTR(s, -n) returns the last n characters, the same as RIGHT(s, n). A start position of 0 returns an empty string.
why: A — Wrong. RMA is SUBSTR('INFORMATICS', 5, 3) — it treats -5 as +5 (counting from the left). A negative position is counted from the right end.

B — Wrong. TIC would need the start at T, but T is position -4 (S = -1, C = -2, I = -3, T = -4). Starting one place too far to the right is a common off-by-one slip; position -5 is A, so the result is ATI.
C — Correct. From the end: S = -1, C = -2, I = -3, T = -4, A = -5. Three characters from A are A, T, I → ATI.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT SUBSTR('INFORMATICS', -5, 3);
work:
INFORMATICS has 11 letters: I1 N2 F3 O4 R5 M6 A7 T8 I9 C10 S11
From the end: S = -1, C = -2, I = -3, T = -4, A = -5 → start at position 11 − 5 + 1 = 7
3 characters from position 7 → A, T, I → 'ATI'
Run on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): SUBSTR('INFORMATICS',-5,3) → ATI; SUBSTR('INFORMATICS',5,3) → RMA
tip: Negative start = count from the right, -1 = the last character. As a normal position: length − n + 1.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, which of the following expressions return the string 'PUT'?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MID('COMPUTER', 4, 3) = PUT, and SUBSTR('COMPUTER', -5, 3) = PUT because position -5 from the end is P. RIGHT('COMPUTER', 4) = 'UTER', and the LEFT 3 of that is 'UTE', so C is false.
concept: LEFT(str, n) returns the first n characters and RIGHT(str, n) the last n characters. MID / SUBSTR / SUBSTRING(str, pos, n) returns n characters from position pos (counted from 1; a negative pos is counted from the end). Nested functions are worked out from the inside: the result of the inner function becomes the string for the outer one.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. C(1) O(2) M(3) P(4) U(5) T(6) …, so 3 characters from position 4 are P, U, T.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. COMPUTER has 8 letters; position -5 is 8 − 5 + 1 = 4, the letter P, so 3 characters give PUT.
C — Wrong. RIGHT('COMPUTER', 4) is 'UTER' (the last 4 letters), and LEFT('UTER', 3) is 'UTE', not 'PUT'. RIGHT(LEFT('COMPUTER', 6), 3) would give PUT.
D — Correct. A and B both return 'PUT', so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
C1 O2 M3 P4 U5 T6 E7 R8
A: MID(…, 4, 3) → positions 4–6 → PUT ✓
B: -5 → 8 − 5 + 1 = 4 → positions 4–6 → PUT ✓
C: RIGHT(…, 4) → UTER; LEFT('UTER', 3) → UTE ✗
Run on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): PUT, PUT, UTE (and RIGHT(LEFT('COMPUTER',6),3) → PUT)
tip: For nested string functions, work from the innermost bracket outwards and write down each in-between string.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what does SELECT CONCAT('Roll-', 5, NULL); return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In MySQL, CONCAT returns NULL if any of its arguments is NULL. So the whole result is NULL, even though 'Roll-' and 5 are known.
concept: CONCAT(s1, s2, …) joins its arguments into one string; numbers are converted to text, so CONCAT('Roll-', 5) = 'Roll-5'. But if any argument is NULL, MySQL's CONCAT returns NULL, because joining with an unknown value gives an unknown result. To skip NULLs, use CONCAT_WS(separator, …), which ignores NULL arguments, or replace the NULL first with IFNULL(x, ''). Oracle is different: there CONCAT and || treat NULL like an empty string.
why: A — Wrong. 'Roll-5' is the result of CONCAT('Roll-', 5). Adding a NULL argument makes MySQL's CONCAT return NULL; it does not simply skip the NULL (CONCAT_WS would skip it).
B — Wrong. NULL is not the text 'NULL'; it is a marker for a missing value, so it is never joined as the four letters N-U-L-L.
C — Correct. MySQL's CONCAT returns NULL as soon as any argument is NULL.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT CONCAT('Roll-', 5, NULL);
work:
CONCAT('Roll-', 5) → 'Roll-5' (5 is converted to text)
One more argument is NULL → MySQL rule: any NULL argument → result NULL
Run on MariaDB in its default mode (same rule as MySQL 8): CONCAT('Roll-',5) → Roll-5; CONCAT('Roll-',5,NULL) → NULL; CONCAT_WS('-','Roll',NULL,5) → Roll-5
tip: MySQL: CONCAT + any NULL = NULL. Oracle's CONCAT and || ignore NULL. In MySQL use IFNULL or CONCAT_WS to be safe.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what does the query below return? (The second string has TWO spaces before Hi and TWO spaces after there.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: TRIM(LEADING '*' FROM …) removes the stars only from the start, leaving 'Ram**'. LTRIM removes only the 2 leading spaces, so 'Hi there  ' has 8 + 2 = 10 characters.
concept: MySQL's trimming functions: LTRIM(s) removes leading (left) spaces, RTRIM(s) removes trailing (right) spaces, and TRIM(s) removes both. The full form TRIM([BOTH | LEADING | TRAILING] [chars] FROM s) can remove any given character, such as '*', from both ends (BOTH, the default), only the start (LEADING) or only the end (TRAILING). Characters in the middle of the string are never removed. LENGTH(s) counts every character, spaces included.
why: A — Wrong. 'Ram' and 8 would come from TRIM(BOTH '*' …) and LENGTH(TRIM(…)), which work on both ends. LEADING removes only from the start, and LTRIM removes only the left spaces.
B — Correct. LEADING keeps the stars at the end → 'Ram**'; LTRIM leaves 'Hi there' plus 2 trailing spaces → 10 characters.
C — Wrong. '**Ram' is the result of TRAILING (remove from the end). LEADING removes from the start, so the stars at the end stay.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
SELECT TRIM(LEADING '*' FROM '**Ram**'),
       LENGTH(LTRIM('  Hi there  '));
work:
TRIM(LEADING '*' FROM '**Ram**') → remove '*' at the start only → 'Ram**'
'  Hi there  ' = 2 + 8 ('Hi there') + 2 = 12 characters
LTRIM → 'Hi there  ' → 8 + 2 = 10
Run on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): 'Ram**', 10 (TRAILING → '**Ram', BOTH → 'Ram'; LENGTH(TRIM(…)) → 8)
tip: LEADING = start (left), TRAILING = end (right), BOTH = default. LTRIM and RTRIM remove only spaces.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In MySQL, what does SELECT MONTHNAME('2024-08-15'), DAYNAME('2024-08-15'); return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MONTHNAME gives the name of the month (August) and DAYNAME gives the name of the weekday; 15 August 2024 was a Thursday.
concept: Common MySQL date functions: NOW() gives the current date and time; CURDATE() the current date; DATE(dt) the date part of a date-time; MONTH(d) the month number 1–12; MONTHNAME(d) the month name; YEAR(d) the year; DAY(d) the day of the month 1–31; DAYNAME(d) the weekday name, such as 'Monday'. The functions ending in NAME return text; the others return numbers.
why: A — Correct. MONTHNAME('2024-08-15') = 'August' and DAYNAME('2024-08-15') = 'Thursday'.
B — Wrong. 8 and 15 are the results of MONTH() and DAY(), which return numbers. The NAME functions return words.
C — Wrong. August is right, but 15 is what DAY() returns (the day of the month). DAYNAME returns the name of the weekday, Thursday.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code: SELECT MONTHNAME('2024-08-15'), DAYNAME('2024-08-15');
work:
'2024-08-15' → year 2024, month 8, day 15
MONTHNAME → month 8 → 'August'
DAYNAME → 15 August 2024 was a Thursday
Run on MariaDB (same as MySQL 8): August, Thursday (MONTH → 8, DAY → 15, YEAR → 2024)
tip: …NAME() functions return words (August, Thursday); MONTH(), DAY() and YEAR() return numbers.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q:
Consider the following statements about MySQL date-time functions:
I. In SELECT NOW(), SLEEP(2), NOW(); both NOW() values are the same, because NOW() returns the time at which the statement began.
II. In SELECT SYSDATE(), SLEEP(2), SYSDATE(); the two values differ by about 2 seconds, because SYSDATE() returns the time at which it actually runs.
III. CURDATE() returns the current date together with the current time.
Which of these are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and II are true: NOW() is fixed at the start of the statement, while SYSDATE() reads the clock each time it runs. III is false: CURDATE() returns only the date, such as '2024-08-15'.
concept: NOW() (also CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) returns the current date and time as a constant for the whole statement: the time at which the statement began. SYSDATE() returns the exact time at the moment it is evaluated, so it can change within one statement. CURDATE() (also CURRENT_DATE) returns only the date, in 'YYYY-MM-DD' form; DATE(NOW()) gives the same value. SLEEP(n) simply pauses for n seconds and returns 0.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is also true: SYSDATE() reads the clock again when it is evaluated, so after SLEEP(2) it shows a time about 2 seconds later.
B — Correct. I and II are true; III is false because CURDATE() gives only the date.
C — Wrong. Statement III is false: CURDATE() returns only the date (for example 2024-08-15). NOW() and SYSDATE() are the functions that also give the time.
D — Wrong. Only option B matches the correct set of statements; the other options list a wrong set, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. Option B gives exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Run on MariaDB (same documented behaviour as MySQL 8):
SELECT NOW(), SLEEP(2), NOW(), SYSDATE(), SLEEP(2), SYSDATE() →
  NOW() = 06:23:04 and NOW() = 06:23:04 (same)
  SYSDATE() = 06:23:06 and SYSDATE() = 06:23:08 (2 seconds apart)
SELECT CURDATE() → 2026-10-22 (date only); DATE(NOW()) = CURDATE() → 1 (true)
tip: NOW() = time the statement started (fixed). SYSDATE() = time it actually runs. CURDATE() = date only.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In a Python program, mycon = mysql.connector.connect(…) creates a connection object. Which method of mycon returns True if the connection to the MySQL server is working?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The connection object of mysql.connector has the method is_connected(), which returns True when the connection to the server is available and False otherwise (for example, after close()).
concept: The usual Class 12 (CBSE) steps for Python–MySQL connectivity: (1) import mysql.connector; (2) mycon = mysql.connector.connect(host=…, user=…, passwd=…, database=…); (3) check it with if mycon.is_connected(): print('Connected'); (4) create a cursor with cur = mycon.cursor(); (5) run SQL with cur.execute(query); (6) read the result with fetchone(), fetchall() or fetchmany(n), or call mycon.commit() after INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; (7) close with mycon.close().
why: A — Wrong. The connection object has no method named connected(); calling it raises an AttributeError.
B — Wrong. isopen() is not a method of mysql.connector's connection object either; it would raise an AttributeError.
C — Correct. is_connected() returns True for a working connection (and False after mycon.close()).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested with mysql.connector against MariaDB: hasattr(mycon, 'is_connected') → True; hasattr(mycon, 'connected') → False; hasattr(mycon, 'isopen') → False.
print(mycon.is_connected()) → True; after mycon.close() → False.
tip: Seven steps: import → connect → is_connected → cursor → execute → fetch / commit → close.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In mysql.connector, which of the following keyword arguments can be used to give the password in the call mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root", …, database="school")?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: password is the official argument name, and passwd is accepted as a synonym (for compatibility with the older MySQLdb module); Class 12 textbooks usually write passwd. pwd is not recognised and raises an error.
concept: mysql.connector.connect() takes keyword arguments such as host (the server, for example 'localhost'), user, password and database. For compatibility with older Python MySQL modules it also accepts passwd as another name for password, and db as another name for database. Any other name, such as pwd, gives an error, because connect() does not know it.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. passwd is accepted as a synonym of password; Class 12 textbook examples usually write passwd="…".
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. password is the name used in the MySQL Connector/Python documentation.
C — Wrong. pwd is not an argument of connect(); mysql.connector raises AttributeError: Unsupported argument 'pwd'.
D — Correct. A and B both work, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested with mysql.connector against MariaDB (socket connection as root, whose password is empty here; Connector/Python 26.7.0 and 9.4.0, C extension and pure Python gave the same results):
connect(…, passwd="") → connected, is_connected() → True
connect(…, password="") → connected, is_connected() → True
connect(…, pwd="") → AttributeError: Unsupported argument 'pwd'
tip: In mysql.connector.connect(): password = passwd and database = db.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: After cur.execute("SELECT * FROM student") in a Python program that uses mysql.connector, which of the following statements is NOT correct?
opts: cur.fetchone() returns None when there are no more rows to read
cur.fetchall() returns all the remaining rows as one single tuple
cur.fetchmany(3) returns a list of at most 3 rows, each row being a tuple
More than one of the above
exp: fetchall() returns a LIST of tuples (one tuple per row), not one single tuple. A and C are correct descriptions.
concept: The fetch methods read the result of a SELECT. fetchone() returns the next row as a tuple, or None when no rows are left. fetchmany(n) returns a list of the next n rows (fewer if fewer remain, an empty list if none). fetchall() returns a list of all the remaining rows (an empty list if none). Each row is a tuple, so data[0][1] is the second column of the first row.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is correct: once all rows have been read, fetchone() returns None, which is how a while loop knows when to stop. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Correct. This statement is wrong, so it satisfies the NOT stem: fetchall() returns a list such as [(1, 'Ravi', 85), (2, 'Meena', 57)], one tuple per row — not one tuple holding everything.
C — Wrong. This statement is correct: fetchmany(3) returns a list of up to 3 tuples (fewer if fewer rows remain), so it does not fit the NOT stem.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the NOT stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. B satisfies the NOT stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested with mysql.connector against MariaDB (5-row STUDENT table, SELECT * FROM student; pure Python and C extension gave the same results):
fetchone() → tuple (1, 'Ravi', 85)
fetchmany(3) → list [(2, 'Meena', 57), (3, 'Amit', 72), (4, 'Sita', 49)]
fetchall() → list [(5, 'Arjun', 91)] (a list even when only one row is left)
On a 2-row result, fetchone() called 4 times → row 1, row 2, None, None; fetchall() when nothing is left → []
tip: fetchone → one tuple or None; fetchmany(n) and fetchall → a list of tuples (maybe empty).

q: Table STUDENT of database school has the 5 rows shown. What does the following Python program print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: For a normal (unbuffered) cursor, rowcount after a SELECT counts the rows fetched so far. Two fetchone() calls have read 2 rows, so the program prints 2, which is not listed.
concept: cursor.rowcount is a read-only attribute. After a SELECT it gives the number of rows fetched so far: just after execute() no row has been read, so the pure-Python connector shows -1, meaning 'not known yet' (the C extension shows 0), and it goes up by 1 for every row read with fetchone(), fetchmany() or fetchall(). (A cursor made with cursor(buffered=True) reads all rows at once, so its rowcount is the full count straight away.) After INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, rowcount gives the number of rows affected.
why: A — Wrong. -1 means 'not known yet'; the pure-Python connector shows it just after execute(), before any row is fetched (the C extension shows 0 there). Two rows have been fetched since then.
B — Wrong. 5 is the total number of rows in the result. rowcount shows only the rows read so far, and only 2 have been read.
C — Wrong. 1 would be the count after a single fetchone(). Each fetchone() adds 1, and there are two calls.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The program prints 2 (two rows fetched so far), which is not among A–C.
code:
STUDENT
Roll | Name  | Marks
1    | Ravi  | 85
2    | Meena | 57
3    | Amit  | 72
4    | Sita  | 49
5    | Arjun | 91

import mysql.connector
mycon = mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root",
                                passwd="tiger", database="school")
cur = mycon.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT name FROM student ORDER BY roll")
r1 = cur.fetchone()
r2 = cur.fetchone()
print(cur.rowcount)
mycon.close()
work:
execute() → nothing fetched yet (rowcount -1 in pure Python, 0 with the C extension)
fetchone() → ('Ravi',) → rowcount = 1
fetchone() → ('Meena',) → rowcount = 2
print → 2
Run for real against MariaDB with mysql.connector (Connector/Python 26.7.0 pure Python, and 9.4.0 both with its C extension and pure Python); the connection line was replaced by an equivalent socket connection (user root) to a scratch copy of database school with the same rows. Output: 2 in every case.
tip: rowcount after a SELECT = rows fetched SO FAR, not the size of the result.

q: Table STUDENT of database school has the 5 rows shown. What does the following Python program print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: fetchmany(3) reads rows 1–3; fetchall() then reads only the REMAINING 2 rows; rowcount counts all the rows fetched so far, 3 + 2 = 5.
concept: A cursor works like a reading pointer that moves forward through the result. Every fetch continues from where the previous one stopped, so a row is never returned twice. fetchall() therefore returns only the rows not yet read. For a SELECT, rowcount is the total number of rows fetched so far by all the fetch calls together.
why: A — Correct. a has 3 rows, b has the remaining 2, and 5 rows have been fetched in total.
B — Wrong. fetchall() does not start again from the first row; it returns only the 2 rows that fetchmany(3) did not read.
C — Wrong. rowcount is not the number of rows read by the last call; it is the running total of rows fetched since execute(), 3 + 2 = 5.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
STUDENT
Roll | Name  | Marks
1    | Ravi  | 85
2    | Meena | 57
3    | Amit  | 72
4    | Sita  | 49
5    | Arjun | 91

import mysql.connector
mycon = mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root",
                                passwd="tiger", database="school")
cur = mycon.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM student")
a = cur.fetchmany(3)
b = cur.fetchall()
print(len(a), len(b), cur.rowcount)
mycon.close()
work:
execute() → pointer before row 1, nothing fetched yet
fetchmany(3) → rows 1, 2, 3 → len(a) = 3, rowcount 3
fetchall() → rows 4, 5 → len(b) = 2, rowcount 5
print → 3 2 5
Run for real against MariaDB with mysql.connector (Connector/Python 26.7.0 pure Python, and 9.4.0 both with its C extension and pure Python); the connection line was replaced by an equivalent socket connection (user root) to a scratch copy of database school with the same rows. Output: 3 2 5
tip: All fetch calls share one pointer: fetchmany followed by fetchall gives the rest, never a repeat.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In mysql.connector, the values can be passed separately to execute() of an ordinary cursor (cur = mycon.cursor()), as in cur.execute(query, (6, 'Kiran', 66)). Which placeholder must be written in the query string for these values?
opts: %d for the numbers and %s for the string
%s for every value, whatever its type
More than one of the above
exp: With an ordinary cursor, mysql.connector expects %s for every value, whether it is a number, a string or a date (or %(name)s when a dictionary is passed). The connector converts and quotes each value itself.
concept: A parameterized query keeps the SQL text and the data apart: cur.execute("INSERT INTO student VALUES (%s, %s, %s)", (6, 'Kiran', 66)). mysql.connector replaces each %s with the matching value from the tuple, adding quotes and escaping where needed. Here %s is only a marker, not Python's string-format code, so it is used for every data type. This is safer than building the query with format() or %, because it prevents SQL injection. (The ? marker is used by Python's sqlite3 module; in mysql.connector it works only with the special prepared cursor made by mycon.cursor(prepared=True), not with the ordinary cursor.)
why: A — Wrong. %d is Python's integer format code, but mysql.connector does not accept it as a placeholder; it raises 'Not all parameters were used in the SQL statement'. Numbers also use %s.
B — Correct. With an ordinary cursor, mysql.connector's placeholder is %s for every type of value (or %(name)s when a dictionary is passed).

C — Wrong. ? is the placeholder of the sqlite3 module (qmark style). The ordinary mysql.connector cursor does not understand it and raises the same error. (Only the special prepared cursor, mycon.cursor(prepared=True), accepts ?.)
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Tested with mysql.connector against MariaDB (Connector/Python 26.7.0 and 9.4.0, C extension and pure Python):
… WHERE roll = %s AND marks > %s with (3, 70) → [('Amit',)]
… WHERE roll = %d AND marks > %d with (3, 70) → ProgrammingError: Not all parameters were used in the SQL statement
… WHERE roll = ? AND marks > ? with (3, 70) → the same ProgrammingError
INSERT … VALUES (%s, %s, %s) with (6, 'Kiran', 66.0) → 1 row inserted
Checker re-run (Connector/Python 26.7.0, pure Python and C extension): ordinary cursor with ? → ProgrammingError; prepared cursor mycon.cursor(prepared=True) with ? → 1 row inserted (it also accepts %s).
tip: mysql.connector with an ordinary cursor: always %s. sqlite3: ? (qmark style).

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: Table STUDENT (InnoDB, MySQL's default storage engine) has 5 rows. What does the following Python program print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: mysql.connector does not autocommit. Inside the first connection the uncommitted row is visible, so COUNT(*) is 6. The connection is closed without commit(), so the INSERT is rolled back, and the new connection sees 5 rows.
concept: mysql.connector follows the Python DB-API, so autocommit is OFF by default. An INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE starts a transaction: its changes are visible inside the same connection but become permanent only after mycon.commit(). If the program closes the connection (or ends) without commit(), the server rolls the transaction back. That is why Class 12 programs always call mycon.commit() after statements that change data. (MyISAM tables have no transactions, so this applies to InnoDB tables, the default.)
why: A — Correct. The same connection sees its own uncommitted INSERT (6), but without commit() the INSERT is undone when the connection closes, so the new connection counts 5.
B — Wrong. The second count would be 6 only if mycon.commit() had been called before close(). Without commit, the new row is rolled back.
C — Wrong. A transaction always sees its own changes, so the first COUNT(*), run in the same connection, already includes Kiran and gives 6.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
import mysql.connector
mycon = mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root",
                                passwd="tiger", database="school")
cur = mycon.cursor()
cur.execute("INSERT INTO student VALUES (6, 'Kiran', 66)")
cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM student")
print(cur.fetchone()[0])
mycon.close()

mycon = mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root",
                                passwd="tiger", database="school")
cur = mycon.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM student")
print(cur.fetchone()[0])
mycon.close()
work:
Connection 1: INSERT row 6 → transaction open, not committed
COUNT(*) in the same connection → 6 (its own change is visible)
close() without commit() → the server rolls back the INSERT
Connection 2: COUNT(*) → 5
Run for real against MariaDB with mysql.connector (Connector/Python 26.7.0 pure Python, and 9.4.0 both with its C extension and pure Python); the connection line was replaced by an equivalent socket connection (user root) to a scratch copy of database school with the same rows. Output: 6, then 5. mycon.autocommit is False by default.
tip: No commit() → no permanent change. Always call mycon.commit() after INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE.

D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.

q: In Oracle, what Pay values does the query below return for Asha, Vikas and Neha (in that order)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: NVL2(x, a, b) returns a when x is NOT NULL and b when x is NULL. Asha's Comm is NULL → Sal = 30000; Vikas → 25000 + 1500 = 26500; Neha's Comm is 0, which is not NULL → 28000 + 0 = 28000.
concept: Oracle's NULL functions: NVL(x, y) returns y if x is NULL, otherwise x. NVL2(x, a, b) returns a if x is NOT NULL and b if x is NULL, so it lets you choose a different expression for each case. Zero is a real value, not NULL, so it counts as 'not null'. The standard function COALESCE(x1, x2, …) returns the first non-NULL argument.
why: A — Wrong. NULL would come from writing Sal + Comm directly, because adding NULL gives NULL. NVL2 avoids this: when Comm is NULL it returns its third argument, Sal = 30000.
B — Correct. NULL Comm → Sal (30000); non-NULL Comm → Sal + Comm (26500 and 28000).
C — Wrong. 1500 and 0 are the Comm values themselves. NVL2 never returns its first argument; when Comm is not NULL it returns the second argument, Sal + Comm.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
EMP
EName | Sal   | Comm
Asha  | 30000 | NULL
Vikas | 25000 | 1500
Neha  | 28000 | 0

SELECT EName, NVL2(Comm, Sal + Comm, Sal) AS Pay
FROM EMP;
work:
Asha: Comm NULL → third argument Sal → 30000
Vikas: Comm 1500 is not NULL → Sal + Comm = 25000 + 1500 = 26500
Neha: Comm 0 is not NULL → Sal + Comm = 28000 + 0 = 28000
Logic checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB with the equivalent CASE WHEN Comm IS NOT NULL THEN Sal + Comm ELSE Sal END → 30000, 26500, 28000 (NVL2 itself is Oracle-only).
tip: NVL2(x, value-if-NOT-null, value-if-null). Zero is NOT null.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In Oracle, what does the query below show in the Remark column for Meena and for Sita?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DECODE compares Grade with 'A' and then with 'B'. Meena's 'C' matches neither, and Sita's NULL matches neither, so both rows get the default value 'Average'.
concept: DECODE(expr, s1, r1, s2, r2, …, default) is Oracle's older form of a CASE expression: it compares expr with each search value s1, s2, … in order and returns the result paired with the first match. If nothing matches, it returns the default; if no default is given, it returns NULL. Standard SQL writes the same thing as CASE expr WHEN s1 THEN r1 WHEN s2 THEN r2 ELSE default END. One difference: DECODE treats two NULLs as equal, so DECODE(Grade, NULL, 'No grade', …) would match Sita's NULL, while CASE Grade WHEN NULL never matches.
why: A — Correct. Neither 'C' nor NULL equals 'A' or 'B', so DECODE returns the default 'Average' for both rows.

B — Wrong. A NULL Grade does not make DECODE return NULL; NULL simply fails to match 'A' and 'B', so the default 'Average' is returned. When nothing matches, DECODE returns NULL only if no default is given.
C — Wrong. DECODE never returns the input value itself when nothing matches; it returns the default (the last, unpaired argument).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
RESULT
Name  | Grade
Ravi  | A
Meena | C
Amit  | B
Sita  | NULL

SELECT Name,
       DECODE(Grade, 'A', 'Excellent', 'B', 'Good', 'Average') AS Remark
FROM RESULT;
work:
Ravi: 'A' = 'A' → Excellent
Meena: 'C' ≠ 'A', 'C' ≠ 'B' → default → Average
Amit: 'B' → Good
Sita: NULL matches neither 'A' nor 'B' → default → Average
Logic checked on SQLite, PostgreSQL 16 and DuckDB with the equivalent CASE expression → Meena Average, Sita Average (DECODE itself is Oracle-only).
tip: DECODE(value, search, result, search, result, …, default) — the last unpaired argument is the default.
