q: In Oracle, table STU(roll, name) already exists, and the statements below are run in one session. What does the last SELECT print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The first NEXTVAL returns the start value 100, the second 110 and the third 120. CURRVAL returns the last value given by NEXTVAL in this session, 120, which is not listed.
concept: An Oracle SEQUENCE is a database object that generates numbers, often used for key columns. The first reference to seq.NEXTVAL returns the START WITH value; each later NEXTVAL adds the INCREMENT BY amount and returns the new value. seq.CURRVAL returns the value most recently produced by NEXTVAL in the current session and does not change the sequence. CURRVAL cannot be used in a session until NEXTVAL has been called at least once (error ORA-08002).
why: A — Wrong. 100 is the first value, given to Ravi. After three NEXTVAL calls the sequence has moved on to 120.
B — Wrong. 110 is the second value, given to Meena. Amit's INSERT called NEXTVAL a third time, giving 120.
C — Wrong. 130 would be the NEXT value. CURRVAL does not move the sequence forward; it repeats the last value, 120.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. CURRVAL is 120 (the value given to Amit), which is not among A–C.
work:
NEXTVAL #1 → 100 (Ravi)
NEXTVAL #2 → 110 (Meena)
NEXTVAL #3 → 120 (Amit)
CURRVAL → the last value from NEXTVAL → 120
Model run on PostgreSQL 16 (CREATE SEQUENCE roll_seq START WITH 100 INCREMENT BY 10; nextval three times; currval) → 120; rows 100, 110, 120.
tip: NEXTVAL moves the sequence forward; CURRVAL only repeats the last NEXTVAL of your session.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q:
Consider the following statements about Oracle pseudocolumns:
I. ROWID gives the address of a row; it is the fastest way to reach that single row.
II. SELECT * FROM emp WHERE ROWNUM > 1; returns every row of EMP except the first one.
III. ROWNUM numbers the rows of a query result 1, 2, 3, … in the order in which Oracle selects them.
Which of these are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: I and III are true. II is false: the first candidate row gets ROWNUM 1, fails ROWNUM > 1 and is dropped; the next row then also gets ROWNUM 1 and fails too, so the query returns no rows at all.
concept: A pseudocolumn behaves like a column but is not stored in the table. ROWID holds the address of a row in the database (which data object, file, block and slot it is in); it is the fastest way to locate one row. ROWNUM is a number given to each row as the query selects it: 1 for the first row that passes the WHERE condition, 2 for the next, and so on. Because a number is used up only when a row passes, conditions such as ROWNUM = 1 or ROWNUM <= n work, but ROWNUM > 1 or ROWNUM = 2 are never true.
why: A — Wrong. Statement II is false: WHERE ROWNUM > 1 returns no rows, not 'all rows except the first'.
B — Wrong. Statement II is false (see above), and this option also leaves out statement I, which is true.
C — Correct. ROWID is the row's address (I) and ROWNUM numbers the selected rows from 1 (III); II is false.
D — Wrong. Only option C matches the correct set of statements; the other options list a wrong set, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. Option C gives exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Trace of WHERE ROWNUM > 1: row 1 is given ROWNUM 1 → 1 > 1 is false → rejected; the number 1 is not used up, so row 2 is also given ROWNUM 1 → rejected; … every row is rejected → 0 rows.
Oracle SQL Language Reference, ROWNUM pseudocolumn: 'Conditions testing for ROWNUM values greater than a positive integer are always false. For example, this query returns no rows: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE ROWNUM > 1;'
ROWID pseudocolumn: 'returns the address of the row'; rowids are the fastest way to access a single row.
tip: ROWNUM = 1 and ROWNUM <= n work; ROWNUM > 1 and ROWNUM = 2 return nothing.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: Which of the following statements about Oracle PL/SQL are correct?
opts: In a PL/SQL block, only the executable part BEGIN … END is compulsory; the DECLARE and EXCEPTION parts are optional
The declaration v_sal emp.sal%TYPE; gives v_sal the same data type as the column sal of table EMP
The declaration r emp%ROWTYPE; declares a record that can hold one complete row of table EMP
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true: a block needs only BEGIN … END; %TYPE copies the data type of a column or variable; %ROWTYPE declares a record with one field for every column of the table.
concept: A PL/SQL block has up to three parts: DECLARE (optional — variables, constants, cursors), BEGIN (compulsory — the statements to run) and EXCEPTION (optional — error handlers), followed by END;. Anchored declarations save you from repeating data types: x emp.sal%TYPE takes the type of column emp.sal, and r emp%ROWTYPE creates a record whose fields match all the columns of EMP, used as r.ename, r.sal. If the column type changes later, these declarations follow it automatically. In SQL*Plus, Oracle's command-line tool, SET SERVEROUTPUT ON is needed to see DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE output, and a / on a line by itself runs the block.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Oracle describes a block as an optional declarative part, a required executable part and an optional exception-handling part.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. %TYPE anchors a variable to the data type of a column (or of another variable).

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. %ROWTYPE declares a record whose fields have the same names and data types as the columns of the table.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Only BEGIN … END is a must. %TYPE = the type of one column; %ROWTYPE = a whole row.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In Oracle PL/SQL, the statement SELECT sal INTO v_sal FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'; is run, and three employees work in the IT department. Which predefined exception is raised?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SELECT … INTO must return exactly one row. Three rows are more than one, so Oracle raises TOO_MANY_ROWS (ORA-01422).
concept: SELECT … INTO copies one row into PL/SQL variables, so it must return exactly one row. If it returns no row, the predefined exception NO_DATA_FOUND (ORA-01403) is raised; if it returns more than one row, TOO_MANY_ROWS (ORA-01422) is raised. Other common predefined exceptions are ZERO_DIVIDE (ORA-01476, division by zero), VALUE_ERROR (a conversion or size error) and DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX (a duplicate value in a unique column). They are handled in the EXCEPTION part, for example WHEN TOO_MANY_ROWS THEN …; WHEN OTHERS catches any remaining error. To process many rows, use a cursor.
why: A — Wrong. NO_DATA_FOUND is raised when SELECT … INTO returns zero rows. Here it returns three.
B — Correct. More than one row from SELECT … INTO raises TOO_MANY_ROWS.
C — Wrong. ZERO_DIVIDE is raised when a number is divided by zero; there is no division here.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: SELECT … INTO: 0 rows → NO_DATA_FOUND; 2 or more rows → TOO_MANY_ROWS.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In SQL Server, which system database holds temporary tables and other temporary objects, and is re-created every time SQL Server starts?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: tempdb is SQL Server's workspace for temporary tables, table variables and intermediate results. It is re-created every time SQL Server starts, so nothing in it is kept permanently.
concept: SQL Server has four main system databases. master records all the system-level information of the instance (logins, configuration settings, the list of databases). model is the template: every new database starts as a copy of it. msdb is used by SQL Server Agent to store jobs and alerts, and also keeps backup history. tempdb is a workspace for temporary tables (such as #temp), table variables and intermediate results; it is re-created at every start of SQL Server. SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is the graphical tool used to manage all of these.
why: A — Wrong. master stores the instance's system-level information, such as logins, configuration and the existence of every database. It is permanent and must never be lost.
B — Wrong. model is the template copied whenever a new database is created (tempdb itself is also built from it at startup), but temporary objects are not kept in model.
C — Correct. tempdb holds temporary tables and intermediate results and is re-created fresh each time SQL Server starts.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: master = system information, model = template, msdb = Agent jobs and backup history, tempdb = temporary, emptied at every restart.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In SQL Server, members of which fixed server role can create, alter, drop and restore any database?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The fixed server role dbcreator lets its members create, alter, drop and restore any database on the server.
concept: Fixed server roles give permissions on the whole SQL Server instance: sysadmin — can do anything; serveradmin — change server-wide settings and shut down the server; securityadmin — manage logins and their permissions; processadmin — end running processes; setupadmin — add and remove linked servers; bulkadmin — run BULK INSERT; diskadmin — manage disk files; dbcreator — create, alter, drop and restore any database. Fixed database roles (names starting with db_, such as db_owner) work inside one database only.
why: A — Correct. The dbcreator role allows its members to create, alter, drop and restore any database.
B — Wrong. diskadmin is the fixed server role for managing disk files; it does not give the right to create or drop databases.
C — Wrong. setupadmin lets its members add and remove linked servers (links to other database servers); it is not about creating databases.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The role name tells the job: dbcreator → databases, diskadmin → disk files, setupadmin → linked servers, bulkadmin → BULK INSERT.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: In SQL Server, table ORDERS is created as below, and three rows are inserted without giving an OrderID. What OrderID does the third row get?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: IDENTITY(seed, increment): the first row gets the seed 100, and each next row adds 5, giving 100, 105, 110. So the third row gets 110.
concept: IDENTITY(seed, increment) makes SQL Server generate a column's values automatically: seed is the value for the very first row, and increment is added for each following row. With IDENTITY(1,1) — the default when no numbers are given — the values are 1, 2, 3, … A table can have only one identity column, and you normally do not insert values into it yourself (that needs SET IDENTITY_INSERT ON). Similar features are AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL and SEQUENCE objects or identity columns in Oracle.
why: A — Wrong. 105 is the second row's value (100 + 5). The third row adds another 5.
B — Correct. Row n gets seed + (n − 1) × increment = 100 + 2 × 5 = 110.
C — Wrong. 115 comes from giving the first row 100 + 5. The first row gets the seed itself, 100.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Row 1 (Pen) → seed = 100
Row 2 (Ink) → 100 + 5 = 105
Row 3 (Book) → 105 + 5 = 110
Formula: seed + (n − 1) × increment = 100 + 2 × 5 = 110
Model run on PostgreSQL 16 with an identity column START WITH 100 INCREMENT BY 5 → 100, 105, 110.
tip: IDENTITY(seed, increment): the first row gets the seed itself, NOT seed + increment.

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q:
Consider the following statements about indexes in SQL Server:
I. A table can have only one clustered index, because the data rows themselves can be stored in only one order.
II. A table can have many nonclustered indexes.
III. If a table has no clustered index, a PRIMARY KEY constraint creates a clustered index on the key by default.
Which of these are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are true. A clustered index decides the physical order of the rows, so there can be only one; nonclustered indexes (up to 999 per table) are separate structures; and PRIMARY KEY creates a clustered index by default when the table does not already have one.
concept: In a clustered index, the table's data rows themselves are stored in the order of the index key — like a dictionary, where the entries are kept in alphabetical order. Since rows can be sorted in only one way, a table has at most one clustered index. A nonclustered index is a separate structure holding key values with pointers to the rows — like the index at the back of a textbook; SQL Server allows up to 999 of them per table. Creating a PRIMARY KEY makes a unique clustered index automatically, unless a clustered index already exists or NONCLUSTERED is written.
why: A — Correct. Statements I, II and III are all true.
B — Wrong. Statement III is also true: by default a PRIMARY KEY creates a clustered index when the table has none.
C — Wrong. Statement I is also true: only one clustered index is possible, because the rows can be physically sorted in only one order.
D — Wrong. Only option A matches the correct set of statements; the other options list a wrong set, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Wrong. Option A gives exactly the correct statements, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Clustered = the book itself kept in sorted order (only 1). Nonclustered = the index pages at the back (many).

topic: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server & Python–SQL Connectivity
q: Which of the following statements about SQL Server (T-SQL) is NOT true?
opts: @@ROWCOUNT returns the number of rows affected by the last statement
@@ERROR returns 0 if the previous T-SQL statement ran without an error
GO is a T-SQL statement that the database engine executes to commit the current transaction
More than one of the above
exp: GO is not a T-SQL statement at all. It is a batch separator understood by client tools such as SSMS and sqlcmd: they send the statements written before GO to the server as one batch. It does not commit anything. A and B are true.
concept: T-SQL (Transact-SQL) is Microsoft's extension of SQL used by SQL Server, with variables, IF/WHILE, TRY…CATCH and system functions. @@ROWCOUNT returns the number of rows affected by the last statement; @@ERROR returns the error number of the last statement, or 0 if it succeeded. GO is a command of the client tools (SSMS, sqlcmd, osql), not of the server: it marks the end of a batch, and the tool sends that batch to the server. Transactions are ended with COMMIT or ROLLBACK, not with GO.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true: @@ROWCOUNT gives the number of rows affected by the last statement (for example 3 after an UPDATE that changed 3 rows). So it does not fit the NOT stem.
B — Wrong. This statement is true: @@ERROR is 0 after a successful statement and holds the error number otherwise. So it does not fit the NOT stem.
C — Correct. This statement is false, so it satisfies the NOT stem: GO is a batch separator recognised by SSMS and sqlcmd, not a T-SQL statement, and it never commits a transaction.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the NOT stem; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the NOT stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: GO = 'send this batch' (a tool command). COMMIT = 'make it permanent' (a T-SQL statement).

q: SQL views are also known as
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A view is a saved query that looks and behaves like a table but holds no rows of its own, so it is called a virtual table.
concept: A view is a named SELECT query stored in the database, for example CREATE VIEW it_staff AS SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'. When you query the view, the DBMS runs the saved query and shows the result as if it were a table. The rows really live in the base tables (the real, stored tables); the view itself stores no data. Because it looks like a table but is not physically stored, a view is called a virtual table.
why: A — Wrong. 'Simple table' is not another name for a view. Books do speak of a 'simple view' (a view built from one table without functions or grouping), but that is one kind of view, not a name for all views.
B — Correct. A view has no stored data of its own; its rows are produced from the base tables each time it is used, so it is a virtual table.
C — Wrong. 'Complex table' is not a standard term. A 'complex view' (a view built from several tables, or with joins, functions or GROUP BY) is one kind of view, not a name for views in general.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Base table = real table stored on disk. View = virtual table (a saved query). Materialized view = a view whose result is actually stored and refreshed from time to time.

q: How many primary keys can be there in a table?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A table can have only one primary key. That one key may consist of one column or of several columns (a composite key), but it is still a single primary key.
concept: A primary key is the key the designer chooses to identify each row; its values must be unique and never NULL. A table may have several candidate keys (column sets that could identify rows), but only one of them becomes the primary key; the others are called alternate keys and are usually declared UNIQUE. A primary key made of two or more columns is called a composite key, and it still counts as one primary key.
why: A — Correct. SQL allows only one PRIMARY KEY constraint per table. Declaring two gives an error, e.g. PostgreSQL says 'multiple primary keys for table are not allowed'.

B — Wrong. No rule allows exactly two primary keys. If two columns can each identify a row, one is made the primary key and the other an alternate (UNIQUE) key; if they are needed together, they form one composite primary key.
C — Wrong. The number of columns can decide how many columns the key contains (a composite key), not how many primary keys exist. A table with 10 columns still has exactly one primary key.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Common confusion: PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, subject) has two columns but is ONE primary key. Many candidate keys, only one primary key.

q: Which of the following is NOT a constraint in SQL?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL are constraints (rules on the values a column may hold); UNION is a set operator that combines the results of two queries.
concept: A constraint is a rule the DBMS enforces on table data so that invalid data cannot be stored. The SQL constraints are NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK, and many textbooks (and SQL Server) also list DEFAULT as a constraint. UNION is not a rule on data at all: it is a set operator that merges the result rows of two SELECT queries and removes duplicates (UNION ALL keeps them).
why: A — Wrong. PRIMARY KEY is a constraint: it forces the key column(s) to be unique and not NULL, so every row can be identified.
B — Wrong. NOT NULL is a constraint: it forbids missing (NULL) values in that column.
C — Correct. UNION is a set operator, not a constraint. It joins the rows returned by two queries, e.g. SELECT city FROM a UNION SELECT city FROM b, and places no rule on stored data.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not a constraint); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C is not a constraint, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK (DEFAULT). Set operators: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle).

q: Which of the following is NOT a valid aggregate function?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: COUNT and SUM are standard aggregate functions; COMPUTE is not a function at all (it was an old SQL Server clause for printing totals).
concept: An aggregate function takes many values (a whole column, or one group of rows) and returns a single value. The five standard aggregate functions are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX; they appear in the SELECT list or in HAVING, often with GROUP BY. COMPUTE is not an aggregate function: old versions of Microsoft SQL Server had a COMPUTE / COMPUTE BY clause that printed summary rows, and it was removed in SQL Server 2012.
why: A — Wrong. COUNT is a valid aggregate function: COUNT(*) counts rows and COUNT(col) counts the non-NULL values in a column.

B — Correct. COMPUTE is not an aggregate function. SELECT COMPUTE(sal) FROM emp fails with 'function does not exist' in PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB. The old SQL Server COMPUTE clause only displayed totals calculated by real aggregates such as SUM.
C — Wrong. SUM is a valid aggregate function: it adds up the non-NULL values of a numeric column.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not a valid aggregate function); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. B is not a valid aggregate function, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Five standard aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. All of them except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs. Common mistake: FIRST() and LAST() are MS Access functions, not standard SQL aggregates.

q: If we have not specified ASC or DESC after an SQL ORDER BY clause, which of the following is used by default?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: ORDER BY sorts in ascending order (ASC) unless DESC is written after the column.
concept: ORDER BY sorts the rows of a query result. After each sort column you may write ASC (ascending: small to large, A to Z, older date to newer date) or DESC (descending: large to small). If you write neither, SQL uses ASC. For example, SELECT name, marks FROM student ORDER BY marks lists the lowest marks first. Directions can be mixed: ORDER BY class ASC, marks DESC.
why: A — Wrong. DESC (descending order) is used only when you write it, e.g. ORDER BY marks DESC.
B — Correct. ASC is the default. ORDER BY x on the values 3, 1, 2 returns 1, 2, 3 in PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB, and the same holds in Oracle, MySQL and SQL Server.
C — Wrong. The SQL standard does fix a default direction for ORDER BY: ascending.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Where NULLs appear in the sort differs by product (Oracle and PostgreSQL put NULLs last in ascending order; MySQL and SQL Server put them first), but the default direction is ASC everywhere.

q: Which of the following is true about the HAVING clause?
opts: Similar to the WHERE clause but is used for columns rather than groups
Similar to WHERE clause but is used for rows rather than columns
Similar to WHERE clause but is used for groups rather than rows
More than one of the above
exp: HAVING is a filter like WHERE, but it filters the groups formed by GROUP BY, while WHERE filters individual rows.
concept: A grouped query is processed in this order: FROM (take the rows) → WHERE (keep some rows) → GROUP BY (put rows into groups) → HAVING (keep some groups) → SELECT → ORDER BY. WHERE works on single rows before grouping, so it cannot use aggregate functions such as SUM. HAVING works on whole groups after grouping, so it can use them, e.g. SELECT dept, SUM(sal) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING SUM(sal) > 1000.
why: A — Wrong. Neither WHERE nor HAVING chooses columns; choosing columns is the job of the SELECT list (projection). Also, HAVING works on groups, the opposite of what this option says.
B — Wrong. Filtering individual rows is what WHERE itself does, so this describes no difference at all. HAVING is not a row filter.

C — Correct. HAVING tests a condition on each group made by GROUP BY. HAVING SUM(sal) > 1000 keeps only departments whose total salary is above 1000, while writing WHERE SUM(sal) > 1000 gives an error ('aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE').
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: WHERE = row filter (before grouping, no aggregates). HAVING = group filter (after grouping, aggregates allowed).

q: _____ clause creates temporary relation for the query on which it is defined.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The WITH clause defines a temporary named relation (a common table expression) that exists only for the query in which it is written.
concept: The WITH clause gives a name to a sub-result so that the main query can use it like a table. Korth describes it as 'a way of defining a temporary relation whose definition is available only to the query in which the with clause occurs'; such a named sub-result is also called a common table expression (CTE). Example: WITH d(dept, total) AS (SELECT dept, SUM(sal) FROM emp GROUP BY dept) SELECT dept FROM d WHERE total > 1000. The relation d exists only while this one query runs.
why: A — Correct. WITH creates a temporary relation (CTE) that can be used only inside the query where it is defined and disappears when that query ends.

B — Wrong. FROM lists the relations a query reads. It names existing tables; it is not the clause that defines a named temporary relation. (A subquery written inside FROM does produce a temporary 'derived table', but the textbook clause for defining a named temporary relation for the query is WITH.)
C — Wrong. WHERE only gives a condition that filters rows; it does not create any relation.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: WITH = temporary, query-local named result (CTE). CREATE VIEW = a named query saved permanently. CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE = a real table that lasts for the session.

opts: More than one of the above
exp: A negative second argument rounds to the left of the decimal point: −1 means 'round to the nearest ten', so 65.726 becomes 70.
concept: ROUND(n, d) rounds the number n to d digits. If d is positive it rounds to d places after the decimal point (ROUND(65.726, 1) = 65.7); if d is 0 or omitted it rounds to a whole number (66). If d is negative it rounds to the left of the decimal point: −1 gives the nearest ten, −2 the nearest hundred. DUAL is Oracle's built-in dummy table with one row and one column, used when you want to compute a value without reading a real table.
why: A — Correct. Rounding 65.726 to the nearest ten gives 70.
B — Wrong. A negative digit count is perfectly legal in Oracle; it does not give 'garbage' or an error. It simply rounds to the left of the decimal point.
C — Wrong. 726 is just the digits after the decimal point. No rounding rule produces it; ROUND never throws away the whole-number part.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
work:
Step 1: d = −1 means round to the tens place.
Step 2: In 65.726 the tens digit is 6; the digit just to its right is 5.
Step 3: 5 or more rounds up, so 60 + 10 = 70.
Check: SELECT ROUND(65.726, -1) gives 70 in PostgreSQL and DuckDB; Oracle documents the same rule (ROUND(15.193, -1) = 20).
Note: SQLite does not support negative digits; it treats −1 like 0 and prints 66, so SQLite cannot be used to check this question.
tip: Common mistake: SQL ROUND on exact numbers is not 'banker's rounding'. ROUND(2.5) = 3 and ROUND(-2.5) = -3 (half away from zero) in Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL. Compare TRUNC(65.726, -1) = 60, which just cuts off.

q: _____ command makes the updates performed by the transaction permanent in the database.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: COMMIT ends a transaction and makes all of its changes permanent; ROLLBACK undoes them.
concept: A transaction is a group of SQL operations treated as one unit of work, such as debiting one account and crediting another. TCL (Transaction Control Language) commands control it: COMMIT saves all changes of the current transaction permanently, ROLLBACK cancels all changes made since the last COMMIT, and SAVEPOINT marks a point you can roll back to. After COMMIT the changes survive even a system crash (durability) and can no longer be undone with ROLLBACK.
why: A — Wrong. ROLLBACK does the opposite: it undoes the changes made by the transaction since the last COMMIT (or back to a SAVEPOINT).
B — Correct. COMMIT makes the transaction's updates permanent and visible to other users.

C — Wrong. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that removes all rows from a table; its job is not to save a transaction's updates. (In Oracle and MySQL any DDL statement, TRUNCATE included, causes an automatic commit as a side effect, but the command meant for making updates permanent is COMMIT.)
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: TCL = COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT (and SET TRANSACTION). COMMIT = save, ROLLBACK = undo.

q: Which of the following is the basic approach for joining tables?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Tables can be combined with the join technique (natural join, union join and other join types) and with the subquery technique, so more than one option is a basic approach.
concept: Joining means combining rows of two or more tables through related columns. Textbooks such as Hoffer's Modern Database Management describe two basic approaches for processing several tables: the join technique (inner/equi-join, natural join, outer join, union join) and the subquery technique, where an inner query's result is used by the outer query, e.g. WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT dept_id FROM dept WHERE city = 'Patna'). A natural join matches rows on all columns with the same name and shows each common column once. A union join (defined in SQL-92 and SQL:1999, later dropped from the standard) keeps every row of both tables without matching them.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. UNION JOIN was a join type in the SQL-92 and SQL:1999 standards: it returns all rows of both tables, unmatched and padded with NULLs; few products implemented it and it was dropped in SQL:2003.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Natural join is the textbook basic join: it matches rows on all same-named columns and keeps one copy of each common column.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Subqueries are the second basic approach: the inner query finds values (for example department IDs) and the outer query uses them, often giving the same result as a join.
D — Correct. Natural join and subqueries are clearly basic approaches for combining tables, and union join is also listed among the join types, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. At least natural join and subqueries are genuine approaches for combining tables, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: The wording is loose ('the basic approach' suggests one answer). This question matches a common MCQ ('one of the basic approaches for joining tables') whose key is 'all of the mentioned', so the intended answer is D. Even if you doubt UNION JOIN, B and C are both true, so D still holds. Common mistake: an equi-join keeps both copies of the common column; only a natural join shows it once.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of DBMS?
opts: Minimum duplication and redundancy of data
More than one of the above
exp: A DBMS supports many users at the same time (concurrent access); 'single-user access only' is the opposite of a DBMS feature.
concept: A DBMS (Database Management System) is software that stores data centrally and controls how it is used. Its main features are: reduced redundancy (data stored once instead of being copied into many files), consistency and integrity, security (users get only the permissions they need), multi-user concurrent access with concurrency control, backup and recovery, and support for ACID transactions. The older file-processing system, where each program kept its own files, lacked most of these.
why: A — Wrong. Minimum duplication (redundancy) of data is a real DBMS feature: data is stored once and shared instead of being repeated in many files.
B — Wrong. A high level of security is a real feature: the DBMS checks user accounts, roles and privileges (GRANT/REVOKE) before allowing any access.
C — Correct. A DBMS is built for multi-user access: many users can read and change data at the same time while concurrency control keeps it correct. Being limited to a single user is not a feature.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not a feature of DBMS); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C is not a feature of DBMS, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The same idea returns in TRE 2 Q126. Features to remember: low redundancy, consistency, security, multi-user access, backup and recovery, ACID.

q: The values appearing in given attributes of any tuple in the referencing relation must likewise occur in specified attributes of at least one tuple in the referenced relation, according to _____ integrity constraint.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This is Korth's definition of the referential integrity constraint, which is enforced by a foreign key.
concept: Referential integrity says that a foreign key value must point to something that really exists. The table that holds the foreign key is the referencing (child) relation; the table it points to is the referenced (parent) relation. Example: every dept_id in EMP must appear as a dept_id in DEPT (or be NULL); inserting an employee with dept_id 99 when DEPT has no 99 is rejected. It is declared with FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES.
why: A — Correct. The sentence is the textbook definition of referential integrity: values in the referencing relation must appear in the referenced relation.
B — Wrong. There is a primary key constraint (and 'entity integrity': no part of a primary key may be NULL), but it is about uniqueness inside one table, not about values matching another table.
C — Wrong. 'Referencing' is the name of the child relation in the definition, not the name of a constraint. Students pick it only because the word appears in the stem.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Entity integrity → primary key cannot be NULL. Referential integrity → a foreign key must match an existing key value (or be NULL). Domain integrity → values must belong to the column's allowed set.

q: What is a database?
opts: Organized collection of information that cannot be accessed, updated and managed
Organized collection of data or information that can be accessed, updated and managed
Organized collection of data that cannot be updated
More than one of the above
exp: A database is an organized collection of related data that can be easily accessed, updated and managed.
concept: Data are raw facts, such as 85 or 'Ravi'; information is data processed into something meaningful, such as 'Ravi scored 85 in Physics'. A database is an organized collection of related data, stored so that it can be easily accessed (read), updated (changed) and managed. The software that does this work is the DBMS (Database Management System), e.g. MySQL, Oracle or PostgreSQL.
why: A — Wrong. The whole purpose of a database is that its data can be accessed, updated and managed. A collection that cannot be accessed would be useless.
B — Correct. This is the standard definition: an organized collection of related data that can be accessed, updated and managed.
C — Wrong. Databases are updated all the time with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Being unchangeable is not part of what a database is.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which type of data can be stored in the database?
opts: Data in the form of audio or video
More than one of the above
exp: Databases store text and numbers and also images, audio, video and whole files (in large-object types such as BLOB), so all three options are true.
concept: Besides numbers, dates and short text, a database can store multimedia and documents. Large data is kept in large-object (LOB) types: BLOB (Binary Large Object) for binary data such as photos, audio, video and PDF files, and CLOB (Character Large Object) for long text. Oracle has BLOB and CLOB, MySQL has BLOB and LONGBLOB, and PostgreSQL uses BYTEA. Many applications store only the file's path in the table and keep the file itself on disk.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Images can be stored as BLOB values, e.g. each student's photo in a STUDENT table.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Text is the most common kind of stored data (CHAR, VARCHAR, CLOB), and whole files such as PDFs can be stored as BLOBs.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Audio and video are binary data and can be stored in BLOB columns or in multimedia databases.
D — Correct. Images, text and files, and audio or video can all be stored in a database, so more than one option is true.
E — Wrong. All of A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: Almost anything digital can be stored in a database: structured values in ordinary columns, and images, audio, video or documents as BLOB/CLOB.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of database?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Network (a data model) and distributed (by location) are standard database types; 'decentralized' is not one of the textbook types.
concept: Databases are classified in a few standard ways. By data model: hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented. By where the data is kept: centralized (all data at one site) and distributed (one logical database spread over several sites on a network). By number of users: single-user and multi-user. 'Decentralized database' is not one of these textbook categories.
why: A — Wrong. Network is a classic database type (data model): records are linked like a graph, and a child record may have several parents (the CODASYL/DBTG model).
B — Wrong. Distributed is a standard type: one logical database whose parts are stored at several sites connected by a network, e.g. a bank with servers in different cities.
C — Correct. 'Decentralized' is not a database type in DBMS textbooks. The textbook pair is centralized versus distributed.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not a type of database); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C is not a textbook type of database, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The wording is loose: 'decentralized' is used today for blockchain-style systems, but it is not a textbook database type, so the intended answer is C. Textbook pair to remember: centralized vs distributed.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of DBMS?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Microsoft Access and IBM Db2 are DBMS products; Google is a company (best known for its search engine), not a DBMS.
concept: A DBMS is software used to create, store, query and manage databases. Well-known examples are Oracle Database, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Microsoft Access, IBM Db2, SQLite and MongoDB. A company name or a website is not a DBMS, even if the company uses or sells databases.
why: A — Wrong. Microsoft Access is a DBMS: a desktop relational DBMS in Microsoft Office with tables, queries, forms and reports.
B — Wrong. IBM Db2 is a DBMS: IBM's relational database product, widely used by banks and large companies.

C — Correct. Google is a company and its best-known product is a search engine; neither is a DBMS. (Google does build database products such as Bigtable and Cloud Spanner, but 'Google' itself is not a DBMS.)
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not an example of DBMS); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C is not an example of DBMS, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of DBMS?
opts: Minimum duplication and redundancy of data
More than one of the above
exp: A DBMS supports many users at once; 'single-user access only' is not a feature, while low redundancy and ACID support are.
concept: ACID names the four properties a DBMS guarantees for transactions: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (the database moves from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not disturb each other) and Durability (committed changes survive crashes). Together with low redundancy, security, multi-user access and backup/recovery, ACID support is a key DBMS feature. Being limited to a single user is a limitation, not a feature.
why: A — Wrong. Minimum duplication and redundancy is a real feature: data is stored once in a shared database instead of being copied into many separate files.
B — Correct. A DBMS lets many users work at the same time, using concurrency control (locks, timestamps) to keep the data correct. 'Single-user access only' is not a feature.
C — Wrong. Supporting the ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) is one of the most important DBMS features; it makes transactions safe.
D — Wrong. Only B satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not a feature of DBMS); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. B is not a feature of DBMS, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: This repeats TRE 1 Q86 with one option changed, so expect repeats. ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the database?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A database system stores, manipulates and protects data; analysing program code is the work of compilers and code-analysis tools.
concept: The main functions of a database system are: storing data, retrieving it, manipulating it (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE through DML, the Data Manipulation Language), keeping it secure (user accounts and access rights), keeping it consistent (integrity constraints), handling many users at once, and backup and recovery. Analysing source code (checking syntax, finding bugs) is done by compilers, interpreters and static-analysis tools, not by a database.
why: A — Wrong. Manipulating data is a core function: DML commands such as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change the stored data.
B — Wrong. Security for stored data is a core function: the DBMS checks who the user is and what the user may do (GRANT/REVOKE, roles, views).

C — Correct. Analysing code is not a database function. A DBMS does parse and optimize the SQL queries sent to it, but analysing program code in general is the job of compilers and code-analysis tools.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not a function of the database); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C is not a function of the database, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is information about data called?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Metadata means 'data about data', such as a table's name, its column names, data types and constraints.
concept: Metadata is data that describes other data. In a DBMS the metadata (table names, column names and types, constraints, indexes, users and privileges) is kept in the data dictionary, also called the system catalog. Example: the fact that the column marks is of type INT and cannot be NULL is metadata; the value 85 stored in it is data.
why: A — Wrong. Teradata is the name of a company and its data-warehouse DBMS product, not a term for 'data about data'. It is a distractor because it sounds similar.
B — Correct. Metadata = data about data, stored in the data dictionary (system catalog).
C — Wrong. A relation is a table in the relational model (rows = tuples, columns = attributes). It holds data; it is not the name for information about data.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Data dictionary = system catalog = the store of metadata. You can see it in PostgreSQL through information_schema and in Oracle through views such as USER_TABLES.

q: The DBMS acts as an interface between _____ and _____ of an enterprise-class system.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Application programs do not touch the stored files directly; they send requests to the DBMS, which reads and writes the database for them.
concept: In an enterprise system many application programs (payroll, billing, a website) need the same data, and none of them reads the data files directly. Each application sends a request, usually in SQL, to the DBMS; the DBMS checks it, applies security and concurrency rules, finds the data in the database and returns the result. So the DBMS sits between the database applications and the database, like a librarian between readers and the shelves.
why: A — Wrong. The DBMS cannot be an interface between the data and itself, because it is one of the two sides named. The DBMS manages the data; it does not stand between the data and the DBMS.
B — Correct. The DBMS is the layer between database applications (programs that use the data) and the database (the stored data).

C — Wrong. 'The user and the software' is too vague, and the DBMS is itself software. Users reach the DBMS through applications or query tools; the precise textbook pairing is database application and database.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Picture three layers: application programs → DBMS → database (stored data). The DBMS is the middle layer.

q: _____ is a set of one or more attribute(s) taken collectively to uniquely identify a record.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: This is Korth's definition of a superkey: any set of one or more attributes that, taken together, identifies each record uniquely.
concept: A superkey is any set of attributes whose combined values never repeat in two different rows, so it identifies each record. A superkey may contain unnecessary extra attributes: if roll_no is a superkey, so is {roll_no, name}. A candidate key is a minimal superkey (no attribute can be removed), and the primary key is the one candidate key chosen by the designer. So every primary key is a superkey, but not every superkey is a primary key.
why: A — Wrong. A primary key does identify records, but it is a special, minimal key chosen by the designer from the candidate keys. The general sentence 'a set of one or more attributes taken collectively to uniquely identify a record' is the textbook definition of a superkey.
B — Wrong. A foreign key does not identify the records of its own table; it refers to the primary key of another (or the same) table, and its values may repeat.
C — Correct. The sentence is the textbook definition of a superkey (Korth: 'a set of one or more attributes that, taken collectively, allow us to identify uniquely a tuple in the relation').
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Superkey ⊇ candidate key ⊇ primary key. The phrase 'set of one or more attributes taken collectively' is the superkey definition, so the intended answer is C, even though a primary key also identifies records.

q: Which of the following commands is correct to delete the values in the relation teaches?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DELETE FROM teaches; with no WHERE clause deletes all the rows (values) of teaches but keeps the empty table.
concept: DELETE is a DML command that removes rows from a table. Without a WHERE clause it removes every row; with WHERE it removes only the rows that match the condition. The table itself (its columns and constraints) remains, so new rows can be inserted later. To remove the table definition as well you use DROP TABLE, and to empty a table quickly as a DDL operation you use TRUNCATE TABLE.
why: A — Correct. DELETE FROM teaches; removes all the tuples (values) of teaches and leaves the empty relation in place, exactly Korth's form 'delete from r'.

B — Wrong. 'Null' in quotes is an ordinary 4-letter text value, not NULL, so the command deletes only rows whose Id is the word Null — normally none. Even Id = NULL (without quotes) would match nothing; testing for a missing value needs Id IS NULL.
C — Wrong. REMOVE TABLE is not an SQL command and gives a syntax error. Removing the whole table (structure and data) is DROP TABLE teaches;.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
code:
Relation from the Korth university schema:
teaches(ID, course_id, sec_id, semester, year)
work:
Test table teaches(ID, course_id, sec_id, semester, year) with 4 rows, one of them with ID = NULL.
A: DELETE FROM teaches; → rows left = 0 in SQLite, PostgreSQL and DuckDB; the empty table still exists.
B: DELETE FROM teaches WHERE ID = 'Null'; → rows left = 4. No ID equals the string 'Null' (even the row whose ID really is NULL is kept).
C: REMOVE TABLE teaches; → syntax error in all three engines; REMOVE is not an SQL command.
tip: DELETE FROM t; → empties the rows, keeps the table (DML). TRUNCATE TABLE t; → empties the rows quickly (DDL). DROP TABLE t; → removes the rows AND the table definition.

q: The top level of the hierarchy consists of _____ each of which can contain _____.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the SQL naming hierarchy, catalogs are at the top; each catalog contains schemas, and schemas contain tables, views and other objects.
concept: To avoid name clashes, SQL uses a three-level naming hierarchy (Korth, 'Catalogs, Schemas and Environments'). The top level is the catalog; each catalog contains schemas; each schema contains SQL objects such as tables, views and procedures. A table can be named fully as catalog.schema.table, e.g. univ_db.main.student. A user's SQL environment is the default catalog and schema (and user identity) that the connection uses.
why: A — Wrong. This reverses the order: schemas live inside catalogs, not catalogs inside schemas.
B — Wrong. A schema does not contain an 'environment'. The SQL environment is the default catalog, schema and user identity that a connection uses; it is not a level inside a schema.
C — Correct. Korth: 'The top level of the hierarchy consists of catalogs, each of which can contain schemas.' Schemas then contain tables and views.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Think of folders: catalog (big folder) → schema (sub-folder) → table (file). Full name: catalog.schema.table.

q: The user IDs can be added or removed using which of the following fixed roles?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In Microsoft SQL Server, members of the db_accessadmin fixed database role can add or remove database access (database users) for logins.
concept: SQL Server has fixed database roles, each a ready-made set of permissions inside one database. Examples: db_owner (can do everything in the database), db_accessadmin (adds or removes database access for logins, i.e. user IDs), db_securityadmin (manages role membership and permissions), db_ddladmin (creates and alters objects), db_backupoperator, db_datareader and db_datawriter. Fixed server roles such as sysadmin and securityadmin act on the whole server, not on one database.
why: A — Wrong. There is no fixed database role called db_sysadmin. The similar name 'sysadmin' is a fixed SERVER role whose members can do anything on the server.
B — Correct. Members of db_accessadmin can add or remove access to the database for Windows logins, Windows groups and SQL Server logins, i.e. add or remove user IDs.
C — Wrong. db_securityadmin members manage permissions and membership of custom roles; adding or removing users is not their job.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Link the name to the job: ACCESSadmin = who gets ACCESS to the database (add/remove users); SECURITYadmin = which permissions and roles they have.

q: The traditional storage of data organized by the customer, stored in separate folders in filing cabinets is an example of
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A filing cabinet holds folders and each folder holds one customer's papers: a strict parent → child tree, which is how the hierarchical model organizes data.
concept: The hierarchical model stores data as a tree: each parent record can have many children, but each child has exactly one parent (one-to-many links only). A paper filing system works the same way: cabinet → drawer → one folder per customer → the documents inside it, and each document sits in exactly one folder. IBM's IMS is the classic hierarchical DBMS. In the network model a record may have several parents (a graph); in the relational model data sits in tables linked by matching key values.
why: A — Wrong. A relational DBMS stores data in tables of rows and columns linked by keys, not in nested folders. A filing cabinet has no tables or joins.

B — Wrong. In the network model a record can have several parents (many-to-many links, like a graph). In a filing cabinet each paper sits in exactly one folder, so the structure is a tree, not a network.
C — Correct. Cabinet → folder per customer → papers is a one-parent tree, which is the hierarchical model.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The wording is loose: paper files are not a 'DBMS' at all. The examiner means 'which model does this organization resemble?', and the intended answer is hierarchical (C): one folder per customer, each paper in one folder = tree.

q: After groups have been established, SQL applies predicates in the _____ clause, allowing aggregate functions to be used.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Korth: SQL applies predicates in the HAVING clause after groups have been formed, so aggregate functions may be used there.
concept: A predicate is a condition that is true or false for each row or group, such as sal > 1000. Predicates in WHERE are checked on single rows before groups are made, so they cannot use aggregates. GROUP BY then forms the groups, and predicates in HAVING are checked on each group afterwards, so they can use aggregates such as COUNT(*) > 2 or AVG(sal) > 5000.
why: A — Correct. HAVING holds the predicates that are applied to groups after GROUP BY has formed them, and these predicates may use aggregate functions.
B — Wrong. GROUP BY forms the groups (rows with equal values go together); it does not hold conditions that filter the groups.
C — Wrong. WITH defines a temporary named relation (a common table expression) used by the main query; it is not the clause that filters groups.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Order of processing: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.

q:
Which of the following is NOT the utility of DBMS?
I. Backup
II. Loading
III. Process organization
IV. File organization
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Backup, loading and file (re)organization are standard DBMS utilities; process organization is not. The options are lists of the genuine utilities, so the intended answer is A (I, II and IV), leaving III as the one that is not a utility.
concept: DBMS utilities are helper programs that the database administrator (DBA) uses to maintain the database (Elmasri–Navathe). The usual ones are: loading (bulk-loading data from files into the database), backup (copying the database, e.g. to tape or another disk, so it can be recovered after a failure), file reorganization (rearranging stored files and indexes to improve performance) and performance monitoring. 'Process organization' is not a DBMS utility; organizing and scheduling processes is the work of the operating system.
why: A — Correct. I (backup), II (loading) and IV (file organization/reorganization) are the genuine DBMS utilities, and III (process organization) is the odd one out. Every option lists three items, so the examiner is asking you to separate the three real utilities from the one that is not, and A is that set.
B — Wrong. This set includes III, process organization, which is not a DBMS utility (process management is an operating-system job), and leaves out file organization, which is one.
C — Wrong. This set includes III (not a utility) and leaves out II, loading, one of the most common DBMS utilities.
D — Wrong. Only set A correctly separates the utilities from the non-utility, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be right.

E — Wrong. On the intended reading A is the matching set. (Read word for word, the stem asks for the non-utility, which is III alone, and no option says 'III only'; that literal reading is the only argument for E — see the tip.)
tip: The wording is loose: the stem says 'NOT the utility', yet every option is a list of three items and only III is not a utility, so the examiner most likely meant 'Which ARE the utilities?' and the intended answer is A. A strictly literal reading would point to E. Learn the fact itself: utilities = loading, backup, file reorganization, performance monitoring; process organization is not one.

q: For designing a normal RDBMS, which of the following normal forms is considered adequate?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In practice a design normalized up to 3NF (or BCNF) is considered good enough for most relational databases.
concept: Normalization splits tables to remove redundancy and update anomalies. 1NF: atomic (indivisible) values. 2NF: no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: no transitive dependency (a non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute). Most real designs stop at 3NF (or BCNF), because it removes the common anomalies while keeping dependencies and reasonable query speed; a lossless, dependency-preserving 3NF design always exists. 4NF and 5NF handle rarer multivalued and join dependencies.
why: A — Wrong. 4NF removes redundancy caused by multivalued dependencies, which is uncommon in ordinary business data. It is usually not needed, so it is more than what is called 'adequate'.
B — Correct. 3NF is the standard practical target: it removes partial and transitive dependencies, and a lossless, dependency-preserving 3NF design can always be found.
C — Wrong. 2NF still allows transitive dependencies (e.g. emp_id → dept_id → dept_name), which cause update anomalies, so it is not considered adequate.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Exam line: '3NF is considered adequate for most practical database designs.' Common mistake: BCNF is free only from FD-based redundancy; redundancy caused by multivalued dependencies remains until 4NF.

q: What happens if a piece of data is stored in two places in the db?
opts: Storage space is wasted and changing the data in one spot will cause data inconsistency
Changing the data in one spot will cause data inconsistency
More than one of the above
exp: Duplicate data has two bad effects at once: it wastes storage, and if only one copy is changed the two copies disagree (inconsistency). Option A states both effects, so it is the complete answer.
concept: Data redundancy means the same fact is stored in more than one place. It causes two problems. First, extra storage space is used. Second, and more serious, whenever the fact changes every copy must be updated; if one copy is missed, the database holds two different values for the same fact, which is called data inconsistency (an update anomaly). A central DBMS and normalization reduce redundancy to avoid both problems.
why: A — Correct. It gives both effects of storing the same data twice: wasted storage space, and inconsistency when only one copy is changed. It is the complete answer.
B — Wrong. This is only half of the answer. Inconsistency is a real effect, but the option leaves out the wasted storage, which also happens every time data is duplicated.
C — Wrong. This is only half of the answer. Storage is wasted, but the more serious effect, inconsistency after an update, is left out.
D — Wrong. B and C are not false, but each is incomplete; the examiner wrote A as their combination, so A is the expected single answer rather than D.
E — Wrong. A correctly describes what happens, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: The wording is arguable: B and C are each true on their own, so a strict reader could choose D. The examiner deliberately built A as the combination of B and C, so the intended answer is A, the most complete option. When one option is exactly the union of two others, examiners usually intend that combined option.

q: Which data type can store unstructured data in a column?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In Oracle, RAW holds raw binary bytes that the database does not interpret, so it is the type meant for unstructured data; NUMERIC and VARCHAR hold structured numbers and character strings.
concept: Structured data has a fixed format the DBMS understands and checks, such as numbers (NUMBER, NUMERIC, INT) or character strings (CHAR, VARCHAR2). Unstructured data is a stream of bytes the DBMS does not interpret, such as part of an image, a sound sample or an encrypted value. Oracle's RAW type (up to 2000 bytes by default) stores such binary data as-is, without converting it between systems; larger unstructured data goes into LONG RAW (old) or BLOB.
why: A — Correct. RAW stores binary data (raw bytes) without interpreting it, which is how unstructured data is kept in a column in Oracle.
B — Wrong. NUMERIC (NUMBER) stores numbers with a fixed precision and scale, e.g. NUMERIC(8,2). The DBMS checks and interprets every value, so this is structured data.

C — Wrong. VARCHAR stores character strings in a known character set, and the DBMS interprets them as text (sorting, comparing, case conversion). It is meant for structured text values, not raw binary data.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The wording is loose (free text in a VARCHAR column is sometimes loosely called unstructured), but the intended answer is RAW: binary data stored exactly as given. Oracle binary types: RAW, LONG RAW, BLOB, BFILE.

q: Which of the following is NOT a type of DBMS?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Relational and object-oriented are types of DBMS (named after their data models); 'sequential' describes a file organization, not a type of DBMS.
concept: Types of DBMS are named after the data model they use: hierarchical (tree), network (graph), relational (tables), object-oriented (objects with attributes and methods), object-relational, and NoSQL kinds such as document and key-value stores. 'Sequential' is a way of arranging records in a file: records are stored one after another in key order and read from start to end, like songs on a cassette tape. That is a file organization, not a DBMS type.
why: A — Wrong. Relational DBMS is the most common type: data is kept in tables (relations) linked by keys, e.g. MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL.
B — Wrong. Object-oriented DBMS is a real type: data is stored as objects with attributes and methods, as in object-oriented programming, e.g. ObjectDB, db4o.
C — Correct. There is no 'sequential DBMS' type. Sequential is a file organization (records stored in order and read one after another), not a data model.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the only one that is not a type of DBMS); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C is not a type of DBMS, so it satisfies the stem and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: DBMS types follow data models: hierarchical, network, relational, object-oriented (plus object-relational and NoSQL). File organizations: heap, sequential, indexed, hashed.

q: In a relational database, what is a primary key?
opts: A key used to uniquely identify each record in a table
A key used to establish relationships between tables
A key used to sort records in a table
More than one of the above
exp: A primary key uniquely identifies each record (row) in a table; its values must be unique and not NULL.
concept: A primary key is a column, or a set of columns, whose value is different in every row and never NULL, so each record can be found exactly; for example roll_no in a STUDENT table. A foreign key is a column in another table that refers to this primary key, and that is what links (relates) the tables. Sorting is done with ORDER BY, not by declaring a key.
why: A — Correct. This is the definition of a primary key: it uniquely identifies each record and cannot be NULL.

B — Wrong. Establishing relationships between tables is the job of a foreign key. A foreign key points to a primary key, so the primary key takes part in the link, but its own purpose is identification.
C — Wrong. Sorting records is done with ORDER BY. Some products store rows in primary-key order (a clustered index), but that is a storage detail, not what a primary key is.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Primary key = identifies (unique + not NULL). Foreign key = relates (points to a primary key). ORDER BY = sorts.

q: Which normal form ensures that every non-prime attribute in a table is fully functionally dependent on the primary key?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 'Every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the key' (no partial dependency) is the definition of 2NF.
concept: A non-prime attribute is one that is not part of any candidate key. Full functional dependency means the attribute depends on the whole key, not on just a part of it. Example: in ENROL(roll_no, course_id, student_name, grade) with key (roll_no, course_id), student_name depends on roll_no alone — a partial dependency — so the table is not in 2NF. 2NF = 1NF + no partial dependency; 3NF = 2NF + no transitive dependency.
why: A — Wrong. 1NF only requires atomic (single, indivisible) values in every cell, with no repeating groups. It says nothing about how attributes depend on the key.
B — Correct. The rule 'every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the primary key' is exactly the definition of 2NF.

C — Wrong. 3NF's own rule is that no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the key (no non-key → non-key dependency). A 3NF table also meets the 2NF rule, because 3NF includes 2NF, but the normal form defined by full functional dependency is 2NF.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Strictly, tables in 3NF or BCNF also meet this rule (they include 2NF), but the question asks which normal form the rule defines, so the intended answer is 2NF. Keywords: atomic → 1NF; full / no partial dependency → 2NF; no transitive dependency → 3NF; every determinant is a candidate key → BCNF.

q: Which SQL command is used to add new rows to a database table?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: INSERT INTO adds new rows; CREATE makes new objects such as tables, and ADD is only a keyword used inside ALTER TABLE.
concept: SQL commands are grouped by purpose. DDL (Data Definition Language) defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE. DML (Data Manipulation Language) works on rows: INSERT (add rows), UPDATE (change rows) and DELETE (remove rows); SELECT reads rows. Example: INSERT INTO student (roll_no, name) VALUES (1, 'Ravi');
why: A — Wrong. ADD is not a command on its own. It is used inside ALTER TABLE to add a column or a constraint, e.g. ALTER TABLE student ADD email VARCHAR(50); — that changes the structure, not the rows.
B — Wrong. CREATE is a DDL command that makes new objects (CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE INDEX). It does not add rows of data.
C — Correct. INSERT is the DML command that adds new rows: INSERT INTO table_name VALUES (...).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Rows → DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). Structure/columns → DDL (CREATE, ALTER ... ADD, DROP).

q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of using a distributed database system?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Keeping copies at many sites in step is hard, so data can become inconsistent; better accessibility is an advantage, and security becomes harder, not stronger.
concept: A distributed database stores one logical database at several sites connected by a network. Advantages: data is near the users who need it (faster local access), better availability and reliability (one site failing does not stop the others), and easy growth by adding sites. Disadvantages: more complex software and administration, higher cost, harder security (more sites and network links to protect), and difficulty keeping replicated copies consistent, because every update must reach every copy (this needs protocols such as two-phase commit).
why: A — Wrong. Improved data accessibility is an advantage: users reach data stored at a nearby site, and data stays available if one site fails.

B — Wrong. 'Increased data security' is not a disadvantage; if security really increased, that would be an advantage. In fact distributed systems make security harder, because data travels over networks and sits at many sites.

C — Correct. When the same data is replicated at several sites, an update that reaches some copies but not others leaves the data inconsistent. Preventing this needs extra protocols (two-phase commit, replica control), so the risk of inconsistency is a recognized disadvantage.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The wording is loose: textbooks speak of 'difficulty in maintaining consistency of replicated data' rather than plain 'data inconsistency', but that is what the examiner means, so the intended answer is C.
